MetaCyc_Comment: 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase is an enzyme of the oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway. Three crystal structures of the enzyme in complex with substrate and cosubstrate compounds have been solved. Binding of NADP+ may induce a conformational change in the enzyme. A catalytic mechanism has been proposed |CITS: |. gnd is a highly polymorphic gene within E. coli populations, likely due to interstrain transfer and recombination. This may be a result of its proximity to the rfb region, which determines O antigen structure |CITS: |. Expression of 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase is growth rate-regulated |CITS: |. Most of the growth rate-dependent increase in Gnd levels is due to increased transcription, leading to higher mRNA levels |CITS: |. Posttranscriptional regulation |CITS: | involves a secondary structure element between codons 67 and 78 of the gnd mRNA |CITS: |. This region may function by sequestration of the translation initiation region into an mRNA secondary structure, thus reducing the efficiency of translation initiation |CITS: |. However, the effector of this regulatory mechanism has apparently not yet been identified. truA (hisT) mutants reduce the growth rate-dependent increase of Gnd expression by post-transcriptional regulation |CITS: |. Growth under acidic conditions upregulates expression of gnd |CITS: |. gnd is one of the most consistently flux-coupled genes (FCGs), which are genes whose expression transition patterns upon perturbations are correlated with their corresponding flux values |CITS: |. Certain growth conditions selected for a deletion mutation in the promoter region that results in increased transcription of gnd and increased enzyme activity |CITS: |. An edd gnd double mutant is unable to grow on gluconate |CITS: |. A null mutation in gnd does not significantly alter the growth rate. However, cellular metabolism and metabolic flux is changed |CITS: |; succinate production is increased during growth on glucose or glycerol |CITS: |. A gnd deletion mutant shows enhanced ethanol and H2 production compared to wild type during anaerobic growth on glycerol |CITS: |, whereas in a different, heavily engineered strain, overexpression of gnd increases ethanol and H2 production |CITS: |. Stasis-induced carbonylation of 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase is increased in lon and hslVU mutants |CITS: |. Gnd: "gluconate-6-phosphate dehydrogenase" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

This protein has similarity to the SdhA subunit of succinate dehydrogenase |CITS: |. A 2.2 Å crystal structure of L-aspartate oxidase suggests that an unusual tertiary structure is shared by L-aspartate oxidase, the SdhA subunit of succinate dehydrogenase, and the FrdA subunit of fumarate reductase |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: NADH:quinone oxidoreductase II (NDH-2) is a type IIA NADH dehydrogenase that catalyzes the transfer of electrons from NADH to the quinone pool in the cytoplasmic membrane. NDH-2 is one of two distinct NADH dehydrogenases in E. coli. In contrast to |FRAME: NADH-DHI-CPLX "NDH-1"| (encoded by the nuo genes), NDH-2 utilizes NADH exclusively, and electron flow from NADH to ubiquinone does not generate an electrochemical gradient |CITS: |. During glucose limited aerobic growth E. coli directs electron flux through both NADH dehydrogenases |CITS: |. Electron transport from NADH to oxygen is not affected in a strain lacking NDH-I but is significantly reduced in a strain lacking NDH-II; similarly nitrate respiration with NADH was only slightly affected in a strain lacking NDH-I but significantly reduced in a strain lacking NDH-II. This suggests that NDH-II is used preferentially in aerobic and nitrate respiration |CITS: |. NDH-2 is a strongly membrane-associated protein; it contains an FAD cofactor and copurifies with phospholipids |CITS: |. Phosphatidylethanolamine appears to be required for full enzymatic activity in vivo |CITS: |. The enzyme contains a thiolate-bound Cu(I) ion, and a putative copper binding site has been identified |CITS: |. Heterooligomers of NDH-1 and NDH-2 have been identified by electrophoresis and sucrose gradient centrifugation is suggestive of a supramolecular organisation in the membrane |CITS: |. NDH-2 can generate superoxide radicals and hydrogen peroxide by autooxidation of the FAD cofactor |CITS: | when the enzyme is overproduced or in the absence of quinones |CITS: |. However, under regular growth conditions, it is not the primary source of intracellular hydrogen peroxide |CITS: |. NDH-2 also has cupric reductase activity that is dependend on FAD or quinones. Under experimental conditions, the reductase activity was observed simultaneously with the dehydrogenase function linked to the respiratory chain |CITS: |. NDH-2 mutants are more sensitive to copper toxicity; NDH-2 may have a role in copper homeostasis |CITS: , |. Sequence analysis predicts that NDH-2 contains four domains: a FAD binding domain containing a conserved FAD binding motif; and NADH binding domain with a conserved NADH binding motif, a membrane anchoring domain containing two predicted transmembrane regions and a copper binding domain containing two conserved cysteine residues that may be copper ligands |CITS: |. Based on the remote similarity of NDH-2 to the SCOP family of FAD/NAD-linked reductases, a structural model of NDH-2 has been proposed |CITS: |. The originally isolated ndh mutant |CITS: | was not a single-locus mutant; it also contained a disruption of the nuo locus, encoding NDH-1 |CITS: |. Only strains containing mutations in both NADH dehydrogenases are unable to grow on mannitol as the sole source of carbon |CITS: |. Metabolic effects of an ndh null mutation alone and in combination with various other mutations have been investigated |CITS: |. ndh is subject to complex transcriptional regulation. Expression of ndh is repressed during anaerobic growth in an FNR dependent manner; expression of ndh varies during the growth cycle regulated by the transcription factors Fis and IHF |CITS: |. In an F1-ATPase-defective mutant, ndh transcription and NDH-2 activity is increased |CITS: |. Several metabolic genes, including ndh, were found upregulated in two MG1655 lysogens carrying closely related Stx2a phages O104 and PA8 |CITS: 31208335|. Ndh: "NADH dehydrogenase" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: SodA, or MnSOD, is one of three superoxide dismutases in E. coli |CITS: |. The three enzymes differ in their metal cofactor requirement; MnSOD contains manganese. Superoxide dismutase is implicated in the response to a large number of environmental changes that lead to the generation of superoxide radicals. MnSOD and the iron-containing enzyme |FRAME: SUPEROX-DISMUTFE-MONOMER FeSOD| (SodB) are not functionally equivalent; MnSOD is more effective than FeSOD in preventing damage to DNA, while FeSOD seems more effective in protecting a cytoplasmic superoxide-sensitive enzyme |CITS: |. However, both enzymes were shown to protect dihydroxy acid dehydratase from inactivation by oxidative stress |CITS: |. MnSOD binds DNA non-specifically |CITS: | with a Ka of 3 x 105 M-1 |CITS: |. The superoxide dismutases contribute to reducing iron toxicity |CITS: |. The enzyme is highly specific for the manganese cofactor; an iron-substituted MnSOD is catalytically inactive |CITS: |, although it was recently suggested that iron-substituted MnSOD has peroxidase/catalase activity |CITS: |. The binding constant for Mn(II) is 3.2 x 108 M-1 |CITS: |, and the process of manganese acquisition has been studied |CITS: |. Metal uptake appears to be cooperative and requires dimer dissociation |CITS: |. The apo-form of a Gln146Glu mutant is much more stable than the apo-form of the wild type enzyme; conversely, the wild type, but not the mutant enzyme is stabilized by metal binding. This suggests that enzyme stability was sacrificed for enhanced metal binding ability during evolution of MnSOD |CITS: |. The Glu170 residue is essential for metal selectivity and is thought to form a hydrogen bond with His171 of the second monomer in the homodimeric enzyme |CITS: |. A Gly165Thr mutation confers some activity using Fe as the metal cofactor |CITS: |. Crystal structures of wild type and mutant apo- and MnSOD have been solved |CITS: |. The catalytic mechanism and involvement of the metal cofactor have been studied |CITS: |. Superoxide dismutase is also part of the ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase activating system. The system is composed of three proteins, flavin reductase, superoxide dismutase and a protein fraction named fraction b whose function is poorly defined |CITS: |. MnSOD was identified as the enzyme present in the system |CITS: |, but other species of the enzyme could substitute |CITS: |. Production of MnSOD is not dependent on the SOS system |CITS: |. The complex transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation of sodA expression has been studied in detail |CITS: |. An sodA mutant is more sensitive to paraquat than wild type |CITS: | and shows an increased mutation rate that is dependent on the presence of oxygen |CITS: |. A sodA sodB double mutant is especially sensitive to DNA damage induced by hydrogen peroxide |CITS: |. Under aerobic conditions, a sodA sodB double mutant is able to grow slowly on rich medium, but not on minimal glucose medium. The double mutant is able to grow under anaerobic conditions or by supplementing the minimal medium with a full complement of amino acids |CITS: |. The amino acid auxotrophic phenotypes can be explained by oxidative inactivation of dihydroxy acid dehydratase |CITS: | and transketolase |CITS: |. A sodA sodB double mutant is more susceptible to killing by human serum and neutrophils |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

Merged_Functions: AspC encodes an aspartate aminotransferase in E. coli that can catalyze the transamination of aromatic keto‑acid intermediates such as para‑amino‑phenylpyruvate (APP) to the corresponding amino acid (L‑para‑amino‑phenylalanine). In the engineered pathway for PAPE and 4‑APA production, AspC competes with the desired flux by diverting APP away from decarboxylation, and its deletion was shown to increase product titers. {PubMed:30662895}. The aspC gene encodes the Escherichia coli aspartate aminotransferase, a 43 kDa PLP‑dependent enzyme that catalyzes reversible transamination reactions. It transfers the amino group from glutamate (or other donors) to oxaloacetate, producing aspartate and 2‑oxoglutarate, and thus participates in the final steps of biosynthesis of aspartate, tyrosine and phenylalanine in vivo. The enzyme shows broad substrate specificity, similar to mammalian aspartate aminotransferases, and functions as a homodimer with structural features (coenzyme‑binding and substrate‑binding sites) conserved with pig mitochondrial and cytoplasmic isoenzymes. Overproduction of AspC restores growth of aminotransferase‑deficient strains and yields high aspartate aminotransferase activity in crude extracts. {PubMed:3521591}. In the article, aspC encodes the native aspartate aminotransferase (AspC) that catalyzes the transamination of oxaloacetate (OAA) with glutamate to form L‑aspartate and α‑ketoglutarate. This reaction provides the aspartate precursor for β‑alanine biosynthesis. However, the authors observed that overexpressing or adding extra copies of the native aspC did not significantly increase β‑alanine production, indicating that its catalytic activity was insufficient in the engineered strain. Consequently, they replaced aspC with the heterologous L‑aspartate dehydrogenase gene PaeAspDH to achieve a more efficient conversion of OAA to aspartate and improve β‑alanine yields. {PubMed:31989219}. AspC encodes the L‑aspartate aminotransferase, an enzyme that catalyzes the reversible transamination between oxaloacetate and L‑glutamate to form L‑aspartate and α‑ketoglutarate. In the engineered E. coli strains it was overexpressed to drive L‑aspartate production from oxaloacetate. The enzyme also exhibits broad substrate specificity, being able to use pyruvate as an amino‑group acceptor to generate L‑alanine, which was observed when oxaloacetate supply was limited. {PubMed:31063790}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the reversible transamination of oxaloacetate and L‑glutamate to L‑aspartate and α‑ketoglutarate. {PubMed:3521591, PubMed:31989219, PubMed:31063790}. Exhibits broad substrate specificity, also transaminating pyruvate to L‑alanine and aromatic keto‑acids such as para‑amino‑phenylpyruvate to L‑para‑amino‑phenylalanine. {PubMed:3521591, PubMed:30662895, PubMed:31063790}. Contributes to the biosynthesis of aspartate, tyrosine and phenylalanine by providing L‑aspartate as a precursor. {PubMed:3521591}. Supplies the aspartate precursor required for β‑alanine biosynthesis. {PubMed:31989219}. Competes with engineered pathways for PAPE and 4‑APA production by diverting para‑amino‑phenylpyruvate, and its deletion enhances product titers. {PubMed:30662895}. Restores growth of aminotransferase‑deficient strains when overproduced, yielding high aspartate aminotransferase activity. {PubMed:3521591}. Functions as a homodimeric PLP‑dependent enzyme with conserved coenzyme‑ and substrate‑binding sites. {PubMed:3521591}.

Alkaline phosphatase is a metalloenzyme, binding two zinc atoms and one magnesium ion per monomer |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: The lepB gene encodes the sole catalytically active Signal Peptidase I (SPase) in Escherichia coli. SPase is an essential membrane‑bound enzyme that cleaves N‑terminal signal peptides (15–30 aa) from precursor proteins, thereby releasing exported proteins from the membrane. Because this processing step is required for the maturation of many secretory and membrane proteins, lepB is essential for bacterial growth and division. Under‑expression of lepB reduces cellular SPase levels, slows growth, and sensitizes cells to SPase inhibitors, confirming its vital role in protein export and cell viability. {PubMed:12384363}. LepB encodes the essential type I signal peptidase of *Escherichia coli*, a 36 kDa inner‑membrane serine protease that spans the membrane twice and uses a Ser‑90/Lys‑145 catalytic dyad to cleave the short N‑terminal leader peptide (15–30 aa) of secreted and membrane proteins, thereby releasing mature proteins into the periplasm as part of the protein export machinery. In addition to this canonical catalytic activity, LepB possesses a non‑catalytic, chaperone‑like structural role that is crucial for the import of nuclease‑type bacteriocins such as colicin D and Klebicin C/D. LepB binds with nanomolar affinity (Kd ≈ 10⁻⁹ M) to a conserved 28‑amino‑acid peptide motif (the LepB‑binding site, LBS) located in the central domain of these toxins. This stable 1:1 interaction promotes the association of the toxin’s central domain with the inner membrane, facilitates FtsH‑dependent proteolytic processing of the toxic C‑terminal domain, and enables subsequent translocation of the toxin into the cytoplasm. The binding interface involves residues in the short C‑terminal Box E of LepB (e.g., Gly‑272, Asn‑274, Asn‑277, Ala‑279). Thus, LepB functions both as a signal‑peptide cleaving enzyme and as a moonlighting membrane protein that structurally assists the entry of specific bacteriocins into target cells. {PubMed:26499796}. In Rickettsia rickettsii and R. typhi, lepB is co‑transcribed with secF, nuoF, and rnc in a polycistronic operon, and its product can complement a temperature‑sensitive Escherichia coli lepB mutant, restoring preprotein processing and growth at non‑permissive temperatures. {PubMed:12867468}. The periplasmic domain folds after full translocation, generating a pulling force detectable by force‑profile analysis. Thus, LepB functions as a membrane‑bound protease whose periplasmic domain is cotranslationally translocated and post‑translationally folded. {PubMed:33989648}. MetaCyc_Comment: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (Ppc) is an anaplerotic enzyme that replenishes oxaloacetate in the tricarboxylic acid cycle. The carboxylation of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to form oxaloacetate and Pi proceeds in two steps: formation of carboxyphosphate and the enolate form of pyruvate, followed by carboxylation of the enolate and release of phosphate and oxaloacetate. Ppc activity is allosterically regulated by many kinds of effectors |CITS: | that interact with several distinct binding sites. The in vivo concentrations of the various regulators differ depending on the growth conditions, resulting in different levels of enzyme activity |CITS: |. The primary activator was thought to be acetyl-CoA; fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (FBP) and GTP can act synergistically with acetyl-CoA |CITS: |. A mechanism for synergistic activaton of the enzyme by different effectors was proposed |CITS: |. In a proteome-wide screen, Ppc was found to bind citrate, ATP, and FBP. Citrate inhibits Ppc activity in vitro; the presence of FBP or acetyl-CoA had no effect on the inhibition |CITS: |. Analysis of metabolomics and metabolic flux data after removal of glucose shows a buildup of PEP and a 99% decrease of Ppc activity; this effect is due to the decreased level of FBP and the ultrasensitive response of Ppc to FBP levels in the presence of acetyl-CoA and aspartate. The highly sensitive regulation of Ppc activity enables adaptation to variable carbon availability and prevents a futile cycle during gluconeogenesis |CITS: |. Crystal structures for Ppc complexed with L-aspartate, Mn2+, Mn2+ and/or a PEP analog were determined |CITS: |. Ppc is a homotetramer in a dimer-of-dimers arrangement |CITS: |. The binding site for the inhibitor L-aspartate is located approximately 20Å away from the catalytic site |CITS: |. Additional crystal structures with Mn2+ and a PEP analog enabled identification of the active site and proposals for the reaction mechanism and the mechanism for allosteric regulation |CITS: |. Ppc may be a target for the antimicrobial peptide Lactoferricin B |CITS: |. Various Ppc mutants have been isolated or generated by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. A ppc point mutant (Thr188Ile) grows similarly to wild type on TCA cycle intermediates as the sole carbon source, but grows very slowly on glucose. This mutant contains Ppc that is primarily in the homodimeric form; it can be activated by acetyl-CoA, but not by various co-activators |CITS: |. An Arg438Cys mutant is also predominantly homodimeric |CITS: |. An Arg313Gln mutant is desensitized to activation by FBP |CITS: |. A Lys620Ser mutant is less sensitive to inhibition by aspartate and malate |CITS: |. Two mutations, Ile829Ser and Arg849Ser, were identified by adaptive laboratory evolution and also cause decreased sensitivity to inhibition by L-aspartate |CITS: |. Both the conserved His138 |CITS: | and Arg587 |CITS: | residues are required for catalysis of the second half-reaction, the carboxylation of the enolate form of pyruvate |CITS: |. Overexpression of Ppc improves the growth yield on glucose |CITS: |, increases production of succinate from glucose by fermentation |CITS: |, and reduces acetate excretion |CITS: |. Gene expression, enzyme activities, metabolite concentrations and metabolic flux have been measured in a ppc mutant |CITS: |. Metabolic modeling of ppc mutants is enhancing comprehension of the metabolic network and enabling predictions for metabolic engineering |CITS: |. In a high-throughput experiment evaluating growth of single-gene deletion mutants on a variety of carbon sources, the Δppc mutant was only able to grow efficiently with acetate, α-ketoglutarate, fumarate, malate, succinate, or ribose as the sole source of carbon |CITS: |. Ppc activity was initially measured to be highest during growth on glucose |CITS: |. Further comparisons showed that it is highest during growth on glycerol as the sole source of carbon, followed by gluconate and glucose; growth on acetate represses the activity |CITS: |. Using an engineered promoter library, the optimal expression level for ppc resulting in the highest biomass yield during growth on glucose minimal media was determined |CITS: |. rne mutants produce significantly less Ppc than wild type |CITS: |. Both deletion and increased expression of ppc has been used to increase the yield of a variety of products in metabolic engineering studies. Reviews: |CITS: |

Merged_Functions: The ilvI gene encodes the catalytic subunit of acetohydroxy acid synthase III, the enzyme that catalyzes the first common step in the biosynthetic pathways for the branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine and valine in Escherichia coli K‑12. The ilvI product works together with the ilvH regulatory subunit to form the active synthase complex, and its activity is subject to feedback inhibition by valine. {PubMed:3881131}. The article states that ilvI encodes the large subunit of acetohydroxy acid synthase III (AHAS III), one of the three acetohydroxy acid synthase enzymes (ilvB, ilvG, ilvI). These AHAS enzymes are involved in the pathways of branched‑chain amino acid synthesis. Like the other AHAS proteins, the IlvI product is a flavoprotein that uses α‑ketoacid substrates in the presence of thiamine pyrophosphate and Mg²⁺. {PubMed:3016647}. The ilvI gene encodes the large catalytic subunit of the valine‑sensitive acetohydroxyacid synthase III (AHASIII) in Escherichia coli K12. AHASIII catalyzes the first common step in the biosynthetic pathway of the branched‑chain amino acids (valine, leucine, and isoleucine). The ilvI‑encoded protein forms part of the AHASIII enzyme complex together with the smaller IlvH subunit, which provides valine sensitivity. Thus, ilvI functions as the catalytic component of AHASIII, enabling the synthesis of branched‑chain amino acids while being subject to regulation by valine. {PubMed:6308579}. ilvI encodes the large catalytic subunit (LSU) of acetohydroxyacid synthase III (AHAS III) in Escherichia coli. When isolated, ilvI exhibits only ~3 % of the activity of the complete holoenzyme and requires association with a small regulatory subunit (normally ilvH) to achieve full catalytic activity. The article demonstrates that ilvI can also be activated by heterologous small subunits such as ilvM (the AHAS II regulatory subunit) or truncated versions of ilvH, although these hybrid enzymes are not subject to valine feedback inhibition. {PubMed:19653643}. The ilvI gene encodes the large subunit of acetohydroxy acid synthase (ALS) III, an enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the biosynthetic pathway for the branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine and leucine. In Salmonella typhimurium LT2 the ilvI gene contains a nonsense mutation that prevents expression of functional ALS III, whereas natural isolates possess an intact ilvI allele that yields an active ALS III isozyme. {PubMed:7557326}. Encodes the enzyme pyruvate oxidase (PoxB), a peripheral membrane flavoprotein that catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetate and CO₂ in the presence of the cofactor thiamine pyrophosphate. The enzyme forms a homotetramer (≈62 kDa per subunit) and its activity is dramatically enhanced (20‑25‑fold increase in specific activity and ~10‑fold decrease in Km for pyruvate) by binding of various lipids or detergents to a C‑terminal region. Lipid binding protects the protein from proteolytic cleavage; removal of a small C‑terminal peptide (~2.6 kDa) eliminates lipid activation. The protein shares homology with the large subunits of acetohydroxyacid synthases (IlvB, IlvG, IlvI) and belongs to the flavoprotein family that utilizes α‑ketoacid substrates together with Mg²⁺. {PubMed:3016647}. The article describes b0077 (ilvH) as encoding the small regulatory subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase III (AHAS III). This polypeptide does not possess catalytic activity itself but confers valine sensitivity to the AHAS III enzyme complex, thereby modulating the enzyme’s activity in response to valine levels. {PubMed:6308579}. Encodes the enzyme pyruvate oxidase (PoxB), a peripheral membrane flavoprotein that catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetate and CO₂. The reaction requires the co‑factor thiamine pyrophosphate and is markedly stimulated (20–25‑fold increase in activity and ~10‑fold decrease in Km for pyruvate) by association with various lipids or detergents. The enzyme functions as a homotetramer (≈62 kDa per subunit) and is involved in ubiquinone reduction. The C‑terminal region of the protein participates in lipid binding, and limited proteolysis of this region releases a small peptide (~2.6 kDa) that abolishes lipid activation. Activity of PoxB is dramatically stimulated (20‑25‑fold increase and ~10‑fold decrease in Km) by binding of lipids or detergents to its C‑terminal region, which also protects the protein from proteolytic cleavage; removal of a C‑terminal peptide abolishes this activation. {PubMed:3016647}. Merged_Functions: The b0078 gene encodes IlvH, the small regulatory (SSU) subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase (AHAS) isozyme III in Escherichia coli. IlvH forms a dimer and interacts with the large catalytic subunit (LSU) to activate the holoenzyme. Its N‑terminal ACT domain binds the feedback inhibitor valine, while the C‑terminal domain mediates inter‑monomer contacts that are required for proper transmission of the valine‑binding signal and for maintaining high affinity of the holoenzyme for valine. Mutations or truncations in the C‑terminal domain disrupt valine binding and render the enzyme insensitive to feedback inhibition, although the mutant SSU can still activate the LSU. Thus, b0078/IlvH functions as a regulatory subunit that both activates AHAS III and confers valine‑dependent feedback inhibition. {PubMed:21224018}. The gene encodes the IlvH polypeptide, the small regulatory subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase III (AHASIII) in Escherichia coli K12. IlvH partners with the larger catalytic subunit IlvI to form the functional AHASIII enzyme, which catalyzes the first step in branched‑chain amino‑acid biosynthesis. The IlvH subunit specifically confers valine sensitivity to the enzyme, modulating its activity in response to valine levels. {PubMed:6308579}. The ilvH gene encodes the small regulatory subunit (SSU) of acetohydroxyacid synthase III (AHAS III) in Escherichia coli. IlvH pairs with the large catalytic subunit IlvI to form the active AHAS III holoenzyme. It is required for valine feedback inhibition, conferring valine sensitivity to the enzyme; only the full‑length IlvH transmits this inhibition, whereas truncated N‑terminal ACT‑domain peptides can activate IlvI but lack valine responsiveness. Thus, IlvH functions both to activate the catalytic subunit and to mediate allosteric regulation by valine in the AHAS III complex. {PubMed:19653643}. The ilvH gene encodes the small (regulatory) subunit of acetohydroxy acid synthase III (AHAS III), one of three AHAS isozymes in Escherichia coli K‑12. Together with the larger subunit encoded by ilvI, the IlvH protein forms the AHAS III holoenzyme that catalyzes the first common reaction in the biosynthesis of the branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine, leucine, and valine—the synthesis of α‑acetolactate from pyruvate. The IlvH subunit modulates the enzyme’s kinetic properties and its sensitivity to feedback inhibition by valine; a missense mutation (ilvH612) reduces valine inhibition, lowers the apparent Kₘ for pyruvate, and increases specific activity, thereby enhancing growth under certain amino‑acid conditions. {PubMed:3053650}. The ilvH gene encodes the subunit of acetohydroxy acid synthase III (AHAS III), the enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step in the biosynthesis of the branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine and valine. AHAS III condenses pyruvate (and/or 2‑ketobutyrate) to form acetolactate, initiating the pathway that ultimately yields valine and isoleucine. The enzyme activity is normally inhibited by valine; mutations in ilvH (e.g., ilvH865, ilvH866) produce a valine‑resistant form of AHAS III, altering carbon flow toward these amino acids and restoring normal attenuation control of the ilvGEDA operon in certain regulatory mutant backgrounds. {PubMed:6365098}. ilvH encodes the small regulatory subunit (SSU) of acetohydroxyacid synthase (AHAS) isozyme III. The SSU activates the large catalytic subunit of AHAS, and together they form the holoenzyme that catalyzes the first step in branched‑chain amino‑acid biosynthesis. The N‑terminal ACT domain of IlvH binds the end‑product valine and confers feedback inhibition on the holoenzyme. The C‑terminal domain does not bind valine directly but is required for proper transmission of the valine‑binding signal, likely through inter‑monomer contacts that stabilize a conformation of the SSU that allows high‑affinity valine binding and inhibition of catalytic activity. Mutations or truncations in the C‑terminal domain disrupt these contacts, leading to loss of valine sensitivity while retaining activation of the catalytic subunit. {PubMed:21224018}. The ilvH gene encodes the regulatory subunit of acetohydroxy acid synthase III (AHAS III) in Escherichia coli K‑12. This subunit is required for feedback inhibition of the enzyme by valine, conferring valine sensitivity to the AHAS III complex, and it also contributes to the efficient catalytic activity of the enzyme. Truncation of ilvH eliminates valine inhibition and markedly reduces AHAS III activity, indicating that ilvH is essential for both regulation and optimal function of the acetohydroxy acid synthase III isozyme. {PubMed:3881131}. IlvH encodes the small (≈160‑aa, ~17.5 kDa) regulatory subunit of the valine‑sensitive acetohydroxyacid synthase III (AHAS III). Together with the larger catalytic IlvI subunit, IlvH forms the functional AHAS III enzyme and confers sensitivity to inhibition by valine, thereby modulating the first step of branched‑chain amino‑acid biosynthesis. {PubMed:6308579}. ilvH encodes the regulatory subunit (RSU) of Escherichia coli acetohydroxyacid synthase III (AHAS III). The RSU binds to the catalytic subunit (CSU, ilvL) and is required to activate the enzyme’s catalytic activity. In addition to activation, the full‑length ilvH mediates feedback inhibition of AHAS by branched‑chain amino acids, particularly valine. The study identified a minimal activation motif within ilvH (the ΔN14‑ΔC89 peptide, comprising residues 15–89) that retains the ability to activate the CSU of E. coli AHAS I and III as well as CSUs from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Arabidopsis thaliana, and Nicotiana plumbaginifolia, but this truncated peptide no longer confers valine‑dependent feedback regulation, indicating that distinct regions of ilvH are responsible for activation versus feedback inhibition. {PubMed:23512804}. IlvH is the regulatory subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase (AHAS) in Escherichia coli (AHAS III). It forms a heterodimeric enzyme together with the catalytic subunit (IlvI) and is responsible for mediating feedback inhibition of AHAS activity by the branched‑chain amino acid valine. Mutations in IlvH that alter residues near the valine‑binding site (e.g., Asn11Ala, Gly14Asp, Asn29His, Leu131Ala/Arg, Val153Ala/Asp) reduce the sensitivity of the enzyme to valine, leading to increased valine production. In this study, IlvH served as a comparative model to design analogous mutations in the yeast regulatory subunit Ilv6. {PubMed:29477860}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of a heterotetrameric complex that catalyzes the two-step biosynthesis of anthranilate, an intermediate in the biosynthesis of L-tryptophan. In the first step, the glutamine-binding beta subunit (TrpG) of anthranilate synthase (AS) provides the glutamine amidotransferase activity which generates ammonia as a substrate that, along with chorismate, is used in the second step, catalyzed by the large alpha subunit of AS (TrpE) to produce anthranilate. Merged_Functions: Encodes D‑serine ammonia lyase (also known as D‑serine dehydratase), a pyridoxal‑5′‑phosphate‑dependent enzyme that specifically deaminates D‑serine (and, with lower activity, D‑threonine and allothreonine) to produce pyruvate, ammonium and water. In E. coli the enzyme detoxifies D‑serine, allowing the bacterium to use D‑serine as a carbon and nitrogen source. When expressed in plants, the enzyme removes D‑serine toxicity, conferring resistance to D‑serine and providing a selectable marker for plant transformation. {PubMed:15830131}. The dsdA gene encodes D‑serine deaminase, an enzyme that specifically degrades D‑serine to pyruvate and ammonia. In uropathogenic E. coli strain CFT073, DsdA activity enables catabolism of the abundant D‑serine present in urine. Deletion of dsdA prevents D‑serine degradation, leading to intracellular accumulation of D‑serine during urinary tract infection. This accumulation triggers up‑regulation of the D‑serine‑responsive transporter gene dsdX and a broader D‑serine‑dependent regulon, resulting in altered expression of multiple virulence factors (e.g., P fimbriae, hemolysin, F1C fimbriae) and a hypermotile, hypercolonizing phenotype in the mouse urinary tract. Thus, dsdA functions in D‑serine catabolism and signaling that modulates global virulence gene regulation in uropathogenic E. coli. {PubMed:17074858}. The dsdA gene encodes the structural component of D‑serine deaminase, an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of D‑serine into pyruvate and ammonia. This enzymatic activity is central to the D‑serine deaminase system in Escherichia coli, allowing the bacterium to metabolize D‑serine. The gene is transcribed divergently from the regulatory dsdC gene, and its expression is tightly controlled by the D‑serine‑responsive activator protein DsdC, as well as by cAMP‑cAMP‑binding protein, leading to a massive induction (3,000‑ to 5,000‑fold) upon exposure to D‑serine. {PubMed:3029015}. The article describes dsdA as the gene encoding D‑serine deaminase. It is one of the highly prevalent virulence‑associated regulatory genes in uropathogenic E. coli (found in >96% of isolates). While not identified as a decisive virulence factor, dsdA is implicated in the bacterial ability to survive in the urinary tract, particularly in the urethra, likely by metabolizing D‑serine. {PubMed:28104383}. Encodes the D‑serine deaminase enzyme that degrades D‑serine to ammonia and pyruvate. This activity enables E. coli to utilize D‑serine as a sole carbon and nitrogen source and provides resistance to the bacteriostatic effect of D‑serine in urine. When DsdA is absent, D‑serine accumulates intracellularly, acting as a signal that up‑regulates virulence genes and leads to a hypercolonization phenotype during murine urinary tract infection. {PubMed:17785472}. The dsdA gene encodes D‑serine deaminase, an enzyme that detoxifies D‑serine by catalyzing its conversion to pyruvate and ammonia through a multistep dehydratase reaction. This activity removes the toxic effect of D‑serine on Escherichia coli K‑12, which otherwise inhibits L‑serine and pantothenate synthesis, and enables the bacterium to use D‑serine as a sole carbon and nitrogen source. Expression of dsdA is strongly induced (several hundred‑fold) in the presence of D‑serine and requires the trans‑acting LysR‑type regulator DsdC together with the cAMP‑CRP complex for full transcriptional activation. {PubMed:7592420}. The dsdA gene encodes a PLP‑dependent serine dehydratase (also referred to as D‑serine ammonia lyase) in Pediococcus pentosaceus. The enzyme catalyzes the deamination of both L‑serine and D‑serine, producing pyruvate as the reaction product. This pyruvate can be further converted into flavor compounds such as diacetyl and acetoin, linking dsdA activity to diacetyl formation from serine. Recombinant DsdA from strain FAM19132 displayed Michaelis‑Menten kinetics with Km values of ~7.5 mM for L‑serine and ~0.5 mM for D‑serine, and optimal activity between pH 6.5 and 7.4 (≈70 % activity retained at pH 5.5). Enzyme activity is modestly inhibited by increasing NaCl for L‑serine but enhanced for D‑serine, indicating functionality under the low‑pH, high‑salt conditions typical of cheese. Size‑exclusion chromatography suggests the native enzyme forms a dimer (~120 kDa apparent mass). Functional dsdA is present in P. pentosaceus strains that exhibit serine dehydratase activity; mutations (frameshifts, nonsense, or missense affecting PLP‑binding residues) render the gene product inactive in other strains. The gene is absent in P. acidilactici. While not essential for growth in rich medium, dsdA may contribute to detoxification of D‑serine and provide an energy source via pyruvate generation during cheese ripening. {PubMed:23241976}.

MetaCyc_Comment: It was established long ago that E. coli is able to deaminate serine |CITS: | and that the activity is inducible by D-serine |CITS: |. D-serine ammonia-lyase (DsdA) catalyzes the deamination of D-serine to form pyruvate and ammonia. D-serine has a bacteriostatic effect on E. coli; thus, when D-serine is present, detoxification is necessary for cell growth |CITS: |. Once the cell expresses DsdA, D-serine can be utilized as the sole source of carbon and nitrogen |CITS: |. Toxicity of D-serine in minimal medium appears to be due to an effect on biosynthesis of L-serine and pantothenate |CITS: |. The cofactor requirements and reaction mechanism of the enzyme have been investigated. Binding of the pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) cofactor has been studied in detail |CITS: |. The reaction involves a transient Schiff base intermediate of α-aminoacrylate and PLP |CITS: |. The G279D and G281D mutations eliminate enzyme activity |CITS: | due to altered interactions with PLP |CITS: |. More conservative substitutions at G278, G279, and G281 result in reduced or altered enzymatic activity |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme have been solved, confirming results from the analysis of mutant enzymes, and leading to the proposal of a catalytic mechanism |CITS: |. Regulation of DsdA expression has been extensively investigated and was shown to involve positive regulation by DsdC and cAMP-CRP |CITS: |. DsdA: "D-serine deaminase" |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Adenylate cyclase catalyzes the synthesis of cyclic AMP (cAMP) by an intramolecular transfer of the adenylyl group of ATP to the 3'-hydroxy group, releasing pyrophosphate. cAMP is an important signaling molecule; the role of cAMP in regulating the production of metabolic enzymes was first summarized in |CITS: |. The absence of cAMP affects the expression of alternative carbon source uptake and degradation systems involved in central metabolism |CITS:|. Via binding to the CAP/CRP protein (see |FRAME: CPLX0-226|), it participates in the regulation of transcription of many genes. Adenylate cyclase is present at very low levels of approximately 15 molecules/cell |CITS: |. Its rare UUG initiation codon, which was confirmed by N-terminal sequencing of the purified protein |CITS: |, limits the translation of cyaA |CITS: |. Polyamines stimulate synthesis of adenylate cyclase at the level of translation initiation |CITS: |. The regulation of adenylate cyclase has been studied for many years, but the results were often contradictory. Proteins of the PEP:sugar phosphotransferase system (PTS) were implicated early, and regulation of adenylate cyclase in cell extracts could be reconstituted by addition of PTS proteins |CITS: |. Experiments with various mutants finally showed that the phosphorylated form of IIAGlc appears to be responsible for activating adenylate cyclase |CITS: |, although some results remained unexplained; see, for example, |CITS: |. An experiment attempting to reconstitute regulation of adenylate cyclase in vitro showed that a membrane-targeted adenylate cyclase interacts directly with IIAGlc, but regulation of the enzyme still requires additional factor(s) present in cell extract |CITS: |. Other possible regulators of adenylate cyclase activity, such as inhibition by CAP/CRP |CITS: | and stimulation by EF-Tu |CITS: |, have been reported. Expression of cyaA is repressed by cAMP-CRP |CITS: |. This transcriptional regulation is only partly responsible for downregulation of cAMP levels by CRP; the majority of the effect is due to posttranscriptional regulation |CITS: | via reducing the level of phosphorylated IIAGlc |CITS: |. The enzyme is composed of an N-terminal catalytic domain and a C-terminal regulatory domain |CITS: |. Amino acid residues that are important for catalytic activity have been identified by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |, and a two-metal ion catalytic mechanism has been proposed |CITS: |. The C-terminal 48 residues are required for posttranscriptional regulation of adenylate cyclase by CRP |CITS: |. Overexpression of cyaA is lethal in a crp wild-type background |CITS: |. A cyaA mutant shows a slow-growth phenotype when grown aerobically on glucose, but appears to have no effect on overall metabolic flux |CITS: |. Growth of a cyaA mutant is negatively affected by increased external pH |CITS: |. cyaA mutants are resistant to fosmidomycin due to regulation of expression of the GlpT transporter by cAMP |CITS: |. cyaA mutants showed similar survival rates in the presence of antibiotics and carbon source consumption as cell persisters, indicating a key component in metabolism of these phenotypic variants |CITS:|. MetaCyc_Comment: Mannose-6-phosphate isomerase (phosphomannose isomerase, PMI) catalyzes the reversible isomerization of mannose-6-phosphate and fructose-6-phosphate. This reaction is the first committed step in the synthesis of GDP-α-D-mannose (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-5659|). The enzyme is required for growth on mannose as the sole source of carbon and energy. It is also required for the formation of GDP-L-fucose, a building block of capsular polysaccharide |CITS: | (see pathways |FRAME: MANNCAT-PWY| and |FRAME: COLANSYN-PWY|). PMI activity is increased by growth on p-fluorophenylalanine (FPA), which leads to formation of mucoid colonies |CITS: |. A manA mutant is unable to grow on mannose as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: | and has a defect in the maintenance of colonization of the mouse intestine |CITS: |. The manA gene can be used as a selectable marker |CITS: |. Pmi: "phosphomannose isomerase" The E. coli enzyme is a type I PMI, a monofunctinal, Zn2+-dependent metalloenzyme found in most bacteria and mammals |CITS: |. Crystal structures have been determined for the PMI from Salmonella typhimurium bound to metal atoms and substrate |CITS: |. A novel tandem mass spectrometry based assay for the quantification of phosphorylated aldose-ketose sugar isomers has been described which differentiates between the isomeric aldose and ketose 6-phosphates. This enabled measurement of the equilibrium constant of the reversible reaction catalyzed by E. coli PMI, as well as its kinetic parameters in both directions |CITS: |. Electrospray ionization Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry was used to probe the noncovalent complexes of E. coli PMI with its ligands including the Zn2+ cofactor, mannose-6-phosphate, and fructose-6-phosphate, as well as the two inhibitors erythrose 4-phosphate and mannitol 1-phosphate |CITS: |. The E. coli enzyme has also been included in several inhibitor studies because PMI is of interest as a drug target. Its activity is essential for the survival and pathogenesis of several microorganisms |CITS: |. Deletion of manA was part of a strategy for the metabolic engineering of E. coli to produce mannosylglycerate from externally added mannose |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: Isoleucine-tRNA ligase (IleRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. IleRS belongs to the Class I aminoacyl tRNA synthetases |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNAIle that are important for recognition by IleRS have been identified |CITS: |. The presence of the t6A modification at position 37 of tRNAIleGAU strongly enhances the aminoacylation rate by IleRS |CITS: |. Residues within IleRS that interact with tRNAIle have been identified |CITS: |. IleRS specifically acylates the 2'-OH and deacylates the 3'-OH of tRNAIle |CITS: |. The aminoacyl linkage between Ile and tRNAIle is the most stable among the 12 pairs of cognate amino acid-tRNA pairs measured by |CITS: |. The reaction mechanism of IleRS has been studied |CITS: |. Aminoacylation proceeds via the aminoacyl adenylate pathway |CITS: |. IleRS contains two zinc atoms per active site |CITS: |. One zinc atom bound near the N-terminal catalytic core is important for amino acid binding and utilization |CITS: |. The second zinc binding site has been mapped near the C terminus of IleRS |CITS: | and is required for the tRNA binding step in aminoacylation |CITS: |. The C-terminal peptide containing this site can complement the specific tRNA binding and catalytic activity of the N-terminal domain in trans |CITS: |. If separately expressed, the three domains of IleRS can form an active complex and complement each other in trans |CITS: |. The dispensable CP1 domain interrupts the nucleotide binding domain within IleRS |CITS: |. IleRS binds one molecule of tRNA per molecule of enzyme |CITS: |. Affinity labeling experiments were used to identify various binding and active sites of IleRS |CITS: |. Binding specificity of IleRS for various aliphatic amino acids and aminoalkyl adenylates has been determined; none of the tested isoleucine analogs bind as tightly as isoleucine itself |CITS: |. Both amino acid discrimination and proofreading contribute to the specificity of Ile charging onto tRNAIle |CITS: |, and experimental data is consistent with the existence of both a pre- and a post-transfer editing capability of the enzyme, depending on the amino acid |CITS: |. The body of tRNAIle appears to modulate the pre-transfer editing activity of IleRS, while the 3' end of tRNAIle is required for post-transfer editing |CITS: |. Misactivated homocysteine undergoes pre-transfer editing |CITS: |. Although valine is discriminated against at the amino acid recognition stage, IleRS misactivates valine at a significant rate. A single point mutation, G56A, eliminates the ability to discriminate against valine, and valine is then discriminated against by hydrolytic editing |CITS: |. The presence of misacylated tRNA was thought to be required for both pre- and post-transfer editing |CITS: |. IleRS appears to be the only class I enzyme for which pre-transfer editing is important. The rates of hydrolysis of a pre-transfer amino-adenylate and a misacylated tRNA are approximately equal for IleRS |CITS: |. The tRNA-dependent pre-transfer editing activity accounts for approximately 1/3 of the total proofreading activity. The conserved Tyr59 residue within the tRNA aminoacylation active site is involved in tRNA-dependent pre-transfer editing |CITS: |. tRNAIle stimulates pre-transfer editing and decreases the affinity of IleRS toward amino acids |CITS: |. The editing response was initially thought to be triggered by specific bases in the effector and to not require a tRNA-like structure or active acceptor hydroxyl groups |CITS: |, and was thought to involve translocation of the misactivated amino acid from the active site to the editing site |CITS: |. The post-transfer editing site maps to the CP1 domain, an insertion that interrupts the Rossman fold nucleotide-binding domain |CITS: |. The isolated CP1 domain alone has post-transfer editing activity |CITS: |. The editing site is distinct from the active site for aminoacylation |CITS: |. Distinct residues within the editing site are required for editing the misactivated adenylate form and the aminoacyl ester |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis identified the isoleucine binding site |CITS: |. Labeling studies with pyridoxal-5'-phosphate identified residues that may be important for binding of the phosphates of ATP |CITS: |. An editing-deficient IleRS mutant strain has a growth yield advantage under specialized conditions, generating "statistical proteins" containing norvaline |CITS: |, but under most conditions, it has a lower growth rate |CITS: |. Pseudomonic acid A (mupirocin) is an inhibitor of IleRS activity |CITS: |. Expression of ileS and the downstream gene, lspA, appear to be tightly coupled |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Alanine—tRNA ligase (AlaRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. AlaRS belongs to the Class IIC aminoacyl tRNA synthetases |CITS: |. AlaRS was seen as a homotetramer in solution |CITS: |. Later experiments determined that AlaRS is homodimeric in solution |CITS: | and can exist in an equilibrium between a homodimeric and a homodecameric state, depending on temperature |CITS: |. The enzyme contains one molecule of zinc per AlaS polypeptide |CITS: |; zinc binds cooperatively and induces a conformational change in AlaRS |CITS: |. Zinc is important for tRNA recognition |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNAAla that are important for recognition by AlaRS have been identified |CITS: |. A single nucleotide base pair in the acceptor helix of tRNAAla, G3-U70, is necessary and sufficient for aminoacylation of that tRNA with alanine |CITS: |. A mutation in alaS which compensates for a mutant tRNAAla containing a G3-C70 base pair has been isolated |CITS: |. Discrimination of the G3-U70 base pair maps to a 76 amino acid region outside the catalytic center of AlaRS |CITS: |. The nucleotide at position 73 modulates the efficiency of the transfer step of aminoacylation |CITS: |. Specificity determinants and residues within AlaRS that are important for catalytic activity have been investigated |CITS: |. An N-terminal 461 amino acid fragment of the AlaS polypeptide was shown to complement a temperature-sensitive alaS allele in vivo; the C-terminal portion of the enzyme appears to be dispensable for catalytic activity, but is required for formation of the tetramer |CITS: |. Mutagenesis of an N-terminal domain peptide reveals residues that increase catalytic activity of the fragment |CITS: |. A central region of AlaRS is essential for interaction with alanine-specific tRNA |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis has identified the Arg69 residue within motif 2 |CITS: |, the Cys665 residue |CITS: | and the Asp235 residue |CITS: | as important for catalysis. The Lys73 residue is important for recognition of tRNAAla |CITS: |. Single turnover kinetics experiments showed that a step prior to aminoacyl transfer is rate limiting |CITS: |. Kinetic parameters for binding of AlaRS to tmRNA have been determined |CITS: |. The central domain of AlaRS is the editing domain. Many aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases have been shown to have editing functions. AlaRS misactivates glycine and serine, but has a pre-transfer editing function, hydrolyzing the non-cognate amino acid before transfer to tRNAAla, and a post-transfer editing function that deacetylates mischarged tRNAAla |CITS: |. A series of crystal structures, together with kinetic analysis and mutagenesis, has allowed elucidation of the basis for recognition of alanine by AlaRS and provides a structural and evolutionary explanation for the interaction with serine |CITS: |. The covalently continuous two-domain structure of the tRNA is required to enable editing |CITS: |. The editing domain alone is able to specifically recognize mischarged tRNAAla, utilizing the same discriminator base pair within the tRNA as the aminoacylation domain |CITS: |. It deacylates misacylated Ser-tRNAAla with a kcat/KM of 6.6 x 105 M-1 s-1. The site-directed mutants Q584H, I667E, and C666A have decreased editing activity; interestingly, the C666A mutation is 1.7-fold more active on Ala-tRNAAla than on the mischarged Ser-tRNAAla |CITS: |. A homologous free-standing protein with editing activity, AlaX, exists in other organisms; the protein family may have evolved from an ancestral form that was able to deacylate multiple tRNAs |CITS: |. |FRAME: CPLX0-3581| is able to edit Gly-tRNAAla more efficiently than AlaRS |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain (C-Ala) plays a role in activating the catalytic sites of the N-terminal domain |CITS: |. C-Ala represents the major tRNA binding module of AlaRS |CITS: |; this tRNA binding activity is required for efficient editing activity by the central editing domain |CITS: |. The C-Ala domain serves to bring the aminoacylation and editing domains of AlaRS together to bind to the acceptor stem of tRNAAla |CITS: | and is important for dimerization of the enzyme |CITS: |. AlaRS represses transcription of the alaS gene by binding to a region flanking the transcription start site, and thus autoregulates its own expression. The autoregulatory effect depends on the concentration of alanine, with higher concentrations leading to lower levels of alaS transcription. At physiological levels of AlaRS, repression of alaS transcription is solely mediated by alanine levels |CITS: |. The designed alaS triple mutant T567F/S587W/C666F is unable to edit mischarged Ser-tRNAAla and Gly-tRNAAla. When combined with a dtd deletion, the strain shows a synthetic growth defect and becomes sensitive to added glycine |CITS: |. The alaS21 allele leads to increased resistance to novobiocin |CITS: |. Mutations in ribosomal proteins S5 and S20 partially suppress the temperature sensitive growth defect of an alaS mutation |CITS: |. The mechanism of suppression is thought to be a reduction in the rate of polypeptide synthesis |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Methionine-tRNA ligase (MetRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. MetRS belongs to the Class I aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases; apart from sequence motifs whithin the active site, the different enzymes show little similarity in their primary amino acid sequences |CITS: |. The biochemical properties and reaction mechanism of MetRS have been studied extensively; e.g. |CITS: |. MetRS acylates both initiator tRNAfMet and elongator tRNAMet; acylation of tRNAfMet appears to be more efficient |CITS: |. MetRS contains one zinc atom per active site that is coordinated by four cysteine residues which are essential for activity |CITS: |. Crystal structures of MetRS have been determined |CITS: |. The structural domains can be expressed separately and can reconstitute active MetRS enzyme |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain can function independently for specific binding of the tRNA anticodon stem-loop |CITS: |. The ATP binding site was identified by affinity labeling |CITS: |. Catalysis is proposed to involve an induced fit mechanism |CITS: |. The evaluation of enzymes containing point mutations in residues that may link the anticodon binding motif to the catalytic domain |CITS: | as well as comparisons between crystal structures of the apo- and methionine-bound enzyme |CITS: | support this hypothesis. Molecular dynamics simulations confirm significant motility of the enzyme, suggesting that Trp461 mediates the distribution of structural ensembles |CITS: | and confirming the pathways of communication between distant sites |CITS: |. The methionine binding site was predicted |CITS: |, and non-hydrolyzable ATP analogues and methionine and methionyl adenylate analogues have been used to study conformational changes during catalysis |CITS: |. Regions within MetRS that interact with tRNAfMet |CITS: | and tRNAMet |CITS: | have been determined |CITS: |. The Trp461 residue may interact directly with the tRNA anticodon loop |CITS: |; Asp391 may interact directly with U36 |CITS: |. Suppressor enzymes that are able to aminoacylate methionine amber tRNA carry mutations in the vicinity of Trp461 |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis and analysis of the mutant enzymes has been used to study the domain structure, catalytic properties and the roles of active site residues of the enzyme |CITS: |. Lys335 is required for methionine activation |CITS: |; Tyr358 |CITS: | contributes to the ATP-PPi exchange reaction. MetaCyc_Comment: Glutamine-tRNA ligase (GlnRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. GlnRS belongs to the Class I aminoacyl tRNA synthetases |CITS: |; apart from sequence motifs within the active site, the different enzymes show little similarity in their primary amino acid sequences. Substrate recognition and discrimination by GlnRS has been studied extensively. Binding of tRNA and ATP to GlnRS is cooperative, and transfer of the aminoacyl adenylate to the tRNA is the rate determining step |CITS: |. Interactions between the tRNA identity nucleotides and GlnRS modulate the affinity of the enzyme for glutamine |CITS: |, and the terminal adenosine base of tRNAGln mediates amino acid recognition |CITS: |. tRNA binding to GlnRS results in conformational changes in the active site |CITS: |; induced-fit changes in the active site structure by both amino acid and tRNA binding may contribute to enzyme specificity |CITS: |. Reports differ on whether the properties of the amino acid binding site allow the enzyme to specifically recognize glutamine and select against glutamate |CITS: | or function as a negative determinant, binding glutamate in a non-productive orientation |CITS: |. The glutaminyl adenylate intermediate is hydrolyzed by the GlnRS-tRNAGln complex and is analogous to pre-transfer editing reactions catalyzed by editing aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases like IleRS |CITS: |. A substrate-assisted catalytic mechanism is supported by single-turnover kinetic analysis |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics simulations of tRNA binding to GlnRS have been performed |CITS: |. Various crystal structures of GlnRS have been solved |CITS: |. GlnRS mutants that allow recognition and mischarging of su+3 tRNATyr and others have been identified |CITS: |, and their relaxed specificity has been interpreted in light of their location within the crystal structure |CITS: |. Overexpression of wild type GlnRS also leads to mischarging of su+3 tRNATyr |CITS: |; concomitant overexpression of the cognate tRNAGln2 abolishes this effect, indicating that proper balance between the tRNA and the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase is critical |CITS: |. A "minimal" GlnRS enzyme retains catalytic activity |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNA that are important for recognition by GlnRS have been identified; see, for example, |CITS: | and references therein. GlnRS enzyme levels increase with increasing growth rate |CITS: |. GlnRS expression is regulated at the transcriptional as well as posttranscriptional levels |CITS: |. The tRNAGln/GlnRS pair has been engineered for incorporation of unnatural amino acids into proteins |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: The lactose permease LacY is a galactoside:proton symporter, responsible for the uptake of lactose and other galactosides. LacY is a member of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) of transporters |CITS: | and is probably the best characterised secondary transporter. β-galactoside transport was first described in the mid twentieth century (reviewed in |CITS: | and studies of lactose transport were instrumental in elucidating and confirming the chemiosmotic theory for energy transfer in cells |CITS: |. The lacY gene was the first transporter gene to be cloned and sequenced |CITS: |. The lactose permease has been solubilised, purified, reconstituted into liposomes, and shown to mediate lactose:proton symport with a 1:1 stoichiometry |CITS: |. The substrate specificty of LacY has been surveyed - compounds were assayed as inhibitors of o-nitrophenyl-β-D-galactopyranoside (ONPG) uptake |CITS: | (refer to list of inhibitors below). Results suggest a specific requirement for the galactopyranosyl ring of D configuration with a free hydroxyl group. The size of the aglycone group appeared to be more important than its chemical nature - an increase in aglycone size was associated with enhanced binding. Aromatic α and β-D-galactopyranosides are high-affinity inhibitors but not all are transported. LacY transports the D-galactopyranosides lactose and melibiose, with similar affinities (Km = 0.1-1 mM) |CITS: |. Purified LacY functions as a monomer |CITS: |. The secondary structure is predominantly α-helical, consisting of 12 transmembrane regions with the N and C termini located in the cytoplasm |CITS: |. Crystal structures of mutant LacY (Cys154 → Gly) with and without bound ligand and native LacY have been obtained. The twelve TM helices are organised into two bundles of six connected by a long flexible loop. A central hydrophilic cavity contains the sugar binding site and the residues involved in proton translocation. The structures are 'inward-facing', that is they are oriented with the cavity open to the cytoplasm |CITS: |. This is believed to be the conformation of the transporter that is present in bacterial membranes in the absence of bound substrate |CITS: |. The introduction of tryptophan replacements for glycine-glycine pairs (G46/G262 and G46/G370) results in the formation of a stable outward-facing LacY structure |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the double tryptophan mutant (G46W G262W) with bound substrate has been obtained. The substrate is bound within an almost occluded central cavity that has a narrow opening to the periplasmic side and is completely sealed on the cytoplasmic face. Amino acids ligating the sugar are Glu-126, Arg-144, Trp-151, Glu-269, Asn-272, and His-322 |CITS: |. Substrate transport occurs by an 'alternating access mechanism', in which conformational change of the transporter allows alternating access of single sugar and proton binding sites to either side of the membrane (reviewed by |CITS: | and |CITS: |. Sugar binding is associated with opening of a wide hydrophilic cleft on the periplasmic side of the membrane and closing of a large cytoplasmic facing cavity |CITS: |. LacY mutants with single cysteine 154 → glycine replacements are able to bind substrate but have no transport activity |CITS: | due to constitutive opening of the periplasmic cleft |CITS: |. Introduction of large thiol groups into the periplasmic cleft also blocks transport without affecting substrate binding |CITS: |. Specific lipid-protein interactions affect the conformational dynamics of LacY; phosphotidylethanolamine disrupts a charge-relay network (Asp-68, Lys-131, Glu-139 and Lys-335) present on the intracellular side of LacY and triggers a conformational shift towards the inward facing state in vitro |CITS: |. LacY has been extensively mutagenised (reviewed in |CITS: |. A functional Cys-less transporter has been generated and Cys-scanning mutagenesis has altered every residue in this transporter to a cysteine. Only six residues (Glu-126, Arg-144, Glu-269, Arg-302, His-322 and Glu-325) are absolutely essential for lactose transport |CITS: |. Glu-126 and Arg-144 are essential for sugar binding |CITS: | and along with Trp-151 and Glu-269 form the substrate binding/recognition site |CITS: |. There is a salt bridge between Glu-126 and Arg-144, which is broken upon substrate binding |CITS: |. The galactopyranosyl ring of the substrate has a direct stacking interaction with the indole ring of Trp-151 |CITS: |. Glu-269 is predicted to participate in substrate recognition by hydrogen bonding to the C-3 OH group of the galactopyranosyl ring |CITS: |. Glu-269 may be the primary protonation site |CITS: |. Asn-272 is part of the sugar binding site |CITS: |. Residues involved in the proton translocation pathway (Tyr231, Asp240, Arg-302, Lys319, His-322, and Glu-325) are mainly located in the C-terminal helix bundle and are positioned on the opposite side of the cavity to the substrate binding site |CITS: |. Protonation is required for sugar binding |CITS: |. At physiological pH, sustrate binds to fully protonated LacY |CITS: |. Residues involved in proton translocation do not form a pathway across the membrane but form a highly connected salt bridge cluster |CITS: | - water molecules coordinated within this cluster may function as the protonation site during transport |CITS: |. Glu-126 and Arg-144 are not required for sugar binding, though they do play a role in maintenance of secondary structure |CITS: |. LacY has also served as a model for studying the contribution of membrane lipids and lipid headgroups to membrane protein assembly |CITS: |. The lacY gene forms part of the well known lactose-inducible lac operon with the lacZ gene encoding β-galactosidase, the lacA gene encoding thio-β-galactoside transacetylase and the lacI gene encoding the lactose repressor. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Mediates the transport of melibiose and other galactosides by a symport mechanism (PubMed:2185831, PubMed:3311166, PubMed:3316227, PubMed:45782, PubMed:7703254). Can use sodium, lithium and protons as coupling cations, depending on the sugar substrate and the cationic environment (PubMed:3311166, PubMed:3316227, PubMed:45782, PubMed:7703254). Alpha-galactosides (melibiose, raffinose, p-nitrophenyl-alpha-galactoside or methyl-alpha-galactoside) are cotransported with either Na(+) or H(+), whereas beta-galactosides (lactose, L-arabinose-beta-D-galactoside, D-fructose-beta-D-galactoside, methyl-beta-galactoside or p-nitrophenyl-beta-galactoside) are cotransported with Na(+) or Li(+) but not H(+) (PubMed:3311166, PubMed:45782). The monosaccharide D-galactose can use either Na(+) or H(+) for cotransport whereas D-fucose, L-arabinose and D-galactosamine can use only Na(+) (PubMed:3311166). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:2185831, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3311166, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3316227, ECO:0000269|PubMed:45782, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7703254}.

MetaCyc_Comment: MelB is a melibiose-cation cotransport protein belonging to the Glycoside-Pentoside-Hexuronide:Cation Symporter Family (GPH) |CITS: |. Proteins in the GPH family facilitate sugar-cation symport |CITS: |. MelB has been purified, solubilized and reconstituted into liposomes and demonstrated to mediate melibiose symport with sodium, lithium, or proton as the coupling ion |CITS: |. The effects of sodium ion, lithium ion, and proton on the sugar binding constants of MelB were studied in de-energized membrane vesicles incubated in media containing various concentrations of the co-transported cations |CITS: |. It was observed that, in a similar fashion, sodium ions and lithium ions activate sugar binding by selectively increasing the permease affinity for the co-transported sugar. This suggests that the two monovalent cations have comparable activation strengths |CITS: |. Hydropathy analysis, proteolytic digestion, and PhoA fusions suggest a 12 transmembrane segment topology, with the N and C termini located on the cytoplasmic face of the membrane |CITS:|. The susbtrate specificity of MelB was studied in a lactose transport negative strain of E.coli possessing an inducible melibiose transport system. α-galactopyranosides (methyl α-D-galactopyranoside, raffinose and p-nitrophenyl-α-galactoside) are cotransported with either H+ or Na+ while β-galactopyranosides (lactulose, lactose, methyl β-D-galactopyranoside and o-nitrophenyl-β-D-galactoside) are cotransported with Na+. The monosaccharides D-fucose, L-arabinose and D-galactosamine are cotransported with Na+ while D-galactose can be cotransported with either H+ or Na+ |CITS: |. Two-dimensional crystallization of MelB permease was achieved, and a projection map at 8.0 Å resolution was derived by electron crystallography, suggesting an asymmetric protein unit hosting 12 potential transmembrane alpha -helices that are distributed in two domains lining a central and curve-shaped cleft. |CITS:|. The melibiose transport system is temperature sensitive in E.coli K-12, it is active at 30oC but not at 37 oC |CITS: |. Reviewed in |CITS: , , |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter complex RbsABC involved in ribose import. Binds ribose. Also serves as the primary chemoreceptor for chemotaxis. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:25533465, ECO:0000269|PubMed:4608146, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6327617, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7982928}.
MetaCyc_Comment: RbsB is the periplasmic ribose binding protein of an ATP-dependent ribose uptake system; ligand bound RbsB also interacts with the |FRAME: EG11018 "Trg"| sensory protein to mediate taxis to ribose. The ribose binding protein is required for chemotaxis towards ribose; mutants lacking this protein do not demonstrate ribose mediated taxis |CITS: |. The RbsB molecule consists of two similar structured domains linked by a hinge region consisting of three short peptide stretches; bound β-D-ribopyranose is completely enclosed in a cleft between the domains |CITS: |. Non-liganded (open) structures of RbsB have also been obtained and conformational changes that the molecule undergoes during ligand binding and release are proposed |CITS: |. Regions/residues of RbsB involved in interaction with RbsC and with the chemosensory receptor have been identified |CITS: | RbsB has been used in the development of a TNT bioreporter |CITS: |. rbsB was found to be downregulated in a MG1655 lysogen carrying the Stx2a phage PA8 |CITS: 31208335|.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Interacts with outer membrane receptor proteins that carry out high-affinity binding and energy dependent uptake into the periplasmic space of specific substrates such as cobalamin, and various iron compounds (such as iron dicitrate, enterochelin, aerobactin, etc.). In the absence of TonB these receptors bind their substrates but do not carry out active transport. TonB also interacts with some colicins and is involved in the energy-dependent, irreversible steps of bacteriophages phi 80 and T1 infection. It could act to transduce energy from the cytoplasmic membrane to specific energy-requiring processes in the outer membrane, resulting in the release into the periplasm of ligands bound by these outer membrane proteins. Implicated in hydroxy radical-mediated cell death induced by hydroxyurea treatment (PubMed:20005847). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:20005847}.
MetaCyc_Comment: TonB is a component of the energy transducing Ton system which functions to harness the energy of the proton motive force (pmf) at the cytoplasmic membrane to support active transport of iron-siderophore complexes and vitamin B12 across the outer membrane. Early studies characterized tonB mutants which were defective in iron and Vitamin B12 transport, resistant to various phages and colicins and resistant to the sideromycin, albomycin |CITS: | and suggested that TonB function couples the energized state of the inner membrane to the binding and translocation processes of outer membrane proteins |CITS: |. The TonB protein is predicted to anchor to the inner membrane by its amino terminus while the bulk of the protein extends into the periplasmic space (|CITS: |, see |CITS: |). TonB contains an N-terminal, membrane anchoring domain (residues 1-33), an intermediate periplasmic domain (residues 34-154) and a C-terminal domain that interacts with TonB dependent outer membrane transporters |CITS: |. The intermediate domain contains multiple Glu-Pro and Lys-Pro dipeptide repeats and adopts a rigid, elongated conformation |CITS: |. TonB lacking the repeat motif (TonBΔ66-100) can interact with ExbB and FepA and appears to be functional in energy transduction |CITS: |. TonB localizes with both the inner membrane and outer membranes in approximately equal amounts; the C-terminus is required for association with the outer membrane |CITS: | TonB forms a complex with the inner membrane proteins, ExbB and ExbD |CITS: |. TonB interacts with ExbD; the detection of cross-links between TonB and ExbD requires PMF; TonB and ExbD interact via their periplasmic domains |CITS: |. TonB binds to a conserved region in its partner outer membrane proteins called the Ton box |CITS: |. TonB interacts with BtuB |CITS: |. Purified TonB (residues 147-239) binds to approximately one-half of the periplasmic surface of BtuB in a 1:1 stoichiometry in vitro |CITS: |. Purified TonB (lacking its transmembrane domain) binds to the outer membrane transporters BtuB and FhuA; mutations in the BtuB Ton box disrupt binding and impair transport |CITS: |. TonB interacts with FhuA |CITS: |. Purified TonB (residues 33-239) binds to FhuA in a 1:1 stoichiometry; an interprotein β sheet forms between the FhuA Ton box and a central β sheet of the TonB C-terminal domain |CITS: |. Purified TonB and FhuA form stable 2:1 complexes; FhuA-TonB interactions are multiple and TonB may contain two distinct binding regions for FhuA |CITS: |. TonB binding induces conformational changes in the extraccellular loops of the outer-membrane receptor FhuA |CITS: |. TonB interacts with FecA; this interaction does not require the PMF and is enhanced in the presence of substrate |CITS: |. Various constructs of TonB have been detected as monomers and dimers |CITS: |. The energy transduction cycle may involve transition of TonB through distinct conformations |CITS: |. TonB activity is unaffected when it's amino terminus is trapped as a homodimer (through disulfide cross-linking) but when the carboxy terminus is trapped as a homodimer TonB is inactive and fractionates almost solely with the inner membrane |CITS: |. GFP-TonB fusions localize to the central region of the cell envelope and are largely absent from the cell poles; TonB is a dynamic protein; PMF drives GFP-TonB motion (likely rotational); deletion of exbBD compromises the connection between PMF and TonB motion |CITS: |. TonB interacts with the ferrichrome periplasmic binding protein FhuD; this interaction has a 1:1 stoichiometry in vitro; addition of FhuD to a TonB-FhuA complex results in formation of a trimeric complex in vitro |CITS: |. TonB interacts with the cyanocobalamin periplasmic binding protein, BtuF in vitro |CITS: |. ton: T-one |CITS: | (as cited in |CITS: |) Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: OmpF is a general outer membrane (OM) porin which mediates the non-specific diffusion of small solutes such as sugars, ions and amino acids; the major non-specific OM porins of E. coli K-12 (OmpF and |FRAME: CPLX0-7533 "OmpC"|) are typically defined by an exclusion limit based on substrate mass (~600 daltons) but there are large differences in penetration rates within solutes due to factors such as size, hydrophobicity and charge (discussed in |CITS: |). OmpF acts as a phage receptor (see for example |CITS: |) and is required for the activity of various colicins (see for example |CITS: |). Purified OmpF reconstituted into artificial lipid bilayer membranes forms an ion permeable channel with an estimated pore diameter of 1.1nm; OmpF exhibits a preference for cations |CITS: |. OmpF (protein b) can be isolated associated with the pepidoglycan |CITS: |. OmpF and OmpC are considered to be the two major non-specific trimeric OM porins under standard laboratory growth (see |CITS: | and references within); in the Transporter Classification Database both are members of the General Bacterial Porin (GBP) family |CITS: | which also includes the related porins |FRAME: CPLX0-7530 "PhoE"|, |FRAME: EG10659-MONOMER "NmpC"| and |FRAME: G6700-MONOMER "OmpN"|. Imaging of the OM by atomic force microscopy shows that OmpF foms part of a dense, crowded network of low mobility trimeric porins; the porin network is interupted by nanoscale patches enriched in LPS which may facilitate the insertion of new membrane components as the cell grows |CITS: |. Purified OmpF is trimeric; the OmpF monomer consists of a 16-stranded anti-parallel β-barrel containing an aqueous pore; short β-hairpin turns define the 'smooth' end of the barrel while long, irregular loops are found at the other 'rough' end which faces the extracellular space; one of the long loops (L3) folds into the barrel and forms a constriction zone at about half the height of the barrel |CITS: |. Voltage gating of OmpF and the role of the L3 loop in gating has been widely studied (see reviews by |CITS: | and references within; also |CITS: |). Trimeric OmpF binds specifically to lipopolysaccharide |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |. OmpF-LPS interactions may serve to modulate OmpF activity in vivo |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). OmpF mediates the entry of various antibiotics including β-lactams (|CITS: | quinolones |CITS: | and others |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). OmpF has been implicated in the secretion of the extracellular protein |FRAME: EG11807-MONOMER "YebF"| |CITS: |. OmpF imports the cytotoxic domains of group A colicins E1 and E3 after the colicins bind to the BtuB receptor |CITS: |. The Colicin E9 (ColE9) translocon is a heptameric complex consisting of single copies of the ColE9-immunity protein complex, BtuB, the OmpF trimer and TolB |CITS: |. ColE9's unstructured N-terminal domain occupies two OmpF subunits and captures TolB on the other side of the membrane |CITS: |. Colicin N uses only OmpF for entry |CITS: | - it does not require a separate receptor protein, rather it binds to lipopolysaccharide molecules adjacent to OmpF |CITS: |. Porin genes are subject to complex transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation influenced by factors such as medium osmolarity, temperature and pH (see selected reviews |CITS: |). Polyamines inhibit OmpF activity in vitro |CITS: | and reduce outer membrane permeability (as measured through effects on chemotaxis and permeation of β-lactams) in vivo |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Cadavarine may function as an endogenous modulator of OM permeability via inhibition of porin activity or via a reduction in porin expression |CITS: |. OmpF has been used as a scaffold for the design and engineering of proteins with varying pore size and specific solute selectivity |CITS: | A description of outer membrane protein nomenclature, including early and recommended names can be found in |CITS: |. tolF tolerant (to bacteriocin JF246) |CITS: |Early studies characterizing tolF mutants and outer membrane protein 1a (also called outer membrane protein b) in E. coli K-12 include: |CITS: | Selected related reviews: |CITS: | Please note: extensive characterisation of OmpF has occurred in E. coli B strains. A series of E. coli B strains (the BEstrains) lacking the major outer membrane proteins has been constructed and used as an expression host for purification and characterization of mutant porins including OmpF |CITS: |. While we have attempted to include only information relating to OmpF from K-12, it is possible that some of the studies cited here refer to OmpF from E. coli B strains. The K-12 and B proteins differ by only three amino acid residues (see |CITS: |).
