Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Plays an essential in the initiation and regulation of chromosomal replication. Binds in an ATP-dependent fashion to the origin of replication (oriC) to initiate formation of the DNA replication initiation complex once per cell cycle (PubMed:3036372). Binds the DnaA box (consensus sequence 5'-TTATC[CA]A[CA]A-3') and separates the double-stranded (ds)DNA (PubMed:3036372, PubMed:18216012). Forms a right-handed helical filament on oriC DNA; dsDNA binds to the exterior of the filament while single-stranded (ss)DNA is stabiized in the filament's interior (By similarity). The ATP-DnaA-oriC complex binds and stabilizes the upper strand of the AT-rich DNA unwinding element (DUE) (PubMed:18216012). Mutagenesis of residues that line the central pore blocks dsDNA strand separation (PubMed:18216012). Subsequent binding of DNA polymerase III subunits leads to replisome formation (PubMed:3036372, PubMed:18216012). The DnaA-ATP form converts to DnaA-ADP; once converted to ADP the protein cannot initiate replication, ensuring only 1 round of replication per cell cycle (PubMed:3036372). Binds ATP, ADP and dATP equally well, hydrolyzes ATP with a half-life of about 15 minutes, ATP hydrolysis is not required for pre-priming replisome formation, nucleotide exchange is very slow (PubMed:3036372). Binds acidic phospholipids (PubMed:9478970, PubMed:26272946). DnaA inhibits its own gene expression (PubMed:2981626) as well as that of other genes including dam, rpoH (PubMed:2540187), ftsA and mioC. {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:O66659, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18216012, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2540187, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26272946, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2981626, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3036372, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9478970}.; FUNCTION: Also required for replication of some plasmid DNA; binds 4 DnaA boxes in the minimal plasmid RK2 replication origin (oriV). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15878847, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9242693}.

FUNCTION: Pore-forming subunit of a potassium efflux system that confers protection against electrophiles. Catalyzes K(+)/H(+) antiport. Can also export rubidium, lithium and sodium. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_01413, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17679694, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21041667, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9023177}.
MetaCyc_Comment: KefB and KefC are two independent glutathione-regulated potassium efflux systems, which play a role in protecting the cell from electrophile toxicity. Mutations in kefB and kefC affect potassium efflux at neutral pH, can be complemented by the cloned genes and probably function via potassium/proton antiport |CITS: |. Potassium efflux by KefB or KefC is activated by adducts formed by reaction of glutathione with electrophilic compounds such as N-ethylmaleimide, methylglyoxal and chlorodinitrobenzene |CITS: |. Potassium efflux mediated by KefB and KefC leads to acidification of the cytoplasm, which protects the cell from electrophile toxicity |CITS: |. KefB and KefC differ in their activation by methylglyoxal, with KefC only weakly activated |CITS: |. KefC is a member of the CPA2 family of monovalent cation/proton antiporters. The ancillary protein, KefF, is required for maximum activity of KefC |CITS: |. In addition to KefB and KefC, additional unidentified potassium efflux systems exist. KefC consists of a membrane domain attached to a C-terminal KTN (K+ transport, nucleotide binding) domain via a flexible linker. Mutational analyses suggest the presence of a single binding site for GSH or its adducts at the interface between dimeric KTN domains. The crystal structure of the C terminal domain of KefC in association with KefF has been resolved at 2.4 Å resolution |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the C-terminal domain of KefC in complex with KefF and either the inhibitory ligand GSH or the activating adduct ESG (N-ethylsuccinimido-S-glutathione) have also been solved. Significant conformational change in the KTN domain is associated with binding of the activating adduct but the mechanism by which local conformational change in this region might influence the associated transmembrane pore remains unclear |CITS: |. Overexpression of kefC from an ASKA plasmid leads to a more than 3-fold increase in the MIC of hydrogen peroxide |CITS: |.

This subunit binds the periplasmic potassium ions and delivers the ions to the membrane domain of KdpB through an intramembrane tunnel (PubMed:30478378, PubMed:34272288, PubMed:7896809). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:23930894, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2849541, ECO:0000269|PubMed:30478378, ECO:0000269|PubMed:34272288, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7896809, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8499455}.
MetaCyc_Comment: KdpA is an innner membrane subunit of the potassium ion importing Kdp ATPase |CITS: |; KdpA contains 12 predicted transmembrane regions and forms the K+ transporting channel of the complex; both periplasmic and cytoplasmic K+ binding sites have been identified |CITS: |. More recently, cryo-EM structures of the KdpFABC complex suggest a translocation pathway for K+ via KdpA and KdpB half-channels |CITS: | (and further |CITS: |). KdpA contains 4 M1-P-M2 (MPM) transmembrane motifs and may be homologous to the transmembrane subunits of K+ symporters |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Glutamate-tRNA ligase (GluRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. GluRS belongs to the Class IB aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases |CITS: |. GluRS charges tRNAGlu for both protein and δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthesis. ALA is the first committed tetrapyrrole precursor |CITS: |. The enzyme only aminoacylates the 2'-OH group of tRNA substrates with a terminal 3'-deoxyadenosine base |CITS: |. GluRS can bind both ATP and its tRNA substrate independently, but binding of glutamate requires the presence of tRNAGlu |CITS: |. A two-step catalytic mechanism has been proposed |CITS: |. The contributions of the five domains of GluRS to substrate recognition and catalytic activity have been studied |CITS: |. A tightly bound Zn2+ atom is required for native conformation and catalytic activity |CITS: |; the binding site has been identified by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: | and belongs to the SWIM domain family |CITS: |. The |FRAME: EG10443-MONOMER| phosphorylates the conserved Ser239 residue near the active site of GluRS and inhibits its aminoacylation activity, leading to an increased concentration of uncharged tRNAGlu and triggering (p)ppGpp synthesis |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNAGlu that are important for recognition by GluRS have been identified |CITS: |. The 2-thio element of the hypermodified nucleotide 5-methylaminomethyl-2-thiouridine at position 34 in tRNAGlu is an important recognition element for aminoacylation by GluRS |CITS: |. GluRS competes effectively with TyrRS for aminoacylation of tRNAGlu in vitro |CITS: |. Residues within GluRS that interact with tRNAGlu have been identified |CITS: |. Both the anticodon-binding domain and the catalytic domain of GluRS may participate in tRNAGln discrimination |CITS: |. The Arg266 residue may be uniquely involved in phylum-specific tRNAGlu recognition |CITS: |. Temperature-sensitive alleles of gltX have been isolated |CITS: |. Expression of GluRS may be regulated post-transcriptionally |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

PabB, in the absence of PabA, can catalyze the formation of ADC in the presence of exogenous ammonia. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:16605270, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2251281, ECO:0000269|PubMed:4914080}.

MetaCyc_Comment: PabB (component 1) catalyzes the formation of 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate (ADC) from chorismate and ammonia generated by PabA within the amiodeoxychorismate synthase complex |CITS: |. Kinetic studies support an ordered bi-bi catalytic mechanism with chorismate binding first |CITS: |. In the absence of PabA, PabB can utilize ammonia (at a reduced rate) to aminate chorismate and produce 4-amino-4-deoxychorismate |CITS: |. The reaction catalyzed by PabB in vitro in the presence of ammonia is reversible in the absence of PabC |CITS: |. Crystal structures of PabB have been determined at 2.0 Å resolution; a potential active site has been identified. A deeply embedded tryptophan molecule may play a structural role |CITS: |. Random and site-directed mutagenesis has identified residues important for the interaction with PabA and for catalytic activity |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis supports the function of K274 as the active-site nucleophile |CITS: |, forming a covalent intermediate |CITS: |. The E258 residue acts as a general acid ctalyst for loss of the C4 OH group of chorismate and is required for formation of the covalent intermediate |CITS: |. A homology model for the PabA-PabB complex was constructed. Alanine scanning mutagenesis revealed residues within an interdomain hydrogen bonding network that are important for PabA-PabB complex formation, residues involved in allosteric signaling between the subunits, as well as residues involved in ammonia channeling from the PabA- to the PabB active site |CITS: |. The conserved PabB D308 residue appears to be essential for both complex formation and allosteric signaling |CITS: |. PabB shows sequence |CITS: | and structural |CITS: | similarity TrpE (anthranilate synthase), suggesting common ancestry. Mutations in PabB that enable the additional ability to eliminate pyruvate, i.e. catalyze the anthranilate synthase reaction, were isolated, tested and confirmed |CITS: |. A pabB mutant requires supplementation with p-aminobenzoate for growth |CITS: |. PabB: "p-aminobenzoate" |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Fumarase C (FumC) is one of three fumarase isozymes participating in the TCA cycle. FumC is a tetrameric protein and belongs to the class II, iron-independent fumarases |CITS: |. The cell adapts to changing environmental oxygen conditions by utilizing different isozymes. Both FumA and FumB contain iron-sulfur centers; exposure to oxidative agents such as superoxide results in damage to the metal cofactor and loss of enzyme activity |CITS: |. In contrast, FumC is an iron-independent enzyme and is insensitive to oxidative damage |CITS: |. FumC is made by the cells primarily as a backup enzyme if the FumA or FumB enzymes are damaged by reactive oxygen species. Crystal structures of fumarase C have been solved, allowing identification of the active site |CITS: |. What was thought to be an activator binding site was later determined to be part of the active site, providing a path for transfer of substrate and product between the active site and the bulk solvent |CITS: |. Each active site is composed of residues from three subunits. The function of the SS loop was probed by structural and kinetic characterization of site-directed mutants |CITS: |. The E. coli enzyme has been used to study the effect of disease-associated mutations found in the human ortholog, FH |CITS: |. Fumarase C abundance is more than 38-fold increased during growth with vanillin; a fumC deletion mutant shows a decreased final cell yield when grown in the presence of vanillin |CITS: |. Expression of all three fumarase genes is controlled by oxygen levels. Expression of fumB is four fold elevated under anaerobic cell growth conditions versus aerobic conditions |CITS: |. In contrast, fumA expression is highest only during aerobic growth and where fumC is only weakly expressed. When cells encounter oxidative stress conditions, fumC gene expression is significantly induced by the SoxRS regulatory system |CITS: |. The regulation of fumC expression has been investigated |CITS: |. fumC is a member of the SoxRS regulon; expression can be induced by paraquat |CITS: |. fumA and fumC are under catabolite repression; the transcriptional regulators ArcA and Fnr function to repress fumAC expression under anaerobic conditions |CITS: |. A fumC deletion mutant shows increased biofilm formation |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

Has lower activity towards alkylated DNA containing ethenoadenine, and no detectable activity towards 1-methylguanine or 3-methylthymine. Accepts double-stranded and single-stranded substrates. Requires molecular oxygen, alpha-ketoglutarate and iron. Provides extensive resistance to alkylating agents such as MMS and DMS (SN2 agents), but not to MMNG and MNU (SN1 agents). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12226668, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12594517, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16482161, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19706517, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20084272, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21068844}.

MetaCyc_Comment: AlkB is a Fe(II)-containing, 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase which catalyses the non-mutagenic repair of methyl lesions in DNA and RNA. Purified AlkB is a 2-oxoglutarate and Fe(II) dependent dioxygenase which accurately repairs 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine lesions in DNA |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Purified AlkB accurately repairs 1-methyladenine and 3-methylcytosine in RNA; episomal expression of alkB reactivates methylated RNA phage in vivo |CITS: | (and further |CITS: |). The enzyme is capable of repairing methylation lesions on various nucleic acid substrates (ssDNA, dsDNA, ssRNA, dsRNA and hybrids) in vitro but shows a preference for single-stranded substrate |CITS: |; the enzyme may be active at the replication fork or at sites of transcription in vivo |CITS: |. AlkB repairs 1-ethyladenine and 3-ethylcytosine lesions in DNA |CITS: |; AlkB repairs the minor DNA lesions, 1-methylguanine (1-meG), and to a lesser extent 3-methylthymine (3-meT) |CITS: | (although a later study observed no detectable repair in trinucleotides containing 1-methyl-dG or 3-methyl-dT |CITS: |). AlkB demethylates 2-methylthiocytidine containing tRNAs which are generated from exposure to methylating agents |CITS: |. AlkB is able to repair exocyclic base adducts (eg.3,N4-ethenocytosine, 1,N2-ethenoguanine and 1,N6-ethenoadenine) resulting from oxidative stress or exposure to industrial carcinogens |CITS: |. Purified AlkB is unable to demethylate single, alkylated nucelosides |CITS: |; it can demethylate (with varying efficiency) 1-methyl-deoxyadenosine 5'-phosphate, 1-methyldeoxyadenosine 5'-triphosphate, and 1-methyladenine within an oligonucleotide trimer or dimer; a phosphate residue 5' to the lesion may be important for catalysis |CITS: |. AlkB is not involved in the repair of apyrimidinic and apurinic DNA site lesions or crosslinks (DNA-protein, DNA interstrand) that occur at such lesions; AlkB is not involved in the repair of 3-methyladenine lesions |CITS: |. Overproduction and purification of the protein is described leading to analysis of substrate binding and enzyme assays |CITS: |. Crystal structures of substrate and product complexes of AlkB have been determined |CITS: | (and further |CITS: |). The Fe(II) cofactor of AlkB has been replaced with Cu(II) in a study probing the active site of the enzyme |CITS: |. AlkB-dsDNA complexes containing 3-methyl cytosine, 3-methyl thymine or a cyclic adduct have been crystallised and the structures resolved to high resolution; intermediates of the repair reactions have been characterised after the complexes are subject to 'oxidation in crystallo' |CITS: |. AlkB interacts directly with RecA in vivo; the purified proteins form a stable complex in vitro; RecA stimulates AlkB catalyzed oxidative demethylation in vitro |CITS: |. alkB deficient cells are susceptible to the toxicity and mutagenicity of alkylation lesions |CITS: |. An alkB mutant (alkB22) exhibits increased sensitivity to methyl methanesulfonate (MMS) and a defect in repair of MMS-treated phage, compared to wild type, but shows wild-type sensitivity to UV irradiation and a wild-type response to N-methyl-N'-nitro-N-nitrosoguanidine (MNNG) |CITS: |. The aidD6::Mu d1 (bla lac) mutation disrupts the alkB gene |CITS: |. Regulation has been described |CITS: |. Gene expression is activated by self-methylation of the Ada protein upon interaction with alkylated DNA |CITS: |. Gene expression is induced by the alkylating agents MMS |CITS: |, MNNG |CITS: |, streptozotocin (STZ), and N-methyl-N-nitrosourea (MNU) |CITS: |. Methylation is a more effective inducer than some other types of alkylation |CITS: |. Gene expression is not induced by heat shock |CITS: |, pH changes, thiosalicyclic acid, or N-ethylmaleimide treatment |CITS: |. AlkB has 23% identity to human ABH protein |CITS: | and similarity to human ABH2 and ABH3 |CITS: |. AlkB is a member of the iron-dependent, 2-oxoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase protein family |CITS: |. Expression of ada and alkB genes in human cells increases the cellular resistance to alkylation |CITS: |. Expression of alkB alone in human cells increases resistance specifically to SN2 alkylation compounds but not to SN1 alkylation compounds, the same spectrum of resistance that AlkB provides in E. coli |CITS: |. Expression of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae YFW1, YFW12, or YFW16 gene functionally complements the MMS resistance of an E. coli alkB mutant |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |Related reviews: |CITS: | AidD: "alkylation-inducible" |CITS:|

MetaCyc_Comment: 3-Dehydroquinate dehydratase (DHQ dehydratase) is involved in the 3rd step of the chorismate pathway, which leads to the biosynthesis of aromatic amino acids. DHQ dehydratase catalyzes the conversion of DHQ to 3-dehydroshikimate and introduces the first double bond of the aromatic ring |CITS: |. The first step of the 3-dehydroquinase reaction involves the formation of an imine intermediate between the keto group of 3-dehydroquinate and the e-amino group of a lysine at the active site of the enzyme. Chemical modification and mutagenesis experiments have identified this lysine to be Lys-170 |CITS: |. In addition to the lysine side chain involved in imine formation, the enzyme also requires a basic group for proton abstraction. His-143 has been shown to be essential for catalysis in this enzyme and that this residue may be acting as the general base in the catalytic mechanism. His-143 may also be involved in Schiff base formation/breakdown. |CITS: | The pH activity studies demonstrate that 3-dehydroquinase requires groups with pKa values near 6 in a deprotonated form for maximal activity. Experiments with diethylpyrocarbonate provide evidence that this group is the imidazole side chain of a histidine residue. |CITS:| The reaction exhibits cis stereochemistry in both directions |CITS: |. The structural gene, aroD, has been cloned and overexpressed |CITS: |. Crystals of DHQ dehydratase in E. coli and Salmonella typhi were grown. However, only the S. typhi DHQ dehydratase structure has been resolved to 2.3 Å resolution. The E. coli and S. typhi DHQ dehydratase is 69% identical at the amino acid level |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: Diadenosine tetraphosphate (Ap4A) is a side product of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, including E. coli |FRAME: LYSU-CPLX LysU|. Diadenosine tetraphosphatase (diadenosine 5', 5'''-P1, P4-tetraphosphate pyrophosphohydrolase, ApaH) hydrolyzes Ap4A and related molecules |CITS: |. ApaH decaps RNA molecules that contain Ap4 and Gp4 caps at the 5' end, generating a diphosphorylated RNA product |CITS: |. It has also been shown that ApaH can cleave both methylated and non-methylated NpnN caps |CITS: |. Epistasis experiments suggest an RNA decay pathway involving the consecutive actions of ApaH followed by |FRAME: G7459-MONOMER RppH|, triggering the degradation of Np4-capped RNAs |CITS: |. Substrate specificity and reaction kinetics have been examined |CITS: |. ApaH cleaves after the second phosphate group of the adenosine moiety |CITS: |. An apaH mutation leads to elevated levels of Ap4A |CITS: |, loss of motility due to a decrease in σF-mediated gene expression, and decreased expression of cAMP-CRP-regulated genes |CITS: |. An apaH mutant exhibits decreased heat resistance |CITS: | that can be suppressed by ClpB overproduction |CITS: |, and decreased resistance to mild acid stress |CITS: |. The previously identified cfcB1 mutation |CITS: | is an apaH allele |CITS: |. An apaH null mutant shows a moderately decreased level of persister cell formation |CITS: |. The phenotypes of several apaH point mutations and the effects of a ΔapaH mutation on the proteome were also tested |CITS: |. Both deletion of apaH and overexpression of LysU lead to a large increase in killing by aminoglycoside antibiotics such as kanamycin |CITS: |. Overexpression of apaH decreases the intracellular concentration of dinucleotide tetraphosphates |CITS: |, but does not appear to alter the profile of proteins produced upon heat shock or oxidative damage and does not increase resistance to H2O2 |CITS: |. The ApaH protein of Salmonella Typhimurium is required for wild-type invasion of human cells in vitro |CITS: |. apaH belongs to a network of genes which facilitate stress-induced mutagenesis (SIM) in E. coli K-12 |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: ada encodes a bifunctional methyltransferase and transcriptional regulator which is a key component of the adaptive response - the mechanism of adaption induced after exposure to small amounts of DNA alkylating agents. O6-methylguanine (O6--meG) and O4-methylthymine (O4-meT) are two of a number of nucleobase modifications that result from exposure of DNA to alkylating agents - both chemical and endogenous; O6-meG and O4-meT modifications constitute potentially mutagenic lesions due to their tendency to mispair with thymine and with guanine, respectively, inducing transition mutations (reviewed in |CITS: |). The Ada protein contains two major domains: an N-terminal domain (N-Ada), which demethylates Sp-diastereoisomers of DNA methylphosphotriesters by irreversible methyl transfer to its Cys-38 residue (initially thought to be Cys69) and converts Ada into a transcription regulator, and a C-terminal domain (C-Ada) which demethylates the mutagenic bases, O6-meG and O4-meT, by irreversible methyl transfer to Cys-321. Early characterization of Ada and the inducible response to DNA alkylation was done in E. coli B (see |CITS: |. The proteins from E. coli K-12 and E. coli B differ by 6 amino acid alterations |CITS: |. Ada can be also be activated as a transcriptional regulator through a direct methylation by MMS and methyl iodide |CITS: |. Purified Ada is cleaved by cellular proteinases into two smaller polypeptides derived from the N-terminal and C-terminal halves of the protein |CITS: |. The C-terminal 178 amino acid domain of Ada (from E. coli B) has been purified and crystallised; in this structure Cys-321 is buried suggesting that conformational change is required for contact with the methyl group of a DNA molecule |CITS: |. N-Ada (purifed from E. coli B) binds a zinc molecule which is tetrahedrally coordinated to 4 cysteine residues (Cys38, Cys42, Cys69 and Cys72); zinc is required for correct protein folding |CITS: |. Ada is autoregulated and regulates transcription of the genes encoding |FRAME: EG11222-MONOMER "AlkA"|, |FRAME: EG10037-MONOMER "AlkB"| and |FRAME: CPLX0-7691 "AidB"| proteins |CITS:|. The mechanism of transcription regulation by Ada varies depending on the target promoter |CITS: | (and see review by |CITS: |. Transcription activation by Ada is controlled by a methylation dependent electrostatic switch whereby methylation of Cys38 enhances DNA binding by reducing the electrostatic repulsion between N-Ada and the sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA |CITS: |. Undamaged cells produce, on average, one Ada molecule per generation; some cells have no Ada molecules and thus cannot trigger the adaptive response. The stochastic activation of Ada results in subpopulations that do not repair alkylation damage or that have a delay in such repair, causing an accumulation of mutations that could generate genetic plasticity |CITS: |. We have modified the reported length of the binding site of this protein to 13 bp, according to the proposal by Teo et al |CITS: |. Other authors have proposed different lengths and consensus sequences for Ada |CITS: |, but Nakamura et al showed that deletions in this consensus sequence (AAANNAAAGCGCA) decrease the activity of β-galactosidase |CITS: |. Based on a quantitative model, it was shown that stochastic expression of Ada is responsible for creating stark cellular heterogeneity in the adaptive response |CITS:|. ada: adaptive response to alkylation damage Reviews: |CITS: |.Related reviews: |CITS: |

Electron transfer from D-lactate to oxygen under aerobic conditions and electron transfer from D-lactate to nitrate under anaerobic conditions depends on the presence of a quinone |CITS: |. The protein contains 3 discontinuous domains - a FAD binding domain, a cap domain and a membrane binding domain. The membrane domain of Dld has an electropositive surface; Dld binds to the membrane through electrostatic force |CITS: |. D-lactate dehydrogenase was widely used in experiments investigating the mechanism for energy coupling between respiration and active transport (see articles by |CITS: |, |CITS: | and |CITS: |). MetaCyc_Comment: RsmA is the methyltransferase responsible for dimethylation of 16S rRNA at the two adjacent adenosine bases A1518 and A1519 |CITS: |. In vitro, the enzyme is active on 30S ribosomal subunits, but not the fully assembled 70S ribosome |CITS: |. RsmA may play a role in biogenesis of the small subunit of the ribosome |CITS: |, providing a checkpoint where binding of RsmA keeps immature 30S subunits from entering the translational cycle |CITS: |. RsmA and the ribosome maturation factor |FRAME: EG11178-MONOMER RbfA| function together in checkpointing maturation of the 30S subunit |CITS: |. Methylation of the 16S rRNA by RsmA is important for release of RbfA from the 30S subunit |CITS: |. The evolutionary relationship and functional divergence of this enzyme and its homologs in eukaryotes has been studied |CITS: |. RsmA as well as the dimethylation modification it catalyzes are nearly universally conserved, suggesting an important function |CITS: |. RsmA is unable to methylate free 16S rRNA |CITS: | and is only able to methylate 30S ribosomal subunits in their translationally inactive conformation |CITS: |. RsmA interacts with the decoding site of the 30S subunit, and interactions of 30S with RsmA and IF-3 appear to be mutually exclusive |CITS: |. Lack of RsmA affects the initiation error rate and the kinetics of translation initiation |CITS: |. Methylation of the two adenosine residues is independent of each other |CITS: |. Recognition of the 3' terminal hairpin of 16S rRNA and methylation activity of RsmA have been studied |CITS: |. The loop of helix 24 and the length of helix 45 of 16S rRNA appear to be important for RsmA catalytic activity |CITS: |. Binding of RsmA prevents helix 44 from adopting its position in the mature 30S subunit and blocks the formation of the decoding site |CITS: |. Once the methylation is complete, RsmA dissociates rapidly from 30S, likely due to a methylation-dependent conformational change in the rRNA |CITS: |. Crystal structures of wild type and the L114P mutant of RsmA |CITS: | and cryo-EM structures of RsmA bound to a nonmethylated 30S ribosomal subunit |CITS: | have been solved. Site-directed mutagenesis of conserved residues in the predicted N-terminal SAM binding motifs result in loss of methyltransferase activity |CITS: |. The L114 residue in the active site specifically affects the ability of the enzyme to perform the second methylation reaction at the same adenine base |CITS: |. While the N-terminal catalytic domain contacts the substrate adenosine residues, the C-terminal domain contacts helix 27 and helix 24 of 16S rRNA |CITS: |. Successive methylation of the two adjacent adenosine residues is thought to involve successive flipping of the substrate nucleotides without dissociation of RsmA |CITS: |. Surprisingly, RsmA also exhibits cytosine-DNA glycosylase activity and may play a role in protection of DNA against oxidative stress |CITS: |. Mutation of rsmA causes resistance to kasugamycin (an inhibitor of translation initiation), but no substantial growth defect |CITS: |. The lack of methylation at A1519, but not A1518, appears to be responsible for the kasugamycin resistance phenotype of an rsmA mutant |CITS: |. An rsmA deletion enhances the slow growth phenotype of an rsgA mutation |CITS: |. rsmA was also identified as a multicopy suppressor for a cold-sensitive mutant of era, which encodes an essential GTP-binding protein |CITS: |. The methyltransferase and multicopy suppressor activities of RsmA are separable, indicating a possible second function of RsmA |CITS: |. High-level overexpression of RsmA is toxic, and the cells show increased sensitivity to acid shock |CITS: |. An rsmA deletion strain is cold sensitive and shows an altered ribosome profile and altered 16S rRNA processing, while an rsmA point mutant lacking catalytic activity has a dominant negative effect on growth and ribosome formation |CITS: |. A ΔrsmA mutant shows increased susceptibility to aminoglycoside antibiotics; the phenotype is due to the lack of its methyltransferase activity, which affects translation fidelity |CITS: |. Overexpression of |FRAME: EG11178-MONOMER RbfA| in a ΔrsmA strain leads to a severe growth defect and accumulation of 17S rRNA precursors |CITS: |. In a systematic study of rRNA methyltransferases, rsmA expression was highly induced in early exponential phase. The ΔrsmA mutant of the Keio collection showed no apparent accumulation of ribosomal assembly intermediates, but an increased amount of the 17S rRNA processing intermediate when grown at 20°C. The mutant shows decreased efficiency of exogenous protein synthesis |CITS: |. The RsmA protein binds specifically to its own mRNA and may regulate its own translation |CITS: |. Growth rate positively regulates rsmA expression |CITS: |. KsgA: "kasugamycin resistance" |CITS: | Comment: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: OmpC is a general outer membrane (OM) porin which mediates the non-specific diffusion of small solutes such as sugars, ions and amino acids; the major non-specific OM porins of E. coli K-12 (OmpC and |FRAME: CPLX0-7534 "OmpF"|) are typically defined by an exclusion limit based on substrate mass (~600 daltons) but there are large differences in penetration rates within solutes due to factors such as size, hydrophobicity and charge (discussed in |CITS: |). OmpC acts as a receptor for bacteriophages 434, T4 and Bp7 (see |CITS: | and further |CITS: |). Purified OmpC reconstituted into artificial lipid bilayer membranes forms an ion permeable channel with a slight preference for cations |CITS: |. OmpC and OmpF are considered to be the two major non-specific trimeric OM porins under standard laboratory growth (see |CITS: | and references within); in the Transporter Classification Database both are members of the General Bacterial Porin (GBP) family |CITS: | which also includes the related porins |FRAME: CPLX0-7530 "PhoE"|, |FRAME: EG10659-MONOMER "NmpC"| and |FRAME: G6700-MONOMER "OmpN"|. Imaging of the OM by atomic force microscopy shows that OmpC foms part of a dense, crowded network of low mobility trimeric porins; the porin network is interupted by nanoscale patches enriched in LPS which may facilitate the insertion of new membrane components as the cell grows |CITS: |. Purified OmpC is trimeric; the OmpC monomer consists of a 16-stranded anti-parallel β-barrel containing an aqueous pore; the β-strands show short connections at the periplasmic rim and long irregular loops at the extracellular surface with the exception of loop L3 which folds into the barrel and forms a constriction zone; the OmpC monomers are arranged into trimers via hydrophobic interactions between barrel surfaces and a 'latching loop" L2 which connects one monomer to its neighbour |CITS:|. OmpC is tightly but noncovalently associated with the peptidoglycan layer |CITS:|. OmpC is implicated in a retrograde phospholipid trafficking pathway (the Mla pathway) that functions to maintain lipid asymmetry in the outer membrane; stationary phase ΔompC cells have disrupted outer membrane lipid asymmetry; OmpC interacts physically with the outer membrane lipoprotein |FRAME: G7216-MONOMER "MlaA"|; strong genetic interaction between mlaA and ompC suggests that the proteins function together within the Mla system |CITS: | (see further |CITS: | and also |CITS: |). OmpC mediates the entry of various antibiotics including β-lactams, tetracyclines and others |CITS: |. OmpC is implicated in the secretion of the extracellular protein |FRAME: EG11807-MONOMER "YebF"| |CITS: |. Porin genes are subject to complex transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation influenced by factors such as medium osmolarity, temperature and pH (see selected reviews |CITS: |). MetaCyc_Comment: Pyruvate oxidase is a peripheral membrane enzyme that catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to form acetate and CO2. The reaction is coupled to the electron transport chain via ubiquinone. Metabolism of pyruvate by pyruvate oxidase is less efficient than the route via |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX| (PDH); however, the pyruvate oxidase route is important for wild-type growth efficiency and responsible for a significant amount of pyruvate metabolism under aerobic conditions |CITS: |. PoxB is the main pathway for acetate production in stationary phase |CITS: |. Under aerobic phosphate starvation conditions, metabolic flux is diverted from PDH to PoxB, which may decrease oxidative stress |CITS: |. Modern systems biology approaches have been used to enable a more thorough understanding of the transition to overflow metabolism (excretion of acetate) |CITS: | and growth on glycerol as the carbon source |CITS: |. Activation of the enzyme by phospholipids plays an essential role in vivo |CITS: |. The lipid binding site localizes to the C terminus of PoxB |CITS: |. The enzyme is a homotetramer. Multimerization does not appear to be necessary for enzyme activity |CITS: |; however, the domain that interacts with lipid appears to be formed by contribution from two subunits |CITS: |. The presence of the substrate pyruvate and the TPP cofactor causes a conformational change in the C terminus, which goes from a solvent-inaccessible state in which the C termini within the tetramer do not interact with each other to a solvent-accessible state in which C termini are proximal |CITS: |. The active site residue V380 is an important determinant of substrate specificity |CITS: |. Mutations of poxB that abolish pyruvate oxidase enzymatic activity were isolated by selecting for lack of growth in the absence of acetate in an aceEF mutant background |CITS: |. Limited proteolytic digestion of PoxB activates the enzyme by removing the C-terminal amphipathic α-peptide that may be responsible for interaction with membrane phospholipids |CITS: |. The poxB3 mutant allele is altered in lipid binding and has 15% of wild type activity |CITS: |. Both the poxB3 (P536S) and poxB4 (A467T) alleles localize to the C-terminal domain |CITS: |. A mutant protein lacking the C-terminal 24 amino acids is active in vitro, but can not be activated by lipids and is not active in vivo |CITS: |. The study of additional mutants has contributed to a detailed understanding of PoxB interaction with and activation by lipids |CITS: |. Crystal structures of full-length PoxB and the proteolytically activated Δ23 protein have been solved at 2.9 and 2.5 Å resolution, showing that activation is the result of a conformational rearrangement that uncovers the active site |CITS: |. PoxB is evolutionarily related to the large subunits of E. coli acetohydroxy acid synthases (AHAS) IlvB, IlvG, and IlvI |CITS: | and glyoxylate carboligase |CITS: |. Gene expression and/or protein abundance increases at stationary phase |CITS: |, in response to the herbicide and acetolactate synthase inhibitor, sulfometuron methyl |CITS: |, in response to osmotic stress |CITS: |, and during growth on glycerol compared to growth on glucose as the carbon source |CITS: |. poxB is part of the σS regulon |CITS: |. Gene expression decreases under anaerobic conditions |CITS: |. poxB transcript levels are higher in a K-12 strain than in E. coli B, contributing to higher acetate production in K-12 strains |CITS: |. Manipulation of metabolic flux through pyruvate has been successfully used as a strategy in metabolic engineering; e.g. |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

FUNCTION: Involved in the restart of stalled replication forks, which reloads the replicative helicase (DnaB) on sites other than the origin of replication; the PriA-PriB pathway is the major replication restart pathway (PubMed:11532137, PubMed:37169801, PubMed:22636770). There are several restart pathways, the PriA-PriB pathway is subdivided into 2 distinct pathways (PubMed:34423481). priB and priC have redundant roles in the cell (PubMed:10540288). During primosome assembly it facilitates complex formation between PriA and DnaT on DNA; stabilizes PriA on DNA, presumably by preventing or inhibiting PriA DNA translocation activity (PubMed:8663104, PubMed:8663105, PubMed:8663106). Forms a branched DNA-PriA-PriB complex when the lagging strand is single-stranded (ss)DNA (PubMed:16188886). Binds ssDNA in the presence and absence of ssDNA DNA-binding protein (SSB), does not bind branched structures (PubMed:8366072, PubMed:16188886). DNA binding, forming spiral filaments on ssDNA, is cooperative (PubMed:16899446). Stimulates the helicase activity of PriA (PubMed:16188886, PubMed:37169801, PubMed:34423481). The homodimer binds 12 nucleotides of ssDNA (PubMed:20156448). Binds homo-pyrimidine tracts better than homo-purine tracts (PubMed:15383524, PubMed:20156448). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11532137, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15383524, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16188886, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1646811, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16899446, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1856227, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20156448, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22636770, ECO:0000269|PubMed:34423481, ECO:0000269|PubMed:37169801, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8366072, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8663104, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8663105, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8663106}.; FUNCTION: Genetic interactions among priB, dam, lexA, nagC, polA, rdgB, rdgB, rep and uup link the PriA-PriB replication restart pathway to DNA double-strand break repair. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:36326440}.

MetaCyc_Comment: The ushA gene of E. coli encodes a bifunctional enzyme with 5'-nucleotidase and UDP-sugar hydrolase activities. It has relatively broad substrate specificity, hydrolyzing 5'-ribonucleotides and 5'-deoxyribonucleotides |CITS: |, bis(5'-nucleosidyl)polyphosphates |CITS: |, UDP sugars |CITS: |, and CDP-alcohols |CITS: |. It also hydrolyzes the synthetic substrates bis(p-nitrophenyl)phosphate and p-nitrophenyl phosphate |CITS: |. UshA localizes to the periplasm where it is able to catalyze the degradation of external UDP-glucose to uridine, glucose-1-phosphate and inorganic phosphate which are then utilized by the cell. The nucleoside diphosphate sugar hydrolase activity is specific for UDP sugars |CITS: |. The periplasmic location suggests a general role for this enzyme in utilization of extracellular nucleotides |CITS: |. UshA is also involved in the degradation of internally formed nucleotides during degradation of cellular RNA |CITS: , |. ushA knockout mutants lack major 5'-nucleotidase activity. An ushA aphA double knockout mutant is unable to utilize purine nucleotides as the sole carbon source |CITS: |. In addition to its 5'-nucleotidase activity, UDP-sugar hydrolase activity, and dinucleoside polyphosphate hydrolase activity, UshA has a novel, highly efficient CDP-alcohol hydrolase activity. The E. coli enzyme and its ortholog in Yersinia intermedia have CDP-alcohol hydrolase activity against CDP-glycerol, CDP-ethanolamine and CDP-choline. CDP-glycerol hydrolysis by the Yersinia enzyme produces cytidine, L-glycerol-3-phosphate and inorganic phosphate |CITS: |. The activities of both the UDP-sugar hydrolase and the nucleotidase are inhibited by an (unidentifed) intracellular protein; this inhibition may serve to protect the cytoplasmic nucleotide pool prior to secretion of UshA to the periplasm |CITS: |. X-ray structures indicate that UshA is a monomer consisting of a larger N-terminal domain that coordinates two catalytic divalent metal ions, linked by an α helix to a smaller C-terminal domain which provides the substrate specificity pocket for the nucleotides. Substrate binding is at the interface of the two domains. A large domain rotation is associated with catalysis |CITS: |. UshA belongs to the calcineurin superfamily of dinuclear metallophosphatases and is homologous to the mammalian ecto-5'-nucleotidases |CITS: |. ush: UDP-sugar hydrolase |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: appA encodes a periplasmic protein with phosphoanhydride phosphatase and multiple inositol-polyphosphate phosphatase activity. The purified protein (initially isolated from E. coli K-10) has phosphoanhydride phosphatase activity that is optimal at pH2-4; the enzyme is not active on most phosphomonoesters and preferentially hydrolyses the distal phosphoryl residues of GTP and of the regulatory nucleotide guanosine 5',3'-bisphosphate |CITS: |. The expression of the enzyme is subject to complex regulation; it is induced by anoxia, influenced by the phase of growth, and the concentration of phosphate |CITS: |. The biological significance of AppA is not clear; the enzyme is apparently not able to supply the cell with inorganic phosphate split from exogenous phosphorylated compounds or polyphosphates. Its complex regulatory characteristics, and in particular its synthesis in response to oxygen deprivation have suggested a possible relationship with fermentation or respiration |CITS: |. Purified AppA has multiple inositol-polyphosphate phosphatase activity; it dephosphorylates myo-inositol hexakisphosphate (phytate) in a sequential manner to produce |FRAME: CPD-6746 "myo-inositol monophosphate"| (myo-inositol 2-monophosphate). The hydrolysis rate decreases markedly during the later steps possibly due to inhibition by the phosphate product |CITS: , , |. Inositol-polyphosphate phosphatase activity is expressed under anaerobic conditions and in late stationary phase growth |CITS: |. The enzyme may exist as a dimer or higher order oligomer in vivo; two isoforms can be distinguished on the basis of isolelectric point; the two isoforms have similar kinetic and biochemical properties |CITS: |. Purified, crystallized AppA is monomeric and contains an α domain and an αβ domain; the active site is located at the interface of the two domains; phytate binding induces conformational change near the active site |CITS: |. AppA is a Group III histidine acid phosphatase (HAP); group III HAPs are capable of hydrolysing metal free phytate plus various other phosphate esters at acidic pH |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: PutP is a member of the SSS family of sodium/solute transporters |CITS:|. PutP is a sodium/proline symporter responsible for the uptake of proline. Mutations in putP decrease proline transport and can be complemented by the cloned putP gene |CITS:|. The PutP protein has been purified, reconstituted into proteoliposomes, and shown to mediate proline transport in the presence of a sodium or lithium ion gradient |CITS:,|. Mutant phenotype and expression analysis also suggest that PutP may be responsible for the transport of the short chain fatty acid propionate |CITS:|. Kinetic analysis has shown that PutP binds proline with a Km of approximately 2 μM and sodium with a Km of approximately 700 μM |CITS:|. Sodium and proline are transported by PutP with a stoichiometry of 1:1 |CITS:|. The transport activity of PutP is associated with charge translocation |CITS:,|. Sodium ions and/or proline induce a charge displacement and conformational alteration through the binding process at the cytoplasmic face of the protein |CITS:|. Genetic and spectroscopic analyses indicate that PutP consists of 13 transmembrane helices with the N-terminus on the periplasmic side of the membrane and the C-terminus facing the cytoplasm |CITS:,|. PutP has been found as a dimer in the inner membrane |CITS:|. The structure of transmembrane domain IX of PutP, thought to form part of the ion and/or proline translocation pathway |CITS: , | has been modeled using pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) measurements on spin-labeled mutants |CITS:|. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the attachment of valine to tRNA(Val). As ValRS can inadvertently accommodate and process structurally similar amino acids such as threonine, to avoid such errors, it has a 'posttransfer' editing activity that hydrolyzes mischarged Thr-tRNA(Val) in a tRNA-dependent manner.
Catalytic activity: CATALYTIC ACTIVITY: Reaction=tRNA(Val) + L-valine + ATP = L-valyl-tRNA(Val) + AMP + diphosphate; Xref=Rhea:RHEA:10704, Rhea:RHEA-COMP:9672, Rhea:RHEA-COMP:9708, ChEBI:CHEBI:30616, ChEBI:CHEBI:33019, ChEBI:CHEBI:57762, ChEBI:CHEBI:78442, ChEBI:CHEBI:78537, ChEBI:CHEBI:456215; EC=6.1.1.9;
MetaCyc_Comment: Valine-tRNA ligase (ValRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. ValRS belongs to the Class I aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases |CITS: |. ValRS contains a conserved proline triplet that is critical for activity; it therefore requires |FRAME: EG12099-MONOMER EF-P| for expression, which may explain evolution of the EF-P system |CITS: |. ValRS is a monomer in solution |CITS: |. A single binding site for tRNAVal was thought to exist |CITS: |, but evidence for a second binding site has been reported |CITS: |. The reaction mechanism of ValRS includes the formation of an aminoacyl adenylate intermediate, which then serves as the animo acid donor in the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase reaction |CITS: |. The enzyme rapidly forms a valyl-adenylate and binds a second molecule of valine slowly |CITS: |. Residues in contact with valine and residues that may be part of the editing site have been determined |CITS: |. The ATP binding site of ValRS was determined by affinity labeling |CITS: |. Investigation of pre-steady-state and single turnover kinetics of ValRS show that the enzyme exhibits burst kinetics and is rate-limited by release of aminoacyl-tRNA, distinguishing it from class II aminoacyl tRNA synthetases |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNAVal that are important for recognition by ValRS have been identified |CITS: |. The anticodon is sufficient for distinguishing tRNAMet and tRNAVal |CITS: |. ValRS specifically acylates the 2'-OH of tRNAVal, while the 3'-OH is important for preventing misacylation |CITS: |. The U73 mutant of tRNAVal is valylated at either the 2' or the 3'-OH group |CITS: |. Many aminoacyl tRNA synthetases have been shown to have editing functions. ValRS misactivates threonine, cysteine and α-aminobutyrate (αBut) |CITS: |, but has a post-transfer editing mechanism which hydrolyzes a mischarged αBut-tRNAVal and others |CITS: |. Editing occurs almost exclusively via post-transfer hydrolysis of the mischarged aminoacyl-tRNA within the editing domain |CITS: |. The editing site of ValRS recognizes adenosine at the 3' end of tRNA |CITS: |; further requirements for editing have been determined |CITS: |. The nature of the mischarged tRNA does not influence its transfer to the editing site on ValRS |CITS: |. Mutations that allow charging of tRNAVal with cysteine have been identified and lie in the editing site of ValRS |CITS: |; the Lys277 residue is important for the editing activity |CITS: |. D286A, K277P, and K277P/D286A mutants within the post-transfer editing domain are unable to deacylate misacylated tRNA |CITS: |. Isoleucine is selected against by a steric exclusion mechanism |CITS: |. The β-phosphate-γ-phosphate interchange reaction of ATP contributes to the prevention of tRNA aminoacylation by non-cognate amino acids |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: Encodes the ribosomal protein L20 (rplT), a primary 23S rRNA‑binding protein that is a component of the 50S ribosomal subunit. The article identifies JW1703 as the himA gene, which encodes the α‑subunit of Integration Host Factor (IHF). IHF is a basic, class II DNA‑binding protein that forms a heterodimer with the β‑subunit encoded by hip (himD). The HimA protein participates in a variety of cellular processes: it binds specific DNA sites to facilitate site‑specific recombination of bacteriophage λ and Mu, influences DNA supercoiling, and acts as a transcriptional regulator. Within the pheST‑himA operon, HimA exerts autoregulatory control by forming repressor complexes that inhibit transcription initiation at two promoters (p3 upstream of pheST and p4 located inside pheT). This negative feedback is modulated by the SOS response; LexA‑dependent SOS induction relieves HimA‑mediated repression at both promoters, although no LexA binding site is present in the promoter regions. Additionally, HimA expression is coupled to the attenuation mechanism governing pheST transcription, allowing the intracellular concentration of HimA to be linked to the functional state of the translational apparatus. In summary, JW1703 (himA) encodes the IHF α‑subunit, a DNA‑binding protein essential for phage integration, global transcriptional regulation, and feedback control of its own expression. {PubMed:3326947}. The gene encodes the ribosomal protein L20 (previously called P12). L20 is a primary 23S ribosomal RNA‑binding protein that forms part of the 50S ribosomal subunit. Its synthesis is coordinated with other ribosomal proteins, reflecting its role in ribosome assembly and function. {PubMed:6317865}. The article identifies b1713 as the himA gene, which encodes the α‑subunit of Integration Host Factor (IHF). IHF is a basic, class II DNA‑binding protein that forms a heterodimer with the β‑subunit (encoded by hip/himD). The HimA protein participates in several cellular processes: it binds specific DNA sites to facilitate site‑specific recombination events such as λ phage integration and Mu development; it influences DNA topology and supercoiling; and it acts as a transcriptional regulator, forming part of operator‑repressor complexes that negatively control its own transcription as well as the transcription of the upstream pheST operon. HimA‑mediated regulation occurs at two promoters (p3 upstream of pheST and p4 within pheT) and is modulated by the SOS response, although no LexA binding site is present in these promoters. Additionally, HimA contributes to an attenuation mechanism that couples its expression to the functional state of the translational apparatus, linking intracellular HimA levels to phenylalanyl‑tRNA synthetase activity. {PubMed:3326947}. The article describes pheT as encoding the β‑subunit of phenylalanyl‑tRNA synthetase (PheRS) in Escherichia coli. Together with the α‑subunit encoded by pheS, PheRS forms an α₂β₂ hetero‑tetrameric enzyme that catalyzes the esterification of phenylalanine to its cognate tRNA (tRNA^Phe). The β‑subunit (PheT) is responsible for recognition of the tRNA, binding of the aminoacyl‑adenylate intermediate, and editing of misacylated tRNA. The study highlights that the glutamic acid residue at position 571 (Glu₅₇₁) of PheT is critical for the thermal stability of the PheRS enzyme; a G1711→A1711 transition causing an Glu₅₇₁→Lys substitution (named pheT36) renders cells temperature‑sensitive, demonstrating the vital role of this residue in maintaining enzyme function at elevated temperatures. {PubMed:29660847}. The pheT gene encodes the β (beta) subunit of phenylalanyl‑tRNA synthetase. Together with the α subunit encoded by pheS, it forms the heterotetrameric (α₂β₂) phenylalanyl‑tRNA synthetase enzyme that catalyzes the attachment of phenylalanine to its cognate tRNA (tRNA^Phe), a crucial step in protein synthesis. The article also notes that pheT is co‑transcribed with pheS as part of the same operon. {PubMed:6368838}. The pheT gene encodes the large (β) subunit of Escherichia coli phenylalanyl‑tRNA synthetase, which together with the small (α) subunit encoded by pheS forms the α₂β₂ tetrameric enzyme that catalyzes the attachment of phenylalanine to its cognate tRNA. The gene is located immediately downstream of pheS and is transcribed as part of the same operon (pheS‑pheT), whose expression is controlled by a phenylalanine‑mediated attenuation mechanism. {PubMed:6317865}. The pheT gene encodes the β‑subunit (≈785 aa, ~87 kDa) of the phenylalanyl‑tRNA synthetase (PheRS) in Thermus thermophilus HB8. This large subunit, together with the α‑subunit encoded by pheS, forms the heterotetrameric α₂β₂ enzyme that catalyzes the ATP‑dependent attachment of phenylalanine to its cognate tRNA (tRNA^Phe). The β‑subunit contributes directly to the enzyme’s active site and participates in tRNA binding, as indicated by conserved arginine and lysine residues that correspond to tRNA‑interacting residues identified in yeast and E. coli PheRSs. Structural features of the β‑subunit include clusters of hydrophilic residues, several predicted α‑helical regions, and a leucine‑zipper motif that may be involved in subunit dimerization or regulatory interactions. {PubMed:1508711}. Encodes one of the two structural subunits of the Escherichia coli phenylalanyl‑tRNA synthetase (the pheST operon). The pheST operon provides the enzyme that amino‑acylates tRNA^Phe with phenylalanine, and its transcription is regulated by a tRNA^Phe‑dependent attenuation mechanism. In addition, a promoter located within the 3′ end of pheT (designated p4) can initiate transcription of the downstream himA gene. {PubMed:3326947}.

MetaCyc_Comment: DdlB is one of two D-alanine—D-alanine ligases in E. coli |CITS: |. D-alanine—D-alanine ligase, along with alanine racemase, makes up the D-alanine branch of peptidoglycan biosynthesis. The enzyme combines two molecules of D-alanine to form D-alanyl-D-alanine, which is then added to the growing cell wall precursor. DdlB belongs to the ATP grasp superfamily. The enzyme is similar to VanA, a DD-ligase with modified substrate specificity that occurs in vancomycin-resistant enterococci |CITS: |. D-alanine—D-alanine ligase is an antibacterial drug target; it has long known to be the target of D-cycloserine |CITS: |. Structural and functional studues revealed that it is the phosphorylated form of D-cycloserine that inhibits DdlB |CITS: |. Crystal structures of DdlB have been solved, and a reaction mechanism was proposed |CITS: |. Kinetic analysis of mutants in predicted active site residues has allowed confirmation and refinement of the proposed reaction mechanism |CITS: |. The reaction involves rapid formation of an enzyme-bound D-alanyl phosphate intermediate |CITS: |. Several active site mutants have gained ligase functions similar to the VanA enzyme involved in vancomycin resistance of enterococci |CITS: |. Crystal structures of wild type and mutant DdlB in a complex with an inhibitor allowed insights into substrate specificity and reasons for the weaker inhibition of VanA |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics simulations of the transition between the open and closed conformation enabled virtual screening and discovery of inhibitors of DdlB |CITS: |. The second D-alanine substrate (D-Ala2) is bound in its zwitterionic state, suggesting that the specificity of VanA for D-lactate as the second substrate arises from differences in ligand ionization rather than differences in catalytic behavior |CITS: |. A ddlB insertion mutant is lethal due to a polar effect on the essential cell division genes that lie downstream in the same transcription unit |CITS: |. A potential RNA G-quadruplex structure, formed by guanine-rich sequences located in the coding sequence region of the gene, was identified for ddlB . This structure could regulate the expression of the gene, as observed for hemL gene expression |CITS: |.

Merged_Functions: The ilvB gene is part of the ilvB operon that encodes acetohydroxy acid synthase I, a 60 kDa enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the biosynthesis of the branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine and valine in Escherichia coli K‑12. The cloned fragment contains the ilvB structural gene together with its native promoter and regulatory region, which control transcription of the operon. Expression of ilvB is negatively regulated by leucine and valine (repression) and positively regulated by cyclic AMP and the stringent response alarmone ppGpp. The functional ilvB promoter drives transcription of the downstream tet^r gene in the cloning vector, demonstrating that the promoter is active and responsive to the same regulatory signals that modulate chromosomal ilvB expression. {PubMed:6181375}. ilvB encodes the large catalytic subunit of Escherichia coli acetohydroxyacid synthase I (AHAS I). The enzyme catalyzes the first committed step in the biosynthetic pathway for the essential branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine, leucine and valine by converting pyruvate (and/or 2‑oxobutyrate) to acetolactate (or acetohydroxybutyrate). The ilvB protein is organized into three domains (α, β and γ); the β‑domain binds the flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) cofactor, while the α‑ and γ‑domains contain the thiamine‑pyrophosphate (TPP) binding sites that together form the active site at the inter‑subunit interface. ilvB interacts with the small regulatory subunit ilvN, which binds near the FAD‑binding site in the β‑domain and also contacts the α‑domain, modulating enzyme activity and possibly influencing feedback inhibition. Overall, ilvB provides the catalytic core required for acetolactate formation in branched‑chain amino acid biosynthesis. {PubMed:18193896}. The ilvB gene encodes the promoter‑proximal (large) subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase I (AHAS I), the enzyme that catalyzes the first committed step in the biosynthetic pathway to the branched‑chain amino acids leucine and valine (formation of acetolactate from two molecules of pyruvate). It is part of an operon (ilvB‑ilvN) that together produces both the large (IlvB) and small (IlvN) subunits of AHAS I, enabling the enzyme to function in the synthesis of these essential amino acids. {PubMed:2989781}. The ilvB gene encodes acetohydroxyacid synthase I (AHAS I), the enzyme that catalyzes the first step common to the biosynthesis of the branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine and valine in Escherichia coli. The AHAS I activity is sensitive to feedback inhibition by valine (and also by leucine) and is regulated by a multivalent attenuation mechanism involving a leader peptide rich in valine and leucine codons, as well as by catabolite repression mediated through CRP‑cAMP. {PubMed:6346263}. The ilvB gene encodes the structural component of acetolactate synthase isoenzyme I (AHAS I; EC 4.1.3.18), an enzyme that catalyzes the carbon‑to‑carbon condensation step required for branched‑chain amino acid biosynthesis in Escherichia coli K12. Specifically, AHAS I synthesizes acetolactate (and acetohydroxybutyrate) from pyruvate, representing the first step in the valine pathway and the second step in the isoleucine pathway. Mutations in ilvB reduce total AHAS activity and produce an Ilv⁻ phenotype when combined with mutations in other ilv genes. {PubMed:7009323}. The ilvB gene encodes acetohydroxy acid synthase (AHAS), the enzyme that catalyzes the second reaction in the isoleucine biosynthetic pathway of Corynebacterium glutamicum. Together with ilvA (threonine dehydratase) and ilvC (isomeroreductase), ilvB provides a key, rate‑limiting step for the formation of L‑isoleucine. The gene is part of a tightly linked ilvBC cluster but is transcribed independently of ilvC. {PubMed:1551588}. The ilvB gene encodes acetohydroxy acid synthase I, the biosynthetic isozyme that catalyzes the first committed step in the synthesis of the branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine and valine in Escherichia coli K‑12. This enzyme is part of the ilvB‑encoded acetohydroxy acid synthase activity and is subject to complex regulation: it is repressed by end‑product (leucine and valine) levels, positively regulated by the alarmone ppGpp, and uniquely activated by cyclic AMP (cAMP). The cAMP effect on ilvB expression can replace the requirement for ppGpp, leading to large increases (up to ~24‑fold) in enzyme activity when cAMP is added under conditions of limited ppGpp and cAMP. Thus, ilvB provides the catalytic function for the biosynthetic pathway of branched‑chain amino acids and its expression is tightly controlled by nutritional and stress signals. {PubMed:6247617}. Encodes the large (≈60 kDa) subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase I (AHAS I). AHAS I catalyzes the first committed step in the biosynthetic pathway of the branched‑chain amino acids leucine, valine and isoleucine by condensing two molecules of pyruvate to form acetolactate (and also condensing pyruvate with 2‑ketobutyrate to form acetohydroxybutyrate). The ilvB (JW3646) gene is part of the ilvB‑ilvN operon, which together encode the two subunits (large IlvB and small IlvN) that assemble into the functional AHAS I enzyme. {PubMed:2989781}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the condensation of two molecules of pyruvate to acetolactate and of pyruvate with 2‑oxobutyrate to acetohydroxybutyrate, the first committed step in the biosynthesis of the branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine, leucine and valine. {PubMed:18193896, PubMed:2989781, PubMed:7009323, PubMed:6346263, PubMed:1551588}. Binds flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) in the β‑domain and thiamine‑pyrophosphate (TPP) in the α‑ and γ‑domains, cofactors required for catalytic activity. {PubMed:18193896}. Interacts with the small regulatory subunit IlvN, which binds near the FAD‑binding site and modulates enzyme activity and feedback inhibition. {PubMed:18193896}. Is feedback‑inhibited by the end‑products valine and leucine. {PubMed:6346263, PubMed:18193896}. Is transcriptionally repressed by leucine and valine and activated by cyclic AMP and the stringent response alarmone ppGpp, and is further controlled by catabolite repression (CRP‑cAMP) and attenuation mediated by a valine/leucine‑rich leader peptide. {PubMed:6181375, PubMed:6346263, PubMed:6247617}. Mutations reduce acetohydroxyacid synthase activity and, in combination with other ilv mutations, yield an Ilv⁻ phenotype. {PubMed:7009323}. Provides the rate‑limiting step for L‑isoleucine formation in Corynebacterium glutamicum by catalyzing the second reaction of the isoleucine biosynthetic pathway. {PubMed:1551588}.

MetaCyc_Comment: E. coli contains two different phosphoribosylglycinamide (GAR) transformylases, both of which can catalyze the third step in de novo purine biosynthesis. The transformylase encoded by purN utilizes 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate as the formyl donor. The second transformylase encoded by purT utilizes formate, which is provided by PurU-catalyzed hydrolysis of 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate |CITS: |. The existence of these two transformylase enzymes was determined by mutant studies. A strain containing a knockout insertion in purN did not result in purine auxotrophy |CITS: |. Only mutants defective in both purN and purT required exogenously added purine for growth |CITS: |. There is no significant homology between the two transformylases |CITS: |. In early work using E. coli B, 10-formyltetrahydrofolate was identified as the formyl donor for this enzyme |CITS: |. Later work using E. coli K-12 showed that the enzyme is monofunctional and catalyzes a reaction involving the transfer of a formyl group from 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate to the amino nitrogen of 5-phospho-ribosyl-glycineamide (GAR), producing 5'-phosphoribosyl-N-formylglycineamide (FGAR) and tetrahydrofolate |CITS: |. The PurN catalyzed reaction is one of two reactions in the de novo purine biosynthesis pathway that require reduced folate cofactors. The other is the |FRAME: AICARTRANSFORM-ENZRXN| activity of the bifunctional product of purH. A random sequential kinetic mechanism for PurN was proposed |CITS: |. Asp144 was identified as a functional active site residue |CITS: | and catalytically important residues Asn106, His108, Ser135 and Asp144, were also identified by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. The crystal structure of the enzyme has been solved |CITS: |. Although E. coli PurN was shown to be a monomer in solution |CITS: |, it was a dimer in the crystal structure |CITS: |. The important role of E. coli PurN in purine de novo biosynthesis has made it a model for inhibitor development |CITS: |. The human enzyme is a target for the development of antineoplastic drugs |CITS: |. A novel, engineered PurN heterodimer has been produced with activity and kinetics similar to wild-type |CITS: |. A novel, engineered hybrid PurN/PurU enzyme was also constructed and its phosphoribosylglycinamide formyltransferase (GAR transformylase) efficiency was improved by combinatorial mutagenesis |CITS: |. The subcellular location of E. coli PurN was studied using GFP-labeled protein. It was shown to be diffused throughout the cytoplasm, thus eliminating the possibility of complex formation with other pathway enzymes mediated by cytoskeletal or membrane elements |CITS: |. Review: Jensen, K.F., G. Dandanell, B. Hove-Jensen, and M. Willemoes (2008) "Nucleotides, Nucleosides and Nucleobases" EcoSal 3.6.2 |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: During de novo tetrahydrofolate biosynthesis, dihydrofolate synthetase encoded by folC catalyzes the addition of the glutamyl residue to dihydropteroate (7,8-dihydropteroate) to form dihydrofolate (7,8-dihydrofolate monoglutamate) in an ATP-dependent reaction |CITS: | (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-6614|). In E. coli FolC is a bifunctional enzyme that also catalyzes the subsequent additions of L-glutamate to tetrahydrofolate (folylpoly-γ-glutamate synthetase activity). This latter activity can also utilize the 10-formyl and methylene derivatives of tetrahydrofolate as substrate |CITS: | (see pathway |FRAME: PWY-2161|). The folC gene has been shown to be essential in E. coli because this organism lacks specific folate transporters |CITS: |. Recombinant FolC has been overexpressed as a soluble protein, purified and characterized |CITS: |. The enzyme is a member of the Mur synthetase superfamily. The crystal structure of FolC has been determined at 2.1 Å resolution and analysis of crystallographic data suggested the existence of different binding sites for dihydropteridine and tetrahydrofolate on FolC. Its dihydrofolate binding site was found to be distinct from that of Lactobacillus casei, which is a model for the human enzyme, making the E. coli enzyme a possible drug target |CITS: |. However, mutant studies have shown that dihydrofolate synthase and folylpolyglutamate synthetase activities could not be separated |CITS: |. A later mutant study showed that the amino terminal domain of FolC (residues 1-287) binds tetrahydrofolate and dihydroptroate with the same affinity as the intact enzyme |CITS: |. The antifolate drug trimethoprim is an inhibitor of |FRAME: DIHYDROFOLATEREDUCT-MONOMER| (DHFR) encoded by folA. Trimethoprim also indirectly blocks the folylpolyglutamate synthetase activity of FolC due to the accumulation of inhibitory dihydrofolate species that results from DHFR inhibition |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: The nirB gene encodes the NirB nitrite reductase, a soluble siroheme‑containing enzyme that uses NADH as an electron donor to reduce nitrite in the cytoplasm of Escherichia coli.  Expression of the nirB operon is induced during anaerobic growth and is maximally activated when extracellular nitrate or nitrite concentrations are high, i.e., when these anions exceed the cell’s capacity to consume them.  Under such conditions the NirB enzyme functions primarily in nitrite detoxification and in recycling excess NADH by oxidizing it while reducing nitrite.  Consequently, NirB synthesis is optimal in environments where nitrate or nitrite is abundant, complementing the low‑nitrate‑induced NrfA nitrite reductase. {PubMed:11004182}. The article identifies nirB as the structural gene encoding the 88 kDa apoprotein of the NADH‑dependent nitrite reductase (nitrite oxidoreductase, EC 1.6.6.4). This enzyme catalyzes the reduction of nitrite to ammonia using NADH as electron donor and is the major contributor to anaerobic nitrite reduction in Escherichia coli. Mutations in nirB abolish NADH‑dependent nitrite reductase activity while leaving other reductases (e.g., NADPH‑dependent sulphite reductase, formate hydrogenlyase) and cytochrome c₅₅₂ synthesis unaffected, indicating that nirB specifically provides the protein component required for the NADH‑dependent nitrite reduction pathway. {PubMed:3906030}. The nirB gene encodes the structural component of the NADH‑dependent nitrite reductase enzyme in Escherichia coli. It is responsible for producing the 88 kDa nitrite reductase apoprotein that catalyzes the rapid reduction of nitrite to ammonia during anaerobic growth, using NADH as an electron donor. The enzyme contains the prosthetic group sirohaem, which is also required for NADPH‑dependent sulphite reductase activity. Overexpression of nirB leads to a marked increase in nitrite reductase activity and associated NAD⁺‑stimulated cytochrome c reductase activity, confirming its role as the essential structural gene for this enzymatic function. {PubMed:2993824}. The nirB gene encodes the NADH‑dependent nitrite reductase, the first gene of the nir operon in Escherichia coli. Its promoter (the nirB promoter) is naturally induced under anaerobic conditions and is up‑regulated by the presence of nitrite or nitrate. Transcriptional activation requires the FNR (fumarate and nitrate reductase regulatory) protein binding sites at –30 and –52 relative to the transcription start site, as well as additional regulatory elements such as NarL and NarP binding sites. The enzyme catalyzes the reduction of nitrite using NADH as an electron donor, playing a key role in anaerobic nitrate/nitrite respiration. {PubMed:25368804}. In the article, nirB refers to an anaerobically‑induced promoter derived from the native nirB gene. This promoter is activated under anaerobic conditions and was employed to drive the expression of the heterologous genes raiP, kivD, and padA in engineered Escherichia coli. By using the nirB promoter, the authors achieved high‑level, cost‑effective production of 5‑aminovalerate without the need for expensive exogenous inducers such as IPTG. {PubMed:33751934}. The nirB gene encodes the apoprotein of the NADH‑dependent nitrite reductase, the structural component of the major nitrite reductase activity in Escherichia coli. The NirB protein binds several prosthetic groups—FAD, an iron‑sulfur cluster (likely a [4Fe‑4S] type associated with Cys‑Xaa‑Xaa‑Cys repeats), and sirohaem—and together with the sirohaem‑synthesizing product of cysG catalyzes the reduction of nitrite to ammonia using NADH as electron donor. {PubMed:2200672}. The nirB gene (identical to cysG) encodes an enzyme required for the synthesis of sirohaem, a prosthetic group essential for the six‑electron reduction reactions catalyzed by NADH‑dependent nitrite reductase (nitrite → ammonia) and NADPH‑dependent sulphite reductase (sulphite → sulfide). Consequently, nirB is necessary for functional nitrite reductase activity and for normal sulphite reduction, and its loss leads to loss of NADH‑dependent nitrite reductase activity, slow nitrite reduction, and cysteine auxotrophy. {PubMed:6262434}. The nirB gene encodes the structural apoprotein of the NADH‑dependent nitrite reductase enzyme complex in Escherichia coli. This enzyme catalyzes the reduction of nitrite to ammonia, providing the primary pathway for nitrite detoxification under anaerobic conditions. nirB transcription is strictly anaerobic, requiring the transcriptional activator Fnr, and is further up‑regulated by the presence of nitrite. It is the first gene of the nirB operon, which also includes downstream genes (nirD, nirE, nirC, and cysG) that are co‑transcribed from the same promoter. {PubMed:2200673}. The nirB gene encodes the NADH‑dependent nitrite reductase (EC 1.6.6.4), an enzyme that reduces nitrite during anaerobic growth. Its transcription is induced by anaerobiosis via the FNR regulatory protein and is further enhanced by the presence of nitrite, requiring separate promoter regions for the FNR‑dependent response (between –54 and –30) and the nitrite‑mediated response (between –87 and –149). {PubMed:2845227}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the reduction of nitrite to ammonia using NADH (EC 1.6.6.4). {PubMed:3906030, PubMed:2993824, PubMed:11004182, PubMed:2200672}. Binds the prosthetic groups sirohaem, FAD and an iron‑sulfur cluster ([4Fe‑4S]), which are required for activity. {PubMed:2200672}. Provides the primary pathway for anaerobic nitrite detoxification and recycles excess NADH under nitrate or nitrite‑rich conditions. {PubMed:11004182, PubMed:3906030}. Is required for synthesis of sirohaem, a cofactor essential for both NADH‑dependent nitrite reductase and NADPH‑dependent sulfite reductase; loss leads to loss of nitrite reductase activity, slow nitrite reduction and cysteine auxotrophy. {PubMed:6262434, PubMed:2200672}. Is transcriptionally induced under anaerobic conditions; expression requires the FNR regulator and NarL/NarP binding sites, with distinct promoter regions mediating FNR‑dependent and nitrite‑responsive activation. {PubMed:25368804, PubMed:2200673, PubMed:2845227}. Overexpression markedly increases nitrite reductase activity and NAD⁺‑stimulated cytochrome c reductase activity. {PubMed:2993824}. Its promoter drives strong anaerobic expression of heterologous genes without the need for exogenous inducers. {PubMed:33751934}.

MetaCyc_Comment: L-ribulose 5-phosphate 4-epimerase catalyzes the third step in the pathway for degradation of L-arabinose, the epimerization at the C4 carbon to form D-xylulose-5-phosphate, which enters the |FRAME: NONOXIPENT-PWY|. The enzyme catalyzes epimerization via a carbon-carbon bond cleavage analogous to a class II aldolase reaction |CITS: |. The H97N and other mutants can catalyze an aldolase reaction |CITS: |. The binding site for Zn2+, the physiological metal cofactor, has been identified by sequence similarity and mutagenesis |CITS: | as well as in the crystal structure |CITS: |. Mutagenesis of the predicted phosphate-binding pocket results in a significant increase in Km, and Asp120 was identified as one of two key catalytic acid/base residues |CITS: |. The enzyme was crystallized |CITS: |, and crystal structures of the wild type |CITS: | and a mutant enzyme |CITS: | have been solved. Consistent with its aldolase-type reaction mechanism, the structure shows close overall similarity to that of L-fuculose-1-phosphate aldolase |CITS: |. (Note: Several of the recent studies, including crystallization of the enzyme, appear to be using the enzyme from E. coli B/r UP1000 (gene originally cloned by |CITS: |) |CITS: |.) Most studies of the enzyme and its genetics were done in E. coli B/r. Earlier studies of the enzyme from E. coli B/r described its purification |CITS: |, its catalytic mechanism |CITS: | and summarized its properties |CITS: |.
