MetaCyc_Comment: UDP-N-acetylglucosamine enolpyruvoyl transferase (MurA) catalyzes the first committed step in the assembly of peptidoglycan |CITS: |. In exponentially growing cells, the intracellular concentration of UDP-N-acetylglucosamine is approximately 100 µM, while the concentration of the MurA product, UDP-N-acetylglucosamine enolpyruvate is only 2 µM |CITS: |. MurA activity is feedback-inhibited by UDP-MurNAc, the product of the second enzyme in the |FRAME: PWY-6387| pathway |CITS: |. The reaction mechanism of the enzyme has been investigated. A tetrahedral adduct can be formed at the active site of the enzyme during catalyis |CITS: |. However, covalent enzyme adduct formation is not required for catalysis |CITS: |. The stereochemical course of the reaction has been investigated |CITS: |. Catalysis involves conformational transitions within the enzyme |CITS: |. MurA is the site of action for the antibiotic fosfomycin. Inactivation of MurA is dependent on the presence of the substrate UDP-GlcNAc |CITS: |. The antibiotic covalently binds to the active site nucleophile Cys115 of the enzyme |CITS: |. A C115D mutant is active, but resistant to fosfomycin |CITS: |. Overexpression of MurA increases resistance to fosfomycin |CITS: |; it is the only chromosomally encoded protein whose overexpression yields fosfomycin resistance |CITS: |. A murA mutant with increased resistance to fosfomycin was identified |CITS: |; the temperature-sensitive phenotype of that mutant may be unrelated to the murA mutation |CITS: |. Novel inhibitors of MurA activity have been sought and investigated |CITS: |. MurA is also the primary physiological target of the nonnatural toxin bromoacetate |CITS: |. Crystal structures of wild-type and mutant MurA in various complexes have been solved |CITS: |. Reinterpretation of existing crystal structure data suggests that under physiological conditions, MurA exists in a dormant complex containing UDP-N-acetylmuramic acid (UNAM) and the covalent PEP adduct at Cys115 |CITS: |. murA is an essential gene |CITS: |. A strain containing a conditionally lethal amber mutation in murA has been generated |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminase (NagB) catalyzes the second cytoplasmic reaction in the metabolism of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine. The deamination of glucosamine-6-phosphate generates ammonia and fructose-6-phosphate, which can enter glycolysis directly. Both N-acetylglucosamine and glucosamine can serve as the sole source of carbon for E. coli. Utilization of several amino sugars as carbon sources converges on NagB; additionally, NagB activity needs to be regulated to avoid a futile cycle with |FRAME: L-GLN-FRUCT-6-P-AMINOTRANS-MONOMER GlmS|. It is therefore not surprising that a number of regulators have been identified to date. The first to be identified was the compound N-acetyl-D-glucosamine-6-phosphate (GlcNAc6P), which allosterically activates NagB |CITS: |. Both substrate binding and the allosteric transition are entropy-driven processes |CITS: |. However, the growth rate on glucosamine is limited by the supply of substrate to NagB rather than the absence of GlcNAc6P |CITS: |. Replacement of NagB with an orthologous enzyme that is not allosterically regulated has surprisingly little effect on the growth rate or fitness of E. coli; therefore, the physiological role of allosteric regulation of NagB activity is still unclear |CITS: |. Recently, several enzymes of central metabolism were found to regulate NagB activity. Unphosphorylated |FRAME: PTSH-MONOMER| is an allosteric activator of NagB. The specific amino acid residues involved in the interaction have been modeled |CITS: |. Additional allosteric activators are |FRAME: NANE-MONOMER NanE| and |FRAME: URIDYLYL-PII|. The HPr+U-PII and HPr+NanE pairs appear to have synergistic effects on NagB, and modeling of their binding sites suggest that they can interact with NagB simultaneously |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme have been solved |CITS: |. The enzyme is a trimer of dimers that are linked by an interchain disulfide bridge |CITS: |. Extensive site-directed mutagenesis and analysis of the mutant enzymes has allowed identification of residues that play roles in catalysis, coupling binding in the active site to the allosteric pocket, and binding of the allosteric effector N-acetyl-D-glucosamine-6-phosphate |CITS: |. A fluorescently labelled derivative allowed monitoring of the allosteric transition of the enzyme |CITS: |. Nanoencapsulation, which keeps NagB in the T quaternary conformation, was used to study the allosteric activation process. The results are consistent with the Tertiary Two-States model |CITS: |. nagB mutants are unable to grow on N-acetylglucosamine as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: |. Several point mutants that affect N-acetyl-D-glucosamine-6-phosphate binding, the active site, and the active site lid in vitro were tested for their effect on the growth rate with glucosamine or N-acetylglucosamine as the source of carbon and energy in vivo |CITS: |. Overexpression of nagB can suppress the defect of a glmS mutant, showing that glucosamine-6-phosphate deaminase can act in the biosynthetic direction, supplying glucosamine-6-phosphate for the synthesis of UDP-GlcNAc. To avoid a futile cycle, proper regulation of both enzymes is thus essential |CITS: |, and it has been hypothesized that allosteric activation of NagB by N-acetyl-D-glucosamine-6-phosphate plays this role |CITS: |. NagB: "N-acetylglucosamine" |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: The MntH protein is a member of the natural resistance-associated macrophage proteins (NRAMP) family of metal ion transporters. The protein has 11 putative membrane spanning alpha helices. This permease is involved in the uptake of Metal2+. Uptake of Mn2+ is mediated by a high affinity proton symport reaction. The permease also transports Fe2+ at a lower affinity. Mutation of five of the six acidic residues in MntH, Asp-34, Glu-102, Asp-109, Glu-112, and Asp-238, shows they are important for function of the protein. The lack of function of the protein upon mutation of the residues in the DPGN signature sequence of the Nramp family suggests that these helix-breaking residues form a binding pocket for Mn2+ transport |CITS: |. Manganese can help protect cells against oxidative stress. E. coli strains that lack catalases and peroxidases (Hpx-) accumulate intracellular H2O2 to toxic levels and activate expression of the OxyR regulon. Hpx-ΔmntH strains show profound growth defects which can be suppressed by manganese supplementation |CITS: |. Hpx-ΔmntH cells do not degrade H2O2 any more rapidly than Hpx- mntH+ cells and manganese does not prevent H2O2 accumulation by Hpx- and Hpx-ΔmntH cells |CITS: |. This suggests that the protective effect of manganese is not related to its chemical ability to scavenge H2O2 and superoxide.

Preferentially hydrolyzes diadenosine penta-phosphate with ATP as one of the reaction products (PubMed:11479323). Also able to hydrolyze diadenosine hexa- and tetra-phosphate (PubMed:11479323). Has no activity on diadenosine tri-phosphate, ADP-ribose, NADH and UDP-glucose (PubMed:11479323). In an RNase PH (rph) wild-type strain background, RppH is not required for maturation of tRNAs; however, strains with the truncated rph allele (for example K12 W1485 and its derivatives MG1655 and W3110) require RppH for maturation of certain monocistronic tRNAs with short (<5 nucleotides) leader sequences (PubMed:28808133). MetaCyc_Comment: Pyridoxine 5'-phosphate synthase (PdxJ) is one of the key enzymes in de novo pyridoxine 5'-phosphate synthesis. It catalyzes a complicated ring-closure reaction involving the condensation of 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate (DXP) and 3-amino-1-hydroxyacetone 1-phosphate to form pyridoxine 5'-phosphate (PNP) |CITS: |. Crystal structures of PdxJ have been solved |CITS: |. The enzyme is an octamer in solution |CITS: |. The octamer is organized as a tetramer of active dimers; each monomer consists of a (β/α)8 TIM barrel domain. Structures of enzyme/substrate and enzyme/product complexes allowed localization of the active site within a deep cavity which is closed in the presence of the product |CITS: |. Each subunit of the octamer has a unique conformation that is correlated with the occupancy of the active site. The substrate-binding sites are located at the interface of two subunits |CITS: |. A reaction mechanism involving Schiff base formation, water elimination and addition, phosphate elimination, ring closure, and various proton shifts has been proposed |CITS: |. The open state accepts substrates and releases products, while most of the catalytic events occur in the closed state. Glu72 appears to be the central acid-base catalyst of the enzyme |CITS: |. A Mini-Tn10 insertion mutant within pdxJ requires pyridoxine for growth |CITS: |. acpS, encoded downstream of pdxJ in the same operon, is essential for viability |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Phosphoglycerate kinase encoded by gene pgk catalyzes the reversible phosphorylation of 3-phospho-D-glycerate to 1,3-bisphospho-D-glycerate during glycolysis and gluconeogenesis in E. coli. In the glycolytic reaction direction the enzyme catalyzes the transfer of a phosphoryl group from 1,3-bisphospho-D-glycerate to ADP, forming ATP and 3-phospho-D-glycerate. Pgk cDNAs from a variety of organisms have been isolated. Their protein products are all monomers of similar size, with similar tertiary structures |CITS: |. The amino acid sequence of the E. coli enzyme is highly homologous to that of eukaryotes |CITS: |. Part of gene pgk showed similarity to an ORF found in the enterobacterial fish pathogen Edwardsiella ictaluri |CITS: |. The gene order around pgk in the Enterobacteriaceae differs from that in most other bacteria and transcriptional regulation of the E. coli epd-pgk-fbaA region has been studied |CITS: |. In earlier work, phosphoglycerate kinase was purified to near homogeneity from cell extracts of E. coli K-12. When assayed in the reverse direction its activity was dependent upon the presence of ATP and 3-phospho-D-glycerate |CITS:|. A pgk mutant cannot grow on sugars or gluconeogenic substrates |CITS: |. A mapping study using transductional crosses determined a gene order in the pgk region |CITS:|. Pgk synthesis was shown to be induced over 10-fold during the transition from exponential to stationary growth phase. The position of the protein on two-dimensional gels indicated that it is one of the proteins induced by anaerobiosis |CITS:|. The crystal structure of E. coli K-12 Pgk has been determined at 2.40 Å resolution and compared with that of yeast. Both enzymes have very similar tertiary structures and measured global stabilities. Although E. coli Pgk shows 39% homology and 56% similarity with that of yeast, the E. coli enzyme is more resistant to proteolysis. Pgk consists of N and C domains that are connected by an α-helical linker. Biophysical studies suggested that cooperativity between the N and C domains of E. coli Pgk results in more rigidity and is the basis of the increased stability |CITS: |. A novel use of the N-domain of E. coli Pgk as a fusion partner to express heterologous proteins that are prone to aggregation has also been reported |CITS: |. A series of vectors inducibly expressing paired-terminus antisense RNAs was constructed to silence central carbon metabolism in host E. coli K-12 MG1655. A vector that silenced pgk at 79% efficacy did not cause severe growth inhibition, possibly due to residual activity |CITS: |. Co-overexpression of several genes including pgk in an engineered E. coli strain was a strategy for improving polyhydroxybutyrate production in an E. coli host |CITS: |.

Fatty acids that are endogenously synthesized are attached to ACP and exogenously added fatty acids are attached to CoA |CITS: 6355102|. In E. coli phospholipids the sn 1 position is occupied mainly by either palmitate, or cis-vaccenate, whereas the sn 2 position is predominantly palmitoleate, or cis-vaccenate. This is thought to result from the substrate preferences of the PlsB and PlsC enzymes |CITS: |. The plsB gene has been shown to be regulated by stress response regulators such as |FRAME: RPOE-MONOMER| and |FRAME: GUANOSINE-5DP-3DP| |CITS: |. PlsB is part of a protein network for phospholipid synthesis and interacts with |FRAME: ACP| (ACP), |FRAME: EG11110-MONOMER| (YbgC) and |FRAME: PHOSPHASERSYN-MONOMER| (PssA) to form a complex at the cytoplasmic side of the inner membrane |CITS: |. plsB is essential for growth |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis and chemical modification studies have demonstrated catalytically important amino acid residues in PlsB, including an invariant histidine residue that is essential for catalysis |CITS: |. Genetic studies have identified the plsB locus as involved in the formation of multidrug tolerant persister cells |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (PyrD) catalyzes the oxidation of dihydroorotate to orotate in the pathway for de novo biosynthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides. PyrD is a member of the membrane-associated family 2 dihydroorotate dehydrogenases and is linked with the electron transport system of the cell. When purified away from the membrane, the enzyme can be assayed as a dehydrogenase, using various quinones as well as ferricyanide or 2,6-dichlorophenolindolphenol (DCIP) as electron acceptors |CITS: |. There is evidence that the physiological electron acceptor is ubiquinone under aerobic conditions and menaquinone under anaerobic conditions |CITS: |. The enzyme works by a two-site ping-pong mechanism |CITS: |. The catalytically competent intermediate is the reduced enzyme - orotate complex |CITS: |. A reaction model for the first half reaction, flavin reduction, has been proposed |CITS: |. The available evidence is consistent with a stepwise mechanism of flavin reduction |CITS: |. The role of conserved residues near the active site has been investigated by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. A crystal structure of PyrD has been solved at 2.5 Å resolution. The structure shows the enzyme in monomeric form |CITS: |; it is thought that the soluble purified enzyme is a multimer due to the lack of its normal hydrophobic interactions with the membrane. The interaction of PyrD with phospholipid vesicles has been studied |CITS: |.

Merged_Functions: The b3185 gene encodes ObgE, an evolutionarily conserved essential small GTPase that functions primarily in ribosome biogenesis. ObgE binds to the ribosome and acts as an anti‑association factor, preventing premature joining of the 30S and 50S subunits by mimicking a tRNA in the peptidyl‑transferase centre. It also binds the alarmone ppGpp, linking its activity to the stringent response. Although the article notes additional phenotypes associated with obgE mutants—such as effects on chromosome segregation, cell division, resistance to DNA damage, persister formation and antibiotic tolerance—its core function described here is to assist proper assembly of the 50S ribosomal subunit and to coordinate its expression with that of ribosomal proteins L21 (rplU) and L27 (rpmA) as part of a polycistronic operon. Expression of b3185 is growth‑phase dependent and is indirectly regulated by ppGpp and DksA. {PubMed:27137500}. The article describes an open reading frame (ORF2) located downstream of the ribosomal protein genes rplU and rpmA. This ORF encodes a ~35 kDa polypeptide whose deduced amino‑acid sequence shows significant similarity to prenyltransferases and to prephytoene‑pyrophosphate dehydrogenase (CrtE), enzymes that participate in carotenoid biosynthesis and other isoprenoid pathways. The authors tentatively name this gene “cel” (crtE‑like) and suggest that it may function as a prenyltransferase involved in the synthesis of isoprenoid compounds, although its exact biochemical role in *E. coli* has not been experimentally confirmed. {PubMed:8312607}. The rpmA gene encodes the 50S ribosomal protein L27, a component of the large ribosomal subunit in Escherichia coli. It is co‑transcribed with the upstream rplU gene (encoding ribosomal protein L21) and downstream genes yhbE and obgE as part of the rplU‑rpmA‑yhbE‑obgE operon. Expression of rpmA follows the typical pattern of ribosomal protein genes: it is highest during exponential growth and sharply declines as cells enter stationary phase. A transcriptional terminator located between rpmA and yhbE attenuates read‑through, limiting the amount of rpmA‑derived transcript that continues to downstream genes. Thus, rpmA contributes to ribosome biogenesis by providing the L27 protein required for proper assembly and function of the 50S subunit. {PubMed:27137500}. The rpmA gene encodes the ribosomal protein L27, a component of the 50S subunit of the Escherichia coli ribosome. It is co‑located with rplU (encoding L21) in an operon and is transcribed together with rplU. The L27 protein contributes to the structure and function of the ribosome during protein synthesis, but evidence in the article suggests it does not act as a regulatory protein for its own synthesis. {PubMed:8312607}. The rpmA gene encodes the bacterial ribosomal protein L21, a component of the 50S ribosomal subunit. L21 is bacteria‑specific and has been reported to interact with 23S rRNA, suggesting a role in ribosome assembly or function, although its precise functional importance remains poorly understood. {PubMed:27381917}. The rpmA gene encodes the 50S ribosomal subunit protein L27. L27 is a small, highly basic protein that resides near the base of the central protuberance of the 50S subunit, in the vicinity of the peptidyl‑transferase center. It is required for proper assembly of the large ribosomal subunit; loss of rpmA leads to accumulation of a 40S precursor lacking several other proteins (L16, L20, L21) and severely perturbs 50S formation. In addition, L27 is essential for full peptidyl‑transferase activity and for correct binding of aminoacyl‑tRNA to the A site, likely by directly participating in the catalytic center. Complementation of an rpmA deletion mutant with either the native E. coli rpmA or a homologous rpmA from Aquifex aeolicus restores growth and ribosomal function, although the heterologous protein does not aid assembly. Thus, rpmA’s primary function is to produce L27, a ribosomal protein critical for 50S subunit assembly and for the catalytic activity of the ribosome during protein synthesis. {PubMed:11673426}. The rpmA gene encodes ribosomal protein L27, a small basic protein of the Escherichia coli 50 S ribosomal subunit. L27 is located at the base of the central protuberance near the peptidyl‑transferase center (PTC) and interacts closely with domain V of the 23 S rRNA. It plays two major roles: (1) it is required for efficient in vivo assembly of the 50 S subunit, acting early enough to influence the incorporation of other large‑subunit proteins such as L16, L20 and L21; loss of rpmA leads to accumulation of a 40 S precursor lacking these proteins and slows cell growth. (2) L27 contributes directly to the catalytic activity of the PTC by facilitating proper positioning of the 3′‑terminal adenosine of A‑site aminoacyl‑tRNA, thereby enhancing EF‑Tu‑dependent tRNA binding and accelerating peptide‑bond formation. Deletion of rpmA reduces the affinity of aminoacyl‑tRNA for the A site, lowers peptidyl‑transferase activity (3–4‑fold), and impairs puromycin reactivity, while P‑site binding of peptidyl‑tRNA remains largely unaffected. Thus, rpmA/L27 is essential for both the structural maturation of the large ribosomal subunit and the functional efficiency of translation. {PubMed:9677420}. The rpmA gene encodes the 50S ribosomal protein L27, a component of the bacterial large ribosomal subunit that is located near the peptidyl‑transferase center. Its N‑terminal region stabilizes A‑site tRNAs during peptide‑bond formation, thereby contributing to efficient translation. In the context of this study, mutations in rpmA (e.g., G23A) impair the formation of peptide bonds, particularly affecting the translation of the proline‑rich leader peptide mgtL. This reduced efficiency of mgtL translation leads to altered folding of the mgtA 5' leader RNA and derepression of mgtA transcription, demonstrating that RpmA/L27 plays a critical role in coupling Mg²⁺‑dependent translation dynamics to transcriptional regulation of the mgtA Mg²⁺ transporter. {PubMed:27849575}.

Is a putative prenyltransferase likely involved in the biosynthesis of isoprenoid compounds such as carotenoids. {PubMed:8312607}. Merged_Functions: The rpmB gene encodes ribosomal protein L28, a component of the 50S subunit of the Escherichia coli ribosome. The article reports that the nucleotide sequence of rpmB yields an amino‑acid sequence identical to the previously characterized L28 protein, confirming its identity as a translation‑associated ribosomal protein. As part of the ribosome, L28 contributes to ribosome assembly and the overall process of protein synthesis. {PubMed:7035835}. The rpmB gene is part of the rpmB‑G operon and encodes ribosomal protein L28, a component of the large (50S) ribosomal subunit in Escherichia coli. L28 is required for normal ribosome assembly: loss of rpmB (and thus L28) prevents formation of complete 70S ribosomes, leading to accumulation of precursor particles such as '30S material' and '47S particles'. Supplying L28 from a plasmid restores normal growth, ribosome synthesis kinetics, and coordination of ribosomal protein production, indicating that L28 plays a crucial role in the proper assembly of the 50S subunit and overall ribosome biogenesis. {PubMed:9294008}. The rpmB gene encodes the ribosomal protein L28, a bacteria‑specific component of the 50S ribosomal subunit. L28 is essential for proper ribosome assembly: loss of rpmB results in a severe reduction of 70S ribosomes and accumulation of immature 30S and 47S particles, which can be rescued by supplying L28 in trans. The rpmB gene is part of the rpmB‑rpmG operon (L28‑L33) whose transcription is down‑regulated by the ppGpp/DksA‑mediated stringent response during amino‑acid starvation, but the operon does not exhibit autogenous translational feedback regulation. {PubMed:27381917}. The rpmB gene is the first gene of the rpmB,G operon in Escherichia coli and encodes the ribosomal protein L28. L28 is a component of the 50S ribosomal subunit and participates in the normal assembly of ribosomes. The article reports that the rpmB,G operon produces the ribosomal proteins L28 (from rpmB) and L33 (from rpmG). Mutations that reduce or eliminate translation of rpmB (e.g., insertion of IS1 into rpmB or a Shine‑Dalgarno mutation) lower the synthesis of L28, which in turn perturbs ribosome assembly, leading to accumulation of abnormal precursor particles (47S) and altered RNA content. Thus, rpmB’s primary function is to provide the structural protein L28 required for proper 50S subunit formation and efficient ribosome biogenesis. {PubMed:7685806}. Encodes ribosomal protein L28, a constituent of the 50S ribosomal subunit. The article shows that L28 is essential for ribosome assembly in vivo: loss of rpmB (and thus L28) prevents the conversion of 30S material and 47S precursor particles into mature 70S ribosomes, causing linear rather than exponential growth and accumulation of RNA. Supplying L28 from a plasmid restores normal 70S ribosome formation, exponential growth, and normal rates of RNA and protein synthesis. Therefore, rpmB’s product is required for proper assembly of the large ribosomal subunit and for functional protein synthesis. {PubMed:9044258}. The rpmB gene encodes ribosomal protein L28, a structural component of the 50S large ribosomal subunit in Escherichia coli. It is one of the ribosomal proteins required for proper ribosome assembly and function in protein synthesis. The article confirms that mutations affecting L28 map to rpmB, establishing it as the structural gene for this ribosomal protein. {PubMed:6450866}. Encodes ribosomal protein L28, the product of the promoter‑proximal rpmB gene in the rpmB,G operon. L28 is a component of the 50S ribosomal subunit and participates in the normal assembly of ribosomes in Escherichia coli. The article describes that the rpmB,G operon synthesizes ribosomal proteins L28 and L33, and that mutations affecting rpmB (such as insertion of IS1 or alteration of the Shine‑Dalgarno sequence) reduce L28 production and lead to defects in ribosome assembly, indicating L28’s essential role in forming functional 50S subunits. {PubMed:7685806}.

Merged_Functions: The rpmF gene encodes the ribosomal protein L32, a component of the 50S ribosomal subunit in Escherichia coli. It is located near the pyrC locus (23.4 min) and forms an operon with the downstream g30k gene, which encodes a 30‑kilodalton protein of unknown function. Transcription of the rpmF‑g30k operon yields multiple mRNA species, with the most abundant transcripts initiating at promoter P2 and extending through rpmF. Because rpmF is situated far from the origin of replication, its promoter or translation efficiency appears to be higher than those of other ribosomal protein genes to maintain the required stoichiometry of one L32 molecule per ribosome. {PubMed:2477362}. The rpmF gene encodes the ribosomal protein L32, a structural component of the Escherichia coli ribosome. It is the structural gene whose product (L32) is part of the ribosomal protein complement, and mutations in rpmF result in an altered L32 protein. The gene is located near pyrC and purB on the chromosome, and it is the ribosomal protein gene situated farthest from the origin of replication (oriC), suggesting a lower gene dosage that may require a more efficient promoter for adequate expression. {PubMed:3911025}. The rpmF gene encodes ribosomal protein L32, a component of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit. In the context of the article, rpmF is part of an operon that is cotranscribed with the plsX and several fatty‑acid biosynthetic (fab) genes, suggesting a coordinated regulation of ribosome production and membrane lipid synthesis. {PubMed:7635191}. Encodes ribosomal protein L32, a component of the bacterial ribosome (50S subunit), as identified in the rpmF‑plsX‑fabH gene cluster of Rhodobacter capsulatus. {PubMed:8020746}. The gene encodes the PlsX protein, which participates in membrane lipid synthesis in Escherichia coli. Although its precise biochemical role is not defined, PlsX is required—together with a defective plsB allele—for the manifestation of a glycerol‑3‑phosphate‑auxotrophic phenotype, indicating its involvement in the pathway that supplies glycerol‑3‑phosphate or related lipid intermediates. {PubMed:1447160}.

Merged_Functions: RpmG is a small 53‑amino‑acid protein traditionally annotated as the ribosomal protein L33, but its deletion does not affect ribosome function. In this study, over‑expression of rpmG conferred resistance to the DNA‑crosslinking agent mitomycin C (MMC) in an E. coli ΔruvAB background. This MMC‑resistance phenotype was completely dependent on the presence of the DNA‑glycosylase MutM, which resides in the same operon (yicR‑rpmB‑rpmG‑mutM). Deletions of the neighboring genes yicR or rpmB did not affect the phenotype, indicating that RpmG specifically requires MutM to promote MMC resistance. The authors propose that RpmG acts in a non‑catalytic, extra‑ribosomal capacity, likely by physically interacting with MutM and stimulating its activity during base‑excision repair of MMC‑induced lesions. {PubMed:26704888}. The rpmG gene encodes ribosomal protein L33, a component of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit. It is co‑transcribed with the upstream rpmB (L28) gene in a single operon, and its expression depends on the promoter and 5' sequences of rpmB. As a ribosomal protein, L33 contributes to ribosome structure and function in protein synthesis. {PubMed:7035835}. The rpmG gene encodes the bacterial‑specific ribosomal protein L33, which is a component of the 50S ribosomal subunit. According to the article, L33 has a redundant role in ribosome synthesis and function, as deletion of rpmG does not affect the growth rate of Escherichia coli. The gene is part of the rpmB‑rpmG operon (encoding L28 and L33), and unlike L28, L33 is not essential for ribosome assembly. Additionally, the operon containing rpmG is not subject to autogenous translational feedback regulation. {PubMed:27381917}. The article identifies rpmG as the structural gene encoding ribosomal protein L33. Mutations in rpmG (e.g., in strain JE704) alter the L33 protein, confirming that rpmG directs synthesis of this ribosomal component, which is part of the 50S ribosomal subunit and required for normal ribosome function. {PubMed:6450866}. The rpmG gene encodes ribosomal protein L33, a component of the 50S large ribosomal subunit in Escherichia coli.  Experimental analysis of strains lacking rpmG (and thus L33) showed that the absence of L33 does not impair ribosome assembly kinetics, 70S ribosome formation, or cellular growth rates when protein L28 (encoded by rpmB) is present.  Consequently, L33 appears to be non‑essential for ribosome synthesis and function under the conditions examined, suggesting a redundant or dispensable role in vivo. {PubMed:9044258}. The rpmG gene encodes ribosomal protein L33, a component of the large (50S) ribosomal subunit in Escherichia coli. L33 is part of the rpmB,G operon that also encodes L28. Experimental evidence in the article shows that loss of L33 (e.g., in strain BM108) does not impair ribosome assembly or function when L28 is supplied, suggesting that L33 is not essential for ribosome synthesis under the tested conditions and may be functionally redundant. However, L33 is normally present in mature 50S subunits and is deficient in abnormal 47S precursor particles that accumulate when L28 is absent. {PubMed:9294008}. The rpmG gene encodes ribosomal protein L33, a component of the 50S large ribosomal subunit in Escherichia coli. Protein L33 is produced from the rpmG portion of the rpmBG operon and, together with the upstream-encoded L28, participates in ribosome assembly. Experimental evidence in the article indicates that loss of L33 (e.g., by IS3 insertion into rpmG) has only a minor impact on ribosome assembly and function, suggesting that L33 plays a relatively modest role compared with L28. Additionally, when the rpmG mutation prevents L33 synthesis, the operon may still produce L28 and an unstable N‑terminal fragment of L33, but functional ribosomes can be assembled without full‑length L33. {PubMed:9098043}. Encodes the ribosomal large‑subunit protein L33 (RpmG), a small basic protein that is a component of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit. {PubMed:7968510}. The b3636 gene encodes YgaQ, an uncharacterized 110‑amino‑acid protein that belongs to the α‑amylase family but functions as a DNA nuclease. YgaQ exhibits nuclease activity specific for single‑stranded DNA with a 5′‑terminal end (e.g., 5′‑flap structures) and does not efficiently cleave fully base‑paired duplex DNA or 3′‑ended ssDNA. This activity depends on conserved Asp, Glu, Arg, and Lys residues; mutating these residues abolishes both nuclease activity and the ability of YgaQ to confer resistance to the DNA‑crosslinking agent mitomycin C (MMC). YgaQ‑mediated MMC resistance operates independently of homologous recombination (RecA, RuvABC) but requires the helicase UvrD, suggesting that YgaQ works together with UvrD‑generated ssDNA intermediates during DNA repair of MMC‑induced lesions. {PubMed:26704888}. The article describes b3636 as the gene rpmG, which encodes ribosomal protein L33. L33 is a small basic protein that is a structural component of the 50S subunit of the Escherichia coli ribosome. It participates in the assembly and function of the ribosome, contributing to protein synthesis. The rpmG gene is co‑transcribed with the upstream rpmB (L28) gene in a single operon (rpmBp‑rpmB‑rpmG‑rpmGt), and its expression depends on the promoter and regulatory sequences located upstream of rpmB. {PubMed:7035835}. Encodes ribosomal protein L28 (rpmB), a component of the 50S ribosomal subunit. The article demonstrates that L28 is essential for proper ribosome assembly in Escherichia coli: loss of L28 (together with L33) prevents formation of 70S ribosomes, causing accumulation of 30S material and abnormal 47S precursor particles, and leads to linear (non‑exponential) RNA and protein synthesis. Supplying L28 from a plasmid restores normal growth, ribosome assembly kinetics, and the full complement of ribosomal proteins, indicating that L28 is required for conversion of 47S particles into functional 50S subunits and for overall ribosome biogenesis. {PubMed:9044258}. The b3636 gene encodes the SecE protein, a small (≈59 aa) integral membrane component of the Sec protein translocase in Bacillus subtilis. It contains a single transmembrane helix corresponding to the C‑terminal domain of Escherichia coli SecE and is essential for cell viability. SecE participates in the SecA‑SecYEG secretion pathway, facilitating the translocation and proper processing of secretory proteins such as proOmpA. The B. subtilis SecE can complement a cold‑sensitive secE mutation in E. coli, restoring growth at restrictive temperature and normal precursor processing, confirming its functional role in protein export. {PubMed:7968510}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: The RuvA-RuvB-RuvC complex processes Holliday junction (HJ) DNA during genetic recombination and DNA repair (PubMed:21531731, PubMed:6374379). The RuvA-RuvB complex plays an important role in the rescue of blocked DNA replication forks via replication fork reversal (RFR); RFR and homologous recombination required for UV light survival can be separated (PubMed:16424908, PubMed:18942176, PubMed:21531731, PubMed:9814711). The RuvA-RuvB complex promotes Holliday junction (HJ) branch migration. RuvA binds to HJ cruciform DNA, conferring on it an open structure (PubMed:10890893, PubMed:7885479, PubMed:9628481). In the presence of RuvB, ATP and Mg(2+) the junction is dissociated; hydrolyzable (d)NTPs can replace ATP but other analogs cannot (PubMed:10772859, PubMed:10890893, PubMed:1608954, PubMed:1617728, PubMed:1833759, PubMed:7885479, PubMed:8393934, PubMed:9628481). The RuvB hexamer acts as a pump, pulling dsDNA into and through the RuvAB complex (PubMed:9078376). Can bypass UV-induced lesions (PubMed:1617728) and physically cross-linked DNA strands (PubMed:10662672). RuvA gives specificity by binding to cruciform junctions, while the RuvB ATPase provides the motor force for branch migration; excess RuvB can promote branch migration in the absence of RuvA (PubMed:10662672, PubMed:1617728). Overexpression of RuvA alone leads to UV sensitivity (PubMed:2164626). RuvA stimulates the weak ATPase activity of RuvB in the presence of DNA; the addition of HJ DNA further stimulates ATPase about 10-fold (PubMed:1435721, PubMed:1833759, PubMed:8393934). Inhibits RuvC endoDNase activity by binding to HJ DNA, including DNA to which RuvC is already bound (PubMed:9000618). Does not bind dsDNA (PubMed:11080172). May act as a collar that slides at HJ which promotes branch migration while inhibiting other DNA remodeling activities (Probable). {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00031, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10662672, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10772859, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10890893, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11080172, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1435721, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1608954, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1617728, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16424908, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1833759, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18942176, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21531731, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2164626, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6374379, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7885479, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8393934, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9000618, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9078376, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9628481, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9814711, ECO:0000305|PubMed:16324713}.; FUNCTION: An in vitro resolvase system that forms and processes HJ has been reconstituted with DNA substrates, RuvA, RuvB and RuvC. RuvA-RuvB increases the rate of strand exchange (branch migration), dissociates the RecA filament and allows RuvC to cleave in both orientations at the cruciform junction (PubMed:10421637, PubMed:9160752). HJ-RuvA-RuvB-RuvC complexes resolve Holliday junctions and also undergo branch migration, providing evidence for a coupled branch migration/HJ resolution reaction (PubMed:10421637). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10421637, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9160752}.
MetaCyc_Comment: RuvA is a structure-specific DNA binding protein which has high affinity for Holliday junctions. Together with RuvB it mediates branch migration of Holliday junctions. Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: The RuvABC complex is involved in recombinational repair of UV or chemically damaged DNA (PubMed:6374379). The complex also plays an important role in the rescue of blocked DNA replication forks via replication fork reversal (RFR); RFR and homologous recombination required for UV light survival can be separated (PubMed:16424908, PubMed:18942176, PubMed:9814711). This subunit has a weak ATPase activity that is inhibited by its ADP product; binds ADP better than ATP (PubMed:2529252). Promotes Holliday junction (HJ) branch migration in conjunction with RuvA. Binds to HJ cruciform DNA; in the presence of RuvA, ATP and Mg(2+) the junction is dissociated. Hydrolyzable (d)NTPs can replace ATP but other analogs cannot (PubMed:1608954, PubMed:1617728, PubMed:6374379, PubMed:8393934). The RuvB hexamer acts as a pump, pulling DNA into and through the RuvAB complex (PubMed:9078376). Can bypass UV-induced lesions (PubMed:1617728) and physically cross-linked DNA strands (PubMed:10662672), suggesting RuvB does not unwind large sections of DNA. RuvA gives specificity by binding to cruciform junctions, while the RuvB ATPase provides the motor force for branch migration; excess RuvB can promote branch migration in the absence of RuvA (PubMed:10662672, PubMed:1617728). In vitro the RuvA-RuvB complex has 5'-3' helicase activity that is ATP-dependent and works best on short dsDNA hybrids; 52 and 66-nucleotide (nt) pairs are easily displaced, hybrids greater than 140-nts are not (PubMed:8433990). HJ-RuvA-RuvB-RuvC complexes resolve Holliday junctions and also undergo branch migration, providing evidence for a coupled branch migration/HJ resolution reaction (PubMed:10421637). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10421637, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9160752}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: The RuvA-RuvB-RuvC complex processes Holliday junctions during genetic recombination and DNA repair (PubMed:6374379). Endonuclease that resolves Holliday junction (HJ) intermediates. Cleaves cruciform DNA by making single-stranded nicks across the junction at symmetrical positions within the homologous arms, leaving a 5'-phosphate and a 3'-hydroxyl group; requires a central core of homology in the junction (PubMed:10471285, PubMed:1661673, PubMed:1758493, PubMed:1829835, PubMed:36000732, PubMed:8001122, PubMed:8106500, PubMed:8195150, PubMed:9000618, PubMed:9135161, PubMed:9160752). The consensus cleavage sequence is 5'-(A/T)TT(C>G/A)-3'. Cleavage occurs on the 3'-side of the TT dinucleotide at the point of strand exchange, although there is some flexibility in the position cleaved (PubMed:10471285, PubMed:8001122, PubMed:8195150, PubMed:9135161). The cleavage reactions can be uncoupled; incision requires the presence of two consensus cleavage sequences, although they do not have to be identical (PubMed:9135161). The presence of a 5'-phosphate in a half-cut site accelerates cleavage of the second site, ensuring the second cleavage occurs within the lifetime of a single RuvC-HJ complex (PubMed:19399178). Binds to cruciform DNA in a sequence non-specific manner (PubMed:10471285, PubMed:8106500, PubMed:8195150). {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00034, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10471285, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1661673, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1758493, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1829835, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19399178, ECO:0000269|PubMed:36000732, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6374379, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8001122, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8106500, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8195150, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9000618, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9135161, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9160752}.; FUNCTION: An in vitro resolvase system that forms and processes HJ has been reconstituted with DNA substrates, RuvA, RuvB and RuvC. RuvA-RuvB increases the rate of strand exchange (branch migration), dissociates the RecA filament and allows RuvC to cleave in both orientations at the cruciform junction (PubMed:10421637, PubMed:9160752). HJ-RuvA-RuvB-RuvC complexes resolve Holliday junctions and also undergo branch migration, providing evidence for a coupled branch migration/HJ resolution reaction (PubMed:10421637). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10421637, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9160752}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Methionine adenosyltransferase catalyzes the formation of the sulfonium compound S-adenosylmethionine. The reaction is unusual in that the entire tripolyphosphate chain is cleaved from the ATP molecule, and is further degraded to pyrophosphate and phosphate before the products are released |CITS: |. Due to its importance, the enzyme is a target for the development of antimicrobial and anticancer compounds. The enzyme is a homotetramer in solution |CITS: |; the tetrameric form is required for activity |CITS: |. Various crystal structures of methionine adenosyltransferase have been solved. The enzyme is a dimer of dimers with active sites located at the dimer interfaces |CITS: |. A mobile loop gates access to the active site |CITS: |. Methionine adenosyltransferase requires binding of two divalent cations and one monovalent cation per subunit for full activity |CITS: |. The binding sites have been studied |CITS: |. The reaction proceeds by a sequential mechanism consistent with random binding of substrates and ordered product release |CITS: |. The catalytic mechanism and active site have been studied |CITS: |. The R244 residue plays a role in interactions with the triphosphate chain |CITS: |. A novel catalytic mechanism for SAM formation has been proposed |CITS: |. Novel inhibitors of methionine adenosyltransferase have been discovered by computational docking and were tested in vitro |CITS: |. metK is essential for growth in E. coli |CITS: |. The metK84 mutant has an altered promoter sequence |CITS: | and shows a defect in cell division |CITS: |. Further studies of recruitment of cell division proteins to the septal ring in the metK84 mutant indicate that a methylation reaction is required for complete septal ring assembly |CITS: |. Expression of methionine adenosyltransferase is regulated by MetJ |CITS: |. Transcription of metK is induced upon biofilm formation |CITS: |. |CITS: | reported the presence of two adjacent genes encoding methionine adenosyltransferase, metK and metX; however, as noted by |CITS: |, there is no evidence for the existence of metX in the sequenced genome. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the reversible interconversion of serine and glycine with tetrahydrofolate (THF) serving as the one-carbon carrier. This reaction serves as the major source of one-carbon groups required for the biosynthesis of purines, thymidylate, methionine, and other important biomolecules (PubMed:10858298, PubMed:1517215, PubMed:19883126, PubMed:3891721, PubMed:7925461). Also exhibits THF-independent aldolase activity toward beta-hydroxyamino acids, producing glycine and aldehydes, via a retro-aldol mechanism. Thus, is able to catalyze the cleavage of allothreonine and 3-phenylserine (PubMed:10858298, PubMed:1517215, PubMed:19883126, PubMed:3891721). Also catalyzes the irreversible conversion of 5,10-methenyltetrahydrofolate to 5-formyltetrahydrofolate (PubMed:10858298, PubMed:2201683). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10858298, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1517215, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19883126, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2201683, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3891721, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7925461}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (GlyA) converts serine to glycine, transferring a methyl group to tetrahydrofolate, thus forming 5,10-methylene-tetrahydrofolate (5,10-mTHF). 5,10-mTHF is the major source of C1 units in the cell, making GlyA a key enzyme in the biosynthesis of purines, thymidine, methionine, choline and lipids. The enzyme also catalyzes several side reactions including hydrolysis of 5,10-methenylTHF to 5-formylTHF |CITS: | and the reversible cleavage of 3-hydroxy amino acids (L-threonine, allothreonine, 3-phenylserine) to glycine and an aldehyde |CITS: |. D-alanine inactivates the enzyme by reacting with the pyridoxal phosphate prosthetic group to form pyridoxamine phosphate |CITS: |. The Thr226 residue within a conserved region of the enzyme appears to be involved in substrate discrimination |CITS: |. The His228 residue plays a role in determining reaction specificity |CITS: |. Lys229 does not appear to play a catalytic role |CITS: |. Arg363 appears to be the binding site for the carboxyl group of the amino acid substrate |CITS: |. The hydroxyl group of Tyr65 may be involved in the conversion of the active site from a closed to an open conformation |CITS: |. Both Tyr55 and Arg235 are required for the transaldimination reaction |CITS: |. Studies on refolding of the enzyme indicate that pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) only binds to the dimeric apoenzyme at the end of the folding pathway |CITS: |. The mechanism of PLP addition has been investigated further. At high concentrations of PLP, a second molecule of PLP can bind at Lys346 |CITS: |. A conserved hydrophobic contact area is involved in stability of the PLP binding site |CITS: |. Tyr55 is required for correct positioning of the PLP cofactor |CITS: |. Crystal structures of wild type and mutant serine hydroxymethyltransferase have been solved |CITS: |. glyA mutants can not use glycine as the sole source of nitrogen |CITS: |. A glyA mutant is auxotrophic for glycine |CITS: |; glyA was later shown to be essential for growth on glycerol minimal medium |CITS: |. Sequences 3' to the structural gene within the glyA mRNA are required for mRNA stability |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Responsible for the aerobic transport of the dicarboxylates fumarate, L- and D-malate and to a lesser extent succinate, from the periplasm across the inner membrane. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17088549}.
MetaCyc_Comment: DctA is required for dicarboxylate transport |CITS:|. DctA is a proton motive force-dependent C4-dicarboxylate transporter, responsible for the uptake of fumarate, succinate, L-aspartate and L- and D-malate under aerobic conditions, and also for the uptake of orotate, a pyrimidine precursor |CITS:|. The substrate recognition site of DctA is located on the outer surface of the inner membrane |CITS:,|. DctA and DcuB function as co-sensors with |FRAME: DCUS-MONOMER "DcuS"| - the sensor histidine kinase of the two-component system that controls the expression of genes required for C4-dicarboxylate degradation. DcuS requires the transport proteins DctA or DcuB for normal function. DctA interacts specifically with DcuS in vivo |CITS: |. DctA is predicted to contain eight transmembrane helices with the N and C-termini located in the cytoplasm. Residues important for interaction with DcuS are located in α-helix 8b |CITS: |. DctA's role in the DctA-DcuS sensor complex is not dependent on transport function - DctA mutants with uncoupled regulatory and transport function can be isolated and DctA-DcuS sensor function can be activated by substrates such as citrate that are not transported by DctA |CITS: |. Transcription of dctA is weakly controlled by the DcuSR two-component system in response to dicarboxylates |CITS:,,,,|. DcuR binds upstream of dctA |CITS:|. dctA expression increases during stationary phase |CITS:|. dctA, among other genes involved in carbon source transport and metabolism, was downregulated in two MG1655 lysogens carrying closely related Stx2a phages O104 and PA8 |CITS: 31208335|. dctA is strongly down-regulated by CRP interacting with Eσ54 and is therefore subject to catabolite repression |CITS:,,,,,|. dctA is repressed by ArcA under anaerobic conditions |CITS:|. dctA is also repressed by |FRAME: EG11889-MONOMER "DctR"| in an atp deletion strain preventing growth on C4-dicarboxylates |CITS:|. dctA is transiently induced upon cold shock |CITS:|. Mutants defective in dctA were unable to grow on fumarate or malate, showed decreased growth on succinate and were unable to utilize orotate as a pyrimidine source |CITS:,,|. These defects could be complemented by the cloned dctA gene |CITS:|. There appears to be another transporter, possibly a monocarboxylate carrier, that is able to import succinate at acidic pH in sufficient amounts for aerobic growth on succinate, but cannot exchange fumarate and succinate |CITS:|. The |FRAME: YCHM-MONOMER "DauA"| protein was characterised by |CITS: | as a succinate/fumarate/aspartate transporter active in aerobic and acidic environements. DctA is a member of the Dicarboxylate/Amino Acid:Cation Symporter (DAACS) family of transporters |CITS:|. Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Required for rescue of stalled ribosomes mediated by trans-translation. Binds to tmRNA RNA (also known as SsrA or 10Sa RNA, 363 nucleotides in this organism), required for stable binding of tmRNA to ribosomes (PubMed:10393194, PubMed:11904185, PubMed:11917023). tmRNA and SmpB together mimic tRNA shape, replacing the anticodon stem-loop with SmpB (Probable). tmRNA is encoded by the ssrA gene; the 2 termini fold to resemble tRNA(Ala) and it encodes a 'tag peptide', a short internal open reading frame. Able to recruit charged tmRNA to ribosomes (PubMed:15069072). Does not play a role in transcription, processing or Ala-aminoacylation of tmRNA (PubMed:10393194). Other studies have shown it stimulates aminoacylation of tmRNA (PubMed:11904185, PubMed:11917023). May protect tmRNA from degradation (PubMed:11917023). Binds to tmRNA that cannot be aminoacylated (tmRNA G3A), does not bind to tmRNA mutations near the tRNA-like termini (tmRNA G19C, A334U); other tmRNA mutations that block trans-translation still bind SmpB (PubMed:11917023). With tmRNA may play a role in bacterial persistence (PubMed:23812681). During trans-translation Ala-aminoacylated transfer-messenger RNA acts like a tRNA, entering the A-site of stalled ribosomes, displacing the stalled mRNA. The ribosome then switches to translate the ORF on the tmRNA, the nascent peptide is terminated with the 'tag peptide' encoded by the tmRNA and targeted for degradation. The ribosome is freed to recommence translation, which seems to be the essential function of trans-translation. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10393194, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11904185, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11917023, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15069072, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15699355, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20348441, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20940705, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22622583, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23812681, ECO:0000305|PubMed:20940705}.

FUNCTION: Succinyl-CoA synthetase functions in the citric acid cycle (TCA), coupling the hydrolysis of succinyl-CoA to the synthesis of either ATP or GTP and thus represents the only step of substrate-level phosphorylation in the TCA. The beta subunit provides nucleotide specificity of the enzyme and binds the substrate succinate, while the binding sites for coenzyme A and phosphate are found in the alpha subunit. Can use either ATP or GTP, but prefers ATP. It can also function in the other direction for anabolic purposes, and this may be particularly important for providing succinyl-CoA during anaerobic growth when the oxidative route from 2-oxoglutarate is severely repressed. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00558, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10353839}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Nucleotidase with a broad substrate specificity as it can dephosphorylate various ribo- and deoxyribonucleoside 5'-monophosphates and ribonucleoside 3'-monophosphates with highest affinity to 3'-AMP (PubMed:15489502). Also plays a significant physiological role in stress-response and is required for the survival of E.coli in stationary growth phase (PubMed:15489502). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15489502, ECO:0000303|PubMed:15489502}.

MetaCyc_Comment: UmpG (SurE) is a phosphatase with broad substrate specificity. It efficiently hydrolyzes purine and pyrimidine ribonucleotides and deoxyribonucleotides, and polyphosphate. UmpG and its homologs are widely distributed among bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes |CITS: |. The enzyme was found to participate in the degradation of "overflow" UMP nucleotides |CITS: |. UmpG hydrolyzes purine and pyrimidine ribonucleotides and deoxyribonucleotides, as well as the synthetic substrate p-nitrophenyl phosphate, with pH optima of 7.0-7.2. A divalent metal cation is required and Mn2+, Co2+, Mg2+ or Ni2+ are effective. High affinity substrates include 3'-AMP, 5'-GMP, 5'-dGMP, 5'-AMP and 3'-CMP |CITS: |. UmpG was initially thought to be involved in cell survival during stationary phase |CITS: |, but it has since been shown that the phenotype was due to the presence of an amber mutation in rpoS |CITS: |. UmpG and Pcm may act in parallel protein damage response pathways |CITS: |. A umpG umpH double mutant shows impaired growth upon addition of orotate, an intermediate in the |FRAME: PWY0-162 "pyrimidine biosynthesis pathway"|, to the growth medium. However, growth recovers, and the final culture density is higher than for wild type cells |CITS: |. Transcriptional fusions showed an RpoS-independent increase in umpG transcription during stationary phase |CITS: |. UmpG: "UMP degradation" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the base-exchange of a guanine (G) residue with the queuine precursor 7-aminomethyl-7-deazaguanine (PreQ1) at position 34 (anticodon wobble position) in tRNAs with GU(N) anticodons (tRNA-Asp, -Asn, -His and -Tyr). Catalysis occurs through a double-displacement mechanism. The nucleophile active site attacks the C1' of nucleotide 34 to detach the guanine base from the RNA, forming a covalent enzyme-RNA intermediate. The proton acceptor active site deprotonates the incoming PreQ1, allowing a nucleophilic attack on the C1' of the ribose to form the product. After dissociation, two additional enzymatic reactions on the tRNA convert PreQ1 to queuine (Q), resulting in the hypermodified nucleoside queuosine (7-(((4,5-cis-dihydroxy-2-cyclopenten-1-yl)amino)methyl)-7-deazaguanosine). {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00168, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11714265, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12909636}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Trigger factor (TF) is a ribsome-associated, ATP-independent chaperone that cooperates with downstream proteins such as |FRAME: EG10241-MONOMER DnaK| and |FRAME: CPLX0-3934 GroEL-GroES| in the folding of newly synthesized cytosolic proteins; TF also interacts with nascent secretory proteins and cooperates with the |FRAME: CPLX0-8046 SecB| chaperone to usher a subset of proteins on the post-translational secretory pathway. TF is involved in protection against copper-induced protein aggregation under anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. TF exhibits peptidyl-prolyl isomerase and protein folding activity in vitro; TF associates with ribosome bound nascent cytosolic and secretory polypeptide chains in vitro |CITS: |. Nascent polypeptides interact first with TF |CITS: | at the ribosome, where TF binds at proteins L23/L29 at the polypeptide exit site |CITS: |. TF is thought to interact primarily with short nascent chains |CITS: | and its function overlaps with that of DnaK, which interacts with longer nascent chains downstream of TF |CITS: |. Although deletion mutants of either tig or dnaK are viable, their combined deletion is lethal at temperatures above 30°C |CITS: |. Recruitment of TF occurs in vivo when the ribosome nascent-chain polypeptide is is approximately 100 amino acids in length. Premature engagement of TF (through over-expression of tig) interferes with the co-translational removal of the of the N-terminal formyl methionine residue |CITS: |. TF postpones co-translational folding in model substrates in vitro and can also unfold ribosome tethered polypeptides that have acquired their native folded state |CITS: |. TF stabilizes partially folded states and mediates folding transitions until proteins reach their native structure |CITS: |. TF has foldase activity on protein substrates under tension; at zero force TF stabilizes the unfolded state or protects the partially folded state, in the presence of force (such as that present at the ribosomal exit tunnel) TF decreases the stability of the misfolded state and increases the folding probability of a substrate construct (protein L) |CITS: |. TF is a genuine secretory pathway chaperone; it binds tightly to a subset of secretory preproteins and prevents their aggregation; TF:secretory protein complexes are targeted to the SecYEG-SecA translocase; SecB relieves the inhibitory effect of TF on pre-protein translocation |CITS: |. TF rapidly binds to and dissociates from vacant or translating ribosomes; transient complexes are strongly stabilised when the nascent peptide displays a TF binding sequence; TF and |FRAME: SRP-CPLX SRP| exhibit partial competitive binding to ribosome nascent chain complexes |CITS: |. TF affects cotranslational protein complex assembly; in an engineered E. coli strain, TF increases the specificity of interaction between a fully synthesized subunit encoded by the upstream gene, and a nascent subunit encoded by the downstream gene, of an operon |CITS: |. TF cycles between a dimeric form when free in solution and a conformationally activated monomer induced by ribosome binding; TF may remain bound to substrate proteins post-translationally |CITS: |. TF substrates have been identified by TF copurification and TF resolvable aggregation. Many of the substrates are subunits of multimeric complexes including many ribosomal proteins and a role for TF in the biogenesis of protein complexes has been suggested |CITS: |. Selective ribosome profiling suggests that nascent outer membrane proteins (OMPs) are preferential TF targets in vivo. Consistent with this Δtig cells have decreased OMP levels and phenotypes that are consistent with disrupted outer membrane integrity |CITS: |. Secretory proteins may be directed into a Sec-mediated post-translational pathway by means of their preferential interaction with TF |CITS: |. TF consists of three domains |CITS: | all of which interact with the nascent polypeptide during translation |CITS: |. The N-terminal domain contains the TF signature motif which mediates ribosome binding |CITS: |. The middle domain displays peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerase (PPIase) activity |CITS: | and is dispensable for the chaperone activity of TF in vitro and in vivo |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain is essential for chaperone activity |CITS: |. Three TF molecules are required to bind unfolded alkaline phosphatase (PhoA) in vitro. The 3 TF molecules bind PhoA in discrete regions separated by stretches of about 80-90 amino acids. TF contains 4 sites, which bind unfolded PhoA over a distance of about 90Å. TF binds to PhoA primarily though hydrophobic contacts; interaction between TF and PhoA is dynamic with fast association and dissociation rates. TF is a dimer in solution but PhoA binding results in TF monomerization. TF does not interact with folded MBPmut (an aggregation-prone maltose binding protein variant) but multivalent binding between TF and unfolded MBPmut prevents its aggregation in vitro |CITS: |. TF has insignificant unfoldase activity in solution but strong unfoldase activity when bound to the ribosome |CITS: |. tig shows differential codon adaptation, resulting in differential translation efficiency signatures, in thermophilic microbes. It is therefore predicted to play a role in the heat shock response. A tig deletion mutant is more sensitive than wild-type to heat shock and osmotic stress |CITS: |. A strain containing non-polar deletions of all six cytoplasmic PPIases (Δ6ppi) shows a growth defect at 37°C in rich media and at 43°C in both rich and minimal media |CITS: |. trigger factor: 'triggers membrane assembly-competent folding' |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |Comments: |CITS: |

Merged_Functions: The JW3686 clone corresponds to the E. coli tnaA gene, which encodes the enzyme tryptophanase (TnaA). TnaA catalyzes the degradation of L‑tryptophan into indole, pyruvate and ammonia, and thus participates in amino‑acid catabolism. In this study the JW3686 construct was used to produce His‑tagged TnaA for antibody generation, but the underlying gene product functions as the tryptophan‑degrading enzyme. {PubMed:32123036}. Encodes the cytoplasmic enzyme tryptophanase (TnaA) that hydrolyses L‑tryptophan into indole, pyruvate and ammonia. In Escherichia coli, TnaA is expressed from the tna operon in response to extracellular tryptophan and, together with the tryptophan importer TnaB, converts imported exogenous tryptophan into indole, which is then secreted and functions as a signalling molecule influencing motility, biofilm formation, antibiotic resistance, virulence and other cellular processes. The article demonstrates that indole production is limited almost exclusively by the amount of external tryptophan available and that TnaA does not significantly degrade the internal anabolic tryptophan pool due to its relatively low affinity for tryptophan. {PubMed:23397453}. tnaA encodes the enzyme tryptophanase, a structural gene of the tnaCAB operon in Escherichia coli. Tryptophanase catalyzes the degradation of L‑tryptophan into indole, pyruvate, and ammonia, thereby participating in amino‑acid catabolism. In addition, the TnaA protein exhibits L‑cysteine desulfhydrase activity, converting L‑cysteine to pyruvate, ammonia, and sulfide. Thus, TnaA functions as a key enzyme for the breakdown of tryptophan (and also cysteine) during cellular metabolism. {PubMed:32123036}. The tnaA gene encodes the enzyme tryptophanase, which catalyzes the conversion of L‑tryptophan to indole (and pyruvate and ammonia). TnaA activity is a major source of indole production in Escherichia coli. Expression of tnaA is subject to catabolite repression: its transcription is activated by the cAMP‑CRP complex and is rapidly shut down when preferred carbohydrates such as glucose or arabinose are present. In addition to transcriptional control, TnaA protein activity is regulated post‑translationally; the presence of various carbohydrates (both PTS and non‑PTS sugars) inhibits the enzymatic activity of pre‑formed TnaA and alters its subcellular localization from polar/mid‑cell foci to a diffuse cytoplasmic distribution. This carbohydrate‑dependent inhibition occurs independently of intracellular cAMP levels, cAMP‑CRP, inducer exclusion, pH, or potassium availability, indicating a novel regulatory mechanism linked to the metabolic state of the cell. {PubMed:25061041}. The tnaA gene encodes the enzyme tryptophanase, a pyridoxal‑phosphate (PLP) dependent tetrameric protein that hydrolyzes L‑tryptophan into indole, pyruvate and ammonia. It resides in the tnaCAB operon together with the tryptophan‑specific transporter TnaB. Transcription of tnaA is activated by the cAMP‑CRP complex and induced by high extracellular tryptophan via a Rho‑dependent terminator and the TnaC leader peptide. TnaA activity is modulated post‑translationally: the enzyme can be sequestered into polar or mid‑cell foci where it is largely inactive, and becomes active when it diffuses throughout the cytoplasm. Additional regulation involves a surface loop near the catalytic pocket whose conformation can occlude substrate access, and mutations affecting this loop or inter‑subunit interfaces alter both localization and enzymatic activity. The enzyme’s activity produces indole, a signaling molecule that influences numerous bacterial physiological processes and host‑microbe interactions. {PubMed:25650045}. tnaA encodes a cysteine deaminase (CD) that catalyzes the degradation of L‑cysteine in Escherichia coli. In this study the gene was deleted to reduce L‑cysteine degradation, although the impact on cysteine production was modest compared with other targets. {PubMed:29405609}. tnaA encodes the enzyme tryptophanase (EC 4.1.99.1), a catabolic protein that degrades L‑tryptophan into indole, pyruvate, and ammonia, enabling Escherichia coli to use tryptophan as a source of carbon, nitrogen, and energy. The gene is part of the tna operon, which also includes tnaB (a low‑affinity tryptophan permease), and its expression is regulated at multiple transcriptional steps, including initiation, elongation (via GreA/GreB factors), and termination. {PubMed:15702537}. The tnaA gene encodes the PLP‑dependent enzyme tryptophanase (TnaA), which catalyzes the β‑elimination of L‑tryptophan to produce indole. In Edwardsiella tarda, TnaA‑mediated indole production occurs throughout growth and reaches ~35 µM in stationary phase. Indole generated by TnaA acts as a signaling molecule that positively influences several phenotypes: it supports normal swarming and twitching motilities, promotes lipopolysaccharide (LPS) biosynthesis, contributes to multidrug resistance (especially to penicillins, tetracyclines, phenicols and rifampin), and is required for full virulence in zebrafish (ΔtnaA shows a 55‑fold increase in LD₅₀). Thus, tnaA functions both as the enzymatic source of indole and as a regulator of motility, cell envelope composition, antibiotic resistance, and pathogenicity in E. tarda. {PubMed:23761341}.

Exhibits L‑cysteine desulfhydrase activity, converting L‑cysteine to pyruvate, ammonia and sulfide. {PubMed:32123036}. Requires pyridoxal‑phosphate (PLP) as a cofactor. {PubMed:25650045}. Enables Escherichia coli to use tryptophan as a source of carbon, nitrogen and energy. {PubMed:15702537}. Deletion reduces L‑cysteine degradation, confirming its role as a cysteine deaminase. {PubMed:29405609}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Tryptophanase or tryptophan indole-lyase (TnaA) is an extremely well-studied pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzyme that catalyzes the cleavage of L-tryptophan to indole, pyruvate and NH4+. Together with the tryptophan transporter TnaB, it enables utilization of L-tryptophan as sole source of nitrogen or carbon for growth. In recent years, it has become clear that one of the reaction products, indole, plays a significant role as an extracellular |CITS: | and intracellular |CITS: | signal, even acting as a cell cycle regulator |CITS: |. Indole production by TnaA depends directly on the amount of exogenous tryptophan, and the enzyme does not appear to degrade internal anabolic tryptophan |CITS: |. Tryptophanase is a major contributor towards the cellular L-cysteine desulfhydrase (CD) activity |CITS: |. In vitro, tryptophanase also catalyzes α,β elimination, β replacement, and α hydrogen exchange reactions with a variety of L-amino acids |CITS: |. Tryptophanase is one of the most S-sulfhydrated proteins in E. coli; at least six of its seven Cys residues can be S-sulfhydrated. S-sulfhydration reduces the enzymatic activity of tryptophanase. In a mouse model, a diet high in sulfur-containing amino acids reduces indole levels in the gut and mitigates kidney damage |CITS: |. Molecular and biochemical properties of tryptophanase have been studied in depth by several groups; only a small number of papers can be cited here, with preference given to work performed on the K-12 enzyme. Tryptophanase consists of four identical subunits |CITS: |, each of which contains one molecule of pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) |CITS: |. The dissociated dimeric form of the enzyme appears to be inactive |CITS: |. Dissociation has been studied by site-directed mutagenesis of residues within the subunit interaction interfaces |CITS: |. Crystal structures of wild-type and mutant TnaA apo- and holoenzyme have been solved |CITS: |. The tetramer contains four bound K+ ions |CITS: |. The apo form of the enzyme, lacking PLP, appears to be more flexible than the holo form |CITS: |. Using a method that distinguishes N-phosphorylation from O-phosphorylation, N-phosphorylation was detected in vitro |CITS: |. PLP forms an aldimine bond with Lys270 of the enzyme |CITS: |; binding of PLP induces a conformational change |CITS: |. The enzyme requires K+ for its activity and for tight PLP binding |CITS: |. Analysis of site-directed mutants, e.g. in |CITS: |, has identified a number of residues that are required for interaction with PLP, orienting the substrate-PLP intermediates in the optimal conformation for catalysis, and are important for overall enzyme activity and substrate specificity. The enzyme may react by a rare SE2-type mechanism. Some of this work is reviewed in |CITS: |. Different benzimidazole analogs of the indolenine intermediate/transition state are either substrates or inhibitors of tryptophanase |CITS: |. L-bishomotryptophan is a potent and selective competitive inhibitor of the enzyme |CITS: |. Tryptophanase localizes to a single focus at one of the cell poles, mainly during the logarithmic growth phase. The Min system is involved in localization of the protein |CITS: |. Amino acid residues that affect assembly and localization of the enzyme were identified by site-directed mutagenesis. Sequestration of the enzyme may be an additional mechanism to regulate its activity |CITS: |. When the level and distribution of tryptophanase is analyzed under a variety of concentrations of glucose and tryptophan, formation of foci appears to be more complex |CITS: |. In a strain selected for increased isobutanol tolerance, a tnaA mutation contributes significantly to the tolerance phenotype |CITS: |. A tnaA mutant has decreased viability during long-term stationary phase |CITS: |. Reports disagree on whether indole signaling increases or decreases persister cell formation; |CITS: | report decreased persister cell formation of a tnaA mutant when grown in rich medium. In contrast, |CITS: | report decreased persister cell formation when indole is added to a tnaA mutant and increased persister cell formation when tryptophanase activity is indirectly downregulated by the phosphodiesterase activity of |FRAME: G6783-MONOMER DosP| |CITS: |. The different results may be due to differences in the experimental conditions and strains used. Regulation of expression of tryptophanase has been of interest for a long time and was shown to be induced by L-tryptophan and regulated by catabolite repression |CITS: |. Glucose depletion triggers synthesis of tryptophanase |CITS: |. Regulation by L-tryptophan is exerted via antitermination in the leader region |CITS: | that is facilitated by the TnaC leader peptide |CITS: |. For a description of the attenuation mechanism, please see |FRAME: TU00085| and the review by |CITS: |. tnaA mRNA levels are significantly downregulated in E. coli cells inoculated on lettuce leaves |CITS: |. During exponential growth under anaerobic nitrate respiration conditions, transcription of tnaCAB is repressed by the NarXL and NarPQ two-component systems via FNR, thereby avoiding the conversion of indole into mutagenic nitrosative derivatives |CITS: |. TnaA protein levels are significantly increased by growth at high external pH |CITS: | and growth on glycerol |CITS: |. tnaA mRNA levels are significantly decreased under moderately acidic conditions |CITS: |. Increased TnaA expression via TorRS is involved in survival of alkaline stress conditions due to TMAO respiration |CITS: |. Increased tnaA expression at the onset of stationary phase is dependent on σS |CITS: | and Crl |CITS: |. Expression of the toxin |FRAME: G6109-MONOMER YafQ| reduces TnaA levels, possibly by cleavage of the tnaA mRNA at the in-frame YafQ cleavage cites |CITS: |. Addition of glucose and other carbohydrates inhibits TnaA function, suggesting an additional level of carbohydrate-dependent post-translational regulation |CITS: |. Increased degradation of tnaA mRNA upon a shift to acidic growth conditions is dependent on RNase E |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Transaldolase B is an enzyme of the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway. Along with transketolase, transaldolase creates a reversible link between the pentose phosphate pathway and glycolysis. It catalyzes the interconversion of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate and sedoheptulose-7-phosphate to fructose-6-phosphate and erythrose-4-phosphate. The reversibility of this reaction and carbon flux through the pentose phosphate pathway has been addressed both experimentally (summarized in |CITS: |) and theoretically |CITS: |. There are two closely related transaldolases in E. coli, encoded by talA and talB. Only transaldolase B has been biochemically characterized. TalB is a dimer in solution |CITS: | and in the crystal structure |CITS: |. Mutation of the R300 residue leads to the formation of catalytically active monomers |CITS: |. Catalytically important active site residues have been identified by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. Crystal structures of transaldolase B have been determined, confirming the presence of a Schiff-base intermediate at the active site and leading to a proposed reaction mechanism |CITS: |. A talB null mutant has no growth defect on minimal media with glucose as the carbon source |CITS: |. TalB: "transaldolase B" |CITS: | Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: tRNA m1G37 methyltransferase (TrmD) catalyzes the addition of a methyl group to G37 of certain tRNAs |CITS: |. Specificity of this activity is controlled by tRNA structure, specifically including the V, T and D side loops and the presence of G36pG37 |CITS: |. TrmD can accomodate both A and G at position 36 in tRNAAsp and tRNAPhe |CITS: |. Analysis of enzyme activity with truncated tRNAs showed that TrmD minimally requires the anticodon loop and a 9 bp stem in vitro, distinguishing the prokaryotic enzymes from the archaeal and eukaryotic Trm5 |CITS: |. The catalytic mechanisms of TrmD- and Trm5-type enzymes differ, and kinetic assays that distinguish their activities have been described |CITS: |. The m1G37 modification of tRNAs contributes to the prevention of +1 frameshift errors during translation, particularly at the second codon of an open reading frame |CITS: |, and is required for translation of the proline-encoding CC codons |CITS: |. CC codons at codon 2 are overrepresented in ORFs encoding membrane proteins; accordingly, TrmD deficiency results in a variety of membrane-related phenotypes |CITS: |. Distinct from the frameshifting mechanism, lack of the m1G37 modification leads to ribosome stalling at codons that are normally translated by m1G37-containing tRNAs |CITS: |. Aminoacylation of tRNAPro that lacks the m1G37 modification is less efficient than that of the modified tRNA. An experimental evolution experiment showed that the growth defect due to TrmD deficiency can be suppressed by point mutations in |FRAME: CPLX0-3950 ProRS| that enable more efficient aminoacylation of unmodified tRNAPro |CITS: |. The crystal structure of the TrmD homodimer bound to S-adenosyl homocysteine was determined to 2.5 Å resolution. The subunits consist of an N-terminal domain with AdoHcy bound to a trefoil knot, and a flexible linker connecting the C-terminal domain. Predicted active site residues were mutagenized, and the kinetic parameters of the resulting enzymes were analyzed |CITS: |. The knot appears to remain even in the unfolded state |CITS: |. Protection of tRNA and conformational changes during methylation have been analyzed |CITS: |. Pre-steady state kinetic analysis showed that, unlike the archaeal Trm5 enzyme, TrmD does not show burst kinetics, and only one of the two active sites in the dimeric enzyme is functional at any given time |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics simulations and kinetic analysis of site-directed mutants suggest that the knot undergoes conformational changes during the catalytic cycle that supports signaling by the AdoMet substrate across the dimer interface |CITS: |. Adenosine and methionine competitively inhibit TrmD, but not Trm5 |CITS: |. Both the exocyclic 2-amino group of G37 and the adjacent G36 base in the tRNA are important for TrmD activity |CITS: |. TrmD requires a divalent metal ion for catalytic activity; the physiologically relevant ion is Mg2+. It appears to aid the abstraction of the N1 proton and stabilizes the developing negative charge at O6 of the G37 base |CITS: |. A model of the catalytic cycle was proposed based on crystal structures and kinetic analysis of mutants of the Haemophilus influenzae enzyme |CITS: |. Unlike the Staphylococcus aureus enzyme, E. coli TrmD does not bind 3',5'-cAMP and is thus able to discriminate between its substrate AdoMet and the signaling molecule; the Tyr86 residue is important for discrimination |CITS: |. The level of TrmD activity is not growth rate-dependent |CITS: |. The enzyme is present in very low amounts |CITS: |. TrmD is encoded within an operon together with the ribosomal proteins S16 and L19, and its lower abundance appears to be regulated at the translational level |CITS: |. A high-throughput experiment initially identified the trmD gene as essential for growth |CITS: |. trmD has been the subject of a pilot study to screen for genetic interactions with null alleles in the Keio collection |CITS: |. The originally isolated trmD mutant is a temperature-sensitive allele |CITS: |. A S88L mutation causes a temperature-sensitive growth phenotype due to a decrease in TrmD activity at increased temperatures |CITS: |. Non-polar trmD mutants grow several fold slower |CITS: | and experience more frameshifting than wild-type E. coli |CITS: |. The strongest effect of TrmD depletion is on frameshifting at the second codon of an open reading frame, when that codon is CCC-C |CITS: |. TrmD depletion, and thus m1G37 deficiency, weakens the cell envelope and sensitizes the cells to several classes of antibiotics |CITS: |. TrmD depletion leads to decreased aminoacylation of substrate tRNAs and a gene expression phenotype reminiscent of the stringent response |CITS: |. TrmD: "tRNA methylation" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |
