MetaCyc_Comment: UbiE is a C-methyltransferase that catalyzes reactions in both ubiquinone (Q) and menaquinone (MK) biosynthesis. Q biosynthesis and MK biosynthesis diverge after the formation of chorismate and the pathways proceed independently except for the C methylation step. In Q biosynthesis, UbiE catalyzes the conversion of 2-octaprenyl-6-methoxy-1,4-benzoquinone to 2-octaprenyl-3-methyl-6-methoxy-1,4-benzoquinone. In MK biosynthesis, UbiE catalyzes the conversion of demethylmenaquinone to menaquinone |CITS: |. UbiE localizes to both soluble and membrane fractions. The seven ubiquinone biosynthesis proteins UbiE, UbiF, UbiG, UbiH, UbiI, UbiJ, and UbiK form a 1 MDa complex in the cytosol |CITS: |. A ubiE mutant accumulates 2-octaprenyl-6-methoxy-1,4-benzoquinone, an intermediate in ubiquinone (Q) biosynthesis |CITS: |, and is unable to convert demethylmenaquinone (DMK) to menaquinone (MK), accumulating DMK |CITS: |. A ubiE mutant strain thus does not contain Q and MK, but does contain DMK, and is able to grow on non-fermentable substrates like glucose, as well as grow by respiration using fumarate, TMAO and DMSO, but not nitrate |CITS: |. The original ubiE401 mutant allele was found to be a missense mutation resulting in an Asp142Gly substitution |CITS: |. Inactivation of ubiE results in dependence on an intact RecA |CITS: |. ubiE, ubiF, ubiX, ubiG, and ubiH mutants from the Keio K-12 mutant collection showed elevated resistance to the broad-spectrum antibiotic D-cycloserine (DCS) when grown in complex media, suggesting that they may be involved in DCS sensitivity |CITS: |. ubiE belongs to a network of genes which facilitate stress-induced mutagenesis (SIM) in E. coli K-12 |CITS: |. The ubiE, ubiJ, and ubiB genes appear to form an operon |CITS: |. UbiE: |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Sulfur carrier protein involved in sulfur trafficking in the cell. Part of a sulfur-relay system required for 2-thiolation during synthesis of 2-thiouridine of the modified wobble base 5-methylaminomethyl-2-thiouridine (mnm(5)s(2)U) in tRNA (PubMed:16387657). Interacts with IscS and stimulates its cysteine desulfurase activity (PubMed:16387657, PubMed:23281480). Accepts an activated sulfur from IscS, which is then transferred to TusD, and thus determines the direction of sulfur flow from IscS to 2-thiouridine formation (PubMed:16387657). Also appears to be involved in sulfur transfer for the biosynthesis of molybdopterin (PubMed:23281480). Seems to affect the stability of sigma-S, particularly during the logarithmic growth phase (PubMed:9555915). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:16387657, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23281480, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9555915}.

FUNCTION: Modulates the synthesis of GlmS, by affecting the processing and stability of the regulatory small RNA GlmZ. When glucosamine-6-phosphate (GlcN6P) concentrations are high in the cell, RapZ binds GlmZ and targets it to cleavage by RNase E. Consequently, GlmZ is inactivated and unable to activate GlmS synthesis. Under low GlcN6P concentrations, RapZ is sequestered and inactivated by an other regulatory small RNA, GlmY, preventing GlmZ degradation and leading to synthesis of GlmS (PubMed:17824929, PubMed:23475961). Displays ATPase and GTPase activities in vitro. Can also hydrolyze pNPP (PubMed:19074378). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17824929, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19074378, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23475961}.

FUNCTION: Single strand-specific metallo-endoribonuclease involved in late-stage 70S ribosome quality control and in maturation of the 3' terminus of the 16S rRNA. Acts together with the RNase R to eliminate defective 70S ribosomes, but not properly matured 70S ribosomes or individual subunits, by a process mediated specifically by the 30S ribosomal subunit. Involved in the processing of 16S, 23S and 5S rRNAs, with a particularly strong effect on maturation at both the 5'- and 3'-ends of 16S rRNA as well as maturation of the 5'-end of 23S and 5S rRNAs. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00009, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16511207, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20639334, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20807199, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23273979}.

FUNCTION: Acts as a ribosome collision sensor (PubMed:35264790). Detects stalled/collided disomes (pairs of ribosomes where the leading ribosome is stalled and a second ribosome has collided with it) and endonucleolytically cleaves mRNA at the 5' boundary of the stalled ribosome (PubMed:35264790). Stalled/collided disomes form a new interface (primarily via the 30S subunits) that binds SmrB (PubMed:35264790). Cleaved mRNA becomes available for tmRNA ligation, leading to ribosomal subunit dissociation and rescue of stalled ribosomes (PubMed:35264790). {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_01042, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35264790}.

MetaCyc_Comment: YmdB is a macrodomain family protein with O-acetyl-ADP-ribose deacetylase activity |CITS: |. O-acetyl-ADP-ribose is produced by NAD+-dependent protein deacetylation. The YmdB protein inhibits the acitivity of |FRAME: CPLX0-3281| by interacting direcly with the enzyme. Amino acids 120-140 in the catalytic region of RNase III are necessary for YmdB binding |CITS: |. The interaction was modeled, and site-directed mutagenesis confirmed that residues R40 of YmdB and D128 of RNase III are important for the interaction |CITS: |. A protein inhibitor of RNase III was first identified by Makarov and Apirion |CITS: |. Crystal structures of YmdB have been solved, and a catalytic mechanism was proposed |CITS: |. Expression of ymdB increases in early stationary phase and during cold shock |CITS: |; this response is dependent on the alternative sigma factor RpoS (σS) |CITS: |. Downregulation of RNase III activity during cold shock requires YmdB, while decreased RNase III activity during stationary phase does not appear to depend on YmdB |CITS: |. Genes whose expression is modulated by YmdB were identified by microarray analysis |CITS: |. Overexpression of YmdB inhibits biofilm formation |CITS: |. This effect is independent of RNase III, and may be due to an interaction with RpoS |CITS: |. Overexpression of ymdB increases the susceptibility to apramycin; this effect depends on the presence of RNase III |CITS: |. A ymdAB-clsC triple knockout mutant showed greater biofilm formation than a ymdB single mutant. Resistance to apramycin was increased in ymdB knockout cells compared with wild-type cells |CITS: |. Full complementation of a clsC mutant requires co-expression with ymdB |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: The UvrABC repair system catalyzes the recognition and processing of DNA lesions. A damage recognition complex composed of 2 UvrA and 2 UvrB subunits scans DNA for abnormalities. Upon binding of the UvrA(2)B(2) complex to a putative damaged site, the DNA wraps around one UvrB monomer. DNA wrap is dependent on ATP binding by UvrB and probably causes local melting of the DNA helix, facilitating insertion of UvrB beta-hairpin between the DNA strands. Then UvrB probes one DNA strand for the presence of a lesion. If a lesion is found the UvrA subunits dissociate and the UvrB-DNA preincision complex is formed. This complex is subsequently bound by UvrC and the second UvrB is released. If no lesion is found, the DNA wraps around the other UvrB subunit that will check the other stand for damage. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12145219}.

MetaCyc_Comment: RlmH is a methyltransferase that catalyzes the addition of a methyl group in the N3 position of the pseudouridine (Ψ) residue at nucleotide 1915 in 23S rRNA |CITS: |. The enzyme requires the intact ribosome and the presence of pseudouridine at position 1915 in 23S rRNA for activity |CITS: |. m3Ψ1915 is the only currently known methylated pseudouridine residue in bacterial RNAs. Computational docking between RlmH and the ribosome shows contacts with both ribosomal subunits |CITS: |, consistent with the requirement for intact ribosomes for in vitro activity |CITS: |. RlmH is a member of the SPOUT superfamily of methyltransferases |CITS: | and belongs to the α/β knot superfamily of proteins |CITS: |. Thermodynamic and kinetic analysis of folding of RlmH shows that the protein folds via a simple three-state sequential mechanism |CITS: |. Folding may involve a slipknot intermediate |CITS: |. The RlmH polypeptide chain has a trefoil knot conformation even in the denatured state |CITS: |, but its overall structure is random coil-like |CITS: |. A circularly permuted RlmH that lacks the trefoil knot forms a domain-swapped dimer that is less stable and does not bind SAH |CITS: |. RlmH is a dimer in solution |CITS: |. Backbone NMR assignments for urea-denatured RlmH have been reported |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the homodimeric RlmH showed that the SAM-binding pocket is composed of residues in the knotted core of one monomer; the C-terminal tail of the second monomer completes the active site. Site-directed mutagenesis of conserved residues within the predicted active showed that mutation of E138 or residues in the C terminus led to loss of catalytic activity |CITS: |. RlmH activity is influenced by the presence of specific nucleotides in stem-loop 69 (H69) surrounding Ψ1915 in 23S RNA |CITS: |. An rlmH deletion mutant lacks the m3Ψ1915 modification |CITS: | and has a slightly lower growth rate than wild type |CITS: |. RlmH: "rRNA large subunit methyltransferase H" |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Serine-tRNA ligase (SerRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. SerRS belongs to the Class II aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, which share three regions of homology |CITS: |. SerRS is a dimer in solution |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNASer that are important for recognition by SerRS have been identified |CITS: |. SerRS also aminoacylates a special tRNA, tRNASec, with serine |CITS: |. The charging efficiency for tRNASec is approximately 1% of that for tRNASer |CITS: |. The serine residue of Ser-tRNASec is subsequently converted to selenocysteine by |FRAME: CPLX0-1141|. tRNASec recognizes the stop codon UGA. SerRS lacks an editing domain, but pre-transfer editing (hydrolysis) of non-cognate aminoacyl adenylate intermediates may proceed within the enzyme active site itself |CITS: |. The reaction mechanism of SerRS includes the formation of an aminoacyl adenylate intermediate, which then serves as the animo acid donor in the aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase reaction |CITS: |. The N-terminal coiled coil domain of SerRS is required for its aminoacylation activity, but is not required for amino acid activation |CITS: |. This domain is an autonomously folding unit |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain contains the dimer interface and the active site |CITS: |; the Glu355 residue is conserved and important for activity |CITS: |. Crystal structures of SerRS in various conformations have been solved |CITS: |; however, they have not been deposited in PDB. Reviews: |CITS: |

Merged_Functions: The article describes b0930 (pepN) as encoding aminopeptidase N, a cytoplasmic peptidase that participates with other peptidases in the degradation of peptides generated during intracellular protein turnover. The enzyme removes N‑terminal amino acids from peptide substrates, contributing to overall peptide catabolism. The protein lacks a signal peptide and is not produced as a precursor, supporting a location on the inner face of the cytoplasmic membrane rather than being secreted. {PubMed:2869947}. The b0930 gene encodes the Escherichia coli asparaginyl‑tRNA synthetase (Asn‑tRNA synthetase, encoded by asnS). This enzyme belongs to the class II aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetases and catalyzes the ATP‑dependent attachment of L‑asparagine to its cognate tRNA^Asn, thereby generating Asn‑tRNA^Asn required for ribosomal protein synthesis. In the study, a temperature‑sensitive mutant (N4316) carrying a lesion in the motif 2 domain of this synthetase displayed defective growth at non‑permissive temperatures and abnormal translation (reduced protein synthesis, altered protein copy number, increased frameshifting and nonsense‑codon read‑through). Complementation with a wild‑type copy of b0930 restored normal growth and partially corrected the translation defects, indicating that the primary function of the gene is to provide functional Asn‑tRNA synthetase activity essential for accurate and efficient translation. {PubMed:1425658}. Encodes the small protein YbjC of unknown function. The article shows that ybjC is co‑transcribed with the nitroreductase gene nfsA from a common SoxS‑dependent promoter, forming an operon that is induced by the superoxide‑generating compound paraquat. No specific biochemical or physiological role for YbjC is described beyond its expression and operon membership. {PubMed:11741843}. The gene encodes aminopeptidase N, a cytoplasmic/membrane‑associated peptidase of Escherichia coli. Aminopeptidase N participates in the degradation of peptides generated during intracellular protein turnover, acting together with other peptidases to hydrolyze N‑terminal amino acid residues from peptide substrates. The protein lacks a signal peptide and is not produced as a precursor, suggesting it functions on the inner face of the plasma membrane. {PubMed:2869947}. The article identifies JW0913 as the pepN gene, which encodes Aminopeptidase N, a peptidase enzyme present in Escherichia coli. Aminopeptidase N belongs to a family of numerous peptidases that cleave N‑terminal amino acids from peptide substrates. The protein has an estimated molecular weight of ~90 kDa. {PubMed:6140621}. AsnS encodes asparagine synthetase, an ATP‑dependent amidotransferase that synthesizes asparagine and glutamate from aspartate and glutamine. The enzyme contains two catalytic domains: an N‑terminal domain that hydrolyzes glutamine to produce ammonia, and a C‑terminal domain that activates the aspartate carboxyl group by forming a β‑aspartyl‑AMP intermediate using ATP and Mg²⁺. The generated ammonia travels through an intramolecular tunnel to the activated intermediate, resulting in asparagine formation. This reaction supplies cellular asparagine, consumes glutamine and aspartate, and produces glutamate, playing a key role in nitrogen metabolism and cellular response to amino‑acid stress. {PubMed:29084849}. The ASNS gene encodes asparagine synthetase, a metabolic enzyme (EC 6.3.5.4) that catalyzes the ATP‑dependent conversion of L‑aspartate and L‑glutamine into L‑asparagine and L‑glutamate (L‑aspartate + L‑glutamine + ATP + H₂O → L‑asparagine + L‑glutamate + AMP + PPi). The enzyme consists of a glutamine amidotransferase domain (aa 2‑191) and an asparagine synthetase domain (aa 213‑536), linking the metabolism of four amino acids (aspartate, glutamine, asparagine, glutamate). ASNS is expressed ubiquitously, with particularly high levels in the brain and very low levels in liver. {PubMed:30057589}. The asnS gene encodes the enzyme asparaginyl‑tRNA synthetase, a class IIb aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase. This enzyme catalyzes the two‑step ligation of L‑asparagine to its cognate tRNA (tRNA^Asn): first, asparagine is activated by ATP to form an asparaginyl‑adenylate intermediate, and second, the asparaginyl moiety is transferred to the 3′ end of tRNA^Asn, producing asparaginyl‑tRNA ready for incorporation into nascent proteins during translation. The enzyme functions as a homodimer, contains conserved class‑II motifs (motifs 1, 2, and 3) that form the catalytic domain and participate in substrate (ATP, Mg²⁺, asparagine) and tRNA anticodon binding. While primarily essential for accurate protein biosynthesis, the article also notes that asparaginyl‑tRNA synthetases can have additional roles, such as acting as protective antigens in certain parasites and influencing ribosomal frameshifting or nonsense codon read‑through in E. coli. {PubMed:8706760}. The article identifies asnS as the gene encoding the asparaginyl‑tRNA synthetase in Escherichia coli. This enzyme catalyzes the attachment of asparagine to its cognate tRNA (tRNA^Asn), a crucial step in protein synthesis. Mutations in asnS (e.g., asnS459) reduce the overall rate of protein synthesis, which can suppress growth and protein‑secretion defects of secA mutants by lowering the demand on the compromised secretory apparatus. {PubMed:3519584}. The asnS gene encodes the Escherichia coli asparaginyl‑tRNA synthetase, a class II aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase (~466 amino acids, ~52 kDa per monomer) that functions as an α₂ homodimer (~100 kDa). Its primary biochemical role is to catalyze the ATP‑dependent attachment of L‑asparagine to its cognate tRNA^Asn, thereby generating charged Asn‑tRNA required for protein synthesis. In the temperature‑sensitive mutant strain N4316, a lesion within the conserved motif 2 of Asn‑tRNA synthetase abolishes this activity at non‑permissive temperatures, leading to reduced overall protein synthesis, altered protein copy numbers, increased ribosomal frameshifting, and enhanced read‑through of nonsense codons. Supplying wild‑type Asn‑tRNA synthetase (the “complementing factor”) restores growth at 43 °C and partially corrects the translation defects, indicating that the enzyme also contributes to translational fidelity and proper regulation of protein expression. The gene includes upstream regulatory sequences that may interact with tRNA^Asn, suggesting additional layers of expression control. {PubMed:1425658}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the attachment of threonine to tRNA(Thr) in a two-step reaction: L-threonine is first activated by ATP to form Thr-AMP and then transferred to the acceptor end of tRNA(Thr) (PubMed:10881191, PubMed:15079065, PubMed:18997014). The rate-limiting step is amino acid activation in the presence of tRNA (PubMed:18997014). The 2'-OH of the acceptor base (adenine 76, A76) of tRNA(Thr) and His-309 collaborate to transfer L-Thr to the tRNA; substitution of 2'-OH of A76 with hydrogen or fluorine decreases transfer efficiency 760 and 100-fold respectively (PubMed:18997014). The zinc ion in the active site discriminates against charging of the isosteric amino acid valine (PubMed:10881191). Also activates L-serine, but does not detectably transfer it to tRNA(Thr) (PubMed:15079065). Edits incorrectly charged L-seryl-tRNA(Thr) via its editing domain (PubMed:15079065, PubMed:11136973, PubMed:15525511), in a post-transfer reaction probably via water-mediated hydrolysis (PubMed:15525511). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10319817, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10881191, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11136973, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15079065, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15525511, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18997014}.; FUNCTION: ThrS is also a translational repressor protein, it controls binds its own mRNA in the operator region upstream of the start codon (PubMed:3086882). X-ray structures prove that operator mRNA and tRNA bind to overlapping sites in the protein (PubMed:10319817, PubMed:11953757). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10319817, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11953757, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2254931, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3086882}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Threonine-tRNA ligase (ThrRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. ThrRS belongs to the Class IIA aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases |CITS: |. Kinetic analysis of ThrRS supports a two-step reaction mechanism with an induced fit conformational change for the adenylation reaction |CITS: |. A proton relay model involving an active site histidine residue has been proposed |CITS: |. The tightly binding noncompetitive inhibitor borrelidin acts at the threonine activation step |CITS: |. Mutations in the zinc binding site inactivate the enzymatic function of ThrRS, but not its regulatory function, leading to a dominant negative phenotype when overexpressed in wild-type |CITS: |. Acetylation of several lysine residues within ThrRS reduces the tRNA charging activity of the enzyme |CITS: |. ThrRS has both pre- and posttransfer editing activities |CITS: |. A zinc ion at the active site provides the ability to discriminate against the isosteric amino acid valine at the activation step |CITS: |. In the absence of tRNA, amino acid activation is asymmetric; serine is activated at rates similar to threonine, but the seryl-adenylate is hydrolyzed. When tRNA is present, seryl transfer to tRNA is only 2-fold slower than threonyl transfer |CITS: |. The N-terminal domain of ThrRS contains a post-transfer editing function that is able to deacylate mischarged Ser-tRNAThr |CITS: |. Oxidative stress leads to oxidation of the Cys182 residue to cysteine sulfenic acid |CITS: |, which impairs the editing activity and leads to formation of Ser-tRNAThr, protein mistranslation, and impaired growth |CITS: |. ThrRS can not effectively discriminate against the unnatural amino acid β-hydroxynorvaline |CITS: |. Editing of mischarged Ser-tRNAThr is negatively affected by acetylation of the Lys169 residue in ThrRS |CITS: |. ThrRS is able to cross-edit mischarged human Ala-tRNAThr, which is not known to occur in bacteria. This activity is proposed to enable the evolution of the mischargeable G4:U69-containing tRNAThr in vertebrates |CITS: |. Threonyl-tRNA synthetase represses its own expression at the translational level |CITS: |. Mutations that affect autoregulation map to a region between the transcription start site and the start of the thrS open reading frame; the site has sequence and structural similarity to parts of tRNAThr |CITS: |. ThrRS interacts with two stem-loop structures in the mRNA leader region |CITS: |. Defects in the regulatory and aminoacylation functions in ThrRS are correlated, suggesting that the enzyme recognizes its mRNA and tRNA ligands in analogous ways |CITS: |; however, one ThrRS dimer binds only one operator region, but each of the two ThrRS subunits binds one tRNAThr |CITS: |. The transmembrane helices are positioned to form two menaquinone binding pockets |CITS: | Despite similar function, hydrophobicity, and protein size, the FrdC and FrdD subunits of fumarate reductase do not share significant sequence identity with the corresponding membrane-binding subunits of succinate dehydrogenase, SdhC and SdhD |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Two distinct, membrane-bound, FAD-containing enzymes are responsible for the catalysis of fumarate and succinate interconversion; fumarate reductase is used in anaerobic growth, and succinate dehydrogenase is used in aerobic growth. Anchors the catalytic components of the fumarate reductase complex to the cell inner membrane, binds quinones (PubMed:10373108). The QFR enzyme complex binds 2 quinones in or near the membrane; 1 near the [3Fe-4S] cluster (QP is proximal to the [3Fe-4S] cluster, on the cytoplasmic side of the membrane) while QD (the distal cluster) is on the other side of the membrane. It is not clear if both of the quinol-binding sites are functionally relevant (PubMed:10373108, PubMed:11850430). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10373108, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11850430}.

FUNCTION: Controls the transcription of genes involved in arginine and lysine metabolism. Activates transcription of several genes, including argO, lysP, lysC, asd, dapB, dapD, lysA, gdhA and argK. Acts by binding directly to their promoter or control region (PubMed:10600368, PubMed:15150242, PubMed:17504942, PubMed:21441513, PubMed:21890697). ArgP dimer by itself is able to bind the argO promoter-operator region to form a binary complex, but the formation of a ternary complex with RNA polymerase is greatly stimulated only in presence of a coeffector. Both arginine and lysine are coeffectors at the argO promoter, but only arginine is competent to activate transcription. Lysine has repressive effects (PubMed:15150242, PubMed:17504942). ArgP also mediates lysine repression of dapB, and gdhA in vivo, but via an alternative mechanism: ArgP binding is directly reduced upon the addition of lysine (PubMed:21890697). Binds in vitro to the promoter region of dnaA and to the upstream region of the nrd promoter, but these genes are probably not regulated by ArgP in vivo (PubMed:21890697, PubMed:9254708, PubMed:9819053). In vitro, also binds to the three 13-mers located in the origin region (oriC) and blocks the initiation of replication (PubMed:1733927). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10600368, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15150242, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1733927, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17504942, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21441513, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21890697, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9254708, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9819053}.

FUNCTION: Member of a network of 50S ribosomal subunit biogenesis factors (ObgE, RluD, RsfS and DarP) which assembles along the 30S-50S interface, preventing incorrect 23S rRNA structures from forming (PubMed:33639093). Promotes peptidyl transferase center (PTC) maturation (PubMed:33639093). Binds pre-50S ribosomal subunits near the 23S rRNA L1 stalk, where it may mediate correct positioning of the L1 stalk (PubMed:33639093). Plays a dual role in the late stages of assembly of the 50S ribosomal subunit; promotes peptidyl transferase center (PTC) maturation by modulating the docking of 23S rRNA helix H68, and maintains the stability of helix H89 with the help of uL16 (rplP), facilitating the final maturation of the PTC (Probable) (PubMed:38842932). Overexpression slows growth at 37 degrees Celsius (PubMed:38842932). {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00765, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33639093, ECO:0000269|PubMed:38842932, ECO:0000305|PubMed:38842932}.

FUNCTION: Nucleotidase that shows high phosphatase activity toward non-canonical pyrimidine nucleotides and three canonical nucleoside 5'-monophosphates (UMP, dUMP, and dTMP), and very low activity against TDP, IMP, UDP, GMP, dGMP, AMP, dAMP, and 6-phosphogluconate. Appears to function as a house-cleaning nucleotidase in vivo, since the general nucleotidase activity of YjjG allows it to protect cells against non-canonical pyrimidine derivatives such as 5-fluoro-2'-deoxyuridine, 5-fluorouridine, 5-fluoroorotate, 5-fluorouracil, and 5-aza-2'-deoxycytidine, and prevents the incorporation of potentially mutagenic nucleotides into DNA. Its dUMP phosphatase activity that catalyzes the hydrolysis of dUMP to deoxyuridine is necessary for thymine utilization via the thymine salvage pathway. Is strictly specific to substrates with 5'-phosphates and shows no activity against nucleoside 2'- or 3'-monophosphates. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15489502, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17189366, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17286574}.

MetaCyc_Comment: YjjG is a monophosphatase whose activity is essential for thymine salvage in a thyA (|FRAME: THYMIDYLATESYN-CPLX|) mutant. The dUMP phosphatase activity of YjjG generates deoxyuridine, which can be used by DeoA to liberate the deoxyribose-1-phosphate required for salvage of thymine |CITS: |. YjjG was first identified as a pyrimidine nucleotidase belonging to the superfamily of haloacid dehalogenase (HAD)-like hydrolases. YjjG has phosphatase activity towards UMP, dUMP, and dTMP, and the activity is inhibited by nucleoside di- and triphosphates |CITS: |. The enzyme shows a low level of substrate discrimination among its preferred substrates |CITS: |. The phosphatase activity of YjjG was also shown in a high-throughput screen of purified proteins |CITS: |. The general nucleotidase activity of YjjG allows it to protect cells against the potentially mutagenic noncanonical pyrimidine nucleotides, preventing their incorporation into DNA |CITS: |. YjjG is oligomeric in solution |CITS: |. The enzyme is likely identical to a partially purified 5'-nucleotidase from E. coli B |CITS: |. A yjjG thyA double mutant is unable to use thymine for growth on glucose minimal medium |CITS: |. A yjjG mutant is sensitive to toxic noncanonical pyrimidine derivatives such as 5-fluorodeoxyuridine |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Required for optimal enterobactin synthesis. Acts as a proofreading enzyme that prevents EntB misacylation by hydrolyzing the thioester bound existing between EntB and wrongly charged molecules. Displays esterase activity toward a wide range of substrates, including acyl-CoAs and aryl-CoAs. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15808744, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17675380, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19119850, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19193103, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24992697}.
MetaCyc_Comment: EntH is a thioesterase that is involved in the biosynthesis of enterobactin |CITS: |. It acts as a proofreading enzyme that hydrolyzes misacylated EntB aryl intermediates |CITS: |. |CITS: | reports that the catalytic activity of EntH is sensitive to the pattern of hydroxyl groups on the aryl-CoA substrates |CITS: |, while |CITS: | saw no such effect. Although EntH can utilize both CoA and holo-EntB as the substrate thioester, holo-ACP is a very poor substrate |CITS: |. While EntH is not required for enterobactin synthesis in vitro |CITS: |, it is required for optimal synthesis in vivo |CITS: |. EntH interacts with phosphopantetheine-modified |FRAME: ENTB-CPLX EntB| in vivo |CITS: |. Esterase activity of EntH was first discovered in a high-throughput screen of purified proteins |CITS: |. Benzoyl-CoA was found to be a good substrate, with a Km of 82 µM |CITS: |. Crystal structures of EntH have been determined |CITS: |. The quarternary structure is best described as a dimer of dimers |CITS: |. Enzymes with mutations in predicted active site residues have been purified and kinetically characterized |CITS: |. EntH belongs to the 4-hydroxybenzoyl-CoA thioesterase subfamily of the hot dog fold superfamily of proteins |CITS: |. Structural and functional comparisons between EntH and its paralog |FRAME: G6912-MONOMER MenI| provided insight into the substrate specificity and evolution of the hotdog fold enzymes |CITS: |. EntH production is increased under iron starvation conditions; overproduction of EntH inhibits production of enterobactin |CITS: |. EntH: "enterobactin" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: With TolR probably plays a role in maintaining the position of the peptidoglycan cell wall in the periplasm (Probable). Plays a role in resistance to environmental stress, and a role in outer membrane functionality and cell shape (PubMed:11906175, PubMed:361695). Non-covalently binds peptidoglycan (Probable) (PubMed:25135663). Acts as a porin with low permeability that allows slow penetration of small solutes (PubMed:1370823, PubMed:20004640, PubMed:21069910). A very abundant protein, there can be up to 210,000 OmpA molecules per cell (PubMed:24766808). Reconstitution in unilamellar lipid vesicles shows only about 3% of the protein is in an open conformation, which allows diffusion of L-arabinose at a rate comparable to that of OmpF porin; the pores interconvert very rarely (PubMed:7517935). Native and reconstituted protein forms ion channels with 2 conductance states of (50-80 pS) and (260-320 pS); the states are interconvertible in this study. Interconversion requires refolding of the periplasmic domain (PubMed:10636850). Small pores are converted into large pores by increasing temperature; in this model the C-terminal periplasmic domain forms 8 more beta sheets to form a larger pore (PubMed:15850404). The center of the isolated beta-barrel is polar and has a central gate (involving Glu-73, Lys-103, Glu-149 and Arg-159, sandwiched between Tyr-29, Phe-40 and Tyr-94), with no obvious passage for water or ions (Probable) (PubMed:9808047). Gating involves the Glu-73-Arg-159 salt bridge; gate opening probably involves formation of alternate salt bridges Glu-149-Arg-159 and Glu-73-Lys-103 (PubMed:17041590). Modeling suggests that non-covalent binding of OmpA (from the outer membrane) and TolR (from the inner membrane) to peptidoglycan maintains the position of the cell wall in the periplasm, holding it approximately equidistant from both the inner and outer membranes. Trimeric Lpp controls the width of the periplasm, adjusts its tilt angle to accommodate to the available space, and can compensate in part for an absence of OmpA (Probable). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10636850, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11906175, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1370823, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15850404, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17041590, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20004640, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21069910, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24766808, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25135663, ECO:0000269|PubMed:361695, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7517935, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9808047, ECO:0000305|PubMed:17041590, ECO:0000305|PubMed:27866852, ECO:0000305|PubMed:28978443, ECO:0000305|PubMed:30713026}.; FUNCTION: Required for F plasmid cell conjugation; purified protein plus lipopolysaccharide (LPS) inhibits conjugation in a concentration-dependent manner. OmpA probably acts as the receptor on recipient cells (Probable) (PubMed:321438). Required for the stabilization of mating aggregates during F plasmid conjugative transfer, may interact with F plasmid-encoded TraN, but not with TraN from plasmid R100-1 (PubMed:16272376, PubMed:9696748). All 4 external, surface-exposed loops are required for F plasmid conjugation (PubMed:10368142). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10368142, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16272376, ECO:0000269|PubMed:321438, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9696748, ECO:0000305|PubMed:4604263}.; FUNCTION: (Microbial infection) Mutants with decreased or altered protein are resistant to bacteriophage TuII* (PubMed:1107069, PubMed:791936). Mutants which have no or greatly reduced protein levels are resistant to a number of bacteriophages, including K3, K4, K5, Ox2, Ox3, Ox4, Ox5, Ml, and Ac3 (Probable) (PubMed:3902787, PubMed:783129). Mutations in this protein render the bacteria partially or completely susceptible to a number of bacteriophages for which is it probably the receptor (PubMed:3902787, PubMed:6086577). All but the last external, surface-exposed loops are required for phage K3 infection (PubMed:10368142). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10368142, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1107069, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3902787, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6086577, ECO:0000269|PubMed:783129, ECO:0000269|PubMed:791936, ECO:0000305|PubMed:4604263}.; FUNCTION: (Microbial infection) A mutation in this locus (called tolG) renders the cell tolerant to bacteriocin JF246 but does not affect its sensitivity to colicins A, C, El, E2, E3, K, Ia, or Ib (PubMed:4591955). MetaCyc_Comment: E. coli contains three phosphatidylglycerophosphatases - |FRAME: EG10704 "PgpA"|, PgpB and |FRAME: EG11371 "PgpC"| - which catalyse the dephosphorylation of phosphatidylglycerol phosphate (PGP) to phosphatidylglycerol (PG), an essential phospholipid of the inner and outer membrane in E. coli. PgpA and PgpC appear to be specific for PGP |CITS: | whereas PgpB is a multifunctional enzyme that is also active on undecaprenyl diphosphate, phosphatidicic acid and lysophosphatidic acid |CITS: |. The main physiological activity of PgpB may be its diacylglycerol pyrophosphate (DGPP) phosphatase activity. Phosphatidate (PA), lyso-PA, and phosphatidylglycerophosphate are alternative substrates for the enzyme |CITS: |. PgpB is unusual in that it appears to be located in both the outer and cytoplasmic membranes |CITS: |. Topological studies shows that PgpB is constituted by six transmembrane segments, with the N- and C-terminal regions localized in the cytoplasm and the active site located on the outer side of the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: |. Its activity varies according to the subcellular location. PGP phosphatase activity is higher in the cytoplasmic membrane, while PA and LPA phosphatase activities are higher in the outer membrane |CITS: |. A pgpB null mutant has no obvious growth defect |CITS: |. Simultaneous inactivation of pgpB, bacA, and ybjG is lethal. Depletion of BacA in the triple mutant strain causes changes in cell morphology and lysis. Overexpression of pgpB, yeiU, bacA, and ybjG leads to increased undecaprenyl pyrophosphate (C55PP) phosphatase activity in crude membrane extracts. Expression of C55PP phosphatase activity from any one of the three genes pgpB, bacA, and ybjG appears to be sufficient for synthesis of undecaprenyl phosphate and survival |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: mltA encodes a membrane bound lytic murein transglycosylase which cleaves the β-1,4 glycosidic bond between N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) and N-acetylmuramic acid (MurNAc) residues of peptidoglycan with the concomitant formation of a 1,6-anhydro ring at the MurNAc residue. MltA is an outer membrane lipoprotein |CITS: |. Purifed MltA degrades insoluble murein sacculi to produce soluble muropeptides and degrades isolated linear glycan strands (poly GlcNAc-MurNAc) to produce anhydro-disaccharide units |CITS: |. Purified MltA degrades the purified cell wall sacculus to produce the following major products (in order of abundance): tetra-A1 (GlcNAc-1,6-anhydro-MurNAc monomer with tetrapeptide stem); tetra2-A2 (a GlcNAc-1,6-anhydro-MurNAc dimer with crosslinked tetrapeptide stems); tri-A1 (GlcNAc-1,6-anhydro-MurNAc monomer with tripeptide stem) plus other variations in smaller amounts. The reaction generates both cross-linked and non-crosslinked products; it does not generate products that are indicative of an endolytic transglycosylase reaction |CITS: |. Purified MltA interacts with |FRAME: EG10605-MONOMER "PBP1B"|, |FRAME: G7322-MONOMER "PBP1C"|, |FRAME: EG10606-MONOMER "PBP2"|, |FRAME: EG10341-MONOMER "PBP3"|, |FRAME: EG10748-MONOMER "PBP1A"| (through an unknown periplasmic factor), and |FRAME: G6968-MONOMER "MipA"| |CITS: |. MltA, PBP1B and MipA form a trimeric complex in vitro |CITS: |. Purified, crystallized MltA (lacking its lipid anchor) is a 'kidney bean' shaped monomer; the protein contains two domains separated by a large groove which may constitute the substrate binding site |CITS: |. Crystal structures have also been obtained for an inactive MltA mutant, in apo form and in complex with chitohexaose - a substrate analog |CITS: |. Induced overexpression of MltA results in spheroblasting and lysis of cells grown at 30° C, the optimal temperature for enzymatic activity |CITS: |. A strain lacking three lytic transglycosylases, MltA, MltB and Slt70 shows no change in morphology or growth but significant changes to peptidoglycan composition including decreased anhydromuropeptide content and an increase in L-D peptide cross links |CITS: |. A strain lacking MltA, MltB and Slt70 shows a significant reduction in murein turnover without affecting growth |CITS: |. E. coli K-12 contains other lytic murein transglycosylases including |FRAME: G7410-MONOMER "MltB"|, |FRAME: G7533-MONOMER "MltC"|, |FRAME: EG10246-MONOMER "MltD|, |FRAME: EG11373-MONOMER "MltF"|, |FRAME: G6622-MONOMER "EmtA"| and |FRAME: EG10950-MONOMER "Slt70"|. |FRAME: EG11494 "MltG"|, an inner membrane protein and potential PG terminase, also has lytic murein transglycosylase activity. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in the degradation of glucose via the Entner-Doudoroff pathway (PubMed:15659677, PubMed:1624451). Catalyzes the reversible, stereospecific retro-aldol cleavage of 2-keto-3-deoxy-6-phosphogluconate (KDPG) to pyruvate and D-glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (PubMed:11342129, PubMed:17962400, PubMed:17981470). In vitro, can also catalyze the cleavage of 2-keto-4-hydroxy-4-(2'-pyridyl)butyrate (KHPB), 2-keto-3-deoxy-6-phosphogalactonate (KDPGal), and of the substrate analogs 2-keto-3-deoxy-gluconate (KDG) and 2-keto-4-hydroxyoctonate (KHO) (PubMed:17962400). Can accept some nucleophiles other than pyruvate, including 2-oxobutanoate, phenylpyruvate and fluorobutanoate (PubMed:17981470). In addition to its KDPG aldolase activity, catalyzes the reversible cleavage of 2-keto-4-hydroxyglutarate (KHG) to glyoxylate and pyruvate (PubMed:1098660, PubMed:1339418, PubMed:4560498, PubMed:7016177). The enzyme is stereoselective for the S-enantiomer of KHG (PubMed:1098660, PubMed:4560498). Cleavage of KHG could serve in tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle regulation or, when operating in the reverse direction, in the detoxification of glyoxylate (Probable). Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Confers DNA tethering and processivity to DNA polymerases and other proteins. DNA bound in the ring is bent 22 degrees, in solution primed DNA is bound more tightly than dsDNA, suggesting the clamp binds both ss- and dsDNA (PubMed:18191219). Initially characterized for its ability to contact the alpha subunit (dnaE) of DNA polymerase III (Pol III), tethering it to the DNA and conferring very high processivity (PubMed:2040637). Pol III is a complex, multichain enzyme responsible for most of the replicative synthesis in bacteria; it also exhibits 3'-5' exonuclease proofreading activity. MetaCyc_Comment: ftnA encodes the iron-storage protein ferritin, which is similar to human ferritin H |CITS: |. Ferritin forms a multi-subunit, hollow spherical shell of 24 individual ferritin polypeptides that can sequester more than 2000 iron atoms in the center |CITS: |. Ferritin and |FRAME: CPLX0-1421| are distantly related |CITS: |. The crystal structure of ferritin has been determined, identifying three iron-binding sites per subunit |CITS: |. Two of these sites form a dinuclear iron center where oxidation of Fe(II) occurs, allowing iron to be stored as ferric phosphate |CITS: |. The third site appears to modulate Fe2+ binding to the dinuclear iron center |CITS: |. No protons are released upon initial binding of Fe2+. Subsequent oxidation of Fe2+ leads to production of H2O2, which is itself utilized for oxidation of Fe2+ bound at other ferroxidase centers |CITS: |. In vitro, FtnA was shown to sequester iron released from damaged clusters of IscU. Iron sequestered by FtnA can be transferred to IscA, but not IscU |CITS: |. Overexpression of ftnA rescues the oxygen sensitivity of a Δfur ΔrecA mutant, presumably by preventing toxic iron accumulation |CITS: |. An ftnA mutant shows impaired growth in iron-deficient media |CITS:|. Expression of ftnA is higher in stationary phase than log phase cells and is dependent on iron and Fur |CITS: |. Although ftnA expression was thought to be regulated by RyhB |CITS: |, microarray experiments indicated that it is not dependent on RyhB |CITS: |. It was later shown that ftnA expression is directly regulated by Fur, which reverses silencing by H-NS |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Cyclopropane fatty acyl phospholipid synthase (CFA) catalyzes a modification of the acyl chains of phospholipid bilayers through methylenation of unsaturated fatty acyl chains to their cyclopropane derivatives |CITS: |. It is one of the few enzymes known to act on the nonpolar portion of phospholipids dispersed in a vesicle. The enzyme acts on the double bond of a phospholipid unsaturated fatty acid residue, which must be 9-11 carbon atoms removed from the glycerol backbone of the molecule. |CITS: | Studies using analogs of S-adenosyl-L-methionine suggest that the reaction proceeds via methyl transfer followed by proton loss |CITS: |. CFA synthase is thought to operate via a carbocation mechanism |CITS: |. The presence of a bicarbonate ion in the active site was predicted by similarity to the M. tuberculosis cyclopropane synthases. The presence of bicarbonate enhances the Vmax of CFA synthase 3-fold |CITS: |. Mutants in residues predicted to interact with bicarbonate show reduced catalytic efficiency, and some mutants can be rescued by the addition of free bicarbonate. A reaction mechanism has been proposed |CITS: |. It has since been shown that the reaction does not involve proton exchange, and that both steps of the reaction, the methyl addition to the double bond and the deprotonation, are rate determining |CITS: |. A G236E mutant in the active site catalyzes the formation of novel fatty acids, providing evidence for a carbocation reaction intermediate |CITS: |. CFA synthase shows some association with the cytoplasmic membrane and shows specific binding to unsaturated fatty acid- or cyclopropane fatty acid-containing phospholipid vesicles |CITS: |. A crystal structure of CFA synthase has been solved at 2.07 Å resolution |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain of each monomer provides the dimerization interface. An E308Q mutation converts the dimeric wild-type enzyme into a monomeric species and causes loss of enzymatic activity. A surface area of the N-terminal domain carries a positive charge and may be involved in an interaction with the negatively charged head groups of the lipid bilayer. A model for the enzymatic function of CFA synthase at the membrane surface was proposed |CITS: |. Mutants show a reduced resistance to acid shock |CITS: | and extreme acid |CITS: |, freeze-thaw cycles |CITS: |, increased pressure |CITS: |, and heat |CITS: | compared to wild type. Mutants do not exhibit obvious phenotypic defects under a range of other conditions |CITS: |. A Δcfa mutant is less susceptible to the proline-rich antimicrobial peptide apidaecin 1b |CITS: | and shows a slightly increased growth rate compared to wild type |CITS: |. A cfa rpoS double mutant shows enhanced acid sensitivity compared to either single mutant |CITS: |. Overproduction of cfa does not cause obvious growth defects |CITS: |. An RpoS-dependent promoter directs stationary-phase transcription of cfa, while a σ70-type promoter directs constitutive transcription |CITS: |. Phospholipid-mediated enzyme stabilization |CITS: | and degradation by a heat-shock-dependent mechanism |CITS: | also have regulatory effects. Moderate aciditity (pH 5) induces gene expression, resulting in an acid-acclimation effect |CITS: |. Stringent control regulation has been observed, with increases in enzyme activity upon entry into stationary phase and during isoleucine starvation |CITS: |. The nucleotide guanosine-3',5'-bisdiphosphate (ppGpp) has an indirect regulatory effect via induction of RpoS |CITS: |. Crp, Fur |CITS: | and FNR |CITS: | were identified as repressors of cfa expression, while neutal acetate stimulates transcription directly |CITS: |. Cyclopropane fatty acid levels under a variety of conditions have been measured |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: RbsK is a ribokinase that belongs to the ribokinase subfamily of sugar kinases |CITS: |. Crystal structures of ribokinase alone and in ternary complexes have been solved |CITS: |. They suggest an ordered reaction mechanism |CITS: | with a critical role for conformational changes |CITS: |; monovalent cation binding leads to a conformational change and activation of the enzyme |CITS: |. The rare codon AGG, encoding the Arg307 and Arg309 residues, together with the inefficient termination codon UGA lead to tagging of 10-25% of newly synthesized molecules of RbsK by the SsrA system |CITS: |. An rbsK mutant can not utilize D-ribose as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: |. In an rbsK mutant, D-ribose is able to leak from the cell |CITS: |. rbsK belongs to a network of genes which facilitate stress-induced mutagenesis (SIM) in E. coli K-12 |CITS: |. rbsK was found to be downregulated in a MG1655 lysogen carrying the Stx2a phage PA8 |CITS: 31208335|.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the phosphate (Pho) regulon, which plays a key role in phosphate homeostasis. Encoded together with proteins of the phosphate-specific transport (Pst) system in the polycistronic pstSCAB-phoU operon. PhoU is essential for the repression of the Pho regulon at high phosphate conditions. In this role, it may bind, possibly as a chaperone, to PhoR, PhoB or a PhoR-PhoB complex to promote dephosphorylation of phospho-PhoB, or inhibit formation of the PhoR-PhoB transitory complex. Is also part of complex networks important for bacterial virulence, tolerance to antibiotics and stress response. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17420206, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6310121}.

FUNCTION: Folding helper with both chaperone and peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (PPIase) activities. Chaperone activity prevents aggregation of unfolded or partially folded proteins and promotes their correct folding. PPIases catalyze the cis-trans isomerization of Xaa-Pro bonds of peptides, which accelerates slow steps of protein folding and thus shortens the lifetime of intermediates. Both strategies lower the concentration of intermediates and increase the productivity and yield of the folding reaction. SlyD could be involved in Tat-dependent translocation, by binding to the Tat-type signal of folded proteins. MetaCyc_Comment: SlyD is a peptidyl prolyl cis/trans-isomerase (PPIase) and chaperone. The protein has a C-terminal metal binding domain and binds Zn2+ and Ni2+ ions |CITS: | as well as Cu+ and Co2+ in vitro |CITS: |. Its PPIase activity is regulated by Ni2+ binding to the histidine-rich C-terminus |CITS: |. Ni2+ binding increases the thermodynamic stability of both SlyD domains |CITS: |. In vivo under anaerobic conditions, SlyD can specifically influence the balance of nickel ions in the cell |CITS: |. SlyD serves as a Ni2+ reservoir for -hydrogenase biosynthesis |CITS: |. The binding of Cu+ and Ni2+ to two C-terminal peptides has been studied |CITS: |. Together with |FRAME: G6925-MONOMER RflP|, SlyD appears to regulate the DNA binding ability of |FRAME: EG10359 Fur| in response to iron deficiency |CITS: |. A protein consisting of the N-terminal 165 amino acids of SlyD (SlyD*) efficiently catalyzes refolding of reduced and carboxymethylated RNase T1; the enzyme is inhibited by FK506, and kinetics of the refolding activity have been measured |CITS: |. The "insert-in-flap" (IF) chaperone domain near the prolyl isomerase active site within SlyD* appears to be necessary and sufficient to confer chaperone activity for proline-limited folding |CITS: |; it recognizes and binds unfolded and partially folded proteins |CITS: |. After the IF domain forms an initial dynamic complex with unfolded proteins, they are transferred to the prolyl isomerase domain |CITS: |. The substrate specificity of SlyD* was measured using a library of fluorescent peptides, showing high activity with hydrophobic residues such as Leu, Tyr, and Phe preceding proline |CITS: |. However, in a protein context, activity was not dependent on the amino acid residue before the proline |CITS: |. SlyD promotes very fast prolyl isomerization in an unfolded protein; in proteins that already contain the correct prolyl isomer, SlyD thus retards conformational folding |CITS: |. SlyD is involved in the insertion of Ni2+ during the maturation of hydrogenases and may have a role in regulating which of the three hydrogenases is synthesized |CITS: |. SlyD has been shown to interact directly with |FRAME: EG10484-MONOMER HypB|, an accessory protein required for hydrogenase maturation |CITS: |, and transfers Ni2+ to HypB |CITS: |. A loop in the SlyD chaperone domain is required for interaction with HypB, and the interaction is important for hydrogenase maturation. The C-terminal metal-binding domain of SlyB is required for stimulating metal release from HypB and for hydrogenase activation |CITS: |, while the PPIase activity is not required for hydrogenase maturation |CITS: |. Contributing to the metal specificity of hydrogenase maturation, SlyD stimulates Ni2+ dissociation, but prevents Zn2+ dissociation from HypB |CITS: |. Interaction with SlyD increases the GTPase activity of HypB |CITS: |, and HypB and SlyD form a tighter complex in the presence of GDP |CITS: |. SlyD also interacts directly with |FRAME: HYCELARGE-MONOMER HycE|, the large subunit of hydrogenase 3, via its IF domain |CITS: |. Although a truncated mutant protein, SlyD155, is able to bind a single Ni2+ ion and interacts with HypB, it is unable to activate release of Ni2+ from HypB and does not activate hydrogenase |CITS: |. In competitive binding experiments, SlyD is able to block the interaction of HypB with HypA; a hierarchy of binary protein-protein interactions supports the nickel delivery process |CITS: |. SlyD (as well as DnaK) binds to Tat signal sequences in vivo and in vitro |CITS: |. SlyD binds ATP, but does not hydrolyze it; binding is enhanced by bivalent transition metal ions, especially Zn2+ and Ni2+ |CITS: |. SlyD is required for phage φX174-induced cell lysis |CITS: |. Its function appears to be in the stabilization of the φX174 lysis protein E |CITS: |. An interaction of nascent lysis protein E with SlyD is essential for maintaining membrane insertion competence of the toxin |CITS: |. A peptide consisting of the N-terminal transmembrane domain of protein E inhibits the peptidyl prolyl isomerase activity of SlyD |CITS: |. Gel filtration experiments indicate that SlyD is a dimer in solution |CITS: |, while an N-terminal fragment of SlyD (aa 1-165) appears to be monomeric |CITS: |. A later study indicated that SlyD is monomeric and contains multiple metal binding sites |CITS: |. Solution structures of full-length SlyD |CITS: | and SlyD* |CITS: | have been solved. The FKBP and IF domains do not have a fixed relative location |CITS: |. An additional C-terminal α-helix is packed against the atypical PPIase domain and appears to be involved in nickel ion binding and conformational rearrangement of the PPIase domain |CITS: |. The kinetics of folding of the SlyD* protein with or without the IF domain (a "guest domain" located in a loop of the FKBP domain) has been studied |CITS: |. Overexpression of slyD is toxic, causing filamentation |CITS: |. In the E. coli B and C strains, slyD mutations cause a significant growth rate defect |CITS: |. SlyD: "sensitivity to lysis D" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: The FklB protein is an FKBP (FK506 binding protein)-type peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (PPIase) that may be located in the periplasm. Sequence analysis indicates that FklB is related to the Mip (macrophage infectivity potentiator)-like FKBPs which occur in many intracellular pathogens |CITS: |. Substrates were identified by pull-down assay and include Rob, Crl, PcnB, and ObgE |CITS: |. Purified FklB (from E. coli K-12 HB101) is a dimer in solution; the enzyme shows a preference for substrate with a hydrophobic side chain in position P1 (eg Suc-Ala-Leu-Pro-Phe) and also for a lysyl residue at this position (Suc-Ala-Lys-Pro-Phe); PPIase activity is inhibited in vitro by the immunosuppressive drug FK506 |CITS: |. Based on sequence similarity, FklB appears to have a domain structure consisting of an N-terminal dimerization domain, a long α-helix linker, and a C-terminal domain that is implicated in binding FK506 and rapamycin |CITS: |. Mutations in the linker helix affect the chaperone activity, structure and stability of FklB, but have little effect on rapamycin binding |CITS: |. The Tyr15 residue of the N-terminal domain is additionally required for dimerization |CITS: |. Mutants in putative active site residues were assayed for potential substrate binding and PPIase activity |CITS: |. The putative periplasmic localization of FklB was shown using a polyclonal antibody against FKBP25mem from Legionella pneumophila Philadelphia I |CITS: |; it may have thus detected a different PPIase of similar molecular weight. fklB appears to be either poorly expressed or tightly controlled |CITS: |. A strain containing non-polar deletions of all six cytoplasmic PPIases (Δ6ppi) shows a growth defect at 37°C in rich media and at 43°C in both rich and minimal media |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: Phosphate acetyltransferase (Pta) catalyzes the reversible conversion between acetyl-CoA and acetylphosphate, a step in the metabolism of acetate. Both pyruvate and phosphoenolpyruvate activate the enzyme in the direction of acetylphosphate synthesis and inhibit the enzyme in the direction of acetyl-CoA synthesis |CITS: |. The |FRAME: PWY0-1312| pathway has been the target of metabolic engineering to reduce the flux to acetate and increase the production of commercially desired end products; see, for example, |CITS: |. It has also been studied using systems biology approaches such as metabolic modeling and flux balance analysis; see, for example, |CITS: |. Pta is composed of three domains; only the C-terminal domain is required for phosphate acetyltransferase activity. The N-terminal domain is involved in stabilization of the native quarternary structure and metabolic regulation |CITS: |. Pta may be able to utilize both acetyl-CoA and propionyl-CoA. An ack pta double mutant has reduced levels of propionate from L-threonine, suggesting that the enzyme is part of the anaerobic pathway metabolizing L-threonine to propionate |CITS: | (see |FRAME: PWY-5437|). A pta mutant does not grow on acetate as the sole source of carbon |CITS: |. Both pta and pta ackA mutants are impaired in their ability to survive glucose starvation |CITS: |. The growth defect of a pta mutant appears to be due to perturbation of acetyl-CoA flux |CITS: |. pta mutants produce large amounts of lactate when grown on glucose as the carbon source under microaerophilic conditions |CITS: |. The effect of a pta mutation on metabolism, enzyme activity and gene expression has been thoroughly studied recently |CITS: |. pta and recBC mutants are synthetically growth inhibited |CITS: |. Levels of Pta are decreased by growth on acetate |CITS: | and under low pH conditions |CITS: |. pta belongs to the CreBC regulon |CITS: |. FNR has a slightly positive effect on pta expression |CITS: |. The growth-rate dependent expression pattern of pta-ackA was measured |CITS: |. Pta: "phosphotransacetylase" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

Merged_Functions: The article states that trxB encodes thioredoxin reductase, a component of the thioredoxin system that maintains cellular redox balance. MetaCyc_Comment: Under anaerobic conditions, the multifunctional enzyme AdhE catalyzes the sequential reduction of acetyl-CoA to acetaldehyde and then to ethanol (see the |FRAME: FERMENTATION-PWY| pathway). The two catalytic functions are conferred by its N-terminal aldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) domain and C-terminal iron-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) domain. The unusual quarternaty structure of AdhE was noticed very early; 20-60 subunits are helically arranged to form rod-like ultrastructures that appear to change conformation in the presence of Fe2+ and NADH |CITS: |. More recently, cryo-EM structures confirmed the higher-order helical architecture and conformational changes upon cofactor addition |CITS: |. The two active sites are topologically separated; ALDH active sites face the outer surface, while ADH active sites face the inner surface |CITS: |. Helical filament formation is essential for AdhE function in vitro and in vivo; the extended conformation allows substrate channeling between the two active sites |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the apo- and cofactor-bound alcohol dehydrogenase domain of AdhE have been solved at 1.95 and 1.65 Å resolution, respectively |CITS: |. Using a method that distinguishes N-phosphorylation from O-phosphorylation, N-phosphorylation was detected in vitro |CITS: |. AdhE is one of the major proteins damaged by oxidative stress, and its expression is low under aerobic conditions |CITS: |. However, AdhE mutants that confer the ability to grow aerobically on ethanol can be selected |CITS: |; their in vivo activity depends on protection against metal-catalyzed oxidation by the chaperone DnaK |CITS: |. A Glu568Lys substitution identified in the adhC mutant also confers high activity of the enzyme under aerobic assay conditions |CITS: |. AdhE's aerobic role is uncertain, but it may protect against oxidative stress, acting as a hydrogen peroxide scavenger |CITS: |. Under aerobic conditions, AdhE may be protected against metal-catalyzed oxidation in the presence of copper |CITS: | and heat inactivation |CITS: | by the heat shock proteins IbpA and IbpB. AdhE appears to interact directly with the ribosome at the head of the small subunit, where it may unwind RNA helices |CITS: |. Ribosomes containing the |FRAME: EG30090 rrsH| variant of the 16S rRNA have enhanced interactions with AdhE, leading to phenotypic changes |CITS: |. In the pathogenic E. coli O157:H7, AdhE activity affects the regulation of virulence genes in various ways; an adhE mutant is significantly less virulent than wild type |CITS: |. The pyruvate formate-lyase deactivase activity of AdhE described by |CITS: | has been questioned. |CITS: | were unable to reproduce the PFL deactivase activity; they noted that small molecule thiols can effect deactivation. Expression of adhE is induced under anaerobic |CITS: | and microaerobic |CITS: | growth conditions and repressed in the presence of nitrate |CITS: |. The half-maximal increase (pO0.5) for adhE expression is at 0.8 mbar oxygen |CITS: |. adhE expression is correlated with the NADH:NAD+ ratio in the cell |CITS: |. Transcriptional regulation is complex; expression involves two promoter regions, is repressed by |FRAME: PD00521 Cra| |CITS: | and NarL in the presence of nitrate |CITS: |, and induced by |FRAME: PD00196 Fis| |CITS: | and |FRAME: PD00197 FNR| |CITS: |. |FRAME: CPLX0-3281| cleavage of the adhE mRNA is required for translation, perhaps eliminating a secondary structure that occludes the ribosome binding site |CITS: |. adhE mRNA is a target for degradation by |FRAME: EG11299-MONOMER| |CITS: |. Mutants overproducing alcohol dehydrogenase are able to use ethanol as the sole source of carbon |CITS: |. Temperature-sensitive mutants have been isolated |CITS: |. Null mutants are unable to grow anaerobically with glucose unless an external electron acceptor such as nitrate is supplied |CITS: |. An F670E mutant disrupts the helical superstructure and affects ALDH catalytic activity more significantly in the direction of acetyl-CoA reduction |CITS: |. A Δ446-449 mutant that shortens the linker between the ALDH and ADH domains also prevents helical filament formation and affects ALDH catalytic activity, and phenocopies a ΔadhE mutant in vivo |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: Encodes lactaldehyde oxidoreductase (also called L‑1,2‑propanediol oxidoreductase), an NADH‑linked, iron‑dependent group III dehydrogenase that normally reduces lactaldehyde during catabolism of deoxy sugars such as fucose. The enzyme functions as a homodimer, each subunit containing an active site, and displays a broad substrate range that includes the toxic lignocellulose‑derived compound furfural. By catalyzing the NADH‑dependent reduction of furfural to its less toxic alcohol, FucO enhances Escherichia coli’s tolerance to furfural and improves growth and product formation (e.g., ethanol, lactic acid) in fermentations. Overexpression of fucO from plasmids increases furfural tolerance, and specific mutations (e.g., L7F) can further raise enzyme activity and affinity for furfural. {PubMed:23475621}. The fucO gene encodes the enzyme 1,2‑propanediol oxidoreductase (also called propanediol oxidoreductase), an iron‑activated alcohol dehydrogenase that functions in the L‑fucose catabolic pathway of Escherichia coli. Under anaerobic conditions, the enzyme reduces L‑lactaldehyde (produced from L‑fuculose‑1‑phosphate) to 1,2‑propanediol, which is then excreted from the cell. Expression of fucO is induced by the presence of L‑fucose, producing a ~2.1 kb transcript, and the protein is a 383‑amino‑acid, ~40.6 kDa monomer that shares ~40 % identity with iron‑containing alcohol dehydrogenase II from Zymomonas mobilis and ADH4 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, defining a new family of unusual alcohol dehydrogenases. {PubMed:2661535}. The fucO gene encodes an iron‑activated, NADH‑dependent oxidoreductase (propane‑diol oxidoreductase) that normally catalyzes the interconversion of L‑lactaldehyde and L‑1,2‑propanediol during anaerobic fucose catabolism. In addition to its native substrates, FucO exhibits NADH‑dependent reductase activity toward furfural and 5‑hydroxymethylfurfural (5‑HMF), converting these toxic aldehydes to their less‑toxic alcohols (furfuryl alcohol and HMF alcohol). Overexpression of fucO in engineered Escherichia coli strains increases the rate of furfural reduction, raises the minimum inhibitory concentration for furfural, and improves production of ethanol or lactate under furfural stress, especially when combined with silencing of the NADPH‑dependent furfural reductase YqhD. {PubMed:21685167}. The fucO gene encodes the enzyme lactaldehyde:propanediol oxidoreductase (FucO), an iron‑dependent group III dehydrogenase that catalyzes the reversible interconversion of L‑lactaldehyde and L‑1,2‑propanediol. Under anaerobic conditions, FucO uses NADH to reduce the metabolic intermediate L‑lactaldehyde (generated from L‑fucose or L‑rhamnose catabolism) to L‑1,2‑propanediol, which is excreted as a fermentation product. In the reverse direction, the enzyme oxidizes L‑1,2‑propanediol back to L‑lactaldehyde, which can then be further oxidized to L‑lactate by an aldehyde dehydrogenase. The enzyme requires Fe²⁺ as a catalytic metal ion (tetrahedrally coordinated by Asp196, His200, His263, and His277) and is specific for NAD⁺/NADH; it does not utilize NADP⁺ due to steric hindrance by Asp39. FucO functions as a homodimer, with each subunit comprising an N‑terminal α/β dinucleotide‑binding domain and a C‑terminal all‑α domain, and remains active in the absence of oxygen but is inactivated by oxidative metal‑catalyzed mechanisms or by competing metals such as Zn²⁺. {PubMed:15995211}. The fucO gene encodes L‑1,2‑propanediol oxidoreductase, an NADH‑linked oxidoreductase that catalyzes the reduction of L‑lactaldehyde to L‑1,2‑propanediol during anaerobic metabolism of L‑fucose (and, via cross‑induction, L‑rhamnose). This reaction converts the aldehyde product of the aldolase step into the excreted diol, allowing regeneration of NAD⁺ under anaerobic conditions. The enzyme is essential for anaerobic growth on fucose or rhamnose and becomes constitutively expressed in mutants selected for growth on propanediol as the sole carbon source. {PubMed:3325779}. In the article, fucO is described as encoding an enzyme that functions as an L‑lactaldehyde and 1,2‑propanediol oxidoreductase.  It was identified among candidate isobutyraldehyde reductases (IBRs) and experimentally shown to possess activity toward isobutyraldehyde, converting it to isobutanol.  Overexpression of fucO in an engineered E. coli strain restored isobutanol production, indicating its role as an aldehyde reductase.  Enzyme assays demonstrated that FucO reduces both acetaldehyde and isobutyraldehyde, with a strong preference for NADH as the cofactor (approximately six‑fold higher activity with NADH than NADPH).  Thus, fucO encodes a NADH‑dependent aldehyde reductase/oxidoreductase that can reduce isobutyraldehyde (and other aldehydes) to their corresponding alcohols. {PubMed:22731523}.

MetaCyc_Comment: L-1,2-propanediol oxidoreductase is an iron-dependent group III dehydrogenase. It anaerobically reduces L-lactaldehyde, a product of both the L-fucose and L-rhamnose catabolic pathways, to L-1,2-propanediol, which is then excreted from the cell |CITS: |. A mutant's ability to grow on L-1,2-propanediol as the source of carbon and energy is due to constitutive production of FucO, and the enzyme then serves as a propanediol dehydrogenase |CITS: |. Another mutant strain was selected for the ability to utilize ethylene glycol as a carbon source. This ability is in part due to a regulatory mutation that increases the activity of FucO, which can utilize ethylene glycol as an alternate substrate |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme have been solved, showing a domain-swapped dimer in which the metal, cofactor and substrate binding sites could be located |CITS: |. An aspartate and three conserved histidine residues are required for Fe2+ binding and enzymatic activity |CITS: |. Full activity of FucO requires growth on L-fucose or L-rhamnose under anaerobic conditions |CITS: |. FucO expression is induced by growth on L-fucose under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions, but the enzyme is only catalytically active under anaerobic conditions due to inactivation of the enzyme under aerobic conditions |CITS: |. In vitro, the enzyme can be reactivated by high concentrations of NAD |CITS: | and efficiently inactivated by a mixture of Fe3+ and ascorbate or Fe2+ and H2O2 |CITS: |. Metal-catalyzed oxidation of the conserved His277 residue is proposed to be the cause of the inactivation |CITS: |. FucO mutants with increased resistance to oxidative stress can be isolated |CITS: |. Expression of FucO enables engineered one-turn reversal of the β-oxidation cycle |CITS: |. FucO activity contributes to the conversion of isobutyraldehyde to isobutanol in an engineered strain |CITS: |. A fucAO deletion mutant colonizes the mouse intestine and maintains its population at a lower level than wild type; the accumulation of fuculose-1-phosphate appears to enable the mutant to switch to utilization of ribose for growth |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: D-3-phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (SerA) catalyzes the first committed step in the biosynthesis of L-serine. The enzyme is regulated by allosteric end-product inhibition that shows cooperativity. Inhibition by serine acts primarily through reduction of catalytic velocity and has only a small effect on the Kms of the substrates; SerA is thus classified as a type V allosteric enzyme. SerA also has an α-ketoglutarate reductase activity, producing 2-hydroxyglutarate. Kinetically, the best SerA substrates are 3-phosphohydroxypyruvate (3PHP) and α-ketoglutarate (αKG), i.e. in vitro, the reaction equilibrium is skewed towards production of 3-phosphoglycerate (3PG) rather than the 3PHP intermediate required for serine biosynthesis |CITS: |. The hypothesis that the activities and reaction equilibria of SerA may play a role in recycling NADH back to NAD+ |CITS: | is supported by experimental data |CITS: |. Unlike enzymes from some other organisms, E. coli SerA utilizes an intrinsic interconversion cycle between NAD+ and NADH that is coupled to utilization of αKG, which is the side product of the reaction catalyzed by SerC that follows SerA in the serine biosynthesis pathway |CITS: |. A K141R mutant in a sequence motif that distinguishes αKG-utilizing from non-utilizing enzymes decreases the catalytic efficiency of the E. coli enzyme with the αKG substrate 50-fold |CITS: |. The basis for allosteric and cooperative inhibition of SerA by serine has been studied extensively. Occupation of two of the four serine binding sites in the homotetramer results in 85% inhibition of activity |CITS: |. Further binding of serine shows negative cooperativity |CITS: |. Phosphate is able to reduce the site-to-site cooperative effects on serine binding |CITS: |; the effect was mainly due to the presence of intrinsically bound NADH |CITS: |. A Trp139Gly mutation results in a homodimeric enzyme that has lost cooperativity in serine binding and allosteric inhibition |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis of residues within the effector binding site, the regulatory interface between subunits, and a flexible hinge region support a model where movement of adjacent domains is involved in inhibition of the enzymatic activity |CITS: |. Transient kinetic analysis showed that the cooperativity of inhibition of catalytic activity results from a conformational change due to serine binding |CITS: |. An enzyme missing the regulatory domain is no longer inhibited by serine, but other kinetic parameters remain the same |CITS: |. Hybrid tetramers provided further insight into the mechanism of allosteric inhibition |CITS: |. Novel allosteric sites were predicted by computational modeling and tested in vitro |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis has allowed the identification of residues within the active site that contribute to substrate binding and catalysis |CITS: |. Mutations in the hinge region between the substrate and nucleotide binding domains affect the kcat of the enzyme; certain mutations uncouple serine binding and catalytic inhibition |CITS: |. Extensive site-directed mutagenesis and structural studies have contributed to a detailed view of the interactions between allosteric regulation, cooperativity and catalytic activity |CITS: |. Further insight into the catalytic pathway was provided by stopped-flow kinetic analysis, indicating that the rate-limiting step in both catalytic directions is a conformational change of the enzyme |CITS: |. Serine binding appears to lead to the formation of a dead-end quaternary complex between the enzyme, coenzyme, substrate, and effector that eliminates the conformational change subsequent to substrate binding |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the wild type enzyme and various mutants have been solved |CITS: |. The structure showed that each subunit of the homotetramer consists of three distinct domains, a nucleotide binding domain, a substrate binding domain, and a regulatory/serine binding domain |CITS: |. serA is essential for growth on glycerol minimal medium; the growth defect can be rescued by addition of serine |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: LptB is a cytoplasmic ATPase that energises the transport and assembly of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) by the Lpt system. Depletion of LptB results in impaired LPS transport and outer membrane biogenesis |CITS: |. LptB forms a complex with LptF, LptG and LptC |CITS: |. Sequence analysis suggests that LptB has an ATP binding fold |CITS: |. Purified LptB has ATPase activity in vitro; purified LptB has a KM for ATP of 0.56 mM; ATP binding to LptB is cooperative |CITS: |. Crystal structures of LptB bound to ADP and a catalytically inactive LptB mutant (LptBE163Q) bound to ATP have been obtained and suggest that ATP hydrolysis induces conformational change in LptB |CITS: |. Purified, crystallised LptB is an L-shaped molecule consisting of an ATPase domain containing the characteristic motifs (Walker A and B, and Q loop) and an α-helical domain |CITS: |. LptB contains a binding site (which includes residues F90, R91, L93 and R150) which contacts the coupling helices of LptF and LptG |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain of LptB (defined as residues 230-241) is functionally important; the region forms crucial interactions with the ATP binding site; characterization of mutations which impair distinct steps of the ATP cycle support the contention that LPS transport is driven by ATP binding |CITS: | (see further |CITS: |) LptB is found in the inner membrane fraction of whole cell lysates |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: A translation factor that gates the progression of the 70S ribosomal initiation complex (IC, containing tRNA(fMet) in the P-site) into the translation elongation cycle by using a mechanism sensitive to the ATP/ADP ratio. Binds to the 70S ribosome E-site where it modulates the state of the translating ribosome during subunit translocation. Stimulates dipeptide bond synthesis in the presence of ATP (cell in high energy state), but inhibits dipeptide synthesis in the presence of ADP (cell in low energy state), and thus may control translation in response to changing ATP levels (including during stationary phase).
