Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Formate dehydrogenase allows E.coli to use formate as major electron donor during anaerobic respiration, when nitrate is used as electron acceptor. Subunit gamma is the cytochrome b556 component of the formate dehydrogenase-N, and also contains a menaquinone reduction site that receives electrons from the beta subunit (FdnH), through its hemes. Formate dehydrogenase-N is part of a system that generates proton motive force, together with the dissimilatory nitrate reductase (Nar). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11884747}.
MetaCyc_Comment: fdnI encodes the γ subunit of formate dehydrogenase-N (Fhd-N); it is an integral membrane protein with four transmembrane helices, which, together with the single transmembrane helix of FdnH and a cardiolipin molecule, form a tightly packed trimer in the inner membrane. The γ subunit contains two heme b groups - heme bP located towards the periplasmic side of the membrane and heme bC located towards the cytoplasmic face of the membrane - and a site for menaquinone reduction |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Allows to use formate as major electron donor during aerobic respiration. Subunit gamma is probably the cytochrome b556(FDO) component of the formate dehydrogenase.
MetaCyc_Comment: fdoI encodes the γ subunit of formate dehydrogenase O. It has 45% amino acid identity (over an alignment of 156 residues) with the heme b binding, γ subunit (FdnI) of formate dehydrogenase-N |CITS: |. Both the N- and C-terminus of FdoI appear to be located in the cytoplasm and it is predicted to have 4 transmembrane regions |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: FkpB is a peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase (PPIase) of the FK506-binding protein type |CITS: |. FkpB also has chaperone activity; a number of ribosomal proteins appear to be natural substrates |CITS: |. Substrates were identified by pull-down assay and binding affinity measurements and include RpoE, RseA, RpsB and AphC |CITS: |. A crystal structure has been solved at 1.35 Å resolution. Serendipidously, the linker region of the purification tag of a different FkpB polypeptide is found in the chaperone binding groove of the insert-in-flap (IF) domain of FkpB, mimicing a chaperone substrate. A proline residue within the linker peptide appears to be specifically recognized and is important for binding |CITS: |. A solution structure of FkpB suggested that the orientation of the F37 residue is a reason for the moderate PPIase activity of FkpB; domain-swap experiments support this interpretation |CITS: |. Mutants in potential active site residues were assayed for potential substrate binding and PPIase activity |CITS: |. A strain containing non-polar deletions of all six cytoplasmic PPIases (Δ6ppi) shows a growth defect at 37°C in rich media and at 43°C in both rich and minimal media |CITS: |. FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter complex TcyJLN involved in L-cystine import (PubMed:20351115, PubMed:25139244, PubMed:25837721, PubMed:26350134). This high affinity cystine transporter is involved in resistance to oxidative stress by forming a L-cysteine/L-cystine shuttle system with the EamA transporter, which exports L-cysteine as reducing equivalents to the periplasm to prevent the cells from oxidative stress. Exported L-cysteine can reduce the periplasmic hydrogen peroxide to water, and then generated L-cystine is imported back into the cytoplasm via the TcyJLN complex (PubMed:20351115, PubMed:25837721). Functions at low cystine concentrations (PubMed:26350134). The system can also transport L-cysteine, diaminopimelic acid (DAP), djenkolate, lanthionine, D-cystine, homocystine, and it mediates accumulation of the toxic compounds L-selenaproline (SCA) and L-selenocystine (SeCys) (PubMed:25139244, PubMed:26350134). Binds cystine and DAP (PubMed:4564569, PubMed:8450713). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:20351115, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25139244, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25837721, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26350134, ECO:0000269|PubMed:4564569, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8450713}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Flavin reductase (Fre) catalyzes the reduction of free flavins (riboflavin, FMN, or FAD) by NADPH or NADH |CITS: |. The enzyme appears to be an important physiological source of superoxide radicals |CITS: |. The enzyme follows a sequential ordered reaction mechanism, with binding of NADPH followed by flavin binding |CITS: |. After both NADPH and riboflavin are bound, a charge-transfer complex of NADPH and riboflavin is formed as the first intermediate, followed by a second charge-transfer intermediate of enzyme-bound NADP+ and reduced riboflavin |CITS: |. The enzyme is A-side-specific, selectively transfering the pro-R hydrogen from the C-4 position of the nicotinamide group |CITS: |. Flavin reductase utilizes flavins only as substrates, not as cofactors. The interaction of the enzyme with its flavin substrates has been studied |CITS: |. FAD appears to interact with Fre at a site overlapping with the NAD(P)H-binding site, binding more tightly than either FMN or riboflavin. In the presence of both FMN and FAD, Fre preferentially reduces FAD; FAD thereby inhibits Fre activity at low NADH concentrations |CITS: |. Fre interacts with the |FRAME: G7060-MONOMER|; Fre uses the MsrQ FMN cofactor as a substrate to catalyse reduction of the MsrQ heme in the presence of NADH; the Fre-MsrQ interaction is a two-component protein system that together with |FRAME: G7059-MONOMER MsrP| serves to repair the oxidized methionine residues of functionally diverse periplasmic proteins |CITS: |. Although Cys5, Cys149 and Cys214 are not required for enzymatic activity, they are responsible for N-ethylmaleimide inactivation of the enzyme |CITS: |. The Ser49 residue is important for recognition of the isoalloxazine ring of flavins |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the enzyme has been solved, showing structural similarity to the ferredoxin reductase family of flavoproteins |CITS: |. The conformational dynamics of the Fre-FAD complex has been studied |CITS: |. Flavin reductase is part of the ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase activating system that is able to regenerate the tyrosyl radical of |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-DIP-REDUCTI-CPLX|. The system is composed of three proteins, flavin reductase, |FRAME: SUPEROX-DISMUTMN-CPLX| and a protein fraction named fraction b whose function is poorly defined |CITS: |. In a fre mutant, |FRAME: SULFITE-REDUCT-CPLX| can substitute for this activity |CITS: |. In the presence of a flavin, Fre also acts as a ferric reductase, reducing Fe+++ to Fe++; however, it is the reduced flavin rather than the Fre enzyme that donates the electron for reduction of Fe+++ |CITS: |. Again in the presence of a flavin, Fre is able to reduce chromate to a soluble and stable Cr(III)-NAD+ complex |CITS: |. Overexpression of Fre leads to increased sensitivity to H2O2 under anaerobic conditions. Addition of cyanide has a synergistic effect, which is due a block in respiration that leads to accumulation of NADH. NADH can then be used by Fre to produce FADH2, which in turn efficiently reduces Fe+++ to Fe++. Fe++ reacts with H2O2 to produce hydroxyl radicals which damage DNA |CITS: |. fre was initially thought to be identical to ubiB |CITS: |, but it was later shown that fre is not involved in ubiquinone synthesis |CITS: |. fre belongs to a network of genes which facilitate stress-induced mutagenesis (SIM) in E. coli K-12 |CITS: |. fre shows differential codon adaptation, resulting in differential translation efficiency signatures, in aerotolerant compared to obligate anaerobic microbes. It was therefore predicted to play a role in the oxidative stress response. An fre deletion mutant was shown to be more sensitive than wild-type specifically to hydrogen peroxide exposure, but not other stresses |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: The glycerol facilitator, GlpF, allows the facilitated diffusion of glycerol across the inner membrane for utilization inside the cell. It is a member of the major intrinsic protein (MIP) family of transmembrane channel proteins, along with AqpZ, a water channel. GlpF is predicted to be monomeric |CITS:,|. A projection map at a resolution of 3.7 Å reveals GlpF forms a tetramer of four channels |CITS:,|. Interactions between purified GlpF show it forms multiple oligomeric complexes |CITS:|. The tetrameric structure has a funnel on its periplasmic surface which help in recruitment of glycerol to the transporter |CITS:|. The structure of GlpF with glycerol has been determined by X-ray crystallography to a resolution of 2.2 Å |CITS:|. The structure of GlpF has also been determined using cryo-electron microscopy of two dimensional crystals to a resolution of 6.9 Å |CITS:|. The GlpF channel contains hydrophobic residues on one side and hydrophilic residues on the other side, possibly limiting water permeation |CITS:|. Real time molecular dynamics (MD) simulations indicate GlpF is a two stage filter |CITS:|. GlpF prevents proton transport either by orienting water molecules in a bipolar water file |CITS:,| or by an electrostatic mechanism |CITS:|. In order to select for glycerol over water transport, it is believed GlpF has a glycerol-mediated induced fit gating motion |CITS:|. MD simulations show water is necessarily cotransported with glycerol because competition with water for hydrogen bonding sites is required for movement of glycerol through the pore |CITS:|. Glycerol is transported equally well in either direction |CITS:|. glpF mutants have impaired growth on low concentrations of glycerol |CITS:|. glpF mutants also had reduced uptake of DL-glyceraldehyde, glycine, urea, erythritol, D-arabitol, L-arabitol, ribitol, xylitol, D-galactitol, D-mannitol, D-sorbitol |CITS:|, AsOH3 |CITS:|, and SbOH3 |CITS:|. Complementation studies have demonstrated that the cloned glpF gene can complement glycerol transport mutants |CITS:|. Voltage clamp experiments showed that GlpF was not voltage-activated for ion transport; it mediates glycerol diffusion via a pore type mechanism |CITS: |. GlpF interacts with glycerol kinase (GlpK) leading to activation of GlpK |CITS:|. Expression of glpF is regulated by GlpR and cAMP-CRP |CITS:|. Reviews: |CITS:,|

MetaCyc_Comment: gss encodes a bifunctional protein with two domains: an N-terminal glutathionylspermidine (GSP) amidase domain and a C-terminal GSP synthetase domain. The enzyme catalyzes both the formation and hydrolysis of an amide bond between glutathione and spermidine. The net reaction of the two component activities is ATP hydrolysis, a potential futile cycle |CITS: |. Glutathionylspermidine levels in E. coli have been measured; levels increase in stationary phase, especially under anaerobic conditions |CITS: | and after treatment with hydrogen peroxide |CITS: |. The function of glutathionylspermidine metabolism in E. coli has been unclear. Recently it was proposed that the GSP amidase activity plays a role in reduction of Gsp-S-S-Gsp and Gsp-S-protein adducts |CITS: |. Regulation of GSP amidase/synthetase at the enzyme level is required to avoid futile cycling. The two domains can be physically separated and fold and function independently. If expressed independently, the GSP amidase domain has significantly higher amidase activity than the full-length protein. Thus, in the context of the full-length protein, the amidase domain is negatively autoregulated |CITS: |. However, amidase activity increases up to 15-fold by addition of synthetase substrates |CITS: |. Hydrogen peroxide selectively inactivates the amidase, but not the synthetase activity of Gss |CITS: |; amidase activity recovers significantly after four hours |CITS: |. The catalytic mechanism for the amidase function is thought to involve a nucleophilic attack involving cysteine as the catalytic nucleophile and an acyl-enzyme intermediate. Cys59 was found to be essential for amidase activity |CITS: |. Various synthetic inhibitors have been designed and tested |CITS: |. Crystal structures of Gss alone or in complex with substrate, product or inhibitor have been solved; the structures are consistent with the proposed reaction mechanism |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the amidase domain alone, in complex with its substrate, and modified by hydrogen peroxide treatment have been solved |CITS: |. Gsp: "glutathionylspermidine" |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: malE encodes the periplasmic substrate-binding component of the maltose ABC transporter. MalE, or maltodextrin binding protein (MBP) can bind linear maltodextrins, cyclic maltodextrins and various maltodextrin analogues although only linear maltodextrins up maltoheptaose are substrates for transport |CITS: |. Non-polar malE deletion mutants do not show appreciable growth on media containing maltose concentrations up to 25 mM |CITS: |. MBP consists of two globular domains separated by a deep groove which contains the maltodextrin binding site. MBP adopts two distinct conformations - an open unliganded form in which the two globular domains are far apart and the binding groove is accessible and a closed liganded structure. Bound maltose is almost completely enclosed and is held in place by hydrogen bonds and Van der Waals interactions |CITS: |. Crystal structures of MalE bound to cyclomaltoheptaose |CITS: |, of MalE bound to the modified sugars maltotriitol and maltotetraitol |CITS: |, of MalE complexed with xenon |CITS: | and of various mutant MalE proteins |CITS: | are available. Maltose bound MBP has a strong stimulatory effect on the ATPase activity of the maltose transporter (MalFGK2) in vitro |CITS: , |. Both liganded and unliganded forms of MBP interact with the membrane components of the maltose transporter in vitro |CITS: , | and unliganded MBP is also able to stimulate the ATPase activity of MalFGK2 |CITS: |. The interaction of both liganded and unliganded MalE with MalFGK2 in different nucleotide states (apo, ADP and ATP) has been investigated |CITS: |. Dissociation of MBP is not a prerequisite for substrate translocation |CITS: |. MBP is expressed at very high levels in the periplasm of E. coli growing on maltose |CITS: , |. In addition to being the periplasmic substrate-binding component of the maltose ABC transporter, MalE with bound substrate is also able to bind to the chemoreceptor Tar to induce chemotaxis toward maltose. MalE mutants have been identified which are chemotaxis negative for maltose |CITS:,, |. Export of proMalE to the periplasm is dependent on the cytoplasmic chaperone |FRAME: EG10937 "SecB"| and this process has been extensively studied |CITS:| (and reviewed by |CITS: |) . Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Efflux pump driven by the proton motive force. Confers resistance to a broad spectrum of chemically unrelated drugs. Confers resistance to a diverse group of cationic or zwitterionic lipophilic compounds such as ethidium bromide, tetraphenylphosphonium, rhodamine, daunomycin, benzalkonium, rifampicin, tetracycline, puromycin, and to chemically unrelated, clinically important antibiotics such as chloramphenicol, erythromycin, and certain aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones. Overexpression results in isopropyl-beta-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) exclusion and spectinomycin sensitivity. Transport of neutral substrates is electrogenic, whereas transport of cationic substrates is electroneutral. In addition to its role in multidrug resistance, confers extreme alkaline pH resistance, allowing the growth under conditions that are close to those used normally by alkaliphiles. This activity requires Na(+) or K(+). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12578981, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15371593, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9079913, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9644262, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9811673}.
MetaCyc_Comment: The MdfA protein, also known as Cmr, is a multidrug efflux protein belonging to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) |CITS:|. Overexpression of MdfA confers resistance to a broad range of antibiotics and toxic molecules including tetracycline, chloramphenicol, erythromycin, daunomycin, puromycin, benzalkonium, rifampin, some aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones and organic cations such as ethidium bromide and tetraphenylphosphonium |CITS:|. Deletion of mdfA results in increased susceptibility to ethidium bromide and benzalkonium chloride |CITS:|. Transport experiments suggest that MdfA confers resistance via an efflux mechanism dependent on the proton motive force |CITS:|. Consistent with this, chloramphenicol/proton antiport is observed in membrane vesicles prepared from cells overexpressing mdfA |CITS:|. Overexpression of mdfA results in spectinomycin sensitivity and isopropyl-Β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) exclusion via an unknown mechanism |CITS:| (see also |CITS: |). Sequence analysis and experimental topology analysis indicate that MdfA contains12 transmembrane domains with the N and C-termini located in the cytoplasm |CITS: |. MdfA catalyses drug:proton antiport with a stoichiometry of 1; MdfA-catalyzed transport of neutral substrates is electrogenic, resulting in a net movement of electric charge, whereas transport of cationic substrates is electroneutral with no net movement of charge, driven primarily by proton chemical gradient |CITS:|. The negatively charged, membrane embedded, amino acid residues glutamic acid 26 (E26) and aspartic acid 34 (D34) and the positively charged arginine residue at position 112 (R112) have been implicated in transport function |CITS: ,|. R112 is located within a predicted drug binding pocket and a positive charge at this position is essential for transport function |CITS: |. No single replacement of any acidic residue with a neutral residue abolishes activity of the transporter, however an E26C/D34C double mutation disrupts MdfA-mediated resistance to a variety of test drugs |CITS:|. Aspartic acid at position 34 (D34) is the proton binding carboxylic residue |CITS: |. Substrate and protons compete for binding to MdfA but they bind at different sites within the protein |CITS: |. Insertion of an additional acidic residue into the predicted substrate binding pocket of MdfA broadens the substrate specificity of the transporter to include divalent cationic compounds |CITS: |. Wild-type MdfA can transport symmetric divalent cationic compounds when the two positively charged moieties are separated by a long linker (eg.dequalinium); transport of these compounds may proceed in a processive manner whereby each cationic moiety is treated as a separate substrate |CITS: |. Crystal structures of MdfA in alternative conformational states - inward facing with chloramphenicol bound |CITS: | and outward open |CITS: | - have been reported. MdfA consists of 12 transmembrane (TM) helices (helices 1-6 constitute the N-terminal domain or lobe and helices 7-12 constitute the C-terminal domain or lobe) and a 12-residue amphipathic linking helix (α6-7); the 12 TM helices form four pseudo-symmetrical 3 helix repeats with helices 1, 4, 7 and 10 contributing to the formation of a central substrate binding cavity which is lined with hydrophobic residues and contains the two proton-titratable residues, E26 and D34. D34 is directly involved in chloramphenicol binding and is likely to be the residue that gets deprotonated upon chloramphenical binding |CITS: |. Elements of the MdfA-mediated transport cycle vary from those predicted by the canonical alternating access mechanism; MdfA may have a lateral gate exposed to the inner membrane for the entry of lipophilic substrates |CITS: |. In addition to its role in multidrug resistance, MdfA also plays a physiological role in alkaline pH tolerance. mdfA null mutants are sensitive to mild alkaline conditions; overexpression of mdfA confers extreme alkaline pH resistance, allowing growth of cells under conditions that are close to those used normally by alkaliphiles (up to pH 10). Purified MdfA catalyzes Na+ or K+-dependent proton transport in vitro |CITS:|. mdfA has been implicated in arabinose efflux |CITS: |. mdfA: multidrug facilitator A |CITS: |cmr: chloramphenicol resistance |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS:|

MetaCyc_Comment: E. coli MetF is a flavoprotein capable of catalyzing the NADH-linked reduction of 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate to 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. The enzyme is a tetramer of four identical subunits with a beta8alpha8 barrel catalytic domain. Each of the four subunits of MetH contains a molecule of noncovalently bound flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) at the C-termini of the beta strands |CITS: |. Each of the four subunits of MetH contains a molecule of noncovalently bound flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD). In the reaction, NADH transfers reducing equivalents to the FAD cofactor, which in turn transfers them to methyltetrahydrofolate. This reaction provides methyltetrahydrofolate to be used for methylation of homocysteine to form methionine |CITS: |. NADPH also serves as a reductant, but much less effectively than NADH. MetF can also catalyze the oxidation of methyltetrahydrofolate to methylenetetrahydrofolate in the presence of menadione, which serves as an artificial electron acceptor |CITS: |. The enzyme catalyzes these oxidoreductions by a ping-pong Bi-Bi mechanism. Reoxidation of the reduced flavin by methylenetetrahydrofolate is rate limiting in the physiological NADH-methylenetetrahydrofolate oxidoreductase reaction. In the NADH-menadione oxidoreductase reaction, the reduction of the flavin by NADH is rate limiting |CITS: |. The mutation A177V near the catalytic domain of MetF increases the chance to lose its essential flavin cofactor |CITS: |. Flavin dissociation is associated with the loss of enzymatic activity. The native tetramer of the enzyme dissociates into dimers preceding flavin release at low enzyme concentration. An enzymatically active holodimer of MetF is the smallest functionally active unit of the enzyme because the FAD dissociation occurs only on unfolding of the holodimer to monomer |CITS: |. Studies with Asp120Asn and Glu28Gln mutant enzymes support the involvement of conserved acid residues Asp120 and Glu 28 present at the flavin active site in catalysis of folate binding and reduction |CITS: |. Asp120 is not critical for flavin reduction by NADH |CITS: |. Asp120 adopts "open" and "closed" conformations to ensure differential recognition of NADH and folate |CITS: |. Conformationally mobile Phe223 or Leu223 plays role in both NADH and folate binding |CITS: |. metJ mutants show that MetJ proteins regulate the vitamin B12-mediated MetF expression |CITS: |.

Cell division inhibitors MinC and MinD act in concert to form an inhibitor capable of blocking formation of the polar Z ring septums. FUNCTION: MotA and MotB comprise the stator element of the flagellar motor complex. Required for the rotation of the flagellar motor. Probably a linker that fastens the torque-generating machinery to the cell wall. Overexpression of this protein with MotA improves motility in a pdeH disruption, (a c-di-GMP phosphodiesterase) suggesting there is an interaction (direct or indirect) between the c-di-GMP-binding flagellar brake protein YcgR and the flagellar stator. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:20346719}.

MetaCyc_Comment: The mtn gene encodes 5'-methylthioadenosine/S-adenosylhomocysteine nucleosidase |CITS: |. The enzyme catalyzes glycosidic bond cleavage in S-adenosylhomocysteine and 5'-methylthioadenosine substrates, with a higher Vmax toward 5'-methylthioadenosine |CITS: |. Although MTA was thought to be the preferred substrate |CITS: |, it was later shown that 5'-methylthioadenosine, S-adenosylhomocysteine and 5'-deoxyadenosine are hydrolyzed with similar catalytic efficiency |CITS: |. The E. coli B enzyme has been characterized in detail |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme bound to adenine (1.9 Å resolution) |CITS: |, formycin A (2.2 Å resolution) |CITS: |, and 5'-methylthiotubercidin (2.0 Å resolution) |CITS: | are presented, and the implications of the structures with respect to catalysis are discussed |CITS: |. Additional crystal structures of the wild-type and mutant enzymes have been determined, allowing analysis of the conformational motions occuring during the catalytic cycle |CITS: |. Conformational flexibility of the active site appears to be important for substrate specificity of the enzyme |CITS: |. Transition state analogue inhibitors of the enzyme have been designed and tested |CITS: |. Mtn has potential as a drug target |CITS: |. Expression of mtn increases at the end of log phase growth and can be increased by salt stress |CITS: |. An mtn mutant is auxotrophic for biotin due to the accumulation of 5'-deoxyadenosine, which inhibits biotin synthase activity |CITS: |. Deletion of mtn decreases AI-2 production and biofilm formation |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in peptidoglycan biosynthesis. Transports lipid-linked peptidoglycan precursors from the inner to the outer leaflet of the cytoplasmic membrane. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_02078, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18708495, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18832143, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25013077}.
MetaCyc_Comment: MurJ is the inner membrane protein responsible for flipping lipid II from the inner face of the inner membrane to the outer face prior to peptidoglycan (PG) polymerization; MurJ is essential for PG synthesis |CITS:, ,|. There are conflicting reports on MurJ binding to lipid II: MurJ does not interact directly with lipid II in vitro and does not affect MrcB mediated lipid II polymerization in vitro |CITS: |; purified MurJ binds lipid II with high affinity (Kd of 2.9 µM for binding of the first lipid II) |CITS: |. MurJ has 14 transmembrane (TM) domains with the N and C-termini located in the cytoplasm |CITS:, |. MurJ contains a solvent exposed central cavity located within the membrane region which is consistent with a role in transport; the central cavity is lined by TM domains 1, 2, 7 and 8 and charged residues within the cavity are critical for function |CITS: , |. The crystal structure of substrate-free MurJ in an inward-open conformation has been reported: the protein consists of two six-helix TM bundles which form a bilobed structure with a central hydrophobic cavity that extends almost completely across the membrane; a pair of carboxy-terminal helices (TM13 and 14) lie outside the bundles and form a deep groove which is believed to be the binding site for the isoprenoid tail of lipid II |CITS: |. High-throughput mutagenesis has identified functionally important regions of the protein |CITS: |. The pyrophosphate, MurNAc and GlcNAc moieties of lipid II are implicated in recognition/binding by MurJ |CITS: |. MurJ co-purifies with cardiolipins and other low molecular mass phospholipids; MurJ binds to cardiolipin with µM affinity; cardiolipin interferes with lipid II binding to MurJ in vitro |CITS: |. Binding of lipid II to purified MurJ is sensitive to pH but is not affected by changes in Na+ concentration |CITS: |. MurJ mediated lipid flipping requires membrane potential (Δψ); dissipating the membrane potential alters MurJ conformation and inhibits transport function in vitro |CITS: |. MurJ can adopt both inward and outward facing conformations in vivo, consistent with an alternating access mechanism of lipid translocation |CITS: | (see further |CITS: |). Labeled MurJ localizes in the lateral wall and at midcell; midcell localization is dependent on the assembly of the divisome, the activity of |FRAME: EG10341-MONOMER "PBP3"| and the synthesis of lipid II; midcell localization requires a functional |FRAME: EG10344-MONOMER "FtsW"|; MurJ function is not required for lateral wall and midcell localization |CITS: |. Depletion of MurJ causes cells to swell and burst |CITS:,|. Expression of |FRAME: UPPSYN-CPLX "ispU"| (which encodes an undecaprenyl diphosphate synthase involved in PG synthesis) from a multicopy plasmid suppresses the growth defect of a temperature-sensitive murJ mutant |CITS:|. Incorporation of radiolabeled diaminopimelic acid into PG intermediates is increased in a murJ mutant, but incorporation into the PG layer is reduced |CITS:,|. murJ has a potential σ54-dependent promoter |CITS:|. murJ is one of a number of genes whose expression increases when |FRAME: EG10935 "sdiA"| is expressed from a high copy number plasmid |CITS:|. MurJ is a member of the Multidrug/Oligosaccharidyl-lipid/Polysaccharide (MOP) Flippase Superfamily |CITS:|. The inner membrane protein |FRAME: EG10344-MONOMER "FtsW"| has also been shown to act as a lipid II flippase in vitro |CITS: |. The inner membrane protein |FRAME: EG10607-MONOMER "RodA"| has been implicated in lipid II translocation |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |Related reviews: |CITS: |Comments: |CITS: |

Catalyzes the hydrolysis of the N-acetyl group of N-acetylglucosamine-6-phosphate (GlcNAc-6-P) to yield glucosamine 6-phosphate and acetate. In vitro, can also hydrolyze substrate analogs such as N-thioacetyl-D-glucosamine-6-phosphate, N-trifluoroacetyl-D-glucosamine-6-phosphate, N-acetyl-D-glucosamine-6-sulfate, N-acetyl-D-galactosamine-6-phosphate, and N-formyl-D-glucosamine-6-phosphate. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:16630633, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17567047, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17567048, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2190615, ECO:0000269|PubMed:4861885, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9143339}.

MetaCyc_Comment: N-acetylglucosamine-6-phosphate deacetylase catalyzes the first cytoplasmic reaction in the metabolism of N-acetyl-D-glucosamine. N-acetylglucosamine can serve as the sole source of carbon for E. coli and is transported into the cell via phosphotransferase transport systems. It thus reaches the cytoplasm in the phosphorylated form, N-acetylglucosamine-6-phosphate. A catalytic mechanism of NagA involving the formation of a tetrahedral intermediate has been proposed |CITS: |, and the function of amino acids and the Zn2+ within the active site has been modelled |CITS: |. The rate-limiting step is the cleavage of the amide bond |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the apoenzyme, the Zn2+-containing enzyme, and a mutant have been solved |CITS: |. The enzyme is a homotetramer both in solution |CITS: | and in the crystal structure |CITS: |. nagA mutants are unable to grow on N-acetylglucosamine as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: |. NagA: "N-acetylglucosamine" |CITS: | Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: UmpH is a ribonucleoside tri-, di-, and monophosphatase with a preference for purines |CITS: |. The enzyme was found to degrade "overflow" UMP nucleotides and is required for optimal growth in response to environmental pyrimidine intermediates |CITS: |. UMP accumulation to levels above the Km of the enzyme, triggered by environmental conditions or artificially induced by mutations in the normal feedback regulation of the pyrimidine biosynthesis pathway, appear to cause the overflow degradation of UMP by UmpH |CITS: |. Though UmpH is a member of the nag N-acetylglucosamine utilization operon, it is a fairly general ribonucleotide monophosphatase |CITS: |. A type IIA member of the HAD protein superfamily, UmpH shows peak activity with UMP, but is also a very effective phosphatase with AMP, GMP and CMP |CITS: |. The structure of UmpH has been solved to 1.8 Å resolution |CITS: |. A umpH null mutant shows somewhat impaired growth upon addition of orotate, an intermediate in the |FRAME: PWY0-162 "pyrimidine biosynthesis pathway"|, to the growth medium. However, growth recovers, and the final culture density is higher than for wild type cells |CITS: |. Overexpression of umpH induces a stress response, including increased expression of rpoH, and enables improved expression of certain recombinant membrane proteins |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Non-essential, abundant cell division factor that is required for proper Z-ring formation. It is recruited early to the divisome by direct interaction with FtsZ, stimulating Z-ring assembly and thereby promoting cell division earlier in the cell cycle. Its recruitment to the Z-ring requires functional FtsA or ZipA. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:18394147}.
FUNCTION: High-affinity transporter for guanine and hypoxanthine. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:24214977}.

GhxP has been implicated in transport of the purine base analogs |FRAME: CPD-15922|, |FRAME: CPD-15921|, |FRAME: CPD-15916|, |FRAME: CPD-5721| and |FRAME: CPD-15920| |CITS: |. GhxP is a member of the nucleobase-cation symporter-2 (NCS2) family of transporters |CITS: |. A ghxP transposon mutation suppresses the sensitivity of a Δ|FRAME: G6487 "ycbX"| strain to the purine analogues, 6-hydroxyaminopurine and 2-amino-6-hydroxyaminopurine. A ΔghxP strain is also less sensitive to 6-mercaptopurine and 6-thioguanine than wild type |CITS: |. ghxP contains a PurR binding motif |CITS: | and PurR dependent repression of ghxP is induced by exogenous adenine |CITS: |. Membrane topology predictions using experimentally determined C terminus locations indicate that GhxP has 13 transmembrane helices and the C-terminus is located in the periplasm |CITS: , |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Antitoxin component of a type V toxin-antitoxin (TA) system. Neutralizes the toxic effects of toxin GhoT by digesting ghoT transcripts in a sequence-specific manner (PubMed:22941047). In concert with GhoT is involved in reducing cell growth during antibacterial stress (PubMed:24373067). Overexpression leads to transcript level reduction of 20 other mRNAs involved in purine or pyrimidine synthesis and transport. Not seen to bind its own promoter DNA (PubMed:22941047). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:22941047, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24373067}.

FUNCTION: Required for the formation of a threonylcarbamoyl group on adenosine at position 37 (t(6)A37) in tRNAs that read codons beginning with adenine. Is probably involved in the transfer of the threonylcarbamoyl moiety of threonylcarbamoyl-AMP (TC-AMP) to the N6 group of A37, together with TsaD and TsaB. TsaE seems to play an indirect role in the t(6)A biosynthesis pathway, possibly in regulating the core enzymatic function of TsaD. Displays ATPase activity in vitro. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:22378793}.
MetaCyc_Comment: TsaE is involved in the biosynthesis of the threonylcarbamoyladenosine (t6A) residue at position 37 of ANN-decoding tRNAs. A mixture of purified |FRAME: G7698-MONOMER TsaC|, |FRAME: EG11171-MONOMER TsaD|, |FRAME: G6991-MONOMER TsaB|, and TsaE proteins catalyzes formation of t6A in the presence of a tRNA substrate, ATP, threonine and bicarbonate in vitro |CITS: |. The three essential proteins TsaE, TsaB and TsaD form an interaction network. TsaB can interact with both TsaE and TsaD directly, and the interactions appear to be mutually exclusive |CITS: |. Purified TsaE forms a heterogeneous mixture of oligomers in vitro |CITS: |. The protein is broadly conserved in bacteria and contains motifs characteristic of P-loop ATPases |CITS: |. A crystal structure of Haemophilus influenzae TsaE shows a nucleotide binding fold |CITS: |. Measurements of TsaE's low intrinsic ATPase activity and ADP binding vary; |CITS: | measured ATPase activity with a Km of 1.4 mM and a kcat of 12 h-1 and ADP binding with a Kd of 32 µM; |CITS: | measured ATPase activity with a Km of 169 µM and a Kcat of 0.0026 s-1; |CITS: | measured ADP binding with a Kd of 6.54 µM. The ATPase activity of TsaE is activated by the TsaB-TsaD heterodimer. Site-directed mutants in the predicted ATP binding site and switch regions were generated and biochemically characterized |CITS: |. TsaE belongs to the widely conserved Ubiquitous bacterial Kinase (UbK) family of protein kinases and is able to autophosphorylate in vitro |CITS: |. TsaE is essential for growth in complex media under aerobic conditions |CITS: |, but not under anaerobic conditions |CITS: |. Depletion of the protein results in the formation of enlarged, elongated cells with an unusual distribution of DNA |CITS: |. |FRAME: G6864 rstA| was identified as a multicopy suppressor of the lethal phenotype of a strain with a conditional tsaE deletion |CITS: |. Other multicopy suppressors indicate a link between purine biosynthesis and TsaE function |CITS: |. Other genetic interactions were found |CITS: |. A deletion/insertion mutant containing an extra copy of tsaE suppresses the effects of a tsaDts allele |CITS: |. Expression of tsaE is induced by norfloxacin and other fluoroquinolone antibiotics |CITS: |. TsaE: "threonylcarbamoyl-6(six)-adenosine" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: nhaB encodes a Na+:H+ antiporter |CITS: | implicated in alkaline pH homeostasis. E. coli contains other transporters which mediate active proton uptake for alkaline pH homeostasis including |FRAME: CPLX0-7629 "NhaA"| (the prominent Na+:H+ antiporter), |FRAME: CHAA-MONOMER "ChaA"|, |FRAME: CMR-MONOMER "MdfA"| and |FRAME: YJIO-MONOMER "MdtM"|, each of which may function under varying conditions of external pH and cation composition (see |CITS: |) Purified, reconstituted NhaB is an electrogenic antiporter with a stoichiometry of 3H+:2Na+ |CITS: |. NhaB also contributes to Li+ export (Li+:H+ antiport) at high external Li+ concentrations (0.2 M LiCl) |CITS:|. The E. coli K-12 mutant strain EP432 (ΔnhaA ΔnhaB) is Na+ sensitive and membrane vesicles isolated from this strain lack Na+:H+ antiporter activity |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). The E. coli K-12 mutant strain KNabc (ΔnhaA ΔnhaB ΔchaA) cannot export Na+ and is unable to grow in the presence of of 0.2 M NaCl (or 10 mM LiCl); membrane vesicles prepared from KNabc cells do not show any Na+:H+ antiporter activity |CITS: |. Characterization of mutant strains containing varying combinations of NhaA, NhaB and ChaA is also reported in |CITS: |) (and further |CITS: |). NhaB may be the constitutive Na+:H+ antiporter |CITS: | NhaB is an inner membrane protein with 12 predicted transmembrane segments |CITS:|. Under oxygen limitation nhaB expression shows a complex response to pH; under aerobic conditions expression is highest at acid pH (5.7) |CITS: |. Related reviews: |CITS:|

This latter system is constitutive in nature and catalyses an electrogenic metal phosphate:H+ symport |CITS: |. Pi uptake via Pit is dependent on the presence of divalent cations, like Mg2+, Ca2+, Co2+, or Mn2+, which form soluble metal phosphate (MeHP04) complexes |CITS: |. The Pit system in E. coli K-12 consists of two transporters - PitA and PitB - which have 81% sequence identity at the protein level; pitA is likely constitutive while pitB is repressed or inactivated through the pho regulon; both proteins may have contributed to the kinetic values and substrate specificities determined in earlier studies |CITS: |. The Pit proteins are predicted to contain 10 transmembrane helices |CITS: |. The Pit system also transports the phosphate analogue, arsenate |CITS: | while PitA (but not PitB) has been implicated in the import of tellurite |CITS: |. pitA insertion mutants have increased resistance to Zn(II) associated with reduced uptake of the metal ion (probably as a ZnHPO4 complex) |CITS: |. pitA transcription is regulated by the availability of Zn(II) and Pi; Zn(II) is taken up by the PitA transporter in competition with Mg(II) |CITS: |. PitA is regulated by the |FRAME: RNA0-348| and the small protein |FRAME: MONOMER0-766 "MgtS"|; this regulation impacts bacterial growth under Mg2+ limiting conditions |CITS: |. The PitA phosphate transporter is a member of the Inorganic Phosphate Transporter (PiT) family |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: | * The Pit system is lacking in many E. coli K-10 strains |CITS: |.

PpiA is a homolog of the human enzyme cyclophilin; unlike that enzyme, PpiA activity is only inhibited by high concentrations of cyclosporin A |CITS: | or FK506 |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Exopolyphosphatase (PPX) degrades inorganic polyphosphates (polyP). It has a strong preference for long-chain polyphosphates; activity decreases with smaller size polyP of about 15 residues. PPX acts on the ends of the polyP chain, removing orthophosphate processively |CITS: |. Steady-state levels of polyP are dependent on the level of PPX in the cell |CITS: |. pppGpp and ppGpp strongly inhibit PPX activity while also acting as a substrate; however, GppA is the major source of pppGppase activity in the cell |CITS: |. PPX activity is redox-regulated; the enzyme is highly sensitive to inactivation by oxidation. Thus, oxidative stress conditions lead to accumulation of poly(P), which acts as a global chaperone |CITS: |. The N terminus of PPX contains the active site and belongs to the ASKHA (acetate and sugar kinases, Hsp70, actin) phosphotranferase superfamily, while the C terminus binds polyphosphate. The halves can be expressed separately and combined to form a functional enzyme |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme have been solved at 1.9 Å |CITS: | and 2.2 Å |CITS: | (using E. coli O157:H7, with 100% identical sequence) resolution. The enzyme consists of four domains, with the active site located at the interface between domains I and II. The location of the active site was confirmed by deletions and site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. The active site region opens to a "canyon" that extends along the dimer interface, which may represent the polyP binding site |CITS: |. A strain overexpressing ppx together with ppk has decreased levels of intracellular polyphosphate and increased tolerance to heavy metals such as cadmium compared to a strain that only expresses ppk |CITS: |. Both ppx and ppk ppx mutants are deficient in biofilm formation |CITS: |. A Δppx mutant accumulates polyP that is dispersed throughout the cell; under wild type conditions, polyP forms foci primarily at the cell poles |CITS: |. Expression of Ppx is induced by growth under low phosphate conditions |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: | Note that |CITS: | has been retracted due to phage contamination |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: DauA is an inner membrane protein that transports C4 dicarboxylates in an aerobic, acidic (pH 5) environment. DauA transports the monoanion and dianion form of succinate and fumarate, and the dicarboxylic amino acid aspartate. At pH 5, DauA is the main succinate transporter and |FRAME: DCTA-MONOMER "DctA"|, which is active for dicarboxylate transport at pH 7, is not produced |CITS: |. DauA is required for the optimal expression of DctA at pH 7 |CITS: |. In liquid culture (pH 5) with succinate as the sole carbon source a dauA deletion mutant and a dauA dctA double deletion mutant are unable to grow. In liquid culture (pH 7) with succinate as sole carbon source a dctA deletion mutant grows poorly when compared to a dauA deletion mutant and both grow less than the wild type |CITS: |. DauA can be detected during growth with succinate at pH 5 or pH 7 |CITS: |. Measurement of kinetic parameters for succinate transport indicates that DauA has a weaker affinity for succinate than DctA and a lower maximal transport rate |CITS: |. DauA is present at consistent levels in both wild type and dcuS deleted strains when cultures are grown with succinate as sole carbon source at pH 5 or pH 7 suggesting that, unlike DctA, DauA is not induced by the DcuSR two-component system |CITS: |. DauA is a member of the SLC26 (solute carrier 26)/SulP (sulphate permease) family of anion transporters responsible for the transport of sulphate, chloride and bicarbonate across the plasma membrane |CITS: |. dauA and related sequences from bacteria form a cluster within the SLC 26 family that is independent from the "BicA-like" transporters predicted to be involved in bicarbonate transport |CITS: |. Topology predictions suggest the presence of 12 transmembrane regions and a C-terminal cytoplasmic domain containing a STAS (sulphate transporter antagonist of anti-sigma factor |CITS: |) domain |CITS: , |. The DauA STAS domain co-purifies in a 1:1 complex with |FRAME: EG50003-MONOMER "acyl carrier protein (ACP)"| |CITS: |. DauA consistently co-purifies with proteins involved in fatty acid metabolism - FabA, FabR, FadE and FadJ |CITS: |. dauA and dauA STAS region deletion mutants show reduced growth compared to the wild type at alkaline pH and a dauA deletion shows altered bicarbonate incorporation |CITS: |. DauA is thus predicted to form part of a 'membrane metabolon' which functions to channel external bicarbonate/carbonate directly to enzymes of fatty acid metabolism sequestered by its STAS domain |CITS: |. Bicarbonate transport by DauA was not detected by |CITS: |. Transcription is induced upon biofilm formation |CITS: |. dauA: dicarboxylic acid uptake system A Related reviews: |CITS: |

FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter complex TcyJLN involved in L-cystine import (PubMed:20351115, PubMed:25139244, PubMed:25837721, PubMed:26350134). This high affinity cystine transporter is involved in resistance to oxidative stress by forming a L-cysteine/L-cystine shuttle system with the EamA transporter, which exports L-cysteine as reducing equivalents to the periplasm to prevent the cells from oxidative stress. Exported L-cysteine can reduce the periplasmic hydrogen peroxide to water, and then generated L-cystine is imported back into the cytoplasm via the TcyJLN complex (PubMed:20351115, PubMed:25837721). The system can also transport L-cysteine, diaminopimelic acid (DAP), djenkolate, lanthionine, D-cystine, homocystine, and it mediates accumulation of the toxic compounds L-selenaproline (SCA) and L-selenocystine (SeCys) (PubMed:25139244, PubMed:26350134). Also has weak LD-carboxypeptidase activity on L-mDAP-D-Ala peptide bonds. Partially suppresses a prc disruption mutant. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:23062283, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9158724}.

Incorporation of labelled mDAP into the peptidoglycan sacculi is decreased by up to 80% in the triple deletion strain. Over-expression of any of the three genes from a plasmid allows the triple deletion mutant to grow normally. This suggests that MepS, MepM and MepH perform essential and redundant functions in vivo |CITS: |. mepS encodes a predicted periplasmic surface outer membrane lipoprotein. MepS is monomeric in solution; the C-terminal 126 residues of MepS adopt an α+β fold consisting of four α helices and a sheet of six antiparallel β strands; a Cys-His-His catalytic triad is present in the active site of the protein |CITS: |. mepS is expressed under aerobic and anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Enhances distal genes transcription elongation in a specialized subset of operons that encode extracytoplasmic components. RfaH is recruited into a multi-component RNA polymerase complex by the ops element, which is a short conserved DNA sequence located downstream of the main promoter of these operons. Once bound, RfaH suppresses pausing and inhibits Rho-dependent and intrinsic termination at a subset of sites. Termination signals are bypassed, which allows complete synthesis of long RNA chains. Enhances expression of several operons involved in synthesis of lipopolysaccharides, exopolysaccharides, hemolysin, and sex factor. Also negatively controls expression and surface presentation of AG43 and possibly another AG43-independent factor that mediates cell-cell interactions and biofilm formation. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00951, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10660066, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11983161, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12007406, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1584020, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16452414, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8606157, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8951819, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9171395, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9426123}.

FUNCTION: During stationary phase, converts 70S ribosomes to an immature dimeric form (90S ribosomes) which are converted to inactive 100S ribosomes (a process called ribosomal hibernation) by the hibernation promoting factor HPF (PubMed:18174192, PubMed:7677746). Inactivates ribosomes by covering the peptidyl transferase (PTase) center of the 23S rRNA and the entrance of peptide exit tunnel (PubMed:12473202, PubMed:15066119). However crystallization with T.thermophilus 70S ribosomes shows it binds near the 3'-end of the 16S rRNA near the anti-Shine-Dalgarno sequence, where it would sterically hinder translation initiation (PubMed:22605777). In this crystal binding of RMF induces movement of the 30S head domain away from the rest of the ribosome, presumably so they would more easily form dimers (PubMed:22605777). Also involved in protection against heat stress, but this role is not dependent on the maintenance of ribosome dimers (PubMed:15278243). {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00919, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12473202, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15066119, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15278243, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18174192, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19170772, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7677746, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8440252, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9278503}.

FUNCTION: During stationary phase, promotes and stabilizes dimerization of 70S ribosomes by the ribosome modulation factor (RMF), leading to the formation of inactive 100S ribosomes (PubMed:18174192). Converts immature 90S particles formed by RMF into 100S ribosomes (PubMed:16324148). Crystallization with T.thermophilus 70S ribosomes shows it binds in the channel between the head and body of the 30S subunit, where mRNA, tRNAs, initiation factors IF1 and IF3 and elongation factor G would bind; however RMF is still able to bind (PubMed:22605777). In this crystal binding of HPF induces movement of the 30S head domain away from the rest of the ribosome, presumably so they would more easily form dimers (PubMed:22605777). May also function as a potential translational inhibitor (PubMed:18174192). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11168583, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16324148, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18174192, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19170772, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22605777}.

FUNCTION: An anti-sigma factor for extracytoplasmic function (ECF) sigma factor sigma-E (RpoE). ECF sigma factors are held in an inactive form by an anti-sigma factor until released by regulated intramembrane proteolysis (RIP). RIP occurs when an extracytoplasmic signal triggers a concerted proteolytic cascade to transmit information and elicit cellular responses. The membrane-spanning regulatory substrate protein is first cut periplasmically (site-1 protease, S1P, DegS), then within the membrane itself (site-2 protease, S2P, RseP), while cytoplasmic proteases finish degrading the anti-sigma factor, liberating sigma-E. Overexpression of RseA blocks sigma-E from acting, results in cell lysis in stationary phase and temperature-sensitivity above 37 degrees Celsius. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:23687042, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9159522, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9159523}.

FUNCTION: Negatively modulates the activity of sigma-E (RpoE) by stabilizing RseA under non-stress conditions. Although not essential for association of sigma-E with Rsea it increases their affinity 2- to 3-fold. When bound to RseA it prevents proteolysis by DegS, which is probably relieved by lipopolysaccharide binding (LPS). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10500101, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17360428, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21245315, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23687042, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9159522, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9159523}.

Required for the transport of microcin B17 (MccB17), microcin 25 (Mcc25) and proline-rich antimicrobial peptides (such as Cathelicidin-3, Arasin 1 and Dro/Drosocin) into the cell. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17725560, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3543211, ECO:0000269|PubMed:36997646, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7768835, ECO:0000305|PubMed:26860543}.

FUNCTION: Negative regulator of replication initiation, which contributes to regulation of DNA replication and ensures that replication initiation occurs exactly once per chromosome per cell cycle. Binds to pairs of hemimethylated GATC sequences in the oriC region, thus preventing assembly of replication proteins and re-initiation at newly replicated origins. Repression is relieved when the region becomes fully methylated. Can also bind to hemimethylated GATC sequences outside of oriC region. Binds, with less affinity, to fully methylated GATC sites and affects timing of replication. May play a role in chromosome organization and gene regulation. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00908, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10931282, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11080170, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20689753, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7553853, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7891562, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8011018}.

SspB activates the ATPase activity of ClpX. This mechanism prevents the premature segregation of damaged DNA to daughter cells during cell division. MetaCyc_Comment: Ribulose-5-phosphate 3-epimerase (Rpe) is an enzyme of the non-oxidative branch of the pentose phosphate pathway. Rpe requires ferrous iron for activity and is vulnerable to damage by H2O2 due to Fenton chemistry. Mn2+, Co2+ and Zn2+ can substitute for Fe2+ to varying degrees, and Rpe containing these alternative cations is not vulnerable to H2O2. Induction of the managnese transporter can protect Rpe from H2O2 damage |CITS: |. An rpe mutant strain does not grow on minimal medium containing either ribose or xylose, but grows when both sugars are present |CITS: |. rpe mutant strains have a growth defect in complex medium and a more severe growth defect in minimal medium containing glycolytic carbon sources or gluconate |CITS: |. A mutation in rpe, drsE30, supresses the temperature-sensitive growth defect of the dnaR130 mutant allele |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: In eubacteria ppGpp (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-diphosphate) is a mediator of the stringent response which coordinates a variety of cellular activities in response to changes in nutritional abundance. This enzyme catalyzes both the synthesis and degradation of ppGpp. The second messengers ppGpp and c-di-GMP together control biofilm formation in response to translational stress; ppGpp represses biofilm formation while c-di-GMP induces it. ppGpp activates transcription of CsrA-antagonistic small RNAs CsrB and CsrC, which down-regulate CsrA's action on translation during the stringent response (PubMed:21488981). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:14622409, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19460094, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21488981}.

MetaCyc_Comment: SpoT is a key enzyme involved in the stringent response in Escherichia coli. It is a bifunctional enzyme with both hydrolase and synthetase activities |CITS: |. The ppGpp hydrolase activity of SpoT has a major physiological role in ppGpp degradation |CITS: | and is inhibited under conditions of physiological stress. Its amino acid sequence has been shown to be extensively related to that of RelA |CITS: |. RelA is involved in the E. coli stringent response triggered by amino acid starvation, activating (p)ppGpp synthesis via a ribosomal mechanism |CITS: |. SpoT provides the hydrolase activity for this RelA-dependent synthetase activity. The physiological role of the RelA-independent, spoT-encoded synthetase activity is less clear. This activity is also referred to as ppGpp synthetase II or PSII, whereas the RelA synthetase activity is referred to as PSI |CITS: |. PSII activity was demonstrated in relA null mutants and it was shown that relA/spoT null mutants did not synthesize ppGpp |CITS: |. The SpoT PSII activity has been proposed to have a role in maintaining the basal level of ppGpp during exponential growth. PSII is relatively inactive during amino acid starvation, is activated by other sources of stress, and is active during exponential growth. In contrast, the RelA-encoded PSI activity is activated by amino acid starvation and has little activity during exponential growth |CITS: |. Although incompletely understood, the regulation of ppGpp levels by the spoT-encoded hydrolase and PSII synthetase activities involves sensing sources of nutrient stress other than amino acid starvation. These include a limitation in fatty acid synthesis |CITS: |, phosphate starvation (which elevates (p)ppGpp levels by a mechanism involving IraP, RssB and RpoS) |CITS: |, and iron limitation |CITS: |. SpoT PSII activity may be necessary for increasing the ppGpp levels in these conditions, although how it detects them is still under investigation. In the case of fatty acid starvation, there is in vivo and in vitro evidence for a model in which acyl carrier protein specifically interacts with SpoT and may trigger a SpoT conformational change leading to (p)ppGpp accumulation. The interaction between ACP and SpoT was demonstrated in co-purification experiments and in a bacterial two-hybrid system |CITS: |. Another interaction has been reported between SpoT and the 50S ribosomal subunit-associated GTPase, CgtAE (ObgE). The two proteins were shown to co-purify. The possible involvement of CgtAE in the control of SpoT function, or an effect of SpoT on CgtAE activity were suggested |CITS: |. In addition to the ppGpp hydrolase and synthetase activity of SpoT, SpoT also has pppGpp hydrolase activity |CITS: | and possibly pppGpp synthetase activity. The putative pppGpp synthetase activity is based the observation that in ΔrelA/Δgpp mutants starved for glucose pppGpp accumulates, which suggests phosphoryl group transfer to GTP as well as GDP, although the phsophoryl donor is not known (cited as unpublished data in Cashel et. al. (1996) "The Stringent Response", chapter 92, in |CITS: |). SpoT has been studied both mutationally and biochemically. Deletion mutants of spoT were analyzed for their ability to complement chromosomal mutations defective in synthetase or hydrolase activities. This allowed mapping of ppGpp hydrolase activity to the first 203 amino acids and the PSII activity to an overlapping region comprising amino acids 67-374. This suggested separate, but closely linked catalytic sites in the amino acid sequence |CITS: |. A site-directed mutagenesis study suggested that Asp293 is required for ppGpp synthetase activity |CITS: |. Proteolysis studies of partially purified, recombinant SpoT identified two major domains (Met1-Phe373 and Glu374-Asn702) each containing two minor sub-domains. In vivo expression studies suggested that ppGpp synthetic activity was associated with the N-terminal domain |CITS: |. In comparison, proteolysis studies done on the bifunctional Rel/Spo homolog from Streptococcus equisimilis localized hydrolase and synthase activities to the N-terminal half of the protein, whereas the C-terminal half appeared to have a regulatory function |CITS: |. The crystal structure of a fragment containing the catalytic region of this S. equisimilis protein was determined at 2.1 Å resolution |CITS: |. A relA spoT mutant was found to form biofilms with reduced catalase activity and elevated levels of hydroxyl radicals; the biofilms of mutants were more sensitive to the antibiotics ofloxacin and tobramycin than were biofilms formed by wild type |CITS: |. Spot mutant strains with missense mutations in the relA gene showed an increase in glycogen content and elevated levels of glycogen gene expression when these strains were grown in Kornberg medium |CITS: |. Mutant strains lacking SpoT functions are incapable of growth in minimal medium M9 |CITS: |.

FUNCTION: Binds 16S rRNA, required for the assembly of 30S particles and may also be responsible for determining the conformation of the 16S rRNA at the A site.

FUNCTION: One of the primary rRNA binding proteins, it binds specifically to the 5'-end of 16S ribosomal RNA (PubMed:4598121). Also plays a role in translational accuracy; neamine-resistant ribosomes show reduced neamine-induced misreading in vitro (PubMed:765484, PubMed:781296). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:4598121, ECO:0000269|PubMed:765484, ECO:0000269|PubMed:781296}.

FUNCTION: Required for translation of most natural mRNAs except for leaderless mRNA (PubMed:12068815, PubMed:17376482, PubMed:24339747, PubMed:7003157, PubMed:9677288). Binds mRNA upstream of the Shine-Dalgarno (SD) sequence and helps it bind to the 30S ribosomal subunit; acts as an RNA chaperone to unfold structured mRNA on the ribosome but is not essential for mRNAs with strong SDs and little 5'-UTR structure, thus it may help fine-tune which mRNAs that are translated (PubMed:24339747). Unwinds dsRNA by binding to transiently formed ssRNA regions; binds about 10 nucleotides (PubMed:22908248). Has a preference for polypyrimidine tracts (PubMed:778845). Negatively autoregulates its own translation (PubMed:2120211). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12068815, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15340139, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1712292, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17376482, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2120211, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22908248, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24339747, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7003157, ECO:0000269|PubMed:778845, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9677288}.; FUNCTION: It is not clear if it plays a role in trans-translation (a process which rescues stalled ribosomes). Evidence for its role; binds to tmRNA with very high affinity, is required for binding of tmRNA to 30S subunit (PubMed:11101533, PubMed:15340139). Thought to play a role only in translation of the tmRNA in vitro (PubMed:17392345). Evidence against its role; overexpression of whole protein or various S1 fragments inhibits translation, they have no effect on trans-translation, and an in vitro system with S1-less ribosomes performs trans-translation (PubMed:15340139, PubMed:17376482). In trans-translation Ala-aminoacylated transfer-messenger RNA (tmRNA, product of the ssrA gene; the 2 termini fold to resemble tRNA(Ala) while it encodes a short internal open reading frame (the tag peptide)) acts like a tRNA, entering the A-site of the ribosome and displacing the stalled mRNA (which is subsequently degraded). The ribosome then switches to translate the ORF on the tmRNA, the nascent peptide is terminated with the 'tag peptide' encoded by the tmRNA and thus targeted for degradation. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11101533, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15340139, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17376482, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17392345}.; FUNCTION: (Microbial infection) During infection by bacteriophage Qbeta, part of the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase complex; this subunit is required for RNA replication initiation activity during synthesis of (-) strand RNA from the (+) strand genomic RNA but not for (+) strand synthesis from the (-) strand (PubMed:25122749, PubMed:6358207). Binds an approximately 70 nucleotide RNA internal to the viral replicase gene (the M-site) (PubMed:25122749). Others have reported it is not involved in RNA replication initiation but rather in termination of RNA synthesis and is required for termination whether it is the (+) or (-) strand that is being synthesized (PubMed:23653193). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:23653193, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25122749, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6358207, ECO:0000269|PubMed:816798}.; FUNCTION: (Microbial infection) During infection by bacteriophage T4, plays a significant role in substrate choice by viral endoribonuclease RegB. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17130171}.

Exhibits sequence and structure-selective cleavage of four-way DNA junctions, where it introduces symmetrical nicks in two strands of the same polarity at the 5' side of CC dinucleotides. Corrects the defects in genetic recombination and DNA repair associated with inactivation of ruvAB or ruvC.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter complex UgpBAEC involved in sn-glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P) import (PubMed:23013274, PubMed:2842304). Can also transport glycerophosphoryl diesters, which are hydrolyzed to G3P and alcohol during transport (PubMed:2842304). The G3P moiety can be detected in the cytoplasm whereas the corresponding alcohol is usually found in the culture medium (PubMed:2842304). Binds G3P and glycerophosphocholine, but not glycerol-2-phosphate (PubMed:23013274). It was proposed by Yang et al that the complex could also transport glycerol-2-phosphate (G2P) in vivo, but as it was shown later by Wuttge et al that UgpB does not bind G2P, this transport activity is questioned (PubMed:19429609, PubMed:23013274). G2P might be converted in the periplasm to G3P before its transport (PubMed:23013274). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19429609, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23013274, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2842304}.; FUNCTION: In the absence of G3P, UgpB can serve as a potent molecular chaperone that exhibits anti-aggregation activity against bile salt-induced protein aggregation (PubMed:32882062). The substrate G3P, which is known to accumulate in the later compartments of the digestive system, triggers a functional switch between UgpB's activity as a molecular chaperone and its activity as a G3P transporter (PubMed:32882062). Chaperone and G3P binding activities are likely mutually exclusive activities (PubMed:32882062). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:32882062}.

FUNCTION: Part of the Sec protein translocase complex. Interacts with the SecYEG preprotein conducting channel. SecDF uses the proton motive force (PMF) to complete protein translocation after the ATP-dependent function of SecA. The large periplasmic domain is thought to have a base and head domain joined by a hinge; movement of the hinge may be coupled to both proton transport and protein export, with the head domain capturing substrate, and a conformational change preventing backward movement and driving forward movement. Expression of V.alginolyticus SecD and SecF in E.coli confers Na(+)-dependent protein export, strongly suggesting SecDF functions via cation-coupled protein translocation. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:21562494}.
MetaCyc_Comment: SecD is an inner membrane protein that is part of the heterotrimeric Sec translocon accessory complex. Early studies characterized the secD locus, composed of yajC-secD-secF, and implicated the products of secD and secF in protein export |CITS:|. SecD and SecF are not absolutely essential but are required for efficient protein transport; secDF double null mutants have a severe protein export defect at 37°C which is exacerbated at 23 °C; overexpressing SecD and SecF improves the export of proteins with a defective signal sequence |CITS: |. SecD and SecF are implicated in SecA membrane cycling at SecYEG in vitro |CITS: | (see further |CITS: |). Function [CC]: FUNCTION: The central subunit of the protein translocation channel SecYEG. Consists of two halves formed by TMs 1-5 and 6-10. These two domains form a lateral gate at the front which open onto the bilayer between TMs 2 and 7, and are clamped together by SecE at the back. The channel is closed by both a pore ring composed of hydrophobic SecY resides and a short helix (helix 2A) on the extracellular side of the membrane which forms a plug. The plug probably moves laterally to allow the channel to open. The ring and the pore may move independently. SecY is required to insert newly synthesized SecY into the inner membrane. Overexpression of some hybrid proteins has been thought to jam the protein secretion apparatus resulting in cell death; while this may be true, overexpression also results in FtsH-mediated degradation of SecY.
MetaCyc_Comment: The SecY inner membrane protein is the core component of the heterotrimeric SecYEG preprotein translocase; SecY forms the protein conducting channel with channel plug and hydrophobic seal; SecY contains a signal sequence binding pocket and cytosolic loops that interact with partner proteins (see |CITS: | and |CITS: |). SecY is required for efficient protein translocation across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: |. A temperature sensitive SecY mutant (ts24) accumulates the precursor form of periplasmic and envelope proteins (OmpA and MBP) in the cytoplasm when grown at the non-permissive temperature |CITS: |. SecY supports the posttranslational translocation of proOmpA across the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: |. SecY is essential when translocation is reconstituted in proteoliposomes in vitro |CITS: |; SecY, SecE and an unidentified polypeptide termed 'band1' (later shown to be SecG |CITS: |) form a stable complex which supports precursor protein translocation in vitro |CITS: |. Precursor proteins interact with SecY during translocation |CITS:|. SecY binds synthetic signal peptide in vitro |CITS: |. The insertion of mannitol permease into the inner membrane requires SecY |CITS: |. SecY interacts with FtsY in vitro |CITS:|; FtsY binds SecY to form a 400-kD FtsY-SecY translocon complex |CITS: |. During cotranslational targeting, FtsY interacts with the cytosolic loops of SecY which also serve as docking sites for the ribosome and SecA |CITS: |. SecY is an integral inner membrane protein |CITS: |. Sec Y contains contains 10 transmembrane domains, 5 periplasmic domains and 6 cytosolic domains. The N and C-termini are located in the cytoplasm |CITS: |. SecY oligomers mediate translocation: one copy of the SecY complex forms the translocation pore while a nontranslocating SecY molecule provides the interaction site for SecA |CITS: |. SecY molecules can associate with one another in the membrane but single molecules are sufficient for both co- and post-translational translocation in vivo |CITS: |. Cardiolipin binds to SecY; SecY variants which have reduced affinity for cardiolipin are associated with decreased stimulation of SecA ATPase activity and less efficient Sec-mediated protein translocation in vitro; additionally the PMF stimulation of translocation observed in wild type SecYEG inner membrane vesicles is lost when using these SecY variants |CITS: |. The SecY translocon is involved in CDI toxin import |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). secY: secretion |CITS: |prlA: protein localization: |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |Related reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Sigma factors are initiation factors that promote the attachment of RNA polymerase to specific initiation sites and are then released. This sigma factor is involved in regulation of expression of heat shock genes. Intracellular concentration of free RpoH protein increases in response to heat shock, which causes association with RNA polymerase (RNAP) and initiation of transcription of heat shock genes, including numerous global transcriptional regulators and genes involved in maintaining membrane functionality and homeostasis. UhpT has been purified and reconstituted into liposomes and demonstrated to transport hexose 6-phosphates via an inorganic phosphate antiport mechanism |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: SodC, or CuZnSOD, is one of three superoxide dismutases in E. coli that convert superoxide radicals to hydrogen peroxide and water. The three enzymes differ in their metal cofactor requirement. SodC is the only periplasmic enzyme |CITS: |. Periplasmic superoxide may be generated by autooxidation of dihydromenaquinone in the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: |. SodC is inactivated by cyanide and diethyldithiocarbamate, suggesting that it contains both copper and zinc |CITS: |. Both metal ions can be identified in the crystal structure |CITS: |. Addition of either copper or zinc increases the thermal stability of the purified enzyme |CITS: |. SodC is monomeric even at high protein concentration and in a number of buffers |CITS: |. Charged residues in portions of the protein that are typically hydrophobic dimer interfaces may explain this |CITS: |. A crystal structure of SodC has been solved at 2 Å resolution |CITS: |. Unlike the bovine enzyme, SodC from E. coli is quite resistant to inactivation by hydrogen peroxide. SodC may protect E. coli from killing by macrophages |CITS: |. Diethyldithiocarbamate inhibits SodC activity and inhibits aerobic growth of a sodA sodB mutant strain |CITS: |. A sodC mutant is more sensitive to hydrogen peroxide at the onset of stationary phase than wild type |CITS: |. Decreased expression of sodC confers resistance to exogenous methylglyoxal |CITS: |. SodC expression is repressed during anaerobiosis |CITS: | and is induced in stationary phase by RpoS, which helps diminish the enhanced sensitivity to hydrogen peroxide that occurs for several hours after entry into stationary phase following aerobic growth |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: SodB, or FeSOD, is one of three superoxide dismutases in E. coli |CITS: |. The three enzymes differ in their metal cofactor requirement; FeSOD contains iron. Superoxide dismutase is implicated in the response to a large number of environmental changes that lead to the generation of superoxide radicals. FeSOD and the manganese-containing enzyme MnSOD (SodA) are not functionally equivalent; MnSOD is more effective than FeSOD in preventing damage to DNA, while FeSOD seems more effective in protecting a cytoplasmic superoxide-sensitive enzyme |CITS: |. However, both enzymes were shown to protect dihydroxy acid dehydratase from inactivation by oxidative stress |CITS: |. The reaction mechanism involves cycling of the metal ion between the +3 and +2 oxidation states; the midpoint potential of the metal ion determines what redox reactions are possible, and is thus precisely tuned |CITS: |. Crystal structures of FeSOD have been solved |CITS: |. Tyr34 is required for maximal activity |CITS: |; its contribution to substrate binding has been evaluated |CITS: |. The enzyme is highly specific for the iron cofactor; a manganese-substituted FeSOD is catalytically inactive |CITS: |. Mutations in Q69 and A141 alter metal selectivity and catalytic activity |CITS: |. The activity of FeSOD correlates with the chemical properties of glutamine at position 69 |CITS: |; hydrogen bonding interactions of Glu affect the the pK of the Fe-bound solvent ligand |CITS: |. Under anaerobic conditions, FeSOD is the only superoxide dismutase enzyme present in E. coli |CITS: |. A sodB mutant shows a lag period when an anaerobic culture is shifted to aerobic conditions; this is due to damage to enzymes in the branched chain amino acid biosynthesis pathway |CITS: |. Expression of FeSOD is dependent on Fur |CITS: | and is induced by high temperatures |CITS: |. Positive regulation by Fur is indirect via the small RNA RyhB |CITS: |. SodB expression is induced by acidic pH |CITS: |. In minimal medium, a sodB mutant is more sensitive to paraquat than wild type |CITS: |. Under aerobic conditions, a sodA sodB double mutant is able to grow slowly on rich medium, but not on minimal glucose medium unless it is supplemented with a full complement of amino acids |CITS: |. The ssa suppressor mutation in dapD enables growth under these conditions |CITS: |. The sodA sodB double mutant is able to grow under anaerobic conditions |CITS: |. The sodA sodB double mutant has an increased mutation rate in the presence of oxygen |CITS: | and is more sensitive to aerobic heat stress than wild type |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

The sstT gene has been cloned and shown to complement a serine transport mutant |CITS:|. The SstT protein has been purified and demonstrated in reconstituted proteoliposomes to mediate the transport of serine driven by electrochemical sodium ion gradient with a Km and Vmax of 0.82 μM and 0.37 nmol/min/mg protein respectively. Serine transport was inhibited by L-threonine, but not by other amino acids |CITS:|.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the reduction of quinones (PubMed:14766567). Acts by simultaneous two-electron transfer, avoiding formation of highly reactive semiquinone intermediates and producing quinols that promote tolerance of H(2)O(2). Quinone reduction is probably the primary biological role of ChrR (By similarity). Can also reduce toxic chromate to insoluble and less toxic Cr(3+). Catalyzes the transfer of three electrons to Cr(6+) producing Cr(3+) and one electron to molecular oxygen without producing the toxic Cr(5+) species and only producing a minimal amount of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Chromate reduction protects the cell against chromate toxicity, but is likely a secondary activity (PubMed:14766567, PubMed:17088379, PubMed:22558308). Can also reduce potassium ferricyanide, 2,6-dichloroindophenol, V(5+), Mo(6+), methylene blue, cytochrome c and U(6+) (PubMed:14766567, PubMed:17088379). During chromate reduction, is able to use both NAD or NADP equally well (PubMed:14766567). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:Q88FF8, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14766567, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17088379, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22558308}.

MetaCyc_Comment: YieF is a flavoprotein containing the FMN cofactor; it belongs to the flavodoxin superfamily of enzymes |CITS: |. The enzyme is able to reduce chromate in vitro |CITS: |. Chromate (VI) is primarily an anthropogenic environmental contaminant, and thus it is unlikely that YieF has evolved specifically for Cr(VI) detoxification. YieF was shown to possess quinone reductase activity which may guard against oxidative stress by preventing redox cycling of quinones which would otherwise generate ROS, and by maintaining a pool of reduced quinone in the cell that is able to quench ROS directly (|CITS: | and Ackerley et al., unpublished). The quinone reductase activity of YieF is likely the primary biological role of this enzyme |CITS: |. Evidence is consistent with the model of an obligatory four-electron reduction of chromate, where the enzyme transfers three electrons to Cr(VI), producing Cr(III), and one electron to molecular oxygen or an oxygen equivalent - without producing the toxic Cr(V) species and only producing the minimal amount of reactive oxygen species (ROS) |CITS: |. Chromate reductase may be inhibited by certain divalent cations |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the enzyme has been solved at 2.2 Å resolution, showing a dimer-of-dimers quarternary structure |CITS: |. An earlier study reported a homodimeric structure |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis of residues forming a hydrogen bond network at the dimer-dimer interface result in improved chromate reductase activity |CITS: |. The dynamic behavior of FMN-bound YieF has been simulated |CITS: |. Expression of yieF is induced in stationary phase and by the presence of chromate |CITS: |. Overexpression of YieF results in a two-fold increase in chromate reduction without affecting growth |CITS: | and increases hydrogen peroxide tolerance and scavenging (Ackerley et al., unpublished). A yieF mutant has increased sensitivity to chromate |CITS: |. An evolved derivative of YieF with improved chromate reductase activity is being investigated as a prodrug-activating enzyme in cancer chemotherapy |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Succinyl-CoA synthetase functions in the citric acid cycle (TCA), coupling the hydrolysis of succinyl-CoA to the synthesis of either ATP or GTP and thus represents the only step of substrate-level phosphorylation in the TCA. The alpha subunit of the enzyme binds the substrates coenzyme A and phosphate, while succinate binding and nucleotide specificity is provided by the beta subunit. Can use either ATP or GTP, but prefers ATP. It can also function in the other direction for anabolic purposes, and this may be particularly important for providing succinyl-CoA during anaerobic growth when the oxidative route from 2-oxoglutarate is severely repressed. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_01988, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10353839}.

MetaCyc_Comment: SucD is the α subunit of succinyl-CoA synthetase. His246 is the phosphorylated residue of the reaction intermediate. A His246Asp mutant can not autophosphoryate and has no catalytic activity |CITS: |. A His142 mutant is catalytically inactive for the overall reaction, but the enzyme can be phosphorylated with ATP and dephosphorylated with succinate |CITS: |. Glu208 is essential for phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of His246 |CITS: |. The conserved Cys123 is not required for catalytic activity |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Stimulates the cysteine desulfurase activity of CsdA. Contains a cysteine residue (Cys-61) that acts to accept sulfur liberated via the desulfurase activity of CsdA.
