MetaCyc_Comment: XylE is a D-xylose/proton symporter, one of two systems in E. coli K-12 responsible for the uptake of D-xylose - the other being the ATP-dependent ABC transporter XylFGH. The cloned xylE gene has been shown to complement xylE mutants in vivo |CITS: |. XylE-mediated transport in whole cells is inhibited by protonophores and elicits an alkaline pH change |CITS: |. Experiments using xylE and xylF mutants have established that XylE has a Km of 63-169 μM for D-xylose |CITS: |. Crystal structures of XylE bound to the ligands D-xylose, D-glucose and the chemically synthesized glucose derivative, 6-bromo-6-deoxy-D-glucose have been obtained at 2.6 - 2.9 Å. Structures were captured in an outward facing conformation. XylE contains 12 transmembrane (TM) helices organised into two distinct domains with amino and carboxy termini located on the cytosolic side of the membrane. XylE also contains an intracellular domain consisting of 4 helices - 3 of these connect the TM domains, the fourth is located at the C-terminal end of the protein |CITS: |. Crystal structures of XylE in an inward open conformation are also available |CITS: , |. D-glucose is a strong inhibitor of xylose transport in in vitro sugar competition assays. Other hexose and pentose sugars (D-galactose, L-fucose, L-arabinose, D-mannose and L-rhamnose) had no effect |CITS: |. D-glucose does not induce the XylE transport system |CITS: |. XylE mutants with neutral replacements at Asp27 (XylE D27N and XylE D27A) do not catalyse D-xylose:H+ symport although binding and counterflow activity remain similar to the wild-type suggesting that Asp27 is involved in proton transport. A XylE double mutant Q175I / L297F transports D-glucose although at a lower level than D-xylose |CITS: |. Specific lipid-protein interactions affect the conformational dynamics of XylE; phosphotidylethanolamine disrupts a charge-relay network present on the intracellular side of XylE and triggers a conformational shift towards the inward facing state in vitro |CITS: |. XylE is a member of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) of transporters |CITS: |. The xylE gene probably constitutes a monocistronic operon whose expression is inducible by D-xylose. Imported xylose is catabolised to xylulose-5-phosphate by the action of the XylA and XylB enzymes.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the anaerobic formation of alpha-ketobutyrate and ammonia from threonine in a two-step reaction. The first step involved a dehydration of threonine and a production of enamine intermediates (aminocrotonate), which tautomerizes to its imine form (iminobutyrate). Both intermediates are unstable and short-lived. The second step is the nonenzymatic hydrolysis of the enamine/imine intermediates to form 2-ketobutyrate and free ammonia. In the low water environment of the cell, the second step is accelerated by RidA. TdcB also dehydrates serine to yield pyruvate via analogous enamine/imine intermediates. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10388709, ECO:0000269|PubMed:13405870, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15390404}.

ThiL catalyzes the phosphorylation of thiamine monophosphate to yield thiamine diphosphate in the presence of ATP and Mg2+ |CITS: |. Mutations in thiL resulted in a requirement for thiamine pyrophosphate for growth |CITS: |. In Salmonella typhimurium, altered ThiL activity resulted in decreased repression of transcription of thiamine pyrophosphate-regulated genes |CITS: |. The ThiL structure with substrate and product complexes in Aquifex aeolicus was determined |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Thioesterase that has relatively broad substrate specificity, hydrolyzing primarily medium- and long-chain acyl-CoA substrates to free fatty acids and CoA (PubMed:1645722, PubMed:20547355, PubMed:24271180). Functions in the thioesterase-dependent pathway of beta-oxidation of oleate and conjugated linoleate ((9Z,11E)-octadecadienoate or CLA), which provides all energy and carbon precursors required for the growth of E.coli. Thus, supports growth on oleate or conjugated linoleate as the sole source of carbon by hydrolyzing 3,5-tetradecadienoyl-CoA, the terminal metabolite of oleate beta-oxidation via the alternative thioesterase-dependent pathway, and 3,5-dodecadienoyl-CoA, the end product of CLA beta-oxidation, respectively (PubMed:14707139, PubMed:18702504). MetaCyc_Comment: Thioesterase II (TesB) is one of a number of thioesterases present in E. coli. The enzyme has relatively broad substrate specificity, cleaving medium- and long-chain acyl-CoA substrates |CITS: |. Thioesterase II is one of the thioesterases supporting growth on oleate or conjugated linoleic acid as the sole source of carbon |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the enzyme has been solved at 1.9 Å resolution. TesB appears to be a homodimer in the crystal structure |CITS: |, while data from non-denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis suggested a homotetrameric structure |CITS: |. The D204 residue was predicted to be in the active site; its importance was confirmed by kinetic analysis of mutants |CITS: |. Strains either lacking or overproducing tesB have no obvious defect |CITS: |. Overproduction of TesB relieves inhibition of fatty acid synthesis by long-chain acyl-ACP molecules that accumulate upon glycerol starvation |CITS: |. TesB has been used in the engineered production of enantiopure |FRAME: CPD-335| and |FRAME: CPD-1843| |CITS: | and in the engineered reversal of the β-oxidation cycle |CITS: |.

Toxin transport is strain-specific, mutations in this gene do not confer resistance to several other tested CdiA toxins. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:26305955}.
MetaCyc_Comment: RbsC is predicted to be the inner membrane subunit of an ATP-dependent ribose uptake system |CITS: |. Topology analysis suggests that it contains 6 transmembrane regions with the N and C-termini located in the cytoplasm |CITS: |. RbsC has been implicated in the import of specific toxins of contact-dependent growth inhibition (CDI) systems in gram-negative bacteria; rbsC transposon insertion mutants and rbsC in-frame deletion mutants are resistant to the CdiA-CT1Dd3937 toxin; inner membrane proteins such as RbsC are thought to act as receptors which bring the nuclease domain of CDI toxins into close proximity with the inner membrane of target cells |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: Tyrosine-tRNA ligase (TyrRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. TyrRS belongs to the Class IC aminoacyl tRNA synthetases |CITS: |. The enzyme is a homodimer in solution |CITS: |. TyrRS binds one molecule of tRNATyr per TyrRS dimer and has two binding sites for tyrosine with different dissociation constants |CITS: |. Other reports find two equivalent tyrosinyl-5'-AMP binding sites |CITS: |; the binding data may require more complex analysis |CITS: |. The reaction mechanism of TyrRS has been studied |CITS: |. Aminoacylation proceeds via the aminoacyl adenylate pathway |CITS: |. TyrRS also aminoacylates tRNATyr with D-tyrosine |CITS: |; the resulting D-Tyr-tRNATyr can be hydrolyzed by |FRAME: EG11852-MONOMER D-Tyr-tRNATyr deacylase| |CITS: |. Discrimination by TyrRS against phenylalanine appears to be at the level of amino acid recognition |CITS: |. The substrate range of TyrRS for non-standard amino acids has been investigated |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNATyr that are important for recognition by TyrRS were found to consist of the discriminator base at position 73 and the first base of the anticodon of tRNATyr |CITS: |. Residues within TyrRS that interact with tRNATyr have been identified |CITS: |, and the Lys237 residue has been implicated in ATP binding |CITS: |. An F130S mutation allows efficient charging of azatyrosine onto tRNATyr |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the catalytic domain of TyrRS in complex with L-tyrosine and Tyr-AMS have been solved at 2 and 2.7 Å resolution |CITS: |. Crystal structures of a mutant protein which recognizes 3-iodo-L-tyrosine have been solved |CITS: |. Several lysine acetylation sites within TyrRS have been identified in proteomics experiments. TyrRS can be non-enzymatically acetylated by acetyl-CoA and acetyl-phosphate and enzymatically deacetylated by CobB. Acetylation at Lys85 or Lys235 significantly decreases the catalytic activity of TyrRS |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the prenylation of para-hydroxybenzoate (PHB) with an all-trans polyprenyl group. Mediates the second step in the final reaction sequence of ubiquinone-8 (UQ-8) biosynthesis, which is the condensation of the polyisoprenoid side chain with PHB, generating the first membrane-bound Q intermediate 3-octaprenyl-4-hydroxybenzoate (PubMed:4552989). Geranyldiphosphate (GPP), all-trans-farnesyldiphosphate (FPP) and all-trans-solanesyldiphosphate (SPP) are also accepted as side chain precursors (PubMed:8155731). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:4552989, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8155731}.

MetaCyc_Comment: 4-Hydroxybenzoate octaprenyltransferase is the second enzyme in the pathway of ubiquinone biosynthesis. It is responsible for the prenylation of 4-hydroxybenzoate using a polyprenyldiphosphate as a side chain precursor. UbiA is an inner membrane protein with seven predicted transmembrane domains. The C terminus is located in the periplasm |CITS: |. Earlier work experimentally localized UbiA to the membrane fraction |CITS: |. The structure of the enzyme and its active site have been modelled |CITS: |. In subsequent work a 3D structural model was developed that places UbiA in SCOP family 48 583. The model was experimentally supported by site-directed mutagenesis studies |CITS: |. ubiA mutants can grow on glucose as the sole source of carbon, but can not grow on succinate |CITS: |. A ubiA- mutant grows more slowly on glucose and accumulates acetate and lactate |CITS: |. The sdgG10 mutation, which suppresses a conditional mutation in dnaG (DNA primase), has been localized to either the ubiC, ubiA or yjbI gene |CITS: |. ubiA belongs to a network of genes which facilitate stress-induced mutagenesis (SIM) in E. coli K-12 |CITS: |. Radiotracer studies have suggested that UbiA, UbiD, and UbiI can utilize p-aminobenzoate, or intermediates derived from it, as substrates |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

FUNCTION: Toxic component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system (PubMed:9767574). A sequence-specific, ribosome-dependent mRNA endoribonuclease that inhibits translation during amino acid starvation (the stringent response). In vitro acts by cleaving mRNA with high codon specificity in the ribosomal A site between positions 2 and 3. The stop codon UAG is cleaved at a fast rate while UAA and UGA are cleaved with intermediate and slow rates. In vitro mRNA cleavage can also occur in the ribosomal E site after peptide release from peptidyl-tRNA in the P site as well as on free 30S subunits (PubMed:12526800). In vivo cuts frequently in the first 100 codons, most frequently after the second and third base and rarely near the stop codon (PubMed:21324908). Overexpression of RelE results in the inhibition of bacterial growth and a sharp decrease in colony-forming ability which is neutralized by the labile cognate antitoxin RelB. Overexpression also sharply increases persisters (cells that neither grow nor die in the presence of bactericidal agents and are largely responsible for high levels of biofilm tolerance to antimicrobials) (PubMed:15576765). Plays a role in dormancy when expressed in high-density cells in the absence of antitoxin RelB; amino acid starvation and an unidentified extracellular factor promote dormancy, while expression of antitoxin RelB restores cell culturability (PubMed:22210768). Acts with RelB as a corepressor of relBE transcription, considerably increasing the repression of RelB alone. 2 RelB dimers bind to 2 operator sequences; DNA-binding and repression is stronger when complexed with toxin/corepressor RelE by conditional cooperativity (PubMed:18501926, PubMed:19747491, PubMed:22981948, PubMed:9767574). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11274135, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11717402, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12123459, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12526800, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15576765, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18501926, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18532983, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19747491, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20005802, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21324908, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22210768, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22981948, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24251350, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9767574}.; FUNCTION: Seems to be a principal mediator of cell death in liquid media (PubMed:19707553). Implicated in hydroxy radical-mediated cell death induced by hydroxyurea treatment (PubMed:20005847). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19707553, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20005847}.; FUNCTION: Cross-talk can occur between different TA systems. Ectopic expression of this toxin induces transcription of 7 tested TA systems (dinJ/yafQ, hicAB, mazEF, mqsRA, prlF(sohA)/yhaV, relBEF and yefM/yoeB) with specific cleavage of the relBEF mRNA produced immediately upstream and within the relB coding sequence. The cleaved mRNA can be translated into RelE, leading to a positive feedback cycle of RelE expression. The relBEF operon is required for transcription of the mazEF TA system operon during amino acid starvation. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:23432955}.

FUNCTION: Antitoxin component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system. Counteracts the effect of cognate toxin RelE via direct protein-protein interaction, preventing RelE from entering the ribosome A site and thus inhibiting its endoribonuclease activity. MetaCyc_Comment: SrkA is a serine/threonine protein kinase that protects cells from several types of lethal stress |CITS: |. SrkA is able to autophosphorylate at serine and threonine, but not tyrosine residues |CITS: |. The protein kinase activity is required for stress protection by SrkA |CITS: |. SrkA is also able to phosphorylate a general kinase substrate, myelin basic protein, in vitro. The native substrate for SrkA has not been identified yet |CITS: |. A crystal structure of SrkA has been determined at 2.8 Å resolution and shows structural similarity to protein kinases |CITS: |. A D217A mutation abolishes catalytic activity |CITS: |. A ΔsrkA mutant is hypersusceptible to the lethal effects of UV light, hydrogen peroxide, nalidixic acid and certain other antibiotics, but does not affect their minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC). Deletion of mazEF rescues the hypersusceptibility phenotype of the ΔsrkA mutant |CITS: |. The dsbA gene is partly cotranscribed from the srkA promoter, which is activated by CpxR |CITS: |. A yihE insertion mutation decreases the abundance of periplasmic DsbA, but does not appear to affect periplasmic disulfide bond formation |CITS: |. RdoA is the YihE homolog in Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium |CITS: | and Shigella flexneri |CITS: |, where it is involved in cellular stress responses. SrkA: "stress response kinase A" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Proton symporter that senses osmotic shifts and responds by importing osmolytes such as proline, glycine betaine, stachydrine, pipecolic acid, ectoine and taurine. It is both an osmosensor and an osmoregulator which is available to participate early in the bacterial osmoregulatory response. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10026245, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3082857, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8421314}.
MetaCyc_Comment: ProP is an osmosensing transporter which mediates the uptake of zwitterionic osmolytes such as proline and glycine betaine; ProP function protects cells from dehydration under conditions of hyperosmotic stress. The proP locus was first defined in E. coli K-12 (strain RM2 ΔputPA) by mutations which eliminate an inducible proline uptake activity and increase resistance to the toxic proline analaog, 3,4-dehydroproline |CITS: |. ProP mediated proline uptake is induced and stimulated by osmotic stress |CITS: |; ProP has similar affinity for proline and glycine betaine |CITS: |. ProP catalyses active proline uptake in cytoplasmic membrane vesicles; ProP activity measured in whole cells is eliminated by the uncoupling agent CCCP and the respiration inhibitor KCN |CITS: |. ProP functions as a proline:H+ symporter |CITS: |; purified ProP reconstituted in liposomes catalyses the active accumulation of proline, this activity requires both membrane potential and an osmotic upshift and maximum uptake occurs in the presence of a pH downshift |CITS: |. ProP also transports the osmoprotectants taurine, ectoine, carnitine, pipecolate, proline betaine, N,N-dimethylglycine, and 1-carboxymethylpyridinium |CITS: |; ProP transports the L-proline analog, 5-hydroxy-L-pipecolic acid |CITS: | and the toxic proline analog 3,4-dehydroproline |CITS: |. ProP transports glycine betaine, dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) and dimethylsulfonioacetate (DMSA) but (unlke ProU) it does not provide osmoprotection at very low concentrations of these substrates (1 nM to 1 µM) |CITS: |. Choline, alanine, trigonelline and sarcosine are all inhibitors of proline import but are not transport substrates |CITS: |. ProP activity is stimulated by exogenous K+ |CITS: | although this may represent a K+ requirement for respiration rather than direct involvement in transport |CITS: |. As a component of the pmf, membrane potential (ΔΨ) contributes to ProP catalysed symport; ΔΨ also controls osmosensing - ProP appears to progress from an off to an on and then an osmolality-sensitive state as the membrane potential increases from 0 to -137mV |CITS: |. Conformational change of ProP (as measured by the accessibility of introduced cysteine residues to alkylation) has been observed in response to osmolality |CITS: |. ProP consists of 11 or 12 predicted transmembrane regions and a cytoplasmic C-terminal domain which is required for activity |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Mechanosensitive channel that participates in the regulation of osmotic pressure changes within the cell, opening in response to stretch forces in the membrane lipid bilayer, without the need for other proteins. The channel is sensitive to voltage; as the membrane is depolarized, less tension is required to open the channel and vice versa. MetaCyc_Comment: MscS is a mechanosensitive channel of small conductance; MscS conductance is 0.8-1 nanosiemens in E. coli giant protoplasts |CITS: |. MscS activity is adaptive, that is, it declines in response to sustained stimulation |CITS: |. In patch clamp experiments MscS activity occurs in short bursts that last for a few seconds |CITS: |. Gating of MscS is controlled by tension within, or voltage across the lipid bilayer |CITS: |. Activation of MscS depends upon tension, while inactivation is both tension and voltage dependent; channel activation requires a high rate of increase in membrane tension; slower rates of increase can be ignored |CITS: |. MscS is a homoheptamer |CITS: | with three transmembrane (TM) domains per subunit and a large cytoplasmic chamber |CITS: |. The N-terminus of each subunit forms a mixed helical hairpin structure located at the periplasmic interface of the lipid bilayer |CITS: |. The functional state represented in the crystal structure of |CITS: | - conducting |CITS: | or non-conducting |CITS: | - is unclear. A model for closed |CITS: | and open |CITS: | conformations of MscS has been proposed. The inhibition of MscS channel activity due to crosslinking of the C-terminus or adding Ni2+ to C-terminally, hexahistidine tagged proteins suggests that the C-terminus acts as a cytoplasmic gate and moves apart upon activation of the channel |CITS: |. Deletion of the C-terminus of MscS resulted in decreased stability and activity |CITS: |. Crosslinking studies of cysteine substitutions reveal the very flexible architecture of the MscS channel and support predictions that MscS undergoes dramatic displacement of domains upon activation and deactivation |CITS: |. MscS fluorescent fusion proteins, expressed at basal levels, are evenly distributed and mobile throughout the membrane |CITS: |. A strain lacking MscS, MscK and MscL exhibits defects in Z-ring placement in the presence of the septation inhibitor, cephalexin |CITS: |. Parabens induce MscS activity which allows leakage of cell contents, suggesting a mechanism for their antimicrobial activity |CITS: | although later experiments |CITS: | suggest that MscS may not be the primary target for parabens. MscS is slightly anion-selective |CITS: |. mscS expression is induced by RpoS upon entry into stationary phase and by osmotic stress |CITS: |. FUNCTION: DegP acts as a chaperone at low temperatures but switches to a peptidase (heat shock protein) at higher temperatures (PubMed:10319814). MetaCyc_Comment: In the E. coli K-12 strains MG1655 (represented in EcoCyc) and W3110, the rph gene contains a frameshift mutation (rph-1) resulting in a shortened open reading frame. As characterized in strain W3110, Rph is truncated at the C-terminus and lacks the weak poly(A) phosphorylase activity associated with RNase PH. The strains also show a pyrimidine starvation phenotype due to a PyrE deficiency that results from the polar effect of the rph frameshift mutation on the downstream pyrE gene (|CITS: | and discussed in |CITS: |). In the absence of the |FRAME: G7459-MONOMER| RppH, the rph-1-encoded truncated RNase PH inhibits |FRAME: CPLX0-1382|-mediated maturation of certain pre-tRNAs. It is thought that the truncated RNase PH protein creates a steric hindrance and reduces access of RNase P to the pre-tRNA |CITS: |. Further descriptions of RNase PH here refer to the wild-type version of the enzyme present in other E. coli K-12 strains, or to a rph+ derivative designated MG1655(Seq)* described in |CITS: |. The rph gene was previously named orfE |CITS: |. Ribonuclease PH (RNase PH) is a divalent cation-dependent and inorganic phosphate-dependent exoribonuclease that acts in processing of the tRNA 3' terminus |CITS: |. There is also evidence for its role in the processing of rRNAs, small stable RNAs and mRNA fragments containing secondary structure |CITS: |. Like polynucleotide phosphorylase (PNPase), RNase PH catalyzes phosphorolysis rather than hydrolysis of RNA substrates, yielding nucleoside diphosphate products |CITS: |. The enzyme also has a weak poly(A) phosphorylase activity relative to PNPase |CITS: |. Recombinant Rph has been overexpressed, purified and its RNase PH activity characterized. It has helix-turn-helix sequence motifs and binds nonspecifically to DNA |CITS: |. It is a multimeric enzyme of undefined subunit stoichiometry |CITS: |. Crystal structures of RNase PH from other organisms reveal a homohexamer |CITS: |. RNase PH is a member of the PDX family of 3' to 5' phosphate-dependent exoribonucleases and has homologs in many other organisms containing RNase PH domains. The enzyme activity has been studied in vitro |CITS: |. The reaction is reversible in vitro, but probably unidirectional in vivo |CITS: |. In vivo and in vitro evidence for an interaction between a basic stretch of 80 amino acids in wild-type RNase PH and an acidic stretch of 16 amino acids in RNase E has been presented |CITS: |. An rph mutation causes synthetic phenotypes, including synthetic lethality, in combination with various other RNase mutations |CITS: |. Quintuple mutation of exoribonucleases RNase II, D, BN, T, and PH is lethal, whereas quadruple mutants are viable, but not wild-type |CITS: |. Mutant data suggest that RNase PH and RNase T are involved in the regulation of tRNA processing by competing with poly(A) polymerase I for the 3'-ends of tRNAs |CITS: |. In the case of the three proline tRNAs, the endoribonuclease RNase E appears to be responsible for their maturation |CITS: |. Double mutation of PNPase and RNase PH causes ribosomal defects |CITS: |. In the absence of the exoribonucleases RNase II, R and PNPase, RNase PH can carry out the 3' processing of 16S rRNA at a slow rate |CITS: | and has a role in the rRNA starvation degradation pathway |CITS: |. A strain containing deletions of the RNase PH and RNase II genes shows accumulation of precursor 23S rRNA and ribosome assembly defects |CITS: |. Strains with mutations in RNases I, PH and R, or RNases I, II, PH and PNPase genes show increased sensitivity to the aminoglycoside antibiotics neomycin and paromomycin that affect translation and inhibit ribosome subunit assembly |CITS: |. Mutants lacking RNase PH and PNPase accumulate secondary structure-containing mRNA fragments, and RNase PH can utilize duplex RNA as a substrate |CITS: |. Both RNase PH and PNPase are involved in the stabilization of Hfq-bound small noncoding RNAs (sRNAs) which regulate target mRNAs |CITS: |. RNase PH may also have a role in the maturation of small stable RNAs |CITS: |. Regulation of the rph-pyrE operon has been described |CITS: |. RNase PH is named for phosphate-dependent nuclease |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: A small protein (arrest peptide) encoded upstream of inducible ornithine carboxylase gene (speF) that controls expression of downstream genes (speF and patE) by nascent chain-translational arrest and transcriptional attenuation. In the presence of ornithine a toeprint due to ribosomal arrest can be seen on the speFL transcript. Only L-ornithine (not other tested amino acids) has this effect (PubMed:32094585). MetaCyc_Comment: L-aspartate oxidase (NadB) is the first enzyme in the de novo |FRAME: PYRIDNUCSYN-PWY| pathway, catalyzing the FAD-dependent oxidation of L-aspartate to iminoaspartate |CITS: |. NadB activity is required for NAD biosynthesis under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions |CITS: |; fumarate is the more efficient electron acceptor and is used under anaerobic conditions, while oxygen appears to be the predominant electron acceptor under aerobic conditions due to the lower fumarate levels |CITS: |. The enzyme can exist in monomeric and dimeric form depending on pH |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the apo- and holoenzyme have been determined, suggesting that an unusual tertiary structure is shared by L-aspartate oxidase, the SdhA subunit of succinate dehydrogenase, and the FrdA subunit of fumarate reductase |CITS: |. NadB may have evolved from succinate dehydrogenase/fumarate reductase-type enzymes |CITS: |. NadB is a predominant source of hydrogen peroxide under aerobic conditions |CITS: |. Amino acid residues important for enzymatic activity have been identified by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. The E121 residue is essential and thought to be required for orienting the L-aspartate substrate in a productive binding mode; mutants lose L-aspartate oxidase activity, but retain fumarate reductase activity |CITS: |. Measurement of various kinetic isotope effects elucidated the catalytic mechanism of NadB. Similar to typical amino acid oxidases, deprotonation and hydride transfer appear to occur in a concerted manner, where the hydride transfer from the C2 of L-aspartate to FAD is rate-limiting |CITS: |. The fumarate reductase activity of NadB can provide succinate for growth of a Δ lipB ΔsdhB strain |CITS: |. NadB: "NAD biosynthesis" |CITS: | Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: NarK is a nitrate/nitrite transporter with a physiological role in nitrate-dependent respiration. NarK mediates the uptake of nitrate and the extrusion of nitrite - the exact mechanism of transport has been debated but structural constraints suggest that NarK functions as a nitrate:nitrite exchanger |CITS: |. Purified NarK, reconstituted in liposomes functions as a nitrate:nitrite antiporter |CITS: |. The location of nitrate and nitrite ions in crystal structures of NarK suggest that the two ions bind to the same site competitively |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Early studies characterizing narK mutant alleles in E. coli K-12 include |CITS: | and |CITS: |. Physiological studies of narK deletion mutants implicated the protein in nitrate and nitrite transport and proposed that NarK functions as a nitrate:nitrite antiporter |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). The suggestion that NarK functions primarily as a nitrite extrusion protein |CITS: | is now thought to be incorrect. NarK consists of an amino terminal domain and a carboxy terminal domain each containing 6 transmembrane (TM) helices. NarK contains two nitrogen signature (NS) motifs located in TM5 and TM11. The substrate translocation pathway lies at the domain interface and polar residues lining the central pore form a substrate binding pocket. The substrate pathway is positively charged and does not contain protonatable residues suggesting that NarK functions as a nitrate:nitrite exchanger |CITS: |. E. coli K-12 contains a second nitrate transport protein, |FRAME: NARU-MONOMER NarU|, whose function confers selective advantage during nutrient starvation or slow growth |CITS: |. In the Transporter Classification Database |CITS: | NarK is a member of the Nitrate/Nitrite Porter (NNP) family within the Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS). Related reviews: |CITS:|

MetaCyc_Comment: Cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase (MetH) is a large modular protein that catalyzes the transfer of a methyl group from 5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate to homocysteine to form methionine in the final step of the |FRAME: HOMOSER-METSYN-PWY| pathway. The reaction can be catalyzed by either of two transmethylases, |FRAME: HOMOCYSMET-MONOMER MetE| or MetH. MetH, described here, is dependent on vitamin B12 (cobalamin) as a cofactor, whereas MetE is not. MetH can utilize either the mono- or triglutamate forms of folate, while MetE can use only the triglutamate form |CITS: |. MetE and MetH lack sequence similarity, suggesting that these proteins arose by convergent evolution |CITS: |. MetH is composed of four functionally distinct modules that are arranged linearly with single interdomain linkers. The N-terminal module binds homocysteine, while the second module binds methyl-tetrahydrofolate (methylTHF) |CITS: |. The third module binds the cobalamin cofactor |CITS: |; the C-terminal module binds S-adenosyl-L-methionine (AdoMet) and is necessary for the reductive methylation of the cobalamin cofactor of MetH |CITS: |. The cobalamin cofactor serves as a methyl group carrier and is activated by transfer of a methyl group from AdoMet |CITS: |. Kinetic studies provided evidence for an ordered sequential mechanism in which methylTHF binding precedes binding of homocysteine, and release of methionine precedes release of tetrahydrofolate |CITS: |. MetH first catalyzes methyl transfer from enzyme-bound methylcobalamin to homocysteine to produce methionine and cob(I)alamin |CITS: |. MethylTHF then remethylates cob(I)alamin within MetH to regenerate methylcobalamin |CITS: |. Although exogenously supplied cobalamin can be utilized for catalysis of the two methylation half reactions by the isolated N-terminal half of MetH |CITS: |, MetH requires the bound cofactor for efficient catalysis |CITS: |. The movement of a proton during catalysis has been investigated |CITS: |. Zinc is required for methyl transfer from methylcobalamin to homocysteine |CITS: |; the zinc ion is coordinated by the cysteine residues 247, 310 and 311 and the L-homocysteine substrate |CITS: |. The cobalamin cofactor appears to be oxidized once every approximately 2,000 catalytic cycles |CITS: | and must be reactivated by the uptake of an electron from reduced |FRAME: FLAVODOXIN1-MONOMER| acting together with |FRAME: FLAVONADPREDUCT-MONOMER Fpr| |CITS: |. Ferredoxin can not substitute for flavodoxin as an electron donor |CITS: |. The presence of the oxidized cob(II)alamin cofactor appears to lead to a global conformation change in MetH that allows the interaction of cob(II)alamin with flavodoxin and AdoMet, reactivating the cofactor by reductive methylation |CITS: |. Reduction of cob(II)alamin to cob(I)alamin is followed by methyl transfer from AdoMet and a slow change from a five-coordinate methylcobalamin to the active six-coordinate methylcobalamin |CITS: |. The Tyr1139 active site residue within the reactivation domain mediates lengthening of the Co-OH2 bond in the presence of AdoMet |CITS: |. Glu61 of flavodoxin interacts with Lys959 of the C-terminal activation domain of the enzyme |CITS: |. The enzyme undergoes global conformational changes to allow the cobalamin-binding domain to react with three different substrates, homocysteine, methyltetrahydrofolate, and AdoMet |CITS: |. The His759 residue |CITS: | as well as the presence of the ligands methylTHF, flavodoxin and the β-ligand of cobalamin |CITS: | influence the transition between the catalytic and reactivation conformations of MetH. A crystal structure of the cobalamin-binding domain of MetH revealed a conformational change in cobalamin upon binding to MetH, as well as a cap domain that appears to protect the cofactor |CITS: |. A structure containing both the cobalamin- and AdoMet-binding domains in the activation conformation shows displacement of the cap domain and formation of a new interface |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the C-terminal AdoMet-binding domain have been solved |CITS: |. Disulfide crosslinking was used to lock a C-terminal fragment of MetH in the reactivation conformation; its crystal structure showed that the His759 residue dissociated from cobalamin and formed contacts within the AdoMet-binding domain |CITS: |. Additional structures elucidated the steps in reactivation, involving the transition between coordination states of the cobalt atom |CITS: |. A number of crystal structures of the reactivation domain enabled identification of residues involved in substrate binding |CITS: |. Mutation of Cys310 or Cys311 in the N-terminal catalytic domain to either alanine or serine result in loss of catalytic activity |CITS: |. Specific recognition of AdoMet within the C-terminal reactivation domain is promoted by the Glu1097 and Glu1128 residues |CITS: |. metH mutants are methionine auxotrophs and are unable to utilize vitamin B12 supplied in minimal medium |CITS: |. Expression of metH is positively regulated by MetR |CITS: |; the presence of homocysteine decreases the positive regulation by MetR |CITS: |. MetR-dependent transcription activation requires different C-terminal domain residues and orientation of the α subunit of RNA polymerase for metE vs. metH promoters |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: There are two distinct catalases in E. coli. The KatG enzyme is the bifunctional hydroperoxidase I (HPI), with both catalase and peroxidase activity. A monofunctional catalase, HPII, is encoded by katE |CITS: |. Endogenously produced H2O2 is primarily scavenged by a third enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX0-245|, while catalase is the primary scavenger at high H2O2 concentrations |CITS: |. The catalase activity uses one molecule of H2O2 as the electron donor and a second molecule of H2O2 as the electron acceptor, producing oxygen and water. At lower concentrations of H2O2, the peroxidase activity is able to utilize a suitable electron donor other than H2O2 |CITS: |. For both activities, the initial step is the reduction of H2O2 to H2O by a ferric heme, producing the ferryl porphyrin cation radical intermediate known as compound I. In the catalase reaction, compound I is returned directly to the ferric state by oxidizing a second molecule of H2O2 to O2. Under certain conditions, KatG associates with thioredoxin, which hypothetically could act as the external electron donor |CITS: |. In the presence of H2O2, overexpressed |FRAME: EG11404-MONOMER "YchF"| was found to interact directly with KatG and to inhibit its activity |CITS: |. KatG was initially thought to be periplasmic |CITS: |, but was later localized to the cytoplasm |CITS: |. KatG consists of two large domains that may have arisen from a gene duplication event |CITS: |. Although the C-terminal domain of KatG is not predicted to bind heme or have catalytic activity itself, it is required for KatG activity |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the C-terminal domain of KatG have been solved |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain may serve as a platform where its I'-helix directs structural adjustments of the N-terminal domain |CITS: |. The dimeric form of KatG is the smallest active species of the enzyme |CITS: |. Under some conditions, KatG was observed to exist as an isoenzyme pair, HPI-A and HPI-B |CITS: |. KatG activity is much more sensitive to elevated temperature than KatE |CITS: |. The catalytic activity of site-directed mutants in predicted active site residues has been investigated |CITS: |. A W105F mutant has severely reduced catalase activity, but slightly increased hydroperoxidase activity |CITS: |. Monofunctional and bifunctional peroxidases share highly similar active sites. A 35 amino acid structure connecting the F and G helices in KatG is unique to the bifunctional enzyme; deletion of this loop causes loss of 99.8% of catalase activity, while the mutant enzyme retains 50% of its peroxidase activity |CITS: |. Mutagenesis of the LL1 loop similarly reduces catalase activity and enhances peroxidase activity |CITS: |. KatG production can be induced by ascorbate |CITS: | or H2O2 |CITS: |. Expression of katG increases at stationary phase |CITS: |, but regulation does not appear to be dependent on RpoS |CITS: |. KatG is required for rapid recovery of transport function in H2O2-treated |CITS: | or near-UV exposed |CITS: | cells. Overexpression of katG suppresses H2O2 sensitivity of an oxyR mutant strain |CITS: |. An ahpCF katG double mutant is extremely sensitive to the increased endogenous production of peroxides during phosphate starvation |CITS: |. Hpx- mutants lacking all three H2O2-scavenging enzymes (katG katE ahpCF) grow poorly under aerobic conditions |CITS: |. Overexpression of katG from an ASKA plasmid leads to a more than 3-fold increase in the MIC of hydrogen peroxide |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: FecA is the outer membrane receptor protein in the Fe(3+) dicitrate transport system.
MetaCyc_Comment: FecA is an outer membrane (OM) protein which mediates the citrate dependent import of ferric iron; FecA mediated transport across the OM is energized by the inner membrane proton gradient; energy transduction is facilitated by the |FRAME: CPLX0-1923| (reviewed in |CITS: |). FecA also signals the extracellular presence of iron to the FecR/FecI anti-sigma factor/sigma factor pair in the Fec signaling pathway. The outer membrane protein, FecA, is expressed under iron-limiting growth conditions in the presence of citrate |CITS: |. fecA forms an operon with fecBCDE encoding a ferric dicitrate ABC transporter; the operon responds to ferric citrate induction and Fur-Fe2+ repression |CITS: |. Ferric citrate does not have to enter the cell to induce transcription of the operon; FecA (and the Ton complex) are directly involved in fec operon induction independent of their role in transport; substrate binding to FecA initiates a signal that is transferred across the inner membrane by |FRAME: EG10292-MONOMER "FecR"| to activate the the iron starvation responsive sigma factor |FRAME: PD00440 "FecI"|, which facilitates binding of RNA polymerase to the upstream region of fecA |CITS: | (and see |CITS: |). The N-terminal, periplasmic region of FecA interacts with the C-terminal portion of FecR |CITS: | (see further |CITS: |). FecA consists of three structural domains: a monomeric 22-stranded β-barrel in the membrane; a globular plug domain which occludes the channel, and an N-terminal flexible extension (also called the transcriptional domain) which extends into the periplasm; crystal structures of unliganded FecA and its complex with ferric chloride suggest the protein mediates transport by a bipartite gating mechanism |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). FecA interacts with TonB; this interaction does not require the PMF and is enhanced in the presence of substrate; in-frame deletion of the FecA 'TonB box' results in loss of both transport and signaling functions |CITS: |. TonB-energy transduction serves to drive transport and bring the FecA N-terminal transcriptional domain into proximity of the inner membrane receptor FecR |CITS: |. Early studies characterized a citrate-dependent system of iron uptake in E. coli K-12 wild-type and mutant strains |CITS: |. fec mutants grow normally on low-iron media containing 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate but are unable to grow in the presence of citrate |CITS: |. fec: ferric citrate

A fes insertion mutant shows a SpoT-dependent increase in the ppGpp pool |CITS: |. A Δfes mutant is hypersensitive to the antimicrobial peptide wrwycr |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: NhaA is an Na+:H+ antiporter with a prominent role in sodium ion and alkaline pH homeostasis. NhaA mediates the active uptake of protons in exchange for cytoplasmic Na+ - a crucial mechanism that supports the maintenance of cytoplasmic pH under alkali challenge (see |CITS: |). Purified, reconstituted NhaA is an electrogenic antiporter with a stoichiometry of 2H+:Na+ |CITS: |. NhaA is also capable of transporting Li+ and is involved in lithium detoxification |CITS:|; NhaA is a Li+:H+ antiporter with a stoichiometry of 2H+:Li+ |CITS: |. NhaA mediated Na+ efflux (in an in vitro system) is stimulated 2000-fold upon an increase in pH from 6.5 to 8.5 |CITS: |; pH-induced activation is associated with conformational change |CITS: |. Purified, reconstituted NhaA catalyses Na+:Na+, Na+:Li+ |CITS:|, Ca2+:H+ and Ca2+:Na+ exchange |CITS:|. NhaA has an important role in maintaining antibiotic tolerance under starvation; nhaA is upregulated during nutrient starvation and the starvation-induced ampicillin tolerance levels of an nhaA knockout strain are significantly reduced over both a 6 and 30 day period |CITS: |. NhaA exists as a dimer within the membrane |CITS: |. NhaA monomers are functional for Na+:H+ antiport but dimers are important under conditions of extreme stress, possibly due to increased stability |CITS:, |. The monomer contains 12 transmembrane (TM) helices with both N and C termini located in the cytoplasm |CITS:,|. Crystal structures of the NhaA monomer |CITS: | and dimer |CITS: |, both crystallised at low pH (3.5 - 4) have been reported; see reviews by |CITS: | and |CITS: | for a detailed discussion of NhaA structure. Mass spectrometry analysis of NhaA released from C8E4 (tetraethylene glycol monooctyl ether) micelles shows binding of cardiolipin and phospholipids to intact dimers; tandem mass spectrometry suggests that cardiolipin stabilizes the dimer structure |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). NhaA has been extensively mutagenised to study structure-function relationships |CITS: |. Binding of Li+ and H+ is coupled and antagonistic in agreement with the proposed alternative access mechanism for secondary transporters |CITS: |. Binding of lithium to NhaA induces global conformational change resulting from two movements which affect the cytoplasmic and periplamic funnels and are consistent with an alternating-access mechanism of transport |CITS: |. E. coli K-12 contains other sodium:proton antiporters including |FRAME: NHAB-MONOMER "NhaB"| (a second electrogenic H+:Na+ antiporter), |FRAME: CHAA-MONOMER "ChaA"| and the multidrug efflux transporters |FRAME: CMR-MONOMER "MdfA"| and |FRAME: YJIO-MONOMER "MdtM"|. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Translation factor necessary for the incorporation of selenocysteine into proteins. It probably replaces EF-Tu for the insertion of selenocysteine directed by the UGA codon. SelB binds GTP and GDP.
MetaCyc_Comment: SelB is a specialized translation factor that takes the place of elongation factor EF-Tu for the insertion of selenocysteine into a peptide chain at the site of a UGA codon. Most UGA codons signal chain termination; a UGA codon that encodes selenocysteine insertion is distinguished from those that signal chain termination by a structured sequence, called SECIS (SElenoCysteine Insertion Sequence), immediately downstream of the UGA codon |CITS: |. SelB recognizes and binds to identical bases within the loop region in the SECIS hairpin structure of both fdhF and fdnG mRNAs, and thereby brings the charged |FRAME: modified-charged-selC-tRNA selenocysteyl-tRNASec| (Sec-tRNASec) into the neighborhood of the UGA codon |CITS: |. Structures of several intermediates during delivery of Sec-tRNASec to the ribosome have been solved by single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, elucidating the dynamics of codon recognition and GTPase activation |CITS: |. SelB is found at a level of approximately 1100 copies per cell |CITS: |. The N-terminal domain of SelB shares extensive sequence similarity with EF-Tu and IF2 |CITS: |; this domain binds specifically to Sec-tRNASec |CITS: |. Its structure was modeled based on that of Thermus thermophilus EF-Tu |CITS: |. Like EF-Tu, SelB binds GTP and exhibits a low GTPase activity which is stimulated by the presence of 70S ribosomes, the UGA codon and the SECIS element |CITS: |. An additional C-terminal domain of SelB consisting of four tandem winged-helix motifs is responsible for binding to the SECIS mRNA structure |CITS: |. A crystal structure of a fragment of SelB in complex with the hairpin SECIS element has been solved at 2.3 Å resolution |CITS: |. Suppressor mutations within selB that suppress the effect of defined mutations within the SECIS element have been isolated |CITS: |. The kinetics of the interactions of SelB with guanosine nucleotides, the SECIS element, and Sec-tRNASec have been studied, shedding light on the mechanism of SelB action compared to the standard elongation factor EF-Tu |CITS: |. Measurement of dissociation constants suggest that SelB-GTP first interacts with tRNA-Sec before recognition of the SECIS element |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Releases the supercoiling and torsional tension of DNA, which is introduced during the DNA replication and transcription, by transiently cleaving and rejoining one strand of the DNA duplex. Merged_Functions: Encodes an intracellular aminopeptidase P (PepP) that hydrolyzes N‑terminal Xaa‑Pro peptide bonds, removing dipeptides where proline occupies the penultimate position. The PepP enzyme is a ~54 kDa subunit that functions as a homodimer and contributes to the degradation of N‑terminal peptide fragments in Streptomyces lividans. {PubMed:8422994}. pepP encodes an aminopeptidase. In the study, an insertion sequence disrupting pepP caused a polar effect that strongly reduced expression of the downstream gene ubiH, which participates in ubiquinone (co‑enzyme Q) synthesis. The resulting decrease in ubiquinone production impairs the electron‑transport chain, leading to the small‑colony variant phenotype observed in the mutant. Thus, while pepP’s primary role is as an aminopeptidase, its disruption indirectly affects ETC function through down‑regulation of ubiH. {PubMed:27606007}. The pepP gene encodes an intracellular aminopeptidase P (EC 3.4.11.9) that hydrolyzes amino‑acyl‑Pro bonds where proline occupies the penultimate position from the N‑terminus (Xaa‑Pro). This enzyme participates in N‑terminal peptide degradation by cleaving Xaa‑Pro dipeptides, thereby allowing subsequent removal of the exposed N‑terminal proline by a proline iminopeptidase and further degradation by other peptidases. The PepP protein is a ~54 kDa subunit that forms a homodimer and lacks a secretion signal, confirming its intracellular location. {PubMed:8422994}. pepP encodes a dipeptidase that specifically hydrolyzes proline‑containing dipeptides (i.e., dipeptidases with specificity for proline at the C‑terminus). In E. coli it is one of only two genes (pepP and pepQ) that provide this proline‑specific dipeptidase activity. {PubMed:20422176}. The pepP gene encodes the bacterial aminopeptidase P enzyme. Aminopeptidase P cleaves N‑terminal amino‑acid residues that lie immediately before a proline residue. In this study it was shown to remove the Ala^16 residue from the N‑terminus of recombinant human cationic trypsinogen, producing a Pro^17‑Phe^18 N‑terminal sequence. Deletion of pepP eliminated this unwanted N‑terminal trimming, enabling expression of trypsinogen with its authentic native N‑terminus. {PubMed:16542853}. The article reports pepP as an open reading frame situated directly downstream of uvrA that shares ~50% sequence identity with an aminopeptidase P gene from Lactococcus lactis, suggesting that pepP encodes a putative aminopeptidase P enzyme. {PubMed:11566996}.

MetaCyc_Comment: PurL catalyzes the fourth step in the E. coli purine de novo biosynthesis pathway. It converts 5'-phosphoribosyl-N-formylglycineamide (FGAR) to 5-phosphoribosyl-N-formylglycineamidine (FGAM) in the presence of glutamine and ATP. It is the second glutamine amidotransferase in the pathway, the other being PurF. PurL is a large, 141 kDa polypeptide that was shown by genetic complementation tests to contain three different domains. The N-terminal Domain I contains a potential ATP binding motif, the C-terminal Domain III is similar to several glutamine amidotransferases, and Domain II contains elements observed in the triosephosphate isomerase family. Thus, PurL may have arisen from the fusion of at least three different gene families |CITS: |. The enzyme mechanism was studied using initial velocity, dead-end inhibition, and substrate/product exchange studies. A sequential mechanism was suggested in which glutamine binds first, followed by rapid equilibrium binding of MgATP, followed by binding of FGAR |CITS: |. The apparent molecular mass was determined to be 135 kDa by SDS-PAGE and 125 kDa by gel filtration chromatography, indicating a single polypeptide |CITS: |. The crystal structure of the ortholog from Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium has been determined. Four distinct domains were identified and analyzed, providing further insight into the catalytic mechanism |CITS: |. Review: Jensen, K.F., G. Dandanell, B. Hove-Jensen, and M. Willemoes (2008) "Nucleotides, Nucleosides and Nucleobases" EcoSal 3.6.2 |CITS: |

Also shows cysteinylglycinase activity, which is sufficient for E.coli to utilize cysteinylglycine as a cysteine source. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11157967, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20067529, ECO:0000269|PubMed:355237, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7988883}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Peptidase D (PepD) is a dipeptidase capable of breaking down a number of dipeptides with unblocked N termini |CITS: |, including cysteinylglycine, a breakdown product of glutathione |CITS: |. Neither proline nor non-protein amino acids are accepted in the C-terminal position |CITS: |. Transcription of pepD increases five fold during phosphate starvation |CITS: |. Overexpression of pepD negatively affects biofilm formation |CITS: |. Using a method that distinguishes N-phosphorylation from O-phosphorylation, N-phosphorylation was detected in vitro |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: Phosphoribosylamine—glycine ligase (glycinamide ribonucleotide synthetase, GAR synthetase) catalyzes the ligation of glycine to 5-phospho-β-D-ribosyl-amine (PRA) to produce 5-phospho-ribosyl-glycineamide (GAR) in the second step of the E. coli purine de novo biosynthesis pathway. Its kinetic mechanism for substrate binding and product release has been described as sequential and ordered. PRA was suggested to bind first, followed by ATP and glycine, with phosphate leaving first, followed by ADP and GAR. However, PRA is unstable and can hydrolyze to ribose-5-phosphate and ammonia under physiological conditions |CITS: |. A hypothetical docking and channeling model for the transfer of PRA from PurF to the PurD monomer has been proposed |CITS: |. A recombinant, poly-His-tagged Pro294Leu mutant enzyme was crystallized and its structure determined at 1.6 Å resolution |CITS: |. Review: Jensen, K.F., G. Dandanell, B. Hove-Jensen, and M. MetaCyc_Comment: Deoxyguanosinetriphosphate triphosphohydrolase (dGTPase, Dgt) is a unique nucleoside triphosphatase which specifically hydrolyzes dGTP to deoxyguanosine and inorganic tripolyphosphate |CITS: |. Possible physiological roles of the enzyme have only recently been elucidated. Dgt may be involved in replication fidelity via its effect on the cellular pool of dGTP |CITS: |. The level of Dgt expression correlates with the ability of cells to salvage thymine in the absence of functional de novo biosynthesis in a thyA mutant, presumably due to its effect on the intracellular deoxyribose-1-phosphate pool |CITS: |. dGTPase is able to bind single-stranded DNA with relatively high affinity |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme have been solved |CITS: |. Although dGTPase was thought to be a homotetramer based on a prior measurement of its native molecular weight |CITS: |, the crystal structure showed a homohexameric conformation. Subunits with bound ssDNA show significant conformational changes, including in the active site. DNA binding activates the enzyme, lowering the Km for dGTP. An S34D G37E double mutant abolishes binding and stimulation of enzymatic activity by DNA |CITS: |. At physiologically relevant GTP:dGTP ratios (higher than 10:1), GTP appears to act as a competitive inhibitor of dGTPase |CITS: |. Crystal structures of various free and ligand- or inhibitor-bound forms of the enzyme enabled investigation of the substrate selectivity of dGTPase. dGTP, but not GTP binding results in conformational changes within the active site. Mutagenesis of the active site residues H126, E129, or Y272 to alanine resulted in loss of catalytic activity. The binding pocket forms a tight fit with extensive hydrogen bonding around dGTP |CITS: |. The optA1 allele of dgt, a promoter mutation |CITS: |, causes increased production of dGTPase, which makes the cells unable to support growth of phage T7 containing mutations in gene 1.2 |CITS: |. The wild-type gene 1.2 protein is a specific inhibitor of dGTPase by binding to the enzyme |CITS: |. A dgt null mutation has no detectable growth phenotype in rich medium |CITS: |. Several dgt transposon insertion mutants were shown to have a mutator phenotype |CITS: |. When an optA1 gpt double mutant is grown in a medium lacking an exogenous source of purines, the dGPT pool collapses, and the cells eventually die in a manner similar to thymineless death |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Shikimate dehydrogenase (AroE) catalyzes the NADPH-linked reduction of 3-dehydroshikimate to shikimate |CITS: |. The reaction is part of the |FRAME: ARO-PWY| pathway, which provides the common precursor for the biosynthesis of aromatic amino acids, folate, quinones and enterochelin. Phylogenomic analysis of the shikimate dehydrogenase family showed that the two enzymes encoded in E. coli, AroE and |FRAME: CPLX0-7462 YdiB|, belong to different subclasses; the authors suggested that YdiB was acquired by horizontal gene transfer. Common and subclass-specific catalytic residues and substrate binding motifs were identified |CITS: |. AroE is NADP+-specific and has much higher catalytic efficiency than YdiB, which has broader substrate specificity and can use either NADP+ or NAD+ as a co-substrate |CITS: |. Mutant data and the results from metabolic engineering experiments strongly suggest that YdiB is unable to replace AroE under normal physiological conditions. AroE transfers hydrogen stereospecifically from the A-side of NADPH |CITS: |. The structure of AroE with bound NADP+ was determined at 1.5 Å resolution. Although AroE and YdiB have low sequence similarity, they have high structural similarity with two α/β domains separated by a wide cleft |CITS: |. The cosubstrate specificity of AroE was switched from NADP+ to NAD+ by first engineering a consensus Rossmann nucleotide binding domain followed by rational design towards the NAD+ consensus binding domain. A variant with four specific mutations, S131A, L135A, N149D and V152F, shows a five-fold preference for NAD+ over NADP+ |CITS: |. In the "reverse" direction, AroE appears to be able to further dehydrogenate 3-dehydroshikimate to 3,5-dehydroshikimate, which can spontaneously convert to gallic acid |CITS: |. The physiological relevance is unclear. Although an aroE mutant is unable to grow on medium supplemented with shikimate alone, it is able to grow on medium supplemented with shikimate, phenylalanine and tyrosine |CITS: |. An aroE mutant transferred to minimal medium accumulates dehydroshikimate |CITS: |. Shikimate dehydrogenase appears to be expressed constitutively |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Glucose dehydrogenase (Gcd) is a membrane-bound enzyme. Its role in glucose utilization is not fully clear, because under ordinary conditions it exists as an apoprotein. The enzyme requires the cofactor pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) for activity, yet E. coli lacks the ability to synthesize PQQ |CITS: |. However, E. coli exhibits chemotaxis towards environmental PQQ |CITS: |, and may thus use an externally supplied cofactor. Once functional, the enzyme is able to oxidize glucose and feed electrons into the respiratory chain |CITS: |, but does not generate a proton motive force |CITS: |. The topological structure of Gcd within the membrane has been investigated and revealed five N-terminal membrane-spanning segments, with the N terminus located in the cytoplasm and the C terminus is located in the periplasm |CITS: |. The C-terminal periplasmic domain binds PQQ, contains the catalytic activity and is able to interact with ubiquinone in the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: |. A ubiquinone-interacting site is located close to the membrane surface |CITS: |. Further experiments showed that Gcd contains two ubiquinone binding sites |CITS: |. In addition to the PQQ cofactor, a tightly bound ubiquinone-8 molecule is located very close to PQQ at an estimated distance of 11-13 Å |CITS: | and mediates the electron transfer from PQQ to the membrane ubiquinone pools |CITS: |. Menaquinone can substitute for ubiquinone in this function |CITS: |. Bound ubiquinone and may be involved in the oxidation of glucose in addition to the intramolecular electron transfer from PQQ |CITS: |. The residues thought to interact with PQQ and the bound ubiquinone have been identified by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. The specificity for Mg2+ as the metal cofactor has been studied |CITS: |. A gcd insertion mutant has no detectable growth rate defect; however, in a strain with a phosphotransferase system mutation and in the presence of the PQQ cofactor, a gcd mutant can no longer utilize glucose as the sole source of carbon |CITS: |. Overexpression of Gcd may alter sugar utilization preferences |CITS: |. Expression of gcd is increased in the presence of glucose and under aerobic growth conditions |CITS: | and may be repressed by FNR |CITS: |. Combined site-directed mutagenesis and homology modeling studies of E. coli Gcd have suggested that conserved amino acid residues Asp204 and Gly776 are functionally important |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: AroP is an aromatic amino acid permease that is a member of the APC Superfamily of transporters |CITS: |. AroP is referred to as the general aromatic amino acid permease because it is responsible for the transport of all three aromatic amino acids, phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan, across the inner membrane |CITS: , |. Based on the hydrophobicity profile and distribution of charged amino acid residues, AroP was shown to have 12 membrane-spanning regions connected by hydrophilic loops |CITS: |. This topographical model is very similar to that reported for the PheP permease, a phenylalanine-specific transporter, which has 61% amino acid sequence identity with the AroP permease. However, despite their high degree of sequence similarity, the substrate specificities and affinities of the AroP and PheP permeases differ |CITS: |. AroP transports each of the aromatic amino acids with a Km of less than 1 μM |CITS: |. A key residue involved in tryptophan transport is tyrosine at position 103 |CITS: |. Studies with uncouplers of oxidative phosphorylation and with strains deficient in F0F1-ATPase indicate that transport via the AroP system is driven by the proton motive force |CITS: , |. Expression of aroP is subject to regulation involving the TyrR protein |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: Dimethylallyl diphosphate:tRNA dimethylallyltransferase (DMAPP-tRNA transferase, MiaA) catalyzes the first step in the pathway for hypermodification of the A37 base of certain tRNAs such as tRNATyr and tRNAPhe. Further thiomethylation of the A37 position is dependent on the presence of the isopentenyl modification |CITS: |. MiaA transfers the dimethylallyl moiety of DMAPP to the N6 position of A37, which is adjacent to the anticodon |CITS: |. This modification is required for efficient binding of tRNATyr to ribosomes |CITS: | and is important in preventing frameshifts and other mutations |CITS: |. MiaA-catalyzed tRNA modification is involved in regulating the translation efficiency of modification-tunable transcripts (MoTTs) |CITS: |. MiaA can act on isolated tRNA stem-loops, as long as the helix stem and the A36-A37-A38 motif are both present |CITS: |. Co-crystal structures of MiaA in complex with tRNAPhe have been solved, showing a mutually induced fit mechanism of recognition involving structural rearrangement of the anticodon loop of the tRNA |CITS: |. No substantial change in the structure of the catalytic domain of MiaA is seen upon tRNA binding |CITS: |. Both reports rely for comparison on apo-MiaA structures of the protein from other organisms. An ordered sequential mechanism of substrate binding and catalysis has been suggested |CITS: |. Modification of tRNAs by MiaA is important in preventing various mutations. miaA mutants show increased +1 (but not -1) frameshifting as well as GC to TA transversions, the latter requiring active recombination |CITS: |. miaA mutations also increase the general rate of spontaneous mutations and alter readthrough and suppression of nonsense codons |CITS: |. In miaA mutants, the altered efficiency of translation by tRNAs lacking the dimethylallyl modification affects regulation by attenuation of several operons, including pheA, trp, pheMST and tnaCA |CITS: |. A mutation in miaA inhibits growth and, when combined with a mutation in rpsL, leads to streptomycin dependence |CITS: |. Deletion of miaA increases the evolvability of resistance to ciprofloxacin |CITS: |. A miaA insertion mutant causes hypersensitivity to azacytidine-induced DNA-protein crosslinks; the phenotype may result from a defect in azacytidine-induced tmRNA tagging |CITS: |. Mutation of miaA is lethal in a strain lacking functional tRNA6Leu |CITS: |; a miaA insertion mutant shows decreased levels of |FRAME: RPOS-MONOMER RpoS| |CITS: |. MiaA-catalyzed tRNA modification is required for efficient decoding of UUX-leucine codons, and thus at least in part responsible for efficient translation of RpoS and IraP |CITS: |. MiaA appears to have an indirect role in biofilm formation, perhaps through its regulation towards RpoS |CITS: |. The miaA gene is part of a superoperon with complex patterns of transcription and mechanisms of regulation |CITS: |. The superoperon includes a number of heat shock promoters, and miaA is essential for growth at high temperatures |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

FUNCTION: Catalyzes the attachment of proline to tRNA(Pro) in a two-step reaction: proline is first activated by ATP to form Pro-AMP and then transferred to the acceptor end of tRNA(Pro). As ProRS can inadvertently accommodate and process non-cognate amino acids such as alanine and cysteine, to avoid such errors it has two additional distinct editing activities against alanine. One activity is designated as 'pretransfer' editing and involves the tRNA(Pro)-independent hydrolysis of activated Ala-AMP. The other activity is designated 'posttransfer' editing and involves deacylation of mischarged Ala-tRNA(Pro). Misacylated Cys-tRNA(Pro) is not edited by ProRS, but instead may be edited in trans by YbaK.

MetaCyc_Comment: Proline-tRNA ligase (ProRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. ProRS belongs to the Class IIA aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases |CITS: |. ProRS of E. coli B is a dimer in solution |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNAPro that are important for recognition by ProRS have been identified |CITS: |. The R144 residue within the active site makes a key contact with G72 in the acceptor stem of tRNAPro |CITS: |. Specificity determinants and residues within ProRS that are important for catalytic activity have been investigated |CITS: |. Aminoacylation of tRNAPro that lacks the m1G37 modification is less efficient than that of the modified tRNA. An experimental evolution experiment showed that the growth defect due to |FRAME: CPLX0-3950 TrmD| deficiency can be suppressed by point mutations in ProRS that enable more efficient aminoacylation of unmodified tRNAPro |CITS: |. Many aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases have been shown to have editing functions. ProRS misactivates alanine, but has both a pre-transfer editing function, hydrolyzing the non-cognate amino acid before transfer to tRNAPro, and a post-transfer editing function that deacetylates mischarged Ala-tRNAPro |CITS: |. Pre-transfer editing is not stimulated by the addition of tRNAPro |CITS: | and does not require a separate editing domain |CITS: |. Pre-transfer editing by itself is not sufficient to prevent formation of Ala-tRNAPro; the enzyme's selectivity for proline over alanine is 2000-fold |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNAPro that are important for post-transfer editing are primarily located in the anticodon loop |CITS: |. The C433 |CITS: | and K279 |CITS: | residues in ProRS are critical for the post-transfer editing function. ProRS contains a large insertion domain (INS) between motifs 2 and 3 of the class II aminoacyl tRNA synthetases; this domain is independently folded and plays a role in the editing functions |CITS: |. A chimeric yeast prolyl-tRNA synthetase engineered to contain this domain gains a post-transfer editing function |CITS: |. The specificity of the INS domain for recognition of mischarged Ala-tRNAPro appears to be due to a hydrophobic pocket defined by the residues I263, L266, K279 and T277, where the methyl side chain of alanine binds |CITS: |. The K279 residue is predicted to interact with the phosphate backbone of the acceptor stem; results from site-directed mutants showed that a positive charge at residue 279 is required in the editing active site |CITS: |. Based on hybrid QM/MM calculations combined with biochemical assays, a mechanism for Ala-tRNAPro hydrolysis was proposed |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics simulations and mutagenesis studies showed that the INS domain affects motions within the proline binding loop of the active site |CITS: |. Efficient catalysis requires communication between the aminoacylation and editing domains of ProRS |CITS: |. ProRS exhibits a natural level of mischarging with cysteine, resulting in Cys-tRNAPro, which is not edited by the enzyme. The kcat/Km for proline is 369-fold higher than for cysteine |CITS: |. Cys-tRNAPro is edited by a stand-alone hydrolase, |FRAME: EG12454-MONOMER| (YbaK). ProRS and YbaK interact in vivo |CITS: | Synthesis of ProRS is derepressed by starvation for proline |CITS: |. A temperature-sensitive allele of proS has been isolated |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

Mutants in predicted active site residues were investigated |CITS: |. A CysM mutant in which all cysteine residues were replaced by serine (CysM-C) has higher cysteine synthase activity than wild-type and rescues growth of a ΔcysM cysK mutant. MetaCyc_Comment: The nfsA-encoded nitroreductase is the major oxygen-insensitive nitroreductase present in E. coli. NfsA uses only NADPH and has broad electron acceptor specificity |CITS: |. The physiologically relevant substrates may be quinones |CITS: |. Nitroreductases can be used as prodrug activators in cancer therapy |CITS: |. NfsA catalyzes the reduction of nitrocompounds using a ping-pong Bi-Bi mechanism, transferring two electrons |CITS: |. The mechanism for two-electron reduction of quinones is most consistent with a single-step hydride transfer |CITS: |. Turnover of the enzyme is limited by the oxidative half-reaction |CITS: |. The reduction of nitrocompounds to hydroxylamines occurs via a nitroso intermediate; ascorbate inhibition patterns suggest that the reduction of the nitroso intermediate occurs directly by NADPH rather than enzymatically |CITS: |. The R203 residue plays a key role in binding the NADPH substrate |CITS: |, and F42 is important for activity |CITS: |. A single amino acid substitution, E99G, transforms NfsA into an active flavin reductase |CITS: |. Evolution of NfsA for increased catalytic activity towards chloramphenicol eliminates the enzyme's ability to reduce 1,4-benzoquinone |CITS: |. NfsA has chromate reductase activity |CITS: | which involves a single-electron transfer mechanism and generates a flavin semiquinone form of the enzyme. This leads to the generation of reactive oxygen species |CITS: |. A crystal structure of NfsA was solved at 1.7 Å resolution |CITS: |. Structures of NfsA with ligands also have been determined and modeled |CITS: |. Expression of NfsA is induced by paraquat and glycolaldehyde; induction is dependent on the SoxRS system |CITS: |. Mutations in nfsA cause resistance to nitrofurazone and furazolidone |CITS: |. Resistance to nitrofurantoin via mutation of nfsA reduces the fitness of clinical isolates of E. coli |CITS: |. Overproduction of NfsA causes resistance to adriamycin |CITS: | and increases tolerance to chromate |CITS: |. NfsA has been implicated in the ability to utilize 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT) as a source of nitrogen |CITS: |. An nfsA nfsB double mutant retains 30% of wt nitroreductase activity under aerobic conditions |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: L-glutamine:D-fructose-6-phosphate aminotransferase, or GFAT, catalyzes the first step in hexosamine biosynthesis. The enzyme uses a nucleophilic attack by the thiol group of Cys1 on the δ-carbonyl group of glutamine to form ammonia, which is then channeled through the enzyme to the acceptor group on fructose-6-phosphate. The enzyme can not use exogenous ammonia as the nitrogen donor |CITS: |. The N-terminal domain contains the glutamine amidohydrolase activity, and the C-terminal domain contains the ketose/aldose isomerase activity |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the isolated domains and the full length enzyme have been solved |CITS: |. An 18 Å hydrophobic channel provides a conduit for the transfer of ammonia from the glutamine amidohydrolase active site to the isomerase active site |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics simulations and kinetic analysis of mutants identified roles for W74, A602 and V605 in the opening and closing of the ammonia channel |CITS: |. Major structural changes occur during the catalytic cycle |CITS: |. Mutants of GlmS that show reduced sensitivity to product inhibition by glucosamine-6-phosphate have been isolated |CITS: |. Expression of GlmS is controlled at several levels. glmS mRNA and protein levels are decreased by growth on amino sugars |CITS: |. glmS is cotranscribed together with glmU in the glmUS operon. Expression of GlmS is uncoupled from the expression of GlmU in various ways. RNase E processes the glmUS transcript at sites between glmU and glmS, generating a monocistronic 1.9 kb glmS transcript. This transcript is very unstable, with a half life of 0.72 minutes |CITS: |. The small RNAs GlmY |CITS: | and GlmZ |CITS: | regulate glmS expression posttranscriptionally. Via a regulatory cascade involving processing and stabilization of transcripts, the unprocessed form of |FRAME: SRAJ-RNA| binds to glmS mRNA, uncovering the ribosome binding site and allowing translation |CITS: |. Although |CITS: | reported that glmS mRNA is polyadenylated, epistasis experiments and direct assays for polyadenylation show that glmS mRNA is not polyadenylated, and the effect of |FRAME: EG10690-MONOMER| |CITS: | on the stability of glmS mRNA is indirect, via polyadenylation of |FRAME: TKE1-RNA| |CITS: |. A glmS mutant requires glucosamine or N-acetylglucosamine for growth |CITS: |. Overexpression of the catabolic D-glucosamine-6-phosphate isomerase, NagB, can suppress the requirement for glmS |CITS: |. The transcription terminator region of glmS contains the unique insertion site for the transposon Tn7 |CITS: |. GlmS: "glucosamine" Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Initiates the restart of stalled replication forks, which reloads the DnaB replicative helicase on sites other than the origin of replication (PubMed:11532137, PubMed:11929519). Serves as the scaffold for primosome assembly (PubMed:1313026, PubMed:8663104, PubMed:8663105, PubMed:8663106). There are several restart pathways, the PriA-PriB pathway is the major replication restart pathway (PubMed:11532137, PubMed:37169801, PubMed:22636770). The PriA-PriB pathway is subdivided into 2 distinct pathways (PubMed:34423481). The PriA-PriC pathway is a minor restart pathway (PubMed:11532137, PubMed:22636770). Recognizes and binds the arrested nascent DNA chain at stalled replication forks. Unwinds the lagging strand at DNA replication forks in the presence of DNA single-stranded binding protein (SSB) (PubMed:10356325, PubMed:30201718). A 3'-5' DNA helicase that requires (d)ATP and is enhanced by DNA single-stranded binding protein (SSB) and/or PriB (PubMed:2825188, PubMed:2833507, PubMed:1313026, PubMed:16188886, PubMed:23193948, PubMed:34423481). Can remodel the DNA duplex, via its helicase activity, and promotes assembly of the primosome and loading of the major replicative helicase DnaB onto DNA (PubMed:1313026, PubMed:10356325). Helicase activity is not essential for primosome assembly in the PriA-PriB pathway (PubMed:1313026, PubMed:8631700, PubMed:10835375), but is required for the PriA-PriC pathway (PubMed:11532137). Binds to branched DNA structures that resemble D-loops, stalled replication forks or to the primosome assembly site (PAS) in some phage (PubMed:8366072, PubMed:10572298, PubMed:10356325, PubMed:12622722, PubMed:12917421, PubMed:16188886). Binds to DNA in two distinct modes, either dependent on or independent of, recognition of the 3' terminus (PubMed:17483094). MetaCyc_Comment: UbiG is an S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM)-dependent O-methyltransferase that catalyzes both O-methylation reactions in the biosynthesis of ubiquinone and is a component of the Ubi complex metabolon |CITS: |. The enzyme is mostly cytoplasmic, but also shows some association with the membrane |CITS: |. Purified UbiG binds to liposomes, with preferences for phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin |CITS: |. Crystal structures of wild-type and mutant UbiG in complex with S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH) have been determined |CITS: |. A unique, conserved membrane-binding region was identified and its function confirmed by mutating amino acid residues within this region |CITS: |. Interaction of this region with the cytoplasmic membrane may open a channel that provides access for SAM to its binding site |CITS: |. Liposome-associated UbiG has ~11-fold increased affinity for SAH |CITS: |. However, whether or not the membrane association of UbiG contributes to its catalytic activity has not yet been investigated. The seven ubiquinone biosynthesis proteins UbiE, UbiF, UbiG, UbiH, UbiI, UbiJ, and UbiK form a 1 MDa complex in the cytosol |CITS: |. Gel filtration data showed the apparent molecular mass of UbiG is approximately 50 kDa, suggesting a homodimer |CITS: |. However, the protein appears monomeric in crystal structures |CITS: |. A genetic interaction between ubiX and ubiG was shown. Expression of UbiX can restore the final O-methylation reaction of the ubiquinone biosynthesis pathway in the IS16 mutant strain with the UbiG L132Q mutation |CITS: |. Two leaky ubiG mutants accumulate 2-octaprenylphenol and OMHMB |CITS: |. An independently isolated ubiG mutant is unable to grow aerobically on non-fermentable substrates |CITS: |, and ubiG deletion mutants are respiration-defective and thus unable to grow on succinate |CITS: | or glycerol |CITS: | as the sole source of carbon. ubiG, ubiF, ubiX, ubiH, and ubiE mutants from the Keio K-12 mutant collection showed elevated resistance to the broad-spectrum antibiotic D-cycloserine (DCS) when grown in complex media, suggesting that they may be involved in DCS sensitivity |CITS: |. A ΔubiG mutant is significantly more sensitive to hyperosmotic stress than wild type; salt tolerance can be restored by addition of the human analog of Q8, Q10 |CITS: |. ubiG expression is higher under aerobic than anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. SpeA is specific to arginine, and can neither decarboxylate nor be inhibited by L-ornithine or L-lysine |CITS: |. The active form of SpeA is a tetramer with one molecule of pyridoxal 5' phosphate bound per subunit |CITS: |. This tetrameric conformation depends on the presence of the Mg2+ cofactor. In its absence, arginine decarboxylase exists in equilibrium between the monomeric and dimeric forms, with the exact distribution of forms depending on pH |CITS: |. A crystal structure of SpeA has been solved at 3.1 Å resolution and shows a dimer-of-dimers arrangement |CITS: |. In experiments with an E. coli W strain, |CITS: | showed that putrescine biosynthesis preferentially utilized exogenously added arginine. Cells grown with exogenous arginine preferentially utilize the |FRAME: PWY-40| (SpeA-SpeB) pathway |CITS: |. A significant portion of SpeA is associated with the cell envelope, suggesting that it is primarily involved in the conversion of exogenous rather than endogenous arginine to putrescine |CITS: |. SpeA appears to localize to the envelope via a signal sequence. It was initially proposed that signal sequence cleavage would convert SpeA from a 74 kDa form to a 70 kDa form |CITS: |. However, alternative N termini of SpeA were observed by |CITS: |, one of which coincides with an internal translation initiation site for SpeA located at codon Met27. This translation initiation site was detected by retapamulin-enhanced Ribo-seq analysis and may generate the 70 kDa form detected in the earlier work by Buch et al. |CITS: |. The ribosomal proteins S20/L26 (RpsT, antizyme 1) and L34 (RpmH, antizyme 2), originally identified as inhibitors of the biosynthetic ornithine decarboxylase, also inhibit SpeA activity in vitro |CITS: | and in vivo |CITS: |. Interestingly, transcription of rpsT, rpmH, speC and speA is sensitive to polyamines |CITS: |. cAMP-CRP represses expression of SpeA |CITS: |. Conversely, |CITS: | reported that speA expression is not sensitive to catabolite repression; this result seems to be strain-specific, and cAMP appears to act indirectly |CITS: |. In addition to its role in directly inhibiting SpeA activity, putrescine also represses transcription of speA |CITS: |. Expression of speA is repressed by PurR |CITS: |.
