MetaCyc_Comment: There are two distinct catalases in E. coli. The KatE enzyme is the monofunctional catalase HPII. A bifunctional catalase, HPI, is encoded by katG |CITS: |. Aerobically grown E. coli produce sufficient endogenous H2O2 to cause toxic levels of DNA damage via the Fenton reaction |CITS: |; endogenously produced H2O2 is primarily scavenged by a third enzyme, |FRAME: CPLX0-245|, while catalase is the primary scavenger at high H2O2 concentrations |CITS: |. While most heme proteins contain |FRAME: PROTOHEME| as the prosthetic group, HPII contains a unique cofactor, |FRAME: HEME_D|. It has been suggested that heme d is formed in a reaction catalyzed by HPII itself. Based on this model, HPII first binds protoheme, which is subsequently hydroxylated by HPII utilizing one of the first H2O2 substrate molecules |CITS: |. Later work has supported this theory. While HPII from aerobically grown E. coli contains heme d, HPII purified from microaerobic or anaerobic cultures contains a mixture of heme d and |FRAME: PROTOHEME|. The protoheme of HPII obtained from such cells can be converted into heme d by treatment of the purified enzyme with hydrogen peroxide. The His128 residue of HPII is required for this conversion |CITS: |. A number of crystal structures of wild type and mutant forms of KatE have been reported |CITS: |. The apparent hexameric structure of HPII was noted to be unusual |CITS: |; however, crystal structures show a homotetrameric enzyme, each subunit containing a cis-heme d group |CITS: |. The heme d group is rotated 180° with the respect to the orientation found for protoheme IX in beef liver catalase |CITS: |. The Ile274 residue influences heme orientation |CITS: |. The proximal ligand for the heme group is Tyr415 |CITS: |. His392 and Tyr415 are linked by a bond between the Nδ of His and the Cβ of Tyr. Although the bond was initially only apparent in subunits that contained a heme d group |CITS: |, it was later found that His-Tyr bond formation and heme oxidation can be uncoupled |CITS: |. The catalytic activity of various site-directed mutants in active site residues N201 and H128 has been analyzed. Formation of heme d from protoheme may occur via a protoheme compound I |CITS: |. The S234 and E530 residues also appear to have a role in the oxidation of the heme b to heme d |CITS: |. The active site heme groups are deeply buried within the enzyme, requiring substrates and products to move through channels within the enzyme. Various mutants have been constructed, and activity measurements and crystal structures of the resulting enzymes have elucidated the structure and function of those channels |CITS: |. Compared to some other catalases, HPII contains both N- and C-terminal extensions. Both domains are required for accumulation of active enzyme |CITS: |. Approximately 90 residues of the N-terminus of each subunit are inserted into a loop on the adjacent subunit. This interwoven structure was thought to contribute to the exceptional thermal stability of the enzyme |CITS: |, but a later study showed that C-terminal truncation had a larger effect on stability |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain is a divergent member of the type I glutamine amidotransferase (GAT) superfamily; it lacks the catalytic triad and thus also enzymatic activity |CITS: |. A proteolytically truncated form of HPII that lacks 36% of its sequence has been analyzed |CITS: |. KatE production is increased in stationary phase |CITS: | and by hyperosmotic stress |CITS: | and is four-fold higher under aerobic compared to anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. Expression is dependent on σS (KatF) |CITS: |. Overexpression of katE suppresses H2O2 sensitivity of an oxyR mutant strain |CITS: |. A katE mutant is more sensitive to chromate than wild type |CITS: |. Overexpression of katE from an ASKA plasmid leads to a more than 3-fold increase in the MIC of hydrogen peroxide |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: YhbA is a pyridoxal phosphate phosphatase that contributes to PLP homeostasis within the cell. Addition of pyridoxal to a wild-type strain grown in minimal medium leads to an extended lag phase, and cells accumulate PLP. Overexpression of YhbA alleviates this phenotype. Conversely, overexpression of YbhA in cells grown in minimal medium leads to a reduced growth rate and decreased levels of intracellular PLP; the growth defect can be rescued by addition of pyridoxal to the growth medium |CITS: |. The phosphatase activity of YbhA was first discovered in a high-throughput screen of purified proteins |CITS: |. YbhA is a promiscuous phosphatase belonging to the superfamily of haloacid dehalogenase (HAD)-like hydrolases. Its preferred substrates are pyridoxal phosphate and fructose 1,6-bisphosphate |CITS: |. In addition, YbhA appears to have a low level of phosphotransferase activity using monophosphates as the phosphate donor |CITS: | and a low β-phosphoglucomutase activity |CITS: |. YbhA may exist as a homodimer in solution; gel filtration analysis of purified recombinant protein showed the presence of both a monomer and a homodimer |CITS: |. E. coli encodes several enzymes with fructose 1,6-bisphosphate phosphatase activity; YbhA appears to be a less efficient fructose 1,6-bisphosphate phosphatase than Fbp, GlpX and YggF |CITS: |. An open reading frame downstream of and in the same orientation as modABC, modD, was originally annotated at this genome location |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: Cysteine-tRNA ligase (CysRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. CysRS belongs to the Class I aminoacyl tRNA synthetases |CITS: |. CysRS is a monomer in solution |CITS: |. The N-terminal domain of CysRS is active in adenylate synthesis, while the C-terminal domain is able to bind and discriminate tRNA. The two domains can not complement each other in trans, showing that full enzymatic activity requires covalent continuity |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics analysis of the enzyme has allowed identification of key residues involved in communication between the two domains, and kinetic analysis of mutant enzymes confirmed their importance |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNACys that are important for recognition by CysRS have been identified |CITS: |. Specificity determinants and residues within CysRS that are important for catalytic activity have been investigated |CITS: |. Recognition of the 1-72 base pair of the tRNA acceptor end is accomplished by an α-helical motif insertion in the Rossmann-fold domain of CysRS |CITS: |. A crystal structure of CysRS bound to tRNACys was determined at 2.3 Å resolution, showing extensive base-selective and shape-specific RNA-protein interactions |CITS: |. The efficiency of CysRS aminoacylation is modulated by the G15-G48 Levitt pair together with tertiary nucleotides surrounding it in tRNACys |CITS: |. Investigation of pre-steady-state and single turnover kinetics of CysRS show that the enzyme exhibits burst kinetics and is rate-limited by release of aminoacyl-tRNA, distinguishing it from class II aminoacyl tRNA synthetases |CITS: |. Unlike other aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, CysRS does not possess an editing mechanism to discriminate against non-cognate amino acids |CITS: |. Crystal structures of CysRS in the apo- and cysteine-bound state have been determined at 2.3 and 2.6 Å resolution, revealing a zinc ion at the base of the active site cleft |CITS: |. The zinc ion is responsible for the ability of CysRS to bind cysteine specifically, although CysRS does not possess amino acid editing activity |CITS: |. Unlike other class I aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, CysRS is able to attach cysteine to both the 2' and 3' hydroxyl groups of A76 in tRNACys. However, aminoacylation of the 3' hydroxyl group has a 20-fold lower kcat/Km than that of the 2' hydroxyl group. The conserved nucleotide U73 in tRNACys appears to confer this flexibility |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase is the initial enzyme of one of two 4-aminobutyrate (GABA) degradation pathways |CITS: |. It belongs to the aminotransferase subgroup II of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP)-dependent enzymes |CITS: |. GabT also functions as a 5-aminovalerate aminotransferase during degradation of L-lysine |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the free and inhibitor-bound enzyme and various point mutants have been reported |CITS: |. Although a dimer by gel filtration |CITS: |, the enzyme appears as a tetramer in the crystal structure; tetramer formation is promoted by increasing concentration of PLP |CITS: |. A reaction mechanism was proposed based on analysis of kinetic properties and crystal structures of point mutants in active site residues |CITS: |. The redundancy and promiscuity among aminotransferase enzymes has been investigated. Four enzymes, ArgD, AstC, GabT, and PuuE, show some level of ACOAT activity involved in arginine biosynthesis. On minimal medium lacking arginine, single argD or astC mutants have subtle growth defects, and an argD astC double mutant has a slower doubling time than wild type. An argD astC gabT triple mutant does not grow on medium lacking arginine. Accumulation of suppressor mutations eventually allows growth of the triple mutant; an additional deletion of puuE eliminates this effect |CITS: |. Expression of gabT is upregulated in a ΔargD mutant grown on minimal medium |CITS: |. In the hands of |CITS: |, the triple deletion mutant ΔargDΔastCΔgabT shows an extensive lag phase on glucose minimal medium; a quadruple deletion mutant that includes ΔpuuE does not grow. The normal activities of two enzymes, ArgD and SerC, are sufficient for succinyldiaminopimelate (SDAP) and lysine biosynthesis; a third enzyme, AstC, is sufficient for SDAP biosynthesis, but alone can not fulfill the cell's requirement for lysine. Additional enzymes, including GabT and PuuE, may be able to contribute to SDAP biosynthesis. Expression of argD, astC, serC, aspC, gabT, hisC, ilvE, patA, puuE, or tyrB from a plasmid allows growth of the triple ΔargD serC astC mutant on minimal medium |CITS: |. The three major transaminases in alanine biosynthesis are AvtA, AlaA and AlaC. Expression of aspC, gabT, puuE, tyrB, or ygjG from a plasmid partially suppresses the growth defect of a ΔavtA alaA alaC mutant |CITS: |. A gabT mutant can not utilize GABA as the sole source of nitrogen at 37°C |CITS: |. Regulation of the operon containing gabT has been studied extensively |CITS: |. Expression can be induced by growth in high pH medium |CITS: |. gabT was also identified in a screen for genes which are activated by self-produced extracellular signals |CITS: |. Mutational knockout of gabT has been used as part of a strategy to increase GABA yield in E. coli strains metabolically engineered to produce GABA |CITS: |. GabT: "gamma-aminobutyrate utilization; transaminase" |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) carboxykinase (Pck) is an enzyme involved in gluconeogenesis. Growth on succinate as the carbon and energy source is limited by the level of Pck in the cell |CITS: |. PEP carboxykinase is unusual in that it appears to be a monomeric enzyme with an allosteric site |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme have been solved |CITS: |, providing insight into the mechanistic details of the enzymatic reaction |CITS: | and into the mechanism of activation by Ca2+ |CITS: |. Transcription of pck is regulated by catabolite repression and is induced at the onset of stationary phase |CITS: | and is regulated by CsrA |CITS: |. Overexpression of pck during growth on glucose leads to reduced growth yield and increased excretion of fermentation products such as acetate |CITS: |. Expression of Pck is upregulated when acetate is used as the source of carbon |CITS: |. A double mutant defective in both PEP carboxykinase and |FRAME: PEPSYNTH-CPLX| is unable to utilize C4-dicarboxylic acids such as succinate and malate as the sole source of carbon and energy |CITS: |. The salvage pathways can convert adenine, adenosine and deoxyadenosine to guanine nucleotides |CITS: | (see pathways |FRAME: PWY0-1296|, |FRAME: PWY0-1297|, |FRAME: PWY-6605|, |FRAME: PWY-6609| and |FRAME: PWY-6611|). The enzyme was shown to be induced in E. coli B by the presence of adenine or hypoxanthine in the culture medium |CITS: |. The native apparent molecular mass of the enzyme from E. coli K-12 was determined to be 29 kDa by gel filtration chromatography, using either purified enzyme, or enzyme from crude extracts |CITS: |. E. coli adenosine deaminase shares approximately 33% amino acid sequence identity and 50% overall homology with mammalian adenosine deaminases, suggesting structural and functional similarity |CITS: |. Murine adenosine deaminase is a monomeric enzyme that requires Zn2+ as a cofactor. Its crystal structure has been determined |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Plays a central role in chromosome condensation, segregation and cell cycle progression. Functions as a homodimer, which is essential for chromosome partition. MetaCyc_Comment: LdtD is a periplasmic L,D-transpeptidase that catalyses the formation of meso-diaminopimelyl → meso-diaminopimelyl cross links (also called DAP3→DAP3 or 3-3 cross-links) in peptidoglycan. LdtD is a stress reponse L,D-transpeptidase with a role in the protective remodeling of peptidoglycan during cell envelope stress |CITS: |, Muropeptides obtained from the peptidoglycan of an |FRAME: G7073 ldtA| |FRAME: G6422 ldtB| |FRAME: G6571 ldtC| ldtD |FRAME: G6904 ldtE| quintuple mutant (BW25113Δ5) do not contain meso-DAP3-meso-DAP3 cross-links, tripeptide stems substituted by a fragment of the Braun lipoprotein, free tripeptide stems nor tetrapeptide stems with Gly as the fourth amino acid |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Expression of ldtD in the BW25113Δ5 mutant restores production of meso-DAP3-meso-DAP3 cross-links, hydrolysis of D-Ala4, and exchange of D-Ala4 by Gly |CITS: |. E. coli K-12 constains a second enzyme (LdtE) that forms DAP3→DAP3 cross-links in peptidoglycan; growth of a strain lacking both LdtD and LdtE (Δldt2) is not affected under a wide variety of conditions, but their absence contributes to the growth defect of an Δldt5 strain (ΔldtABCDE) grown on minimal DAP medium |CITS: |. Purified, soluble LdtD, incubated with a peptidoglycan disaccharide-tetrapeptide catalyses the formation of DAP3→DAP3 cross links and also displays L,D-carboxypeptidase activity; purified, soluble LdtD is irreversibly acylated by β-lactams of the the carbapenem class while adducts resulting from acylation by β-lactams of the penam and cephem classes are prone to hydrolysis |CITS: |. LdtD over-production and increased synthesis of the alarmone (p)ppGpp confers broad-spectrum resistance to β-lactams (with the exception of carbapenems) in E. coli mutant strain M1; in the presence of ampicillin, peptidoglycan polymerization requires the L,D-transpeptidase activity of LdtD, the glycosyltransferase activity of PBP1b, and the D,D-carboxypeptidase activity of PBP5 |CITS: |. Copper inhibits purified LdtD at submillimolar concentration and in a concentration-dependent manner; copper prevents the LdtD-mediated β-lactam resistance of E. coli M1 |CITS: |. LdtD is activated in response to outer membrane damage; LdtD transpeptidase activity increases the level of meso-DAP3-meso-DAP3 cross-links to fortify the peptidoglycan during cell envelope stress |CITS: |. LdtD physically interacts with PBP1b when cells are experiencing OM stress; LdtD, cooperates with (trans-peptidase inactive) |FRAME: CPLX0-3951 PBP1B|, LpoB and |FRAME: CPLX0-8252 PBP5| or |FRAME: CPLX0-8254 PBP6a| to produce a highly 3-3 cross-linked nascent PG in vitro |CITS: |. The structure of LdtD with bound meropenem has been reported; LdtD consists of a catalytic domain (residues 375-576 with canonical L,D-transpeptidase fold plus a unique a substrate capping subdomain), a scaffolding domain which may be involved in protein interactions, a putative peptidoglycan binding domain (residues 234 -351), and a linker region |CITS: | LdtD is the main L,D-transpeptidase incorporating the D-alanine fluorescent probe NADA into peptidoglycan, at neutral pH during exponential growth; PBP1B, LpoB and CpoB are required for efficient NADA incorporation by LdtD |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). E. coli K-12 incorporates exogenously supplied D-methionine into peptidoglycan stem tetrapeptides; the percentage of muropeptides that contain D-methionine is reduced to varying extents in all single ldt insertion mutants* and is reduced by ~75% in the double ldtD ldtE insertion mutant |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Deletion of ldtD together with ldtE also reduces detection of D-cysteine in peptidoglycan |CITS: |. ldtD shows delayed upregulation in response to an acid shift |CITS: |. Constitutive activation of the Cpx two component pathway results in upregulation of ldtD and a resultant increase in the level of DAP3→DAP3 crosslinks; ldtD is a member of the CpxR regulon |CITS: |. LdtD is predicted to be a bitopic inner membrane protein |CITS: |. LdtA, B, C and E are all of similar size and share 42-62% sequence similarity; LdtD is a larger protein and shares only 11-17% sequence similarity with the others; the putative active site cysteine is located in a conserved motif towards the C-terminus |CITS: |. Overexpression of ldtD from an ASKA plasmid leads to a more than 3-fold increase in the MIC of hypochlorous acid |CITS: |. *|FRAME: G6108-MONOMER ldtF| was not included in this analysis

MetaCyc_Comment: TrmA is the methyltransferase that catalyzes methylation of U54 in the TΨ loop of tRNAs |CITS: | as well as methylation of the corresponding U341 residue within the tRNA-like domain of |FRAME: SSRA-RNA| |CITS: |. In addition to its catalytic activity, TrmA also acts as a tRNA chaperone |CITS: |. tRNAs carry multiple modifications, often in nearby nucleotide residues. The preferred substrate for the TrmA methyltransferase activity is unmodified tRNA, while its binding activity is highest with Ψ55-modified tRNA |CITS: |. The catalytic mechanism involves formation of a covalent complex between the catalytic Cys324 residue of the enzyme and tRNA |CITS: | and occurs by single SN2 displacement |CITS: |. Stereochemically, the reaction proceeds by cis addition followed by trans elimination |CITS: |. Random and site-directed mutagenesis of conserved residues allowed identification of residues involved in formation of the TrmA-tRNA intermediate, enzymatic activity |CITS: |, as well as SAM and tRNA binding |CITS: |. Glu358 acts as a general base, abstracting a proton from C5 of the methylated reaction intermediate |CITS: |. TrmA is also able to methylate 16S rRNA at the U788 residue in vitro, possibly due to the sequence and structural similarity of that rRNA region to the TΨ stem-loop |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within the tRNA encompass both the primary and secondary structure of the T-arm |CITS: |; a 2-5 bp stem and 7 nt loop as well as the U54 methyl acceptor and C56 are required |CITS: |. The crystal structure of a complex between TrmA E358Q and a 19-mer RNA fragment corresponding to the covalently bound reaction intermediate has been solved at 2.4Å resolution. The U54 base is flipped out of the T loop, and other bases adopt a specific fold that differs from the mature tRNA fold |CITS: |. The enzyme is present in both a free form and strongly bound to tRNA and 16S rRNA in vivo, but is not associated with the ribosome |CITS: |. The trmA5 point mutant that lacks all m5U modification of tRNA has essentially no detectable phenotype, although it is outcompeted by wild type in mixed populations |CITS: |. Various trmA point mutants unable to bind or methylate tRNA are also outcompeted by wild type |CITS: |. Introduction of the trmA5 to a double truB trmH mutant, resulting in lack of m5U54, ψ55, and Gm18 modifications to tRNA, only slightly worsens the growth rate defect of the truB trmH mutant |CITS: |. An earlier report suggested that the trmA gene is essential for viability, implying a second, vital function in addition to m5U modification of tRNA |CITS: |, but trmA deletion strains were later obtained |CITS: |. Expression of trmA is growth rate-dependent |CITS: |. TrmA: "transfer RNA methylation" |CITS: |

Crystal structures of the enzyme in the unligated form and in complex with the substrate analog α-methyl-L-glutamate have been solved, and a molecular reaction mechanism was proposed |CITS: |. In serine biosynthesis, α-ketoglutarate (αKG) is the side product of the SerC-catalyzed reaction that follows SerA in the pathway. MetaCyc_Comment: Phosphatidylserine synthase (PssA) catalyzes the de novo synthesis of phosphatidylserine, the first committed step to phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthesis from precursors. Some of the enzymes involved in phospholipid biosynthesis interact and may form a functional complex in the membrane |CITS: |. The enzymatic activity of phosphatidylserine synthase is modulated by the membrane phospholipid composition and may constitute a regulatory mechanism |CITS: |. Catalysis by PssA appears to involve a two-step ping-pong mechanism that involves an enzyme-bound phosphatidyl intermediate |CITS: |. The enzyme is unique among the phospholipid biosynthetic enzymes in that it is tightly associated with ribosomes in crude extracts |CITS: |. Increased ionic strength or addition of the polyamine spermidine leads to dissociation from the ribosomal fraction |CITS: |, while addition of membranes containing either the substrate CDP-diacylglycerol or the product phosphatidylserine lead to membrane association |CITS: |. The enzymatic activity is modulated by the structure of the lipid vesicles and the type of phospholipids present |CITS: |. Both of the major anionic membrane lipids stimulate phosphatidylserine synthase activity |CITS: |. Temperature-sensitive pssA mutants, when shifted to the non-permissive temperature, become filamentous |CITS: | and are defective in flagellar motility and chemotaxis |CITS: |. Both inner and outer membranes show increased levels of cardiolipin |CITS: |. The growth arrest phenotype caused by depletion of phosphatidylserine synthase activity can be rescued by the addition of the divalent metal ions Ca2+, Mg2+ or Sr2+ at millimolar concentrations |CITS: |. The |FRAME: PWY0-1485| is activated in a pss-93 mutant (phosphatidylethanolamine-deficient) strain |CITS: |. Overexpression of PssA from a plasmid has little effect on the phospholipid composition of the cells |CITS: |. However, a later publication showed that overexpression of pssA from a strong promoter increases phosphatidylethanolamine levels and decreases phosphatidylglycerol and cardiolipin levels compared to wild type; the increased levels of PE enhanced tolerance to octanoate by improving membrane integrity and electrochemical potential, cellular hydrophilicity and intracellular pH |CITS: |. Overexpression of pssA leads to increased resistance to the aminoglycoside antibiotic sisomicin |CITS: |. Sparrow and Raetz |CITS: | isolated a mutant, pssR1, that caused increased expression of PssA and was thought to map to a transcriptional repressor. FUNCTION: Member of the two-component regulatory system PhoP/PhoQ involved in adaptation to low Mg(2+) environments and the control of acid resistance genes. In low periplasmic Mg(2+), PhoQ functions as a membrane-associated protein kinase that undergoes autophosphorylation and subsequently transfers the phosphate to PhoP, resulting in the expression of PhoP-activated genes (PAG) and repression of PhoP-repressed genes (PRG). In high periplasmic Mg(2+), acts as a protein phosphatase that dephosphorylates phospho-PhoP, resulting in the repression of PAG and may lead to expression of some PRG (By similarity). PhoP-regulated transcription is redox-sensitive, being activated when the periplasm becomes more reducing (deletion of dsbA/dsbB, or treatment with dithiothreitol). MgrB acts between DsbA/DsbB and PhoP/PhoQ in this pathway; the 2 periplasmic Cys residues of MgrB are required for its action on PhoQ, which then acts on PhoP. Mediates magnesium influx to the cytosol by activation of mgtA. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter complex OppABCDF involved in the uptake of oligopeptides (PubMed:2187863). Plays an important nutritional role (Probable). Binds peptides containing from two to five amino acid residues (PubMed:21983341, PubMed:3536860). Displays a preference for tripeptides and tetrapeptides over dipeptides and pentapeptides, for peptides composed of L-amino acids and for positively charged peptides (PubMed:21983341, PubMed:3536860). Cannot bind the cell wall peptide L-Ala-D-Gly-gamma-meso-diaminopimelic acid (PubMed:21705338). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:21705338, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2187863, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21983341, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3536860, ECO:0000305}.
MetaCyc_Comment: OppA is the periplasmic binding protein of an ABC transporter that mediates the high affinity uptake of oligopeptides. The crystal structure of OppA complexed with peptide ligand (modeled using a tripeptide) is highly similar to that of the well characterized S. typhimurium OppA (see |CITS: |); the ligand is bound in a closed cavity deep inside the protein; the binding cavity contains large hydrated pockets believed to allow the presence of chemically diverse peptide side chains |CITS: |. OppA has a preference for positively charged tripeptides and tetrapeptides |CITS: |. A periplasmic binding protein (suggested to be OppA) purified from E. coli W binds the tripeptide Ala-Phe-Gly with a Kd of 0.1 µM and a stoichiometry of 1:1; it does not bind amino acids or dipeptides and tolerates a wide variety of amino acyl side chains |CITS: |. OppA from E. coli has 85% sequence identity with OppA from S. typhimurium and is a class II, cluster C type substrate binding protein |CITS: |. oppA shows differential codon adaptation, resulting in differential translation efficiency signatures, in thermophilic microbes. It is therefore predicted to play a role in the heat shock response. An oppA deletion mutant is more sensitive than wild-type specifically to heat shock, but not other stresses |CITS: |. OppA has chaperone-like properties; the purified protein increases the refolding of denatured substrate, protects against thermal denaturation, and interacts with a model unfolded protein (reduced carboxymethyl a-lactalbumin) |CITS: |. Overproduction of OppA stabilises a highly unstable MBP mutant; purified OppA inhibits the aggregation of lactate dehydrogenase and α-lactalbumin |CITS: |. Resequencing of multiple isolates of the MG1655 strain has identified several genetic variations compared to the reference sequence, including an IS5 insertion in the region upstream of oppA which may alter its regulation |CITS: |. This EcoliWiki page summarizes these sequence differences. The oppA mutation known as oppA462, initially reported to be a non-polar mutation |CITS: | was later shown to be a polar mutation |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: CysN along with CysD are the two subunits which form sulfate adenylyltransferase |CITS: |. CysN contains a GTP-binding consensus sequence and stimulates the synthesis of |FRAME: APS| (APS) by a GTPase mechanism |CITS: |. Sulfate adenylyltransferase is involved in the assimilation of sulfate and catalyzes two reactions, GTP hydrolysis and activation of intracellular sulfate to APS which generates a sulfate-phosphate anhydride linkage. This linkage facilitates an energetically-downhill entry into the subsequent metabolic fates of reduction and group transfer. The rate of APS formation is enhanced by both a protein activator and by GTP hydrolysis |CITS: |. Disruption of the cysN gene prevents sulfate activation and decreases expression of the downstream cysC gene |CITS: |. cysN, along with cysD and cysC, resides in the sulfate activation operon |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter DppABCDF involved in dipeptide transport (PubMed:10537211, PubMed:1702779, PubMed:7536291). Binds dipeptides and accepts a wide range of side chains, including small neutral, bulky hydrophobic, and positively and negatively charged groups (PubMed:10537211). Tripeptides are poor substrates (PubMed:10537211). DppA alone controls the specificity of the Dpp transporter (PubMed:10537211). In addition, plays a role in chemotaxis toward peptides via interaction with the chemotaxis protein Tap (PubMed:3520334, PubMed:8563629). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10537211, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1702779, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3520334, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7536291, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8563629}.; FUNCTION: Binds heme. When a foreign outer membrane heme receptor is expressed in E.coli, DppABCDF can also transport heme and its precursor, 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA), from the periplasm into the cytoplasm. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:16905647, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8444807}.
MetaCyc_Comment: DppA is the periplasmic binding protein of a dipeptide ABC transport system. dppA mutation results in the inability of a proline auxotroph to utilize Pro-Gly as a proline source; DppA accumulates to high levels when E. coli K-12 strain JM101 is grown in minimal medium; osmotic shock treatment releases DppA into the supernatant |CITS: |. Purified DppA binds ala-ala and ala-phe dipeptides with a 1:1 stoichiometry and substrate specificity has been tested through competitive binding assays; tripeptides are poor substrates as are dipeptides containing one or more D residues |CITS: |. Purified DppA binds heme |CITS: |. Crystal structures of 'open', unliganded DppA (two α/β domains separated by a cleft and connected by two hinge segments) and 'closed' DppA with bound glycyl-L-leucine (three α/β domains; domains I and III connected by 2 strands; dipeptide ligand buried completely) have been reported |CITS: |. The DppA binding site recognizes the peptide backbone while allowing for accommodation of various side chains |CITS:|. DppA is required for dipeptide chemotaxis |CITS: |. Overproduction of DppA stabilises a highly unstable MBP mutant; purified DppA inhibits the aggregation of α-lactalbumin |CITS: |. dppA expression is regulated by the small, non-translated RNA |FRAME: GCVB-RNA "GcvB"| |CITS: |. DppA levels increase in response to glucose-limitation |CITS: |; DppA levels decrease after 4 hours exposure to zinc stress |CITS: |. DppA levels decrease in response to phosphate limitation; a putative Pho box is located upstream of dppA |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: The phage shock protein (psp) operon (pspABCDE) may play a significant role in the competition for survival under nutrient- or energy-limited conditions. PspE catalyzes the sulfur-transfer reaction from thiosulfate to cyanide, to form sulfite and thiocyanate. Also able to use dithiol (dithiothreitol) as an alternate sulfur acceptor. Also possesses a very low mercaptopyruvate sulfurtransferase activity.

MetaCyc_Comment: PspE is a periplasmic sulfurtransferase of the rhodanese family that catalyzes the transfer of sulfur from thiosulfate to a recipient compound such as cyanide |CITS: |. The role of PspE in the cell is still unknown. Based on analysis of deletion mutants, PspE appears to carry out about 85% of the thiosulfate sulfurtransferase activity, with |FRAME: CPLX0-242 "GlpE"| accounting for approximately 10% |CITS: |. Solution structures of the sulfur-free and persulfide intermediate forms of PspE have been solved, indicating that there are no significant conformational changes during the catalytic cycle |CITS: |. The persulfide-modified form of PspE is present when the native protein is purified |CITS: |. Overexpression of PspE does not confer increased resistance to cyanide |CITS: |, and deletion of pspE does not increase sensitivity to cyanide |CITS: |. pspE does not appear to be co-regulated with the other members of the psp operon; rather, PspE activity is carbon source regulated |CITS: |. It was previously shown that the pspE gene may also be transcribed from its own promoter |CITS: |. pspE may be an evolutionarily recent addition to the Psp response |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in the restart of stalled replication forks, which reloads the replicative helicase (DnaB) on sites other than the origin of replication (PubMed:10540288, PubMed:10835375, PubMed:22636770). Recognizes abandoned replication forks and remodels DNA single-stranded binding protein (SSB) on ssDNA to uncover a loading site for DnaB (PubMed:23629733, PubMed:27382050). There are several restart pathways, the PriA-PriC pathway is a minor restart pathway (PubMed:11532137, PubMed:22636770). Also part of the minor PriC-Rep pathway for restart of stalled replication forks, which has a different substrate specificity than PriA (PubMed:10835375, PubMed:17382604). priB and priC have redundant roles in the cell (PubMed:10540288). Stimulates the 3'-5' helicase activity of Rep helicase in vitro (PubMed:17382604). In vitro can load the DnaB replicative helicase from a DnaB-DnaC complex on an SSB-coated stalled replication fork with no leading- or lagging-strand (or with a gap between the leading strand and fork junction) in the absence of other primosome proteins (PriA, PriB or DnaT) (PubMed:15749022, PubMed:23629733, PubMed:27382050). Also part of the major restart pathway with PriA, PriB, DnaB, DnaT and DnaG primase (PubMed:8663105). PriC may contribute to the stability of the preprimosome complex (Probable) (PubMed:8663105). Preferentially binds approximately 7-9 nucleotides of single-stranded (ss)DNA, also binds double-stranded (ds)DNA (PubMed:23819889, PubMed:23868391, PubMed:23629733). PriB is probably more important in the cell than PriC (PubMed:10540288, PubMed:22636770). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10540288, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10835375, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11532137, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15749022, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17382604, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1856227, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22636770, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23629733, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23819889, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23868391, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27382050, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8663105, ECO:0000305|PubMed:8663105}.

FUNCTION: Antitoxin component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system. Neutralizes the toxic effect of cognate toxin HipA (PubMed:20616060). Binds to operator sites with the consensus sequence 5-'TATCCN(8)GGATA-3' to repress the hipBA operon promoter (PubMed:8021189, PubMed:19150849); binding of HipB(2) to DNA induces a 70 degree bend (PubMed:19150849). FUNCTION: Toxic component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system, first identified by mutations that increase production of persister cells, a fraction of cells that are phenotypic variants not killed by antibiotics, which lead to multidrug tolerance (PubMed:16707675, PubMed:26222023, PubMed:6348026, PubMed:8021189). Persistence may be ultimately due to global remodeling of the persister cell's ribosomes (PubMed:25425348). Phosphorylates Glu-tRNA-ligase (AC P04805, gltX, on 'Ser-239') in vivo (PubMed:24095282, PubMed:24343429). Phosphorylation of GltX prevents it from being charged, leading to an increase in uncharged tRNA(Glu). This induces amino acid starvation and the stringent response via RelA/SpoT and increased (p)ppGpp levels, which inhibits replication, transcription, translation and cell wall synthesis, reducing growth and leading to persistence and multidrug resistance (PubMed:24095282, PubMed:24343429). Once the level of HipA exceeds a threshold cells become dormant, and the length of dormancy is determined by how much HipA levels exceed the threshold (PubMed:20616060). The hipA7 mutation (a double G22S D291A mutation) leads to increased generation of persister cells (cells that survive antibiotic treatment) probably by entering into a dormant state, as well as cold-sensitivity (PubMed:14622409, PubMed:16707675). Wild-type cells produce persisters at a frequency of 10(-6) to 10(-5) whereas hipA7 cells produce about 100-fold more persisters (PubMed:14622409, PubMed:16707675, PubMed:25425348). hipA7 decreases the affinity for antitoxin HipB, leading to increased HipA levels and persistence (PubMed:20616060); depending on the protein level, can be toxic enough to reduce cell growth or even kill cells. Generation of persister cells requires (p)ppGpp as cells lacking relA or relA/spoT generate fewer or no persister cells respectively compared to hipA7 (PubMed:14622409). The toxic effect of HipA is neutralized by its cognate antitoxin HipB (PubMed:20616060). Also neutralized by overexpression of gltX (PubMed:24343429, PubMed:28430938). With HipB acts as a corepressor for transcription of the hipBA promoter (PubMed:8021189); binding of HipA-HipB to DNA induces a 70 degree bend (PubMed:19150849, PubMed:26222023). This brings together and dimerizes 2 HipA molecules, which distorts the promoter region, preventing sigma-factor binding; additionally HipA and HipB would physically prevent RNA core polymerase from contacting the -35 promoter box (PubMed:26222023). May play a role in biofilm formation (PubMed:23329678). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:14622409, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16707675, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17041039, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19150849, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20616060, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23329678, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23667235, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24095282, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24343429, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25425348, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26222023, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28430938, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6348026, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8021189}.

MetaCyc_Comment: The puuC gene was first reported as a gene encoding a putative aldehyde dehydrogenase of unknown function. The product of the gene shares 40% identity and over 60% similarity, with both the cytosolic and the mitochondrial forms of mammalian aldehyde dehydrogenases |CITS: |. It was later inferred to be the γ-glutamyl-γ-aminobutyraldehyde dehydrogenase in a putrescine utilization pathway; together with PuuB, γ-glutamyl-γ-aminobutyrate is produced from γ-glutamylputrescine |CITS: |. The purified enzyme was shown to have somewhat promiscuous aldehyde dehydrogenase activity; γ-glutamyl-γ-aminobutyraldehyde was not tested as a substrate in that study |CITS: |. A later study has shown that the enzyme was able to catalyze three separate reactions involved in putrescine catabolism: |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.99|, |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.19|, and |FRAME: EC-1.2.1.24| |CITS: |. The function of genes in the puu gene cluster was initially inferred by similarity with the ipuABCDEGFH operon in Pseudomonas sp. |CITS: |. The puuC, puuB, and puuE genes may form an operon |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter complex CydDC that exports the reduced low-molecular-weight thiols cysteine and glutathione to the periplasm (PubMed:12393891, PubMed:16040611). Export of these thiol-containing redox-active molecules may be crucial for redox homeostasis in the periplasm, permitting correct assembly of various respiratory complexes and formation of correct disulfide bonds in periplasmic and secreted proteins (Probable). CydC contains transmembrane domains (TMD), which form a pore in the inner membrane, and an ATP-binding domain (NBD), which is responsible for energy generation (PubMed:24958725). Required for the assembly of functional cytochrome bd-type quinol oxidases and periplasmic c-type cytochromes (PubMed:15470119, PubMed:3032907, PubMed:7934832, PubMed:8181727). Overexpression of CydDC under anaerobic conditions also results in the formation of a heme biosynthesis-derived pigment, P-574 (PubMed:12375104). CydDC binds heme b, but heme is probably not transported by the complex and instead has a role in regulating ATPase activity (PubMed:24958725). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12375104, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12393891, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15470119, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16040611, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24958725, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3032907, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7934832, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8181727, ECO:0000305|PubMed:12393891, ECO:0000305|PubMed:16040611, ECO:0000305|PubMed:31279084}.; FUNCTION: Conversely, a more recent study suggests an alternative function of CydDC: authors suggest that CydDC does not mediate the export of L-cysteine but rather reduces cytoplasmic L-cystine to L-cysteine (PubMed:32900959). The principle function of CydDC would be to maintain the reduced state of cytoplasmic L-cysteine, thereby providing an important connection between sulfur metabolism, oxidative stress and resistance to antibiotics (PubMed:32900959). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:32900959}.

Cells carrying a cydC null mutation lack a functional cytochrome d complex - the mutant lacks detectable heme d but is still capable of synthesizing the two subunits of the cytochrome complex in vitro |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: ADP-heptose:LPS heptosyltransferase I (HepI) is the enzyme responsible for transfer of the first heptose sugar onto the Kdo2 moiety of the lipopolysaccharide inner core |CITS: |. HepI is able to catalyze heptose transfer to underacylated and fully deacylated Kdo2-lipid A analogs; this activity does not require addition of detergent. Thus, the enzyme appears to only recognize the Kdo sugar region of these acceptor molecules |CITS: |. Crystal structures of WaaC from the pathogenic strain RS218 have been solved, providing insight into the catalytic mechanism |CITS: |. WaaC is considered to be an antimicrobial drug target, and small molecule inhibitors have been identified |CITS: |. A waaC mutant has a defect in the LPS core heptose region |CITS: |, causing a deep-rough phenotype; the lipopolysaccharide of the mutant strain is heptoseless and contains 2-keto-3-deoxyoctulosonic acid (Kdo) as its only core sugar |CITS: |. A Δ(waaC lpxL lpxM lpxP) strain is viable under slow growth conditions in minimal medium at low temperature (23°C) and synthesizes only Kdo2-lipid IVA. Overexpression of msbA partially rescues the growth defect of that strain. Lack of waaC induces the σE extracytoplasmic stress response |CITS: |. Overexpression of waaC leads to formation of biofilms with abnormal architecture |CITS: |. In waaC, waaE, waaF and waaG mutants biofilm formation was significantly increased relative to the parental strain |CITS: |. The waaC gene is located in the first of three operons in the rfa locus |CITS: |. In E. coli K-12 W3110 inactivation of both chromosomal waaC and the heptosyltransferase waaF by allelic-replacement mutagenesis resulted in Re-LPS with highly 2-aminoethanol phosphate substituted tetrasaccharide |CITS: | (Re-LPS is a rough LPS mutant |CITS: |). In E. coli K-12 strains deficient in waaC and waaF heterologously expressing Chlamydial waaA, it was shown that Kdo-(2->8)-Kdo(2->4), but not Kdo-(2->4)-Kdo(2->4) could serve as a heptose acceptor for E. coli WaaC |CITS: |. Mutant selection on the antibiotic tigecycline included a mutant in waaC with low-level resistance |CITS: |. WaaC was also shown to directly interact with LapB in vivo, the latter being a heat shock protein involved in lipopolysaccharide assembly |CITS: |. The chromosomal waa region (formerly rfa) contains the major core-oligosaccharide assembly operons in E. coli |CITS: ||CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Participates in the efflux of aminoglycosides. Confers resistance to a variety of these substances. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10692383}.
MetaCyc_Comment: AcrD is a member of the resistance-nodulation-division (RND) superfamily |CITS: | and a component of the AcrAD-TolC efflux pump complex in E. coli K-12. AcrD is homologous to the major efflux pump permease AcrB |CITS: |. Disruption of acrD in the K-12 strain JC7623 increases susceptibility to a range of aminoglycoside antibiotics (amikacin, gentamicin, tobramycin, kanamycin and neomycin) and cells accumulate higher levels of labeled dihydrostreptomycin and gentamicin than the parent strain; disruption of acrD in the K-12 strain JC7623 slightly increases susceptibility to erythromycin and puromycin but does not affect susceptibility to a range of other compounds including crystal violet, novobiocin, rifampin, chloramphenicol, carbenicillin, cefoxitin, nalidixic acid, norfloxacin and ampicillin |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Expression of cloned acrD in the K-12 strain KAM3 which lacks AcrB (see |CITS: |) confers increased resistance to deoxycholate, SDS, novobiocin and kanamycin (compared to the mutant parent); overexpression of acrD in the KAM3 strain confers a slightly increased resistance to tetracycline, nalidixic acid, norfloxacin and fosfomycin (compared to the mutant parent) |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Overproduction of AcrD in the K-12 strain KAM3 confers increased levels of resistance to the antibiotics novobiocin, oxacillin, cloxacillin and nafcillin (compared to the mutant parent), restores wild-type levels of resistance to deoxycholate and SDS and confers resistance above the wild-type level to carbenicillin, sulbenicillin and aztreonam; AcrD requires TolC for β-lactam export |CITS: |. AcrD requires AcrA for efflux of novobiocin and bile acids; AcrD interacts physically with AcrA |CITS: |. The two large periplasmic loops determine the substrate specificity of the AcrD and AcrB transporters |CITS: |; the difference in β-lactam selectivity between AcrB and AcrD |CITS: | resides in the proximal binding pocket |CITS: |. AcrD proteoliposomes with an interior-acid ΔpH and entrapped AcrA, mediate efflux of H+ when aminoglycosides (gentamicin, amikacin, tobramycin or kanamycin) are present in the reaction buffer; AcrD proteoliposomes with entrapped AcrA accumulate more labeled gentamicin than control liposomes |CITS: |. AcrD proteoliposomes with an interior-acid ΔpH, entrapped AcrA and entrapped aminoglycosides (gentamycin or amikacin) show enhanced proton efflux compared to AcrD proteoliposomes containing only AcrA |CITS: |. Typical substrates of the AcrB and AcrD systems are hydrophilic and hydrophobic compounds respectively while amphiphilic compounds are transported by both; putative substrate binding sites of AcrB and AcrD have been compared with a view to explaining substrate specificity |CITS: |. By analogy with the AcrB RND permease, AcrD is shown as a homotrimer in the complex. Comments: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Hmp is a flavohemoglobin |CITS: | with multiple enzymatic activities; however, its nitric oxide dioxygenase (NOD) activity appears to be the physiologically relevant function |CITS: |, and is also the major detoxification system |CITS:|. Under aerobic conditions, Hmp detoxifies nitric oxide (NO) and thus protects the respiratory cytochromes bo' or bd |CITS: |. Hmp remains the primary consumer of NO under microaerobic conditions (O2 concentrations as low as 35 mM) |CITS: |. However, in vivo measurements of the dynamics of NO detoxification showed that NO defenses are greatly impaired under microaerobic conditions due to limited activities of both |FRAME: CPLX0-1 NorV| and Hmp |CITS: |. NO tolerance is correlated with virulence |CITS: | and survival in macrophages |CITS: |. The nitric oxide dioxygenase reaction appears to occur in two steps. First, NAD(P)H reduces the bound FAD, which then reduces the heme iron. O2 then binds to the reduced flavohemoglobin, which dioxygenates NO, forming nitrate |CITS: |. However, heme ligand turnover and NADH consumption at different O2/NO concentrations suggests that the enzyme binds NO first; the nitroxyl equivalent is then oxidized |CITS: |. The reaction mechanism has been investigated further |CITS: |. There is some debate whether the reaction follows a dioxygenase or a denitrosylase/NO reductase mechanism |CITS: |. Computer simulations have provided further insights into the catalytic mechanism |CITS: |. The steric and dielectric environment of the heme iron has been investigated |CITS: |. The active site structure appears to be similar to that of peroxidases |CITS: |. A crystal structure of Hmp has been solved at 2.2 Å resolution, showing that the N-terminal globin domain, central FAD-binding domain, and C-terminal NADH-binding domain are arranged in a heart-shaped structure |CITS: |. All domains are required for Hmp function |CITS: |. Folding of the globin domain has been studied |CITS: |. Kinetic competition between Hmp and respiratory cytochromes for oxygen appears to be the cause of impaired NO tolerance under microaerobic conditions |CITS: |. During growth on a limited amount of carbon, Hmp expression is induced, Hmp activity depletes the NADH pool of the cell, and NO detoxification subsequently fails |CITS: |. NO detoxification arises from difficulties associated with Hmp synthesis under concurrent NO and H2O2 stresses. This prioritized detoxification depends on both NsrR and Hmp |CITS:|. Hmp activity causes oxidative stress in the cell due to production of superoxide by its NADH oxidase activity |CITS: |. Hmp can oxidize both NADH and NADPH with a Km of 1.8 and 19.6 µM, respectively |CITS: |. The ferrisiderophore reductase activity |CITS: | and ferric citrate reductase activity |CITS: | of Hmp is a result of the flavin reductase activity of Hmp |CITS: |. Hmp was also shown to have dihydropteridine reductase |CITS: |, cytochrome c reductase and ferric hydroxamate reductase |CITS: | as well as alkylhydroperoxide reductase activity |CITS: |. Hmp binds unsaturated or cyclopropanated fatty acids |CITS: |. The enzyme is inhibited by the imidazole class of antibiotics, including miconazole and econazole |CITS: |. Expression of hmp is regulated in response to oxygen, nitrogen compounds, and iron availability |CITS: | and is induced by acid |CITS: |. NO induction is mediated by Fnr |CITS: | and Fur |CITS: |. An hmp mutant is more sensitive to nitric oxide than wild type |CITS: |, but has a growth advantage in mixed cultures |CITS: |. Expression of hmp under NO stress is decreased in a clpP mutant |CITS: |. The rate of NO reduction in anaerobically grown cells appears to be unaffected in an hmp mutant |CITS: |. Hmp: "haemoprotein" |CITS: | FsrB: "ferrisiderophore reductase B" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: GTPase that associates with the 50S ribosomal subunit and may have a role during protein synthesis or ribosome biogenesis. In vitro, also exhibits ATPase activity. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_00900, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19109926, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19181811, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19824612}.
MetaCyc_Comment: HflX is a heat shock-induced ribosome-dependent GTPase that rescues stalled ribosomes by dissociating vacant and mRNA-associated ribosomes with deacylated tRNA in the peptidyl site |CITS: |. Structural data suggests that HflX disrupts the central bridges between the ribosomal subunits and thereby promotes their dissociation |CITS: |. The HflX protein is a GTPase |CITS: | that interacts with the 50S subunit of the ribosome in the presence of both GTP, GDP, ATP and ADP |CITS: |. The intrinsic GTPase activity of HflX is very slow and can be stimulated 1000-fold by interaction with the 50S subunit |CITS: | as well as 70S ribosomes and poly(U)-programmed 70S ribosomes |CITS: |. GTP hydrolysis is required for ribosome dissociation |CITS: | or the release of HflX from the 50S subunit |CITS: |. HflX binds both GTP and ATP |CITS: |. Both the N-terminal and the C-terminal domain can bind and hydrolyze GTP and ATP |CITS: |. Purine nucleotide binding was studied by equilibrium and pre-steady-state fluorescence techniques. KD values indicate a higher affinity for guanine nucleotides as well as for diphosphates compared to triphosphates; GTP appears to be the physiologically relevant substrate |CITS: |. GTPase activity of HflX is not K+-stimulated |CITS: |. HflX was found to bind (p)ppGpp |CITS: |. A cryo-EM structure of the 50S ribosomal subunit in a complex with HflX and GMP-PNP shows that HflX binds to the intersubunit face of the 50S subunit. The N-terminal domain of HflX contacts several rRNA helices near the peptidyl transferase center, while the C-terminal domain interacts with the L12 stalk base. The 50S subunit itself undergoes conformational changes in the regions involving intersubunit bridges |CITS: |. Although hflX is part of the "hflA" locus which was originally found to change the frequency of λ lysogeny, it does not play a role in this process or in transposition frequency |CITS: |. HflX was thought to be involved in regulation of HflC and HflK activity |CITS: |, but it does not interact with HflK or HflC |CITS: |. Autophosphorylation of HflX in the presence of Mn2+ was observed |CITS: |; based on mutagenesis results, the S211 residue within the P-loop is the GTP-dependent autophosphorylation site |CITS: |. High concentrations of Mn2+ appear to inhibit growth of a ΔhflX mutant |CITS: |. The hflA locus contains the hflC, hflK, and hflX genes |CITS: |. It affects the λ phage lysis/lysogeny switch by playing a role in proteolysis of the λ cII protein |CITS: |. A strain containing an in-frame deletion of hflX shows no change in lysogenic frequency of λ or in frequency of transposition |CITS: |. hflX is part of a complex superoperon |CITS: |. Expression is increased by heat shock |CITS: |, and a hflX mutant shows a growth defect at increased temperatures |CITS: |. Hfl: "high frequency of lysogeny" Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Exhibits a very high intrinsic GTPase hydrolysis rate. Involved in the addition of a carboxymethylaminomethyl (cmnm) group at the wobble position (U34) of certain tRNAs, forming tRNA-cmnm(5)s(2)U34.
MetaCyc_Comment: MnmE is required for wild-type 5-methylaminomethyl-2-thiouridine modification of tRNA |CITS: |. The additional modification of m5U stabilizes the U·G pairing at the wobble position and thus plays a role in decoding NNG codons |CITS: |. Together with MnmG, MnmE is involved in maintenance of the correct reading frame |CITS: |. MnmE also appeared to play a role in oxidation of thiophene and furan compounds |CITS: | and regulates glutamate-dependent acid resistance |CITS: |. MnmE is a GTP-binding protein that also exhibits GTPase activity, showing rapid GTP hydrolysis and low nucleotide affinity. The nucleotide binding and hydrolysis activities are localized within the central 17 kDa GTPase domain |CITS: |. The GTPase activity as well as the Cys451 residue in the C-terminal domain are required |CITS: |, but not sufficient |CITS: | for the wild-type tRNA modification function. Dimerization of the GTPase domain is potassium ion-dependent; subsequent GTP hydrolysis activity is dependent on dimerization |CITS: |. Low pH inhibits the GTP hydrolysis activity |CITS: |. Unlike other GTPases, MnmE does not appear to use an "arginine finger" for catalysis |CITS: |. While the GTPase domain is required for homodimerization, the helical domain of MnmE is responsible for the interaction with MnmG |CITS: |. Nucleotide binding leads to a conformational change in MnmE, and GTP-bound MnmE has a much higher affinity for MnmG |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Aldehyde dehydrogenase A (AldA) is an NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase of relatively broad specificity for small α-hydroxyaldehyde substrates. It is thus utilized in several metabolic pathways |CITS: |. The glycolaldehyde dehydrogenase activity of AldA may serve an essential function in removing the glycolaldehyde side product of |FRAME: H2NEOPTERINALDOL-MONOMER FolB| within the folate biosynthesis pathway. The function can be bypassed by |FRAME: G6198-MONOMER PrpC| |CITS: |. L-fucose and L-rhamnose are metabolized through parallel pathways which converge after their corresponding aldolase reactions yielding the same products: dihydoxy-acetone phosphate and L-lactaldehyde. Aerobically, aldehyde dehydrogenase A oxidizes L-lactaldehyde to L-lactate |CITS: |. In parallel pathways utilizing the same enzymes, D-arabinose and L-lyxose can be metabolized to dihydoxy-acetone phosphate and glycolaldehyde, which is oxidized to glycolate by aldehyde dehydrogenase A |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme alone and in ternary and binary complexes have been solved, suggesting a structural basis for AldA's specificity for NADH |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis of the F180 residue and kinetic characterization of the mutant enzyme showed that this residue is involved in cosubstrate specificity of AldA |CITS: |. Aldehyde dehydrogenase A is only present under aerobic conditions and is most highly induced by the presence of fucose, rhamnose or glutamate |CITS: |. The enzyme is inhibited by NADH, which may act as a switch to shift from oxidation of lactaldehyde to its reduction by propanediol oxidoreductase |CITS: |. Based on sequence similarity, AldA was predicted to be a succinate-semialdehyde dehydrogenase |CITS: |. Regulation of aldA expression has been investigated. The gene is regulated by catabolite repression |CITS: |, repression under anaerobic conditions via ArcA |CITS: |, and induction by the carbon source |CITS: |. AldA expression is upregulated during short-term adaptation to glucose limitation |CITS: | and by the presence of oleate |CITS: |. An aldA mutant shows slower growth on fucose and rhamnose than wild type |CITS: |. aldA and |FRAME: G6198 prpC| are synthetically lethal. Based on the lack of sequence and structural similarity between AldA and PrpC, it seems unlikely that PrpC also catalyzes the glycolaldehyde dehydrogenase reaction. Potential explanations for the synthetic lethality of aldA and prpC were discussed |CITS: |. AldA: "lactaldehyde dehydrogenase"

MetaCyc_Comment: In the absence of exogenously supplied vitamin B12 (cobalamin), E. coli MetE catalyzes the final step of de novo methionine biosynthesis. In the presence of the vitamin B12 cofactor, MetH functions in this reaction and synthesis of MetE is repressed (see pathway |FRAME: HOMOSER-METSYN-PWY|). The metE and metH genes lack similarity in their deduced amino acid sequences, suggesting that these proteins arose by convergent evolution |CITS: |. MetE was shown to utilize only the triglutamate form of folate (5-methyltetrahydropteroyltri-L-glutamate) whereas MetH utilized either the monoglutamate (5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate) or the triglutamate forms of folate |CITS: |. Early studies utilized unpurified or partially purified enzyme |CITS: |. The enzyme was later purified from extracts of E. coli K-12 and characterized |CITS: |. The metE gene was cloned and expressed |CITS: | and the expression of MetE was shown to be repressed by methionine and vitamin B12 |CITS: |. Recombinant enzyme has also been purified and characterized |CITS: |. MetE contains zinc which is necessary for its activity. Cys643 and Cys726 have been identified as two of the zinc ligands and a third may be His641 |CITS: |. Evidence suggested that the sulfur of the homocysteine substrate binds directly to the zinc ion |CITS: |. Modeling of the structure of E. coli MetE based on the crystal structure of MetE from Thermotoga maritima showed a double-barrel structure that likely evolved by gene duplication |CITS: |. Inactivation of MetE has been shown in E. coli cells growing under conditions of transient oxidative stress, resulting in a methionine auxotrophy. Under these conditions MetE protein is found at high levels. A possible mechanism involving reversible inactivation of MetE by oxidized glutathione was proposed and glutathionylation of Cys645 at the entrance to the active site was demonstrated. Thiol-trapping experiments provided direct evidence of MetE oxidation in vivo |CITS: |. It was subsequently shown that a Cys645Ala mutant eliminated the methionine auxotrophy imposed by oxidative stress, suggesting that modulation of MetE activity by Cys645 oxidation has physiological significance under these conditions. Control of methionine availability may modulate cellular growth during oxidative stress |CITS: |. The MetE reaction mechanism has been studied with respect to the kinetic pathway for binding of substrates 5-methyltetrahydropteroyltri-L-glutamate and homocysteine. Binding of these substrates was found to be synergistic. Evidence also suggested that activation of 5-methyltetrahydropteroyltri-L-glutamate for methyl group transfer occurs by protonation of N5, which occurs upon formation of the ternary MetE, homocysteine, 5-methyltetrahydropteroyltri-L-glutamate complex |CITS: |. Adaptation of E. coli to anaerobic growth has been shown to involve the action of a conserved, anaerobically induced small regulatory RNA named FnrS which negatively regulates a set of genes that includes metE (see the illustration above and click on FnrS). FnrS expression is strictly dependent on the anaerobic transcriptional regulator FNR. It was suggested that FnrS-mediated post-transcriptional control may play a role in rapid adaptation during anaerobic-to-aerobic transitions |CITS: |. MetJ and MetR are involved in the overexpression of MetE, which is strongly induced by GroE depletion |CITS: |. Review: Hondrop, E.R. and R.G. Matthews (2006) "Methionine" EcoSal 3.6.1.7 |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Inner membrane protein required for the insertion and/or proper folding and/or complex formation of integral inner membrane proteins. Involved in integration of membrane proteins that insert dependently and independently of the Sec translocase complex, as well as at least 2 lipoproteins. Its own insertion requires SRP and is Sec translocase-dependent. Essential for the integration of Sec-dependent subunit a of the F(0)ATP synthase, FtsQ and SecE proteins and for Sec-independent subunit c of the F(0)ATP synthase, M13 phage procoat and the N-terminus of leader peptidase Lep. Probably interacts directly with Sec-independent substrates. Sec-dependent protein FtsQ interacts first with SecY then subsequently with YidC. Merged_Functions: The article describes maeA as encoding the malic enzyme in Escherichia coli. This enzyme catalyzes the reversible conversion between malate and pyruvate, specifically the reaction Pyr → Mal (pyruvate to malate). It is highlighted as one of the three anaplerotic carboxylation reactions (alongside pyc and ppc) that can replenish four‑carbon intermediates (oxaloacetate and malate) and thereby enhance succinate production, particularly under anaerobic conditions. {PubMed:24103861}. MaeA encodes an NADH‑dependent malic enzyme that catalyzes the reversible carboxylation of pyruvate to malate. In Escherichia coli it is described as a gluconeogenic enzyme whose expression is repressed by glucose. The article reports that overexpression of maeA did not markedly increase malate or succinate production and even decreased cell growth, likely because the NADH/NAD⁺ balance is perturbed. {PubMed:33668723}. The article describes maeA as encoding a malic enzyme (MaeA) that catalyzes the decarboxylation of malate to pyruvate within the proposed POMP pathway (PEP‑oxaloacetate‑malate‑pyruvate). In pyruvate kinase‑deficient E. coli strains, this reaction provides the essential pyruvate needed for growth on glycerol. Deletion of maeA markedly reduces growth on glycerol, confirming its critical role in supplying pyruvate via malate decarboxylation. {PubMed:23957584}. The maeA gene encodes the NAD‑dependent malic enzyme of Escherichia coli. This enzyme catalyzes the decarboxylation of C4 metabolites such as malate (and oxaloacetate) to the C3 metabolite pyruvate, using NAD⁺ as a cofactor and thereby generating NADH. In the study, artificial overexpression of maeA increased intracellular NADH concentrations (up to 5.2 µmol g DCW⁻¹) and, when combined with the pgi knockout, also raised NADPH levels, leading to the highest overall reducing‑power pool among the tested strains. The excess NADH produced by maeA expression was shown to impair growth of wild‑type cells, likely due to an imbalance in NAD⁺/NADH required for glycolysis, whereas the pgi‑disrupted strain could tolerate the increase. Thus, maeA functions as a key NADH‑producing, malate‑decarboxylating enzyme that modulates cellular redox balance and growth phenotypes in engineered E. coli. {PubMed:21272045}. The maeA gene (also called sfcA) encodes a NAD‑dependent malic enzyme (SfcA) in Escherichia coli.  SfcA catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of L‑malate to pyruvate and CO₂, using NAD⁺ as the electron acceptor (producing NADH).  This reaction links the tricarboxylic‑acid cycle to glycolysis/gluconeogenesis at the phosphoenolpyruvate‑pyruvate‑oxaloacetate node, providing pyruvate for the forward glycolytic pathway and, together with phosphoenolpyruvate synthetase, generating phosphoenolpyruvate for gluconeogenesis.  MaeA/SfcA is induced during growth on acetate and contributes to acetate metabolism.  The enzyme functions as a homotetramer (~64 kDa per subunit) and displays kinetic properties characteristic of NAD‑specific malic enzymes (low Kₘ for NAD⁺, high catalytic efficiency with NAD⁺, and lower activity with NADP⁺).  Allosteric regulation includes activation by aspartate and inhibition by CoA, acetyl‑phosphate, palmitoyl‑CoA, and oxaloacetate.  Because of its robust activity and specificity, MaeA has been employed in metabolic‑engineering applications, such as restoring nitrogen fixation in Sinorhizobium meliloti NAD‑ME mutants and improving succinate production. {PubMed:17557829}. The sfcA gene encodes SfcA, a ~64 kDa malic enzyme that functions primarily as an NAD⁺‑dependent oxidative decarboxylase. SfcA catalyzes the conversion of L‑malate to pyruvate and CO₂ while reducing NAD⁺ to NADH (it can also use NADP⁺ with much lower efficiency). The enzyme prefers NAD⁺ (≈15‑fold lower Kₘ than for NADP⁺) and displays a catalytic efficiency ∼100‑fold higher with NAD⁺. SfcA assembles as a homotetramer in solution. In E. coli it participates in the phosphoenolpyruvate‑pyruvate‑oxaloacetate node, providing a route for the flow of carbon from TCA‑cycle intermediates to phosphoenolpyruvate for gluconeogenesis, especially under acetate‑utilizing conditions. Its activity is allosterically activated by aspartate and inhibited by CoA, acetyl‑phosphate, palmitoyl‑CoA, and oxaloacetate. SfcA has been employed in metabolic‑engineering applications (e.g., restoring N₂ fixation in S. meliloti mutants and enhancing succinate production) and is induced during acetate metabolism. {PubMed:17557829}. The article states that sfcA encodes the NAD‑dependent malic enzyme (ME1). This enzyme participates in the malic enzyme reaction, converting malate to pyruvate (and CO₂) while using NAD⁺ as a cofactor. In the study, sfcA was under‑expressed in Acinetobacter schindleri ACE relative to Escherichia coli JM101, resulting in a lower ME1 activity and a higher ME2/ME1 activity ratio in ACE. {PubMed:31281927}. The article states that sfcA encodes the NAD‑dependent malic enzyme A (EC 1.1.1.38). This enzyme catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of L‑malate to pyruvate with the reduction of NAD⁺ to NADH. It is part of an alternative metabolic route (the PEP shunt) that can convert malate to oxaloacetate via malic enzyme, phosphoenolpyruvate synthase, and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, providing a bypass for malate oxidation when the primary malate dehydrogenases are absent. {PubMed:11092847}. The article identifies sfcA as one of the malic enzymes (alongside MaeB) that participate in the phosphoenolpyruvate–pyruvate–oxaloacetate (PEP‑PYR‑OAA) node of central carbon metabolism in E. coli. As a malic enzyme, SfcA catalyzes the conversion of malate to pyruvate (and vice‑versa), thereby linking the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle with glycolysis and gluconeogenesis. Its transcription is modulated under the experimental conditions: sfcA is down‑regulated in the PB11 pykAF‑ppsA‑ mutant (which shows reduced acetate catabolism) and up‑regulated in the evolved PB12 pykAF‑ppsA‑ mutant during simultaneous utilization of glucose and acetate, indicating its role in supplying pyruvate when the usual PEP‑to‑PYR routes (pykA/pykF and ppsA) are blocked. {PubMed:24375081}. The article reports that sfcA is one of the gluconeogenic genes that become up‑regulated in Escherichia coli during carbon‑limited (glucose‑limited) chemostat cultures. Its expression increases together with other gluconeogenic enzymes such as maeB and pck, indicating that sfcA participates in the gluconeogenesis pathway that replenishes precursors for biosynthesis when external glucose is scarce. {PubMed:21881893}. sfcA encodes an NAD⁺‑linked malic enzyme. In Escherichia coli it catalyzes the reversible conversion of malate to pyruvate with concomitant decarboxylation and oxidation (malate + NAD⁺ → pyruvate + CO₂ + NADH). The enzyme is thought to function primarily during gluconeogenesis rather than anaerobic catabolism of glucose, and its kinetic properties favor the dehydrogenation/decarboxylation direction under physiological conditions. Deletion of sfcA in the engineered succinate‑producing strains did not affect succinate yield, indicating that the enzyme is not essential for succinate production under the tested anaerobic conditions. {PubMed:18781696}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the reversible oxidative decarboxylation of L‑malate to pyruvate and CO₂, using NAD⁺ (producing NADH), and the reverse carboxylation of pyruvate to malate. {PubMed:24103861, PubMed:33668723, PubMed:23957584, PubMed:21272045, PubMed:17557829, PubMed:11092847, PubMed:18781696, PubMed:31281927}. Links the tricarboxylic‑acid cycle to glycolysis and gluconeogenesis by providing pyruvate and, together with phosphoenolpyruvate synthetase, generating phosphoenolpyruvate at the PEP‑pyruvate‑oxaloacetate node, thereby contributing to anaplerotic replenishment of four‑carbon intermediates. {PubMed:24103861, PubMed:21272045, PubMed:17557829, PubMed:11092847, PubMed:24375081, PubMed:21881893, PubMed:23957584}. Is transcriptionally induced during growth on acetate and under carbon‑limited conditions, repressed by glucose, and differentially regulated in mutants affecting acetate catabolism or the PEP‑to‑PYR routes. {PubMed:17557829, PubMed:33668723, PubMed:21881893, PubMed:24375081}. Is allosterically activated by aspartate and inhibited by CoA, acetyl‑phosphate, palmitoyl‑CoA and oxaloacetate. {PubMed:17557829}. Modulates cellular redox balance by producing NADH (and NADPH in a pgi‑deficient background); overexpression perturbs the NAD⁺/NADH ratio and reduces cell growth. {PubMed:21272045, PubMed:33668723}. Deletion markedly reduces growth on glycerol, indicating its essential role in supplying pyruvate under this condition. {PubMed:23957584}. Deletion does not affect succinate yield in engineered anaerobic succinate‑producing strains, showing it is non‑essential for succinate production under those conditions. {PubMed:18781696}. Forms a homotetramer of ~64 kDa subunits and exhibits a low Kₘ and high catalytic efficiency for NAD⁺, with markedly lower activity toward NADP⁺. {PubMed:17557829}. Has been employed in metabolic‑engineering applications to restore nitrogen fixation in Sinorhizobium meliloti NAD‑ME mutants and to improve succinate production. {PubMed:17557829}.

MetaCyc_Comment: E. coli encodes two "malic enzymes" that catalyze the decarboxylation of malate to form pyruvate with concomitant reduction of NAD(P)+. One enzyme, MaeA (described here) requires NAD+, while the other, |FRAME: MALIC-NADP-MONOMER MaeB|, requires NADP+ |CITS: |. Metabolic flux through the malic enzymes during growth on glycerol as the sole source of carbon appears to be essentially zero |CITS: |. In a strain blocked in the fermentative metabolism of pyruvate, overexpressed NAD+-dependent malate dehydrogenase can support growth by catalyzing the normally non-physiological reductive carboxylation of pyruvate to form malate |CITS: |. MaeA is present as a mixture of monomer, homotetramer and homooctamer in solution |CITS: |. Mg2+ and Mn2+ appear to stabilize two different conformational states of the enzyme |CITS: |. MaeA has been engineered to untilize the bioorthogonal cosubstrates nicotinamide flucytosine dinucleotide (NFCD) and nicotinamide cytosine dinucleotide (NCD) in place of NAD |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the engineered variant, L310R/Q401C, has been solved |CITS: |. Expression of maeA is induced by growth on acetate |CITS: |. A maeA mutant does not show a defect when grown on acetate; however, a maeB maeA double mutant in a pckA mutant background abolishes growth on acetate |CITS: |. A maeB maeA double mutant alone shows a severe lag phase during the transition from growth on glucose to growth on acetate |CITS: |. Overexpression or deletion of maeA has been utilized in metabolic engineering for production of several compounds, e.g. by |CITS: |. SfcA: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: The lipopolysaccharide of E. coli K-12 consists of two major components: the hydrophobic lipid A moiety inserted into the outer membrane and the phosphorylated core oligosaccharide |CITS: |. WaaO is a nonprocessive α-1,3 glucosyltransferase involved in the synthesis of the R core of lipopolysaccharide |CITS: |. WaaO adds the second glucose (GlcII) to the first glucose (GlcI) of the outer core of LPS |CITS: |. Activity of WaaO requires a functional waaB gene |CITS:|. Note that the E. coli K-12 gene is named waaO but is also referred to in the literature by its synonyms. In Salmonella typhimurium it is named waaI (rfaI). The history of this nomenclature is explained in the comment section of the EcoGene GenePage in the Unification Link. The results of site-directed mutagenesis analysis of WaaO indicate that Asp-131 and -133 (DXD motif in region I) and Asp-220 and -222 (DXD motif in region III) may play a crucial role in the catalytic function of E. coli K-12 WaaO protein |CITS: |. An E. coli K-12 waaO (rfaI) deletion mutant is more susceptible to the antibiotic ciclopirox compared to the parent strain |CITS: |. WaaO from E. coli K-12 has been cloned, overexpressed, purified and its activity characterized. The enzyme requires Mg2+ and utilizes UDP-glucose as sugar donor. In the absence of the lipid acceptor, WaaO can slowly hydrolyze the UDP-glucose sugar donor. It cannot hydrolyze UDP-galactose. It was also shown in vitro that the enzyme can add multiple glucosyl residues to analogs of the WaaG and WaaB acceptors, forming multiglucosylated products over time |CITS: |. In addition to components of the main LPS biosynthetic pathway, some nonstoichiometric substitutions can be found in the inner core such as phosphoethanolamine, rhamnose and an additional Kdo, resulting in additional glycoforms. The chromosomal waa region (formerly rfa) contains the major core-oligosaccharide assembly operons in E. coli |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Transferase involved in the biosynthesis of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) (PubMed:21983211). In vitro, catalyzes the transfer of a polymerized O-antigen molecule from its polyprenyl diphosphate membrane anchor to a terminal sugar of the lipid A-core oligosaccharide, finalizing the biosynthesis of the lipopolysaccharide (PubMed:21983211, PubMed:30047569). The enzyme is functional and can be used to give diverse hybrid O-antigens in vitro, but K12 strains do not produce the O-antigen in vivo due to mutations in the rfb gene cluster (Probable). K12 strains are phenotypically rough, their lipopolysaccharide having a complete core structure, but no O-antigen (Probable). In highly mucoid K12 strains, WaaL can ligate colanic acid (CA or M-antigen) repeats to a significant proportion of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) core acceptor molecules, forming the LPS glycoform M(LPS) (PubMed:17227761). The attachment point was identified as O-7 of the L-glycero-D-manno-heptose of the outer LPS core, the same position used for O-antigen ligation (PubMed:17227761). E. coli K-12 strains are phenotypically rough - their lipopolysaccharide has a complete core structure but does not have an O-specific polysaccharide (O-PS). E. coli K-12 strains do not produce O-PS to attach to the LPS core due to mutations in the rfb gene cluster; in MG1655, the rfb-50 allele, an IS5 insertion, interrupts wbbL encoding rhamnose transferase; an engineered strain of E. coli K-12 with all rfb genes intact synthesizes O16 antigen |CITS: |. WaaL is also able to attach colanic acid, or M-antigen (traditionally considered to be an exopolysaccharide) to the LPS core producing MLPS - a novel LPS glycoform that occurs in a highly mucoid strain of E. coli K-12 |CITS: |. Purified WaaL catalyses transfer of O-antigen from its isoprenoid carrier to E. coli K-12 lipid A-core |CITS: |. WaaL displays specificity for the terminal core acceptor site and lacks specificity for the carrier-linked O-PS; purified WaaL can ligate O-PS substrates from different bacterial species to E. coli lipid A-core |CITS: |; the GlcNAc-HepIV β(1 → 7) linkage of the outer core oligosaccharide defines specificity of WaaL in E. coli K-12 |CITS: |. WaaL is predicted to be an inner membrane protein with 12 transmembrane domains; experimental topology analysis suggests its C terminus is located in the cytoplasm |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). WaaL contains a large periplasmic loop which is required for function |CITS: |. WaaL can form oligomers and likely functions as a dimer in vivo |CITS: |. Inactivation of waaL does not generally cause a detectable morphological phenotype; this is not surprising, because K-12 strains lack O antigen |CITS: |. Inactivation of waaL prevents formation of smooth LPS in a K-12 strain engineered to produce O-PS |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |) and prevents formation of MLPS when colanic acid synthesis is induced |CITS: |.
