MetaCyc_Comment: Transketolase catalyzes the reversible transfer of a ketol group between several donor and acceptor substrates. This key enzyme is a reversible link between glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway. The enzyme is involved in the catabolism of pentose sugars, the formation of D-ribose 5-phosphate, and the provision of D-erythrose 4-phosphate, a precursor of aromatic amino acids and PLP |CITS: |. E. coli contains two transketolase isozymes, TktA and TktB. TktA is responsible for the major transketolase activity |CITS: |. In addition to its function in central carbon metabolism, transketolase appears to also have an unexpected role in chromosome structure; a tktA mutant affects chromosome topology |CITS: |. Crystal structures of TktA in complex with donor and acceptor substrates and inhibitors have been solved, elucidating the reaction mechanism and mode of action of transketolase |CITS: |. A computational model of transketolase activity using a quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical method has been proposed, defining a new route for thiamine diphosphate activation |CITS: |. An ultra-high-resolution crystal structure of apo-TktA supports a catalytic model in which a proton wire synchronizes catalysis at the two active sites of the dimeric enzyme |CITS: |. Inhibition of TktA by 2'-methoxy-thiamine was investigated by ultrahigh-resolution X-ray crystallography and molecular dynamics simulations. The 2'-methoxy group clashes with the side chain of Glu411, prohibiting activation of the cofactor by protonation in the N1 position |CITS: |. The thiol of the Cys157 active site residue undergoes single- or double-oxidation to form a sulfenic acid or sulfinic acid. Single oxidation of Cys157 to the sulfenic acid leads to the formation of a high-affinity PLP binding site in TktA and increased activity of the enzyme |CITS: |, while double oxidation may inactivate the enzyme |CITS: |. Oxidative stress during fermentation appears to lead to formation of the higher-activity enzyme; TktA thus appears to be a redox-regulated enzyme |CITS: |. The urea denaturation pathways of wild type and active site mutants of TktA has been investigated |CITS: |, and the effects of temperature and pH on the structure, stability, aggregation and activity of transketolase have been determined |CITS: |. The acceptor specificity of TktA has been investigated |CITS: |. TktA is also able to irreversibly convert β-hydroxypyruvate and ribose-5-phosphate to sedoheptulose-7-phosphate and CO2 |CITS: |. Directed evolution methods and site-specific introduction of noncanonical amino acids have been used to shift the substrate specificity of TktA |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the S385Y/D469T/R520Q variant has been solved |CITS: |. A tradeoff between stability and activity of this enzyme was identified and addressed by introducing additional mutations |CITS: |. Variants with increased thermal stability have been characterized |CITS: |, and epistatic interactions between single and double point mutants were investigated |CITS: |. A new high-throughput assay has enabled identification of effective inhibitors of TktA activity |CITS: |. Transketolase mutants can not grow on pentoses |CITS: |. Overproduction of TktB causes increased transketolase activity and suppresses the tktA mutant phenotype |CITS: |. A tktA tktB double mutant requires pyridoxine (or 4-hydroxy-L-threonine or glycolaldehyde), aromatic amino acids and vitamins for growth |CITS: |. Mutations that suppress the growth defect of a tktA tktB double mutant in LB were found to constitutively express glpK or inactivate deoB, suggesting that disrupted ribose-5-P metabolism results in glycerol-3-P limitation. Growth of a tktA mutant on casamino acids is inhibited by ribose; this effect is due to glycerol-3-P limitation |CITS: |. Null mutations in tktA lead to metabolic flux alterations that increase intracellular levels of the growth inhibitory metabolite methylglyoxal, and thereby have an increased persistence phenotype |CITS: |. Metabolic engineering for production of certain metabolites often involves transketolase; see |CITS: | and more. TktA abundance is affected by the SOS inducer and mutagen 7-methoxy-2-nitronaphthofuran (R7000) |CITS: |. tktA is negatively regulated during entry into stationary phase. The effect by RpoS is likely indirect and might be mediated by an intermediate regulator that itself is directly regulated by RpoS |CITS |. Expression of tktA and tktB is complementary, resulting in approximately constant levels of transketolase expression throughout growth |CITS: |. Genetic interactions suggest that Acs is acetylated and thereby inactivated through the action of |FRAME: G7350-MONOMER|, and that |FRAME: G6577-MONOMER CobB| catalyzes deacetylation of Acs |CITS: |. However, acetylation of CheY in vivo is largely a result of autoacetylation |CITS: |. An acs mutant has a defect in chemotaxis |CITS: |, which was not seen by |CITS: |. Decreased expression of Acs at high growth rates is primarily controlled by transcript stability |CITS: |. CsrA positively regulates Acs expression |CITS: |. A genome-wide screen to identify all direct or indirect regulators of acs expression has been performed, showing a tight link to metabolic enzymes |CITS: |. acs, among other genes involved in carbon source transport and metabolism, was downregulated in two MG1655 lysogens carrying closely related Stx2a phages O104 and PA8 |CITS: 31208335|. MetaCyc_Comment: UDP-N-acetylmannosaminuronate (UDP-ManNAcUA) is one of the building blocks for the cell surface polysaccharide enterobacterial common antigen (ECA). Enzymatic activity requires the presence of UDP-GlcNAc as an activator |CITS: |. UDP-ManNAc synthesized by WecB is proposed to be the precursor for biosynthesis of a novel surface glycan that is required for bacteriophage N4 infection |CITS: |. Experiments with the BASEL collection of bacteriophages that infect E. coli showed that certain families of phages depend on the presence of WecB for infectivity |CITS: |. The reaction mechanism in the UDP-GlcNAc to UDP-ManNAc direction involves the anti-elimination of UDP from UDP-GlcNAc, generating the intermediate 2-acetamidoglucal, and followed by a syn-addition of UDP |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the enzyme has been solved. Each subunit of the homodimeric enzyme only contains a single substrate binding site, thus ruling out the possibility that regulation by UDP-GlcNAc is allosteric. An interdomain rotation may be involved in regulation of catalytic activity |CITS: |. Predicted active site residues were mutagenized, and their effect on substrate binding, catalysis, and regulation was analyzed |CITS: |. A wecB (rffE) mutation was isolated in a search for mutants that are defective in bacteriophage N4 adsorption |CITS: |. A Tn10 insertion mutant in wecB does not produce ECA |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) catalyze the conversion of ribonucleotides into deoxyribonucleotides, which are required for DNA synthesis and repair. Nucleotide reduction involves a transient protein-based thiyl radical that abstracts a hydrogen atom from the 2'-position of the nucleotide. Three classes of RNR enzymes have been identified; they differ in the metallocofactor required for generating the thiyl radical. E. coli contains three RNRs, the class Ia |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-DIP-REDUCTI-CPLX|, the class Ib |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-DIP-REDUCTII-CPLX|, and the class III anaerobic ribonucleoside-triphosphate reductase (NrdD) described here. The existence of an RNR specifically active under anaerobic conditions was first shown by |CITS: |. The NrdD reductase is activated by a tightly associated activase enzyme (NrdG) under anaerobic conditions |CITS: | and is inactivated by oxygen. Exposure to oxygen results in C-terminal truncation of the protein |CITS: | by cleavage on the N-terminal side of the glycyl radical at position 681 |CITS: |. Activation of the enzyme involves generation of a glycine radical at the C2 position of Gly681 |CITS: |. A G681A mutant lacks the glycyl radical and has no enzymatic activity |CITS: |. A multi-component system is responsible for activation of the enzyme. Electrons are transferred from NADPH by |FRAME: FLAVONADPREDUCT-MONOMER| to flavodoxin |CITS: |. NrdD was initially thought to contain an iron-sulfur cluster |CITS: |; however, it was later found that the signal was likely due to the presence of an iron-sulfur cluster in the NrdG protein |CITS: |. NrdD reduces all four common ribonucleotides; its catalytic activity is allosterically regulated. Competition experiments suggest two binding sites for modulators |CITS: |. The reaction mechanism of NrdD has been investigated |CITS: |. The hydrogen donor of the reductase reaction is formate |CITS: |. This enzyme is a class III ribonucleotide reductase that is essential for anaerobic growth. In E. coli strain DHB4, construction of deletion mutants and analysis of their growth characteristics showed that the main ribonucleotide reductase activity in strict anaerobiosis is provided by the products of nrdDG. Under highly restricted oxygen condtions, |FRAME: RIBONUCLEOSIDE-DIP-REDUCTI-CPLX| can support some growth in a strain containing an nrdDG deletion. Either thioredoxin reductase or glutathione reductase are required for anaerobic growth, suggesting that these reductive pathways contribute to enzyme activity |CITS: |. Binding of Zn2+ to NrdD protects the protein from proteolytic cleavage and plays a role in the formation of the glycyl radical |CITS: |. An nrdD null mutant does not grow under entirely anaerobic conditions, but grows under aerobic or microaerophilic conditions due to the activity of NrdAB |CITS: |. Ribonucleotide reductase catalyzes the rate-limiting step in DNA biosynthesis. Its central role in DNA replication and repair makes its regulation important to ensure appropriate pools of deoxyribonucleotides for these processes. Three major classes I, II and III have been designated that share similar catalytic mechanisms. Enterobacteria, including Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium contain class Ia (encoded by |FRAME: EG10660| and |FRAME: EG10661|), class Ib (encoded by |FRAME: EG20257| and |FRAME: EG12381|) and class III (encoded by |FRAME: EG11417|) enzymes. Class Ia and Ib enzymes are active under aerobic conditions, while class III enzymes are inactivated by oxygen and function under strictly anaerobic conditions. Although there are differences in structure and cofactor use, their catalytic mechanisms involve a transient cysteinyl radical at the active site that inititates ribonucleotide reduction. Regeneration of the enzymes is accomplished by corresponding reductive enzyme systems |CITS: | and discussed in |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the ABC transporter complex CydDC that exports the reduced low-molecular-weight thiols cysteine and glutathione to the periplasm (PubMed:12393891, PubMed:16040611). Export of these thiol-containing redox-active molecules may be crucial for redox homeostasis in the periplasm, permitting correct assembly of various respiratory complexes and formation of correct disulfide bonds in periplasmic and secreted proteins (Probable). CydD contains transmembrane domains (TMD), which form a pore in the inner membrane, and an ATP-binding domain (NBD), which is responsible for energy generation (PubMed:24958725). Required for the assembly of functional cytochrome bd-type quinol oxidases and periplasmic c-type cytochromes (PubMed:15470119, PubMed:7934832, PubMed:8181727). Overexpression of CydDC under anaerobic conditions also results in the formation of a heme biosynthesis-derived pigment, P-574 (PubMed:12375104). CydDC binds heme b, but heme is probably not transported by the complex and instead has a role in regulating ATPase activity (PubMed:24958725). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12375104, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12393891, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15470119, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16040611, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24958725, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7934832, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8181727, ECO:0000305|PubMed:12393891, ECO:0000305|PubMed:16040611, ECO:0000305|PubMed:31279084}.; FUNCTION: Conversely, a more recent study suggests an alternative function of CydDC: authors suggest that CydDC does not mediate the export of L-cysteine but rather reduces cytoplasmic L-cystine to L-cysteine (PubMed:32900959). The principle function of CydDC would be to maintain the reduced state of cytoplasmic L-cysteine, thereby providing an important connection between sulfur metabolism, oxidative stress and resistance to antibiotics (PubMed:32900959). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:32900959}.

MetaCyc_Comment: FtsN is an essential cell division protein present at 3000-6000 molecules per cell; inactivation of ftsN results in filamentation and cell death |CITS: |. FtsN contains a small N-terminal cytoplasmic domain, a membrane-spanning region and a large periplasmic C-terminal domain |CITS: |. FtsN localizes to the septum during division; the periplasmic domain of FtsN is sufficient for correct localization |CITS: |. The cytoplasmic domain and membrane spanning region determine membrane localization, but are not otherwise required for FtsN function |CITS: |. The FtsN periplasmic domain contains an α-helical region located near to the membrane, followed by a long unstructured region and a C-terminal SPOR domain which binds peptidoglycan |CITS: | and is required for efficient accumulation of FtsN at constriction sites |CITS: | (see further |CITS: |). SPOR domains bind to |FRAME: a-denuded-peptidoglycan denuded glycans| which are enriched in septal PG |CITS: |. FtsN is recruited to the septum late in the cell cycle; localization to the Z ring is dependent on |FRAME: EG10347-MONOMER FtsZ|, |FRAME: EG10339-MONOMER FtsA|, |FRAME: G7258-MONOMER ZipA|, |FRAME: EG10341-MONOMER FtsI| (PBP3), and |FRAME: EG10342-MONOMER FtsQ| |CITS: | (and see further |CITS: |). Conversely, |FRAME: G7458-MONOMER AmiC| requires FtsN for localization to the Z ring |CITS: |. FtsN interacts with the peptidoglycan (PG) synthase |FRAME: EG10605-MONOMER MrcB| (PBP1B) in vitro and in vivo; FtsN stimulates PBP1B-catalysed PG synthesis in vitro |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). In vivo FRET experiments indicate that FtsN forms homo-oligomers and interacts with |FRAME: CPLX0-7538 ZapA|, |FRAME: EG10344-MONOMER FtsW| and FtsI |CITS: |. FtsN interacts directly with FtsA in vivo; the cytoplasmic and transmembrane region of FtsN is sufficient for this interaction |CITS: |. FtsN-FtsA interaction facilitates midcell localization of FtsN and precedes SPOR-dependent midcell recruitment |CITS: | (see further |CITS: |). Deprivation of FtsN results in disassembly of divisome components |CITS: |. FtsN is implicated in the regulation of |FRAME: EG10605-MONOMER PBP1B| and |FRAME: EG10341-MONOMER PBP3| within the divisome |CITS: |. ftsN was first identified as a multicopy suppressor of the ftsA12(Ts) mutation; overexpression of ftsN also suppresses the ftsI23(Ts) and ftsQ1(Ts) mutations, suggesting interactions between these proteins |CITS: |. In addition, FtsN overproduction can partially suppress thermosensitive or deletion mutants of ftsK |CITS: |. Overproduction of FtsN does not affect the maturation time of the divisome |CITS: |. Uracil residues in DNA can arise as a result of misincorporation of dUMP residues by DNA polymerase or due to deamination of cytosine. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:37452011}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Ribonuclease II (RNase II) is a single-strand-specific exoribonuclease that cleaves RNA processively from the 3' end to produce ribonucleoside 5'-monophosphates. It has roles in the maturation, turnover and quality control of RNA. RNase II is one of five exonucleases (RNase II, RNase D, RNase BN, RNase T, RNase PH) that can process tRNA and is responsible for the first step in the conversion of precursor tyrosine tRNA to its final form |CITS: |. It has been shown in vitro to cleave long 3' tRNA sequences to yield 2-4 nucleotide intermediates for subsequent processing |CITS: |. It also degrades the polycistronic tryptophan operon mRNA from its primary transcription termination site (trp t') to a secondary termination hairpin (trp t) to yield the mature 3' end of tryptophan operon mRNA |CITS: |. RNase II is responsible for a significant portion of the degradation of artificial hammerhead ribozymes in vivo |CITS: |. RNase II also contributes to the degradation of smaller RNA during carbon starvation, though it has no role in 23 S or 16 S RNA breakdown |CITS: |. In concert with PNPase, RNase II degrades the major 3' cleavage product of the antisense RNA CopA, though it can also protect the 3' end from PNPase degradation |CITS: |. Temperature-sensitive double mutants in RNase II and PNPase are inviable at the nonpermissive temperature and accumulate mRNA fragments of 100 to 1,500 nucleotides in length |CITS: |. Triple mutants in RNase II, PNPase and ams (RNase E) show a three- to four-fold increase in the half life of pulse-labeled RNA including mRNAs |CITS: |. RNase II degrades rpsO mRNA following removal of the transcript's 3' stem-loop structure by RNase E, but protects it from degradation by other factors if the 3' stem-loop is present |CITS: |. RNase II also plays a role in bacteriophage T4 ribonucleic acid metabolism |CITS: |. RNase II has a major role in degradation of Rep mRNA from the ColE2 plasmid |CITS: |. Plasmid-borne RNase II can complement the cold-sensitive phenotype of a Δpnp mutant |CITS: |. RNase II has a role in the A-site mRNA cleavage process during ribosome pausing, degrading ribosome-bound mRNA downstream of the ribosomal A-site |CITS: |. However, RNase II activity does not accelerate ribosome recycling |CITS: |. Overexpression of RNase II or RNase R can suppress the growth defects of cells lacking the phosphorolytic RNases PNPase and RNase PH |CITS: |. RNase II has a role in processing the downstream 3' sequences of leuX precursor tRNA after the action of PNPase or RNase P |CITS: |. RNase II degrades the poly(A) tails of mRNA. In triple mutants lacking RNase II, PNPase and RNase E, the length and abundance of mRNA poly(A) tails increases dramatically |CITS: |. Double mutants in RNase II and PNPase show a twenty- to sixty-fold increase in appearance of poly(A) RNA and a three- to four-fold increase in the length of poly(A) tails relative to wild type, but less than a two-fold change in non-poly(A) RNA levels. poly(A) synthesis is also higher in mutant cells, indicating that the exonucleases tested both degrade polyadenylated mRNA and reduce its rate of synthesis |CITS: |. RNase II removes poly(A) tails from rpsO mRNA. The resulting deadenylated rpsO mRNA is more stable than oligoadenylated rpsO mRNA |CITS: |. RNase II is responsible for most degradation of poly(A) tails associated with 23 S rRNA and can be overexpressed to prevent toxicity due to excessive polyadenylation, which decreases the half-life of mRNA |CITS: |. Hfq blocks the degradation of poly(A) tails by RNase II |CITS: |. Polyadenylation of the mRNA for the ribosomal protein S20 allows RNase II and PNPase to degrade it |CITS: |. RNase II catalyzes the direct removal of ribonucleoside 5'-monophosphates from the 3' end of oligoribonucleotides |CITS: |. It degrades substrates with 3'-hydroxyl or 2',3'-cyclic phosphate ends somewhat more readily than those with 3'-phosphate or 2'-phosphate ends, and degrades substrate at a rate of seventy nucleotides per second at 37 degrees C. Its enzymatic activity has been extensively characterized with regards to substrate and reaction conditions |CITS: |. RNase II preferentially degrades longer ribonucleotides and does so processively, leaving a short oligonucleotide and little evidence of intermediates |CITS: |. It has been shown that the RNase II catalytic site binds the 3' end of substrate RNA and its anchor site binds 15-25 nucleotides from the 3' end, with both bindings needed to maintain the enzyme-RNA complex. The enzyme remains fixed at the anchor point on the RNA, processively cleaving twelve nucleotides from the 3' end and then dissociating |CITS: |. An Asp209Asn mutant of RNase II binds but does not hydrolyze substrate |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis of conserved aromatic residues that position RNA in the active site identified Tyr253 as critical for setting the length of the smallest product |CITS: |. Active site residues Tyr313 and Glu390 are crucial for the RNA (rather than DNA) specificity of the enzyme. Active site Arg500 is important for activity, but not for binding of RNA. A Glu542Ala mutant results in a large decrease in Km and large increase in Kcat for a poly(A) substrate |CITS: |. Although RNase II and RNase R both belong to the RNR family, differences in their nuclease domains |CITS: | and the RNase R S1 domain and C-terminal lysine-rich region |CITS: | may account for the lack of activity of RNase II on double-stranded RNA. Stable stem-loops block RNase II, forcing it to dissociate from the substrate RNA |CITS: |. Stable stem-loops and other secondary structure elements have been shown to block RNase II degradation of the Tn10/IS10 antisense RNA RNA-OUT, rpsO mRNA and glyA mRNA, though stem-loop structures alone do not appear to stall RNase II long enough in vitro to account for their effectiveness in stabilizing mRNA in vivo |CITS: |. In addition to its exonuclease activity, one study suggests a significant endonuclease function for RNase II |CITS: |. A study based on a thermolabile RNase II appears to show that RNase II is not responsible for the majority of ribonucleoside 5'-monophosphate formation in carbon-starved cells |CITS: |. ATP has been reported to be a competitive inhibitor of RNase II |CITS: |. This was subsequently demonstrated to be an experimental artifact caused by the presence of adenylate kinase, which works in concert with nucleoside monophosphate kinases to convert 5'-mononucleosides to insoluble nucleoside diphosphates, thus resulting in an apparent diminishing of enzymatic output |CITS: |. Methods for the purification and characterization of RNase II have been summarized |CITS: |. The properties of purified RNase II have been compared with those of its homolog RNase R |CITS: |, and with RNase D |CITS: |. RNase II appears to function as a monomer |CITS: |. Surface plasmon resonance and electrophoretic mobility shift assay techniques have been used to characterize RNA-RNase II complexes |CITS: |. Crystal structures of RNase II in the bound and unbound states have been determined to 2.74 and 2.44 Å resolution, respectively |CITS: |. Based on these structures, RNase II appears to bind RNAs at two locations, and to constrain catalytic access to single-stranded RNA via a narrow, basic channel. Based on subsequent truncation mutants, the RNase II S1 domain is important for stable protein-RNA complexes, the amino-terminal domain prevents overbinding to poly(A) RNA, and there is a third RNA-binding domain in the amino-terminal portion of the catalytic domain |CITS: |. Domain replacement studies show that the S1 domain is functionally similar in RNase II, PNPase and RNase R |CITS: |. Cell fractionation data suggest that the amino-terminal amphipathic helix of RNase II mediates an association with the cytoplasmic membrane |CITS: |. Immunoprecipitation studies using cell extracts suggest that RNase II may be a component of the degradosome |CITS: |. More generally, double-label localization studies indicate that RNase II and other components of the E. coli RNA degradation and processing network are sequestered within extended cellular structures coiled around the periphery of the cell |CITS: |. However, work on RNase E using epifluorescence microscopy under live cell conditions has questioned the formation of such cytoskeletal-like structures |CITS: |. PNPase degrades rnb mRNA, limiting RNase II expression. PNP expression is increased in an RNase II null strain, suggesting that this mRNA-based regulation is reciprocal |CITS: |. RNase E and RNase III also affect RNase II expression, the latter indirectly and the former directly by cleaving rnb mRNA |CITS: |. Gmr regulates RNase II by modulating its degradation In a gmr deletion mutant, RNase II is three times more abundant than in a wild type background |CITS: |. Strains deleted in five exoribonucleases (RNase II, RNase D, RNase BN, RNase T, RNase PH) are inviable, but any one of them can support growth with no accumulation of precursor RNA or disruption of RNA synthesis |CITS: |. Mutants in RNase II do show reduced DNA degradation, possibly due to competitive inhibition of endonuclease I by RNA |CITS: |. RNA-Seq analysis of wild-type and deletion mutants of RNase II, RNase R and PNPase shows that deletion of RNase II significantly affected 187 transcripts related to flagellum assembly, motility and biofilm formation. RNase II and RNase R mutants produce more biofilm than wild-type |CITS: |. Regulation of RNase II at the protein level has been shown to occur via the acetylation of Lys501 by Pka and its deacetylation by CobB. Acetylation affects substrate binding, decreasing catalytic activity. When the growth of cells is slowed, acetylation levels are higher and RNase II activity is decreased |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

However, overexpression of panB increases the intracellular folate pool. Kinetic modeling of the folate synthesis pathway suggests that a regulatory effect, whereby an initial drop in THF concentration upon PanB overexpression leads to increased expression of enzymes in the THF synthesis pathway, can explain this effect |CITS: |. panB mutants are auxotrophic for pantothenate and can grow on media supplemented with panthothenate, pantoate and ketopantoate, but not β-alanine or α-ketoisovalerate |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: The RND (resistance-nodulation-division) family |CITS: | protein, AcrB, is the inner membrane component of a tripartite, proton dependent, drug efflux pump. AcrB contains 12 potential transmembrane regions and two large hydrophilic domains; the N and C-terminal halves of the protein have symmetrical hydropathy profiles |CITS: |. Purified AcrB reconstituted in lipid vesicles mediates the ΔpH driven expulsion of fluorescent phospholipids; extrusion is inhibited by the antibiotics erythromycin and cloxacillin and the bile compounds glycochenodeoxycholate, glycocholate and taurocholate; the addition of AcrA with Mg2+ stimulates transport; AcrB-containing proteoliposomes (with an interior-acid ΔpH) show proton efflux when a substrate (positively charged, negatively charged or uncharged) is added to the external medium |CITS: |. The crystal structure of AcrB has been determined at 3.5 |CITS: |, 2.9, 3.0 |CITS: |, and 2.8 Å resolution |CITS: |. Crystal structures of AcrB with bound ligands rhodamine 6G, ethidium, dequalinium, and ciprofloxacin |CITS: | and with the secondary bile acid, deoxycholate |CITS: | have been reported. The crystal structure of AcrB in complex with a designed protein that binds and inhibits the pump has been determined at 2.5 Å resolution |CITS: |. The AcrB monomer contains 12 transmembrane (TM) α helices and two large periplasmic loops - one between TM1 and 2, the other between TM7 and 8. The AcrB trimer consists of 3 domains: the transmembrane domain; the periplasmic or porter domain and the TolC binding domain. The AcrB monomers form an asymmetric trimer in which each monomer adopts a different conformation and a functionally rotating, three step (access, binding, and extrusion), peristaltic pump mechanism for the export of substrates |CITS: | has been proposed. Inactivation of any one of the three protomeric units of the trimer inactivates the entire complex |CITS: |. AcrB interacts extensively with membrane lipids |CITS: |. Substrate molecules are captured by AcrB from the periplasm or the periplasm/inner membrane interface |CITS: |. Vestibules (openings between protomers) which are located just outside the external surface of the membrane bilayer may be important for substrate entry |CITS: |. AcrB has multiple entrance channels: CH1 - open to the surface of the cell membrane; CH2 - open to the periplasm and CH3 - open to the central cavity of the trimer (see |CITS: | and references within). AcrB has two multisite drug binding pockets (the proximal or access pocket and the distal or deep pocket) separated by a flexible loop; transport may involve initial binding to the access pocket and subsequent transport to the deep pocket by conformational change |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Multiple entrances and multiple transport pathways may function to extend the substrate specificity of AcrB |CITS: |. AcrB mediated proton transport proceeds by an alternating access mechanism; proton binding sites within the transmembrane domain become alternatively accessible to the periplasm or cytoplasm; AcrB adopts a novel antiport mechanism which involves the coupling of two remote alternating access mechanisms - one for drugs and one for protons - within each AcrB protomer |CITS: |. The crystal structure of AcrB bound by a pyridopyrimidine derived inhibitor has been determined. The inhibitor binds tightly to a hydrophobic 'trap' that is located off the substrate translocation channel and inhibits functional rotation of the AcrB monomer |CITS: |. The intermolecular contacts between AcrB and the periplasmic adaptor protein AcrA have been mapped using an in vivo cross-linking approach and the AcrAB complex has been modelled |CITS: |. AcrB has been subject to site-directed and randomized mutagenesis (see |CITS: |). AcrB may play a role in contact dependent growth inhibition. This activity can be separated from its function as part of the AcrAB/TolC multidrug efflux complex |CITS: |. acrB belongs to a network of genes which facilitate stress-induced mutagenesis (SIM) in E. coli K-12 |CITS: |. acrB: acriflavine resistance protein B (see |CITS: |) Reviews: |CITS: |.Related reviews: |CITS: |Comment: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the RavA-ViaA chaperone complex, which may act on the membrane to optimize the function of some of the respiratory chains (PubMed:16301313, PubMed:24454883, PubMed:27979649, PubMed:36127320, PubMed:36625597). RavA functions as an ATPase (PubMed:16301313, PubMed:27979649, PubMed:31992852, PubMed:37660904). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:16301313, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24454883, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27979649, ECO:0000269|PubMed:31992852, ECO:0000269|PubMed:36127320, ECO:0000269|PubMed:36625597, ECO:0000269|PubMed:37660904}.; FUNCTION: The RavA-ViaA system is involved in the regulation of two respiratory complexes, the fumarate reductase (Frd) electron transport complex and the NADH-quinone oxidoreductase complex (NDH-1 or Nuo complex) (PubMed:24454883, PubMed:27979649). It modulates the activity of the Frd complex, signifying a potential regulatory function during bacterial anaerobic respiration with fumarate as the terminal electron acceptor (PubMed:27979649). Interaction of RavA-ViaA with FrdA results in a decrease in Frd activity (PubMed:27979649). It also interacts with the Nuo complex, known to be involved in both the aerobic and the anaerobic respiration (PubMed:24454883). The RavA-ViaA system binds to specific membrane phospholipids, and might chaperone certain respiratory complexes by acting on lipid microdomains in which these complexes are inserted (PubMed:36127320). The RavA-ViaA system also plays a negative role in bacterial persistence upon treatment with antibiotics through the association of the chaperone complex with Frd (PubMed:37660904). It sensitizes cells to sublethal concentrations of aminoglycoside (AG) antibiotics (PubMed:36127320, PubMed:36625597, PubMed:37660904). The system can facilitate uptake of AG across the membrane when cells are in a low energy state (PubMed:36625597). It sensitizes cells to AG through a proton motive force-dependent mechanism (PubMed:36127320, PubMed:36625597). Under fumarate respiration conditions, it sensitizes cells to AG via a FrdA-dependent mechanism (PubMed:36625597). It does not sensitize cells grown under nitrate respiration to gentamicin (PubMed:36625597). In addition, RavA is involved in the bacterial acid stress response (PubMed:27080013). Acts by binding to the inducible lysine decarboxylase CadA/LdcI, a key enzyme in the acid stress response, which reduces binding of CadA/LdcI to its potent inhibitor, the stringent response alarmone ppGpp, and thus modulates CadA/LdcI activity (PubMed:21148420, PubMed:27080013). RavA also has GTPase activity in vitro (PubMed:16301313). GTP hydrolysis is much slower than ATP hydrolysis at lower enzyme/substrate concentrations but reaches comparable levels with increasing amounts of enzyme/substrate (PubMed:16301313). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:16301313, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21148420, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24454883, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27080013, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27979649, ECO:0000269|PubMed:36127320, ECO:0000269|PubMed:36625597, ECO:0000269|PubMed:37660904}.

MetaCyc_Comment: efeB is predicted to encode a periplasmic component of a ferrous iron transport system (see |CITS: |) that is cryptic in E. coli K-12; EfeB is implicated in exogenous heme iron acquisition. Analysis of transcriptional efe-lacZ fusions suggest that efeB does not possess a proximal promoter and is co-transcribed with efeUO |CITS: |. efeU in E. coli K-12 is disrupted by a frameshift mutation leaving the efeU_1 and efeU_2 fragments nonfunctional; EfeB (and EfeO) are produced despite the frameshift mutation |CITS: |. The functional efeU (ycdN) gene in E. coli Nissle 1917 encodes an oxidase-dependent, OFeT family ferrous iron permease |CITS: |. The efeUOB operon of enterohaemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 lacks any frameshift and is functional |CITS: |. EfeB has been implicated in exogenous heme iron acquisition. Due to the lack of an outer membrane receptor for heme, E. coli K-12 is unable to utilize heme as a source of iron |CITS: |. However, expression of the foreign heme receptor protein HasR from Serratia marcescens enables utilization of heme as a source of iron. Subsequent heme uptake through the E. coli K-12 inner membrane also requires the dipeptide inner membrane transporter or a functional EfeUOB system, such as occurs in enterohemorrhagic E. coli O157:H7 |CITS: |. EfeB and |FRAME: G7266-MONOMER "YfeX"| release iron from heme without destroying the tetrapyrrol ring and are the sole E. coli proteins able to provide iron from exogenous heme sources; a yfeX efeB double mutant in a HasR-expressing strain is unable to use heme as an external source of iron |CITS: |. The function of YfeX and EfeB as heme dechelatases has been disputed |CITS: | (but see also |CITS: |). EfeB is a DyP (dye decolorizing peroxidase)-like protein with a predicted Tat signal sequence; EfeB requires the Tat system for translocation into the periplasm; recombinant EfeB, purified from the periplasm is dimeric and contains noncovalently bound heme, identified as Fe(III)-protoporphyrin IX; the heme iron has a high-spin electron configuration; both holo (heme-containing) and apo (lacking heme) forms of the EfeB precursor protein are detected in the cytoplasm |CITS: |. It is not clear if Fe(III)-protoporphyrin IX is a cofactor or substrate of EfeB (see |CITS: |). EfeB may act to reduce Fe3+ to Fe2+ for transport or to oxidize Fe2+ during transport |CITS: |. EfeB exhibits guaiacol peroxidase activity at an optimum pH of about 4.0 and may function under acid-stress conditions |CITS: |. The crystal structure of EfeB has been determined in the apo form to a resolution of 2.0 Å; crystals with bound haem were obtained and diffract to 2.9 Å |CITS: |. efe: elemental ferrous iron uptake |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: The LptD (lipopolysaccharide transport) protein is an essential outer membrane (OM) protein which, in complex with LptE, functions to assemble lipopolysaccharides at the surface of the OM |CITS:|. LptD exhibits β barrel-like characteristics, including a high incidence of aromatic amino acids (13.1%) |CITS:|. Sequence analyses via the algorithm by Shirmer and Cowan |CITS:| and Zhai |CITS:| suggest that LptD is rich in transmembrane β-strands. LptD contains an N-terminal periplasmic domain and a C-terminal β-barrel domain |CITS: |. LptD contains four cysteines which form non-consecutive disulfide bonds (Cys31=Cys724 and Cys173=Cys755) that bridge the N-terminal and C-terminal domains |CITS: |. LptD is fully oxidised in vivo and formation of at least one correct disulfide bond is required for function |CITS: |. Folding of LptD involves DsbA and proceeds via an intermediate stage containing non-native disulfides |CITS: |. LptE is required for maturation to the active protein |CITS: |. The bi-functional protease/chaperone |FRAME: G7311-MONOMER BepA| is important for LptD quality control |CITS: |. LptD is involved in determining the level of organic solvent tolerance in E. coli |CITS:|. Decreased expression of the lptD gene results in increased sensitivity to organic solvents such as n-hexane |CITS:|. Depletion of lptD results in filamentation (2-8 cells long), loss of membrane integrity, and eventual cell lysis, creating filaments of rod-shaped ghosts |CITS:|. An lptD mutation (imp4213) increases OM permeability making the cell sensitive to many different antibiotics and to bile salts |CITS: , |. This phenotype can be partially suppressed by a null mutation in bamB |CITS: | and an insertion mutation in bamA |CITS: |. The BamB and BamA proteins form part of a multi-protein complex required for the assembly of OM β barrels and this genetic interaction suggests a functional interaction between LPS assembly and protein asembly in the OM |CITS: |. imp4213 cells have reduced outer membrane stiffness and decreased survival time during mechanical perturbation; LPS contributes to the load bearing capacity of the outer membrane in E. coli cells |CITS: |. Expression of lptD occurs from a σE promoter |CITS: | and two σD-like promoters |CITS:|. Imp: increased membrane permeability Ost: organic solvent tolerance

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Protein and nucleotide deglycase that catalyzes the deglycation of the Maillard adducts formed between amino groups of proteins or nucleotides and reactive carbonyl groups of glyoxals (PubMed:26102038, PubMed:26774339, PubMed:28596309). Thus, functions as a protein deglycase that repairs methylglyoxal- and glyoxal-glycated proteins, and releases repaired proteins and lactate or glycolate, respectively. Deglycates cysteine, arginine and lysine residues in proteins, and thus reactivates these proteins by reversing glycation by glyoxals. Is able to repair glycated serum albumin, aspartate aminotransferase, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and fructose biphosphate aldolase. Acts on early glycation intermediates (hemithioacetals and aminocarbinols), preventing the formation of Schiff bases and advanced glycation endproducts (AGE) that cause irreversible damage (PubMed:26102038, PubMed:26774339). Also functions as a nucleotide deglycase able to repair glycated guanine in the free nucleotide pool (GTP, GDP, GMP, dGTP) and in DNA and RNA. Is thus involved in a major nucleotide repair system named guanine glycation repair (GG repair), dedicated to reversing methylglyoxal and glyoxal damage via nucleotide sanitization and direct nucleic acid repair (PubMed:28596309). Has been reported to display chaperone, peptidase and glutathione-independent glyoxalase activities (PubMed:12235139, PubMed:12565879, PubMed:14731284, PubMed:15550391, PubMed:21696459, PubMed:7848303). However, these apparently disparate activities are all recruited to execute its protein deglycase primary function (PubMed:26102038, PubMed:26774339). Plays an important role in protecting cells from carbonyl stress, severe heat shock and starvation, as well as in acid resistance of stationary-phase cells (PubMed:12235139, PubMed:16796689, PubMed:17158627). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12235139, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12565879, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14731284, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15550391, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16796689, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17158627, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21696459, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26102038, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26774339, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28596309, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7848303}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Hsp31 has now been identified as a protein deglycase that repairs glyoxal- and methylglyoxal-glycated proteins |CITS: | as well as a nucleotide deglycase that repairs glycated GTP as well as DNA and RNA |CITS: |. Glyoxalase III converts methylglyoxal to D-lactate in a single glutathione (GSH)-independent step. The other known route for this conversion is the two-step GSH-dependent pathway catalyzed by glyoxalase I and II, |FRAME: PWY-5386|. Glyoxalase III was partially characterized by |CITS: |, although the gene encoding the enzyme was not identified at that time. It was recently shown that glyoxalase III is identical to Hsp31 in E. coli |CITS: |, and that the glyoxalase activity in fact reflects the amino acid deglycase activity of Hsp31 |CITS: |. Active site residues have been predicted |CITS: |. Mutations in predicted residues of the catalytic triad, E77A, C185A and H186A, strongly reduce catalytic activity of the enzyme |CITS: |. Hsp31 was first identified as a chaperone that interacts with partially and fully denatured proteins |CITS: |. At elevated temperatures, Hsp31 homodimers bind to substrates undergoing denaturation, and upon temperature decrease the chaperone dissociates from the renatured substrates |CITS: |. Hsp31 appears to undergo thermal activation that results in formation of a high molecular weight oligomer with enhanced chaperone activity |CITS: |. Each Hsp31 monomer comprises two domains separated by a flexible linker region |CITS: |. Crystal structures are presented at 1.6 Å |CITS: |, 2.2 Å |CITS: |, 2.7 Å |CITS: | and 2.8 Å |CITS: | resolution. NMR backbone resonance assignments of Hsp31 in solution have been published |CITS: |. Analysis of a variety of mutants identified the linker-loop region of Hsp31 as a gate which may control access of nonnative proteins to the high-affinity substrate binding site and which is thermally activated |CITS: |. Extensions of Hsp31 with histidine tags at either its N- or C-terminus abolish chaperone activity |CITS: |. Hsp31 may bind ATP, but does not hydrolyze it |CITS: |. ATP induces conformational changes within Hsp31 and is inhibitory with respect to chaperone activity at high temperatures |CITS: |. Hsp31 appears to have weak proteolytic activity using BSA as a substrate |CITS: |; others have found no endo- or exopeptidase activity |CITS: |. Later, Hsp31 was shown to have an aminopeptidase activity with short peptide substrates that is abolished in a C185A mutant |CITS: |. An hchA mutant has a growth defect at 48°C and is strongly affected in its ability to recover from transient exposure to 50°C |CITS: |. In stationary phase, an hchA mutant is more sensitive to methylglyoxal |CITS: | and acid stress |CITS: | than wild type. An hchA mutant contains increased levels of glycated proteins compared to wild type |CITS: |. An hchA mutant as well as an hchA yhbO yajL triple mutant accumulates glycated DNA and RNA and shows increased mutation frequency, with increased levels of GC→AT and AT→GC transitions |CITS: |. Unlike glyoxalases I and II, glyoxalase III activity increases at the transition to stationary phase; the increase is dependent on RpoS |CITS: |. Glyoxalase III activity is not induced by growth in the presence of methylglyoxal |CITS: |. Expression of hchA is induced by heat shock |CITS: |. hchA is a member of the σS stress regulon |CITS: |, and Hsp31 expression is also induced by osmotic stress |CITS: |. The stability of the hchA transcript is higher at increased temperature |CITS: |. Comment: |CITS: |, Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: 2-Methylcitrate synthase (PrpC) catalyzes the Claisen condensation of propionyl-CoA with oxaloacetate, a reaction in propionate catabolism via the methylcitrate cycle |CITS: |. Production of the enzyme is induced by growth on propionate, but not acetate or glucose |CITS: |. Expression of prpBCDE is regulated by PrpR and catabolite repression |CITS: | and is downregulated in the presence of a variety of sugars |CITS: |. A revertant of a gltA mutant strain produces an enzyme with citrate synthase activity |CITS: | that was later found to be identical to PrpC |CITS: |. The mutation causing the revertant phenotype is unknown. Adaptive laboratory evolution experiments designed to determine whether PrpC can function as a citrate synthase isozyme showed that increased expression and increased copy number of prpC rescued growth of the gltA mutant |CITS: |. prpC and |FRAME: EG10035 aldA| are synthetically lethal. Based on the lack of sequence and structural similarity between AldA and PrpC, it seems unlikely that PrpC also catalyzes the glycolaldehyde dehydrogenase reaction that is thought to be the essential function of AldA. Potential explanations for the synthetic lethality of aldA and prpC were discussed |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: Pantothenate synthetase (PanC) catalyzes the ATP hydrolysis-dependent synthesis of pantothenate from β-alanine and pantoate |CITS: |. The enzyme from strains W or B requires both monovalent and divalent cations |CITS: |. The pantothenate:β-alanine exchange reaction depends on the presence of AMP, which supports the two-step Bi Uni Uni Bi reaction mechanism with pantoyl adenylate as the reaction intermediate |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the full length enzyme |CITS: | and its N-terminal domain |CITS: | have been solved. Pantothenate synthetase is dimeric both in solution and the crystal structure. It is a member of the cytidylyltransferase superfamily, with an N-terminal Rossmann fold domain containing the active site and a C-terminal domain that forms a hinged lid |CITS: |. The substrate pantoate is able to bind within the ATP-binding pocket of the N-terminal domain |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that motions of the C-terminal domain dominate the functional dynamics of the E. coli enzyme |CITS: |. panC mutants are auxotrophic for pantothenate |CITS: |. Various inhibitors of pantothenate synthetase have been tested |CITS: |. PanC: "pantothenate"

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: A low activity DNA endonuclease yielding 3'-hydroxyl ends, equally active on ss or dsDNA, not active on dsRNA (PubMed:28096446). MetaCyc_Comment: The Nnr protein is a bifunctional enzyme that catalyzes both the epimerization between the R and S forms of NAD(P)HX and the ADP-dependent repair of (S)-NAD(P)HX to NAD(P)H. The N-terminal domain appears to be responsible for the epimerase activity, while the C-terminal domain is responsible for the dehydratase activity |CITS: |. Comparative genomics and metabolomics experiments suggest that Nnr, and in particular the epimerase domain, may have a moonlighting function that involves pyridoxal phosphate metabolism |CITS: |. Studies in the 1950s have shown that eukaryotic |FRAME: GAPOXNPHOSPHN-RXN "glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase"| slowly catalyzes the formation of a hydrated form of NADH, called |FRAME: NADHX|, from NADH |CITS: |. The equilibrium of this hydration reaction is in favor (100/1) of the hydrated form |CITS: |, making the reaction virtually irreversible. In addition, NADHX can be formed spontaneously from NADH under slightly acidic conditions. NADHX and NADPHX are known to inhibit dehydrogenases in other organisms |CITS: |, and it may thus be important to eliminate these damaged metabolites. The highly conserved K197 residue (K192 in the publication, where a different start site is used) within the N-terminal epimerase domain is required for the epimerase activity of the enzyme |CITS: |. Neither a Δnnr deletion mutant nor a K197A point mutant show a growth defect in rich or minimal medium. However, the deletion mutant accumulates large amounts of the R, S, and cyclic forms of NADHX and NADPHX. Surprisingly, the general changes in the metabolome of the K197A point mutant clustered further away from wild type than those of the deletion mutant. In particular, the pools of amino acids showed larger changes in the point mutant |CITS: |. Nnr: "nicotinamide nucleotide repair" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: NDH-1 shuttles electrons from NADH, via FMN and iron-sulfur (Fe-S) centers, to quinones in the respiratory chain. The immediate electron acceptor for the enzyme in this species is believed to be ubiquinone. Couples the redox reaction to proton translocation (for every two electrons transferred, four hydrogen ions are translocated across the cytoplasmic membrane), and thus conserves the redox energy in a proton gradient.

MetaCyc_Comment: GDP-mannose mannosyl hydrolase (GDPMH) is able to hydrolyze both GDP-mannose and GDP-glucose. Its biological role is as yet unknown, though it may participate in the regulation of cell wall biosynthesis by influencing the cell concentration of GDP-mannose or GDP-glucose |CITS: |. The enzyme was first identified as a member of the Nudix hydrolase family |CITS: |. However, unlike other Nudix hydrolases, GDPMH catalyzes the nucleophilic substitution at C1' rather than phosphorus |CITS: | and requires one divalent cation per active site to facilitate the departure of GMP |CITS: |. The divalent cation binding site, the general base catalyst, and other residues important for catalytic activity were identified by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. Crystal structures of GDPMH have been solved, and a reaction mechanism with a four-stage catalytic cycle was suggested |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: LplA is a lipoyl-protein ligase |CITS: |. Lipoate modification of the E2 subunits is important for the function of |FRAME: PYRUVATEDEH-CPLX| |CITS: |, |FRAME: 2OXOGLUTARATEDEH-CPLX "α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase"| |CITS: |, and the |FRAME: GCVMULTI-CPLX| |CITS: |. It was initially thought that LplA only utilizes lipoate imported from outside the cell, in contrast to the other lipoyl-protein ligase, LipB, which utilizes octanoyl-ACP. However, E. coli lipB mutants are able to grow with externally supplied octanoate instead of lipoate. Octanoate growth requires both LplA and |FRAME: CPLX0-782|, the enzyme that converts octanoyl side chains to lipoyl side chains, suggesting that LplA attaches octanoate to the E2 domain, and |FRAME: CPLX0-782| converts the octanoate to lipoate |CITS: |. The two-part reaction requires ATP and Mg2+ |CITS: | and proceeds through a lipoyl-AMP intermediate |CITS: |. The conserved Lys133 residue is required for both the lipoate adenylation and the lipoate transfer reaction |CITS: |. LplA can also utilize lipoyl-ACP or octanoyl-ACP, albeit very inefficiently |CITS: |. Determinants of substrate recognition |CITS: | and catalysis are discussed, including structural similarity between lipoylating and biotinylating enzymes and implications with respect to the catalytic site |CITS: |. LplA is a monomeric enzyme that is present at low abundance, with fewer than 10 monomers in each cell |CITS: |. Crystal structures of LplA alone, in complex with lipoate, the post-lipoate adenylation intermediate state and the pre-lipoate transfer intermediate state have been solved |CITS: |. Lipoate adenylation is followed by large conformational changes to accommodate the apoprotein substrate. A reaction mechanism has been proposed |CITS: |. Limited trypsin proteolysis of LplA leads to cleavage of a central loop region; cleavage eliminates catalytic activity |CITS: |. An lplA null mutant has a defect in utilization of externally supplied lipoate for modification of proteins and is resistant to selenolipoate |CITS: |. The slr1 (lplA1) selenolipoate-resistant mutant shows a G76S change in the LplA protein, which causes increased specificity for lipoate over the selenolipoate analog |CITS: |. Genetic interactions have been observed between LplA and the LipA to LipB pathway: phenotypes of a lipB mutant are suppressed by overproduction of LplA, and lplA lipA or lplA lipB double mutants exhibit growth defects, whereas an lplA single mutant does not |CITS: |. Missense mutations in lplA that reduce the enzyme's Km for octanoate can scavenge cytosolic octanoate and thereby suppress the auxotrophic phenotype of a lipB mutant |CITS: |. Engineered LplA derivatives are utilized for fluorescent labeling of proteins in vivo; e.g. |CITS: |. Slr: selenolipoic acid-resistant |CITS: | LplA: lipoate-protein ligase A |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in the heme biosynthesis. Catalyzes the anaerobic oxidative decarboxylation of propionate groups of rings A and B of coproporphyrinogen III to yield the vinyl groups in protoporphyrinogen IX. It can use NAD or NADP, but NAD is preferred. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12114526, ECO:0000269|PubMed:7768836}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Oxidative decarboxylation of coproporphyrinogen III to protoporphyrinogen IX is catalyzed by two enzymes in E. coli. Under aerobic conditions, the |FRAME: EG12189 hemF| gene product is active. Under anaerobic conditions, HemN catalyzes the coproporphyrinogen III dehydrogenase reaction |CITS: |. HemN is monomeric when overproduced and purified under anaerobic conditions and might be membrane-associated in vivo. The enzyme contains an oxygen-sensitive iron-sulfur cluster; mutations in specific residues important for iron-sulfur cluster coordination and catalysis have been analyzed and a catalytic mechanism has been proposed |CITS: |. HemN has been classified as a "Radical SAM" enzyme |CITS: |. S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) is consumed during catalysis; the role of a second SAM binding site in HemN has been investigated by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. The catalytic mechanism has been studied in detail |CITS: |. Recently, |CITS: | proposed a revised catalytic mechanism elucidating the function of the second SAM molecule present in the active site. A crystal structure of HemN has been solved at 2.07 Å resolution. A 4Fe-4S cluster is coordinated by three conserved cysteine residues; two molecules of SAM are present, only one of which has coordination bonds with the 4Fe-4S cluster |CITS: |. Both SAM binding sites are required for catalytic activity |CITS: |. Expression of hemN is increased under anaerobic growth conditions and decreased under conditions of limited iron availability |CITS: |. hemN can complement a Salmonella typhyimurium hemF hemN double mutant under both aerobic and anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. A hemN mutant is defective for cytochrome b and cytochrome c synthesis only under anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the hydrolysis of sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerides (SQDG) to sulfoquinovose (SQ), which is then degraded by E.coli through the SQ Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas (SQ-EMP) sulfoglycolysis pathway as a source of carbon and sulfur. Therefore, is likely involved in the utilization of the sulfoquinovose headgroup found in ubiquitous plant sulfolipids (PubMed:26878550). Is also able to hydrolyze simple sulfoquinovosides such as sulfoquinovosyl glycerol (SQGro) (PubMed:26878550, PubMed:30276262). In vitro, can use the substrate analog para-nitrophenyl alpha-sulfoquinovoside (PNPSQ), but shows no detectable activity toward 4-nitrophenyl alpha-D-glucopyranoside (PNPGlc) (PubMed:26878550, PubMed:30276262). Is a retaining glycoside hydrolase, since it forms the alpha anomer of SQ (PubMed:26878550). Also exhibits some alpha-glucosidase activity against alpha-glucosyl fluoride in vitro, although natural substrates, such as alpha-glucobioses are scarcely hydrolyzed (PubMed:15294295). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15294295, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26878550, ECO:0000269|PubMed:30276262}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Sulfoquinovosidase (YihQ) catalyzes the hydrolysis of terminal non-reducing sulfoquinovoside residues in sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerides and sulfoquinovosyl glycerol, releasing the α anomer of sulfoquinovose |CITS: |. Sulfoquinovosyl glycerol can serve as the sole source of carbon and energy via the |FRAME: PWY-7446| pathway |CITS: |. YihQ is a member of the glycosyl hydrolase 31 family. The best tested substrate was α-glucosyl fluoride; the physiological substrate of the enzyme was unknown at the time |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme have been solved |CITS: | and show an (αβ)8 barrel followed by a β-sheet domain. Within the active site, D405 may serve as the catalytic nucleophile and D472 may serve as the catalytic acid-base residue. Mutations in these residues (D405A, D405N, D472A and D472N) render the enzyme catalytically inactive. The W304, R301 and Y508 residues may have roles in the specific recognition of the sulfonate moiety |CITS: |. Expression of YihQ is induced by growth on |FRAME: CPD-10247| |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

Predicted active site residues were analyzed by site-directed mutagenesis. A crystal structure of the enzyme has been solved at 2.5 Å resolution |CITS: |. YihS may be identical to the enzyme first identified by |CITS: |, although the quarternary structure differs. MetaCyc_Comment: Rhamnulose-1-phosphate aldolase is a class II aldolase that catalyzes the third step in the L-rhamnose degradation pathway. The enzyme contains 2 molecules of zinc per enzyme complex |CITS: |. If cobalt or selected other divalent metal ions are artificially substituted for zinc, the enzyme has an oxygenase activity in the presence of dihydroxyacetone phosphate |CITS: |. The enzyme has been crystallized |CITS: |, and crystal structures have been solved |CITS: |. A catalytic mechanism was proposed based on results from site-directed mutagenesis in combination with structural information |CITS: |. Anisotropic mobility of the N-terminal "antenna domain" supports catalysis |CITS: |. Stereospecificity of RhaD has been investigated |CITS: |. For the aldol addition reaction, RhaD accepts a range of aldehydes in place of L-lactaldehyde; this property has been used for synthesis of a variety of compounds of interest |CITS: |. RhaD (there called Rua) was used in a study of designed protein-protein associations; certain mutations generated a new contact surface and allowed formation of an octamer |CITS: |. Expression of RhaD is induced by L-rhamnose as well as L-lyxose |CITS: |. Expression is downregulated under simulated microgravity conditions |CITS: |. rhaD mutants can not utilize rhamnose as a source of carbon |CITS: |.

L-rhamnose isomerase is also capable of using L-lyxose as a substrate |CITS: |. Conditioned on activation of |FRAME: LYXK-CPLX|, RhaA contributes to E. coli's ability to metabolize the uncommon sugar, L-lyxose |CITS: |. Crystal structures of L-rhamnose isomerase have been determined. Despite low sequence similarity, the enzyme shows structural similarity to xylose isomerase from Streptomyces rubiginosus. The data suggests the possibility of a metal-mediated hydride shift reaction mechanism |CITS: |. Expression of rhaA is induced by L-rhamnose |CITS: |. L-lyxose can also induce expression of rhaA |CITS: |. rhaA mutants can not utilize rhamnose as a source of carbon |CITS: |.

Uridine triphosphate (UTP), cytidine 5-triphosphate (CTP), guanosine 5-triphosphate (GTP), and thymidine triphosphate (TTP) also can act as phosphoryl donors. It can also phosphorylate L-fuculose and L-xylulose. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_01535, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14264882, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16674975, ECO:0000269|PubMed:5341476}.

The substrate spectrum of L-rhamnulose kinase has been investigated; the enzyme shows a broad tolerance for structural modifications of the natural substrate |CITS: |. Rare sugars have been modeled into the active center of the crystal structure |CITS: |. L-rhamnulose kinase is a monomer in solution |CITS: |. Crystal structures of L-rhamnulose kinase as an apo- and holo-enzyme as well as the ternary complex including the sugar have been determined and show that the enzyme belongs to the hexokinase-hsp70-actin superfamily. A catalytic mechanism has been proposed |CITS: |. A mutated form of RhaB has been shown to also phosphorylate L-xylulose to L-xylulose 1-phosphate and to allow growth of E. coli on L-lyxose |CITS:|. The enzyme was first identified in E. coli B |CITS: |. rhaB mutants are unable to utilize rhamnose as a source of carbon |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Transfers a GMP moiety from GTP to Mo-molybdopterin (Mo-MPT) cofactor (Moco or molybdenum cofactor) to form Mo-molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide (Mo-MGD) cofactor. Is also involved in the biosynthesis of the bis-MGD form of the Moco cofactor (Mo-bisMGD) in which the metal is symmetrically ligated by the dithiolene groups of two MGD molecules. Is necessary and sufficient for the in vitro activation of the DMSOR molybdoenzyme that uses the Mo-bisMGD form of molybdenum cofactor, which implies formation and efficient insertion of the cofactor into the enzyme without the need of a chaperone. Is specific for GTP since other nucleotides such as ATP and GMP cannot be utilized. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10978348, ECO:0000269|PubMed:1648082, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21081498, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8020507}.

MetaCyc_Comment: MobA is required for the biosynthesis of the molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide (MGD) cofactor |CITS: |. The enzyme catalyzes the transfer of a GMP moiety from GTP to Mo-molybdopterin, forming MGD |CITS: |. The MGD cofactor can be further modified to |FRAME: CPD-15873 "bis-MGD"|. Formation of bis-MGD is proposed to involve formation of a |FRAME: CPD-15874 "bis-Mo-MPT"| intermediate followed by the addition of two GMP moieties by MobA. This cofactor is then transferred to its target protein TorA |CITS: |. MobA is monomeric in solution |CITS: |. Crystal structures of MobA have been solved |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis of conserved residues showed that Gly15 is essential for MobA function, and Gly82 stabilizes the product-bound form of the enzyme |CITS: |. The enzyme's specificity for GTP was also investigated |CITS: |. MobA directly interacts with both MoeA and MobB |CITS: |. In the presence of the enzyme-specific chaperone NarJ and the mature molybdenum cofactor, MobA, MobB, MoeA and MogA interact with apo-NarG |CITS: |. TorD may act as the enzyme-specific chaperone for molybdenum cofactor insertion into TorA |CITS: |. A mobA mutant contains elevated levels of molybdopterin, but no detectable molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide (MGD) |CITS: |. The mob locus is expressed at a low level under both aerobic and anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. mobA was initially identified as one of several genes that, when mutated, result in resistance to chlorate. Chlorate resistance of the chlB mutants is the result of inactive nitrate reductase, which is a molybdoenzyme |CITS: |. However, 2-phosphoglycolate is formed during repair of DNA strand breaks with 3'-phosphoglycolate ends; such breaks can be caused by radiomimetic drugs like bleomycin |CITS:|. Gph was shown to be involved in the recovery of glycolate from 2-phosphoglycolate released by the activity of DNA repair enzymes after bleomycin treatment |CITS:|. Deletion of gph resulted in loss of induction of the glc operon by glycolate after bleomycin treatment |CITS:|. gph mutants also failed to recover as quickly as wild type after bleomycin treatment |CITS:|. In a previous study gph deletion mutation had no apparent physiological effect |CITS:|. Expression of gph appears to be constitutive |CITS:|. Gph: "phosphoglycolate phosphatase" |CITS: |

PBP6b DD-carboxypeptidase activity contributes to the maintenance of cell shape at low pH |CITS: |. The predicted amino acid sequence of PBP6b is 47.4% identical to |FRAME: CPLX0-8252 "PBP5"| and 47.7% identical to |FRAME: CPLX0-8254 "PBP6"| |CITS: |. Increased expression of dacD in a strain that contains dacA and dacC null alleles reduces the amount of pentapeptide muropeptides in peptidoglycan |CITS: |. DacD contains the conserved motif sequences, SxxK (SLTK), xN (SGN) and G (KTG), of the serine acyltransferase superfamily |CITS: |; DacD binds benzylpenicillin |CITS: |. DacD does not contribute to intrinsic β-lactam resistance in E. coli K-12, however overexpression of dacD partially complements the β-lactam sensitivity of a ΔdacA mutant |CITS: |. Purified, soluble DacD binds Bocillin FL penicillin and has moderate deacylation activity; it also exhibits DD-carboxpeptidase activity with the model substrate diacetyl-Lys-D-Ala-D-Ala and with the the peptidoglycan mimetic pentapeptide substrate, L-Ala-γ-D-Glu-L-Lys-D-Ala-D-Ala |CITS: |. Single dacD insertion mutants grow normally under typical laboratory condiition as do ΔdacA dacD::Cm, ΔdacA ΔdacC dacD::Cm and ΔdacA ΔdacB ΔdacC dacD::Cm strains |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Genetic interaction implicates dacD in the maintenance of normal morphology |CITS: |. Overexpression of DacD in early exponential growth leads to cell lysis |CITS: |. PBP5/DacD hybrid proteins, in which the C-terminal membrane anchor of PBP5 is replaced by the homologous membrane anchor of PBP6, bind to the membrane and like PBP5, can complement the morphological defects of a strain lacking seven PBPs (PBPs 4, 5, 6, and 7, DacD, AmpC and AmpH) |CITS: |. PBP6b has strong DD-carboxypeptidase activity at pH 5.0; dacD transcription and translation increase at pH 5.0; purified PBP6b binds a penicillin derivative faster at pH 5.0 than at pH 7.5 and has increased DD-carboxypeptidase activity against pentapeptide-rich peptidoglycan at pH 5.0; this higher activity is due to both enhanced protein stability and enhanced substrate binding at acidic pH |CITS: |. At pH 5.0, active PB6b is required to produce cells with normal morphology |CITS: |, dacD is implicated in the productive biogenesis of the GOB-18 metallo-β-lactamase (Elizabethkingia meningoseptica pre-apo-gob-18 expressed in trans in E. coli); ΔdacD mutants show increased ability to develop biofilm |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: The native biological role of the YebF protein encoded by b1847 is not known. This study demonstrates that YebF is naturally secreted by Escherichia coli: it is exported from the cytoplasm to the periplasm via the Sec pathway, processed to a mature form, and then released into the extracellular medium by an unidentified outer‑membrane mechanism. Moreover, YebF can act as a carrier protein, directing fusion partners (e.g., human IL‑2, α‑amylase, alkaline phosphatase) across the outer membrane and into the culture medium while retaining their activity. {PubMed:16369539}. The article identifies JW1836 as the yebF gene, encoding a small (~10.8 kDa) soluble protein that is naturally exported from the cytoplasm to the periplasm via the Sec pathway and then secreted into the extracellular medium by an unknown outer‑membrane mechanism. Its native physiological role is described as “unknown,” but experimentally it functions as an efficient carrier that can fuse to heterologous proteins (e.g., human IL‑2, α‑amylase) and direct their secretion into the culture medium without causing cell lysis or outer‑membrane leakage. {PubMed:16369539}. The native biological role of YebF is not known; however, the article demonstrates that YebF is a small (≈10.8 kDa) soluble protein that is naturally secreted by laboratory strains of Escherichia coli. It is exported from the cytoplasm to the periplasm via the Sec-dependent pathway and then released into the extracellular medium by an as‑yet unidentified outer‑membrane mechanism. Because YebF can be fused to heterologous proteins and efficiently transport these fusions across the outer membrane, it functions experimentally as a carrier protein for extracellular secretion of recombinant proteins. {PubMed:16369539}. YebF is a ~13 kDa periplasmic protein of previously unknown biological role that is exported to the extracellular medium by a two‑step secretion process in Escherichia coli. After Sec‑dependent translocation into the periplasm, YebF is exported across the outer membrane through a pathway that requires the major porins OmpF and OmpC and the auxiliary outer‑membrane protein OmpX. The protein possesses a cystatin‑like folded core and a highly dynamic, positively charged surface that is essential for its interaction with these porins and for efficient secretion. In addition to being secreted itself, YebF can act as a carrier that enables the extracellular secretion of C‑terminally fused heterologous proteins of various sizes and functions. {PubMed:22658749}. YebF is an endogenous Escherichia coli protein that is naturally secreted into the extracellular medium. It is first exported to the periplasm via the Sec-dependent signal peptide and then traverses the outer membrane, a step that likely involves the OmpF/C porins. In its native role, YebF functions as a carrier protein that can fuse to heterologous “passenger” proteins at its C‑terminus, enabling those proteins to be delivered across the periplasm and outer membrane and accumulate in the culture supernatant in biologically active form. Consequently, YebF is widely used as a secretion tag for extracellular expression of recombinant proteins, including enzymes, human cytokines, and other therapeutic or industrial proteins. {PubMed:24200127}. In the study, YebF is described as a secretion‑tag protein that is exported from the cytoplasm to the periplasm via the Sec pathway and then released into the extracellular medium by an unknown outer‑membrane mechanism. When fused to the antimicrobial peptide Art‑085 (forming YebF‑Art‑085), YebF directs the fusion protein to the periplasm where the Art‑085 moiety can access and degrade the peptidoglycan layer, thereby inducing rapid lysis of the engineered E. coli host. Thus, YebF functions as a carrier that enables periplasmic delivery and subsequent lytic activity of the fused killing protein. {PubMed:28441472}. YebF is a small (13 kDa) native E. coli protein that serves as a carrier in a two‑step secretion system. Its N‑terminal Sec‑leader directs it to the periplasm via the Sec pathway, where the leader is cleaved to a mature 10.8 kDa form. The mature YebF is then exported across the outer membrane through a mechanism involving the porins OmpF and OmpC, enabling fused passenger proteins (e.g., CotA laccase) to be secreted into the culture medium. {PubMed:27738721}. YebF is a periplasmic protein of Escherichia coli that is exported via a Sec-type signal peptide, processed in the periplasm, and efficiently released into the extracellular medium. Its precise physiological role is unknown, but it is a substrate of the oxidative‑folding enzymes DsbA and DsbC, forming a conserved intramolecular disulfide bond. Because of its efficient secretion, YebF has been exploited as a carrier protein to transport heterologous passenger proteins through the cell envelope and release them into the medium. {PubMed:21037007}. In the study, YebF is described as a protein of unknown intrinsic function that is naturally secreted from the periplasm of Escherichia coli into the culture medium. By fusing the tox‑1 mini‑cellulase gene to the C‑terminus of YebF, the researchers used YebF as a secretion carrier to export the TOX‑1 peptide outside the cell. This chimerization helped circumvent toxicity and other production issues associated with intracellular expression of the cellulase, allowing the enzyme to act on extracellular substrates such as carboxymethyl cellulose. {PubMed:27229865}.

MetaCyc_Comment: E. coli contains two different phosphoribosylglycinamide (GAR) transformylases, both of which can catalyze the third step in de novo purine biosynthesis. The transformylase encoded by purN utilizes 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate as the formyl donor. The second transformylase encoded by purT utilizes formate, which is provided by PurU-catalyzed hydrolysis of 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate |CITS: |. The existence of these two transformylase enzymes was determined by mutant studies. A strain containing a knockout insertion in purN did not result in purine auxotrophy |CITS: |. Only mutants defective in both purN and purT required exogenously added purine for growth |CITS: |. There is no significant homology between the two transformylases |CITS: |. Kinetic studies of wild-type and mutant PurT, as well as positional isotope exchange studies, demonstrated a formyl phosphate intermediate in the catalytic mechanism of the GAR transformylase reaction |CITS: |. GAR transformylase 2 can also catalyze a second, side reaction that is different from its transformylase activity. The second activity is acetate kinase, which cleaves ATP in the presence of acetate to produce acetylphosphate and ADP |CITS: |. The crystal structure of phosphoribosylglycinamide transformylase 2 has been determined in complex with substrate and/or nucleotide analogs |CITS: |. The enzyme was determined to be a monomer in solution |CITS: |, but a homodimer in the crystal |CITS: |. It belongs to the ATP-grasp superfamily |CITS: |. E. coli naturally lacks the fhs gene encoding formyltetrahydrofolate synthetase, but possesses purT. In strains engineered to contain either fhs, purT, or both genes, growth competition assays in mixed cultures showed that strains with only a single gene had a fitness advantage |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: NuoL is part of the inner membrane component of NADH dehydrogenase I |CITS: |. The protein has 14 transmembrane helices and a 110 Å long amphipathic α-helix that spans almost the entire length of the membrane domain |CITS: |. Transmembrane helices were assigned to locations in the crystal structure using Fourier transform analysis |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the membrane component at higher resolution has allowed better identification of the unusual arrangement of the transmembrane helices |CITS: |. NuoL was proposed to be located at the distal end of the membrane arm of NDH-1 |CITS: | and to function in proton translocation |CITS: |. The striking placement within the NDH-1 complex of NuoL's long amphipathic α-helix suggested that proton translocation may be facilitated by a piston-like movement of this helix |CITS: |. A modified indirect coupling mechanism was later proposed by |CITS: |. However, analysis of an extensive set of NuoL mutants now indicates that the amphipathic helix of NuoL does not function as a mechanical piston and may instead function like a clamp for the NuoLMN subunits during catalytic turnover |CITS: |. An analysis of movement of the amphipathic helix utilizing cysteine-scanning and labeling of individual sites revealed only minor conformational rearrangements |CITS: |, and constraining its movement by crosslinking did not affect NDH-1 activity |CITS: |. Introduction of small infrared labels at the K551 and Y590 residues allowed enhanced visualization of movement and showed that the labeled residues relocate to a more hydrophobic environment upon NADH reduction |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis of residues that are conserved between NuoL and Na+/H+ antiporters as well as studies using specific inhibitors indicate that NuoL is involved in the indirect coupling mechanism for proton pumping |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis of the three antiporter-like subunits NuoL, M and N indicate that these subunits have a common role in NDH-1 |CITS: |. When the NDH-1 complex is reconstituted with NuoL subunits that are truncated at various points in the amphipathic helix, proton translocation is diminished, but not abolished, arguing for at least two coupling sites for proton translocation, with NuoL being essential for the translocation of 2H+/2e- |CITS: |. However, additional reports using C-terminally truncated forms of NuoL indicated that intact NuoL is required for correct assembly of NDH-1 |CITS: |. Yet, overexpression of all NDH-1 subunits except NuoL is reported to result in formation of a ΔNuoL NDH-1 complex that is capable of the electron transfer reaction, and whose proton translocation activity is approximately half that of wild type |CITS: |. A ΔNuoL complex I also lacked NuoM, but not NuoN, and only contained ~1 molecule of ubiquinone |CITS: |. A point mutation in the conserved D563 residue within the amphipathic helix of NuoL also results in significantly reduced proton translocation |CITS: |. Several additional NuoL point mutants in reconstituted NDH-1 were tested in vitro for proton pumping activity |CITS: |. The V259A mutation (analogous to the V253A mutation in human mitochondrial ND5 of a patient) abolishes NDH-1 activity due to instability of the complex |CITS: |. The specific functional complementation by NuoL of a B. subtilis ΔmrpA Na+ channel mutant indicates that NuoL may transport Na+ as well |CITS: |. A C-terminally truncated fragment of NuoL was previously shown to function as a Na+ pump |CITS: |. NDH-1 lacking the NuoL subunit does not appear to transport Na+ |CITS: |. Null mutants of all individual nuo genes have a growth defect under aerobic conditions in rich medium |CITS: |. A nuoL mutant contains two populations of partially assembled complex I, one with electron transfer activity and about half of the proton transfer activity of wild type, and one inactive complex that is associated with CadA |CITS: |. nuoL belongs to a network of genes which facilitate stress-induced mutagenesis (SIM) in E. coli K-12 |CITS: |. The A1916 base of 23S rRNA is an important specificity determinant |CITS: |. There appear to be different specificity determinants for uridines at different positions of H69. The enzyme shows more stringent specificity in vivo than in vitro |CITS: |. Cryo-EM reconstructions of 50S ribosomal subunit precursors revealed a network of interacting ribosomal biogenesis factors that consists of RluD, RsfS, YjgA, and ObgE |CITS: |. Initial experiments complementing an rluD mutant with catalytically inactive rluD alleles seemed to indicate that lack of pseudouridylation was not responsible for the severe growth defect of an rluD mutant |CITS: |. However, the interpretation of those results was complicated by the use of a truncated rluD gene. Later experiments using an rluD deletion strain showed that the loss of pseudouridylation at positions 1911, 1915, and 1917 in 23S rRNA leads to a defect in ribosome assembly, biogenesis and function |CITS: |. A mutation that suppresses the growth defect of an rluD mutant localizes to prfB, which encodes |FRAME: EG10762-MONOMER| |CITS: |. In the E. coli K-12 background, at least one of the three pseudouridine bases appears to have a function in termination of translation |CITS: |. In an in vitro system, lack of the three pseudouridines in 23S rRNA decreased the activity of RF2 |CITS: |. An rluD deletion enhances the slow growth phenotype of an rsgA mutation |CITS: | and reduces the frequency of single-cell persister resuscitation |CITS: |. Overproduction of RluD increases the frequency of waking and resuscitation of persister cells by BPOET |CITS: |.
