Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Toxic component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system. ChpB is a sequence-specific mRNA and (weak) tmRNA endoribonuclease that inhibits protein synthesis and induces bacterial stasis. Cleavage is independent of the ribosome. Cleavage occurs at ACY sequences where Y is not C. The endoribonuclease activity is not as strong as that of MazF. The endoribonuclease activity (a toxin) is inhibited by its labile cognate antitoxin ChpS. Toxicity results when the levels of ChpS decrease in the cell, leading to mRNA degradation. Both ChpS and ChpB probably bind to the promoter region of the chpS-chpB operon to autoregulate their synthesis. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12972253, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16413033, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21419338, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8226627}.

FUNCTION: Transporter of a GTP-driven Fe(2+) uptake system, probably couples GTP-binding to channel opening and Fe(2+) uptake (PubMed:12446835, PubMed:19629046). A guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G proteins) in which the guanine nucleotide binding site alternates between an active, GTP-bound state and an inactive, GDP-bound state. This protein has fast intrinsic GDP release, mediated by the G5 loop (about residues 149-158). Presumably GTP hydrolysis leads to conformational changes and channel closing (PubMed:19629046). A GDP release mechanism involving a conformational change of the G5 loop (and thus the removal of the nucleotide-binding and stabilizing interactions) would significantly reduce the affinity for GDP, and conceivably be sufficient for catalysing nucleotide release (PubMed:25374115). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12446835, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19629046, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23104801, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25374115, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25517170, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8407793}.
MetaCyc_Comment: FeoB is the inner membrane component of a ferrous iron uptake system which is active under anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. FeoB is composed of a hydrophilic N-terminal domain which specifically binds GTP (the G protein domain; residues 1-170), a GDP dissociation inhibitor-like (GDI-like) domain (residues 171-274) and a C-terminal integral membrane domain which may act as a permease |CITS: |. FeoB's G protein catalyses slow GTP hydrolysis and fast GDP release and is required for Fe(II) uptake |CITS: |. The mechanism of ferrous iron uptake by FeoB may represent an early prototype of the eukaryotic G protein cycle |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the soluble domain of FeoB (nFeoB comprising residues 1-270) in both an apo and GTP-bound conformation have been reported: nFeoB assembles as a funnel-shaped trimer with 3-fold symmetry between the protomers; the trimer binds a single molecule of the nonhydrolysable GTP analogue mGTP and a putative Mg2+ ion; a comparative analysis of the structures suggests that GTP binding leads to opening of a central cytoplasmic pore and a mechanism of G-protein coupled gating of FeoB has been proposed |CITS: |. Conformational change in the nucleotide binding G5 loop is implicated in GDP release |CITS: |. The GTPase activity of nFeoB (residues 1-274) is stimulated by potassium |CITS: |. Early studies in Escherichia coli K-12 strains characterized feo mutants which were defective in the import of ferrous iron |CITS: |. The feo operon consists of three co-regulated genes feoABC |CITS: |. feo is a member of the Fur regulon; expression is repressed by Fur-Fe2+; feo expression is activated by FNR under anaerobic conditions |CITS: |. feo expression is low under aerobic conditions and increases under anaerobic conditions under the positive control of transcription factors ArcA and FNR; Feo-mediated import of Fe2+ promotes Fur-Fe2+ occupancy amd contributes to Fur regulation under anaerobic conditions |CITS: |. FeoB is a member of the 'TrmE-Era-EngA-YihA-Septin like' superfamily within the GTPase superclass of P-loop NTPases |CITS: | and a member of the Ferrous Iron Uptake Family in the Transporter Classification Database |CITS: |. feo: ferrous iron uptake |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

Fe(2+) is an excellent substrate in the presence of excess Cu(2+), but is inactive in the absence of Cu(2+) (PubMed:15516598, PubMed:17804014). Oxidizes the phenolate iron siderophores enterobactin, 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate (2,3-DHB) and 3-hydroxyanthranilate (3-HAA) (PubMed:11466290, PubMed:15317788). Oxidation and thus inactivation of enterobactin could protect cells from the interaction of enterobactin with copper and play a central role as an interface between copper detoxification and iron homeostasis (PubMed:11466290, PubMed:15317788). Also oxidizes a variety of phenolic model substrates, including 2,2'-azinobis(3-ethylbenzthiazolinesulfonic acid) (ABTS), p-phenylenediamine (pPD), 2,6-dimethoxyphenol (2,6-DMP) and 3,4-dihydroxybenzoic acid (3,4-DHB) (PubMed:11466290, PubMed:11527384, PubMed:17804014, PubMed:25679350). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11466290, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11527384, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11867755, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15317788, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15516598, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17804014, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25679350}.

MetaCyc_Comment: CueO multicopper oxidase is a copper-stimulated phenoloxidase and ferroxidase |CITS: | that plays a role in copper homeostasis |CITS: | during aerobiosis |CITS: |. CueO has been observed to offer protective effects from copper-mediated damage |CITS: |. In the presence of copper, CueO can oxidize and thus inactivate the iron siderophores 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate and enterobactin in vitro |CITS: |. A mixture of enterobactin and copper is toxic, and ferric enterobactin may be the natural substrate of CueO in vivo; thus, CueO may play a central role as an interface between copper detoxification and iron homeostasis |CITS: |. The purified protein has cuprous oxidase activity in vitro |CITS: |; CueO functions primarily as a cuprous oxidase in vivo, not as a phenol oxidase |CITS: |. Purified CueO contains four |CITS: | or six |CITS: | atoms of copper per monomer, although the latter value may result from inaccurate protein quantification methods. CueO contains a substrate binding, type 1 ('blue') copper site and a trinuclear copper center (consisting of type 2 and type 3 copper sites) where oxygen binding and reduction takes place; it also contains a methionine rich region which lies over the type 1 copper site and may interfere with substrate binding |CITS: |. Purified CueO binds five copper atoms; a fifth copper atom binds in the methionine rich region and is important for the copper associated activation of enzyme activity |CITS: |. Deletion of the methionine rich region results in a significant reduction in cuprous oxidase activity but an increase in phenoloxidase activity possibly due to increased access to the type 1 copper site |CITS: |. Copper is incorporated sequentially to the three types of binding sites in CueO |CITS: |. The methionine rich region is able to bind additional Cu(I) ions (Cu6 and Cu7 sites) |CITS: |. The fifth copper binding site has a different role in phenol and cuprous oxidation; as a phenol oxidase the T4 site is occupied by Cu(II) and mediates electron transfer from organic substrates such as 2,6-dimethoxyphenol to the T1 site; as a cuprous oxidase the T4 site must be vacant in order to dock a Cu(I) substrate, as demonstrated with the model substrate copper bicinchoninate |CITS: |. Cu6 and Cu7 function as substrate binding oxidation sites; Cu5 acts as an electron transfer site, not a substrate reaction site |CITS: |. CueO crystallized in the presence of Ag(I) contains Ag(I) bound at T4 and at the additional sites (sites 6 and 7) in the Met rich region; binding of Ag(I) inhibits CueO activity |CITS: |. Phenoloxidase activity of CueO was demonstrated against substrates including p-phenylenediamine |CITS: |, 2,6-dimethoxyphenol |CITS: |, and iron siderophores including 2,3-dihydroxybenzoate, enterobactin, and 3-hydroxyanthranilate |CITS: |. CueO is translocated to the periplasm via the Tat pathway |CITS: |. Copper-free, apo-CueO folds to a translocation compatible form in the cytoplasm; CueO is transported without bound copper; CueO assembles copper in the periplasm under copper stress conditions; cofactor assembly stabilizes the protein |CITS: | CueO is a member of the copper responsive, CueR regulon |CITS: |. CueO is the major form of soluble protein-bound copper in E. coli |CITS:|. Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: DsbD is an inner membrane protein which acts within a reductive pathway that maintains the periplasmic disulfide oxidoreductases DsbC and DsbG and the cytochrome c maturation protein CcmG in their catalytically active reduced form. DsbD mediates electron transfer from cytoplasmic thioredoxin to the periplasmic substrate proteins via inter and intra molecular disulfide exchange reactions DsbD consists of three domains: a periplasmic N-terminal domain (nDsbD or DsbDα) which contains an immunoglobulin-like fold, a central transmembrane (TM) domain (tmDsbD or DsbDβ) with eight predicted TM helices and a periplasmic C-terminal domain (cDsbD or DsbDγ) which contains a thioredoxin-like fold |CITS: |. Each domain contains a pair of cysteines which are essential for function |CITS: |. The electron cascade is initiated with the reduction of tmDsbD by thioredoxin, cDsbD then shuttles electrons from tmDsbD to nDsbD and reduced nDsbD passes the electrons on to the periplasmic substrate proteins |CITS: |. DsbD shuffles electrons from the cytoplasm to the periplasm without the involvement of additional cofactors such as quinone, FAD or heme |CITS: |; transfer of electrons across the membrane occurs via thiol disulfide exchange reactions involving the two redox active cysteines contained in each of the three domains of DsbD and reaction intermediates containing mixed disulfide complexes have been isolated |CITS:|. Electron flow from thioredoxin to the periplasmic substrate proteins via DsbD is thermodynamically driven; redox potentials for all the cysteine pairs involved have been determined (see |CITS: | and citations within). dsbD is required for biogenesis of c-type cytochromes in the periplasm |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |. dsbD mutants (dsbD::mini-Tn10Cam) display defects in alkaline phosphatase folding which can be complemented by the addition of reduced dithiothreitol (DTT) |CITS: |. dsbD mutants accumulate oxidised DsbC |CITS: | and oxidised DsbG |CITS: |. Overexpression of dsbD results in phenotypes (loss of alkaline phosphatase activity and loss of motility) that are consistent with the misfolding/reduction of periplasmic proteins containing disulfide bonds; the purified C-terminal domain of DsbD is able to reduce insulin in the presence of DTT; dsbD is essential for growth at temperatures above 42°C |CITS: |. dipZ: disulfide isomerase-like protein Z |CITS: |cutA2: |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |Selected related reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Rescues ribosomes stalled at the 3' end of non-stop mRNAs (PubMed:21062370, PubMed:21435036). This activity is crucial when the stalled ribosome cannot be rescued by the SsrA(tmRNA)-SmpB quality control system (PubMed:21062370, PubMed:21435036). Binds the 30S subunit, contacting 16S rRNA with the N-terminus near the decoding center and its C-terminus in the mRNA entry channel; contacts change in the presence of release factor 2 (RF2, also named PrfB) (PubMed:25355516, PubMed:27906160, PubMed:27906161, PubMed:27934701, PubMed:28077875). Requires RF2/PrfB to hydrolyze stalled peptidyl-tRNA on the ribosome; recruits and probably helps position RF2/PrfB correctly in the ribosomal A site so RF2's GGQ motif can hydrolyze the peptidyl-tRNA bond (PubMed:22857598, PubMed:22922063, PubMed:25355516, PubMed:27906160, PubMed:27906161, PubMed:27934701, PubMed:28077875). Does not release ribosomes with a programmed pause caused by regulatory chains such as SecM-mediated pausing (PubMed:22857598). Binds tRNA which may stimulate its ribosome rescue activity (PubMed:22857598). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:21062370, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21435036, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22857598, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22922063, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25355516, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27906160, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27906161, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27934701, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28077875}.

MetaCyc_Comment: RsmB is the methyltransferase responsible for methylation of 16S rRNA at the C967 nucleotide |CITS: |. In vitro, the enzyme is active on free 16S rRNA, but not 30S ribosomal subunits |CITS: |. Methylation of G966 and C967 in 16S rRNA appears to stabilize the binding of initiator tRNA to the 30S pre-initiation complex prior to recognition of the start codon, thus modulating the early stages of translation initiation |CITS: |. The crystal structure of the apoenzyme has been solved at 1.65 Å resolution, and that of the enzyme complexed with AdoMet at 2.1 Å resolution |CITS: |. A null mutation in rsmB has no significant effect on the growth rate in rich or minimal media |CITS: |, although competitive growth experiments reveal a fitness defect |CITS: |. Deletion of rsmB alters the initiation frequency from certain translation initiation codons |CITS: |. A C375A mutant is catalytically inactive, while a C325A mutant retains activity |CITS: |. RsmB: "rRNA small subunit methyltransferase B" Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: The outer membrane protein PagP catalyses the transfer of a palmitate chain from phospholipid donor to the lipid A moiety of lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a modification that is important for virulence in many gram-negative bacteria. Purified PagP transfers a palmitate chain from the sn-1 position of a phospholipid substrate (phosphatidylcholine substrates and common E. coli phospholipids) to the amide-linked hydroxymyristate chain of the proximal glucosamine unit (GlcN I) of disaccharide lipid A precursors (lipid IVA and Kdo2-lipid IVA) in vitro; the expected physiological substrate of PagP is the lipid A moiety of fully assembled |FRAME: CPD0-939 "LPS"| in the outer membrane; PagP is highly selective for a saturated palmitate chain |CITS: |. PagP is an integral outer membrane enzyme |CITS: |. Purified PagP (refolded in detergent micelles) forms an eight-stranded antiparallel β-barrel with a small amphipathic N-terminal α-helix on the periplasmic side of the membrane; the putative catalytic residues (His-33, Asp-76, and Ser-77) are located on the exterior edge of the outer membrane |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). PagP forms a 'tilted' barrel structure with an internal ligand binding pocket that discriminates between acyl chains with different numbers of carbon atoms |CITS: | (see further |CITS: |. Both phospholipid substrate and LPS must gain access to the active site suggesting that PagP is active when lipid asymmetry is disturbed; PagP activity in vivo depends on aberrant migration of phospholipids to the outer membrane |CITS: |. PagP contains two regions of weakened β-strand hydrogen bonding (the crenel and the embrasure) for controlling lipid diffusion between the barrel interior and the outer membrane external leaflet |CITS: | (see further |CITS: |). pagP expression is induced in mature biofilms and in very late stationary-phase planktonic cultures |CITS: |. crcA: confers resistance to camphor |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Cytochrome peroxidase that enables anaerobic respiration with H(2)O(2) as a terminal electron acceptor (PubMed:28696311). It receives electrons from the quinol pool (PubMed:28696311, PubMed:29550214). Menaquinol is probably the electron donor in vivo (PubMed:28696311, PubMed:29550214). It can use menadiol (a menaquinol analog), hydroquinone, duroquinol and the artificial electron donor ABTS(2-) in vitro, but only menadiol and hydroquinone can efficiently transfer electrons to Ccp, maintaining the catalytic activity of the enzyme (PubMed:29550214). It enables E.coli to grow on a nonfermentable carbon source when H(2)O(2) is supplied (PubMed:28696311). Plays a role in the peroxide stress response under anaerobic conditions (PubMed:17464064). However, it does not degrade H(2)O(2) quickly enough to lower the periplasmic H(2)O(2) level below that of the surrounding medium and protect the cell from its toxic effects (PubMed:28696311). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17464064, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28696311, ECO:0000269|PubMed:29550214}.
MetaCyc_Comment: ccp encodes a periplasmic cytochrome c peroxidase (CCP) that enables E. coli to respire using H2O2 as an anaerobic terminal electron acceptor; Ccp may support growth in environments where H2O2 is produced and oxygen levels are diminished; Ccp activity does not protect the cytoplasm from exogenous H2O2; its physiological role is to exploit H2O2 for respiratory gain while the cytoplasmic peroxidase and catalase activities protect the cell from the toxic effects of H2O2 |CITS: |. Hydroperoxide negative (Hpx-) mutants (ie. strains lacking KatG and KatE catalases plus NADH peroxidase AhpCF) retain a significant ability to degrade H2O2 under anaerobic conditions; Hpx- strains lacking ccp (Hpx- Δccp) show a substantial loss of this ability which can be complemented by overexpression of ccp from a plasmid |CITS: |. Ccp receives electrons directly from the membrane quinone pool for the reduction of H2O2 in the periplasm; Ccp supports anaerobic growth with glycerol as a sole carbon source and H2O2 as the terminal electron acceptor |CITS: |. Like Hpx- Δccp mutants, Hpx- ΔccmABCDEFGH mutants show a significant loss in the ability to degrade H2O2 under anaerobic conditions suggesting that Ccp uses the |FRAME: ABC-35-CPLX "Ccm pathway"| for heme cofactor attachment |CITS: |. E. coli Ccp is a member of a sub-group of bacterial CCPs that contain three heme-binding motifs |CITS: |. Ccp contains the two heme binding sites (CXXCH) which are characteristic of bacterial cytochrome c peroxidases (the electron transferring or E heme and the peroxidatic or P heme) plus an additional c-type heme binding motif in the N-terminal domain (the NT heme); the P heme is His/OH 6-coordinated; the NT and E hemes are both His-Met 6-coordinated |CITS: |. A ccp mutant (W3110 Δccp) shows increased sensitivity to exogenous peroxides |CITS: |. Purified recombinant Ccp, lacking its transmembrane domain is a monomer in solution |CITS: |. Expression of ccp is increased under anaerobic conditions and is dependent on FNR and OxyR |CITS: |; strong expression of a ccp-lacZ transcriptional fusion requires anoxia plus the presence of H2O2; dual regulation by both OxyR and FNR ensures that ccp is expressed when oxygen is absent and H2O2 is present |CITS: | Ccp is predicted to be a bitopic inner membrane protein |CITS: |. Ccp contains a putative signal peptidase II cleavage site |CITS: | .

MetaCyc_Comment: ModA is the periplasmic binding protein of an ABC transporter that mediates the high affinity uptake of molybdate. Purified ModA binds molybdate and tungstate with similar high affinities and in a 1:1 ratio; it does not bind sulfate, phosphate, selenate nor chlorate |CITS: |. Although an early study |CITS: |, indicated that ModA does not bind chromate, later work |CITS: | reported that purified ModA binds chromate with high affinity (Kd approx 100 nM). Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Multidrug efflux pump that probably functions as a Na(+)/drug antiporter. Confers resistance to many drugs such as fluoroquinolones (norfloxacin, ciprofloxacin, enoxacin) and tetraphenylphosphonium ion (TPP) (PubMed:11566977, PubMed:9661020). Also to deoxycholate, doxorubicin, trimethoprim, chloramphenicol, fosfomycin, ethidium bromide and benzalkonium (PubMed:11566977). Cells overexpressing this protein have decreased intracellular levels of Ala-Gln dipeptide, and in a system that produces the Ala-Gln dipeptide overproduction of this protein increases export of the dipeptide (PubMed:20067529). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11566977, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12615854, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20067529, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9661020}.

MetaCyc_Comment: MdtK (also called NorM) is a member of the Multi Antimicrobial Extrusion (MATE) family of transporters (formerly the multidrug and toxic compound extrusion family) within the Multidrug/Oligosaccharidyl-lipid/Polysaccharide (MOP) flippase superfamily |CITS: |. Increased expression of mdtK in an E. coli strain lacking the major drug efflux pump AcrAB (E. coli KAM3) results in increased resistance to norfloxacin, ciprofloxacin, acriflavine and tetraphenylphosphonium (TPP+) |CITS:|. Increased expression of mdtK in E. coli KAM3 results in a 32-fold increase in resistance to TPP+ and deoxycholate, an 8-fold increase in resistance to norfloxacin, enoxacin and doxorubicin, a 4-fold increase in resistance to trimethoprim and a 2-fold increase in resistance to chloramphenicol, fosfomycin, ethidium bromide and benzalkonium |CITS:| (see also |CITS: |). Norfloxacin efflux is disrupted upon the addition of m-chlorophenylhydrazone; MdtK is a putative Na+-driven multidrug efflux pump |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Increased expression of mdtK in an E. coli strain lacking AcrAB (AG100AX) results in increased resistance to a range of antibiotics (norfloxacin, doxorubicin, novobiocin, enoxacin, and ciprofloxacin), dyes (rhodamine 6G, ethidium bromide, acriflavine, and crystal violet) and quaternary ammonium compounds (berberine, benzalkonium and TPP+); increased expression of mdtK in E. coli AG100AX reduces the accumulation of norflaxacin and ethidium bromide; purified MdtK binds rhodamine 6G with micromolar affinity and with a 1:1 stoichiometry of monomeric MdtK to ligand; purified MdtK binds ethidium bromide, proflavine, ciprofloxacin, and norfloxacin with affinities in the micromolar range |CITS: |. Overexpression of mdtK rescues the hypermutable phenotype of an 8-oxoguanine repair deficient E. coli strain possibly by extrusion of molecules that oxidise deoxy-guanine |CITS: |. MdtK is able to transport dipeptides (Ala-Gln and L-alanyl-L-branched chain amino acids) in a dipeptide overproducing strain |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Activator of the cell wall hydrolases AmiA and AmiB. Required for septal murein cleavage and daughter cell separation during cell division. In vitro, exhibits weak endoproteolytic activity on beta-casein. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11976287, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15165230, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19525345, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20300061, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23796240}.
MetaCyc_Comment: EnvC is a divisome associated factor which activates the peptidoglycan (PG) hydrolases |FRAME: NACMURLALAAMI1-MONOMER "AmiA"| and |FRAME: NACMURLALAAMI2-MONOMER "AmiB"| required for septal splitting |CITS: |. EnvC-mediated amidase activation is regulated by direct interaction with the |FRAME: ABC-54-CPLX FtsEX| transmembrane complex (reviewed in |CITS: |). EnvC contains a structural element - the 'restraining arm' - that is implicated in a self-inhibition mechanism; FtsEX interaction with EnvC may drive conformational change that leads to amidase activation |CITS: |. EnvC is not essential for viability; an envC null mutant has cell division and cell envelope integrity defects, an FtsZ ring defect, and is unable to form colonies at 42oC |CITS: |. Temperature sensitivity can be rescued by addition of 5% betaine to the medium |CITS: |. EnvC does not degrade peptidoglycan in solution |CITS: | but does have murein hydrolytic activity in a zymogram assay |CITS: | and also shows weak protease activity toward beta-casein |CITS: |. EnvC was initially shown to localize to the inner membrane and to the cytoplasm |CITS: |; however, a periplasmic localization was shown elsewhere |CITS: |, and an EnvC-green fluorescent protein fusion, when exported to the periplasm, localizes to the septal ring apparatus and functionally complements EnvC- defects |CITS: |. An EnvC mCherry fusion localises to the cell division site |CITS: |. EnvC contains three functional domains: a globular C-terminal LytM domain with similarity to the M23/M37 peptidase family, a central regulatory domain and an N-terminal FtsEX-interacting coiled coil domain |CITS: |. The coiled-coil domain is required for recruitment of EnvC to the divisome |CITS: |. EnvC contains a LytM-like (Pfam: peptidase M23) domain (as do |FRAME: EG12111-MONOMER NlpD|, |FRAME: G7484-MONOMER YgeR| and |FRAME: EG10013-MONOMER MepA|). An E. coli strain lacking all LytM containing proteins shows severe defects in septal peptidoglycan (PG) splitting and forms long cell chains |CITS: |. The LytM domain of EnvC is sufficient for enhancing amidase activity in vitro |CITS: |. The LytM-like domain has a protein fold that is similar to other LytM proteins but the active site region lacks a catalytic metal ion and a metal binding motif. Site directed mutagenesis indicates that residues important for function cluster in and around the 'degenerate' active-site. This is consistent with the hypothesis that EnvC does not itself function to cleave PG but acts to activate other PG hydrolases |CITS: |. The original PM61 mutant strain has an H366Y mutation in EnvC |CITS: |. Overproduction of both wild-type EnvC and the H366Y mutant protein causes a growth defect and cell lysis |CITS: |. An envC mutant exhibits wild-type sensitivity to sodium dodecyl sulfate, ethidium bromide, ethylmethane sulfonate, or nalidixic acid |CITS: |. The envC gene was also identified in a screen for synthetic lethality with minCDE, further arguing for a function of EnvC in cell division |CITS: |. Initial cloning of genes complementing the envC defect in strain PM61 resulted in a plasmid containing the acrE and acrF genes |CITS: |; this is now thought to be the result of multicopy suppression of envC- by acrEF |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes nitrate uptake, nitrite uptake and nitrite export across the cytoplasmic membrane. May function as a nitrate/H(+) and nitrite/H(+) channel. Could confer a selective advantage during severe nutrient starvation or slow growth. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11967075, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15667293, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16804183, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18691156}.
MetaCyc_Comment: NarU catalyses nitrate uptake and nitrite export by an unknown mechanism in E. coli K-12. NarU is a member of the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) of transporters |CITS:|, and is highly similar to the nitrate:nitrite antiporter |FRAME: NARK-MONOMER "NarK"| |CITS:|. narU forms an operon with narZYWV, encoding |FRAME: NITRATREDUCTZ-CPLX| |CITS:|. An |FRAME: RPOS-MONOMER "RpoS"|-dependent promoter is located upstream of the narU transcription start site |CITS:|. narU expressed from a plasmid restores the ability of a strain lacking narK to export nitrite from the cytoplasm |CITS: |. Δ(narUnarK) strains are defective in nitrate dependent growth; single ΔnarU or ΔnarK strains can import nitrate at rates similar to wild-type. A multicopy plasmid expressing narU complements a narK mutation for nitrite excretion but not uptake |CITS: |. Under anaerobic conditions NarU confers a selective advantage during nitrate starvation or very slow growth |CITS: |. NarU catalysed nitrate uptake is mechanistically linked to nitrite expulsion - NarU may function as a nitrate:nitrite antiporter or as a H+ symporter for nitrate import and nitrite export |CITS: |. If NarU functions as a symporter the co-transported ion is unlikely to be a proton but could be a sodium or potassium ion |CITS: |. NarU has 12 transmembrane (TM) helices in two domains - TM 1-6 form the N-terminal domain and TM 7-12 form the C-terminal domain |CITS:, |. 4 conserved residues (Arg87, Arg303, Asn173 and Tyr261) form a putative substrate binding site. NarU binds nitrate with high affinity (KD = 33µM); the binding affinity for nitrite is approximately 10 times lower |CITS: |. Review: |CITS:, |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the reversible reduction of 2,5-diketo-3-deoxygluconate (DKII or 4,6-dihydroxy-2,5-dioxohexanoate) into 2-keto-3-deoxygluconate (KDG or 2-dehydro-3-deoxygluconate) with a concomitant oxidation of NADH (Ref.4). To a lesser extent, can also reduce 5-keto-D-gluconate and oxidize D-gluconate and 1,2-propanediol (PubMed:24509771). Together with KduI, seems to play a role in the catabolism of hexuronates under osmotic stress conditions, substituting for the regular hexuronate degrading enzymes UxaABC and UxuAB whose expression is repressed in these conditions (PubMed:23437267). In vitro, also exhibits NADH-dependent 20-ketosteroid reductase activity against eukaryotic steroid hormone 11-deoxycorticosterone (11-DOC), which is converted into the product 4-pregnen-20,21-diol-3-one. In addition to 11-DOC, five other C21 steroid compounds (11-deoxycortisol, cortisol, corticosterone, cortisone, and 21-hydroxypregnenolone) are reduced by KduD, but steroids lacking the hydroxyl group at C21 position, such as pregnenolone, testosterone propionate, cortisone acetate, or progesterone, cannot be used as substrate (PubMed:24509771). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:23437267, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24509771, ECO:0000269|Ref.4}.

MetaCyc_Comment: CusA is a member of the Resistance-Nodulation-Cell Division (RND) Transporter Superfamily and is involved in the detoxification of copper and silver ions in E. coli as part of the CusCFBA copper/silver efflux system. CusA contains 12 transmembrane (TM) segments and a large periplasmic domain formed from two loops located between TM1 and 2 and TM7 and 8 |CITS: |. As an RND transporter, CusA probably forms trimers in vivo, but it forms a mixture of oligomers in detergent solution |CITS: |. The amino acids M573, M623, M672, D405, E412, and A399 of CusA are essential for copper tolerance |CITS: |. Crystal structures of apo and ion bound CusA suggest that the protein uses methionine pairs or clusters to export copper and silver ions from both the cytoplasm and the periplasm. 3 methionine residues - M573, M623 and M672 coordinate Cu(I) bound in a periplasmic cleft. In addition, 3 pairs of methionine residues - M410/501, M403/486 and M391/1009 - located in the transmembrane region and a further pair (M271/755) located in the periplasmic domain of the protein may form a relay of binding sites for the movement of substrate ions |CITS: |. Copper may bind to CusA by a Met2 O/N motif comprising M573, M672 and E625 |CITS: |. Purified CusA reconstituted into liposomes is able to transport silver ions |CITS: |. Transport is abolished in CusA mutants in which key methionine residues have been substituted |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: The nfsB-encoded nitroreductase is the minor oxygen-insensitive nitroreductase present in E. coli K-12. NfsB reduces a broad range of nitroaromatic compounds |CITS: |, including the antibiotics nitrofurazone and nitrofurantoin |CITS: |. NfsB is a flavin mononucleotide (FMN)-containing protein and uses both NADH and NADPH as a source of reducing equivalents |CITS: |. FAD can substitute for FMN as an effective prosthetic group |CITS: |. NfsB catalyzes the reduction of nitrocompounds using a ping-pong Bi-Bi mechanism |CITS: |. The reduction of nitroaromatic compounds consists of two successive, two-electron transfer reactions to reduce nitroaromatics to their hydroxylamine derivatives |CITS: |. NfsB can also act as a ferric reductase and catalyze a one-electron reduction of hydrogen peroxide, forming hydroxyl radicals |CITS: |. In the presence of free flavins, NfsB is able to release ferrous iron from FtnA and Bfr; NfsB also has a free flavin reductase activity with NADH as the electron donor |CITS: |. An enzyme with dihyropteridine reductase (DHPR) activity |CITS: |, pterin-independent NAD(P)H oxidoreductase activity with potassium ferricyanide as the electron acceptor |CITS: | and dihydrofolate reductase activity |CITS: | has been purified from E. coli; its N-terminal amino acid sequence |CITS: | is highly similar to that of NfsB. Crystal structures of NfsB alone |CITS: |, in complex with the substrate analog nicotinic acid |CITS: | or with nitrofurazone |CITS: |, and of several mutant enzymes |CITS: | have been solved. To investigate the dynamics of NfsB upon ligand binding, NMR backbone assignments with and without nicotinic acid were obtained |CITS: |. Mutations in nfsB lead to increased resistance to nitrofurazone and furazolidone in an nfsA mutant background |CITS: |. Nitrofurantoin resistance due to nfsA/nfsB mutations carries a small fitness cost |CITS: |. An nfsA nfsB double mutant retains 30% of wt nitroreductase activity under aerobic conditions |CITS: |. NfsB has been implicated in the ability to utilize 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT) as a source of nitrogen |CITS: |. nfsB contains a hotspot of IS5 element insertion |CITS: |. IS5 insertion appears to be targeted to superhelical stress-induced DNA destabilization (SSID) regions |CITS: |. Bacterial nitroreductases such as NfsB have been used as prodrug activators for chemotherapy |CITS: |. Mutants that increase its enzymatic activity against prodrugs (e.g. |CITS: |) or to detoxify the anesthetic NBDZ |CITS: | have been identified. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: One of at least 4 proteins (Era, RbfA, RimM and RsgA/YjeQ) that assist in the late maturation steps of the functional core of the 30S ribosomal subunit (PubMed:18223068, PubMed:21102555, PubMed:21303937, PubMed:25904134, PubMed:27382067). Binds the 30S subunit contacting the head, platform, and rRNA helix 44, which may assist the last maturation stages (PubMed:21788480, PubMed:21960487). Removes RbfA from mature, but not immature 30S ribosomes in a GTP-dependent manner; 95% removal in the presence of GTP, 90% removal in GMP-PNP and 65% removal in the presence of GDP (PubMed:21102555, PubMed:25904134). Circulary permuted GTPase that catalyzes rapid hydrolysis of GTP with a slow catalytic turnover (PubMed:12220175). Dispensible for viability, but important for overall fitness. The intrinsic GTPase activity is stimulated by the presence of 30S (160-fold increase in kcat) or 70S (96-fold increase in kcat) ribosomes (PubMed:14973029). Mature 30S ribosomes stimulate intrinsic GTPase more than do immature 30S ribosomes (PubMed:25904134). Ribosome-associated GTPase activity is stimulated by RbfA (PubMed:21102555). The GTPase is inhibited by aminoglycoside antibiotics such as neomycin and paromycin (PubMed:15466596) streptomycin and spectinomycin (PubMed:15828870). This inhibition is not due to competition for binding sites on the 30S or 70S ribosome (PubMed:15828870). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12220175, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14973029, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15466596, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15828870, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21102555, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25904134, ECO:0000305|PubMed:18223068, ECO:0000305|PubMed:27382067}.
MetaCyc_Comment: RsgA, a member of the HAS-GTPase (Hydrophobic Amino acid Substituted for catalytic glutamine GTPases) family, plays a role in the late stages of maturation of the 30S subunit of the ribosome |CITS: |. RsgA induces local conformational changes in the 30S subunit and may thereby destabilize kinetically trapped assembly intermediates |CITS: |. It may also function as a checkpoint protein that tests the decoding center of the 30S subunit |CITS: |. RsgA exhibits GTPase activity |CITS: |, which is stimulated 160-fold by association of RsgA with stochiometric amounts of the 30S subunit of the ribosome |CITS: |. Addition of aminoglycosides that bind to the A site of the 30S ribosomal subunit inhibit that effect |CITS: |. RsgA is a member of a family of P-loop-containing GTPases with an unusual arrangement of GTPase motifs |CITS: |. The N terminus has an OB-fold RNA-binding domain, the central region comprises the GTPase motifs, and the C terminus has a potential zinc knuckle domain |CITS: |. The conserved His248 in the switch 1 region functions as the catalytic residue |CITS: |. The C-terminal zinc finger domain is required for RsgA stability and its interaction with the 30S subunit |CITS: |. The RsgA protein copurifies with ribosomes at a ratio of 1:200. Recombinant RsgA interacts most strongly with the 30S subunit in the presence of 5'-guanylylimidodiphosphate (GMP-PNP), a nonhydrolyzable GTP analog |CITS: |. Binding of RsgA to the 30S subunit induces conformational changes at the A and P site as well as helix 44; GTP hydrolysis may induce partial conformational restoration and dissociate RsgA from the small subunit |CITS: |. The ribosome binding factor |FRAME: EG11178-MONOMER RbfA| promotes association of RsgA with the 30S subunit. RsgA in turn enhances the release of RbfA in a GTP-dependent manner |CITS: |; the C-terminal α helix of RsgA is important for this activity |CITS: |. RsgA is able to bind both mature and immature 30S subunits; its affinity for the mature subunit is much stronger |CITS: |. Binding of Era to the 30S subunit destabilizes helix 44 and prevents binding of RsgA |CITS: |. RsgA was thought to be essential for growth |CITS: |, but a deletion mutant was shown to have a slow growth phenotype and accumulate 30S and 50S ribosomal subunits as well as a 17S rRNA precursor |CITS: |. The structure of the 30S ribosomal subunit of a ΔrsgA mutant was solved by cryo-EM microscopy reconstruction, showing the presence of unprocessed 17S rRNA and absence of some late ribosomal proteins |CITS: |; similar structural defects exist in a ΔrimM mutant |CITS: |. These immature 30S subunits are able to mature slowly |CITS: |. A cryo-EM co-structure shows that RsgA interacts with helix 44, the head and the platform of the 30S subunit, overlapping with the binding sites of |FRAME: EG10505-MONOMER IF2| and |FRAME: EG10506-MONOMER IF3| |CITS: |. A comparison of higher-resolution cryo-EM structures of the mature 30S subunit with and without bound RsgA show stabilization of helix 44 in the presence of RsgA |CITS: |. The protein composition |CITS: | and cryo-EM structure |CITS: | of the 30S subunit from a ΔrbfA ΔrsgA double mutant have been determined. In a genetic interaction screen, two GTPases, |FRAME: EG10270-MONOMER Era| and |FRAME: EG10505-MONOMER IF2|, were found to be multicopy suppressors of the slow growth phenotype, and several synthetic lethal mutants were isolated |CITS: |. Certain mutations in rbfA also suppress the growth and 30S subunit maturation defects |CITS: |, and salt stress suppresses the ribosome assembly and 16S rRNA processing defects |CITS: | of a ΔrsgA mutant. Salt shock leads to a transient decrease in the intracellular level of RsgA; a ΔrsgA mutant is more resistant to high salt stress than wild type |CITS: |. Salt stress resistance appears to be a general feature of many ribosome maturation mutants |CITS: |. An S221A mutation within the central GTPase motif causes a catalytic defect |CITS: |. N-terminal truncation mutants showed that the OB-fold region is essential for ribosome interaction and GTPase stimulation; the N-terminal amino acids 1-20 are essential for GMP-PNP-dependent interaction with the 30S subunit |CITS: |. RsgA: "ribosome small subunit-dependent GTPase A" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Component of the translocation and assembly module (TAM), which facilitates the insertion and assembly of specific beta-barrel proteins into the outer membrane (PubMed:22466966, PubMed:25341963, PubMed:29129383, PubMed:39174534). Promotes the assembly and secretion across the outer membrane of a subset of autotransporters, such as Ag43 (PubMed:22466966, PubMed:25341963). Involved in the assembly of the outer membrane usher protein FimD (PubMed:29129383). In vitro, when TAM is reconstituted into preformed liposomes, it can promote the assembly of several outer membrane proteins, including OmpA, EspP, Ag43 and FadL (PubMed:39174534). TamA is sufficient to catalyze a low level of outer membrane protein (OMP) assembly, but both TamA and TamB are required for efficient OMP assembly (PubMed:39174534). TamB may regulate TamA activity (PubMed:25341963). It could regulate conformational changes in TamA to drive its function in OMP assembly (PubMed:26243377). It could also act as a chaperone that facilitate the transport of nascent membrane proteins across the periplasm to TamA in the outer membrane (PubMed:29129383). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:22466966, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25341963, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26243377, ECO:0000269|PubMed:29129383, ECO:0000269|PubMed:39174534}.; FUNCTION: In addition, is involved in outer membrane lipid homeostasis (PubMed:34781743, PubMed:35226662, PubMed:38913742). Likely transports phospholipids between the inner membrane and the outer membrane (PubMed:34781743, PubMed:35226662, PubMed:38913742). It would provide a bridge-like structure that protects phospholipids as they travel across the periplasm (PubMed:34781743). One possible explanation for the apparent dual function of TAM is that TamB is a somewhat generic transporter of hydrophobic molecules (PubMed:39174534). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:34781743, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35226662, ECO:0000269|PubMed:38913742, ECO:0000269|PubMed:39174534}.; FUNCTION: TamB, YdbH and YhdP are redundant, but not equivalent, in performing an essential function for growth and maintaining lipid homeostasis in the outer membrane (PubMed:34781743). The transport functions of TamB and YhdP could be differentiated according to the fatty acid saturation state of the phospholipids, with TamB transporting more unsaturated phospholipids and YhdP more saturated phospholipids (PubMed:38913742). Any of these three proteins is sufficient for growth (PubMed:34781743). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:34781743, ECO:0000269|PubMed:38913742}.

MetaCyc_Comment: IdnT is a probable L-idonate and D-gluconate transporter. Originally thought to be a subsidiary gluconate uptake system, the primary role of IdnT appears to be in L-idonate transport. The idnT gene is located in the idnDOTR operon involved in metabolising L-idonate to D-gluconate |CITS:|. Expression of this operon is induced by idonate or by 5-ketogluconate |CITS:|. The cloned idnT gene was shown to confer gluconate transport in a gluconate transport negative mutant in whole cell experiments with IdnT displaying a Km of 60 μM for gluconate |CITS:|. While direct transport of L-idonate has not been shown experimentally, IdnT-mediated gluconate transport is strongly inhibited by idonate |CITS:|. IdnT is a member of the Gnt family of gluconate transporters |CITS:| and is homologous to the E. coli GntT and GntU gluconate transporters. Gluconate uptake has been reported to occur via a proton-symport mechanism in E. coli |CITS:|. It seems likely that IdnT mediates L-idonate/proton and D-gluconate/proton symport. Mutant phenotype in growth assays and expression analysis show IdnT also transports 5-keto-D-gluconate |CITS:|.

MetaCyc_Comment: The periplasmic N-acetylneuraminate mutarotase supports the efficient use of α-N-acetylneuraminate (α-NeuNAc) as the sole source of carbon. Sialoglycoconjugates present in vertebrates are linked exclusively by α-linkages; once released by sialidases, spontaneous mutarotation converts the α anomer to β-NeuNAc, which constitutes more than 90% of NeuNAc at equilibrium. FUNCTION: Proton-dependent efflux pump (PubMed:22426385, PubMed:23221628, PubMed:23701827, PubMed:24684269). Confers resistance to a broad spectrum of chemically unrelated substrates (PubMed:11566977, PubMed:22426385, PubMed:23221628, PubMed:23701827, PubMed:24684269). Overexpression confers resistance to acriflavine, chloramphenicol, norfloxacin, ethidium bromide and tetraphenylphosphonium bromide (TPP) (PubMed:11566977, PubMed:22426385). Can also export a broad range of quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs) and contribute to the intrinsic resistance of E.coli to these antimicrobial compounds (PubMed:23221628). In addition to its role in multidrug resistance, MdtM likely plays a physiological role in alkaline pH homeostasis and in resistance to bile salts (PubMed:23701827, PubMed:24684269, PubMed:28962921). May function in alkaline pH homeostasis when millimolar concentrations of sodium or potassium are present in the growth medium (PubMed:23701827). When overexpressed, can confer a tolerance to alkaline pH values up to 9.75 (PubMed:23701827). Probably acts as a low-affinity antiporter that catalyzes the exchange of internal Na(+) and K(+) cations for extracellular protons to maintain a stable internal pH, acid relative to outside, during exposure to alkaline environments (PubMed:23701827). Can also catalyze Rb(+)/H(+) and Li(+)/H(+) antiport, but not Ca(2+)/H(+) exchange (PubMed:23701827). The exact stoichiometry of antiport is unknown (PubMed:23701827). Finally, it could contribute to bile salt resistance by catalyzing the transport of bile salts out of the cell cytoplasm (PubMed:24684269). Mediates a bile salt/H(+) exchange driven by the electrochemical gradient (PubMed:24684269). Binds to cholate and deoxycholate with micromolar affinity and catalyzes both cholate/H(+) and deoxycholate/H(+) exchange reactions (PubMed:24684269). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11566977, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22426385, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23221628, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23701827, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24684269, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28962921}.

MetaCyc_Comment: The MdtM protein is a multidrug efflux protein that belongs to the major facilitator superfamily (MFS) of transporters |CITS:|. Overexpression of the cloned mdtM gene in a drug-sensitive strain results in a four-fold increase in resistance to acriflavine and a two-fold increase in resistance to chloramphenicol, ethidium bromide and tetraphenylphosphonium bromide (TPP) |CITS:|. Strains lacking mdtM show impaired growth in the presence of ethidium bromide and chloramphenicol compared to wild type. Overexpression of cloned mdtM in both a wild type background and in an mdtM null background results in increased resistance to ethidium bromide and chloramphenicol |CITS: |. MdtM is functional in whole cell ethidium bromide transport assays and efflux is disrupted by the addition of the ionophore, carbonyl cyanide 3-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP) |CITS: |. MdtM is able to export a broad range of quaternary ammonium compounds (QACs) and contributes to the intrinsic resistance of E. coli to these antimicrobial compounds |CITS: |. MdtM catalyses the efflux of unconjugated bile salts and contributes to cholate and deoxycholate resistance in E. coli - this may be the natural physiological role of the transporter. Deletion of mdtM results in increased susceptibility to cholate and deoxycholate compared to wild-type. Purified MdtM binds cholate and deoxycholate with high affinity. MdtM catalyses electrogenic bile salt:H+ exchange in inverted membrane vesicles at pH7.2. MdtM acts in synergy with the AcrAB/TolC multidrug efflux system to provide enhanced efflux of unconjugated bile salts in E. coli |CITS: |. MdtM also catalyses Na+:H+ and K+:H+ exchange and contributes to E. coli's adaptive response to alkaline environments. Strains lacking mdtM show growth inhibition at pH9 and pH9.75 compared to wild type. mdtM expressd from a plasmid confers alkali-tolerance to strains lacking chromosomally encoded mdtM or mdfA. MdtM also catalyses Rb+:H+ and Li+:H+ antiport, but not Ca2+:H+ antiport, in vitro. MdtM catalysed Na+:H+ and K+:H+ exchange at alkaline pH is electrogenic but the exact stoichiometry is unknown |CITS: |. Purified MdtM is monomeric in dodecyl-β-D-maltopyranoside solution and binds chloramphenicol with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 0.17µM |CITS: |. The charged amino acid, aspartic acid 22 (D22), is important for function. Expression of a plasmid encoded D22A mutant protein in cells lacking chromosomally encoded MdtM results in impaired growth in the presence of ethidium bromide and disrupts whole cell ethidium bromide transport assays. A D22A mutation disrupts chloramphenicol efflux, however a purified D22A mutant protein retains the ability to bind chloramphenicol (Kd = 0.69 µM) suggesting that the functional significance of D22 is not related to substrate recognition |CITS: |. MdtM expressed from a plasmid can compensate for the loss of the related multidrug efflux protein, |FRAME: CMR-MONOMER "MdfA"| |CITS: |. Overexpression of mdtM increases the MICs for puromycin and lincomycin |CITS: |. MdtM is predicted to contain 12 transmembrane segments with both the the N-termini and C-termini located in the cytoplasm |CITS: |. MdtM is implicated in the uptake of proline-rich antimicrobial peptides (PrAMPS) in cells lacking the peptide uptake permease, |FRAME: CPLX0-8097 "SbmA"| |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

BtsT (YjiY) is predicted to be an inner membrane protein with sixteen |CITS: | or 18 |CITS: | transmembrane domains; topology analysis suggests both termini are located in the cytoplasm |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Phosphatase that hydrolyzes non-canonical purine nucleotides such as XTP and ITP to their respective diphosphate derivatives. Probably excludes non-canonical purines from DNA/RNA precursor pool, thus preventing their incorporation into DNA/RNA and avoiding chromosomal lesions. Purified, crystallised Slt35 consists of an α helical rich α domain, a β domain and a core domain located between the two which binds peptidoglycan strands and contains the active site. E. coli K-12 contains other lytic murein transglycosylases including |FRAME: G7457-MONOMER "MltA"|, |FRAME: G7533-MONOMER "MltC"|, |FRAME: EG10246-MONOMER "MltD|, |FRAME: EG11373-MONOMER "MltF"|, |FRAME: G6622-MONOMER "EmtA"| and |FRAME: EG10950-MONOMER "Slt70"|. |FRAME: EG11494 "MltG"|, an inner membrane protein and potential PG terminase, also has lytic murein transglycosylase activity. AzoR was originally thought to be an acyl carrier protein phosphodiesterase |CITS: |; however, the overexpressed and purified protein has azoreductase activity, but not acyl carrier protein phosphodiesterase activity |CITS: |. The structure of the active site and the FMN cofactor differs between the oxidized and reduced forms |CITS: |. The Arg59 residue may be involved in determining substrate specificity |CITS: |. An E. coli azoR::kan mutant has impaired growth in the presence of 2-methylhydroquinone (2-MHQ), catechol and menadione and shows decreased levels of glutathione. Externally added glutathione can partially restore impaired growth of the azoR mutant caused by 2-MHQ |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: 2,4-Dienoyl-CoA reductase functions in the reductive removal of double bonds extending from even-numbered carbon atoms in unsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids. The product of the reaction catalyzed by E. coli FadH is 2-trans-enoyl-CoA, in contrast with the bovine enzyme, which produces 3-trans-enoyl-CoA. FadH is able to catalyze the reduction of 2-trans,4-cis and 2-trans,4-trans isomers with almost equal efficiency |CITS: |. This is not due to a cis-trans isomerase activity of the enzyme |CITS: |. Kinetic data first suggested that the reaction proceeds via a ping-pong mechanism |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the enzyme has been solved at 2.2 Å resolution. A possible electron transfer pathway from the electron source, NADPH, via FAD, the 4Fe-4S cluster, and FMN was proposed, and the authors conclude that a ping-pong kinetic mechanism is unlikely |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis was used to identify residues involved in catalysis and to support the proposed reaction mechanism |CITS: |. Expression is induced by growth on oleate and is subject to catabolite repression |CITS: |. Regulation of fadH expression was later shown to be complex and involves three independent regulators, FadR, ArcA, and cAMP-CRP |CITS: | as well as HipB |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: An essential GTPase which binds GTP, GDP and possibly (p)ppGpp with moderate affinity, with high nucleotide exchange rates and a fairly low GTP hydrolysis rate. Plays a role in control of the cell cycle, stress response, ribosome biogenesis and in those bacteria that undergo differentiation, in morphogenesis control. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_01454}.; FUNCTION: Required for chromosome segregation (PubMed:11555285). Plays a role in the stringent response, perhaps by sequestering 50S ribosomal subunits and decreasing protein synthesis (PubMed:19555460). Has a non-essential role in the late steps of ribosome biogenesis, coordinating 50S ribosomal subunit assembly (PubMed:24844575, PubMed:33639093). Has high guanosine nucleotide exchange rate constants for GTP and GDP, and a relatively low GTP hydrolysis rate stimulated by the 50S ribosomal subunit. It is estimated there are 34000 molecules in log-phase cells and 5600 molecules in stationary-phase cells. Overexpression increases bacterial persistence (in exponential and stationary phase) in response to antibiotics (PubMed:26051177). Cells expressing high levels of ObgE are more likely to form persister cells upon antibiotic exposure; this requires alarmone (p)ppGpp and acts via induced HokB, depolarizing cells, which probably reduces metabolic activity and induces persistence (PubMed:26051177). The persister phenotype can be separated from the essential phenotype (PubMed:26051177). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11555285, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11976298, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12402086, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15836769, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16980477, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17578452, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17616600, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19555460, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24844575, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26051177, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33639093}.; FUNCTION: Required for correct chromosome partitioning; in temperature-sensitive (ts) mutant nucleoids do not partition but remain in the middle of cell, cells elongate but do not divide (PubMed:11555285). Overexpression protects cells against UV damage. Ts mutants have impaired plasmid and lamdba phage replication, possibly via effects on DnaA (PubMed:12826057). Regulates DnaA levels (PubMed:16518617). Genetic interactions of Val-168 and a C-terminal insertion mutant with the double-strand break repair factors recA and recBCD, and with seqA suggests that ObgE, either directly or indirectly, promotes replication fork stability (PubMed:15721258). May protect replication forks from stress induced by toxic levels of hydroxyl radicals (PubMed:22863262). Initiation of DNA replication continues in ObgE-depleted cells. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11555285, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12402086, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12826057, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12855728, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15721258, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16518617, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17578452, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22863262}.; FUNCTION: Central member of a network of 50S ribosomal subunit biogenesis factors (ObgE, RluD, RsfS and DarP(YjgA)) which assembles along the 30S-50S interface, preventing incorrect 23S rRNA structures from forming (PubMed:33639093). Acts as a ribosome anti-association factor; guanosine nucleotides stimulate ObgE 50S subunit binding and also ObgE-mediated 70S ribosome dissociation (GDP<GTP<GMP-PNP<ppGpp) (PubMed:24844575). Overexpression rescues an rrmJ deletion, stabilizing the 70S ribosome. Even at permissive temperatures the ts mutant (Gln-80/Asn-85) shows disrupted 50S ribosomal subunit assembly, defects in 16 and 23S rRNA processing and altered association of some late-assembling ribosomal proteins (PubMed:11555285). Dissociates from the pre-50S ribosome under conditions of amino acid starvation. The levels of (p)ppGpp rise in the ts mutant (Gln-80/Asn-85), possibly because ObgE controls SpoT. Binds GDP and ppGpp with the same affinity. During ribosome assembly ObgE acts later than the rRNA methyltransferase RrmJ and DEAD-box RNA helicases DeaD and SrmB (PubMed:16980477). Promotes and stabilizes nearly mature conformations of 23S rRNA in late stage pre-50S ribosomal subunits, which may allow integration of late ribosomal proteins uL16 (rplP) and bL36 (rpmJ) (PubMed:33639093). When the 50S subunit is fully assembled (perhaps signalled by the simultaneous presence of uL16 and bL36), changes take place in ObgE that stimulate GTP hydrolysis by ObgE and ultimately lead to its dissociation from the 50S particle (Probable) (PubMed:33639093). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11555285, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11976298, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15292126, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15836769, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16980477, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17616600, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19555460, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24844575, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33639093, ECO:0000305|PubMed:33639093}.

MetaCyc_Comment: ObgE is an essential member of the Obg family of small GTP-binding proteins |CITS: |. A variety of essential cellular processes, including chromosome segregation and ribosome assembly, are affected by ObgE. Purified ObgE has moderate affinity and high guanine nucleotide exchange rate constants for both GTP and GDP and a relatively low GTP hydrolysis rate |CITS: |. The physiologically relevant ligand may be ppGpp. During amino acid starvation, ObgE is important for cell survival and appears to alter the ratio of pppGpp to ppGpp |CITS: |. ObgE also copurifies and interacts with SpoT |CITS: |. ObgE was predicted to be cation-dependent |CITS: |, but it was later shown that ObgE is not activated by K+ |CITS: |. ObgE interacts with the 50S ribosomal subunit and thereby prevents assembly and stimulates disassembly of the intact ribosome; this activity is enhanced in the presence of ppGpp, likely reflecting regulation of ribosome assembly by ppGpp during the stringent response |CITS: |. ObgE is involved in late steps of the assembly of the 50S ribosomal subunit. In cell lysates, the ObgE protein is associated with the 50S ribosomal subunit |CITS: |, but not during amino acid starvation |CITS: |. The GTPase activity of ObgE is stimulated by the 70S ribosome |CITS: |. Cryo-EM reconstructions of 50S ribosomal subunit precursors revealed a network of interacting ribosomal biogenesis factors that consists of ObgE, RluD, RsfS, and YjgA. ObgE coordinates the maturation of the functional core of the 50S subunit |CITS: |. ObgE is involved in 16S and 23S rRNA processing |CITS: |; in the presence of GTP, purified ObgE cosediments with both 16S and 23S rRNA |CITS: |. Purified ObgE also cofractionates with the 30S ribosomal subunit |CITS: | and a number of ribosomal subunit proteins |CITS: |. Earlier experimental results that showed no association of ObgE with the ribosome |CITS: | are thought to be due to instability of the association under the conditions used |CITS: |. A cryo-EM structure of ObgE bound to the 50S ribosomal subunit shows that the N-terminal domain of ObgE resides in the peptidyl transfer center and is a structural mimic of the acceptor arm of A-site tRNA |CITS: |. A crystal structure of ObgE in the GDP-bound state shows the presence of an intrinsically disordered C-terminal domain; this domain contributes specifically to GTP binding |CITS: |. Analysis of the dominant negative ObgE* allele, which contains a K268I mutation located in the G domain of the protein, showed that GTP binding to the G domain appears to lead to a conformational change that is transmitted to the N-terminal domain, conferring toxicity |CITS: |. ObgE may play a role in cell survival after replication fork arrest. A mutant containing a hypomorphic obgE allele (obgE::Tn5) shows increased sensitivity to replication inhibitors such as hydroxyurea (HU) and guanazole, and concomitant loss of recA or recB substantially enhances this phenotype. The obgE::Tn5 allele is synthetically lethal with seqA, suggesting that ObgE plays a role in the regulation of replication or in organization of the replication fork |CITS: |. Cells with depleted ObgE show perturbed SeqA foci |CITS: |. Levels of the replication-initiator DnaA depend directly on the abundance of ObgE |CITS: |, indicating that ObgE acts by regulating DnaA |CITS: |. ObgE mutants that specifically increase sensitivity to HU have been generated and analyzed; HU sensitivity appears to be due to increased levels of cytotoxic hydroxyl radicals |CITS: |. ObgE appers to be involved in cell cycle progression and chromosome partitioning |CITS: |. A heat sensitive mutant exhibits a defect in chromosomal partitioning and elongated cell morphology, but has no defect in DNA replication |CITS: |. Overproduction causes a defect in chromosomal partitioning and leads to oversized cell morphology, but does not cause gross defects in DNA replication, RNA transcription, or protein synthesis |CITS: |. Depletion of ObgE delays chromosome segregation, but is not lethal; growth resumes after expression of ObgE is restored |CITS: |. Purified ObgE associates with DNA and shows some membrane association |CITS: |, but it does not appear to be associated with the nucleoid in vivo |CITS: |. Expression of the dominant negative K268I allele of ObgE (ObgE*) results in cell death in a manner that resembles programmed cell death |CITS: |, but does not involve reactive oxygen species |CITS: |. ObgE* causes irreversible inhibition of the cell cycle after the chromosome segregation step; membrane blebs form at cell division sites, followed by lysis |CITS: |. ObgE controls persister cell formation. ObgE concentration correlates with the probability of transition to the persistent state in individual cells. ObgE's effect on persistence requires ppGpp and is mediated by increased expression of the |FRAME: MONOMER0-1604 HokB| toxin, leading to a decrease in the membrane potential |CITS: |. Most obgE mutant alleles that specifically lost their function in persister cell formation show reduced binding to GDP or ppGpp |CITS: |. Overexpression of ObgE induces protein aggregation in stationary phase and accelerates the development of persister cells |CITS: |. ObgE is an abundant protein |CITS: |, and the growth rate correlates with the cellular level of ObgE |CITS: |. Levels of ObgE protein increase five-fold after exposure to UV irradiation, and moderate overexpression of ObgE leads to increased resistance to UV radiation |CITS: |. obgE is transcribed as the last gene in an operon along with rplU, rpmA, and yhbE. This operon is mainly expressed during exponential growth; reports disagree on whether regulation by ppGpp/DksA is indirect |CITS: | or direct |CITS: |. Furthermore, the amounts of ObgE and YhbE are affected by the presence of a transcription terminator between rpmA and yhbE |CITS: |. Temperature-sensitive obgE mutants were found to have a lower basal level of the RecA repair protein compared with wild-type; recA expression was not stimulated by UV irradiation in these mutants. Taken together, these results strongly suggest that ObgE plays a role in the DNA repair process, most likely through stimulation of the RecA-dependent DNA repair pathway |CITS: |. Overproduction of ObgE suppresses the growth and ribosome assembly defects of a mutant lacking |FRAME: EG11507-MONOMER| |CITS: |. Depletion of ObgE does not appear to affect translation |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine hydrolase (LpxH) catalyzes the fourth step in lipid A synthesis, hydrolyzing UDP-2,3-bis(3-hydroxymyristoyl)glucosamine to yield 2,3-bis(3-hydroxymyristoyl)-β-D-glucosaminyl 1-phosphate (lipid X) |CITS: |. LpxH is a peripheral membrane protein whose activity appears to be stimulated by Mn2+ in vitro. LpxH catalyzes the attack of water on the α-P atom of the UDP moiety to form lipid X and UMP |CITS: |. Although LpxH and |FRAME: CDPDIGLYPYPHOSPHA-MONOMER| (Cdh) are both able to catalyze the hydrolysis of UDP-2,3-diacylglucosamine in vitro, Cdh can not substitute for LpxH in vivo |CITS: |. The Cdh substrate CDP-diacylglycerol is not a substrate for LpxH |CITS: |. A crystal structure of a solubilized, catalytically active mutant of LpxH has been solved at 2 Å resolution. The capping helices covering the active site of the enzyme appear to be flexible in the absence of the substrate/product |CITS: |. In a simulation of the lipid A biosynthesis pathway, it was necessary to include feedback inhibition of LpxH to obtain a steady-state outcome that agreed with the observed lipid A production rate |CITS: |. LpxH is essential for growth |CITS: |. Several lpxH point mutants were isolated in a screen for mutants that provide resistance to the potential antibacterial compound sulfonyl piperazine. The mutations map to the residues G48, L84, F141, and R149 |CITS: |. LpxH: |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: D-arabinose-5-phosphate is a precursor for KDO (2-keto-3-deoxy-octulosonate), a constituent of the cell envelope lipopolysaccharide. Arabinose-5-phosphate isomerase is responsible for the interconversion of D-ribulose-5-phosphate and D-arabinose-5-phosphate, the first committed step in the biosynthesis of KDO. The enzyme was originally isolated and partially characterized from E. coli strain B |CITS: |. KdsD is a tetramer in solution. The reaction kinetics, specificity, and optimal conditions have been characterized, and the physical characteristics of the active site are discussed |CITS: |. Substrate specificity was investigated by saturation transfer difference NMR spectroscopy |CITS: |. The structure of the sugar isomerase domain of KdsD was predicted using homology modeling; site-directed mutagenesis of the conserved Lys59 and His193 residues showed that they were important for catalysis or substrate recognition |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the sugar isomerase domain of a catalytic mutant has been solved at 2.6 Å resolution, and the highly conserved H88 residue was shown to be involved in catalysis |CITS: |. An isozyme, |FRAME: EG10973-MONOMER GutQ|, is present in E. coli; therefore, deletion of kdsD does not lead to a defect in LPS synthesis |CITS: |. A gutQ kdsD double mutant is not viable |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: NanQ catalyzes the conversion of N-acetylneuraminate (Neu5Ac) from its cyclic forms to its linear (aldehydo) form. It preferentially acts on the β anomer, which is also the most prevalent form of Neu5Ac in solution. Addition of NanQ increases the activity of |FRAME: ACNEULY-MONOMER| in vitro, suggesting that linear Neu5Ac is not a tightly bound intermediate in the NanQ catalytic cycle |CITS: |. Purified NanQ was found to contain Zn2+. Zn2+ and other divalent cations themselves increase the rate of formation of the linear form of Neu5Ac, albeit at non-physiological concentrations. The Zn2+ contained in NanQ could therefore play a catalytic role |CITS: |. Growth of a nanQ mutant on Neu5Ac as the sole source of carbon at pH 6 and 20°C is delayed compared to wild-type; in a competition assay, the mutant is 6-fold less abundant than wild-type after six cycles of exponential growth |CITS: |. nanQ is not required for growth on N-acetylmannosamine |CITS: |, Neu5Ac or N-glycolylneuraminate |CITS: | under standard growth conditions. FUNCTION: Protein and nucleotide deglycase that catalyzes the deglycation of the Maillard adducts formed between amino groups of proteins or nucleotides and reactive carbonyl groups of glyoxals (PubMed:26774339, PubMed:28596309). Thus, functions as a protein deglycase that repairs methylglyoxal- and glyoxal-glycated proteins, and releases repaired proteins and lactate or glycolate, respectively. Deglycates cysteine, arginine and lysine residues in proteins, and thus reactivates these proteins by reversing glycation by glyoxals. Is able to repair glycated serum albumin, collagen, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and fructose biphosphate aldolase. Acts on early glycation intermediates (hemithioacetals and aminocarbinols), preventing the formation of advanced glycation endproducts (AGE) that cause irreversible damage (PubMed:26774339). Also functions as a nucleotide deglycase able to repair glycated guanine in the free nucleotide pool (GTP, GDP, GMP, dGTP) and in DNA and RNA. Is thus involved in a major nucleotide repair system named guanine glycation repair (GG repair), dedicated to reversing methylglyoxal and glyoxal damage via nucleotide sanitization and direct nucleic acid repair (PubMed:28596309). In vitro, prevents acrylamide formation in asparagine/glyoxal and asparagine/sugar mixtures at 55 degrees Celsius, likely by degrading asparagine/glyoxal Maillard adducts formed at high temperatures (PubMed:27530919). Also displays an apparent glyoxalase activity that in fact reflects its deglycase activity (PubMed:26678554, PubMed:26774339). Is a general stress protein; is required for the protection of bacterial cells against many environmental stresses, including oxidative, thermal, osmotic, UV, and pH stresses (PubMed:17933887). And plays an important role in protection against electrophile/carbonyl stress (PubMed:26774339). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17933887, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26678554, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26774339, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27530919, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28596309}.

MetaCyc_Comment: YhbO has been identified as a protein deglycase that repairs glyoxal- and methylglyoxal-glycated proteins |CITS: | as well as a nucleotide deglycase that repairs glycated GTP as well as DNA and RNA |CITS: |. YhbO is able to reduce the formation of acrylamide in mixtures of glyoxal/methylglyoxal and asparagine, likely by degrading Maillard adducts |CITS: |. YhbO belongs to the diverse DJ-1/PfpI protein family |CITS: |. It is homologous to a general stress protein from Bacillus subtilis |CITS: | and shares predicted functional site residues with an intracellular protease from Pyrococcus furiosus |CITS: |. However, the purified protein does not have any detectable protease activity using classical biochemical substrates |CITS: |. YhbO does not affect the degradation of damaged proteins and peptides in cells under oxidative stress |CITS: |. Glyoxalase III activity with both glyoxal and methylglyoxal has been measured |CITS: |. The glyoxalase activity may in fact reflect the protein deglycase activity of the enzyme |CITS: |. The purified protein exists as a monomer, trimer and hexamer in solution |CITS: |. The native protein may be a homohexamer |CITS: |. The C104 residue is required for its function in the oxidative stress response |CITS: |. Abundance of YhbO is increased under osmotic stress imposed by NaCl only under aerobic conditions |CITS: |. Expression of yhbO is increased in stationary phase |CITS: |. yhbO belongs to the σS regulon |CITS: |, and it may be part of the Rcs regulon |CITS: |. A yhbO null mutant is sensitive to oxidative, temperature, UV, and pH stresses |CITS: |. A yhbO null mutant contains increased levels of glycated proteins |CITS: | and nucleotides |CITS: | and shows somewhat decreased viability in methylglyoxal- or glucose-containing media, whereas a triple hchA yhbO yajL mutant shows significantly decreased viability |CITS: |. A yhbO mutant as well as an hchA yhbO yajL triple mutant accumulates glycated DNA and RNA and shows increased mutation frequency, with increased levels of GC→AT and AT→GC transitions |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Threonylcarbamoyl-AMP synthase (TsaC) catalyzes the synthesis of threonylcarbamoyl-AMP, an intermediate in the biosynthesis of the threonylcarbamoyladenosine (t6A) modification at position 37 of ANN-decoding tRNAs |CITS: |. Although TsaC (RimN) was initially thought to function as a ribosome maturation factor |CITS: |, new evidence suggested that TsaC is a component of a heteromultimeric complex with threonylcarbamoyltransferase activity |CITS: |. A mixture of purified |FRAME: EG11171-MONOMER TsaD|, |FRAME: G6991-MONOMER TsaB|, TsaC, and |FRAME: EG11757-MONOMER TsaE| proteins catalyzes formation of t6A in the presence of a tRNA substrate, ATP, threonine and bicarbonate in vitro |CITS: |. A crystal structure of TsaC has been determined at 2.0 Å resolution |CITS: |. An NMR solution structure has provided insight into the catalytic mechanism of the enzyme. TsaC is monomeric under NMR conditions; key residues that interact with the substrates L-threonine and ATP were identified |CITS: |. It is known that t6A biosynthesis requires ATP |CITS: |. TsaC was shown to bind ATP and ADP, and the potential nucleotide-binding residues Arg52 and Lys56 are required for function. tsaC complements the t6A- phenotype of a S. cerevisiae SUA5 mutant strain |CITS: |. TsaC binds nucleic acids, with a preference for double-stranded RNA |CITS: |. Specifically, it interacts with both fully and partially modified (lacking t6A37) tRNAThr with high affinity |CITS: |. It was also shown to bind the unmodified anticodon stem-loop of tRNALys(UUU) with higher affinity than the t6A37-modified form |CITS: |. tsaC is an essential gene |CITS: |. A probable null mutant allele of tsaC (ΔtsaC or rimN141) was identified as a suppressor of the temperature-sensitive growth phenotype of the |FRAME: EG10761-MONOMER| mutant allele prfA1 |CITS: |. However, it is not possible to separate the ΔtsaC mutation from the prfA1 allele |CITS: |. RimN: "ribosome maturation" |CITS: |TsaC: "threonylcarbamoyl-6(six)-adenosine" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Mediates coordination of peptidoglycan synthesis and outer membrane constriction during cell division. Promotes physical and functional coordination of the PBP1B-LpoB and Tol machines, and regulates PBP1B activity in response to Tol energy state. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:25951518}.
MetaCyc_Comment: CpoB is a periplasmic protein that mediates physical and functional coordination between the peptidoglycan (PG) synthase |FRAME: CPLX0-3951 "PBP1B-LpoB"| and the energy transducing Tol system; this coordination is required to properly synchronize PG synthesis and outer membrane (OM) constriction during cell division. CpoB, PBP1B-LpoB and the Tol proteins are recruited to the septum at the later stages of cell division and form a higher order complex that spatially links PG synthesis and OM invagination |CITS: |. CpoB interacts with TolA in vivo and in vitro |CITS: |. CpoB forms stable trimers in solution |CITS: |; TolA binding disrupts trimeric CpoB to form CpoB-TolA heterodimers |CITS: | CpoB localizes to sites of envelope constriction in pre-divisional cellls; CpoB interacts with PBP1B in vivo; CpoB forms a ternery complex with TolA and PBP1B; CpoB forms a ternary compex with LpoB and PBP1B. CpoB is present at a copy number of 4550 ± 540 molecules per cell in growing cells. CpoB binding inhibits the transpeptidase activity of the PBP1B-LpoB complex but does not affect the transglycosylase activity - this selective control may be important during cell division |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Genetic interactions implicate CpoB in PBP1B function; ΔcpoB strains show increased sensitivity to β-lactams and have minor OM defects; these phentoypes are exacerbated by the absence of LpoA and are also present in a ΔcpoB ΔmrcA ΔlpoA triple mutant |CITS: |. CpoB contains an N-terminal coiled-coil domain and a C-terminal tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain which contains three consecutive repeats |CITS: |. The N-terminal domain consists of 6 chains arranged to form 2 three-stranded parallel coiled-coil bundles |CITS: | cpoB is the last gene in a three gene operon (tolB-pal-cpoB) |CITS: |. Targeting of CpoB to the Sec-translocase for transport across the inner membrane is SecB-dependent |CITS: |. CpoB: "coordinator of PG synthesis and OM constriction, associated with PBP1B" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat), is an adaptive immune system that provides protection against mobile genetic elements (viruses, transposable elements and conjugative plasmids) (PubMed:21255106, PubMed:24793649, PubMed:24920831). CRISPR clusters contain sequences complementary to antecedent mobile elements and target invading nucleic acids. CRISPR clusters are transcribed and processed into CRISPR RNA (crRNA). The Cas1-Cas2 complex is involved in CRISPR adaptation, the first stage of CRISPR immunity, being required for the addition/removal of CRISPR spacers at the leader end of the CRISPR locus (PubMed:24793649, PubMed:24920831, PubMed:25707795). The Cas1-Cas2 complex introduces staggered nicks into both strands of the CRISPR array near the leader repeat and joins the 5'-ends of the repeat strands with the 3'-ends of the new spacer sequence (PubMed:24920831). Spacer DNA integration requires supercoiled target DNA and 3'-OH ends on the inserted (spacer) DNA and probably initiates with a nucleophilic attack of the C 3'-OH end of the protospacer on the minus strand of the first repeat sequence (PubMed:25707795). Expression of Cas1-Cas2 in a strain lacking both genes permits spacer acquisition (PubMed:24793649, PubMed:24920831). Cas2 not seen to bind DNA alone; the Cas1-Cas2 complex preferentially binds CRISPR-locus DNA (PubMed:24793649). Highest binding is seen to a dual forked DNA complex with 3'-overhangs and a protospacer-adjacent motif-complement specifically positioned (PubMed:26478180). The protospacer DNA lies across a flat surface extending from 1 Cas1 dimer, across the Cas2 dimer and contacting the other Cas1 dimer; the 23 bp-long ds section of the DNA is bracketed by 1 Tyr-22 from each of the Cas1 dimers (PubMed:26478180, PubMed:26503043). Cas1 cuts within the 3'-overhang, to generate a 33-nucleotide DNA that is probably incorporated into the CRISPR leader by a cut-and-paste mechanism (PubMed:26478180). This subunit's probable nuclease activity is not required for spacer acquisition (PubMed:24793649). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:21255106, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24793649, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24920831, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26478180}.

FUNCTION: Peptidoglycan polymerase that catalyzes glycan chain elongation from lipid-linked precursors (PubMed:18165305, PubMed:6368264, PubMed:8772200). May play a role in peptidoglycan assembly during cell division in collaboration with other cell division proteins (PubMed:18165305). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:18165305, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6368264, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8772200}.

MetaCyc_Comment: MtgA is a monofunctional murein glycosyltransferase involved in polymerization of lipid II molecules into glycan strands of peptidoglycan. GFP-MtgA fusions localize to the division site in mrcA(ts) mrcB mutants |CITS:|. Bacterial two-hybrid experiments reveal MtgA interacts with PBP3, FtsW, and FtsN |CITS:|. Assays for peptidoglycan synthesis activity revealed that MtgA has glycosyltransferase activity and polymerizes glycan strands with lipid II as substrate at an optimum pH of 6.0 to 6.5 |CITS:,,|. This differs from the optimum of 7.5 to 8.0 for PBP1B, which is the major bifunctional glycosyltransferase for peptidoglycan synthesis in E. coli |CITS:,|. The glycan strands were then shown to act as substrate for lysozyme |CITS:,,|. Inhibition assays show that Flavomycin does not inhibit this activity as it does with the high-molecular-weight penicillin-binding proteins that have glycosyltransferase activity |CITS:|. Induction of this gene from an expression vector in wild-type W3110 caused cells to immediately stop growing, but not to lyse |CITS:|. mtgA mutants and mtgA pbpC double mutants have elevated levels of tetrapenta muropeptides |CITS:|. Ofloxacin downregulates mtgA expression |CITS:|.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Essential for aminobenzoyl-glutamate utilization. It catalyzes the concentration-dependent uptake of p-aminobenzoyl-glutamate (PABA-GLU) into the cell and allows accumulation of PABA-GLU to a concentration enabling AbgAB to catalyze cleavage into p-aminobenzoate and glutamate. It also seems to increase the sensitivity to low levels of aminobenzoyl-glutamate. May actually serve physiologically as a transporter for some other molecule, perhaps a dipeptide, and that it transports p-aminobenzoyl-glutamate as a secondary activity. The physiological role of abgABT should be clarified. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17307853, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20190044}.
