MetaCyc_Comment: Subject to experimental manipulation, AbgT mediates the transport of p-aminobenzoyl-glutamate - a folate catabolite; the physiological role of the protein has not been confirmed - it may participate in a folate salvage or recycling pathway or it may function to transport an as-yet undefined molecule. Overexpression of abgT supports the growth of p-aminobenzoate auxotrophs on exogenous p-aminobenzoyl glutamate |CITS: |. Overexpression of abgT from a high-copy-number plasmid mediates significant uptake of labelled p-aminobenzoyl-glutamate (KT = 123 µM) in a wild-type background; labelled p-aminobenzoyl-glutamate accumulates in the cell - it does not appear to be metabolized (although overexpression of abgAB, encoding |FRAME: CPLX0-7844 "p-aminobenzoyl glutamate hydrolase"|, may promote its cleavage to p-aminobenzoate and glutamate) |CITS: |. Uptake of p-aminobenzoyl glutamate is inhibited by sodium azide, potassium fluoride and the protonophore uncoupler, carbonyl cyanide 3-chlorophenylhydrazone |CITS: |, suggesting a dependence on the H+ gradient. Overexpression of abgT results in increased sensitivity to the anti-folate compounds, methotrexate and aminopterin |CITS: |. abgT is located in a probable operon with abgA, abgB and ogt; abgT may be cryptic in wild-type E. coli K-12 |CITS: | AbgT has twelve predicted transmembrane regions and is the prototype member of the p-Aminobenzoyl-glutamate Transporter (AbgT) Family within the IT superfamily |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). abg: "p-aminobenzoyl-glutamate utilization" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Amino acid transporter with broad substrate specificity (PubMed:17784858, PubMed:27281193). Can transport various amino acids, including phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan, L-threonine, L-methionine, L-lysine, L-glutamate, L-valine and L-isoleucine (PubMed:17784858, PubMed:27281193). Overexpression confers resistance to phenylalanine and increases export of phenylalanine, tyrosine and tryptophan (PubMed:17784858). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17784858, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27281193}.

MetaCyc_Comment: YddG is an amino acid exporter with broad specificity. YddG is a member of the Aromatic Amino Acid/Paraquat Exporter (ArAA/P-E) Family (TC: 2.A.7.17) within the Drug/Metabolite Transporter (DMT) superfamily |CITS: |. YddG is predicted to be an inner membrane protein with nine or ten transmembrane domains; experimental topology analysis supports a model of 10 transmembrane helices with the N and C-termini located in the cytoplasm |CITS: | Expression of yddG from a multicopy plasmid results in increased resistance to phenylalanine, and to the aromatic amino acid analogues DL-p-fluorophenylalanine, DL-o-fluorophenylalanine, and 5-fluorotryptophane |CITS:|. Overexpression of yddG in E. coli strains engineered to produce aromatic amino acids is associated with accumulation of the respective amino acid (phenylalanine, tyrosine or tryptophan) in the culture medium; overexpression of yddG enhances phenylalanine efflux in the Phe-producing strain |CITS:|. Overexpression of yddG enhances L-tryptophan production in a Trp-producing strain |CITS: |. Purified YddG reconstituted into liposomes transports L-threonine, L-methionine, L-lysine and L-glutamic acid; overexpression of yddG (in both E. coli W3110 wild type and ΔyddG backgrounds) is associated with a consistent increase of valine, threonine and isolecine in the culture medium suggesting that YddG transports a range of amino acids |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Bifunctional protein that catalyzes the synthesis of cyclic-di-GMP (c-di-GMP) in response to reductive stress and then dynamically relocates to the division site to arrest cell division in response to envelope stress. In the presence of high intracellular c-di-GMP levels, and in response to envelope stress, interacts with cell division proteins and halts cell division, without disassembling the Z ring, but by blocking its further progress toward cytokinesis (PubMed:27507823). Part of a network that regulates cell motility by altering levels of c-di-GMP (PubMed:20303158). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:20303158, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27507823}.

MetaCyc_Comment: DgcN is a diguanylate cyclase that dynamically relocates to the division site in response to envelope stress. DgcN localizes to the Z ring in an FtsZ- and ZipA-dependent manner in the presence of high levels of c-di-GMP. |FRAME: G7354-MONOMER YfiR| counteracts relocation of DgcN to the Z ring |CITS: |. DgcN is an inner membrane protein with two predicted transmembrane domains. The C terminus is located in the cytoplasm |CITS: |. DgcN contains an N-terminal CHASE (cyclases/histidine kinases associated sensory) domain |CITS: |. Deletion of dgcN partially restores motility of a pdeH mutant, suggesting that DgcN is one of four diguanylate cyclases that adjust c-di-GMP concentration for motility control |CITS: |. Deletion of dgcN also suppresses the swarming defect of a yfiR deletion mutant |CITS: |. A dgcN deletion mutant shows 18-fold increased early biofilm formation and 10-fold increased swimming motility. Deletion of dgcN does not alter the concentration of c-di-GMP inside the cell |CITS: |. Overexpression of dgcN increases resistance to polymyxin B |CITS: |. In uropathogenic E. coli UTI89, YfiN encodes a diguanylate cyclase that contributes to a cellulose production pathway. YfiN is inhibited by the periplasmic protein YfiR |CITS: |. yfiR, yfiN and yfiB may form an operon in E. coli K-12. In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, this operon is involved in exopolysaccharide synthesis |CITS: |; in uropathogenic E. coli, YfiR and YfiN were shown to have a role in cellulose production, but no evidence implicating YfiB in this process was obtained |CITS: |. E. coli K-12 does not produce cellulose due to a mutation in the bcs operon (see |FRAME: EG12261|). DgcN: "diguanylate cyclase N" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the conversion of 3'-phosphate to a 2',3'-cyclic phosphodiester at the end of RNA. The mechanism of action of the enzyme occurs in 3 steps: (A) adenylation of the enzyme by ATP; (B) transfer of adenylate to an RNA-N3'P to produce RNA-N3'PP5'A; (C) and attack of the adjacent 2'-hydroxyl on the 3'-phosphorus in the diester linkage to produce the cyclic end product. Likely functions in some aspects of cellular RNA processing. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:9738023}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Essential cell division protein that coordinates cell division and chromosome segregation. The N-terminus is involved in assembly of the cell-division machinery. The C-terminus functions as a DNA motor that moves dsDNA in an ATP-dependent manner towards the dif recombination site, which is located within the replication terminus region. Translocation stops specifically at Xer-dif sites, where FtsK interacts with the Xer recombinase, allowing activation of chromosome unlinking by recombination. FtsK orienting polar sequences (KOPS) guide the direction of DNA translocation. FtsK can remove proteins from DNA as it translocates, but translocation stops specifically at XerCD-dif site, thereby preventing removal of XerC and XerD from dif. Stoppage of translocation is accompanied by a reduction in ATPase activity. Also stimulates topoisomerase 4 activity. Required for the targeting of FtsQ, FtsL and FtsI to the septum. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11703663, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11832210, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15522074, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16553881, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18363794, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19246541, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19854947, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20081205, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21371996, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9723913, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9829960}.

FUNCTION: Catalyzes the hydrolysis of 4-amino-2-methyl-5-hydroxymethylpyrimidine pyrophosphate (HMP-PP) to 4-amino-2-methyl-5-hydroxymethylpyrimidine phosphate (HMP-P). Can also hydrolyze other substrates such as MeO-HMP-PP and 4-amino-2-trifluoromethyl 5-hydroxymethylpyrimidine pyrophosphate (CF3-HMP-PP) to give MeO-HMP-P and 4-amino-2-trifluoromethyl-5-hydroxymethylpyrimidine phosphate. This hydrolysis generates resistance to the antibiotics (bacimethrin, CF3-HMP) by reducing the formation of their toxic forms, 2'-methoxythiamin pyrophosphate (MeO-TPP) and CF3-HMP-PP. Also hydrolyzes pyridoxal-phosphate (PLP) and flavin mononucleotide (FMN), and purines (GMP and IMP) as secondary substrates. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_01847, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15292217, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16990279}.

The enzyme is involved in the hydrolysis of HMP-PP, an intermediate in thiamin biosynthesis |CITS: |. In a screen using a variety of compounds, its preferred substrate is pyridoxal phosphate; purine and pyrimidine nucleotides are secondary substrates |CITS: |. Overexpression of Cof from a multicopy plasmid leads to resistance to the HMP (4-amino-2-methyl-5-hydroxymethylpyrimidine) analog bacimethrin (MeO-HMP) |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Global regulator of carbohydrate metabolism (PubMed:10464268, PubMed:11361067, PubMed:11934616, PubMed:9484892, PubMed:9484893, PubMed:9781886). Represses the expression of several genes involved in sugar transport and utilization, in particular phosphoenolpyruvate-carbohydrate phosphotransferase system (PTS) genes (PubMed:10464268, PubMed:9484892, PubMed:9484893, PubMed:9781886). Represses expression of ptsG (EIICB(Glc)), which encodes the PTS system glucose-specific EIICB component (PubMed:9781886). Also represses the expression of the manXYZ operon, encoding the mannose-specific PTS system, expression of malT, encoding the transcriptional activator of the maltose regulon, and expression of the pts operon, composed of the genes ptsH, ptsI and crr (PubMed:10464268, PubMed:9484892, PubMed:9484893). Represses its own expression (PubMed:9484893). Acts by binding to the regulatory region of the target genes (PubMed:10464268, PubMed:9484893, PubMed:9781886). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10464268, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11361067, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11934616, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9484892, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9484893, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9781886}.

FUNCTION: Catalyzes the transfer of the amino group from gamma-aminobutyrate (GABA) to alpha-ketoglutarate (KG) to yield succinic semialdehyde (SSA). PuuE is important for utilization of putrescine as the sole nitrogen or carbon source. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15590624, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20639325}.

MetaCyc_Comment: The 4-aminobutyrate aminotransferase PuuE is the initial enzyme of one of two 4-aminobutyrate (GABA) degradation pathways. PuuE was identified as a putrescine-inducible GABA aminotransferase, which allows cells to grow on putrescine as the sole source of nitrogen even in the absence of GabT |CITS: |. PuuE also functions as a 5-aminovalerate aminotransferase during degradation of L-lysine |CITS: |. The function of genes in the puu gene cluster was initially inferred by similarity with the ipuABCDEGFH operon in Pseudomonas sp. |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis confirmed that the K267 residue is essential for catalytic activity |CITS: |. PuuE activity is induced by growth on putrescine and repressed by addition of succinate and under conditions of limited oxygen availability |CITS: |. The three major transaminases in alanine biosynthesis are AvtA, AlaA and AlaC. Expression of aspC, gabT, puuE, tyrB, or ygjG from a plasmid partially suppresses the growth defect of a ΔavtA alaA alaC mutant |CITS: |. The redundancy and promiscuity among aminotransferase enzymes was further investigated. Four enzymes, ArgD, AstC, GabT, and PuuE, show some level of N-acetylornithine aminotransferase activity involved in arginine biosynthesis. An argD astC gabT triple mutant does not grow on medium lacking arginine. Accumulation of suppressor mutations eventually allows growth of the triple mutant; an additional deletion of puuE eliminates this effect |CITS: |. In the hands of |CITS: |, the triple deletion mutant ΔargDΔastCΔgabT shows an extensive lag phase on glucose minimal medium; a quadruple deletion mutant that includes puuE does not grow. The normal activities of two enzymes, ArgD and SerC, are sufficient for succinyldiaminopimelate (SDAP) and lysine biosynthesis; a third enzyme, AstC, is sufficient for SDAP biosynthesis, but alone can not fulfill the cell's requirement for lysine. Additional enzymes, including GabT and PuuE, may be able to contribute to SDAP biosynthesis. Overexpression of puuE from a plasmid allows growth of the triple ΔargD serC astC mutant on minimal medium |CITS: |. A puuE deletion mutant accumulates GABA |CITS: |. A ΔpuuE ΔgabT double deletion mutant grows more slowly than wild type with putrescine as the sole source of nitrogen, because only one of its two nitrogens can be utilized |CITS: |. GoaG: "GABA or ornithine aminotransferase" |CITS: | PuuE: "putrescine utilization" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in base excision repair of DNA damaged by oxidation or by mutagenic agents. Acts as a DNA glycosylase that recognizes and removes damaged bases. Has a preference for oxidized pyrimidines, such as thymine glycol, 5,6-dihydrouracil and 5,6-dihydrothymine. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the epimerization of L-Ala-D-Glu to L-Ala-L-Glu and has a role in the recycling of the murein peptide, of which L-Ala-D-Glu is a component. MetaCyc_Comment: YcjG is an L-Ala-D/L-Glu epimerase that may play a role in the metabolism of murein peptide. The substrate specificity of the enzyme is not strict. YcjG belongs to the MLE subfamily of the enolase family of enzymes |CITS: |. The crystal structure of YcjG has been solved at 2.6 Å resolution. Although YcjG behaves like a monomer in solution, the crystal structure shows extensive surface contacts between two monomers |CITS: |. A D297G mutant can catalyze both the wild-type reaction as well as the o-succinylbenzoate synthase reaction; thus this substitution relaxes the substrate specificity of the enzyme. O-succinylbenzoate synthase activity of the mutant is sufficient to partially rescue the growth defect of the o-succinylbenzoate synthase-deficient menC mutant under anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. The additional substitution I19F enhances the kinetic constants of the o-succinylbenzoate synthase reaction and growth of the menC mutant strain |CITS: |. YcjG is able to catalyze fluoride elimination in a dipeptide that contains difluorinated alanine at the C terminus, resulting in a 3-fluorodehydroalanine-containing peptide |CITS: |. An electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) showed that PgrR is capable of interacting with the ycjG promoter region; in addition, in a pgrR mutant strain the expression of ycjG was increased |CITS:|. ycjG expression was increased during growth under nitrogen starvation conditions |CITS:|. A mutant that is missing all eight genes involved in polyamine biosynthesis, ΔspeABCDEF cadA ldcC, grows aerobically at a reduced rate. MetaCyc_Comment: TruB is a pseudouridine synthase that catalyzes the pseudouridylation of U55 in tRNA |CITS: |. The base modification generated by TruB activity contributes to the wild-type thermal stability of tRNA |CITS: |. In addition to its catalytic activity, TruB also acts as a tRNA chaperone |CITS: |; early mutagenesis results had already suggested such a role |CITS: |. tRNAs carry multiple modifications, often in nearby nucleotide residues. The preferred substrate for the TruB methyltransferase and tRNA binding activities is unmodified tRNA |CITS: |. Crystal structures of TruB have been solved |CITS: |. TruB recognizes the folded T-loop structure of tRNAs |CITS: | and undergoes significant conformational changes upon tRNA binding |CITS: |. Recognition of the tRNA substrate requires the 53:61 base pair of the T-loop stem as well as several conserved nucleotides within the loop |CITS: |. TruB binds both folded and misfolded tRNAs |CITS: |. The substrate specificity of TruB has been described |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis of the conserved amino acid residue D48 |CITS: | and Y76 |CITS: | yields catalytically inactive enzymes. Oxidation of the D48C mutant (generating the sulfinic acid) restores significant activity |CITS: |. In addition to the catalytic D48 residue, R181 and D90 form an electrostatic network that fine-tunes the D48-R181 interaction |CITS: |. Mutagenesis of nearly invariant lysine and proline residues in Motif I does not have severe effects on catalytic activity, but decreases thermal stability |CITS: |. The reaction does not appear to use a catalytic cysteine |CITS: |. The U55 substrate base is "flipped out" into the enzyme during catalysis |CITS: |. Unlike RluA, TruB activity is not inhibited by RNA containing 5-fluorouridine |CITS: |. The reaction proceeds through formation of a glycal intermediate by deprotonation of C2' |CITS: |. Pre-steady-state kinetic analysis showed that tRNA binding is a fast two-step process; catalysis is the rate-limiting step |CITS: |. A truB deletion mutant lacks the Ψ55 modification in tRNAs |CITS: | and exhibits a competitive disadvantage in a mixed culture. The growth phenotypes of the truB deletion mutant can be complemented by production of the catalytically inactive D48C mutant protein |CITS: |, but not by the K64E mutant protein that lacks tRNA binding activity |CITS: |. Conversely, the mutant's sensitivity to heat shock can only be complemented by the wild type gene. A trmA truB double mutant exhibits more severe sensitivity to heat shock than the single truB mutant |CITS: |. Lack of tRNA Ψ55 modification does not affect the frequency of -1 frameshift errors during translation |CITS: |. TruB: "tRNA pseudo U formation" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Undecaprenyl pyrophosphate (UPP) synthase (IspU) catalyzes the condensation reactions resulting in the formation of UPP, a di-trans,poly-cis-undecaprenyl pyrophosphate that functions as the lipid carrier for bacterial cell wall carbohydrates. To generate UPP, eight isopentenyl diphosphate molecules are sequentially added to farnesyl diphosphate with cis stereochemistry |CITS: |. Under various reaction conditions, the enzyme can produce C50 intermediates as well as larger C60-C75 products in addition to UPP. Triton X-100 activates the reaction by accelerating a step after the rate-limiting IPP condensation reactions |CITS: |. Site-directed mutagenesis of conserved residues identified amino acids that are required for catalysis and/or play a role in binding of IPP |CITS: |, and play a role in product chain length determination |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics simulations indicate that IspU is a highly flexible protein |CITS: |. A conformational change of the enzyme during catalysis is thought to occur |CITS: |. The length of a flexible loop region appears to regulate the conformational change |CITS: |. Single-turnover experiments support a concerted condensation-elimination mechanism for the enzyme |CITS: |. Substrate specificity has been studied, and the shape of both the active site and the product are predicted to determine the chain length of the product |CITS: |. An enzyme containing the W31R mutation has severely decreased enzymatic activity |CITS: |. Crystal structures of IspU have been solved, revealing a possible reaction mechanism |CITS: |. UPP synthase appears to be a dimer in solution and in the crystal structure |CITS: |. ispU is essential in E. coli |CITS: |. Mutants with temperature-sensitive alleles of ispU are sensitive to low osmolarity of the growth medium and have a cell shape defect when grown at the restrictive temperature |CITS: |. Replacing wild type ispU with the uppS31 missense allele is lethal; suppressor mutations in ispH and idi enable growth at low temperature |CITS: |. UPP production and peptidoglycan synthesis are synergistic; lowering both at the same time leads to cell lysis |CITS: |. Inhibitors of the enzyme have been investigated as novel antimicrobial agents |CITS: |. ispU gene expression is repressed by MetJ, which appears to bind a site upstream of this gene |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), which is a major component of the outer leaflet of the outer membranes of Gram-negative bacteria, consists of lipid A linked to a short core oligosaccharide (lipid A-core) plus a distal O-antigen polysaccharide chain (which is absent in E. coli K-12). MsbA, a member of the ATP Binding Cassette (ABC) Superfamily of transporters, is essential for the translocation of lipid A-core from the inner leaflet to the outer leaflet of the inner membrane. MsbA is an inner membrane protein; it consists of an N-terminal membrane spanning domain and a C-terminal nucleotide binding domain |CITS: |. MsbA binds ATP |CITS: |. MsbA is a homodimer; the MsbA monomer consists of an integral membrane domain containing 6 transmembrane alpha-helices and a cytoplasmic nucleotide binding domain |CITS: |. Structures of MsbA (from K-12 or serotype O157:H7) in the inward facing, nucleotide free state with and without LPS bound |CITS: |, of ADP-bound MsbA and of vanadate trapped MsbA |CITS: | have been reported. MsbA may conform to an alternating access model of transport; conformational changes during the transport cycle have been widely investigated (see |CITS: |. Proteoliposomes prepared from purifed MsbA and phospholipids have an intrinsic ATPase activity which is further stimulated by the addition of hexa-acylated Kdo2-lipid A or hexa-acylated lipid A (but not by Lipid A precursors) |CITS: |. LPS transport to the outer membrane in spheroplasts is dependent on the presence of MsbA |CITS: |. MsbA does not function as a phospholipid flippase |CITS: |. Purified, solubilised MsbA is homodimeric and its ATPase activity is stimulated by lipid A; the ATPase activity of MsbA reconstituted in proteoliposomes is inhibited by the phosphate analog, vanadate |CITS: |. Purified MsbA, reconstituted in proteoliposomes, functions as an ATP dependent lipid flippase |CITS: |. MsbA does not transport underacylated lipid A (tetra-acylated and penta-acylated Lipid A) as efficiently as hexa-acylated Lipid A |CITS: |. Overexpression of msbA suppresses the lethality of |FRAME: EG10464 lpxL| null mutants by increasing the translocation of LPS or its precursor, N-acetyl glucosamine, to the outer membrane; depletion of MsbA results in increased retention of labelled N-acetyl glucosamine in the inner membrane |CITS: |. Overexpression of msbA relieves accumulation of tetra-acylated lipid A and glycerophospholipids in the inner membrane to allow growth of lpxL null mutants |CITS: |. Depletion of MsbA results in the the accumulation of hexa-acylated lipid A species and glycerophospholipids within the inner membrane |CITS: |. The transport of lipids (both lipopolysaccharide and phospholipid) to the outer membrane is blocked in an MsbA(A270T) temperature sensitive mutant grown at the non-permissive temperature |CITS: |. Single amino acid substitutions in MsbA or overexpression of msbA suppresses an otherwise lethal |FRAME: KDO Kdo| deletion phenotype |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Cardiolipin impacts transport of LPS across the inner membrane; overexpression of msbA suppresses the lethality of a Δ|FRAME: EG11608 clsA| Δ|FRAME: EG10614 lpxM| double mutant |CITS: |. MsbA has sequence similarity with the human multidrug resistance protein, Mdr1 |CITS: |. Purified MsbA, reconstituted in proteoliposomes, mediates the transport of the DNA dye, Hoechst 33342; MsbA ATPase activity is stimulated by Hoechst 33342 and by the cytotoxic drugs, vinblastine and daunomycin |CITS: |. MsbA expressed in the gram positive organism, Lactococcus lactis, is active as a polyspecific drug efflux system; MsbA catalyses ATP dependent transport of Hoechst 33342 in L. lactis inside-out membrane vesicles; free lipid A binds to MsbA at a different site to Hoechst 33342 |CITS: |. MsbA may use a dual mode of energy coupling; ethidium transport by MsbA is dependent on ATP hydrolysis and the proton electrochemical gradient |CITS: |. The energetics of lipid transport may be substrate dependent; significant MsbA-mediated transport of biotin-labeled phospholipid (biotin-PE) in proteoliposomes requires the simultaneous presence of ATP and a transmembrane chemical H+ gradient (ΔpH) while transport of biotin-labeled Lipid A is observed with ATP only |CITS: |. MsbA is a potential target for the development of new antibiotics |CITS: |. MsbA structures reported by |CITS: | have been retracted |CITS: |. msbA: multicopy suppressor of htrB |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: EF4 (LepA) is a highly conserved protein whose function in translation is still controversial. The most recent results indicate that LepA functions in 30S ribosomal subunit biogenesis |CITS: |. Various experimental results that suggested functions in translation initiation or elongation are summarized below. EF4 competes with EF-G for binding to the ribosome and forms a complex that is an intermediate between the PRE and POST complexes, thus sequestering a catalytically active ribosome |CITS: |. EF4 induces back-translocation of the ribosome and prevents peptide bond formation exclusively in the post-translocation (POST) state of the ribosome. A kinetic model of back-translocation has been proposed |CITS: |. Cryo-EM structures of the ribosome in pre- and post-EF4 states suggest that EF4 enables back-translocation by disengaging the CCA end of tRNA from the peptidyl transferase center of the ribosome |CITS: |. A mechanism for EF4-induced back-translocation was proposed |CITS: |. The back-translocation activity of EF4 could not be reproduced by |CITS: |. EF4 increases the rate of protein synthesis under certain stress conditions |CITS: |. It was recently shown that even in unstressed cells, loss of EF4 reduces the average ribosome density of many coding regions |CITS: |. EF4 is detrimental during severe stress conditions; this effect requires functional |FRAME: SSRA-RNA| and |FRAME: CPLX0-3101| |CITS: |. EF4 has uncoupled ribosome-dependent GTPase activity, and GTP hydrolysis appears to be required for dissociation of EF4 from the ribosome. Addition of EF4 to a coupled in vitro transcription-translation system increases the total protein yield and improves the activity of the produced proteins. A model was proposed in which EF4 recognizes defective translocation states of the ribosome and induces back-translocation, which allows EF-G a second chance to catalyze the formation of a correct POST state |CITS: |. While EF4 does not increase the fidelity of protein synthesis in vivo or in vitro |CITS: |, it does increase the rate of protein synthesis at high salt concentrations or low temperature |CITS: |. The H81 residue is required for GTPase activity |CITS: |. The macrocyclic thiopeptide antibiotic thiostrepton inhibits binding of EF4 to the ribosome as well as ribosome-dependent GTP hydrolysis |CITS: |. EF4 is an extremely highly conserved protein in all domains of life. It also shows high conservation with EF-G, although a domain similar to domain IV of EF-G is absent, and an additional C-terminal domain is present |CITS: |. EF4/EF-G chimeric proteins do not complement EF-G function in vivo |CITS: |. A crystal structure of EF4 has been solved at 2.8 Å resolution. Structural similarity between EF4 and EF-G enabled modelling of EF4 bound to the ribosome, which places the unique C-terminal domain of EF4 in the vicinity of the A site of the 50S subunit |CITS: |. Single-particle cryo-EM was used to visualize EF4 in the process of back-translocation, where it is seen to interact directly with the back-translocated tRNA |CITS: |. A crystal structure of EF4 bound to Thermus thermophilus 70S ribosome has been solved, showing that the C-terminal domain of EF4 interacts with the acceptor stem of the peptidyl-tRNA in the P site |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain is important for ribosome-stimulated GTPase activity of EF4 |CITS: |. Association and dissociation rate and equilibrium binding constants for GDP and GTP have been measured, showing that EF4 has a 5-fold higher affinity for GDP than for GTP |CITS: |. Association of EF4 with the ribosome does not absolutely require the L7/L12 subunit |CITS: |. EF4 was found to bind (p)ppGpp |CITS: |. Expression analysis has shown that the lepA gene is a member of the lep operon along with the downstream gene, lepB, which encodes signal peptidase I |CITS: |. In subcellular fractionation studies, EF4 was detected in the inner membrane fraction |CITS: |. However, under conditions of salt stress, low temperature or low pH, the majority of EF4 protein is released to the cytoplasm |CITS: |. lepA deletion mutants are viable and show no obvious defect in growth or protein export |CITS: | and do not have a significant ribosome assembly defect |CITS: |. However, overproduction of EF4 is lethal on solid agar, and cells become filamentous in liquid cultures after induction |CITS: |. A lepA deletion mutant was found to be hypersensitive to potassium tellurite, but not to other oxidizing agents |CITS: |. Recently, it was shown that a lepA null mutant is outcompeted by wild type in growth competition experiments in minimal media at low temperature, high salt concentrations or low pH |CITS: |, and that it has a growth defect at pH 4 |CITS: |. A ΔlepA mutant has synthetic growth phenotypes with ΔdksA, ΔmolR1, ΔrsgA, ΔtatB, ΔtonB, ΔtolR, ΔubiF, ΔubiG, and ΔubiH |CITS: |. A ΔlepA mutation protects against lethal antimicrobials under aerobic growth conditions; lepA and mazF are epistatic |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: AqpZ is a water channel, or aquaporin, that allows bi-directional passive diffusion of water across the inner membrane. It is a member of the Major Intrinsic Protein (MIP) family, a large and diverse family of transmembrane channels that transport a range of substrates by energy independent mechanisms |CITS: |. AqpZ mediates the rapid entry or exit of water in response to changes in extracellular osmolarity |CITS: |. AqpZ structure has been analysed by electron microscopy |CITS: |, atomic force microscopy |CITS: | and x-ray crystallography |CITS: |. AqpZ contains 6 transmembrane helices and two half membrane helices with the N and C-termini located in the cytoplasm. AqpZ forms homotetramers of 4 monomer channels. The monomer channel adopts an 'hour-glass' structure with periplasmic and cytoplasmic conical shaped vestibules connected by a narrow central amphipathic pore which constitutes a water conduction pathway. A selectivity filter, formed by the side chains of Phe43, His174, Arg189 and Thr183 is located at the narrowest point in the channel. Two distinct conformations of the channel have been obtained, differentiated by the side chain displacement of Arg189. The conformations may represent open and closed forms of the channel or they could be dynamic conformations occurring during water permeation (see also |CITS: |). Purified AqpZ, reconstituted into proteoliposomes, displays high osmotic water permeability |CITS:|. Expression of aqpZ in Xenopus oocytes, produces a marked increase in osmotic water permeability |CITS: |. Expression of aqpZ from a plasmid increases osmotic water permeability |CITS: |. An aqpZ::lacZ-kan knockout mutant is viable but forms small colonies in rich and minimal media and has reduced viability in hypotonic media |CITS:|. No phenotypic effect could be detected in an aqpZ::cam knockout strain under a range of conditions |CITS:|. Cardiolipin stabilises and modulates the function of AqpZ |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). aqpZ mRNA is monocistronic. Expression of aqpZ-lacZ from a low copy plasmid peaks during mid logarithmic growth and is dependent upon the extracellular osmolality |CITS:|. Expression of a chromosomal aqpZ-lacZ fusion is independent of osmolality and increases in a σS-dependent manner as cell growth enters the stationary phase |CITS:|. AqpZ has been used in the development of biomimetic aquaporin membranes |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS:|

FUNCTION: Antitoxin component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system which inhibits the post-segregational killing (PSK) of plasmid-free cells, also referred to as a plasmid addiction system. FUNCTION: Toxic component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system, functioning in plasmid maintainence. Responsible for the post-segregational killing (PSK) of plasmid-free cells, also referred to as a plasmid addiction system. Half-life of over 2 hours. Cell killing by CcdB is accompanied by filamentation, defects in chromosome and plasmid segregation, defects in cell division, formation of anucleate cells, decreased DNA synthesis and plasmid loss. Interferes with the activity of DNA gyrase, inducing it to form a covalent GyrA-DNA complex that cannot be resolved, thus promoting breakage of plasmid and chromosomal DNA. DNA breakage requires hydrolyzable ATP. Toxicity is inhibited by labile antitoxin CcdA, which blocks the activity of CcdB; CcdA also removes bound CcdB protein from the CcdB-GyrA complex by forming a CcdA-CcdB complex, a process termed rejuvenation. Also acts to inhibit partitioning of the chromosomal DNA. Functions as a transcriptional corepressor for the ccdAB operon, repression also requires CcdA. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:1324324, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2615761, ECO:0000269|PubMed:2651399, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6308648, ECO:0000269|PubMed:6327993, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8604132}.

IspG activity depends on additional proteins, most likely involved in the oxidation portion of the reaction |CITS: |. IspG contains a cluster that is required for its activity |CITS: |. Mutations in cysteine residues responsible for Fe-S cluster coordination abolish IspG's enzymatic activity |CITS: |. In vitro, |FRAME: CPLX0-7617 ErpA| can transfer a cluster to apo-IspG |CITS: |. Increased IspG activity was observed under new assay conditions |CITS: |. Flux through the entire MEP pathway was shown to depend on the presence of |FRAME: FLAVODOXIN1-MONOMER|, which may supply reducing equivalents necessary to reduce the Fe-S cluster and yield an active enzyme |CITS: |. A new reaction mechanism was recently proposed |CITS: |. Further studies on the reaction mechanism and reaction intermediate have been published |CITS: |, and potential reaction mechanisms are reviewed in |CITS: |. An ispG mutant does not activate human γδ T lymphocytes due to its defect in production of (E)-4-hydroxy-3-methyl-but-2-enyl pyrophosphate (HMB-PP). This intermediate in the MEP pathway accumulates in an ispH mutant |CITS: |. ispG is essential |CITS: |. Missense mutants which are defective in the MEP pathway |CITS: |, as well as a conditional amber mutant |CITS: | have been isolated. Since the enzymes of the MEP pathway are not found in humans, they have attracted interest for their potential as anti-infective drug targets. A MEP pathway inhibitor has been identified and found to bind IspG |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Sedoheptulose 7-phosphate isomerase catalyzes the first committed step in the biosynthesis of a core component of lipopolysaccharide, the isomerization of D-sedoheptulose 7-phosphate to D-glycero-D-manno-heptose 7-phosphate. Crystal structures of GmhA alone and in complex with the substrate D-sedoheptulose 7-phosphate have been solved. The protein appears to be a tetramer in both the crystal structures and in solution. A reaction mechanism utilizing an enediol intermediate has been proposed |CITS: |. Potential active site residues were mutagenized and their enzymatic activity was measured both in vivo and in vitro |CITS: |. Mutations in gmhA confer novobiocin hypersensitivity |CITS: | and F plasmid conjugation deficiency |CITS: |; gmhA mutants were shown to contain lipopolysaccharides lacking heptose |CITS: |. An IS1 insertion in the Shine-Dalgarno sequence of gmhA was isolated as a suppressor of a ΔlapB mutant |CITS: |. The LPS biosynthesis pathway |CITS: | including GmhA |CITS: | have been explored as a target for development of new antibacterial compounds. Under selection for reduced susceptibility to tigecycline, mutations in gmhA appear |CITS: |. These mutants show increased sensitivity to bile salts |CITS: |. A ΔgmhA mutant shows increased sensitivity to certain cationic antimicrobial peptides |CITS: |. Overexpression of gmhA increases furfural tolerance |CITS: |. LpcA = "LPS-core synthesis" |CITS: | GmhA = "glycero-manno-heptose synthesis" |CITS: | Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: gmhB encodes the D,D-heptose 1,7-bisphosphate phosphatase of the ADP-heptose biosynthesis pathway. GmhB belongs to the superfamily of haloacid dehalogenase (HAD)-like hydrolases. A gmhB deletion strain has a partial defect in LPS core synthesis, but is not completely heptoseless |CITS: |. GmhB has a narrow substrate range, with activity that is specific for ketohexose and ketoheptose bisphosphates, and shows high catalytic efficiency towards its physiological substrate |CITS: |. Crystal structures of apo-GmhB and several liganded forms have been solved, guiding construction of site-directed mutants that provide insight into substrate recognition elements in the catalytic site and suggest a reaction intermediate |CITS: |. It has been proposed that the gmhB gene and the HOL-P phosphatase moiety of hisB evolved via a paralogous duplication event of an ancestral DDDD phosphatase-encoding gene |CITS: |. GmhB is required for toxicity of colicins A and N |CITS: |. Loss of function mutations in gmhB have been identified in E. coli isolates derived from human infections; the mutations lead to increased degradation of OmpF by the periplasmic protease DegP and thereby increased resistance to cefalexin |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in glutaminase-dependent acid resistance (PubMed:30498489, PubMed:8682809). Exchanges extracellular glutamate (Glu) for intracellular gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) under acidic conditions (PubMed:22407317, PubMed:23589309). The protonation states of substrates are crucial for transport. Selectively transports Glu with no net charge and GABA with a positive charge (PubMed:23589309). Also efficiently transports glutamine and, to a smaller extent, methionine and leucine (PubMed:22407317). When the extracellular pH drops below 2.5, can import L-glutamine and export either glutamate or GABA (PubMed:30498489). The ability to survive the extremely acidic conditions of the stomach is essential for successful colonization of the host by commensal and pathogenic bacteria (PubMed:30498489, PubMed:8682809). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:22407317, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23589309, ECO:0000269|PubMed:30498489, ECO:0000269|PubMed:8682809, ECO:0000305|PubMed:30498489, ECO:0000305|PubMed:8682809}.
Catalytic activity: CATALYTIC ACTIVITY: Reaction=4-aminobutanoate(in) + L-glutamate(out) = 4-aminobutanoate(out) + L-glutamate(in); Xref=Rhea:RHEA:28919, ChEBI:CHEBI:29985, ChEBI:CHEBI:59888; Evidence={ECO:0000269|PubMed:22407317, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23589309};
MetaCyc_Comment: GadC, a glutamic acid:γ-aminobutyrate antiporter, is part of the glutamate-dependent acid resistance system 2 (AR2) which confers resistance to extreme acid conditions. When cells are grown at pH 2.5 with glutamate, the internal pH reaches 4.2 which reflects the pH optimum of the glutamate decarboxylases |CITS:|. Insertional inactivation of gadC results in sensitivity to extreme acid conditions (pH 2-3) and eliminates glutamic acid enhancement of acid resistance |CITS:|. GadC mediates export of γ-aminobutyrate in exchange for glutamic acid. GadC is a member of the APC superfamily of amino acid transporters. AR2 also protects the cell during anaerobic phosphate starvation when glutamate is available by preventing damage from weak acids produced from carbohydrate fermentation. gadABC mutants have reduced viability after anaerobic phosphate starvation compared to wild-type |CITS:|. YhiE, GadC, Slp-YhiF, HdeA, and HdeD are involved in the resistance to low pH observed upon overexpression of ydeO |CITS: |. GadC is implicated in maintaining antibiotic tolerance under starvation; gadC is upregulated during nutrient starvation and the starvation-induced ampicillin tolerance levels of a gadC knockout strain are significantly reduced over both a 6 and 30 day period |CITS: |. Regulation has been described |CITS:|. Expression of gadA and gadBC is induced by GadE and GadXW |CITS:|.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of a stress-induced multi-chaperone system, it is involved in the recovery of the cell from heat-induced damage, in cooperation with DnaK, DnaJ and GrpE. Acts before DnaK, in the processing of protein aggregates. Protein binding stimulates the ATPase activity; ATP hydrolysis unfolds the denatured protein aggregates, which probably helps expose new hydrophobic binding sites on the surface of ClpB-bound aggregates, contributing to the solubilization and refolding of denatured protein aggregates by DnaK. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10982797, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12624113, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14640692}.

MetaCyc_Comment: AmiC is an N-acetylmuramyl-L-alanine amidase, which cleaves the peptide moiety from N-acetylmuramic acid, removing murein crosslinks. AmiC is active toward the murein located at the septum and is therefore important for cell separation upon cell division |CITS: |. |FRAME: NACMURLALAAMI1-MONOMER "AmiA"|, |FRAME: NACMURLALAAMI2-MONOMER "AmiB"| and AmiC appear to have overlapping functions |CITS: |. Murein amidase activity produces stemless or |FRAME: a-denuded-peptidoglycan denuded glycans|. AmiC is translocated from the cytoplasm to the periplasm by the twin-arginine transport (Tat) system |CITS: |. During cell division, AmiC specifically localizes to the septal ring; localization is mediated by an N-terminal targeting domain and is dependent on FtsN. In small cells that have not begun dividing, AmiC is located throughout the periplasm |CITS: |. AmiC contains an N-terminal peptidoglycan binding domain and a C-terminal, zinc dependent, catalytic domain. The two domains are linked by a flexible segment |CITS: |. An AmiC mutant which lacks helix α5 in the catalytic domain is constitutively active; an inhibited form of the enzyme is restored by addition of a synthetic peptide mimic |CITS: |. AmiC interacts directly with its cognate activator, |FRAME: EG12111-MONOMER "NlpD"| |CITS: |. AmiC activity is elevated in acidic medium; pH does not directly modulate AmiC activity |CITS: |. |FRAME: G7484-MONOMER ActS| activates AmiC in vitro; ActS interacts with AmiC and may function to activate AmiC under envelope stress conditions |CITS: |. An amiC deletion mutant grows in chains of three to six cells and this phenotype is exacerbated in a ΔamiA,amiB,amiC triple mutant |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: ZntB is a zinc ion transporter; initial investigations conducted concurrently in E. coli and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium implicated ZntB (formerly YdaN) in zinc efflux while later work characterized it as a Zn2+:proton symporter likely mediating zinc ion uptake. An E. coli strain (GR480) which lacks the 5 known Zn2+ transporters ZntA, ZitB, ZupT, ZnuABC and FieF, but retains ZntB (YdaN), exhibits a greater Zn2+ efflux rate than a strain (RS1220) which lacks all 6 transporters suggesting that ZntB is able to facilitate Zn2+ efflux; expression of the cloned homologous gene from Salmonella enterica increases the rate of Zn2+ efflux in E.coli strain RS1220 |CITS: |. Deletion of zntB in Salmonella enterica increases sensitivity to Zn2+ |CITS: |. ZntB consists of a large N-terminal cytoplasmic domain and two transmembrane helices joined by a periplasmic loop; ZntB forms a symmetrical pentamer with a central transmembrane pore |CITS: |. Purified ZntB binds (in order of decreasing affinity) Zn2+, Cd2+, Ni2+ and Co2+ in a 1:1 stoichiometry; purified ZntA reconstituted in liposomes also transports the aforementioned cations; ZntB mediated transport of Zn2+ is driven by the pH gradient; ZntB mediates Zn2+:proton symport in vitro and likely functions as a Zn2+ importer in vivo |CITS: |. YdaN is predicted to be an inner membrane protein with two transmembrane domains; experimental topology analysis suggests the C terminus is located in the cytoplasm |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Represses PhoP/PhoQ signaling, possibly by binding to the periplasmic domain of PhoQ, altering its activity and that of downstream effector PhoP. PhoP-regulated transcription is redox-sensitive, being activated when the periplasm becomes more reducing (deletion of dsbA/dsbB, treatment with dithiothreitol). MgrB acts between DsbA/DsbB and PhoP/PhoQ in this pathway; the 2 periplasmic Cys residues of MgrB are required for its action on PhoQ, and thus PhoP. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:20041203, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22267510}.

FUNCTION: Toxic component of a type IV toxin-antitoxin (TA) system (PubMed:14594833, PubMed:21166897, PubMed:22515815, PubMed:28257056, PubMed:28931012). Acts as a dual toxin inhibitor that blocks cell division and cell elongation in genetically separable interactions with FtsZ and MreB (PubMed:28931012). Interacts with cytoskeletal proteins FtsZ and MreB; inhibits FtsZ GTP-dependent polymerization and GTPase activity as well as MreB ATP-dependent polymerization (PubMed:21166897, PubMed:28931012). Binds to both the N- and C-terminus of FtsZ, likely blocking its polymerization and localization, leading to blockage of cell division (PubMed:21166897, PubMed:28931012). Overexpression results in inhibition of growth in liquid cultures and decrease in colony formation; these effects are overcome by concomitant expression of antitoxin CbeA (YeeU) (PubMed:14594833). In other experiments cells swell, by 6 hours are lemon-shaped and by 24 hours those that have not lysed are spherical with diminished polar regions (PubMed:21166897, PubMed:28931012). Toxic effects are neutralized by cognate antitoxin CbeA, although there is no direct interaction between the 2 proteins (PubMed:14594833, PubMed:22515815). Toxic effects are also neutralized by overexpression of noncogate antitoxins YafW and YpjF (PubMed:28257056). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:14594833, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21166897, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22515815, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28257056, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28931012}.

FUNCTION: Influences nickel and cobalt homeostasis. May act by modulating RcnA-mediated export of these ions to avoid excess efflux. Not involved in nickel import and does not bind nickel or cobalt ions directly. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:21665978}.
FUNCTION: Represses the expression of YqjH which is involved in iron homeostasis under excess nickel conditions. Also represses its own expression. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:21097627}.

FUNCTION: Toxic component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system. Has RNase activity in vitro. Overexpression leads to growth arrest after 30 minutes; these effects are overcome by concomitant expression of antitoxin SohA (PrlF). Massive overexpression is toxic. Unlike most other characterized TA systems degrades rRNA, and co-folding of the both TA proteins is necessary in vitro for inhibition of the RNase activity. It is not known if it has any sequence-specificity. Acts as a transcription factor. The YhaV/PrlF complex binds the prlF-yhaV operon, probably negatively regulating its expression. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17706670}.

FUNCTION: Plays an important role in maintaining outer membrane integrity (PubMed:33315009, PubMed:33847565). Supports proper folding and function of BamA under envelope stress conditions (PubMed:33847565). Binds specifically to anionic phospholipids via the BON 2 domain (PubMed:33315009). This interaction is essential for function and guides the protein to the cell division site (PubMed:33315009). It was reported that DolP is a potential upstream regulator of the amidase activator NlpD (PubMed:28708841). However, later studies suggest that DolP affects cell division and may impact daughter cell separation, but likely not as a regulator of NlpD (PubMed:35604759). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:28708841, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33315009, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33847565, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35604759}.

May act by modulating MlaF structure and stability (PubMed:27529189). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19383799, ECO:0000269|PubMed:27529189}.

MetaCyc_Comment: The rfaD gene encodes ADP-L-glycero-D-mannoheptose-6-epimerase, the last enzyme in the pathway for synthesis of the ADP-heptose precursor of core LPS |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: MalK is the ATP-binding component of the maltose ABC transporter |CITS:|. Opening and closing of the MalK dimer which is associated with ATP binding and hydrolysis is thought to be a key event in the transport cycle. Crystal structures are available for MalK with bound ATP |CITS: |; MalK without nucleotide (in both an open and semi-open conformation) |CITS: | and MalK with bound ADP |CITS: |. In computer simulations, the introduction of MgATP into the active site of MalK is associated with transition from semi-open to closed conformation and from open to semi-open conformation |CITS: |. Computer simulations also suggest that the closed form of MalK is stable when it contains two bound ATP molecules and that a single ATP hydrolysis will induce opening of the dimer |CITS: |. ATP binds along the dimer interface between the nucleotide binding domains (NBDs), positioned between the Walker A motif of one subunit and the signature LSGGQ motif of the other subunit |CITS: |; ATP binding tightly tethers the NBDs of the MalK dimer; the γ phosphate of ATP interacts with the Walker A motif, the Q loop, the switch region histidine of one NBD and the LSGGQ motif of the other NBD |CITS: |. ATP hydrolysis is catalysed by a mechanism in which Glu159 acts as the general base to accept a proton from the attacking water; it is not clear whether one or two ATPs are hydrolyzed during a single transport cycle |CITS: | (and see comment by |CITS: |) Conformational changes in MalK, associated with ATP binding and hydrolysis, modulate its interation with MalF and MalG in vitro |CITS: |. Closure of the MalK dimer interface coincides with opening of MBP and maltose release to the transporter |CITS: |. ATP binding to MalK is associated with conformational change in MalG and MalF periplasmic loops |CITS: |. The N-terminal portion of MalK is the ATP-binding portion which interacts with MalF and MalG, and the C-terminal portion is a regulatory domain that interacts with the transcriptional activator, |FRAME: PD00237 "MalT"| |CITS:,,,|. Over expression of malK prevents induction of the mal regulon by interfering with the activity of MalT |CITS: |. MalK interacts with MalT in vivo and in vitro; the ability to down regulate MalT activity is associated with an inactive, ATP-bound form of MalK |CITS: |. MalK inhibits transcription activation by MalT in vitro and this effect is relieved by maltotriose; MalK and maltotriose compete for MalT binding |CITS: |. Inhibition involves sequestration of MalT by the resting form of the MalFGK transporter, not by free MalK |CITS: |. MalK is also the site of interaction with |FRAME: CRR-MONOMER "EIIAGlc"|; under inducer exclusion MalK binds to the dephosphorylated form of EIIAGlc; the EIIAGlc binding site is separate to the site of ATP binding |CITS: |. Two molecules of EIIAGlc interact with the MalK subunits and stabilise an inward facing conformation of the transporter. This interaction would prevent the structural rearrangements required for ATP hydrolysis and maltose transport. A hydrogen bond is formed between MalK(E122) and EIIAGlc(H90); phosphorylation of H90 is predicted to disrupt the interface |CITS: |. In a reconstituted system EIIAGlc interacts with MalK during all steps of the transport cycle; EIIAGlc binding inhibits transport by preventing closure of the MalK dimer |CITS: |. Commenst: |CITS: |

Because inosine is recognized as guanine by the translation machinery, editing of hokB mRNA changes a tyrosine (TAC) codon into a cysteine (TGC) codon at position 29. FUNCTION: F(1)F(0) ATP synthase produces ATP from ADP in the presence of a proton or sodium gradient. F-type ATPases consist of two structural domains, F(1) containing the extramembraneous catalytic core and F(0) containing the membrane proton channel, linked together by a central stalk and a peripheral stalk. During catalysis, ATP synthesis in the catalytic domain of F(1) is coupled via a rotary mechanism of the central stalk subunits to proton translocation.; FUNCTION: Key component of the F(0) channel; it plays a direct role in translocation across the membrane. A homomeric c-ring of 10 subunits forms the central stalk rotor element with the F(1) delta and epsilon subunits.
MetaCyc_Comment: The c subunit of the Fo complex of ATP synthase is absolutely required for proton translocation and is also necessary for binding of the F1 complex. The number of subunit c monomers determines the number of transported ions per revolution. The stoichiometry of the subunits has been obtained within the range of 9 to 18 |CITS: |; the preferred number of c subunits is 10 |CITS: |. Quantitation, cross-linking and reconstitution experiments with wild-type and mutant F0 show that the stoichiometry of subunit-c is independent of its rate of synthesis |CITS: |. This is the subunit affected by the inhibitor dicyclohexylcarbodiimide. Mutational and cross-linking studies indicate that transmembrane helices (TMH) 4 and 5 of subunit a pack in close proximity to TMH2 of subunit c. Additional studies suggest that pH-dependent conformational change may be related to the proposed role of TMH5 of subunit-a in gating H(+) access from the periplasm to TMH2 of subunit-c |CITS: |. The initiating methionine is cleaved |CITS: |. Chemical modification studies suggest that the ion exit channel lies between the interface of subunit-c and subunit-a. Other models suggest that ions exit through an aqueous channel in subunit-c or a second half channel in subunit-a |CITS: |. It has been suggested that the structural divergence of the c-subunit ring and the a-subunits between bacterial species may allow development of species specific drugs which target these subunits |CITS:|. Insertion of Fo-c into proteliposomes depends on the glycolipid known as |FRAME: CPD-15878| and is stimulated by |FRAME: YIDC "YidC"| |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: The FieF protein is a member of the cation diffusion facilitator (CDF) family of metal cation transporters |CITS:, |. FieF functions as a divalent metal cation transporter which exports Zn2+, Cd2+, and possibly Fe2+ but probably not Hg2+, Co2+, Ni2+, Mn2+, Ca2+ or Mg2+. Metal binding properties of the purified protein identifying zinc and cadmium as substrates have been described |CITS:,,|. FieF forms dimers in detergent-lipid micelles and in reconstituted membranes |CITS:|. The structure of FieF in complex with zinc has been determined by X-ray crystallography to a resolution of 3.8 Å. The FieF homodimer forms a 'Y'-shaped molecule in perpendicular orientation to the plane of the membrane. The transmembrane domains (TMD) of each monomer form a six helix compact bundle; the C-terminal domains (CTD) protrude into the cytoplasm and their association provides the stem of the 'Y'. Two cavities are identifed in the structure - an extracellular cavity exposed to the membrane outer leaflet and an intracellular cavity confined between the TMD and CTD at the inner face of the membrane |CITS:|. The CTD adopts a metallochaperone-like fold and may regulate metal transport activity |CITS: |. Leucine residue 152 constitutes the principle hydrophobic barrier between the two cavities; a putative transmembrane zinc pathway runs from the intracellular cavity through L152 within the inter-cavity seal to the transport site in the extracellular cavity; protein conformational change alternates the on-off mode of zinc binding and protonation-deprotonation of the transport site in a coordinated manner |CITS: | E.coli cells overexpressing fieF exhibited reduced isotopic Fe accumulation, and Zn(II) efflux was shown to be catalyzed through a proton antiport mechanism in membrane eversion studies. Transmembrane flux of iron cations was measured using fluorescence quenching in conjunction with purified and reconstituted FieF. The results suggest that FieF is an iron and zinc efflux system which functions in detoxification |CITS:|. The fieF gene probably constitutes a monocistronic operon. Transcription of fieF has been shown to correlate with iron concentration independent of the ferrous iron uptake regulator Fur. Double fieF and fur led to growth deficiency in complex growth medium, which was partially alleviated by in trans expression of fieF |CITS:|. Experiments with transcriptional fusions showed fieF is strongly induced by zinc and to a lesser extent by cadmium |CITS:|. FieF: ferrous iron efflux

MetaCyc_Comment: Adenylate kinase is an essential enzyme required for the biosynthesis of purine ribonucleotides |CITS: | and has a key role in controlling the rate of cell growth |CITS: |. Adenylate kinase is a relatively small, monomeric protein that consists of three functionally relevant domains: the N-terminal nucleotide binding (NMPbind) domain that binds AMP, followed by the CORE domain that represents the bulk of the enzyme and encloses the LID domain that binds ATP. There are estimated to be approximately 10,000 molecules of adenylate kinase present in the cell |CITS: |. Adenylate kinase activity may be inhibited by interaction with the phosphorylated form of |FRAME: PTSH-MONOMER HPr| |CITS: | and the ribosome |CITS: |. Various crystal |CITS: | and solution |CITS: | structures of the enzyme have been solved, and a reaction mechanism was proposed and refined. Based on new data showing activation of adenylate kinase by direct binding of Mg2+, a new kinetic model for the forward reaction involving a Mg2+-activated random bi-bi mechanism has been proposed. The requirement for binding of Mg2+ before binding of AMP to the enzyme explains the apparent competitive inhibition by AMP |CITS: |. The free energy difference between the open and closed conformation of adenylate kinase is quite small |CITS: |. The site for the initial interaction of ATP with the enzyme in the open conformation has been identified by NMR |CITS: |. Analysis of the open-to-closed transition by X-ray solution scattering and analysis of available crystal structures suggest that the transition initiated by ATP binding follows an induced fit model |CITS: |; single-molecule FRET analysis shows that domain closure in the presence of substrate is two orders of magnitude faster than the catalytic reaction |CITS: |. A mutant enzyme trapped in the closed, catalytically active state was studied |CITS: |. Energy transfer experiments confirmed stepwise domain movement/closure upon binding of the substrates |CITS: |. The dynamics and energetics of domain movements upon substrate binding and catalysis have been further analyzed |CITS: |. Small, fast motion in the hinge regions facilitates larger, but slow movement of the lid domain |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics simulations, NMR spectroscopy and QM/MM calculations of the conformational transition have been reported |CITS: |. A low concentration of urea activates adenylate kinase by modulating its conformational equilibrium |CITS: |. Many additional studies have used E. coli Adk as a model protein to analyze folding and conformational dynamics, often toward the ultimate goal of the rational design of proteins |CITS: |. Site-directed mutants in residues in the nucleotide binding site |CITS: |, in the phosphate binding loop |CITS: |, and in the "second loop" |CITS: | have been kinetically analyzed. Amino acid changes that increase thermal stability of the enzyme have been introduced |CITS: |. The effects of genetic variation in adenylate kinase on cellular fitness depend on its catalytic capacity (the product of cellular abundance and catalytic activity) |CITS: |. The effect of mutations in surface residues that increase local unfolding depend on their location: mutations in the LID domain decrease the affinity for ATP, while mutations in the NMPbind domain increase catalytic activity |CITS: |. Conversely, mutations that stabilize the enzyme show increased substrate inhibition |CITS: |. Adenylate kinase is able to fulfill the role of nucleoside diphosphate kinase in an ndk mutant |CITS: | and participates in the T4 dNTP synthetase complex |CITS: |. Adenylate kinase can combine with |FRAME: PPK-CPLX| to catalyze the formation of ADP from AMP and poly(Pi). This polyP:AMP phosphotransferase (PAP) activity requires both enzymes acting together |CITS: |. Although adenylate kinase is able to catalyze thiamine triphosphate (ThTP) biosynthesis in vertebrates, it is not responsible for ThTP biosynthesis in vivo in E. coli |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Long chain fatty acid CoA-ligase, also known as acyl-CoA synthetase or synthase, plays a pivotal role in the transport and activation of exogenous fatty acids prior to their subsequent degradation or incorporation into phospholipids. This is the rate limiting step of β-oxidation in E. coli |CITS: |. The enzyme catalyzes the esterification of fatty acids into metabolically active CoA thioesters concomitant with transport. The reaction proceeds by a two-step mechanism. The enzyme has broad chain length specificity, with maximal activities associated with fatty acids ranging in length between C-12 and C-18. The enzyme appears to be partially membrane-associated |CITS: |. Early experiments with partially purified enzyme suggested the presence of two enzymes with different preferences for substrate chain length |CITS: |. Long chain fatty acid uptake into inner membrane vesicles is dependent on the level of FadD in the vesicles |CITS: |. Import of labelled oleate is abolished in fadD null strains |CITS: |. Specific mutations in fadD that abolish or reduce the formation of fatty acyl-CoA likewise abolish or reduce the import of exogenous long chain fatty acids |CITS: |. It has been suggested that FadD specifically associates with the inner membrane in response to the presence of long chain fatty acids |CITS: |. FadD is implicated in a transenvelope lipid signaling pathway that detects phospholipid accumulation in the outer membrane (OM) and regulates LPS production to restore OM homeostasis; loss of FadD partially suppresses cell death associated with the gain of function |FRAME: G7216-MONOMER "mlaA*| mutation; loss of FadD prevents the |FRAME: CPLX0-7944 "PldA"|-dependent lipopolysaccharide increase associated with mlaA* |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Heme chaperone required for the biogenesis of c-type cytochromes. Transiently binds heme delivered by CcmC and transfers the heme to apo-cytochromes in a process facilitated by CcmF and CcmH.
MetaCyc_Comment: CcmE is a membrane anchored, periplasmic heme chaperone that is required for |FRAME: PWY-8147 "cytochrome c biogenesis"|. ccmE is part of an 8 gene cluster (ccmABCDEFGH) which bears sequence similarity to Bradyrhizobium japonicum genes that are required for the biogenesis of |FRAME: Cytochromes-c "c-type cytochromes"|; an E. coli ΔccmA-H mutant strain (EC06) is not able to produce mature c-type cytochromes under anaerobic, nonfermentative growth conditions |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). An in-frame ccmE deletion mutant cannot produce mature c-type cytochromes |CITS: |; CcmE binds heme covalently via a conserved histidine residue (His-30) |CITS: |. Heme ligation in CcmE exhibits flexibility and it has been extensively studied (see |CITS: |). The presence of apocytochrome c triggers release of heme from CcmE; heme release is blocked in the absence of CcmFGH |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). During cyctochrome c biosynthesis, heme is moved across the inner membrane concomitant with the formation of a CcmC-heme-CcmE-CcmD complex; subsequent release of holo-CcmE (for eventual heme transfer to apocytochromes c) requires |FRAME: CcmAB-Complex CcmAB|-mediated ATP hydolysis |CITS: |. A stable (intermediate) holo-CcmCDE complex (isolated in the absence of CcmAB) contains oxidized heme (Fe3+) bound to CcmC via His-60 and His-184 axial ligands and to CcmE via a His130 adduct; a purified holo-CcmCDE(H130A) 'pre-adduct' complex contains reduced heme suggesting that the adduct formation in holoCcmE involves oxidation to the Fe3+ state |CITS: |; the identity of the electron acceptor is not known although membrane quinols and other oxidants such as oxygen and nitrate all possess potentials capable of oxidizing 'pre-adduct' CcmCDE heme |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Transfer of heme from holo-CcmE in the periplasm to apocytochromes c is catalysed by the |FRAME: CPLX-9494|, CcmFH |CITS: |. Synthesis of holocytochome c requires both reduction of the heme molecule (mediated by CcmF) and reduction of the cysteine residues of the apocytochrome c. CcmF contains a stably associated b heme which may function to reduce the heme in holoCcmE; the source of reductant for the b heme in CcmF remains unknown although it can be reduced by various quinones in vitro |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). ccm: cytochrome c maturation |CITS: | Related reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in the uptake of ammonium/ammonia (NH(4)(+)/NH(3)) (PubMed:14668330, PubMed:15361618, PubMed:15563598, PubMed:15876187, PubMed:16910683, PubMed:30211659, PubMed:32662768). Transport is electrogenic (PubMed:30211659, PubMed:32662768). Following sequestration of NH(4)(+) at the periplasmic face, NH(4)(+) is deprotonated and neutral NH(3) is transported into the cytoplasm (PubMed:15876187, PubMed:16910683, PubMed:18362341, PubMed:19278252, PubMed:32662768). Neutral NH(3) and charged H(+) are carried separately across the membrane on a unique two-lane pathway, before recombining to NH(4)(+) inside the cell (PubMed:32662768). In vitro can also transport the larger analogs methylamine and methylammonium (PubMed:11847102, PubMed:12023896, PubMed:14668330, PubMed:15876187, PubMed:17998534, PubMed:18362341). Also acts as a sensor of the extracellular ammonium concentration (PubMed:14668330). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11847102, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12023896, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14668330, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15361618, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15563598, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15876187, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16910683, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17998534, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18362341, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19278252, ECO:0000269|PubMed:30211659, ECO:0000269|PubMed:32662768}.
MetaCyc_Comment: AmtB, a member of the Ammonia Channel Transporter (Amt) family, facilitates the uptake of ammonium/ammonia and is important for growth at low external ammonium concentrations. Under nitrogen rich conditions transport of ammonium by AmtB is blocked by the deuridylylated form of |FRAME: PII2-CPLX "PII-2"|, the product of the glnK gene cotranscribed with amtB. The specific substrate of the AmtB transporter is controversial - it has been variously proposed that AmtB transports uncharged ammonia (NH3), cationic ammonium (NH4+) and that NH4+ deprotonation takes place at the periplasmic binding site prior to NH3 conduction through the pore (reviewed by |CITS: |). More recent evidence indicates that following NH4+ deprotonation, H+ and NH3 follow two separated pathways across the membrane before recombining to NH4+ |CITS: | (and see |CITS: |). Disruption of amtB impairs growth at low NH4+ concentration only at pH values less than 7 suggesting that AmtB transports the uncharged form, NH3; this defect could be complemented by the cloned amtB gene |CITS:|. Whole cell transport experiments indicate that AmtB mediates transport of the ammonium analogue, methylammonium, and suggest that transport is dependent on rapid metabolism of the transported substrate |CITS:|. AmtB mediates NH3 uniport in an energy independent, non-concentrative process |CITS: |. AmtB activity is electrogenic |CITS: |; cytoplasmic and periplasmic water wires form a continuous path for H+ movement from its NH4+ sequestration site at the periplasm, to the cytoplasm |CITS: |. AmtB has 11 membrane spanning segments and is trimeric in the native cell membrane |CITS:| (see also |CITS: |). AmtB has an ammonium binding site within the periplasmic vestibule |CITS:|, a hydrophobic pore for ammonia conductance |CITS:|, and a cytoplasmic reprotonation site |CITS:|, though molecular dynamics simulations suggest the pore may also contain water raising the possibility of ammonium conductance as well |CITS:| (see also |CITS: |). Residues important in substrate binding, deprotonation and channel gating have been identified |CITS: |. Phosphatidylglycerol binding stabilizes the AmtB channel |CITS: |. Specific lipid-AmtB interactions can allosterically modulate the binding of lipids of different type in vitro; allosteric lipid-protein interactions may function to define the AmtB-lipid environment in vivo |CITS: |. Lipid-binding to AmtB allosterically modulates the interaction between AmtB and GlnK in vitro; lipid tail length and head group identity affect the allosteric effects observed |CITS: |. The amtB gene forms an operon with the glnK gene, and expression of this operon occurs under nitrogen-limiting conditions and is dependent on the NtrC regulatory protein |CITS:|. GlnK and AmtB have been shown to quickly and reversibly interact after ammonium shock |CITS:|. This reversible sequestration of GlnK by AmtB is rapidly responsive to μM concentrations of ammonia and requires the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain of AmtB |CITS:|. The 1:1 interaction is dependent upon ATP and is sensitive to 2-oxoglutarate when MgCl2 is present |CITS:|. Deuridylylated GlnK is sequestered by AmtB; deuridylylated GlnK inhibits ammonium flux through AmtB by protein-protein interaction |CITS:|. Deletion or mutation of amtB prevents deuridylylation of GlnK due to decreased intracellular glutamine levels - intracellular glutamine levels being the main effector of the uridyltransferase activity of |FRAME: GLND-MONOMER "GlnD"|. Deuridylylation of GlnK and subsequent GlnK-AmtB association is due to increased intracellular glutamine levels |CITS:|. Crystal structures of the AmtB-GlnK complex have been determined to resolutions of 1.96 Å |CITS:| and 2.5 Å |CITS:|. A GlnK trimer, along with its associated 3 molecules of ADP, associates with the cytoplasmic face of the AmtB trimer by inserting the T-loop of each GlnK subunit into the cytoplasmic pore exit of the adjacent AmtB subunit |CITS:|. E. coli amtB expressed in Xenopus oocytes is active as both a CO2 and NH3 channel |CITS:|. Reviews: |CITS:,| Comment: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: HyaA is the small subunit of hydrogenase 1. HyaA contains a distal cluster, a medial cluster and a unique proximal cluster that is essential for oxygen tolerance |CITS: | (and see |CITS: |. The unique proximal cluster is coordinated by six cysteine residues (at positions 17, 19, 20, 1115, 120 and 149 in the mature enzyme); the conserved cysteines at positions 19 and 120 correspond to glycine residues in standard oxygen-sensitive hydrogenases (hydrogenase 2 in E. coli K-12); a HyaA C19G mutation results in hydrogenase 1 enzyme that is devoid of H(2) oxidising activity in the presence of 1% oxygen |CITS: |. The reduction potential of the medial cluster in oxygen tolerant hydrogenases is higher than in standard oxygen sensitive hydrogenases; a P242C mutation results in conversion of the cluster to a cluster and the modified enzyme is unable to sustain H(2) oxidation in the presence of 1% oxygen |CITS: |. Insertion of the C-terminal transmembrane domain of HyaA into the inner membrane is dependent on the Tat translocation system |CITS: |. In the membrane-bound hydrogenase 1 complex, the two transmembrane α helices from two HyaA subunits pack against opposite sides of the HyaC (cytochrome b) subunit |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: An outer membrane lipoprotein that controls the distance between the inner and outer membranes; adding residues to Lpp increases the width of the periplasm (PubMed:29257832). The only protein known to be covalently linked to the peptidoglycan network (PGN) (PubMed:3013869, PubMed:4245367, PubMed:4261992). Also non-covalently binds the PGN (PubMed:3013869). The link between the cell outer membrane and PGN contributes to the maintenance of the structural and functional integrity of the cell envelope, and maintains the correct distance between the PGN and the outer membrane (PubMed:3013869, PubMed:4245367, PubMed:4261992, PubMed:4565677). The most abundant cellular protein in terms of copy number, there can be up to one million Lpp molecules per cell (PubMed:24766808). About one-third of Lpp is bound to the PGN (called bound or periplasmic) the rest is called free or transmembrane (PubMed:4565677). The 'free' form can be surface labeled by membrane impermeable agents and so must cross the outer membrane; it is thought that this transmembrane form is still anchored in the inner leaflet of the outer membrane (PubMed:21219470). Modeling suggests that non-covalent binding of OmpA (from the outer membrane) and TolR (from the inner membrane) to peptidoglycan maintains the position of the cell wall in the periplasm, holding it approximately equidistant from both the inner and outer membranes. Trimeric Lpp controls the width of the periplasm, adjusts its tilt angle to accommodate to the available space, and can compensate in part for an absence of OmpA (Probable). Purified MacA (residues 32-371) forms a hexamer; the MacA protomer consists of an extended α-helical hairpin domain, a lipoyl domain and a β-barrel domain; the 6 protomers pack together in a side-by-side arrangement to form a structure resembling an 'upside-down funnel' |CITS: |. A fourth domain, termed the membrane-proximal, or MP domain is described in |CITS: |. A non-cleavable signal-like sequence anchors MacA to the inner membrane |CITS: , |. MacA interacts with MacB and with TolC. MacA stimulates the ATPase activity of MacB when reconstituted into proteoliposomes and in E. coli membrane vesicles |CITS: |. Binding of MacA to MacB stabilises the ATP bound conformation of MacB |CITS: |. In a cryo-EM structure of the tripartite complex, the helical hairpin domains pack into a cylinder to form a helical barrel which interacts with TolC in the open state to form a long continuous channel and the β-barrel and MP domains interact with MacB. A conserved glutamine residue (Q209) located in the lipoyl domain of the MacA protomer forms a hydrogen-bonded network and constriction point in the hexamer which may serve as a gate favouring outward movement of substrates |CITS: |. Purified MacA contains a tightly bound rough-type lipopolysaccharide (R-LPS) molecule; one molecule of R-LPS appears to bind one MacA molecule; MacAB-TolC may be involved in the transport of outer membrane glycolipids |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: MacB is the ATPase component of a tripartite efflux complex - MacAB-TolC - which contributes to antibiotic resistance in drug-hypersensitive strains and is also implicated in protoporphyrin IX and glycolipid export. MacB contains 4 transmembrane (TM) segments and an N-terminal nucleotide binding domain that is located in the cytoplasm; a large periplasmic loop is located between between TM1 and 2 |CITS: |. MacB is dimeric; MacB interacts with MacA |CITS: |; the periplasmic domain of MacB interacts with the β-barrel and membrane-proximal domains of MacA |CITS: |. MacB is designated as the type specimen for the type VII ABC transporter superfamily; salient features of the MacB fold include its four-transmembrane helix topology and large periplasmic domain which is elevated above the inner membrane by a four helix bundle or 'stalk' |CITS: |. MacB couples cytoplasmic ATP hydrolysis to transmembrane and periplasmic conformational change in a process termed 'mechanotransmission' |CITS: |. Purified MacB, in detergents and reconstituted into proteoliposomes, displays a basal ATPase activity which is stimulated by addition of MacA |CITS: |. Purified MacB binds erythromycin; MacA enhances MacB's capacity to bind erythromycin |CITS: |. MacB lacking the periplasmic loop, retains nucleotide binding capacity and ATPase activity but is uncoupled from macrolide efflux; the periplasmic loop is required for MacA dependent stimulation of ATP hydrolysis and also contributes to the recruitment of TolC into the trans-envelope complex |CITS: |. In a cryo-EM structure of the tripartite complex, MacB is dimeric and has an opening to the periplasm which may represent the access point for periplasmic substrates |CITS: | Related reviews: |CITS: |

CsrA inhibits translation of pgaABCD mRNA by binding to six sites within the pgaABCD leader |CITS: |. NaCl and alkaline pH induction are dependent upon nhaR as deletion of this gene prevented induction |CITS: |. PgaB has similarity to the HmsF protein encoded by the Yersinia pestis hmsHFRST gene cluster, which is involved in plague transmission |CITS: |. Comment: |CITS: |

Sad is the smaller enzyme and preferentially utilizes NAD+ |CITS: |; the gene encoding it was long unknown. Sad also functions as a glutarate semialdehyde dehydrogenase during degradation of L-lysine |CITS: |. YneI was found to be identical to the orphan enzymatic activity of NAD+-dependent succinate semialdehyde dehydrogenase (Sad). Its activity was first predicted using phylogenetic profiles |CITS: | and later confirmed biochemically |CITS: |. Sad has an important role during growth on arginine and is likely required for growth on putrescine as the sole source of nitrogen. Its main function may be to prevent accumulation of the toxic compound succinate semialdehyde |CITS: |. Sad is more important than GabD for growth on putrescine as the sole source of carbon |CITS: |. Growth of a sad deletion mutant is strongly inhibited by succinate semialdehyde. Expression of sad is induced by succinate semialdehyde |CITS: |; Sad activity is induced by growth on GABA as a nitrogen source |CITS: | and by growth on putrescine |CITS: |. sad expression is increased by external acidification |CITS: |.
