MetaCyc_Comment: LdtE (formerly YnhG) is a membrane anchored, periplasmic L,D-transpeptidase that catalyses the formation of meso-diaminopimelate→meso-diaminopimelate cross links (also called DAP3→DAP3 or 3-3 cross-links) in peptidoglycan; LdtE cleaves the m-DAP3→D-ala4 peptide bond of an acyl donor stem tetrapeptide and links the carboxyl group at the L-center of m-DAP3 to the side chain amine of m-DAP3 of an acceptor stem peptide. Muropeptides obtained from the peptidoglycan of a BW25113Δ(|FRAME: G7073 "ldtA"| |FRAME: G6422 "ldtB"| |FRAME: G6571 "ldtC"| ldtE) quadruple mutant (BW25113Δ4) do not contain tripeptide stems substituted by a fragment of the Braun lipoprotein |CITS: |; muropeptides obtained from the peptidoglycan of a BW25113Δ(ldtA ldtB ldtC |FRAME: EG11253 "ldtD"| ldtE) quintuple mutant (BW25113Δ5) do not contain tripeptide stems substituted by a fragment of the Braun lipoprotein, nor do they contain meso-DAP3-meso-DAP3 cross-links, free tripeptide stems or tetrapeptide stems with Gly as the fourth amino acid |CITS:|. Expression of ldtE in the BW25113Δ4 mutant increases the amount of muropeptides with DAP3-DAP3 cross links |CITS: |. Growth of a strain lacking both LdtE and LdtD (Δldt2) is not affected under a wide variety of conditions, but their absence contributes to the growth defect of an Δldt5 strain (ΔldtABCDE) which is also a DAP auxotroph (dapA::cm) |CITS: | (see further |CITS: |). Complementation analysis (|CITS:| results not shown) also suggests LdtE can exchange D-ala4 in peptidoglycan tetrapeptide stems with glycine (|FRAME: RXN-16665 "RXN-16665"|) and hydrolyse D-ala4 to produce tripeptide stems (|FRAME: RXN-16664 "RXN-16664"|). E. coli K-12 incorporates exogenously supplied D-methionine into peptidoglycan stem tetrapeptides; the percentage of muropeptides that contain D-methionine is reduced to varying extents in all single ldt insertion mutants* and is reduced by ~75% in the double ldtD ldtE insertion mutant |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Deletion of ldtD together with ldtE also reduces detection of D-cysteine in peptidoglycan |CITS: |. LdtE and LdtF are implicated in incorporating the fluorescent D-amino acid NADA, into peptidoglycan at acid pH |CITS: |. LdtA, B, C and E are all of similar size and share 42-62% sequence similarity including a putative active site cysteine located in a conserved motif; ldtE and ldtC also contain a LysM domain (see |CITS: |) which is associated with peptidoglycan binding; LtdE shares 17% sequence similarity with LtdD |CITS: |. ldtE is σS-dependent and is upregulated in response to the stationary phase transition, osmotic upshift, and acid stress |CITS:|. Expression of ldtE is induced by acivicin treatment |CITS:| and is supercoiling-dependent |CITS:,|. Expression of ldtE increases in biofilms upon deletion of bhsA |CITS:|. *|FRAME: G6108-MONOMER "ldtF"| was not included in this analysis

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Participates in cysteine desulfuration mediated by SufS. Cysteine desulfuration mobilizes sulfur from L-cysteine to yield L-alanine and constitutes an essential step in sulfur metabolism for biosynthesis of a variety of sulfur-containing biomolecules. Functions as a sulfur acceptor for SufS, by mediating the direct transfer of the sulfur atom from the S-sulfanylcysteine of SufS, an intermediate product of cysteine desulfuration process. Together with the SufBCD complex, it thereby enhances up to 50-fold, the cysteine desulfurase activity of SufS. Component of the suf operon, which is activated and required under specific conditions such as oxidative stress and iron limitation. Does not affect the selenocysteine lyase activity of SufS. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:12876288, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12941942, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14644425}.
MetaCyc_Comment: SufE is part of the Suf iron-sulfur cluster assembly system. SufE acts as a sulfur acceptor for the cysteine persulfide generated by the |FRAME: CPLX0-246 SufS| cysteine desulfurase |CITS: | and transfers the sulfur atoms to the Cys254 residue of |FRAME: G6909-MONOMER SufB| |CITS: |. The Isc system is the "housekeeping" pathway for iron-sulfur cluster assembly in the cell; the Suf system comprises a secondary pathway of iron-sulfur cluster assembly |CITS: | that is required under oxidative stress |CITS: | or iron starvation conditions |CITS: |. IscS-IscU is more susceptible to oxidative modification than SufS-SufE |CITS: |. SufE is both a cosubstrate of SufS, accepting sulfur at its C51 residue from the persulfide at Cys364 of SufS, and an activator for the cysteine desulfurase activity of SufS. SufE binds near the active site of SufS and modulates the site's backbone dynamics |CITS: |. The kinetic mechanism of sulfur transfer between SufS and SufE has been investigated, and a model for a protected sulfur transfer pathway of the Suf system has been proposed |CITS: |. Enhanced cysteine desulfurase activity of SufE-SufS |CITS: | was reported to be dependent on the SufBC components |CITS: | of the |FRAME: CPLX0-1341 SufB-SufC-SufD| complex |CITS: |. The interaction of SufE with the SufB sulfur acceptor requires the presence of SufC |CITS: |. Additional in vivo interaction partners for SufE have been found |CITS: |. Mutation of the conserved cysteine residue C51 eliminates the ability of SufE to enhance SufS activity; this residue may function as the acceptor site for sulfur transfer by SufS |CITS: |. The C51 sulfhydryl group has a pKa of 6.3 |CITS: |. A D74R mutant located in the active site Cys loop increases flexibility and solvent accessibility of the loop and leads to stronger affinity of the mutant protein for SufS |CITS: |. A crystal structure of SufE has been solved at 2 Å resolution, showing structural similarity to |FRAME: G7324-MONOMER IscU| |CITS: |. Although dimeric forms can be detected |CITS: |, the protein is predominantly monomeric in solution |CITS: |. SufE was also shown to transfer sulfur to a cysteine residue of |FRAME: CPLX0-7824 SufA| |CITS: |; however, label transfer experiments don't show interactions between SufA and SufE/S |CITS: |. A mutant deficient in expression of the sufABCDSE operon does not exhibit severe phenotypes, whereas a sufABCDSE isc double mutant exhibits synthetic lethality, indicating that these systems are redundant and that iron-sulfur cluster assembly is essential for viability. Overproduction of the products of the sufABCDSE operon, or regulatory mutations in the sufABCDSE operon, suppress defects of a Δisc strain |CITS: |. A sufE mutant is more sensitive to oxidative stress, acid stress and cadmium than wild type |CITS: |. SufE: "sulfur" Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: DmlA is a D-malate dehydrogenase that is essential for aerobic growth on D-malate as the sole carbon source |CITS: |. DmlA also catalyses the oxidative decarboxylation of 3-isopropylmalate in vitro and in vivo and the non-decarboxylating oxidation of L(+)-tartrate in vitro. DmlA is a generalist enzyme and displays relatively high activity on 3 differing substrates |CITS: |. Expression of dmlA is increased more than 500-fold during growth on D-malate compared to growth on L-lactate |CITS: |, L-malate, glucose or glycerol |CITS: |. Under anaerobic conditions, expression of dmlA is increased even further by the presence of D-malate; however, anaerobic growth on D-malate requires the presence of an additional electron donor such as glycerol |CITS: |. Chromosomal expression of dmlA is able to complement cells lacking leuB-encoded |FRAME: 3-ISOPROPYLMALDEHYDROG-CPLX| (IPMDH) activity. Purified DmlA is active on D-malate, 3-isopropylmalate and L(+)-tartrate; D-lactate, isocitrate and D-tartrate are poor substrates. DmlA has a weaker affinity for L(+)-tartrate than for D-malate or 3-isopropylmalate |CITS: |. Protein levels of DmlA are upregulated in response to Zn(II) stress (growth in 0.2 mM Zn(II) for 4 hours) |CITS: |. DmlA: "D-malate degradation A" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Required for the formation of a threonylcarbamoyl group on adenosine at position 37 (t(6)A37) in tRNAs that read codons beginning with adenine. Is probably involved in the transfer of the threonylcarbamoyl moiety of threonylcarbamoyl-AMP (TC-AMP) to the N6 group of A37, together with TsaD and TsaE. TsaB seems to play an indirect role in the t(6)A biosynthesis pathway, possibly in regulating the core enzymatic function of TsaD. In fact, can act as a protease that specifically degrades TsaD in vitro; therefore TsaB may post-translationally regulate cellular pools of TsaD via proteolytic degradation. Does not show sialoglycoprotease activity against glycophorin A. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19376873, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22378793}.
MetaCyc_Comment: TsaB is involved in the biosynthesis of the threonylcarbamoyladenosine (t6A) residue at position 37 of ANN-decoding tRNAs. A mixture of purified |FRAME: G7698-MONOMER TsaC|, |FRAME: EG11171-MONOMER TsaD|, TsaB, and |FRAME: EG11757-MONOMER TsaE| proteins catalyzes formation of t6A in the presence of a tRNA substrate, ATP, threonine and bicarbonate in vitro |CITS: |. The three essential proteins TsaE, TsaB and TsaD form an interaction network. TsaB interacts with itself; it can interact with both TsaE and TsaD directly, and the interactions appear to be mutually exclusive |CITS: |. The specific interaction between TsaD and TsaB is required for the essential function of these proteins |CITS: |. TsaB and TsaD form a heterodimer; crystal structures of this protein complex have been solved. The structure shows ADP bound at the dimer interface. Site-directed mutants in the TsaB-TsaD interface were generated and biochemically characterized. The C-terminal tail of TsaB is not required for formation of the ternary |FRAME: CPLX0-8182| complex |CITS: |. A preliminary analysis of the crystal structure of TsaB alone has been published |CITS: |; the structure was further analyzed and compared to the structure of the Vibrio parahaemolyticus protein |CITS: |. This analysis suggests two different homodimer architectures corresponding to a free and a nucleotide-bound form |CITS: |. TsaB appears to act a protease that specifically degrades the TsaD protein |CITS: |; this activity may not be reproducible. TsaB is essential for growth in complex media under aerobic conditions |CITS: |. The protein is broadly conserved in bacteria |CITS: |. Depletion of TsaB results in the formation of highly condensed nucleoids |CITS: |. As for tsaE and tsaD, |FRAME: G6864 rstA| was identified as a multicopy suppressor of the lethal phenotype of a strain with a conditional tsaB mutation |CITS: |. Other genetic interactions were found |CITS: |. TsaB: "threonylcarbamoyl-6(six)-adenosine" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: DNA-dependent ATPase and 5'-3' DNA helicase (PubMed:36509145). Has single-stranded (ss)DNA-dependent ATPase activity and 5'-3' helicase activity on forked DNA; both activities were measure in a YoaA:HolC (chi) complex (PubMed:36509145). Requires a 20-35 nucleotide (nt) 5'-ssDNA tail; dsDNA with a 20 nt gap is also unwound (PubMed:36509145). Unwinds damaged 3' nascent ends (such as those terminated by 3' azidothymidine (AZT), 3' dideoxy-C or an abasic site on the translocating strand), to promote repair and AZT excision (PubMed:36509145). Without HolC the protein has much lower activity which could be due to YoaA instability or helicase stimulation by HolC (PubMed:36509145). Genetically identified as involved in the repair of replication forks and tolerance of the chain-terminating nucleoside analog AZT (PubMed:26544712, PubMed:33582602, PubMed:34181484). May act in proofreading during nucleotide misincorporation, it appears to aid in the removal of potential A-to-T transversion mutations in ndk mutants (Probable) (PubMed:34181484). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:P27296, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26544712, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33582602, ECO:0000269|PubMed:34181484, ECO:0000269|PubMed:36509145}.

Of the strains originally tested, the mutant W3110 ΔtrpED102/F'ΔtrpED102 contained the highest amount of D-cysteine desulfhydrase |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Sensor of abasic sites in single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) required to preserve genome integrity by promoting error-free repair of abasic sites (PubMed:30554877). Recognizes and binds abasic sites in ssDNA at replication forks and chemically modifies the lesion by forming a covalent cross-link with DNA: forms a stable thiazolidine linkage between a ring-opened abasic site and the alpha-amino and sulfhydryl substituents of its N-terminal catalytic cysteine residue (PubMed:30554877, PubMed:31235915, PubMed:31504793). The DNA-protein cross-link is then reversed: able to catalyze the reversal of the thiazolidine cross-link and cycle between a cross-link and a non-cross-linked state depending on DNA context: mediates self-reversal of the thiazolidine cross-link in double stranded DNA (PubMed:35934051, PubMed:37519246). May act as a protease: mediates autocatalytic processing of its N-terminal methionine in order to expose the catalytic cysteine (By similarity). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:Q8R1M0, ECO:0000269|PubMed:30554877, ECO:0000269|PubMed:31235915, ECO:0000269|PubMed:31504793, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35934051, ECO:0000269|PubMed:37519246}.

MetaCyc_Comment: DgcQ is a probable inner membrane protein with two predicted transmembrane domains and a C-terminal GGDEF domain with diguanylate cyclase activity |CITS: |. The N-terminal CHASE (Cyclases/Histidine kinases Associated Sensory) domain is predicted to be periplasmic |CITS: |. The C terminus is predicted to localize to the cytoplasm |CITS: |. DgcQ is implicated in phage N4 infection |CITS: |. The diguanylate cyclase domain of DgcQ physically interacts with PyrB, the catalytic subunit of |FRAME: ASPCARBTRANS-CPLX| (PyrBI), an enzyme involved in de novoUMP biosynthesis. The diguanylate cyclase activity of this domain is activated by UTP and inhibited by |FRAME: CARBAMYUL-L-ASPARTATE|, the product of PyrBI |CITS: |. In the commensal E. coli strain 1094, DgcQ is a regulator that constitutively activates cellulose production under all tested environmental conditions |CITS: |. Expression of dgcQ is dependent on σS under a number of stress conditions |CITS: | and increases during transition into stationary phase |CITS: |. DgcQ does not appear to act as a global regulator of gene expression |CITS: |. Deletion of dgcQ partially restores motility of a pdeH mutant, suggesting that DgcQ is one of four diguanylate cyclases that adjust c-di-GMP concentration for motility control |CITS: |. Deletion of dgcQ, |FRAME: EG12396 dgcE|, and |FRAME: G6972 dgcJ| together, fully restores the motility of a ΔpdeH mutant |CITS: |. A dgcQ deletion mutant shows 12-fold increased early biofilm formation and 6-fold increased swimming motility. Deletion of dgcQ does not alter the concentration of c-di-GMP inside the cell |CITS: |. Deletion of dgcQ in a ΔcarB background appears to inhibit cellulose overproduction when the strain is grown in the presence of uracil |CITS: |. An A361E mutation in DgcQ, which causes increased intracellular c-di-GMP levels, leads to improved phototrophic growth in a chemostat evolution experiment with an engineered rhodopsin-expressing E. coli strain grown under illumination with limited glucose |CITS: |. Overexpression of dgcQ from an ASKA plasmid leads to a more than 3-fold increase in the MIC of hypochlorous acid |CITS: |. DgcQ: diguanylate cyclase Q |CITS: | Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: YedX belongs to the family of transthyretin-related proteins (TRP). Transthyretin is a transport protein in extracellular fluids of vertebrates, where it distributes thyroid hormones |CITS: |. YedX is othologous with Bacillus subtilis PucM, which functions to facilitate the hydrolysis of 5-hydroxyisourate (HIU), the end product of the uricase reaction; purified YedX has 5-hydroxyisourate hydrolase (HIUH) activity |CITS: | The physiological significance of HIUH activity in E. coli is unclear. The source of HIU is not known; E. coli degrades purines to form uric acid (see |FRAME: PWY-6608| and |FRAME: SALVADEHYPOX-PWY|), which is a good source of nitrogen in many organisms, but uricase activity has not been identified in E.coli. Alternatively, |CITS: | suggests that uric acid functions as an antioxidant in enterobacteria and that the oxidative (nonenzymatic) decomposition of uric acid would also generate HIU which can spontaneously decompose into, and react with, a variety of free radical compounds. Enzymatic removal of 5-HIU (by periplasmic YedX) would thus prevent accumulation of potentially toxic compounds. YedX contains a cleaved signal sequence and may be located in the periplasm. The protein is a tetramer in solution. E. coli YedX does not bind the thyroid hormones thyroxine and triiodo-thyronine |CITS: |. Purified YedX forms amyloidogenic fibrils at pH 5.8 - pH 6.8 with stirring for 3 days |CITS: | and upon heating at 65°C at pH 7.4 for 3 days without stirring |CITS: |. Purified YedX maintains its tetrameric structure at low pH - separating into monomers at pH 3 - and has a melting temperature (TM) of 66.7°C |CITS: | Crystal structures of YedX have been determined at 1.65 and 2.1 Å resolution. The structures are similar to eukaryotic transthyretins. Zinc ions are located at the putative ligand binding site, although zinc is absent from the purified recombinant protein |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: YfbR is a 5'-deoxynucleotidase that functions as a dCMP phosphohydrolase in a salvage pathway for the synthesis of dUMP in a dcd deoA mutant |CITS: |. The protein contains a conserved HD domain |CITS: |. YfbR has phosphatase activity with deoxyribonucleoside 5'-monophosphates and does not hydrolyze ribonucleotides or deoxyribonucloside 3'-monophosphates. The enzyme requires divalent metal cations for activity |CITS: |. Nucleotidase activity of YfbR was discovered in a high-throughput screen of purified proteins |CITS: |. Crystal structures of YfbR have been solved; based on an analysis of crystal packing and size-exclusion chromatography, it was suggested that the biological unit is a dimer. Site-directed mutagenesis confirmed the importance of certain conserved active site residues, and mechanisms for substrate selectivity and catalysis were proposed |CITS: |. yfbR and alaA may form an operon |CITS: |.

FadR represses transcription of fadIJ in the presence of oxygen |CITS: |. FadI is a putative C-tail-anchored (TA) membrane protein |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: MurQ catalyzes the cleavage of the lactyl ether moiety of N-acetylmuramic acid 6-phosphate (MurNAc-6-P), acting in one of the pathways that recycle murein components |CITS: |. MurQ is the only MurNAc-6-P etherase in E. coli |CITS: |. A reaction mechanism involving β-elimination/hydration has been proposed |CITS: |. Further studies support a mechanism involving syn elimination of lactate followed by syn addition of water. Structural modelling and site-directed mutagenesis implicated the Glu83 and Glu114 residues in catalysis and suggested that Glu83 is required for protonation of the departing lactate |CITS: |. A murQ null mutant strain that is non-polar on murP can not grow on N-acetylmuramic acid as the sole source of carbon and energy. When grown on other carbon sources, a murQ null mutant accumulates MurNAc 6-phosphate |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: A component of the bacterial microcompartment (BMC) shell dedicated to ethanolamine degradation (Probable). Two crystal forms have been seen; a form with a closed central pore that has 3 very small (1.1-2.2 Angstroms) channels per trimer lined by acidic and aromatic residues (PubMed:19451619, PubMed:20044574). A form with a large central pore (8-12 Angstroms) has also been seen; this is probably a functional pore which allows molecules to enter and exit the BMC in a selective, gated manner (PubMed:20044574, PubMed:20851901). Another group only sees the central pore in the presence of Zn(2+); soaking crystals in ZnCl(2) leads to dramatic conformational changes that open a central pore of about 12 Angstroms. Whether Zn(2+) binding is physiologically relevant is unclear, however it suggests a gating mechanism exists (PubMed:20851901). Ethanolamine-binding by the small channels has been hypothesized to stabilize the EutL central pore in a closed (non-transporting) state. An open pore is thought to be large enough to transport ATP and/or cobalamin (By similarity). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:Q8XLZ0, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19451619, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20044574, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20851901, ECO:0000305|PubMed:19451619, ECO:0000305|PubMed:20044574, ECO:0000305|PubMed:20851901, ECO:0007744|PDB:3GFH, ECO:0007744|PDB:3I82, ECO:0007744|PDB:3MPV}.

MetaCyc_Comment: E. coli encodes two "malic enzymes" that catalyze the decarboxylation of malate to form pyruvate with concomitant reduction of NAD(P)+. One enzyme, MaeB (described here) reduces NADP+, while the other, |FRAME: MALIC-NAD-MONOMER MaeA|, reduces NAD+ |CITS: |. MaeB activity is highly regulated by key metabolites |CITS: |. Inhibition by acetyl-CoA may direct carbon distribution at the PEP-pyruvate-oxaloacetate metabolic node |CITS: |. MaeB appears to be important for supplying NADPH during growth on two-carbon compounds |CITS: |; flux-balance analysis predicts flux to pyruvate through MaeB during growth on acetate |CITS: |. Metabolic flux through the malic enzymes during growth on glycerol as the sole source of carbon appears to be essentially zero |CITS: |. A malolactic enzyme activity - decarboxylation of malate to lactate without concomitant reduction of NAD(P)+ - was recently discovered for MaeB; this activity may contribute to maintaining the NADPH/NADH balance of the cell |CITS: |. Purification of the enzyme from E. coli K10 and K-12 indicated that it was composed of 8 subunits |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain of MaeB is similar to phosphotransacetylases; it is not required for catalytic activity, but appears to be required for metabolic regulation and oligomerization |CITS: |. A study using a thiol-based redox proteomic approach showed that the Cys-642 residue of MaeB is modified by peroxynitrite, an antibacterial compound. Reversible modification of specific thiols in AsnB, FrmA, MaeB, and RidA may be involved in adaptation to nitrosative stress |CITS: |. Using a method that distinguishes N-phosphorylation from O-phosphorylation, N-phosphorylation was detected in vitro |CITS: |. Deletion of maeB abolishes NADP+-dependent malic enzyme activity |CITS: |. A maeB mutant does not show a defect when grown on acetate; however, a maeB maeA double mutant in a pckA mutant background abolishes growth on acetate |CITS: |. A maeB maeA double mutant alone shows a severe lag phase during the transition from growth on glucose to growth on acetate |CITS: |. A ΔmaeB mutant is more sensitive to peroxynitrite stress than wild type |CITS: |. Expression of maeB is induced by growth on acetate |CITS: | and is upregulated in a pykF (pyruvate kinase) null mutant |CITS: |. Overexpression of MaeB increases the production of C4 metabolites under anaerobic conditions with supplemental bicarbonate |CITS: |. maeB is among a number of metabolic genes whose expression was downregulated in two MG1655 lysogens carrying closely related Stx2a phages O104 and PA8 |CITS: |. Overexpression or deletion of maeB has been utilized in metabolic engineering for production of several compounds, e.g. by |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the formation of N(4)-acetylcytidine (ac(4)C) at the wobble position of tRNA(Met), by using acetyl-CoA as an acetyl donor and ATP (or GTP). It recognizes the wobble base of tRNA(Met), thus distinguishing between tRNA(Met) and the structurally similar tRNA(Ile2) (PubMed:18668122, PubMed:19322199). Could use an RNA helicase motor driven by ATP hydrolysis to deliver the wobble base of tRNA(Met) to the acetyltransferase domain of TmcA (Probable). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:18668122, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19322199, ECO:0000305|PubMed:19322199}.; FUNCTION: Also functions as a lysine 2-hydroxyisobutyryltransferase to regulate transcription. Can specifically catalyze the 2-hydroxyisobutyrylation (Khib) of the DNA-binding protein H-NS. Hydroxyisobutyrylation of H-NS decreases its DNA-binding activity, promotes the expression of acid-resistance genes and enhances bacterial survival under extreme acid stress. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:34903851}.

MetaCyc_Comment: tRNAMet cytidine acetyltransferase acetylates the wobble base C34 of the |FRAME: Elongation-tRNAMet|. TmcA specifically recognizes the anticodon stem of tRNAMet, thus distinguishing between tRNAMet and tRNAIle2, which is structurally similar and has the same anticodon loop |CITS: |. TmcA was recently also identified as a protein-lysine 2-hydroxyisobutyryltransferase. 467 potential protein modification sites were identified, including the K121 residue of H-NS |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the enzyme complexed with acetyl-CoA and ADP has been solved at 2.35 Å resolution. A modified DEAD-box RNA helicase module is formed by the peripheral N-terminal and the DUF699 PFAM domains. The authors propose that the RNA helicase motor delivers the wobble base substrate of the tRNA to the enzyme active site |CITS: |. The presence of acetyl-CoA is essential for the formation of a stable complex between TmcA and tRNAMet and also activates the intrinsic ATPase activity of TmcA. The substrate tRNA may be transiently rearranged during ATP hydrolysis. Residues essential for either the ATPase or tRNA binding activities were identified by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. In vitro, it was observed that the N4-acetylcytidine (ac4C) modification at wobble position of tRNAMet is important for preventing misreading of the AUA codon |CITS: |. RNA isolated from a tmcA deletion strain lacks the ac4C modification; however, the strain does not show a growth defect. Thus, this modification does not appear to be required for faithful translation in an otherwise wild-type strain. A tmcA |FRAME: EG12022 dusC| double deletion strain has a severe cold-sensitive growth defect |CITS: |. Overexpression of TmcA increases survival under acid stress conditions |CITS: |. TmcA: "tRNAMet cytidine acetyltransferase" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: May mediate protein transfer from the SecYEG translocon to the periplasmic chaperone network via its periplasmic C-terminal region (PubMed:24855643). In addition, at the cytosolic site, acts as a negative regulator of RcsB (PubMed:26092727). In stationary phase, the FtsH-dependent degradation of YfgM ensures the release of RcsB from YfgM and thereby permits cellular protection by the Rcs phosphorelay system (PubMed:26092727). May coordinate stress responses across the inner membrane via a dynamic protein-protein interaction network inside and outside of the membrane (PubMed:26092727). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:24855643, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26092727}.

MetaCyc_Comment: pbpC encodes a HMW penicillin binding protein (PBP) known as PBP1C. PBP1C (like |FRAME: CPLX0-7717 PBP1A| and |FRAME: CPLX0-3951 PBP1B|) contains characteristic transglycosylase and transpeptidase amino acid motifs but only transglycosylase activity has been assayed |CITS: |. PBP1C does not bind most of the β-lactams known to bind other PBPs leading to speculation that PBP1C does not have transpeptidase activity (the transpeptidase region is also responsible for penicillin binding) |CITS: |. PPB1C is predicted to contain a single transmembrane domain which anchors the cell to the inner membrane with the remainder of the enzyme located in the periplasm |CITS: |. PBP1C is responsible for 75% of transglycosylase activity in ether pemeabilized cells, but only less than 3% in crude membranes; PBP1C-specific murein synthesizing activity is sensitive to moenomycin |CITS: |. PBP1C binds 35S-labeled penicillin; maximum binding occurs at pH 5 |CITS: |. PBP1C binds moxalactam poorly |CITS: |. PBP1C binds furazlocillin |CITS: |. PBP1C binds a 125I labelled derivative of ampicillin |CITS: |. Cells lacking PBP1C do not exhibit defects in growth rate, yield or sensitivity to a range of antibiotics; the muropeptide composition of these cells is unaffected except for an increase in the amount of tetra-penta disaccharides |CITS: |. Overproduction of the PBP1C protein does not rescue the defect of an mrcAts mrcB double mutant |CITS: |. Purified PBP1C interacts with PBP1B, |FRAME: EG10341-MONOMER PBP3|, |FRAME: EG10202-MONOMER PBP4|, |FRAME: EG10606-MONOMER PBP2| (through an unknown periplasmic factor), and |FRAME: G7457-MONOMER MltA| |CITS: |. PBP1C interacts with |FRAME: EG10950-MONOMER Slt70| and |FRAME: G7410-MONOMER MltB| |CITS: |. There is no apparent fluctuation in PBP1C level (as measured via the binding of labelled ampicillin) during different points of the cell cycle |CITS: |. pbpC is often found linked to |FRAME: G7323-MONOMER yfhM| homologs (encoding α2-macroglobulins) in bacteria leading to the suggestion that the two enzymes may act together as a defense and repair mechanism to protect the cell from host defenses during colonization |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat), is an adaptive immune system that provides protection against mobile genetic elements (viruses, transposable elements and conjugative plasmids). CRISPR clusters contain sequences complementary to antecedent mobile elements and target invading nucleic acids. CRISPR clusters are transcribed and processed into CRISPR RNA (crRNA).; FUNCTION: A component of Cascade, which participates in CRISPR interference, the third stage of CRISPR immunity. Cascade binds both crRNA and in a sequence-specific manner negatively supercoiled dsDNA target. This leads to the formation of an R-loop in which the crRNA binds the target DNA, displacing the noncomplementary strand. Cas3 is recruited to Cascade, nicks target DNA and then unwinds and cleaves the target, leading to DNA degradation and invader neutralization.

MetaCyc_Comment: HldE catalyzes two reactions in the |FRAME: PWY0-1241| pathway, which provides one of the building blocks for the inner core region of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) |CITS: |. The bifunctionality of HldE results from a fusion of an N-terminal ribokinase superfamily domain and a C-terminal cytidylyltransferase superfamily domain; the two domains are genetically and physically separable |CITS: |. Structural modelling of the ribokinase domain led to the identification of amino acid residues potentially essential for catalysis. Site-directed mutagenesis of potential ATP binding site residues resulted in a dominant negative mutant phenotype |CITS: |. In a genetic screen for heptoseless mutants, a transposon insertion in the hldE gene was identified |CITS: |. Based on increased expression of sulA as a reporter gene, a ΔhldE mutant is more sensitive to exposure to the genotoxic agents nalidixic acid and mitomycin C than wild type |CITS: |. The LPS biosynthesis pathway has been explored as a target for development of new antibacterial compounds |CITS: |; inhibitors of the kinase activity of HldE have been identified |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: The tRNAs specific for glutamate, lysine, and possibly glutamine contain the hypermodified nucleoside 5-methylaminomethyl-2-thiouridine (mnm5s2U) in position 34, the wobble position. The MnmC protein was shown to catalyze the formation of mnm5s2U from 5-carboxymethylaminomethyl-2-thiouridine (cmnm5s2U) in tRNA |CITS: |. Both the tRNA species and growth conditions modulate synthesis of the wobble base modifications |CITS: |. A tentative reaction mechanism has been proposed. The enzyme catalyzes two steps, an initial FAD-dependent demodification of cmnm5s2U to nm5s2U followed by the transfer of a methyl group from AdoMet to nm5s2U to produce mnm5s2U |CITS: |. The second reaction occurs faster than the first reaction, indicating that the enzyme is tuned to produce fully mnm5s2U-modified tRNA without accumulating the nm5s2U-modified tRNA intermediate |CITS: |. tRNAGlncmnm5s2UUG and tRNALeucmnm5UmAA are not substrates for the demodification activity of MnmC |CITS: |. The MnmC protein consists of two conserved domains, an N-terminal methyltransferase domain and a C-terminal FAD-dependent oxidoreductase domain. The purified recombinant protein contains a flavin derivative |CITS: |. As already indicated by the mutant phenotypes of the trmC1 and trmC2 mutant alleles |CITS: |, a structural model of MnmC suggests that the initial demodification reaction is catalyzed by the C-terminal domain of the protein, while the methylation reaction is catalyzed by the N-terminal domain. Site-directed mutagenesis of predicted active site residues and separate expression of the two domains confirmed this hypothesis |CITS: |. The oxidoreductase activity is able to utilize the advanced glycation endproduct (AGE) carboxyethyl-lysine in vitro, restoring it to lysine. A ΔlysA lysine auxotroph was found to be able to utilize carboxyethyl-lysine as the sole source of lysine. Structure-based engineering enabled selection of mutants with increased catalytic activity |CITS: |. A crystal structure of MnmC containing the FAD cofactor has been solved at 3 Å resolution. The catalytic sites of the two domains face opposite sides of the protein, arguing against substrate channeling |CITS: |. A crystal structure of the E. coli B enzyme (which is 99% identical to the K-12 enzyme) containing both FAD and SAM has also been solved |CITS: |. |CITS: | report that an mnmC null mutant has a lower growth rate than wild type, while |CITS: | found no effect of any tested mnmC mutation on growth rate, although growth competition assays showed that the wild type does outcompete certain mnmC mutants. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in disulfide bond formation. DsbG and DsbC are part of a periplasmic reducing system that controls the level of cysteine sulfenylation, and provides reducing equivalents to rescue oxidatively damaged secreted proteins such as ErfK, YbiS and YnhG. Displays chaperone activity in both redox states in vitro. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19965429}.

FUNCTION: Forms pores that allow passive diffusion of cations across the outer membrane. Part of a cation efflux system that mediates resistance to copper and silver. In pathogenic strains it allows the bacteria to invade brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMEC) thus allowing it to cross the blood-brain barrier and cause neonatal meningitis. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:11399769, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12813074, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21249122}.
MetaCyc_Comment: CusC is an outer membrane lipoprotein involved in the detoxification of copper and silver ions in E. coli as part of the CusCFBA copper/silver efflux system. A crystal structure of CusC has been solved to 2.3 Å. The CusC trimer forms a large continuous internal cavity with a cylindrical shape. Each monomer contributes 4 β strands to the outer membrane β barrel structure and 4 α helices to the periplasmic α barrel. The structure also suggests that CusC is triacylated at the N-terminal cysteine residue of each monomer |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: CusF is a periplasmic binding protein involved in the detoxification of copper and silver ions in E. coli as part of the CusCFBA copper/silver efflux system. CusF forms a five-stranded β-barrel and has been crystallized in its apo form as well as with bound Ag(I) or Cu(I) |CITS: |. CusF is a metallochaperone that specifically binds Ag(I) and Cu(I), but not Cu(II) |CITS: | despite earlier evidence regarding binding of Cu(II) |CITS: |. CusF transfers metal directly to CusB for export |CITS: |. CusF is a pink copper-binding protein and binds one copper ion per monomer |CITS: |. The histidine residue at position 58 and the two methionine residues at positions 69 and 71 are essential for copper/silver binding |CITS: |. Cu(I) binding also involves a strong interaction between the metal ion and the aromatic ring of a tryptophan residue at position 44 |CITS: |. The UV-vis spectrum of copper-containing CusF showed an absorption-maximum around 510 nm, which has not been reported for any other copper protein |CITS: |. CusF appears in the periplasmic space after induction with CuCl2 |CITS: |. Comment: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: CusB is a membrane fusion protein involved in the detoxification of copper and silver ions in E. coli as part of the CusCFBA copper/silver efflux system. CusB is monomeric in solution |CITS: |. Three methionine residues (M21, M36, M38) ligate the metal substrate in a 1:1 stoichiometry |CITS: |. Crystal structures of CusB in the absence and presence of silver and copper ions have been described; CusB consists of 4 major domains: 3 β-strand domains and one α-helical domain; two distinct conformations of CusB were found in single crystals suggesting that CusB exhibits conformational flexibility |CITS: |. The function of a membrane fusion protein like CusB may be to bring the outer membrane factor, CusC, closer to the resistance-nodulation-division permease, CusA, consistent with the 'funnel' model of efflux. Alternatively CusB may act as a switch whereby metal binding to CusB promotes opening of a CusA channel and docking of substrate-loaded CusF (reviewed in |CITS: |). Using selenomethionine labeling of active site methionine residues |CITS: | provide in vitro evidence that loaded CusB activates CusA to accept copper from CusF. Back-transfer of copper from CusB to CusF was also observed and this may function as a regulatory mechanism CusB is the key protein for metal induced assembly of the CusCBA tripartite complex; CusB can sense and and bind metal directly in the periplasm; when CusB binds metal, it increases the assembly kinetics and decreases the disassembly kinetics of the CusCBA complex |CITS: |. cusB expression is upregulated by indole in a dose-dependent manner |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: 2-Methylcitrate dehydratase (PrpD) catalyzes the stereospecific dehydration of 2-methylcitrate, a reaction in propionate catabolism via the methylcitrate cycle |CITS: |. PrpD is monomeric in solution |CITS: |. Reports disagree on whether |CITS: | or not |CITS: | PrpD contains an iron-sulfur cluster, and on the substrate specificity of the enzyme |CITS: |. prpD also encodes the residual aconitase-like activity, aconitase C |CITS: |, which constitutes 5% or less of cellular aconitase activity and is observed in an acnA acnB double mutant |CITS: |. Aconitase C activity does not substitute for aconitase A and B activities in vivo and appears not to be reversible, in contrast to true aconitase activity, and is therefore better described as a dehydratase activity |CITS: |. Expression of prpD is induced by propionate, and protein production is observed during growth on propionate, but not acetate |CITS: |. Expression of prpBCDE is regulated by PrpR and catabolite repression |CITS: | and is downregulated in the presence of a variety of sugars |CITS: |.

HxpB is a sugar phosphatase belonging to the superfamily of haloacid dehalogenase (HAD)-like hydrolases. Its preferred substrate is 2-deoxyglucose-6-phosphate |CITS: |. The phosphatase activity of HxpB was first discovered in a high-throughput screen of purified proteins |CITS: |. Phosphatase activity of HxpB is dependent on the presence of a divalent cation such as Mg2+, which appears to affect substrate binding |CITS: |. Mutagenesis of the predicted catalytic Asp residues in HxpB results in loss of phosphatase activity. A hxpB deletion mutant is more sensitive to the presence of 2-deoxyglucose in the growth medium than wild type, while a strain overexpressing hxpB tolerates higher concentrations of 2-deoxyglucose |CITS: |. 2-deoxyglucose is taken up by E. coli and is phosphorylated to 2-deoxyglucose-6P, a toxic analog of glucose-6P |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: The YdjG protein belongs to subfamily 11 of the aldo-keto reductase superfamily. Members of this family generally use NADPH as the cosubstrate, although some are able to use both NADH and NADPH. YdjG is the first member of this family that is only able to use NADH. The crystal structure of the dual-specificity xylose reductase from Candida tenuis identified a conserved glutamic acid residue which appears to allow binding of both NAD+ and NADP+. Mutagenesis of the analogous residue in YdjG, D232A or D232E, converts YdjG into a dual-specificity enzyme |CITS: |. The purified enzyme was found to possess a relatively high activity with methylglyoxal as the substrate (Kcat = 15.7 s-1) |CITS: |. The physiological significance of this activity has not been investigated. YdjG is important for survival under competitive planktonic growth conditions |CITS: |. YdjG protein levels appear to be higher in gnotobiotic mice colonized with E. coli than in comparable growth medium; in an assay for intestinal colonization of gnotobiotic mice, a ydjLKJIHG deletion mutant reached a 1.2-log-lower cecal concentration than the wild type at certain time points during the experiment |CITS: |. Overexpression of ydjG was utilized to increase production of 1,2-propanediol in a metabolically engineered strain |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: N-ethylmaleimide reductase (NemA) is a member of the "old yellow enzyme" family of flavoproteins and catalyzes the reduction of N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) to N-ethylsuccinimide |CITS: |. NEM modifies the cysteine residues of cellular proteins and thus inhibits growth. NemA is probably involved in the degradation of toxic compounds and their reuse as a source of nitrogen |CITS: |. NemA is able to accept a variety of substrates, including the nitrate ester explosives pentaerythritol tetranitrate (PETN) and glycerol trinitrate (GTN) |CITS: |, quinones |CITS: |, and chromate |CITS: |. NemA can activate the nitroaromatic prodrug CB1954 |CITS: |. E. coli K-12 AB1157 can utilize 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene (TNT) as a source of nitrogen. NemA together with NfsA and NfsB is responsible for this ability |CITS: |. NemA activity is induced by menadione, dimethyl maleate and linoleic acid, possibly due to lipid peroxidation |CITS: |. Transcription of nemA is repressed by NemR, which is inactivated by alkylation |CITS: | or reversible oxidation of cysteine residues |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of a signaling cascade that regulates curli biosynthesis. The cascade is composed of two cyclic-di-GMP (c-di-GMP) control modules, in which c-di-GMP controlled by the DgcE/PdeH pair (module I) regulates the activity of the DgcM/PdeR pair (module II), which in turn regulates activity of the transcription factor MlrA and expression of the master biofilm regulator csgD (PubMed:23708798). DgcM stimulates activity of MlrA by direct interaction, leading to the transcription of csgD. It also catalyzes the synthesis of c-di-GMP via the condensation of 2 GTP molecules, which contributes to the c-di-GMP pool generated by module I in a positive feedback loop. Production of c-di-GMP contributes to but is not essential for MlrA activation (PubMed:17010156, PubMed:23708798). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17010156, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23708798}.

MetaCyc_Comment: MppA is the periplasmic binding protein of an ABC transporter that mediates the high affinity uptake of murein tripeptides |CITS: |. mppA mutants cannot use murein tripeptide (L-alanyl-γ-D-glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelate) as a source of diaminopimelic acid (Dap) in a strain that requires Dap for growth |CITS: |. MppA (in the absence of the periplasmic oligopeptide binding protein OppA) supports growth of a proline auxotroph on Pro-Phe-Lys tripeptide; MppA transports murein tripeptide more efficiently than Pro-Phe-Lys |CITS: |. Purified MppA binds murein tripeptide with sub micromolar affinity and the synthetic tripeptide L-Ala-γ-D-Glu-L-Lys with 500-fold lower affinity; it does not bind conventional tripeptides such as Lys-Glu-Lys, Lys-Lys-Lys, Ala-Lys-Lys and others |CITS: |. Crystal structures of MppA in an open, unliganded conformation and in a closed conformation with murein tripeptide bound have been reported; MppA contains two relatively rigid domains connected by a flexible linker; ligand binding is associated with large conformational change wherupon the the molecule transitions from an open form with a solvent accessible cleft to a closed form containing a single molecule of murein tripeptide completely buried within the protein |CITS: |. MppA supports the uptake of heme and the heme precursor γ-aminolevulinic acid, in a recombinant strain of E. coli that expresses an outer membrane heme receptor (HasR from S. marcescens); heme uptake requires the membrane components of the dipeptide ABC transporter (DppBCDF) and either of the periplasmic binding proteins DppA or MppA; purified MppA binds heme; tripeptide is a competitor for heme binding invitro |CITS: |. mppA is implicated in the adaptive response to acetate and propionate; mppA expression decreases after growth in complex medium with acetate or propionate |CITS: |. mppA is a member of the PgrR regulon; PgrR binds to an upstream site of mppA; mppA expression is increased in a pgrR deletion mutant; mppA expression increases under nitrogen starvation |CITS: |. mppA: murein peptide permease A |CITS: | Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Glycerate kinase II (GKII), encoded by glxK, catalyzes the phosphorylation of D-glycerate. The product of the reaction (with the enzyme from E. coli Crooke's strain) was initially identified as 3-phosphoglycerate |CITS: |. More recent biochemical |CITS: | and in vivo metabolic assays showed that the product is in fact 2-phosphoglycerate |CITS: |. There are two glycerate kinases, known as GKI and GKII, in E. coli. GKII is less thermostable and has a narrower pH optimum than GKI |CITS: |. Glycerate kinase II is induced by growth on glycolate as the carbon source |CITS: |. A glxK mutant is unable to utilize glyoxylate |CITS: |. In contrast, |CITS: | state that deletion of glxK does not result in a growth defect with glycolate, glyoxylate or glycerate as sole carbon sources, although the data are not shown.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Chaperedoxin that combines a chaperone activity with a redox-protective function (PubMed:16563353, PubMed:18657513, PubMed:29754824). Involved in the protection against hypochlorous acid (HOCl), the active ingredient of bleach, which kills bacteria by causing protein aggregation (PubMed:29754824). Functions as an efficient holdase chaperone that protects the substrates of the major folding systems GroEL/GroES and DnaK/DnaJ/GrpE from aggregation. In addition, it prevents the irreversible oxidation of its substrates through the formation of mixed disulfide complexes (PubMed:29754824). After bleach stress, it transfers its substrates to the GroEL/GroES and DnaK/DnaJ/GrpE foldases (PubMed:29754824). Lacks oxidoreductase activity (PubMed:21498507, PubMed:29754824). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:16563353, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18657513, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21498507, ECO:0000269|PubMed:29754824}.

MetaCyc_Comment: ArnA is a bifunctional enzyme that acts within a pathway that modifies lipid A phosphates with 4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose (L-Ara4N), which causes increased resistance to polymyxin |CITS: |. ArnA exhibits UDP-glucuronic acid (UDP-GlcA) C-4"-dehydrogenase and UDP-4-amino-4-deoxy-L-arabinose (UDP-L-Ara4N) formyltransferase activities in vitro |CITS: |. The two activities are separable, and both are required for polymyxin resistance |CITS: |. The N-terminal domain is similar to methionyl-tRNAfMet formyltransferase and catalyzes the N10-formyltetrahydrofolate-dependent formylation of the 4'' amine of UDP-L-Ara4N |CITS: |. Crystal structures of this domain have been solved at 1.7, 1.2 and 2.5 Å resolution |CITS: |. The N10-formyltetrahydrofolate binding site has been identified and a reaction mechanism has been proposed; point mutations in the proposed catalytic residues abolish activity |CITS: |. The structure of the N-terminal domain in complex with both the UDP-sugar substrate and N5-formyltetrahydrofolate has provided additional insight into the substrate binding site |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain contains the NAD+-dependent dehydrogenase/decarboxylase activity which catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of UDP-GlcA. Crystal structures of this domain have been solved at 2.4 and 2.3 Å resolution |CITS: |, and active site residues have been identified |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain is also able to inefficiently catalyze the reduction of UDP-α-D-4-ketoxylose to UDP-α-D-xylose in an overall reaction similar to the human UDP-α-D-xylose synthase. Local unfolding of the active site is proposed to direct formation of the preferred product |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the full-length protein in the apo- and substrate-bound forms have been solved |CITS: |. The enzyme forms a homohexamer in a dimer-of-trimers configuration. The dehydrogenase domain undergoes a large conformational change upon binding of the substrate UDP-GlcA; a catalytic mechanism was proposed |CITS: |. A central pocket present in the unliganded structure is proposed to bind a small-molecule effector |CITS: |. ArnA was also identified as a protein that copurifies with the SsrA-SmpB complex |CITS: | and is often a contaminant during purification of recombinant His-tagged proteins |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: During anaerobic β-oxidation of fatty acids, FadI, FadJ, and FadK serve functions parallel to those of FadA, FadB, and FadD in the aerobic pathway |CITS: |. FadJ shows sequence similarity to FadB; the enoyl-CoA hydratase, 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA epimerase, and 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase active site residues appear to be conserved. In a strain engineered for polyhydroxyalkanoate (PHA) production, FadJ is essential for processing of long-chain fatty acids to medium-chain PHA if fadB is absent. Crude cell extracts from a strain that overproduced FadJ contain increased enoyl-CoA hydratase and 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity |CITS: |. FadJ and FadI exhibit partial functional redundancy with FadA and FadB under aerobic conditions; the two complexes are proposed to increase efficiency of β-oxidation by favoring substrates of different chain length |CITS: |. FadR represses transcription of fadIJ in the presence of oxygen |CITS: |. Transcription of fadJ is induced upon biofilm formation compared to planktonic growth in both exponential and stationary phase. Induction of expression was found to be independent of the presence of the F plasmid |CITS: |. A fadJ mutant is impaired in biofilm formation |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: SufS is one of three members of the NifS protein family in E. coli |CITS: |. The protein was initially thought to function mainly as a pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent selenocysteine lyase with high specificity for L-selenocysteine |CITS: |. It was later determined that SufS functions as a PLP-dependent cysteine desulfurase in a secondary pathway of iron-sulfur cluster assembly |CITS: |; the isc operon encodes the major assembly pathway |CITS: |. The Suf system appears to be responsible for Fe-S cluster synthesis when iron or sulfur metabolism is disrupted by iron starvation or oxidative stress |CITS: |. SufS-SufE is less susceptible to oxidative modification than IscS-IscU |CITS: |. The overall cysteine desulfurase reaction involves two half reactions: the desulfurase reaction with release of L-alanine and concomitant formation of a persulfide intermediate on an active site cysteine residue, and a transpersufurase reaction by which the persulfide is transfered to a cysteine residue in an acceptor protein. In the case of SufS, the conserved C364 residue is modified to the persulfide intermediate from which the sulfur can be transferred to Cys51 of |FRAME: G6905-MONOMER SufE| |CITS: |. A "half-sites" mechanism, where catalytic activity alternates between the monomers of the homodimeric SufS, was proposed. Such a mechanism requires communication between the monomers. The dimer interface of SufS indeed undergoes conformational changes upon formation of the C364 persulfide intermediate, which provides a mechanism for communication between its two active sites |CITS: |. Crystal structures of wild-type and mutant SufS confirm that the dimer interface plays a functional role in mediating conformational changes resulting in reorientation of the persulfide intermediate, as well as affecting interactions with SufE |CITS: |. SufE, together with the SufB-SufC-SufD complex, was initially found to stimulate the cysteine desulfurase activity of SufS |CITS: |. SufE is both a cosubstrate, accepting sulfur at its C51 residue from the Cys364 persulfide of SufS, and an activator. SufE binds near the active site of SufS and modulates the site's backbone dynamics |CITS: |. The kinetic mechanism of sulfur transfer between SufS and SufE has been investigated, and a model for a protected sulfur transfer pathway of the Suf system has been proposed |CITS: |. SufS facilitates the formation of the iron-sulfur cluster of ferredoxin in vitro, but does not interact with the IscU scaffold, which acts with IscS in iron-sulfur cluster assembly |CITS: |. Like CsdA and IscS, SufS can transfer sulfur from L-cysteine to activate |FRAME: CPLX0-2502 "MPT synthase"| in vitro. Of the three enzymes, CsdA is the most effective, while SufS shows the lowest activity |CITS: |. SufS does not play a role in formation of the dithiolene group of molybdopterin |CITS: | or in iron-sulfur cluster-independent tRNA thionucleoside modification |CITS: |; SufS does not interact with either TusA or ThiI |CITS: |. However, the SUF system is able to provide iron-sulfur clusters to the thiomodification enzymes TtcA and MiaB |CITS: |. Non-specific incorporation of selenium into proteins appears to occur via synthesis of free selenocysteine by the cysteine biosynthesis pathway |CITS: |. Free selenocysteine it is likely to be toxic to the cell; SufS may be responsible for its degradation |CITS: | and thereby also play a role in the provision of selenium to the selenophosphate synthesis protein |FRAME: EG10943-MONOMER "SelD"| |CITS: |. SufS crystal structures have been solved in various conformations |CITS: |. A C364A mutation at the predicted catalytic cysteine results in a severe defect in L-cysteine desulfurization, but a more mild defect in activity toward L-selenocysteine |CITS: |. sufD, sufS or fhuF mutants exhibit a defect in utilization of ferrioxamine B as a source of iron |CITS: |. A sufABCDSE deletion mutant grows normally, whereas a sufABCDSE isc double mutant exhibits synthetic lethality, indicating that these systems are redundant and that iron-sulfur cluster assembly is essential for viability. Overproduction of the sufABCDSE operon suppresses the growth defects of a Δisc strain |CITS: |. Expression of the suf operon is activated in response to oxidative stress by OxyR |CITS: | and IHF |CITS: | and is regulated in response to iron starvation by Fur |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: JW0474 refers to the Keio knockout strain BW25113 ΔybaS, i.e., the ybaS gene. The article states that ybaS encodes a glutaminase that contributes to acid resistance in Escherichia coli. Under isobutanol stress, ybaS expression is strongly up‑regulated (≈7‑fold). Deletion of ybaS (ΔybaS) leads to a noticeable decrease in growth when the cells are challenged with 1.2% (v/v) isobutanol, indicating that YbaS plays a role in enhancing isobutanol tolerance, likely through its involvement in acid‑stress response. {PubMed:24203355}. The ybaS gene encodes an Escherichia coli glutaminase (EC 3.5.1.2) that catalyzes the hydrolytic deamidation of L‑glutamine to L‑glutamate and free NH₄⁺. YbaS displays strict specificity for L‑glutamine, exhibits a relatively high affinity (Kₘ ≈ 7.3 mM), and functions as a tetrameric enzyme with a β‑lactamase‑like fold and conserved catalytic residues (Ser66, Lys69, Lys259, Ser260, etc.). In addition to its primary metabolic role in controlling intracellular glutamine pools and contributing to glutamine assimilation, YbaS shows increased activity at low pH and is up‑regulated during acid shock, indicating a role in E. coli acid‑resistance mechanisms. The protein also retains low β‑lactamase activity and can be competitively inhibited by β‑lactam antibiotics. {PubMed:18459799}. ybaS encodes a glutaminase (glutaminase A) that hydrolyzes L‑glutamine to L‑glutamate and ammonia. This activity provides Gln‑dependent acid tolerance and supports the glutamate‑dependent acid‑resistance system by supplying intracellular glutamate, which can be decarboxylated to γ‑aminobutyric acid to consume protons. During copper stress, ybaS expression and enzymatic activity are up‑regulated, allowing the cell to convert exogenous glutamine into glutamate and thereby compensate for copper‑induced inhibition of glutamate synthase (GOGAT) and maintain the glutamate pool needed for acid tolerance and overall copper tolerance. {PubMed:28611214}. Encodes the Escherichia coli glutaminase YbaS, a 310‑amino‑acid, tetrameric enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of L‑glutamine to L‑glutamate (glutaminase activity) under acidic conditions (pH 4–6). In the article, YbaS is used as a model enzyme to evaluate how immobilization in mesoporous silica affects its thermostability, aggregation resistance, and catalytic activity. {PubMed:29768820}. YbaS encodes a glutaminase (glutamine ammonia‑lyase) from Escherichia coli that catalyzes the conversion of glutamine to ammonia (and glutamate) without requiring cofactors. In the study, YbaS was displayed on the surface of Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells, where it efficiently deaminated extracellular glutamine, producing high concentrations of ammonia (e.g., 3.34 g/L from 32.6 g/L glutamine, 83.2% conversion) and enabling ammonia production from glutamine present in pretreated soybean residues. {PubMed:32296960}. YbaS encodes an acid‑activated glutaminase that catalyzes the deamidation of L‑glutamine (Gln) to L‑glutamate (Glu) with the release of gaseous ammonia (NH₃). Its enzymatic activity is robust at pH 6.0 or lower (maximal around pH 4.0) and negligible at neutral or alkaline pH. YbaS is essential for Gln‑mediated acid resistance in Escherichia coli: deletion of ybaS abolishes the protective effect of extracellular Gln under extreme acidic conditions (pH 2.5), while complementation with a ybaS‑expressing plasmid restores survival and ammonium production. The ammonia generated is protonated to NH₄⁺, helping to neutralize intracellular protons and raise intracellular pH. YbaS functions together with the amino‑acid antiporter GadC, which imports Gln and exports Glu, forming a two‑component acid‑resistance system that enables E. coli to survive in highly acidic environments. {PubMed:23337585}. Acid‑activated glutaminase that catalyzes the conversion of L‑glutamine to L‑glutamate with concomitant release of ammonia (NH₃). The generated NH₃ can neutralize intracellular protons, thereby raising intracellular pH and contributing to pH‑homeostasis and acid‑resistance (AR2) under acidic conditions and butanol stress. {PubMed:35517002}. Encodes a glutaminase that contributes to acid resistance in E. coli. In the CRP mutant IB2, ybaS expression was strongly up‑regulated (~7‑fold) under isobutanol stress, and deletion of ybaS caused increased isobutanol sensitivity, indicating that ybaS participates in the acid‑resistance response and helps improve isobutanol tolerance, likely acting downstream of CRP via GadX regulation. {PubMed:24203355}. The ybaS gene encodes an acid‑active glutaminase (also referred to as YbaS or GlsA) that catalyzes the deamination of L‑glutamine to L‑glutamate at acidic pH (approximately pH 4–6). This enzyme provides the glutamine‑dependent component of the AR2_Q (glutamine‑dependent acid resistance) system in Enterobacteriaceae such as Escherichia coli. In this system, YbaS supplies glutamate from extracellular glutamine; the glutamate can then be decarboxylated by GadB (glutamate decarboxylase) to γ‑aminobutyrate (GABA), while the antiporter GadC imports glutamine and exports either glutamate or GABA, thereby consuming protons and protecting the cell from extreme acid stress (pH ≤ 2.5). The activity of YbaS is essential for glutamine utilization under acid stress, and loss of ybaS abolishes glutamine consumption and impairs the AR2_Q phenotype. {PubMed:30498489}. glsA1 encodes a bacterial glutaminase belonging to the β‑lactamase superfamily (designated YbaS in Escherichia coli and YbgJ in Bacillus subtilis). The enzyme catalyzes the hydrolytic deamidation of L‑glutamine to L‑glutamate and free NH₄⁺, showing strict specificity for L‑glutamine and no activity toward D‑glutamine or L‑asparagine. It possesses a β‑lactamase‑like fold with a conserved Ser‑X‑X‑Lys catalytic motif (Ser66 in YbaS, Ser74 in YbgJ) that acts as the nucleophile in a mechanism involving a covalent glutamyl‑enzyme intermediate. Kinetic analysis shows a relatively high affinity for glutamine (Kₘ ≈ 7.3 mM for YbaS/YbgJ) compared with the paralogous glutaminase GlsA2. In E. coli, YbaS (GlsA1) contributes to glutamine assimilation as a carbon and nitrogen source and enhances acid resistance, while in B. subtilis YbgJ (GlsA1) is induced by glutamine via the GlnK‑GlnL two‑component system and participates in glutamine uptake and metabolism. The protein functions as a tetramer in solution. {PubMed:18459799}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the hydrolysis of L‑glutamine to L‑glutamate and ammonia (NH₄⁺). {PubMed:18459799, PubMed:24203355, PubMed:28611214, PubMed:30498489, PubMed:32296960, PubMed:35517002, PubMed:29768820}. Contributes to acid resistance by providing glutamate for the glutamine‑dependent AR2_Q system, whereby the generated ammonia neutralizes intracellular protons. {PubMed:18459799, PubMed:23337585, PubMed:35517002, PubMed:30498489, PubMed:24203355}. Enhances tolerance to isobutanol (and other alcohols) through its role in acid‑stress response. {PubMed:24203355, PubMed:35517002}. Is up‑regulated during acid shock, copper stress, isobutanol stress, and butanol stress, indicating involvement in multiple stress responses. {PubMed:18459799, PubMed:24203355, PubMed:28611214, PubMed:35517002}. Functions as a tetrameric enzyme with a β‑lactamase‑like fold and a conserved Ser‑X‑X‑Lys catalytic motif. {PubMed:18459799, PubMed:30498489}. Enables efficient extracellular glutamine deamination when displayed on yeast cells, facilitating ammonia production from glutamine‑rich substrates. {PubMed:32296960}. MetaCyc_Comment: GlsA (YbaS) is a glutaminase that is highly selective for L-glutamine. MetaCyc_Comment: tcyP encodes an inner membrane L-cystine transporter in E. coli K-12 |CITS: |. Two cystine uptake systems (now known to be the ABC transporter |FRAME: CPLX0-8152 "TcyJLN"| and TcyP) were first identified in E. coli W |CITS: |. TcyP is responsible for the majority (approx. 80%) of L-cystine uptake during growth on minimal salts media; transport of labeled L-cystine is inhibited by L-cysteine and to a lesser extent D-cystine |CITS: |. TcyP also mediates the import of S-sulfocysteine for use as a sulfur source |CITS: |. Under aerobic growth conditions, E. coli imports cystine as an economical alternative to sulfate assimilation; E. coli lacks a dedicated cysteine importer and under anaerobic conditions when cysteine remains in the reduced form cells may assimilate sulfur from hydrogen sulfide |CITS: |. TcyP is also able to transport the toxic compounds L-selenaproline and L-selenocystine |CITS: |. TcyP imports L-homocystine as a methionine precursor |CITS: |. Both TcyP and TcyJLN function to replenish cysteine pools in sulfur starved cells; TcyP is the primary transporter when cystine is abundant whereas the high affinity ABC transporter, TcyJLN, functions when cystine is scarce |CITS: |. TcyP may have specificity for compounds containing disulfide bonds that can be reductively cleaved |CITS: |. Disruption of tcyP (ΔcysE ydjN::kan) results in the inability to grow with S-sulfocysteine as the sole source of sulfur; sulfocysteine uptake accelerates when tcyP is overexpressed and is eliminated when tcyP is deleted |CITS: |. ΔtcyP cells have a significantly reduced rate of 14C-cystine import compared to wild type; rapid cystine import by TcyP results in a H2O2 supersensitive phenotype when cells are pregrown in sulfate media and then grown in cystine media and exposed to H2O2 |CITS: |. When cystine is abundant, TcyP imports more than the cell requires; excess cysteine is exported thus setting up a futile import/reduction/export cycle |CITS: |. TcyP, TcyJLN and the L-cysteine exporter |FRAME: EG11639-MONOMER "EamA"| participate in an L-cystine/L-cysteine shuttle system which is suggested to protect the cell membrane under oxidative stress conditions; L-cystine importers (TcyJLN and TcyP) cooperate with an L-cysteine exporter (EamA) to supply reducing equivalents to the periplasm; operation of the shuttle is implicated in the protection against periplasmic H2O2 |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). tcyP is expressed as a monocistronic transcript; expression is regulated by CysB and is induced when cells are grown with poor sulfur sources such as sulfate and djenkolate and repressed during growth with cystine |CITS: |. TcyP belongs to the Dicarboxylate/Amino Acid:Cation Symporter (DAACS) family of transporters |CITS: |. TcyP (and other proteins of the CysB regulon) contain very few cysteine residues which is probably the result of selection against cysteine due to the strict requirement for TcyP (and other CysB regulon proteins) when intracellular cysteine levels fall |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: Succinylornithine transaminase (AstC) catalyzes the third reaction in the ammonia-producing arginine catabolic pathway, |FRAME: AST-PWY|. The astC gene is 60% identical to |FRAME: EG10066 "argD"|, which encodes the arginine-repressible N-acetylornithine aminotransferase |CITS: |. Four enzymes, ArgD, AstC, GabT, and PuuE, show some level of N-acetylornithine aminotransferase (ACOAT) activity involved in arginine biosynthesis. On minimal medium lacking arginine, single argD or astC mutants have subtle growth defects, and an argD astC double mutant has a slower doubling time than wild type. Accumulation of suppressor mutations eventually allows growth of the triple mutant; an additional deletion of puuE eliminates this effect |CITS: |. The normal activities of two enzymes, ArgD and SerC, are sufficient for succinyldiaminopimelate (SDAP) and lysine biosynthesis; AstC is a third enzyme that is sufficient for SDAP biosynthesis, but alone can not fulfill the cell's requirement for lysine. Expression of argD, astC, serC, aspC, gabT, hisC, ilvE, patA, puuE, or tyrB from a plasmid allow growth of the triple ΔargD serC astC mutant on minimal medium |CITS: |. Crystal structures of AstC from E. coli BL21(DE3) have been solved. The enzyme is 99% identical to the E. coli K-12 enzyme |CITS: |. Expression of the enzymes of the AST pathway is regulated by arginine and nitrogen availability |CITS: | via ArgR and NtrC |CITS: |. Substrates include SelO itself, SucA, which is AMPylated on 'Thr-405', and GrxA, AMPylated on 'Tyr-13' (PubMed:30270044, PubMed:32966796). AMPylation of the grx family of enzymes may regulate protein S-glutathionylation levels in cells (PubMed:30270044). AMPylation is probably involved in redox homeostasis (PubMed:30270044). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:30270044, ECO:0000269|PubMed:32966796}.; FUNCTION: Under stress conditions, may act primarily as an uridylyltransferase that catalyzes the UMPylation of various proteins, including chaperones and transcription factors such as FlhDC and Fur (PubMed:32966796, PubMed:35532215, PubMed:35532216). Can also catalyze auto-UMPylation (PubMed:32966796). It can catalyze the Mn(2+)-dependent UMPylation on Tyr and His residues of chaperones such as GroEL, DnaK, HtpG and ClpB, leading to their inactivation (PubMed:32966796). Catalyzes the UMPylation on Ser-31 of the FlhC subunit of the major flagellar transcriptional regulator complex FlhDC (PubMed:35532215). UMPylated FlhDC complex completely loses its DNA binding activity, which inhibits the expression of secondary and tertiary flagellar genes, and interrupts flagellar synthesis (PubMed:35532215). Also catalyzes the UMPylation on His-118 residue of the major iron uptake regulator Fur, which destroys Fur dimers, (PubMed:35532216). Fur loses its DNA binding activity and therefore its repressor activity, which induces the expression of genes involved in iron uptake (PubMed:35532216). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:32966796, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35532215, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35532216}.

MetaCyc_Comment: SelO is a widely conserved member of the SELO family of pseudokinases |CITS: | that catalyzes the transfer of AMP from ATP to Ser, Thr, and Tyr residues on protein substrates (AMPylation) |CITS: |. Protein substrates for SelO include |FRAME: E1O-MONOMER SucA| and |FRAME: RED-GLUTAREDOXIN GrxA| |CITS: |. Active site residues were predicted based on the crystal structure of the Pseudomonas syringae enzyme; mutagenesis of these residues - K107, E130, R170, R177, D246, N247, and D256 - to alanine lead to loss of catalytic activity. Under non-reducing conditions, the formation of an intramolecular disulfide bond between Cys272 and Cys476 reduces the AMPylation activity of SelO |CITS: |. A selO mutant shows a modest decrease in global protein S-glutathionylation; after treatment with |FRAME: OXIDIZED-GLUTATHIONE oxidized glutathione|, the mutant shows a larger decrease in protein S-glutathionylation compared to wild type |CITS: |. Expression of selO is positively regulated by apo-IscR |CITS: |. SelO: "selenoprotein-O" |CITS: | (note that the E. coli protein does not contain a selenocysteine residue) Experiments reported in |CITS: | used E. coli Rosetta, which is a BL21 (DE3) derivative, as the source of the gene/protein and for the gene disruption experiments. The SelO protein sequence is approximately 98% identical to that of the K-12 strain.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Member of gene cluster sufABCDSE that mediates iron-sulfur cluster assembly under oxidative stress and iron limitation conditions (PubMed:17941825). Binds [2Fe-2S] and [4Fe-4S] clusters by mobilizing sulfur atoms provided by the SufS-SufE cysteine desulfurase system and then transfers the assembled Fe-S clusters to target proteins including ferredoxin and aconitase (PubMed:17350000, PubMed:19366265). Seems to act as a Fe-S cluster carrier rather than a scaffold, this role being performed by SufB and SufC (PubMed:19810706, PubMed:23018275). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17350000, ECO:0000269|PubMed:17941825, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19366265, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19810706, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23018275}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Allantoinase catalyzes the hydrolytic ring cleavage of allantoin at the amide bond between N3 and C4, the first step in the assimilation of allantoin. The enzyme has a very narrow substrate specificity |CITS: |. E. coli is able to utilize allantoin as a sole source of nitrogen under anaerobic conditions, but can not utilize it as a sole source of carbon |CITS: |. A crystal structure of allantoinase has been solved at 2.1 Å resolution. The active site residues Asn94 and Ser317 are important for enzymatic activity |CITS: |. Allantoinase activity is induced by growth on allantoin as the sole source of nitrogen |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the oxidation 4-aminobutanal (gamma-aminobutyraldehyde) to 4-aminobutanoate (gamma-aminobutyrate or GABA) (PubMed:16023116, PubMed:3510672). This is the second step in one of two pathways for putrescine degradation, where putrescine is converted into 4-aminobutanoate via 4-aminobutanal, which allows E.coli to grow on putrescine as the sole nitrogen source (PubMed:22636776, PubMed:3510672). Also functions as a 5-aminopentanal dehydrogenase in a a L-lysine degradation pathway to succinate that proceeds via cadaverine, glutarate and L-2-hydroxyglutarate (PubMed:30498244). Can also oxidize n-alkyl medium-chain aldehydes, but with a lower catalytic efficiency (PubMed:15381418, PubMed:16023116). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15381418, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16023116, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22636776, ECO:0000269|PubMed:30498244, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3510672}.

MetaCyc_Comment: γ-aminobutyraldehyde dehydrogenase (PatD) is the second enzyme in one of two pathways for putrescine degradation (|FRAME: PUTDEG-PWY|) |CITS: |. PatD also functions as a 5-aminopentanal dehydrogenase during degradation of L-lysine |CITS: |. It was initially reported that purified γ-aminobutyraldehyde dehydrogenase consists of a dimer of 95 kDa subunits |CITS: |; there are reasons to think that this enzyme was in fact |FRAME: ADHE-MONOMER "AdhE"| |CITS: |. Later purification showed the enzyme to be a homotetramer of 51 kDa subunits |CITS: |. Crystal structures of PatD have been solved. Analysis of the active site configuration as well as enzyme kinetics data suggested that PatD is a medium-chain aldehyde dehydrogenase with a preference for linear n-alkyl medium-chain aldehydes, using NAD as the cofactor |CITS: |. Expression of γ-aminobutyraldehyde dehydrogenase activity is regulated by catabolite repression and by nitrogen source |CITS: |. patD is part of the ydcSTUV-patD operon; transcription is controlled by σS and Nac |CITS: |. A patD mutant lost more than half of its of γ-aminobutyraldehyde dehydrogenase activity; a mutant lacking both patD and puuC lost 85% of this activity and did not utilize putrescine as the sole source of nitrogen |CITS: |. PatD: "putrescine aminotransferase pathway, dehydrogenase" |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Thioesterase III (FadM) is a long-chain acyl-CoA thioesterase that is involved in the β-oxidation of oleic acid. The enzyme is able to hydrolyze a number of related substrates. The best substrate is 3,5-tetradecadienoyl-CoA, which is a minor side product of oleate β-oxidation that is resistant to further degradation. The hydrolysis product, 3,5-tetradecadienoate, is released into the growth medium |CITS: |. Thioesterase III is expressed upon growth on oleic acid as the sole source of carbon |CITS: |. fadM is a member of the fad regulon; expression is induced by a number of fatty acids, with C18:1 as the best inducer |CITS: |. Reports disagree on whether |CITS: | or not |CITS: | conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) induces an even higher level of expression of fadM.

The sulfur is donated as persulfide by IscS. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10722656, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10753862, ECO:0000269|PubMed:18604845}.

MetaCyc_Comment: ThiI is a bifunctional enzyme that is required both for the conversion of uridine to 4-thiouridine (s4U) at position 8 in certain tRNAs and for the synthesis of the thiazole moiety of thiamine. Mutants in the biosynthesis of s4U-modified tRNA were initially identified by their easily selectable phenotype, e.g. |CITS: |. In wild-type strains under near-ultraviolet (UV) light, tRNAs containing s4U8 acquire an intra-tRNA crosslink between U8 and the nearby cytidine base at position 13 |CITS: |. These damaged tRNAs are poor substrates for aminoacylation |CITS: |, and the resulting uncharged tRNAs induce the stringent response and subsequent growth arrest. Mutants that are resistant to exposure to near-UV light were shown to lack s4U at position 8 of tRNAs |CITS: |. ThiI was biochemically identified as the "factor A" component required for s4U-tRNA biosynthesis |CITS: | and later purified based on thiI's ability to complement the nuvA mutant phenotype |CITS: |. The "factor C" component was later identified as |FRAME: G7325-MONOMER IscS| |CITS: |. In vitro studies using radiolabelled sulfur showed transfer of sulfane sulfur from IscS to ThiI; if tRNA is included, the sulfur is incorporated into the tRNA in a ThiI- and ATP-dependent manner |CITS: |. tRNA isolated from a strain containing the thiI D189A or K321M mutants lack s4U; these amino acid residues may be required for activating O4 of the U8 base in tRNA by adenylation |CITS: |. As of July 2020, the presence of an adenylated tRNA intermediate has not been shown directly. The C456 |CITS: | and C344 |CITS: | residues are critical for the sulfur transfer function of ThiI; a mechanism for sulfur transfer including the formation of a tRNA-adenylate intermediate and a disulfide bond between C456 and C344 during turnover has been proposed |CITS: |. Supporting a persulfide-disulfide-thiol cycle at C456, ThiI is unable to catalyze more than a single turnover in the absence of added reductant |CITS: |. The presence of an intra-subunit disulfide bond after a single catalytic turnover has been shown |CITS: |. ThiI was shown to interact with tRNA |CITS: |. The specificity for the U8 base of tRNA appears to be conferred by the secondary and tertiary structure of tRNA |CITS: |. The N-terminal domain of ThiI recognizes the acceptor-stem region of tRNA, while the C-terminal domain appears to induce a conformational change in the full-length tRNA |CITS: |. ThiI is required for the posttranslational formation of a thiocarboxylate modification at the C-terminal glycine residue of |FRAME: THIS-MONOMER| in vivo. ThiS isolated from a thiI-deficient strain does not contain this modification |CITS: |. Nuv: "near-UV" |CITS: |ThiI: |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the oxidation of D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HGA) to 2-oxoglutarate. Appears to be the only D2HGDH in E.coli, providing the way to recycle D-2-HGA produced during L-serine synthesis by SerA, by converting it back to 2-oxoglutarate. The physiological molecule that functions as the primary electron acceptor during D-2-HGA oxidation by YdiJ in E.coli is unknown. Shows strict substrate specificity towards D-2-HGA, since it has no detectable activity on L-2-hydroxyglutarate, L-malate, D-malate, L-lactate, D-lactate, L-tartrate, D-tartrate, L-glycerate, D-glycerate, glutarate, or pyruvate. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:36144368}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: An ATP-independent periplasmic chaperone, decreases protein aggregation and helps protein refolding. Binds substrate over a large region of its convex inner surface (PubMed:21317898, PubMed:24497545). Substrate protein folds while it is bound to chaperone (PubMed:26619265). Increasing Spy flexibility increases its substrate affinity and overall chaperone activity (shown for 3 different substrates) (PubMed:24497545). Protects proteins in vitro against tannin inactivation; tannins have antimicrobial activity (PubMed:21317898). Overexpression enhances the stability of otherwise unstable periplasmic proteins (PubMed:21317898). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:21317898, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24497545, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26619265}.

FUNCTION: Exoribonuclease that catalyzes the last steps of 5S, 16S and 23S rRNA 5'-end maturation. Removes 3 nucleotides (nt) from the 5' end of 5S, 16S and 23S rRNA precursors to generate the mature 5' ends. Precursors with longer extensions are not processed (7 nt at the 5' end of pre-23S rRNA or 66 nt at the 5'-end of 16S rRNA are not processed). 5S and 23S rRNA maturation occurs more efficiently and accurately on ribosomal particles as compared to free RNA; the enzyme overdigests free RNA but generates the correct 5'-end in ribosomes from rnm deletion strains (PubMed:32343306). Efficiently catalyzes the hydrolysis of the 3'-phosphate from 3',5'-bis-phosphonucleotides as well as the successive hydrolysis of 5'-phosphomononucleotides from the 5'-end of short pieces of RNA and DNA, with no specificity toward the identity of the nucleotide base. Is more efficient at hydrolyzing RNA oligonucleotides than DNA oligonucleotides. This enzyme can also hydrolyze annealed DNA duplexes, albeit at a catalytic efficiency approximately 10-fold lower than that of the corresponding single-stranded oligonucleotides. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:25871919, ECO:0000269|PubMed:32343306}.
