MetaCyc_Comment: RNase AM catalyzes the final maturation of the 5' ends of 5S, 16S and 23S rRNA. The enzyme exonucleolytically cleaves the final three nucleotides from the 5' ends of all three rRNAs; maturation takes place more accurately and efficiently in the context of the ribosome. 5' end processing of 23S rRNA is dependent on prior 3' end processing |CITS: |. RNase AM is a metal-dependent 5' → 3' exonuclease with a preference for short RNA oligonucleotides. Substrates must be phosphorylated at the 5'-end of the oligonucleotide; the enzyme does not hydrolyze oligonucleotides that are only phosphorylated at the 3' terminus. The enzyme hydrolyzes ssDNA substrates, but rates of catalysis are generally lower; dsDNA is a poor substrate. Purified RNase AM also hydrolyzes the 3' phosphate from 3'-5' bisphosphonucleotides |CITS: |. A down mutation in the yciV ribosome binding site increases fitness for growth on 18-20% cellulosic hydrolysate |CITS: |. Rnm: "RNase AM" Review: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Part of the outer membrane protein assembly complex (Bam), which is involved in assembly and insertion of beta-barrel proteins into the outer membrane. MetaCyc_Comment: E. coli can utilize alkanesulfonates as a sulfur source for growth. The ssuD gene encodes an FMNH2-dependent alkanesulfonate monooxygenase with a broad substrate range. It is able to desulfonate C-2 to C-10 unsubstituted alkanesulfonates, substituted ethanesulfonic acids, N-phenyltaurine, 4-phenyl-1-butanesulfonic acid and certain sulfonated buffers. The best substrates for the monooxygenase were decanesulfonic acid, octanesulfonic acid and 1,3-dioxo-2-isoindolineethanesulfonic acid |CITS: |. The ssuE-encoded |FRAME: CPLX0-224| provides the alkanesulfonate monooxygenase with FMNH2. The reductase and monooxygenase act as a two-component system |CITS: |. The presence of SsuD and the octanesulfonate substrate changes the kinetics of FMN reduction catalyzed by SsuE |CITS: |. Further studies showed the formation of a stable complex between SsuD and SsuE, which changes the flavin environment of FMN-bound SsuE |CITS: |. These results support a model for direct transfer of the reduced flavin from SsuE to SsuD. A crystal structure of the enzyme has been solved at 2.3 Å resolution. Comparison of the structure to the related structure of LuxA allowed identification of a possible active site |CITS: |. Kinetic studies indicate that ordered substrate binding, with the reduced flavin binding first, is important for SsuD catalytic activity |CITS: |. The Cys54 residue may be involved in stabilizing the C4a-(hydro)-peroxyflavin reaction intermediate |CITS: |. An R227A mutant lacks catalytic activity; Arg227 may therefore be involved in proton abstraction in the active site |CITS: |. The conserved Arg298 residue (position 297 in the mature polypeptide, within a dynamic loop region near the active site) is important for catalytic activity |CITS: |. Conformational changes in this loop region are required for catalysis; it appears to protect the reduced flavin cosubstrate from unproductive oxidation |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics simulations have been performed to study the interactions between the SsuD active site and the substrates as well as the flavin cosubstrate |CITS: |. An ssuD null mutant can not grow on methanesulfonate or L-cysteate as the sole source of sulfur |CITS: |. ssuD shows differential codon adaptation, resulting in differential translation efficiency signatures, in thermophilic microbes. It was therefore predicted to play a role in the heat shock response. An ssuD deletion mutant was shown to be more sensitive than wild-type specifically to heat shock, but not other stresses |CITS: |. SsuD: "sulfonate-sulfur utilization" |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

Uptake is abolished by the addition of the protonophore, carbonyl cyanide m-chlorophenyl hydrazaone |CITS: |. UacT also transports xanthine but with low affinity and low capacity |CITS: |. UacT contains 10 transmembrane helices plus 4 smaller helical segments within the membrane; the amino and carboxy termini are located in the cytoplasm |CITS: |. Amino acid residues critical for function have been identified; threonine at position 100 is essential for uric acid specificity |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) isomerase (Idi) catalyzes the reversible isomerization of isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) to dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP), a key step in the biosynthesis of isoprenoids. Idi catalyzes the reversible isomerization of IPP to DMAPP |CITS: |. The initial 5-6:1 ratio of IPP to DMAPP generated by |FRAME: CPLX0-7564| is adjusted to a final ratio of 3:7 by Idi |CITS: |. The enzyme requires two divalent cations for activity; a Zn2+ ion is located in a hexacoordinate His3Glu2 pocket and is part of the catalytic machinery, while the enzyme-substrate complex contains an additional Mg2+ ion that facilitates substrate binding. A wide variety of divalent metal ions can provide these functions |CITS: |. Crystal structures of free and metal-bound isopentenyl diphosphate isomerase enabled identification of the active site |CITS: |. Crystal structures of complexes with transition state analogues and irreversible inhibitors suggested a catalytic mechanism of protonation/deprotonation involving C67 and E116 |CITS: |, and crystal structures of site-directed mutants in C67 were obtained to confirm the proposed mechanism |CITS: |. Crystal structures of isopentenyl diphosphate isomerase together with the bromohydrin of IPP, an inhibitor of the enzyme, show covalent adducts of C67 and E116 |CITS: |. Crystal structures of mutants in the Y104 residue demonstrate its role in folding of IPP isomerase |CITS: |. The structure of isopentenyl diphosphate isomerase shows similarity to the Nudix hydrolases |CITS: |. E. coli isopentenyl diphosphate isomerase is a Type I enzyme. In contrast, Type II isopentenyl diphosphate isomerases are structurally unrelated and require reduced FMN and Mg2+ for activity |CITS: |. Isotope exchange studies of the reaction mechanism resulted in a proposal that ligand binding to the enzyme is relatively slow. This is due to a significant kinetic barrier to reorganization of the initial encounter complex between enzyme, substrate, and Mg2+ to form the Michaelis complex where the metal cation bridges the protein and the substrate diphosphate group |CITS: |. In metabolic engineering studies, co-expression of the idi gene was useful in increasing the production of lycopene |CITS: | and prenyl alcohols |CITS: | in E. coli. Suppressor mutations in ispH and idi enable growth at low temperature of a strain containing the uppS31 missense allele |CITS: |. idi is not essential for growth |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: GlcA (formerly YghK), is a glycolate transporter that belongs to the Lactate Permease Family (LctP) |CITS: |, due to its strong sequence similarity with the L-lactate permease, |FRAME: LCTP-MONOMER "LldP"|. GlcA transports the 2-hydroxymonocarboxylates, glycolate and L- and D-lactate |CITS: , |. The glcA gene is located downstream from the glcDEFGB encoding the glycolate degradating enzymes malate synthase and glycolate oxidase. Expression studies using Northern blot analysis and lacZ fusion experiments have shown that the glcA gene is transcribed from the same promoter as the other glc structural genes |CITS: |. Expression of this operon is induced by growth on glycolate and is under the control of the transcriptional regulator, |FRAME: G7546-MONOMER "GlcC"| |CITS: |. Growth of a glcA::cat mutant on glycolate was not totally abolished, but its rate was much lower than that of the parental strain, indicating that GlcA probably functions as a glycolate transporter, although glycolate can also enter the cell through another transport system |CITS: |. The lactate permease LldP was also found to be capable of glycolate transport. Growth on glycolate was abolished in a double mutant of the paralogous genes glcA and lldP, and restored with plasmids expressing either GlcA or LldP |CITS: |. Characterization of the putative substrates for these two related permeases showed, in both cases, specificity for the 2-hydroxy-monocarboxylates glycolate, L-lactate, and D-lactate |CITS: |.

FUNCTION: Aldo-keto reductase that catalyzes the stereospecific, NADPH-dependent reduction of L-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (L-GAP) to L-glycerol 3-phosphate (L-G3P) (PubMed:18620424). The physiological role of Gpr is the detoxification of L-GAP, which may be formed via non-enzymatic and/or enzymatic racemization of D-GAP (PubMed:18620424). Also contributes to cellular methylglyoxal detoxification by catalyzing the NADPH-dependent conversion of methylglyoxal to acetol (PubMed:12583903, PubMed:16077126). However, the catalytic efficiency of methylglyoxal reductase activity is more than 2 orders of magnitude lower than the L-GAP reductase activity (PubMed:18620424). MetaCyc_Comment: YghZ is an L-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (L-GAP) reductase |CITS: |; the enzyme is also able to detoxify methylglyoxal at a low rate |CITS: |. YghZ defines the AKR14 (aldo-keto reductase 14) protein family |CITS: |. L-GAP is not a natural metabolite and is toxic to E. coli |CITS: |. L-GAP is a substrate of both the glycerol-3-phosphate and hexose phosphate transport systems of E.coli K-12 |CITS: , |. |CITS: | postulate that the physiological role of YghZ is the detoxification of L-GAP, which may be formed by non-enzymatic racemization of GAP or by an unknown cellular process. Overexpression of yghZ allows a tpiA mutant to grow slowly on L-lactate as the source of carbon. tpiA mutants lack triosephosphate isomerase (TIM), and are thus unable to grow under conditions where gluconeogenesis is required |CITS: |. The YghZ protein does not possess TIM activity |CITS: |. YghZ overproduction results in decreased sensitivity to methylglyoxal, compared to wild type |CITS: |. Growth of a yghZ gloA double mutant is inhibited by 0.3 mM methylglyoxal |CITS: |. Expression of yghZ is not increased in response to methylglyoxal |CITS: |. The crystal structure of the E. coli enzyme has been determined and was suggested to be a tetramer |CITS: |. However, others have found that the protein forms an octamer based on gel filtration and electron micoscopy studies |CITS: | (author statement). Reviews: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Exhibits NADPH-dependent reductase activity for a broad range of short-chain aldehydes (PubMed:18211903, PubMed:19429550, PubMed:19609521, PubMed:20543070). Shows highest catalytic efficiency toward butanal, propanal and the highly toxic aldehydes acrolein and malondialdehyde (MDA), which are produced mainly during lipid peroxidation (PubMed:18211903, PubMed:20543070). Mediates resistance to reactive oxygen species (ROS) elicitors, such as paraquat and potassium tellurite, probably by protecting the cell against the toxic effects of reactive aldehydes derived from membrane lipid peroxidation (PubMed:18211903). Also acts, with lower efficiency, on acetaldehyde, glyceraldehyde, glycolaldehyde, methylglyoxal, glyoxal and hydroxyacetone (PubMed:18211903, PubMed:19609521, PubMed:20543070). Could be involved in glyoxal metabolism, by catalyzing the reduction of glyoxal to glycolaldehyde, and further to 1,2-ethandiol (PubMed:20543070). Catalyzes the reduction of isobutyraldehyde (2-methylpropanal) to isobutanol, and probably contributes to the production of isobutanol (PubMed:19609521). Can probably catalyze the reduction of glutaraldehyde, a widely used biocide, to 1,5-pentanediol, which is non-toxic (PubMed:34248896). Overexpression of YqhD protects the cells against glutaraldehyde toxicity (PubMed:34248896). Can catalyze in vitro the NADPH-dependent reduction of furfural, a natural product of lignocellulosic decomposition, to the less toxic product, furfuryl alcohol (PubMed:19429550). However, it is unlikely that furfural is a physiological substrate (PubMed:19429550). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:18211903, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19429550, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19609521, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20543070, ECO:0000269|PubMed:34248896}.; FUNCTION: In contrast, Sulzenbacher et al. detected significant activities only in the presence of alcohol and NADP(+) (PubMed:15327949). MetaCyc_Comment: YqhD is an NADPH-dependent aldehyde reductase that may be involved in glyoxal detoxification |CITS: | and/or be part of a glutathione-independent response to lipid peroxidation |CITS: |. YqhD appears to be the major glycolaldehyde reductase in E. coli |CITS: |. |CITS: | report that various alcohols, aldehydes, amino acids, sugars and α-hydroxy acids were tested as substrates for YqhD. The purified protein only showed NADP-dependent alcohol dehydrogenase activity, with a preference for alcohols longer than C(3), but with Km values in the millimolar range, suggesting that they are not the physiological substrates |CITS: |. In contrast, |CITS: | report that YqhD does exhibit short-chain aldehyde reductase activity with substrates such as propanaldehyde, acetaldehyde, and butanaldehyde, as well as acrolein and malondialdehyde. In a metabolically engineered strain, phenylacetaldehyde and 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde are reduced to 2-phenylethanol and 2-(4-hydroxyphenyl)ethanol by the endogenous aldehyde reductases YqhD, YjgB, and YahK |CITS: |. Overexpression of YqhD increases 1,3-propanediol oxidoreductase activity of the cell |CITS: |. The use of YqhD in the industrial production of 1,3-propanediol by engineered E. coli has been reviewed in |CITS: |. YqhD activity contributes to the production of isobutanol |CITS: |, 1,2-propanediol |CITS: |, 1,2,4-butanetriol |CITS: |, acetol |CITS: | and ethylene glycol |CITS: | as well. Mutation of yqhD enables production of butanol by an engineered one-turn reversal of the β-oxidation cycle |CITS: |. YqhD has furfural reductase activity, which appears to cause growth inhibition due to depletion of NADPH in metabolically engineered strains that produce alcohol from lignocellulosic biomass |CITS: |. YqhD abundance is almost 35-fold increased during growth with vanillin, and the enzyme has NADPH-dependent vanillin reductase activity |CITS: |. The crystal structure of YqhD has been solved at 2 Å resolution. YqhD is an asymmetric dimer of dimers, and the active site contains a Zn2+ ion. The NADPH cofactor is modified by hydroxyl groups at positions 5 and 6 in the nicotinamide ring |CITS: |. Molecular dynamics simulations with both NADP and NADPH found that the oxidation state of the cosubstrate influences the structure and dynamics of the enzyme |CITS: |. Overexpression of yqhD leads to increased resistance to reactive oxygen-generating compounds such as hydrogen peroxide, paraquat, chromate and potassium tellurite. yqhD mutants shows increased sensitivity to these compounds |CITS: | and to glyoxal |CITS: |, and contains increased levels of reactive aldehydes that are generated during lipid peroxidation |CITS: |. Conversely, yqhD deletion leads to increased furfural tolerance |CITS: |. Transcription of yqhD is induced by exposure to conditions of lipid peroxidation |CITS: |. Various microarray experiments showed induction of yqhD upon cold shock |CITS: |, nutrient limitation |CITS: |, n-butanol stress |CITS: |, and isopentenol stress |CITS: |. Transcription is activated by YqhC and enhanced by addition of glyoxal |CITS: |. Exposure of E. coli BL21 to tellurite leads to increased levels of YqhD |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

Shows broad specificity and can use aromatic aldehydes such as 4-nitrobenzaldehyde, 3-nitrobenzaldehyde and benzaldehyde, and phenylglyoxal (PubMed:16077126). MetaCyc_Comment: DkgA belongs to the aldo-keto reductase (AKR) family and has been shown to have methylglyxoal reductase |CITS: | and beta-keto ester reductase |CITS: | activity. dkgA was reported to encode 2,5-diketo-D-gluconate reductase (25DKGR) A, one of two 25DKG reductases in E. coli. The enzyme uses NADPH as the preferred electron donor and was thought to be involved in ketogluconate metabolism |CITS: |. The specific activity of the enzyme towards 2,5-diketo-D-gluconate was reported to be almost 1000-fold lower than its activity towards methylglyoxal |CITS: |. A crystal structure of DkgA has been solved at 2.16 Å resolution |CITS: |. DkgA abundance is more than 40-fold increased during growth with vanillin, and the enzyme has NADPH-dependent vanillin reductase activity |CITS: |. In a mutant of the ethanologenic E. coli strain LY180 that was selected for furfural resistance, dkgA expression is decreased. Expression of dkgA in this mutant decreases furfural tolerance |CITS: |. Due to its low Km for NADPH, reduction of furans by DkgA may deplete NADPH pools and thereby limit cellular biosynthesis |CITS: |. A broad survey of aldehyde reductases showed that DkgA was one of several endogenous aldehyde reductases that contribute to the degradation of desired aldehyde end products of metabolic engineering |CITS: |. Expression of dkgA is not increased in response to methylglyoxal |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Antitoxin component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system. Labile antitoxin that binds to the MqsR mRNA interferase toxin and neutralizes its endoribonuclease activity. Overexpression prevents MqsR-mediated cessation of cell growth and inhibition of cell proliferation. Initially reported to act as a cotranscription factor with MqsA (PubMed:19690171, PubMed:20105222). Following further experiments, the MqsR-MqsA complex does not bind DNA and all reported data are actually due to a small fraction of free MqsA alone binding DNA. Addition of MqsR to a preformed MqsA-promoter DNA complex causes dissociation of the MqsA-DNA complex, probably causing derepression of MqsA-repressed transcripts (PubMed:23172222). MqsA binds to 2 palindromes in the promoter region of the mqsRA operon activating its transcription. Binds to other promoters, inducing mcbR and spy and repressing cspD among others (PubMed:20105222). Binds to and represses the rpoS promoter, the master stress regulator, resulting in decreased cyclic-di-GMP, reduced stress resistance, increased cell motility and decreased biofilm formation; in these experiments 5 TA systems are missing (lacks MazEF, RelEB, ChpB, YoeB-YefM, YafQ-DinJ) (PubMed:21516113). An earlier study showed overexpression alone increases biofilm formation, perhaps by repressing cspD; in these experiments the 5 TA systems are present (PubMed:20105222). Represses the csgD promoter. In the presence of stress, when this protein is degraded, the promoters it represses are derepressed, leading to biofilm formation (Probable). This TA system mediates cell growth during bile acid deoxycholate stress by degrading mRNA for probable deoxycholate-binding protein YgiS; bile acid detergents such as deoxycholate are important for host defense against bacterial growth in the gall bladder and duodenum (PubMed:25534751). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19690171, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19943910, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20105222, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21516113, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23172222, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25534751, ECO:0000303|PubMed:24212724}.

FUNCTION: Toxic component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system. Plays a significant role in the control of biofilm formation and induction of persister cells in the presence of antibiotics. An mRNA interferase which has been reported to be translation-independent (PubMed:19690171, PubMed:19943910, PubMed:23289863). It has also been reported to be translation-dependent (PubMed:20041169). Cleavage has been reported to occur on either side of G in the sequence GCU (PubMed:19690171). Also reported to cleave after C in GC(A/U) sequences (PubMed:19943910). There are only 14 genes in E.coli W3110 (and probably also MG1655) that do not have a GCU sequence and thus are resistant to the mRNA interferase activity; among these is the gene for toxin GhoT. Overexpression of MqsR causes cessation of cell growth and inhibits cell proliferation via inhibition of translation as well as increasing persister cell formation; these effects are overcome by concomitant or subsequent expression of antitoxin MqsA. Cross-talk can occur between different TA systems. Ectopic expression of this toxin induces transcription of the relBEF TA system operon with specific cleavage of the relBEF mRNA produced (PubMed:23432955). Regulates the expression of GhoT/GhoS, a type V TA system (PubMed:23289863). Persistence depends on toxin GhoT activity, which MqsR controls at the post-transcriptional level by selectively degrading the antitoxin ghoS segment of the ghoST mRNA (PubMed:23289863). Overexpression leads to a dramatic increase in tolerance to the antibiotic ofloxacin. This TA system mediates cell growth during bile acid deoxycholate stress by degrading mRNA for probable deoxycholate-binding protein YgiS; bile acid detergents such as deoxycholate are important for host defense against bacterial growth in the gall bladder and duodenum (PubMed:25534751). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19690171, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19943910, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20041169, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23289863, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23432955, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25534751}.; FUNCTION: Initially reported to act as a cotranscription factor with MqsA (PubMed:19690171, PubMed:20105222). Following further experiments, the MqsR-MqsA complex does not bind DNA and all reported data are actually due to a small fraction of free MqsA alone binding DNA. Addition of MqsR to a preformed MqsA-promoter DNA complex causes dissociation of the MqsA-DNA complex, probably causing derepression of MqsA-repressed transcripts. Does not bind DNA in the presence or absence of MqsA (PubMed:23172222). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19690171, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20105222, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23172222}.

MetaCyc_Comment: NfeF is an NADPH-dependent ferric reductase; the enzyme contains FAD that is used as a cofactor rather than a substrate. The enzyme is only weakly active with purified ferric enterobactin |CITS: |; the hydrolyzed ferric enterobactin complex is the most efficient of the tested substrates |CITS: |. Reports disagree on whether the FAD cofactor is covalently bound to a cysteine sidechain via a thioether bond |CITS: | or not covalently attached |CITS: |. A preliminary report of crystallization and structure analysis of the NfeF protein has appeared. NfeF is structurally related to the NAD(P)H:flavin oxidoreductase superfamily |CITS: |. The reaction mechanism of NfeF has been investigated in detail; a transient flavosemiquinone is involved in the single-electron transfer in a double-displacement (ping-pong)-type reaction. The K55 and R130 residues are required for substrate binding and enzymatic activity. While the enzyme has high affinity for the intact ferric enterobactin, the catalytic turnover rate is much slower than for the hydrolyzed ferric triscatecholate |CITS: |. The slow growth phenotype of a fes deletion mutant is enhanced by deletion of nfeF, supporting a role for NfeF in adaptation to iron starvation. Deletion of nfeF increases the toxicity of nickel |CITS: |. nfeF is part of the Fur regulon |CITS: |; a candidate FUR box has been found upstream of the ORF |CITS: |. Expression of nfeF is repressed by both Fur and NfeR and is induced in response to nickel |CITS: |. NfeF: "Ni-responsive Fe-uptake flavoprotein" |CITS: | Review: |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat), is an adaptive immune system that provides protection against mobile genetic elements (viruses, transposable elements and conjugative plasmids) (PubMed:21255106, PubMed:24793649, PubMed:24920831). CRISPR clusters contain sequences complementary to antecedent mobile elements and target invading nucleic acids. CRISPR clusters are transcribed and processed into CRISPR RNA (crRNA). The Cas1-Cas2 complex is involved in CRISPR adaptation, the first stage of CRISPR immunity, being required for the addition/removal of CRISPR spacers at the leader end of the CRISPR locus (PubMed:24793649, PubMed:24920831, PubMed:25707795). The Cas1-Cas2 complex introduces staggered nicks into both strands of the CRISPR array near the leader repeat and joins the 5'-ends of the repeat strands with the 3'-ends of the new spacer sequence (PubMed:24920831). Spacer DNA integration requires supercoiled target DNA and 3'-OH ends on the inserted (spacer) DNA and probably initiates with a nucleophilic attack of the C 3'-OH end of the protospacer on the minus strand of the first repeat sequence (PubMed:25707795). Expression of Cas1-Cas2 in a strain lacking both genes permits spacer acquisition (PubMed:24793649, PubMed:24920831). Non-specifically binds DNA; the Cas1-Cas2 complex preferentially binds CRISPR-locus DNA (PubMed:24793649). Highest binding is seen to a dual forked DNA complex with 3'-overhangs and a protospacer-adjacent motif-complement specifically positioned (PubMed:26478180). The protospacer DNA lies across a flat surface extending from 1 Cas1 dimer, across the Cas2 dimer and contacting the other Cas1 dimer; the 23 bp-long ds section of the DNA is bracketed by 1 Tyr-22 from each of the Cas1 dimers (PubMed:26478180, PubMed:26503043). Cas1 cuts within the 3'-overhang, to generate a 33-nucleotide DNA that is probably incorporated into the CRISPR leader by a cut-and-paste mechanism (PubMed:26478180). Cas1 alone endonucleolytically cleaves linear ssRNA, ssDNA and short (34 base) dsDNA as well as branched DNA substrates such as Holliday junctions, replication forks and 5'-flap DNA substrates (PubMed:21219465). In vitro catalyzes a concerted transesterification reaction on branched DNA, as would be expected during integration of protospacers into the CRISPR leader sequence; Cas2 is not required in vitro. This reaction requires a 3'-OH group at the branch point (PubMed:26284603). Genetic interactions suggest Cas1 interacts with components of the RecBC and RuvB DNA repair systems (PubMed:21219465). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:21219465, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21255106, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24793649, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24920831, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25707795, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26284603, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26478180}.

CRISPR clusters are transcribed and processed into CRISPR RNA (crRNA).; FUNCTION: A component of Cascade, which participates in CRISPR interference, the third stage of CRISPR immunity. Cascade binds both crRNA and in a sequence-specific manner negatively supercoiled dsDNA target. This leads to the formation of an R-loop in which the crRNA binds the target DNA, displacing the noncomplementary strand. Cas3 is recruited to Cascade, probably via interactions with CasA, nicks target DNA and then unwinds and cleaves the target, leading to DNA degradation and invader neutralization. CasA is not required for formation of Cascade, but probably enhances binding to and subsequent recognition of both target dsDNA and ssDNA.

FUNCTION: Catalyzes the NADPH-dependent reduction of 7-cyano-7-deazaguanine (preQ0) to 7-aminomethyl-7-deazaguanine (preQ1), a late step in the queuosine pathway. Is highly specific for its natural substrate preQ0, since it cannot use various aliphatic, aromatic, benzylic and heterocyclic nitriles, such as acetonitrile, benzonitrile, benzylcyanide and 2-cyanopyrrole, although it can reduce the substrate analog 5-cyanopyrrolo[2,3-d]pyrimidin-4-one with lesser efficiency. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:15767583, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23410922, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23595998}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the removal of elemental sulfur and selenium atoms from L-cysteine, L-cystine, L-selenocysteine, and L-selenocystine to produce L-alanine, and transiently retains the released sulfur atom on a cysteine residue, in the form of a persulfide. Can also desulfinate L-cysteine sulfinate (3-sulfino-L-alanine), which is the best substrate of the enzyme. Functions as a selenium delivery protein in the pathway for the biosynthesis of selenophosphate. Seems to participate in Fe/S biogenesis by recruiting the SufBCD-SufE proteins. Transfers sulfur to CsdE that increases the cysteine desulfurase activity of CsdA. Can also transfer sulfur directly to TcdA/CsdL in vitro. Appears to support the function of TcdA in the generation of cyclic threonylcarbamoyladenosine at position 37 (ct(6)A37) in tRNAs that read codons beginning with adenine. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10829016, ECO:0000269|PubMed:15901727, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20054882, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23242255, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9278392}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the ATP-dependent dehydration of threonylcarbamoyladenosine at position 37 (t(6)A37) to form cyclic t(6)A37 (ct(6)A37) in tRNAs that read codons beginning with adenine. Plays a role in the catabolism of hexuronates under osmotic stress conditions, likely substituting for the regular hexuronate degrading enzyme UxaC whose expression is repressed in these conditions (PubMed:23437267). {ECO:0000250|UniProtKB:Q05529, ECO:0000269|PubMed:23437267}.

MetaCyc_Comment: KduI was a predicted 5-keto 4-deoxyuronate isomerase due to its high sequence similarity to the enzyme from Erwinia chrysanthemi. In unpurified form, the enzyme appeares to be able to utilize both glucuronate and galacturonate, perhaps catalyzing the same reaction as |FRAME: UXAC-MONOMER "UxaC"|. While UxaC expression is repressed under osmotic stress conditions, KduI expression appears to be unaffected, and it could therefore substitute for UxaC |CITS: |. The purified protein was recently shown to catalyze the activity of |FRAME: EC-5.3.1.17| in coupled assays with KduD from Pectobacterium carotovorum or Streptococcus agalactiae |CITS: |. Based on its structural similarity to the Pyrococcus furiosus phosphoglucose isomerase, catalytic activity of KduI was tested with a panel of substrates; the enzyme showed activity with glucose-6-phosphate, glucuronate, and fructose-6-phosphate. The enzyme binds zinc, but catalytic activity is metal-independent |CITS: |. Crystal |CITS: | and solution |CITS: | structures of KduI have been solved. The enzyme binds a metal ion tentatively identified as Zn2+ and is structurally similar to members of the cupin superfamily of proteins |CITS: |. In vivo homomultimeric KduI interaction can be detected in cross-linking experiments |CITS: |. Solution structure data obtained by SAXS suggests the existence of a mixture of high- and low-MM oligomers |CITS: |. Catalytic activity at different enzyme concentrations suggest that the active form of the enzyme is the homodimer |CITS: |. KduI was identified as a protein whose expression is 8-fold lower in E. coli found in the cecum of mice that were fed a casein diet compared to mice fed a starch diet |CITS: |. Expression of kduI is increased in the presence of galacturonate and glucuronate |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Protein and nucleotide deglycase that catalyzes the deglycation of the Maillard adducts formed between amino groups of proteins or nucleotides and reactive carbonyl groups of glyoxals (PubMed:26774339, PubMed:28596309). Thus, functions as a protein deglycase that repairs methylglyoxal- and glyoxal-glycated proteins, and releases repaired proteins and lactate or glycolate, respectively. Deglycates cysteine, arginine and lysine residues in proteins, and thus reactivates these proteins by reversing glycation by glyoxals. Is able to repair glycated serum albumin, collagen, glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, and fructose biphosphate aldolase. Acts on early glycation intermediates (hemithioacetals and aminocarbinols), preventing the formation of Schiff bases and advanced glycation endproducts (AGE) that cause irreversible damage (PubMed:25416785, PubMed:26774339). Also functions as a nucleotide deglycase able to repair glycated guanine in the free nucleotide pool (GTP, GDP, GMP, dGTP) and in DNA and RNA. Is thus involved in a major nucleotide repair system named guanine glycation repair (GG repair), dedicated to reversing methylglyoxal and glyoxal damage via nucleotide sanitization and direct nucleic acid repair. However, is less efficient than Hsp31 and YhbO, suggesting that YajL might be preferentially dedicated to protein repair (PubMed:28596309). Displays a covalent chaperone activity with sulfenylated thiol proteins by forming mixed disulfides with members of the thiol proteome, and preferentially with sulfenylated cellular proteins, upon oxidative stress; these mixed disulfides can be subsequently reduced by low-molecular-weight thiols to regenerate YajL and reduced proteins (PubMed:22157000, PubMed:22321799). Involved in biogenesis of ribosomal proteins, probably as a ribosomal protein-folding chaperone (PubMed:20889753). Confers resistance to oxidative stress (PubMed:20124404, PubMed:22157000, PubMed:22321799). Plays an important role in protection against electrophile/carbonyl stress (PubMed:26774339). The chaperone activity reported for YajL is probably recruited to execute its deglycase activity, to interact with non-native glycated proteins and gain access to partially buried glycated sites (PubMed:25416785, PubMed:26774339). Also displays an apparent glyoxalase activity that in fact reflects its deglycase activity (PubMed:26678554, PubMed:26774339). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:20124404, ECO:0000269|PubMed:20889753, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22157000, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22321799, ECO:0000269|PubMed:25416785, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26678554, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26774339, ECO:0000269|PubMed:28596309}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (FadE) catalyzes the first step in the degradation of fatty acids via the β-oxidation cycle |CITS: |. fadE mutants are unable to utilize oleate and other fatty acids as the sole source of carbon |CITS: |. The fadE62 allele is a single base deletion resulting in a frame shift mutation, and yafH can complement the phenotype of the fadE62 mutant strain |CITS: |. Expression of the enzymes involved in β-oxidation is normally induced by fatty acids of chain length 14 and longer |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Toxic component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system (PubMed:17263853). A sequence-specific mRNA endoribonuclease that inhibits translation elongation and induces bacterial stasis (PubMed:19210620). Cleavage occurs between the second and third residue of the Lys codon followed by a G or A (5'AAA(G/A)3'), is reading-frame dependent and occurs within the 5' end of most mRNAs (PubMed:19210620). Ribosome-binding confers the sequence specificity and reading frame-dependence (PubMed:19210620). When overexpressed in liquid media YafQ partially inhibits protein synthesis, with a reduction in growth rate and colony growth rate. This effect is counteracted by coexpression with cognate antitoxin DinJ (PubMed:17263853). YafQ and DinJ together bind their own promoter, and repress its expression (PubMed:24898247). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17263853, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19210620, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24898247}.; FUNCTION: Cell death governed by the MazE-MazF and DinJ-YafQ TA systems seems to play a role in biofilm formation (PubMed:19707553). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19707553}.

FUNCTION: Antitoxin component of a type II toxin-antitoxin (TA) system (PubMed:17263853). A labile antitoxin that counteracts the effect of cognate toxin YafQ (PubMed:17263853). YafQ and DinJ together bind their own promoter, and repress its expression (PubMed:24898247). There are 2 operators with imperfect inverted repeats (IR) in the dinJ promoter, YafQ-(DinJ)2-YafQ only binds to the first (most upstream) of them to repress transcription; binding to a single IR is sufficient for activity in vivo and in vitro (PubMed:24898247). DinJ alone is as potent a transcriptional repressor as the heterotetramer and also only needs to bind 1 IR to act (PubMed:24898247). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:17263853, ECO:0000269|PubMed:24898247}.; FUNCTION: Cell death governed by the MazE-MazF and DinJ-YafQ TA systems seems to play a role in biofilm formation (PubMed:19707553). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:19707553}.

FUNCTION: Transposase that is always flanked by repeated extragenic palindrome (REP) sequences, which are clustered in structures called bacterial interspersed mosaic elements (BIMEs). RayT catalyzes cleavage and recombination of BIMEs. Binds REP sequences and cleaves BIMEs both upstream and downstream of the REP sequence. Could be important in the creation of BIME variability and amplification. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:20085626, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22199259, ECO:0000269|PubMed:22885300}.

FUNCTION: Poorly processive, error-prone DNA polymerase involved in translesion repair and untargeted mutagenesis (PubMed:10488344, PubMed:10801133). Copies undamaged DNA at stalled replication forks, which arise in vivo from mismatched or misaligned primer ends. These misaligned primers can be extended by Pol IV. Exhibits no 3'-5' exonuclease (proofreading) activity (PubMed:10488344). Overexpression of Pol IV results in increased frameshift mutagenesis. It is required for stationary-phase adaptive mutation, which provides the bacterium with flexibility in dealing with environmental stress, enhancing long-term survival and evolutionary fitness. Not seen to be involved in translesion snythesis even when stimulated by the beta slding-clamp and clamp-loading complex, which do however increase non-targeted DNA polymerase efficiency 3,000-fold, may be due to targeting to stalled replication forks on nondamaged DNA (PubMed:10801133, PubMed:16168375). Involved in translesional synthesis, in conjunction with the beta clamp from PolIII (PubMed:14592985, PubMed:14729336). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10488344, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10801133, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11080171, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11463382, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11751576, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12060704, ECO:0000269|PubMed:14592985, ECO:0000269|PubMed:16168375, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9391106, ECO:0000305|PubMed:14729336}.

Catalyzes the conversion of oxalurate (N-carbamoyl-2-oxoglycine) to oxamate and carbamoyl phosphate (PubMed:38888336). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:34494882, ECO:0000269|PubMed:38888336}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Using genome and metabolic context methods, |CITS: | hypothesize that fdrA encodes an oxamate:CoA ligase which continues the degradation of oxamate produced by the |FRAME: PWY0-41 "anaerobic allantoin degradation pathway"|. The fate of oxamate is not clear; |CITS: | suggest that oxamate is not degraded further and they provide evidence that FdrA is critical for oxamate production during anaerobic allantoin degradation and may be the orphan enzyme |FRAME: OXAMATE-CARBAMOYLTRANSFERASE-RXN oxamate carbomoyltransferase|. In contrast to the wild-type, a ΔfdrA mutant does not produce oxamate during glycerol fermentation with allantoin as the sole nitrogen source |CITS: |. |FRAME: OXALATE Oxalate| production increases under these same conditions via an alternate pathway involving the |FRAME: G6275-MONOMER|-catalysed conversion of ureidoglycolate to urea and glycolate and subsequent oxidation of glycolate to oxalate likely by ldhA-encoded |FRAME: DLACTDEHYDROGNAD-MONOMER lactate dehydrogenase| |CITS: |. An fdrA-lacZ transcriptional fusion is induced by allantoin under anaerobic conditions |CITS: |. An N-terminally truncated version of fdrA acts as a multicopy suppressor of the phenotypes of a dominant negative ftsH mutation |CITS: |. Overexpression of fdrA leads to reduced motility and decreased levels of biofilm formation |CITS: |, while a knockout mutation in fdrA leads to repressed swarming motility |CITS: |. FdrA: "ftsH dominant rescue" |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: NudF is a member of the family of Nudix hydrolases |CITS: | and has ADP-sugar pyrophosphatase activity |CITS: |. ADP-glucose is a precursor molecule for glycogen biosynthesis; thus, it appears that the activity of NudF needs to be regulated. NudF is thought to control the flow of carbon toward glycogen, interconnecting gluconeogenesis with other metabolic pathways |CITS: |. NudF also contributes to the production of dimethylallyl phosphate, which is the substrate for |FRAME: UBIX-MONOMER UbiX|-catalyzed generation of the prFMN cofactor in ubiquinone biosynthesis |CITS: |. Gel filtration experiments indicate that the enzyme is a dimer in solution |CITS: |. Crystal structures of NudF in various forms have been solved, showing a domain-swapped dimer where the Nudix motif residues compose a catalytic center |CITS: |. Binding of the substrate and Mg2+ results in a conformational change from an open to a closed complex. The reaction mechanism involves a nucleophilic attack by water at the phosphorus of the adenosyl phosphate |CITS: |. NudF activity is enhanced by macromolecular crowding and is stimulated by glucose-1,6-bisphosphate and nucleotide sugars |CITS: |. A fraction of the enzyme becomes associated with the membrane during stationary phase |CITS: |. An E. coli enzyme with a similar catalytic activity has been purified and was thought to be localized in the periplasm |CITS: |. There is no effect on cell growth of either a nudF null mutation or nudF overexpression. However, a nudF null mutant contains increased amounts of glycogen, while overexpression of nudF leads to a reduced amount of glycogen in the cell |CITS: |. Transcription of nudF is induced by the CreBC two-component system by minimal media growth conditions |CITS: |. nudF shows differential codon adaptation, resulting in differential translation efficiency signatures, in thermophilic microbes. It was therefore predicted to play a role in the heat shock response. A nudF deletion mutant was shown to be more sensitive than wild-type specifically to heat shock, but not other stresses |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Cyanase is an inducible enzyme in E. coli and was first reported and subsequently studied in E. coli B |CITS: |. The cyanase operon may have evolved to function in detoxification/decomposition of cyanate arising from intra- and extracellular activities |CITS: |. It was shown that bicarbonate (HCO3-) is a substrate of the enzyme, and that water does not participate as a substrate |CITS: |. The initial product carbamate is unstable and spontaneously decomposes to ammonia and carbon dioxide |CITS: |. The enzyme shows competitive substrate inhibition by both substrates |CITS: |. The native enzyme from E. coli B has a molecular weight of ca. 150 kDa and thus appears to be a homodecamer in solution |CITS: |. A crystal structure of cyanase was solved at 1.65 Å resolution; it showed a homodecamer composed of five dimers. The structure allowed identification of the active site, which is located between dimers and is comprised of residues from four adjacent subunits |CITS: |. The free sulfhydryl group of the single cysteine residue is not required for catalytic activity, but plays a role in stabilizing the decameric structure |CITS: |. The single histidine residue is also required for the stability of the decamer and contributes to its catalytic properties |CITS: |. A mutant lacking cyanase is more sensitive to cyanate than the wild type |CITS: |; a cynS mutant is not able to use cyanate as the sole source of nitrogen |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: 2-Dehydro-3-deoxyphosphoheptonate aldolase (DAHP synthase) is involved in the first committed step of the chorismate pathway, which leads to the biosynthesis of aromatic amino acids. DAHP synthase catalyzes an aldol reaction between phosphoenolpyruvate and D-erythrose 4-phosphate to generate 3-deoxy-D-arabino-heptulosonate 7-phosphate (DAHP). |CITS: | There are three isozymes of DAHP synthase, each specifically feedback regulated by tyrosine, phenylalanine or tryptophan |CITS: |. DAHP synthase which is sensitive to tryptophan (DAHP synthase (Trp), AroH) is encoded by aroH. All three isozymes are metalloenzymes, and DAHP synthase (Trp) is activated by Fe2+ |CITS: |. There is a high degree of sequence identity (41%) between the three isozymes and the polypeptides are nearly identical in size |CITS: |. In wild-type cells grown in minimal media, DAHP synthase (Phe) makes up about 80% of the total DAHP synthase activity, DAHP synthase (Tyr) makes up about 20%, and DAHP synthase (Trp) makes up about 1% |CITS: |. Mutations in aroH lead to tryptophan-insensitive DAHP synthase |CITS: |. Essential regions for catalytic activity and feedback regulation have been described |CITS: |. Transcriptional control of aroH is mediated by the trpR repressor with the end products of the pathway acting as co-repressors |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: Bifunctional phosphoribosylanthranilate isomerase / indole-3-glycerol phosphate synthase (TrpC) carries out the third and fourth steps in the tryptophan biosynthesis pathway. The phosphoribosylanthranilate isomerase activity of TrpC catalyzes the Amadori rearrangement of its substrate into carboxyphenylaminodeoxyribulose phosphate |CITS: |. The indole-glycerol phosphate synthase activity of TrpC catalyzes the ring closure of this product to yield indole-3-glycerol phosphate |CITS: |. Early mutant studies identified N-(5'-phosphoribosyl)-anthranilate (PRA) |CITS: | and 1-(o-carboxyphenylamino)-1'-deoxyribulose-5'-phosphate (CDRP) |CITS: | as intermediates in the biosynthesis of tryptophan and provided evidence that a single polypeptide chain catalyzes both the conversion of PRA to CDRP and CDRP to indole-3-glycerol-phosphate (IGP) |CITS: |. These observations were confirmed by kinetic and mutant complementation studies which further demonstrated that the two reactions occur at two distinct, non-overlapping sites on the polypeptide and that CDRP is a free intermediate |CITS: |. Subsequent kinetic and ligand binding studies of the Escherichia coli enzyme, an excised PRA isomerase domain of this enzyme, and the naturally monofunctional PRA isomerase of Saccharomyces cerevisiae led to a proposed mechanism for the PRA isomerase reaction. Interestingly, in this mechanism, the spontaneous conversion of putative enol and keto tautomers of CDRP may limit the rate of tryptophan biosynthesis |CITS: |. In addition, studies involving expression of engineered monofunctional domains of the E. coli enzyme suggested that the PRA isomerase domain may stabilize the IGP synthase domain |CITS: |. Structural and kinetic studies of mutants allowed identification of catalytically important residues for the IGP synthase reaction |CITS: |. A number of structural studies show that TrpC has two individual domains, each catalyzing one of its two activities. Crystal structures to 2, 2.8, and 4 Å resolution, as well as protease studies, show that the two TrpC domains are distinct, each with a folding pattern of an 8-fold parallel β-α barrel |CITS: |. The amino-terminal domain carries out the synthase activity and the carboxy-terminal domain carries out the isomerase activity |CITS: |. The two active sites face away from each other, presumably precluding direct transfer of carboxyphenylaminodeoxyribulose phosphate from the isomerase site to the synthase site |CITS: |. The isolated synthase domain is unstable, suggesting that the combined domains may mutually stabilize each other |CITS: |. Like the α subunit of E. coli tryptophan synthase (TrpA), both the PRA isomerase and IGP synthase domains of E. coli TrpC contain the common (β/α)8-barrel (TIM barrel) protein fold (in |CITS: |). The PRA isomerase domain is of interest in the study of protein folding/unfolding pathways and their intermediates |CITS: | as well as in studies of molecular evolution |CITS: |. In addition, this fold in the IGP synthase domain has been used in studies of protein stability |CITS: |. TrpC is unique among the five enzymes in the tryptophan biosynthesis pathway in that it is not part of a multisubunit enzyme complex |CITS: |.

Merged_Functions: The xylA gene encodes the enzyme xylose isomerase (also referred to as glucose isomerase). This enzyme catalyzes the reversible isomerization of D-xylose to D-xylulose, a key step in the xylose utilization pathway of Clostridium thermosaccharolyticum. The gene product is a 439‑amino‑acid protein with a calculated molecular weight of ~50 kDa. In the organism, xylA is co‑expressed with the downstream xylB gene (encoding xylulokinase) and is likely part of an operon that is induced by xylose and repressed by glucose. The cloned xylA gene confers a xylose‑positive phenotype on an Escherichia coli xylA mutant, indicating that its product restores xylose fermentation capability. Additionally, the enzyme is of biotechnological interest because xylose isomerase is used industrially for large‑scale production of fructose syrups. {PubMed:8163183}. The xylA gene encodes xylose isomerase (EC 5.3.1.5), the enzyme that catalyzes the isomerization of D‑xylose to D‑xylulose, the initial step in the xylose utilization pathway of Escherichia coli. Its expression is induced by xylose and is controlled by a promoter located within a 700 bp BglII‑PvuII fragment upstream of the gene. xylA is organized in an operon with xylB, and the xylose isomerase activity is essential for growth on xylose as a sole carbon source. {PubMed:6330500}. The xylA gene encodes a bacterial xylose isomerase (EC 5.3.1.5). When expressed in the methylotrophic yeast Hansenula polymorpha, the enzyme catalyzes the isomerization of xylose to xylulose (and can also convert fructose to glucose). Expression of xylA restores the ability of an H. polymorpha Δxyl1 mutant (lacking xylose reductase) to grow on xylose as the sole carbon source, providing measurable xylose isomerase activity (approximately 18‑23 % of that in the native bacterial host). The presence of the enzyme does not alter ethanol production compared with the wild‑type yeast strain. {PubMed:16243589}. Encodes xylene oxygenase (XO), the enzyme that initiates the upper pathway of the TOL plasmid by oxidizing toluene and xylenes to their corresponding benzyl alcohols. The article states that xylA encodes xylose isomerase, the first enzyme required for xylose catabolism. The protein’s N‑terminal region is similar to chloroplast‑type ferredoxins, while its C‑terminal region resembles NADH‑ferredoxin reductases. {PubMed:32044035}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Leucine-tRNA ligase (LeuRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. LeuRS belongs to the Class IB aminoacyl tRNA synthetases; apart from sequence motifs within the active site, the different enzymes show little similarity in their primary amino acid sequences |CITS: |. Correct aminoacylation by LeuRS requires both an activation and an editing function |CITS: |. The CCA acceptor end of tRNALeu is essential for both the aminoacylation and editing reaction |CITS: |. Measurement of kinetic parameters for both reactions showed that the rate-limiting step for posttransfer editing is product release, and that its active site functions by kinetic partitioning between hydrolysis and dissociation of misacylated tRNA |CITS: |. LeuRS shows high initial substrate discrimination and appears to correct mistakes by posttransfer editing alone |CITS: |. LeuRS editing defects are lethal to the cell |CITS: |. The CP1 (connective polypeptide 1) domain, which splits the nucleotide binding fold |CITS: |, is required for the posttransfer editing function |CITS: |. The Thr251 residue is a critical specificity determinant |CITS: |, and two conserved Thr residues within CP1 play a central role in amino acid editing, possibly by stabilizing the transition state |CITS: |. The conserved Arg249 residue confers specific amino acid substrate recognition |CITS: |. The β-strands as well as the short flexible "hinges" connecting the CP1 domain to the aminoacylation core are required for editing of mischarged tRNALeu |CITS: |. The effect of point mutations in the β-strands on enzyme activity support the hypothesis that the flexibility and orientation of the β-strands is essential for function |CITS: |. Mutations in both hinge regions allow mischarged tRNAs to bypass the posttransfer editing site |CITS: |. The mechanistic details of posttransfer editing have been elucidated by a series of co-crystal structures of LeuRS with its substrate in the editing and aminoacylation conformations. Translocation of the 3' end of tRNAs from the aminoacylation to the editing site involves correlated rotations of four flexibly linked LeuRS domains |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the editing domain in complex with non-cognate amino acids showed that amino acid discrimination is based on a lock-and-key mechanism |CITS: |. A pretransfer editing activity can be unmasked by secondary mutations within the CP1 domain |CITS: | or by specifically inhibiting the posttransfer editing function |CITS: |. Deletion of the entire CP1 domain results in loss of posttransfer editing and unmasks a tRNA-dependent editing activity that resides in the aminoacylation active site |CITS: |. Deletion of the CP2 domain (residues 194-225) leads to loss of leucine activation, aminoacylation and posttransfer editing activities of LeuRS |CITS: |. In contrast to results with the yeast enzyme, deletion of the C-terminal domain of E. coli LeuRS nearly abolishes aminoacylation and editing activity |CITS: |. The length of the flexible peptide linker which connects the C-terminal domain to the main body of the enzyme is critical especially for the aminoacylation activitiy of the enzyme |CITS: |. The Leu570 residue is important for both amino acid discrimination and tRNA binding |CITS: |. The "leucine-specific domain" (amino acids 572-617) immediately upstream of the catalytic site is required for aminoacylation activity, but not post-transfer editing |CITS: |. leuS is an essential gene |CITS: |. Strains containing an editing-defective mutant allele show a growth defect when grown on medium containing isoleucine, methionine, valine, or various non-standard amino acids |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: GlpT is the major E. coli uptake system for sn-glycerol 3-phosphate, and this transporter belongs to the Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS) of transporters |CITS:|. Uptake of sn-glycerol 3-phosphate via the GlpT transporter leads to the simultaneous counterflow of inorganic phosphate from the cell |CITS:|. GlpT also catalyzes a reversible phosphate:phosphate exchange |CITS:|. Both sn-glycerol 3-phosphate:phosphate and phosphate:phosphate exchange activities were observed in GlpT-reconstituted proteoliposomes |CITS:|. Using phosphate-loaded proteoliposomes, the Km for the transport of sn-glycerol 3-phosphate via GlpT was estimated to be near 20 μM and the Vmax was 130 nmol min-1 mg-1 |CITS:|. GlpT has been crystallized and the structure has been determined by X-ray crystallography to a resolution of 3.3 Å |CITS:,|. The functional form of GlpT is the monomer |CITS:|. GlpT exhibits a rocker-switch mechanism of transport |CITS:| although transport via a 'tilted' mechanism has also been proposed |CITS:|. Experiments using PhoA/LacZ fusions revealed GlpT has twelve transmembrane segments |CITS:|. The residues involved in binding the substrate have been identified as well as the substrate binding mechanism which involves protonation of a histidine residue at the binding site. It has been suggested that translocation of the substrate occurs as a result of salt bridge formation and disruption |CITS:|. GlpT contains a putative charge-relay system located on the intracellular side of the protein; disruption of this network (through targeted mutation) triggers a conformational shift towards the inward facing state in vitro |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Mutants that lack the GlpT system fail to exchange internal phosphate for either external phosphate or sn-glycerol 3-phosphate |CITS:|. Is essential for de novo glutathione synthesis, thereby maintaining cellular redox balance, protecting against oxidative stress, detoxifying xenobiotics and supporting cell proliferation. {PubMed:1687097, PubMed:8828222, PubMed:27498196}. Increases cellular glutathione content when overexpressed, enhancing antioxidant capacity and improving yeast performance in industrial processes such as brewing. {PubMed:15104140}. Maintains intracellular potassium levels and regulates the KefB/KefC K⁺‑efflux channels, influencing ciprofloxacin‑induced K⁺ leakage and antibiotic susceptibility. {PubMed:27498196}. Synthesizes γ‑glutamylcysteine (γGC), the major low‑molecular‑weight thiol in Haloferax volcanii, and complements an Escherichia coli ΔgshA mutant. {PubMed:19525351}. Catalyzes the ligation of L‑glutamate to L‑2‑aminobutyrate, producing γ‑glutamyl‑2‑aminobutyrate, a precursor in the ophthalmic acid biosynthetic pathway. {PubMed:29352090}. Requires the conserved His‑150 residue for catalytic activity. {PubMed:7765288}. Loss of function yields a glutathione‑deficient phenotype with undetectable intracellular GSH. {PubMed:1107813, PubMed:8702583}.

MetaCyc_Comment: γ-Glutamate-cysteine ligase catalyzes the first of two steps in the pathway for the biosynthesis of glutathione. The enzyme is feedback-inhibited by glutathione |CITS: |. The enzyme contains two divalent metal ions which play a role in amino acid binding. Substrate specificity depends on whether Mg2+ or Mn2+ is present; Mn2+ broadens the specificity |CITS: |. Transition state analog inhibitors have been used to study substrate recognition |CITS: |. The enzyme can utilize ethylamine as a substrate, thus producing theanine (γ-glutamylethylamide) |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme from E. coli B (whose wild-type sequence is identical to the K-12 enzyme) have been solved |CITS: |. The structure shows coordination of an inhibitor by three Mg2+ ions, and showing that the binding of cysteine follows an induced-fit model |CITS: |. Although not highly conserved, the cysteine residues C372 and C395 of the intrachain disulfide bond are important for catalytic activity and stability of the enzyme |CITS: |. A gshA insertion mutant is more sensitive to thiol-specific damage |CITS: |, mercury and arsenite |CITS: |, and is unable to grow at high osmolarity |CITS: |, but is not affected in its resistance to oxidative damage |CITS: |. However, a strain overexpressing GshA and GshB is more resistant to radiation than wild type |CITS: |. A gshA trxB double mutant exhibits a severe growth defect which can be suppressed by growth in rich medium containing DTT or by certain mutations in aphC |CITS: |. In cells lacking metal efflux systems, glutathione biosynthesis is required for resistance to Cd2+, Zn2+ and Cu2+ |CITS: |. The resistance of a gshA mutant to a variety of metals has been measured |CITS: |. As shown by the effect of a gshA mutation, glutathione plays a role in formation of the active, cluster-containing form of FNR |CITS: |. Suppressor mutations that allow a ΔgshA strain to grow in the presence of arsenate map to proA and proB; enabling synthesis of glutathione |CITS: |. Transcription of gshA increases with increased cadmium concentration. A microarray analysis measuring the transcriptional response of wild-type and gshA mutant strains to cadmium stress has been performed |CITS: |. Under oxidative stress conditions, translation of gshA is increased by the presence of polyamines. The increase is dependent on the non-canonical UUG start codon of the gshA open reading frame |CITS: |. gshA was first cloned and sequenced from E. coli B |CITS: |; the sequence of the E. coli B and K-12 genes appear to be identical.

MetaCyc_Comment: Nicotinate-mononucleotide adenylyltransferase (NadD) is an essential enzyme involved in both de novo biosynthesis and salvage of NAD+ |CITS: |. Its essentiality makes it a target for the development of antibacterial agents |CITS: |. Both nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN) and nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) are substrates, but the rate of adenylation of NaMN is at least 20 times faster than that of NMN |CITS: |. Crystal structures of the enzyme alone and in a complex with deamido-NAD have been solved and show that ligand binding causes conformational changes in regions surrounding the active site |CITS: |. nadD is essential for growth |CITS: |. The nadD72 mutant allele was first isolated as a spontaneous temperature-sensitive mutation that leads to higher tolerance to fusidic acid. The mutant phenotype is pleiotropic |CITS: |. Further characterization of this mutation showed it to be an allele of nadD with a -1 frameshift mutation that leads to a change in the C terminus of the NadD protein. The mutant synthesizes very little NAD+ and NADPH at the permissive temperature and essentially none at the non-permissive temperature |CITS: |. The newly isolated nadD74 allele causes an amino acid change in the ATP-binding site of NadD. On miminal medium, the mutant shows temperature sensitivity due to a reduction in NAD+ synthesis; at the permissive temperature, NAD+ synthesis is reduced, but sufficient to support normal growth |CITS: |. Additional mutants within the active site and the C terminus of NadD have been isolated and characterized |CITS: |. Mutants that shift the substrate preference of NadD to NMN have been designed and tested |CITS: |. The nadD coding region contains an inhibitory RNA polymerase-binding aptamer (iRAP) that promotes Rho-dependent transcription termination, in particular in stationary phase and under oxidative stress |CITS: |. PIMT was thought to be required for stationary phase survival |CITS: |, but this effect was due to a secondary mutation in rpoS |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: rpmE2 (also known as ykgM) encodes a paralog of the zinc‑binding ribosomal protein L31. Under conditions where the Zur repressor is inactivated (e.g., zinc deficiency or zur mutations), ykgM is expressed and the YkgM protein is incorporated into the 50S ribosomal subunit in place of L31. YkgM binds at the same site as L31 (one copy per ribosome) and fully restores the functions lost in an rpmE (L31) deletion: it promotes 30S–50S subunit association to form 70S ribosomes, supports in vitro translation activity to wild‑type levels, enables formation of 100S dimeric ribosomes in stationary phase, and rescues the slow‑growth phenotype of ΔrpmE cells. Thus, rpmE2 functions as a zinc‑independent L31 replacement that maintains ribosome assembly and translational competence when the canonical Zn‑binding L31 is unavailable. {PubMed:32559334}. In enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7, ykgM is strongly up‑regulated under zinc‑deficient conditions and encodes a protein required for maintaining optimal intracellular Zn²⁺ levels. Loss of ykgM reduces cellular zinc concentration, impairs expression of the curli major subunit gene csgA, diminishes curli fiber production, and consequently decreases bacterial attachment to abiotic (glass) and biotic (epithelial) surfaces. These defects lead to markedly reduced biofilm formation under fluidic, zinc‑limited conditions. Thus, YkgM functions as a zinc‑homeostasis factor that supports curli biogenesis and surface attachment, enabling robust biofilm development in zinc‑deficient environments. {PubMed:21763023}. ykgM encodes a ribosomal protein that is a homolog (paralog) of the Zn(II)-binding ribosomal protein L31. It is strongly up‑regulated under Zn(II)‑deficient conditions (Zur‑regulated) and, unlike L31, does not bind Zn(II). The authors propose that YkgM functions as the “C‑” counterpart in a proposed C⁺/C‑ Zn(II)‑starvation system in E. coli, where it replaces Zn(II)‑bound L31 on the ribosome during Zn(II) starvation, thereby mobilizing ribosome‑associated Zn(II) for cellular use. {PubMed:22196016}. The article describes ykgM as a gene involved in zinc homeostasis in Escherichia coli. It is expressed under zinc‑deficient conditions and contributes to biofilm formation when zinc is limited. Essential‑oil treatments that down‑regulate ykgM expression lead to disrupted zinc homeostasis and reduced biofilm formation, indicating its role in maintaining cellular zinc balance and supporting biofilm development under zinc‑limited environments. {PubMed:33504089}. YkgM is a zinc‑independent paralog of the ribosomal protein L31 (encoded by rpmE). It is transcribed from the ykgM‑ykgO operon, which is repressed by the Zur regulator under zinc‑replete conditions and induced when Zur is inactivated (e.g., during zinc deficiency). YkgM is incorporated into the 50S ribosomal subunit at the same binding site as L31, with a copy number of one per ribosome. When expressed, YkgM restores the weakened 30S–50S subunit association seen in ΔrpmE cells, enables normal 70S ribosome formation, supports the formation of 100S dimeric ribosomes in stationary phase, and rescues the reduced in‑vitro translational activity of ribosomes lacking L31. In summary, YkgM functionally substitutes for L31, maintaining ribosome assembly and translational activity under zinc‑limited conditions. {PubMed:32559334}. Encodes the ribosomal protein bL31B, a non‑zinc‑binding paralog of bL31A (encoded by rpmE). bL31B is incorporated stoichiometrically into the 50S subunit of the 70S ribosome, occupying the same position as bL31A in the central protuberance and contacting the head of the small subunit. Its expression is regulated by the Zur repressor and is induced under zinc‑limiting conditions, leading to replacement of bL31A by bL31B in ribosomes during stationary phase. bL31B‑containing ribosomes confer a lower fitness than bL31A‑containing ribosomes at lower temperatures and during rapid (cyclic) growth, but are tolerated during stationary phase. Functionally, bL31B reduces apparent translation processivity and increases both +1 and –1 frameshifting frequencies, indicating a role in maintaining translation reading‑frame fidelity. Additionally, bL31B has been linked to curli production and biofilm formation in enterohemorrhagic E. coli. {PubMed:32669635}. ykgM encodes a non‑Zn²⁺‑finger paralogue of the ribosomal protein L31. Under severe Zn²⁺ starvation its transcription is up‑regulated (≈2.6‑fold) in a Zur‑dependent manner. The YkgM protein lacks the Zn²⁺‑binding ribbon motif present in the canonical L31 (encoded by rpmE) and is proposed to replace the Zn²⁺‑bound L31 in ribosomes. This replacement allows the Zn²⁺ ion that was coordinated by the canonical L31 to be released and redistributed to other essential Zn²⁺‑requiring enzymes, thereby contributing to cellular Zn²⁺ homeostasis during zinc limitation. {PubMed:19377097}. The ykgM gene encodes the ribosomal protein paralog bL31B, one of two paralogous forms of the large‑subunit ribosomal protein bL31 in Escherichia coli. bL31B lacks the zinc‑binding motif present in the bL31A (rpmE) product and can bind to the same ribosomal site as bL31A, forming part of the intersubunit bridge B1b. During exponential growth, bL31A is the predominant form, but as cells transition to stationary phase, bL31B increasingly replaces bL31A, contributing to ribosome heterogeneity and potentially affecting ribosome stability and function under zinc‑limited or acidic conditions. Expression of ykgM is regulated by the zinc‑dependent ZUR repressor and is induced under zinc‑depleted conditions, ensuring availability of the non‑zinc‑binding bL31B paralog when zinc is scarce. {PubMed:30359641}. The article states that ykgM is up‑regulated during zinc starvation and is predicted to encode a non‑zinc‑containing paralogue of the ribosomal protein L31. In other words, ykgM likely provides a zinc‑independent version of L31 that can substitute for the normal zinc‑binding L31 when cellular zinc levels are low. {PubMed:22016571}. The article describes ykgM as the zinc‑independent paralog of the ribosomal protein bL31 (encoded by rpmE). It is part of the ykgM‑ykgO operon, which is transcriptionally repressed by the zinc‑uptake regulator Zur under normal zinc conditions and becomes highly expressed during zinc starvation (or in a zur‑deficient background). YkgM can replace bL31 on the 50S ribosomal subunit, allowing the cell to free zinc‑binding bL31 for other essential zinc‑requiring enzymes. Additionally, the study provides evidence that YkgM, when induced, can reduce the expression of an rpmE‑lacZ reporter, suggesting that YkgM may also participate in feedback regulation of rpmE expression. {PubMed:32209634}. JW5035 is the Keio knockout strain for the ykgM gene, which encodes the ribosomal protein paralog YkgM. YkgM is a non‑zinc‑binding paralog of the zinc‑binding ribosomal protein L31 (rpmE). Under zinc‑deficient conditions, or when the Zur repressor is inactivated, ykgM is expressed from the ykgM‑ykgO operon and YkgM is incorporated into the 50S ribosomal subunit in place of L31. YkgM binds to the same site as L31, restores 30S–50S subunit association, supports formation of 70S ribosomes, enables formation of 100S dimers in stationary phase, and fully recovers in‑vitro translational activity to the level of ribosomes containing native L31. Thus, YkgM functionally substitutes for L31, maintaining ribosome assembly and translation when L31 is absent or its zinc‑binding site is unavailable. {PubMed:32559334}. JW5035 refers to the Keio collection strain JW5035‑1, which carries a precise deletion of the ykgM gene (ΔykgM::kan). The ykgM gene encodes the ribosomal protein bL31B, a non‑zinc‑binding paralog of the core large‑subunit protein bL31A. bL31B replaces bL31A in ribosomes during the transition from exponential to stationary growth phase, contributing to ribosome heterogeneity and potentially affecting ribosome stability and function under zinc‑limited or acidic conditions. {PubMed:30359641}. The JW5035 locus encodes the bacterial ribosomal protein L31 (bL31), a small (~70 aa), highly basic protein that is a peripheral component of the 50S ribosomal subunit. bL31 participates in the formation of the protein‑protein intersubunit bridge B1b (and, via its C‑terminal domain, also contributes to bridge B1c), thereby stabilizing subunit association and facilitating the rotational movements required for translation. In addition to its structural role, bL31 counteracts ribosome destabilization caused by certain nascent peptide sequences, and it has been implicated in promoting translation initiation and maintaining the correct reading frame. Uniquely, bL31 also functions as an autogenous translational repressor: excess bL31 binds a conserved stem‑loop operator in the 5′‑UTR of its own mRNA (rpmE), inhibiting translation initiation. This repressor activity depends on an intrinsically disordered, lysine‑rich N‑terminal segment (residues 2‑8) of bL31, while the C‑terminal region required for ribosome binding is dispensable for repression. {PubMed:32209634}. Encodes the zinc‑binding ribosomal protein L31 (rpmE). L31 binds to the 50S ribosomal subunit at a specific site, bridges the 30S and 50S subunits, and promotes their association to form functional 70S ribosomes. It is required for efficient in‑vitro translation, proper formation of 100S dimeric ribosomes during stationary phase, and contributes to the late stages of 50S subunit assembly. L31 also participates in cellular zinc storage, releasing Zn(II) under zinc‑limiting conditions when its paralog YkgM replaces it in the ribosome. {PubMed:32559334}.

Merged_Functions: The rpmI gene encodes the ribosomal protein A, also known as L35, which is one of the ribosomal proteins forming part of the bacterial ribosome. It is located in the infC‑rpmI‑rplT operon and contributes to the translational machinery of Escherichia coli. {PubMed:2191140}. The rpmI gene encodes the ribosomal protein L35, a component of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit. L35 is required for proper ribosome assembly and cell growth, as evidenced by the necessity of rpmI expression (along with infC and rplT) for viability in the engineered E. coli strains described in the article. {PubMed:8628231}. The rpmI gene encodes the ribosomal protein L35, a component of the bacterial ribosome. It is transcribed as part of the infC‑rpmI‑rplT operon that also contains the genes for translation initiation factor IF3 (infC) and ribosomal protein L20 (rplT). Expression of rpmI is directly repressed by the ribosomal protein L20 binding to an operator located within infC. Moreover, translation of rpmI is translationally coupled to the downstream rplT gene: when rpmI is translated, ribosomes covering its coding region prevent formation of an mRNA secondary structure that would otherwise sequester the Shine‑Dalgarno sequence of rplT; when rpmI translation is inhibited, the secondary structure forms and blocks rplT translation. Thus, rpmI functions as a structural ribosomal protein and participates in a regulatory network that coordinates the synthesis of L35 and L20. {PubMed:1453449}. The rpmI gene encodes the ribosomal protein L35, the first cistron of the rpmI‑rplT operon. L35 is a component of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit and contributes to ribosome assembly and function. In the context of this study, rpmI expression is subject to autoregulation by the downstream ribosomal protein L20, which binds the rpmI‑rplT mRNA to repress translation of rpmI (and consequently of rplT) via a competition mechanism with the 30S ribosomal subunit. {PubMed:18037435}.

Mutations that affect catalytic activity |CITS: |, subunit interactions |CITS: |, conformational stability |CITS: | and folding |CITS: | have been identified. The crystal structure of the wild-type TrpA protein has been reported at 2.8 Å resolution |CITS: |, 2.5 Å resolution |CITS: | and 2.3 Å resolution |CITS: |. The TrpA protein has been structurally classified as a (beta alpha)(8) TIM barrel protein, a member of the common TIM barrel superfamily. Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopic techniques have been used to investigate its equilibrium folding mechanism in order to obtain insights into the development of structure and stability |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: The udk gene encodes a uridine/cytidine kinase that phosphorylates uridine and cytidine to produce the ribonucleoside monophosphates UMP and CMP. In addition to its enzymatic role, overexpression of udk in Escherichia coli interferes with bacteriophage T7 infection by antagonizing the function of the phage‑encoded transcription inhibitor Gp2. Elevated levels of Udk reduce the stability and functionality of Gp2, preventing Gp2 from binding to the β' jaw domain of the host RNA polymerase, which results in continued transcription from early T7 promoters, accumulation of anti‑terminated early transcripts, and ultimately aborts successful T7 phage replication. {PubMed:23242801}. Encodes the pyrimidine salvage enzyme pyrimidine ribonucleoside kinase (EC 2.7.1.48), which catalyzes the phosphorylation of uridine and cytidine to UMP and CMP, respectively, using GTP as the preferred phosphate donor. {PubMed:8366067}. The article identifies udk as the gene encoding uridine kinase, an enzyme of the pyrimidine salvage pathway. Uridine kinase catalyzes the phosphorylation of uridine to uridine‑monophosphate (UMP), thereby contributing to the conversion of exogenous uridine into nucleotides. The udk locus is used as a chromosomal target for measuring mutation frequencies, and its activity (or loss thereof) is relevant in selection schemes involving the fluoropyrimidine analogue 5‑fluorouridine (FUdR), where uridine kinase activity influences cellular sensitivity to the drug. {PubMed:3033486}. The udk gene encodes a uridine/cytidine kinase that phosphorylates the nucleosides uridine and cytidine to their corresponding ribonucleoside monophosphates (UMP and CMP). The preferred phosphate donors for this reaction are GTP and dGTP. udk is non‑essential in Escherichia coli and functions as part of the pyrimidine ribonucleotide salvage pathway, providing a route to regenerate UMP and CMP from extracellular or intracellular nucleosides. Overexpression of udk does not alter its catalytic activity but leads to a cellular state that impairs T7 bacteriophage growth, likely by preventing adequate inhibition of the host RNA polymerase during infection. {PubMed:18067538}. The article describes UDK as the uridine kinase enzyme found in *Escherichia coli*. UDK catalyzes the phosphorylation of uridine (and the fluorinated analog 5‑fluorouridine) with ATP to generate uridine‑5′‑monophosphate (UMP), thereby contributing to the pyrimidine salvage pathway. This activity enables conversion of 5‑fluorouridine into toxic 5‑fluoro‑UMP, which causes growth inhibition in bacteria expressing the gene. {PubMed:17143579}. The udk gene encodes uridine/cytidine kinase (Udk), an enzyme that participates in the salvage pathway of pyrimidine nucleotide synthesis. It is organized in the udk‑dcd operon, where dcd encodes dCTP deaminase. In Escherichia coli, transcription of udk is positively regulated by the ribose operon repressor RbsR, which activates its expression (as evidenced by decreased udk mRNA levels in an rbsR knockout). Thus, Udk contributes to recycling uridine and cytidine into nucleotide pools. {PubMed:23651393}. The b2066 locus encodes the enzyme uridine/cytidine kinase (Udk), which phosphorylates the nucleosides uridine and cytidine to produce the ribonucleoside monophosphates UMP and CMP.  In the context of bacteriophage T7 infection, over‑expression of Udk interferes with the essential function of the phage‑encoded transcription inhibitor Gp2.  Elevated levels of Udk reduce the stability and functional activity of Gp2, preventing Gp2 from binding to the β' jaw domain of the host RNA polymerase and thereby allowing host RNA polymerase to continue transcribing the early T7 promoters (A0–A3).  This mimics the phenotype of a Gp2‑deficient infection, leading to accumulation of anti‑terminated early transcripts, disruption of coordinated phage gene expression, and ultimately abortive T7 infection.  Thus, b2066/Udk functions as a uridine/cytidine kinase whose over‑production can antagonize Gp2‑mediated host‑RNA‑polymerase inhibition and block successful T7 phage replication. {PubMed:23242801}.
