MetaCyc_Comment: L/F-transferase (Aat) attaches leucine and phenylalanine to exposed amino-terminal arginines and lysines on proteins. This is a key step in the ClpAP-dependent N-end rule degradation pathway. L/F-transferase catalyzes the transfer of leucine and phenylalanine from charged tRNA to amino-terminal lysines and arginines on substrate proteins |CITS: |. When assayed with small peptides, Aat only modifies peptides bearing amino-terminal L-arginine and L-lysine, although the simple dipeptide D-lysyl-D-valine is not a substrate |CITS: |. Testing with purified Aat and actual protein substrates shows that Aat will only transfer to amino-terminal, rather than internal, arginines in proteins |CITS: |. Though addition of both leucine and phenylalanine occurs in vitro, an in vivo experiment with arginine-β-galactosidase yielded only leucine addition |CITS: |. In one case, purified L/F-transferase has been shown to transfer methionine onto the amino-terminus of substrate peptides |CITS: |. L/F-transferase has also been shown to transfer to an unidentified 12 kD protein component of the 30S ribosome |CITS: |. L/F-transferase is required for the degradation of some substrates for the N-end rule pathway, by which a protein undergoes rapid degradation by the ClpAP protease if its amino-terminal residue is arginine, lysine, leucine, phenylalanine, tyrosine or tryptophan. Arginine and lysine are considered secondary destabilizing residues, as the addition of leucine or phenylalanine by L/F-transferase is required to allow degradation |CITS: |. The chaperone protein GroEL copurifies with L/F-transferase. Recombinant L/F-transferase with no RNA present is as active as purified wild-type protein which may contain some RNA |CITS: |. A number of structural studies have been carried out on L/F-transferase. Crystal structures of isolated Aat to 2.4 Å and 1.6 Å resolution and of Aat bound to the aminoacyl-tRNA analog puromycin to 2.8 Å resolution show that Aat comprises two compact domains. Both domains are involved in puromycin, and presumably tRNA, binding via a hydrophobic pocket that is required for Aat activity |CITS: |. Crystal structures of Aat complexed with a phenylalanyl-tRNA analog with or without an associated peptide substrate show that the phenylalanine side chain binds in the hydrophobic pocket as suggested by the puromycin analysis. In addition, this work shows that except for the amino-terminal residue, recognition of peptide substrates by L/F-transferase is sequence independent |CITS: |. Truncation of the Aat amino-terminus by 33 or 78 residues results in a protein that is capable of measureable transferase activity and that has wild type substrate specificity |CITS: |. Mutants lacking L/F-transferase have diminished activities of L-phenylalanyl-transfer ribonucleic acid synthetase and tryptophanase and accumulate high levels of enterochelin during iron limitation. Neither synthetase nor tryptophanase are substrates for L/F-transferase, however |CITS: |. When grown on glycerol, L/F-transferase mutants are partial proline auxotrophs and show a fourfold increase in proline oxidase activity |CITS: |. This increase in activity is due to an increase in the amount of proline oxidase, rather than in the enzymatic activity of individual proline oxidases |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

Merged_Functions: cysE encodes serine transacetylase, an enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of O‑acetylserine from serine and O‑acetyl‑coenzyme A, a key step in the cysteine biosynthetic pathway. {PubMed:1886615}. The cysE gene encodes serine acetyltransferase (SAT), the enzyme that catalyzes the first step of L‑cysteine biosynthesis in Escherichia coli. SAT transfers an acetyl group from acetyl‑CoA to L‑serine, producing O‑acetyl‑L‑serine (OAS). OAS is then converted to L‑cysteine by O‑acetyl‑L‑serine (thiol)‑lyase. The cysE gene is constitutively expressed, but the activity of its product is subject to feedback inhibition by L‑cysteine. Mutations in cysE that reduce this feedback inhibition lead to increased SAT activity and over‑production/excretion of L‑cysteine. {PubMed:3309158}. The cysE gene encodes serine acetyltransferase (SAT), the enzyme that catalyzes the synthesis of O‑acetyl‑L‑serine (OAS) from L‑serine and acetyl‑CoA. OAS is the direct precursor of cysteine, linking serine metabolism to cysteine biosynthesis. SAT activity is inhibited by cysteine, allowing intracellular cysteine levels to regulate OAS production and thus control expression of the cysteine regulon. Mutations in cysE result in cysteine auxotrophy because of loss of SAT activity. {PubMed:2108679}. The cysE gene encodes serine acetyltransferase, an enzyme that catalyzes the acetylation of L‑serine to produce O‑acetyl‑L‑serine (OAS). OAS can spontaneously rearrange at neutral to alkaline pH to form N‑acetyl‑L‑serine (NAS). In the context of the study, CysE activity is essential for the synthesis of a CysE‑dependent extracellular signaling molecule that activates several lacZ reporter fusions (e.g., cma37::lacZ, cma67::lacZ, cma230::lacZ) in both Providencia stuartii and Escherichia coli. Loss of cysE dramatically reduces the ability of conditioned medium to activate these fusions, indicating that the signal requires CysE for its production. Additionally, the cysE mutant exhibits a hyper‑biofilm phenotype, forming biofilms more rapidly and with greater biomass than wild‑type cells; this phenotype can be partially reversed by adding exogenous OAS or cysteine. Thus, CysE functions both in the cysteine biosynthetic pathway (providing the OAS precursor for NAS) and in the generation of an extracellular signal that modulates gene expression and biofilm development. {PubMed:15516574}. SAT catalyzes the transfer of an acetyl group from acetyl‑CoA to L‑serine, forming O‑acetyl‑L‑serine, which is then converted to L‑cysteine by O‑acetylserine sulfhydrylase (CysK). The gene is listed as essential for the survival of several pathogenic bacteria, including Streptococcus pneumoniae, and its product is absent in humans, making it a potential target for antimicrobial development. {PubMed:30734630}. cysE encodes L-serine O‑acetyltransferase (SAT), the enzyme that catalyzes the acetylation of L‑serine to form O‑acetyl‑L‑serine, the first committed step in the biosynthetic pathway that converts L‑serine to L‑cysteine in Escherichia coli. The enzyme is a major rate‑limiting step in L‑cysteine production and is normally subject to feedback inhibition by L‑cysteine; the study employed a feedback‑insensitive mutant version of cysE to relieve this inhibition and increase L‑cysteine accumulation. {PubMed:29405609}. The cysE gene encodes L-serine O-acetyltransferase (SAT), the enzyme that catalyzes the acetylation of L‑serine to form O‑acetyl‑L‑serine, the first committed step in the biosynthetic pathway leading to L‑cysteine. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Involved in disulfide bond formation. Catalyzes a late, reductive step in the assembly of periplasmic c-type cytochromes, probably the reduction of disulfide bonds of the apocytochrome c to allow covalent linkage with the heme. Possible subunit of a heme lyase. DsbE is maintained in a reduced state by DsbD.
MetaCyc_Comment: Apo c-type cytochromes are synthesized in the cytosol and need to be exported into the periplasm (the transport is conducted via the |FRAME: SEC-SECRETION-CPLX|). Once in the cytoplasm, the polypeptide is exposed to the activity of |FRAME: EC-1.8.4.15|, which oxidizes its active thiols forming a disulfide bridge. The reduction of this bridge is essential for the attachment of heme. Two thiol:disulfide oxidoreductases, encoded by the |FRAME: EG12053| and |FRAME: EG12052| genes, have been known for many years to be involved in c-type cytochrome biogenesis |CITS: |. However, specifying the exact reactions ctalyzed by the two enzymes has proved challenging. CcmG is a small protein with a thioredoxin-like motif facing the periplasm, but tethered to the cytoplasmic membrane by a hydrophobic N-terminal domain |CITS: |. A simple relay of disulfide bonds was initially proposed, where CcmG is reduced by |FRAME: EG12178 DsbD| and in turn reduces CcmH, which then reduced apocytochrome c. However, a study of CcmG in 2001 has found that a mutation in |FRAME: EG12053| cannot be compensated by a second mutation in the disulfide-bond-forming proteins |FRAME: EG11297 DsbA| and |FRAME: EG11393 DsbB|, or by chemical reductants. The oxidized form of CcmG accumulated in |FRAME: EG12054| and |FRAME: EG12052| mutants, suggesting that CcmG functions later than CcmF and CcmH in cytochrome c assembly. The authors proposed three alternative models to explain their observation, with the preferred one including a disulfide formation between CcmG and CcmH |CITS: |. A much later study from 2017 has found that CcmG can reduce directly and efficiently the disulfide bond of apocytochrome c. CcmH could also carry out this task, though slower than CcmG. In addition, CcmG could rapidly resolve a mixed disulfide between CcmH and apocytochrome c. The authors concluded that the most likely scenario is that CcmG is the enzyme that initially reduces apocytochrome c. One of the reduced cysteine residues then attacks Cys-45 of oxidized CcmH, yielding a CcmH(Cys-45)--(Cys-34) apocytochrome c mixed disulfide (as has been suggested in the 2001 study), leaving Cys-37 of apocytochrome c available to form a thioether bond with the vinyl-4 of heme, which is still attached to CcmE. This mixed disulfide bond is then be resolved by reduced CcmG, forming a CcmG-(Cys-75)--(Cys-45)-CcmH mixed disulfide, which is resolved by an attack on CcmG-(Cys-75) by the second cysteine of CcmG, yielding oxidized CcmG and restoring a reduced CcmH. According to this model, the second thioether bond between Cys-34 of apocytochrome c and the heme vinyl-2 is formed later, upon resolution of the CcmE-heme-apocytochrome c complex intermediate. By forming only a single heme-thil bond initially, the mechanism ensures stereo-specificity during cytochrome c maturation |CITS: |. For production of CcmG protein for the study the |FRAME: EG12053| gene was cloned with a His6 tag and expressed in E. coli BL21 cells, and the recombinant protein was purified to homogeneity |CITS: |.

Overexpression of mdlB in Escherichia coli enhances tolerance to exogenously added isopentenol and increases isopentenol production titers by ~12 % (up to ~20 % at higher induction levels).  Although its native physiological role is not fully characterized, MdlB appears to function as an exporter that reduces intracellular accumulation of the short‑chain alcohol isopentenol, thereby mitigating solvent stress and improving biogasoline production. {PubMed:25370492}. The mdl gene encodes a single polypeptide with two ATP‑binding domains and two hydrophobic transmembrane domains arranged TM‑ATP‑TM‑ATP, mirroring the domain architecture of eukaryotic multidrug‑resistance (MDR/P‑gp) transporters. This structure predicts that the Mdl protein functions as an energy‑dependent ABC exporter, likely involved in the efflux of small molecules or xenobiotics. Gene‑disruption experiments showed that mdl is not essential for cell growth, and mutants displayed only a modest (~2‑fold) increase in sensitivity to the macrolide antibiotic spiramycin, indicating a limited contribution to drug resistance. Phylogenetic analysis places mdl in a distinct subfamily together with bacterial exporters hlyB, msbA, and cvaB, suggesting functional similarity to MDR‑related exporters, although its exact physiological substrate and role remain undetermined. {PubMed:7904973}. The article describes MdlB (encoded by the mdlB gene) as an ABC‑type efflux pump that provides microbial tolerance to the five‑carbon alcohol isopentenol (3‑methyl‑3‑buten‑1‑ol). In the study, MdlB was fused to GFP (MdlB‑GFP) and used as one of the inner‑membrane proteins to assess how gene deletions affect membrane protein expression. {PubMed:29026162}. The article reports that the mdl gene does not play a role in nitrogen regulation. Experiments showed that deletion of mdl (alone or together with glnK) did not affect glutamine synthetase expression, GS adenylylation, or growth phenotypes related to nitrogen utilization. Thus, within the context of this study, mdl appears to have no observable function in nitrogen regulatory pathways. {PubMed:9720863}. The mdlB gene encodes the mono‑ and diacylglycerol lipase (MdlB) enzyme of Aspergillus oryzae. MdlB is a secreted lipolytic protein that hydrolyzes monoacylglycerols and diacylglycerols (but not triacylglycerols), containing the conserved Gly‑X‑Ser‑X‑Gly motif and catalytic triad (Ser‑Asp‑His) typical of lipases. This activity contributes to lipid metabolism during fermentation, enabling the breakdown of glyceride substrates and the production of mono‑ and diacylglycerols. {PubMed:8807803}. JW5061 encodes GlnK, a PII‑like signal transduction protein that participates in the nitrogen regulatory network of Escherichia coli. GlnK is uridylylated by the UTase/UR enzyme (GlnD) in response to cellular glutamine levels and 2‑ketoglutarate. Through its interaction with the two‑component sensor kinase NRII (GlnL), GlnK modulates the phosphorylation state of the transcriptional activator NRI (GlnG), thereby contributing to the negative regulation of Ntr‑controlled promoters, especially those that require higher NRI~P concentrations for activation (e.g., the glnK promoter). GlnK also interacts with the adenylyltransferase ATase (GlnE) to regulate the adenylylation/deadenylylation cycle of glutamine synthetase (GS, GlnA), influencing GS activity. Unlike the constitutively expressed PII protein (GlnB), GlnK expression is itself tightly regulated by nitrogen availability via an Ntr promoter. Together, GlnK and GlnB provide overlapping but distinct control of nitrogen assimilation: GlnK acts as a slower or “memory” regulator that fine‑tunes NRI~P levels and GS adenylylation, helping prevent inappropriate expression of the Ntr regulon under fluctuating nitrogen conditions. {PubMed:9720863}. The mdlB gene encodes the extracellular lipolytic enzyme L2, a mono‑ and diacylglycerol lipase. The predicted protein is a 306‑amino‑acid precursor (including a 28‑aa signal peptide) that is processed to a mature 278‑aa enzyme (~30 kDa) that hydrolyzes monoacylglycerols and diacylglycerols but not triacylglycerols. The enzyme contains the conserved Gly‑X‑Ser‑X‑Gly motif and the catalytic triad (Ser, Asp, His) typical of lipases. It is highly similar to the MdlA lipase of Penicillium camembertii and is implicated in lipid modification during Aspergillus oryzae fermentation, with potential applications in the biotechnological production of mono‑ and diacylglycerols. {PubMed:8807803}. MdlB is described as a predicted ATP‑binding cassette (ABC) transporter subunit, likely functioning as a multidrug efflux pump. In the study it was identified among genes up‑regulated by isopentenol exposure and, when overexpressed, conferred increased tolerance to exogenous isopentenol and a 12 % improvement in isopentenol production. The native physiological role of MdlB is not well characterized, but it is typically induced under antibiotic stress or DNA‑damage conditions, suggesting a general role in exporting harmful compounds. {PubMed:25370492}. The mdlB gene encodes (S)-mandelate dehydrogenase, an enzyme derived from Pseudomonas putida ATCC 12633 that catalyzes the second step of the engineered mandelate degradation pathway used for benzyl alcohol production in Escherichia coli. Specifically, MdlB oxidizes (S)-mandelate, which is generated from phenylpyruvate by hydroxymandelate synthase (hmaS), to phenylglyoxylate. This reaction provides the substrate for the subsequent decarboxylation step carried out by phenylglyoxylate decarboxylase (mdlC), ultimately leading to benzaldehyde formation and downstream reduction to benzyl alcohol. {PubMed:34150507}. The article states that mdlB encodes (S)-mandelate dehydrogenase (MDH), the second enzyme of the mandelate catabolic pathway in Pseudomonas putida. MDH catalyzes the oxidative conversion of (S)-mandelate to benzoylformate, supplying the substrate for the downstream enzyme benzoylformate decarboxylase (encoded by mdlC). The predicted protein is 393 amino acids long, with a molecular weight of ~43 kDa, and shows sequence similarity to glycolate oxidase and ferricytochrome b₂ lactate dehydrogenase, indicating it belongs to the α‑hydroxy acid dehydrogenase family. {PubMed:2271624}. MdlB encodes an ATP‑binding cassette (ABC) efflux pump. Its primary role is to export the five‑carbon alcohol isopentenol (3‑methyl‑3‑buten‑1‑ol) out of the cell, thereby providing microbial tolerance to this compound. In the study, MdlB was fused to GFP and used as a model inner‑membrane protein to assess how gene deletions affect membrane protein expression. {PubMed:29026162}. The article describes mdlB as encoding an (S)-mandelate dehydrogenase. In recombinant E. coli strains, mdlB catalyzes the oxidation of (S)-3‑ethoxy‑4‑hydroxymandelic acid (S‑EMA) to 3‑ethoxy‑4‑hydroxybenzoylformate, the first step of a modified mandelate pathway that ultimately leads to ethyl vanillin production. The enzyme shows activity toward the (S)‑enantiomer of EMA, while the (R)‑enantiomer is not converted. {PubMed:23430129}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Phosphogluconate dehydratase catalyzes the dehydration of D-gluconate 6-phosphate to 2-dehydro-3-deoxy-D-gluconate 6-phosphate. It is also inactivated by iron chelators and thiol-reactive compounds. Fluoride ions protect the enzyme from the effects of oxidants |CITS: |. Under continuous culture conditions induction of phosphogluconate dehydratase is favored at low oxygen concentrations |CITS: |. Edd from E. coli K-12, a laboratory strain, has not been well characterized biochemically. However, using E. coli strains from the ECOR collection of natural isolates, the Km and Vmax of phosphogluconate dehydratase were determined along with the growth rate in gluconate minimal salts medium |CITS: |. Reduced expression levels of the GroEL-GroES molecular chaperonin complex during steady-state growth increases the synthesis of Edd and Eda, suggesting a regulatory function |CITS: |. Plasmid-encoded Edd overproduction suppresses the stationary phase toxicity of DnaK overproduction |CITS: |. The product of gntR regulates edd inducibility |CITS: |. |FRAME: IDNCAT-PWY| proceeds through the Entner Doudoroff pathway and an edd mutant grows more slowly than wild-type on L-idonate |CITS: |. It also grows more slowly on gluconate which can be metabolized via the |FRAME: PENTOSE-P-PWY| |CITS: |. The protein interacts specifically with the FAD‑binding (β) domain and, to a lesser extent, the α domain of the large catalytic subunit (ilvB), but not with the γ domain. Binding of ilvN to these domains promotes re‑assembly of the holoenzyme, markedly increasing catalytic activity compared with the catalytic subunits alone. The interaction positions ilvN near the FAD‑binding site, likely inducing conformational changes that enhance the geometry of the active site and thereby activate the enzyme. {PubMed:18193896}. IlvN encodes the small regulatory subunit (RSU) of Escherichia coli acetohydroxyacid synthase I (AHAS I). It performs two key roles: (1) activation of the large catalytic subunit (CSU), without which the CSU retains <15% activity; and (2) feedback regulation of the enzyme by binding the end‑product branched‑chain amino acids, specifically valine and isoleucine (but not leucine). Binding of these effectors induces a coil‑to‑helix transition in IlvN, shifting its conformational equilibrium and leading to allosteric inhibition of AHAS I, thereby controlling flux through the branched‑chain amino acid biosynthetic pathway. {PubMed:23205845}. ilvN encodes the small regulatory subunit (SSU) of acetohydroxyacid synthase I (AHAS I) in Escherichia coli. It binds to the large catalytic subunit ilvB to form the active holoenzyme, thereby restoring full catalytic activity that is very low when the LSU is isolated. ilvN is essential for conferring valine‑dependent feedback inhibition on AHAS I; only the native ilvN–ilvB pair exhibits valine sensitivity, whereas heterologous SSUs (e.g., ilvM) activate the LSU without imparting valine inhibition. Thus, ilvN functions as a regulatory partner that both activates the catalytic subunit and mediates valine feedback control of the enzyme. {PubMed:19653643}. IlvN encodes the regulatory (RSU) subunit of the Escherichia coli acetohydroxyacid synthase I (AHAS I) holoenzyme.  It forms dimers (and at higher concentrations can tetramerize) that associate with two catalytic subunits (IlvB) to generate the functional hetero‑hexameric holoenzyme (2 CSU : 4 RSU).  IlvN binds the end‑product branched‑chain amino acids valine and isoleucine at a pocket located at the dimer interface; this binding triggers conformational changes (notably in Cys43 and His53) that mediate feedback inhibition of AHAS I activity.  In addition to its inhibitory role, IlvN is required for activation of the catalytic subunit, providing the platform for RSU–CSU interactions and influencing the oligomeric state of the holoenzyme. {PubMed:30887800}. The ilvN gene encodes the small (≈9–11 kDa) regulatory subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase isozyme I (AHAS I) in Escherichia coli. Together with the large catalytic subunit encoded by ilvB, the IlvN protein forms an equimolar heterodimeric holoenzyme that catalyzes the first step in branched‑chain amino‑acid biosynthesis. The small subunit contributes to the enzyme’s allosteric properties, influencing valine feedback inhibition and overall catalytic activity. {PubMed:16326011}. The ilvN gene encodes the small (≈10‑17 kDa) subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase I (AHAS I) in Escherichia coli K‑12. The IlvN polypeptide partners with the large IlvB subunit to form the active AHAS I holoenzyme. It is required for full catalytic efficiency, contributing to enzyme stability and turnover number, as its absence reduces specific activity by more than ten‑fold. Additionally, IlvN determines the enzyme’s sensitivity to feedback inhibition by L‑valine; loss of IlvN renders AHAS I largely resistant to valine inhibition while still allowing enough activity to support growth. Thus, IlvN functions as an essential structural and regulatory component of AHAS I, influencing both enzymatic activity and valine‑mediated regulation. {PubMed:3011751}. ilvN encodes the small (≈19 kDa) subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase (AHAS) in Methanococcus aeolicus. Together with the large subunit encoded by ilvB, it forms the heteromeric AHAS enzyme that catalyzes the first step in branched‑chain amino‑acid biosynthesis (condensation of pyruvate with 2‑ketobutyrate to form 2‑acetohydroxybutyrate for isoleucine, and condensation of two pyruvate molecules to form 2‑acetolactate for leucine and valine). The small subunit shows ~42 % amino‑acid identity to small subunits of bacterial AHAS enzymes and is positioned downstream of ilvB, likely co‑transcribed, with a possible internal promoter. In bacterial AHAS, loss of the small subunit reduces specific activity and alters feedback inhibition; the archaeal small subunit may play a similar or distinct regulatory role. {PubMed:9099862}. IlvN encodes the 11.2‑kilodalton small subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase I (AHAS I) in Escherichia coli K‑12. The enzyme can function without IlvN, but with reduced activity, indicating that IlvN acts as a regulatory/auxiliary subunit rather than a catalytic one. {PubMed:3294793}. The ilvN gene encodes the small (regulatory) subunit of acetolactate synthase (ALS) in Streptomyces cinnamonensis. This subunit forms a heterotetrameric enzyme together with the large catalytic subunit encoded by ilvB. The regulatory subunit contains the binding site for the end‑product valine and is responsible for mediating feedback inhibition of ALS activity, thereby controlling the flow of carbon into the branched‑chain amino acid biosynthetic pathway (valine and isoleucine synthesis). Mutations in ilvN that alter conserved residues near the N‑terminus or truncate the C‑terminal region abolish or reduce valine sensitivity, leading to deregulated ALS activity. {PubMed:10581183}. ilvN encodes the 22 kDa dimeric regulatory (small) subunit of Escherichia coli acetohydroxyacid synthase (AHAS) isoenzyme I. The regulatory subunit partners with the catalytic (large) subunit encoded by ilvB to form the active holoenzyme that catalyzes the first committed step in the biosynthesis of the branched‑chain amino acids valine, leucine, and isoleucine. IlvN was shown to bind close to the FAD binding site of IlvB |CITS: |. The interactions between the large and small subunits from different isozymes were investigated |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: The ilvM gene encodes the small (≈9.7 kDa) subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase II (AHAS II). This subunit is essential for the formation of active AHAS II, which catalyzes the first two steps in branched‑chain amino acid biosynthesis. In the absence of ilvM, AHAS II activity is reduced to a very low level that is insufficient for valine synthesis and only marginally supports isoleucine synthesis. The study demonstrates that ilvM and the large subunit gene ilvG can be expressed independently, but functional AHAS II requires both subunits, with ilvM being absolutely required for valine biosynthesis and almost essential for isoleucine biosynthesis when other AHAS isoenzymes are absent. {PubMed:3027038}. The ilvM gene encodes the small regulatory subunit (SSU) of acetohydroxyacid synthase II (AHAS II) in Escherichia coli.  IlvM binds to the large catalytic subunits (LSUs) of AHAS enzymes and restores full catalytic activity when the holoenzyme is reconstituted.  Remarkably, ilvM can activate the LSUs of all three AHAS isozymes (ilvG of AHAS II, ilvB of AHAS I, and ilvI of AHAS III), achieving up to 100 % of the activity of the native holoenzymes.  Unlike the SSUs of AHAS I (ilvN) and AHAS III (ilvH), ilvM does not confer feedback inhibition by valine; the hybrid enzymes formed with ilvM remain valine‑resistant.  This lack of valine sensitivity is attributed to the absence of a canonical valine‑binding ACT domain in ilvM, although it likely retains the β‑α‑β‑β‑α‑β fold that mediates interaction with the catalytic subunits.  Thus, ilvM functions as a non‑valine‑responsive regulatory subunit that activates AHAS catalytic subunits across isozymes. {PubMed:19653643}. The ilvM gene encodes the small (≈10–17 kDa) subunit of Escherichia coli acetohydroxyacid synthase (AHAS) isoenzyme II. This small subunit pairs with the large subunit encoded by ilvG to form the active heterotetrameric enzyme that catalyzes the first step in the biosynthesis of the branched‑chain amino acids (valine, leucine and isoleucine). While the large subunit contains the principal catalytic machinery, the small subunit is required for full enzymatic activity, contributes a regulatory role (e.g., it can bind valine), and participates in highly cooperative binding of two small‑subunit monomers to a large‑subunit dimer during enzyme reconstitution. The small subunit alone exhibits only trace activity and does not bind the required cofactors (FAD, ThDP, Mg²⁺) until incorporated into the tetramer. {PubMed:9581571}. The article identifies ilvM as encoding the small subunit of acetolactate synthase isozyme II, a component of the ilvGMEDA operon that participates in the biosynthetic pathway for the branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine and valine. {PubMed:3008097}. The ilvM gene encodes the small (≈9.7 kDa) subunit of Salmonella typhimurium acetolactate synthase isozyme II (ALSII). This subunit pairs with the larger ilvG‑encoded subunit (≈59 kDa) in an equimolar 2 + 2 arrangement to form the active ALSII enzyme. Acetolactate synthase catalyzes the first common step in the biosynthesis of the branched‑chain amino acids valine, leucine, and isoleucine by condensing two molecules of pyruvate (or pyruvate with α‑ketobutyrate) to produce α‑acetolactate (or α‑aceto‑α‑hydroxybutyrate) and CO₂. Thus, ilvM provides the essential small subunit required for the functional acetolactate synthase complex. {PubMed:3907697}. The article states that ilvM encodes the regulatory subunit (RSU) of acetohydroxyacid synthase II (AHAS II) in enterobacterial species.  IlvM forms a dimeric ACT domain that associates with the catalytic subunit encoded by ilvG.  Compared with the regulatory subunit IlvN of AHAS I, IlvM has a much smaller ligand‑binding pocket and lacks key hydrogen‑bonding residues, which makes it resistant to feedback inhibition by the branched‑chain amino acids valine, isoleucine and leucine.  The reduced pocket volume and increased steric bulk are proposed to explain the loss of sensitivity to these effectors.  Additionally, IlvM is reported to be capable of cross‑activating the catalytic subunit IlvB (from AHAS I) and the regulatory subunit IlvH (from AHAS III), suggesting a role in activation of catalytic activity across AHAS isozymes. {PubMed:30887800}. The article states that ilvM encodes the regulatory subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase I (also called acetolactate synthase I). This enzyme complex catalyzes the first step in the biosynthetic pathway for branched‑chain amino acids (valine, leucine, isoleucine). In the study, ilvM was expressed as a fusion protein with cytochrome b5 to improve its solubility and yield. {PubMed:15802225}. The article states that ilvM encodes the small subunit of acetohydroxy acid synthase (AHAS) II, one of three isozymes that catalyze the first step of the parallel pathway for the biosynthesis of the branched‑chain amino acids isoleucine and valine (and leucine). Thus, ilvM functions as part of the enzyme complex that initiates branched‑chain amino acid synthesis in Escherichia coli K‑12. {PubMed:2421252}. The article states that ilvM is the second structural gene of the ilvGMEDA operon and encodes the small subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase II (AHASII), an enzyme involved in the biosynthesis of branched‑chain amino acids. The coding region of ilvM also harbors the internal promoter ilvEp, which drives transcription of downstream genes (ilvE, ilvD, ilvA) under certain conditions. {PubMed:1917871}. The product of JW3742 encodes IlvN, the regulatory (ACT) subunit of acetohydroxyacid synthase I (AHAS I) in Escherichia coli. IlvN forms a dimer (and at higher concentrations can tetramerise) that associates with two catalytic subunits (IlvB) to generate the AHAS I holoenzyme (hetero‑hexameric 2 CSU : 4 RSU). The primary role of IlvN is to bind the end‑product branched‑chain amino acids valine and isoleucine at a pocket located at the dimer interface. Binding of these effectors triggers conformational changes—most notably a concerted side‑chain switch of Cys⁴³ and His⁵³—that mediate feedback inhibition of the holoenzyme. IlvN therefore acts as a sensor of intracellular valine and isoleucine levels, modulating AHAS I activity by either stabilising an inactive “T” state or reducing the stability of the active complex. In the ligand‑free state IlvN exists in an ensemble of oligomeric states (dimer–tetramer equilibrium) and adopts an ACT fold composed of three α‑helices and four β‑strands. The protein also interacts directly with the catalytic subunit IlvB, contributing to holoenzyme assembly and regulation. {PubMed:30887800}.

FUNCTION: Binds RpoD and negatively regulates RpoD-mediated transcription activation by preventing the interaction between the primary sigma factor RpoD with the catalytic core of the RNA polymerase and with promoter DNA. May be involved in replacement of the RNA polymerase sigma subunit from RpoD to RpoS during the transition from exponential growth to the stationary phase. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_01181, ECO:0000269|PubMed:10368152, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9560209}.
MetaCyc_Comment: Rsd exerts its effect via its ability to specifically interact with a number of proteins, including |FRAME: RPOD-MONOMER σ70| |CITS: |, |FRAME: SPOT-MONOMER SpoT| |CITS: | and dephosphorylated |FRAME: PTSH-MONOMER HPr| |CITS: |. Rsd was first identified as an anti-σ factor. It binds specifically to the major σ factor |FRAME: RPOD-MONOMER σ70| |CITS: | with a stoichiometry of 1:1 |CITS: |. Rsd sequesters σ70, making RNAP core enzyme accessible for σS and possibly other σ factors in stationary phase |CITS: |. The dephosphorylated form of |FRAME: PTSH-MONOMER HPr| is able to form a tight 1:1 complex with Rsd and thereby inhibit its interaction with σ70, linking Rsd anti-σ factor activity to nutrient availability |CITS: |. Rsd interacts directly with the TGS domain of |FRAME: SPOT-MONOMER SpoT| and stimulates its (p)ppGpp hydrolase activity; it does not interact with RelA. The stimulatory effect of Rsd on SpoT (p)ppGpp hydrolase activity is negated by the presence of dephosphorylated. Rsd thus functions as a link between PTS-dependent carbon source utilization and the stringent response HPr |CITS: |. Rsd can interact simultaneously with regions 4 |CITS: | and 2 |CITS: | of σ70. Region 4 is involved in recognition of the -35 promoter element, while region 2 is involved in the recognition of the -10 promoter element. Both regions also contain critical determinants for the interaction with core RNA polymerase (RNAP) |CITS: |. The crystal structure of Rsd bound to region 4 of σ70 shows that Rsd binding directly interferes with both the core RNAP-binding and promoter-binding functions of region 4 |CITS: |. A crystal structure of Rsd bound to HPr shows that the binding interfaces on Rsd for σ70 and HPr partially overlap |CITS: |. Rsd was initially isolated in a complex with σ70 from stationary-phase cell extracts |CITS: |. Rsd increases expression from a σS-dependent promoter and reduces expression from certain σ70-dependent promoters |CITS: |. Increasing amounts of Rsd can physically displace σ70 from holo-RNAP in vitro |CITS: |. Rsd protein levels increase as cell growth begins to decrease |CITS: |. Pull-down experiments have demonstrated that Rsd levels are only twofold higher in stationary phase, with approximately 6,000 molecules per cell, compared to levels in exponentially growing cells. Therefore, the concentration of Rsd should be high enough in exponentially growing cells to allow binding to σ70. Yet, the complex between Rsd and σ70 can only be detected in stationary-phase extracts |CITS: |. Expression of rsd is under the control of two promoters, P1 and P2, where P1 is σS-dependent and P2 is σ70-dependent |CITS: |. The P2 promoter is stronger than P1 and active in all phases of growth |CITS: |. Transcriptional regulators of rsd expression have been investigated |CITS: |. 6S RNA appears to regulate Rsd post-transcriptionally |CITS: |. In a high-throughput approach to identify dsRNA fragments that resulted from cleavage by RNase III, rsd mRNA was found to be regulated by RNase III |CITS: |. Global gene expression at different growth stages of wild-type cells compared to Δrsd and ΔrpoS mutants showed that ~75% of genes under σS control were also affected by loss of Rsd |CITS: |. A Δrsd mutation suppresses the growth defect of a ΔrelA mutant under amino acid starvation conditions, indicating that Rsd stimulates SpoT (p)ppGpp hydrolase activity in vivo. A Δrsd mutant also shows a longer diauxic lag phase and less efficient growth on casamino acids post-lag than wild-type |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: TrkH is a potassium ion transporter, closely related to the |FRAME: TRKG-MONOMER "TrkG"| potassium ion transporter. Early studies in E. coli K-12 identified four separate K+ uptake systems: two constitutive systems , a high affinity system (Kdp) and a non-saturable system TrkF |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |. Although initially thought to be a single system TrkA/Trk activity was later shown to result from the activity of two K+ transporters which were named |FRAME: TRKG-MONOMER "TrkG"| and |FRAME: TRKH-MONOMER "TrkH"| |CITS: |. trkG trkH double null mutations abolish saturable K+ uptake in a strain lacking |FRAME: ATPASE-1-CPLX "Kdp"| and |FRAME: KUP-MONOMER "TrkD"| mediated potassium transport |CITS: |. TrkG and TrkH show 41% amino acid identity; inactivation of either trkH or trkG (in a ΔkdpFABC trkD1 background) affects the kinetics of potassium uptake |CITS: |. TrkH and TrkG are both active as low affinity, high rate potassium ion transporters (Km of 1-6 mM) |CITS: | and function in conjunction with |FRAME: TRKA-MONOMER "TrkA"|, a peripheral membrane protein that binds NAD+ and is essential for TrkH/G activity |CITS: |. |FRAME: EG12304 "TrkE"| (also known as SapD), an ATP binding protein, is required for TrkH activity and affects the kinetics of TrkG activity |CITS: , |. In the Transporter Classification Database TrkH and TrkG are members of the K+ transporter (Trk) family within the VIC superfamily |CITS: |. TrkH is an inner membrane protein with 10 predicted transmembrane regions |CITS: |. TrkH is predicted to contain 4 sequential MPM (membrane-pore-membrane) regions plus two additional TM regions |CITS: |. Trk mediated K+ transport in E. coli requires both ATP and the proton motive force |CITS: | however Trk systems are not energised directly by ATP |CITS: |. A full understanding of the mechanism of Trk mediated K+ transport remains outstanding; structural and functional studies of the TrkH K+ transporter from Vibrio parahaemolyticus (see for example |CITS: | indicate that it assembles with the regulatory protein TrkA and operates as an ion channel. trk: transport of K |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: Evidence gathered for orthologous enzymes and genetic interactions indicate that UbiX is a flavin prenyltransferase that produces a novel cofactor for |FRAME: CPLX0-301 UbiD|, |FRAME: CPD-18260| |CITS: |. ubiX was first thought to encode a second 3-octaprenyl-4-hydroxybenzoate decarboxylase in E. coli |CITS: |; however, no biochemical evidence for the enzymatic function of UbiX was available at that time. The fungal genes pad1 and fdc1 are homologs of E. coli ubiX and ubiD, respectively. Coexpression of Fdc1 from both Saccharomyces cerevisiae |CITS: | and Aspergillus niger |CITS: | with either the respective Pad1 enzymes or E. coli UbiX allows isolation of active Fdc1, suggesting that UbiX is isofunctional with Pad1. The enzymatic function of Pseudomonas aeruginosa UbiX and the structure of its product, |FRAME: CPD-18260|, were fully characterized. UbiX is a flavin prenyltransferase that catalyzes the addition of the dimethylallyl moiety of dimethylallyl phosphate to the N5 and N6 atoms of FMNH2. This adds a fourth non-aromatic ring to the flavin isoalloxazine group, producing prenylated FMNH2. Crystallographic, biochemical, and biophysical studies characterized this new cofactor and suggested a UbiX reaction mechanism |CITS: |. The cofactor role of prenylated FMNH2 in UbiD-catalyzed reactions was also investigated |CITS: |. UbiX is found in both the cytosolic and membrane fractions. UbiD and UbiX co-migrate and may form a 700 kDa complex in the cytosol |CITS: |. Based on genetic interactions between ubiX and ubiD as well as their mutant phenotypes, it was initially proposed that UbiX and UbiD interact to be able to carry out the 3-octaprenyl-4-hydroxybenzoate decarboxylase step in ubiquinone biosynthesis during logarithmic growth |CITS: |. A genetic interaction between ubiX and ubiG was shown. Expression of UbiX can restore the final O-methylation reaction of the ubiquinone biosynthesis pathway in the IS16 mutant strain with the UbiG L132Q mutation |CITS: |. Expression of ubiX shows dependence on carbon source and regulation via Fnr, ArcA and HemA |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: In eubacteria ppGpp (guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-diphosphate) is a mediator of the stringent response which coordinates a variety of cellular activities in response to changes in nutritional abundance. This enzyme catalyzes the formation of pppGpp which is then hydrolyzed to form ppGpp. The second messengers ppGpp and c-di-GMP together control biofilm formation in response to translational stress; ppGpp represses biofilm formation while c-di-GMP induces it. ppGpp activates transcription of CsrA-antagonistic small RNAs CsrB and CsrC, which down-regulate CsrA's action on translation during the stringent response (PubMed:21488981). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:14622409, ECO:0000269|PubMed:19460094, ECO:0000269|PubMed:21488981, ECO:0000269|PubMed:26051177}.
Catalytic activity: CATALYTIC ACTIVITY: Reaction=GTP + ATP = guanosine 3'-diphosphate 5'-triphosphate + AMP; Xref=Rhea:RHEA:22088, ChEBI:CHEBI:30616, ChEBI:CHEBI:37565, ChEBI:CHEBI:142410, ChEBI:CHEBI:456215; EC=2.7.6.5;
MetaCyc_Comment: RelA is a key enzyme involved in the stringent response of Escherichia coli to amino acid starvation. It activates the synthesis of the global regulatory molecules of the stringent response ppGpp and pppGpp (referred to collectively as (p)ppGpp) via a ribosomal mechanism (see below). The amino acid sequence of RelA has been shown to be extensively related to that of SpoT |CITS: |. The RelA (p)ppGpp synthetase activity is referred to as (p)ppGpp synthetase I, or PSI. RelA also contains an inactive hydrolase domain (reviewed in |CITS: |). Its catalytic activity is located in the N-terminal portion of the molecule, while the C-terminal portion may have a regulatory function |CITS: |. The bifunctional SpoT protein provides opposing hydrolase activity for RelA synthetase activity, both of which are involved in the regulation of (p)ppGpp levels. SpoT also has a RelA-independent ppGpp synthetase activity, referred to as PSII, that can be demonstrated in relA null mutants (reviewed in Cashel et. al. (1996) "The Stringent Response", chapter 92, in |CITS: |). Mutations in the amino acid residues His219, Glu220, Tyr228, Pro253, Gly318, and Glu351 located in the synthetase domain of RelA resulted in reduced ppGpp synthesis |CITS: |. Strains with missense mutations in different positions of the N-terminal coding regions of relA allowed the synthesis of metabolically stable RelA proteins. Such strains also have a spoT gene mutation and are able to increase the ppGpp levels in the exponential phase when grown on Kornberg medium (KM) |CITS: |. Spot mutant strains with missense mutations in the relA gene showed an increase in glycogen content and elevated levels of glycogen gene expression when the strains were grown in KM. RelA is the major source of ppGpp, compared with SpoT, in cells growing in KM |CITS: |. Homologs of RelA and SpoT are members of the RelA/SpoT Homolog (RSH) superfamily. This superfamily has been divided into 30 subgroups comprising long RSHs, small alarmone synthetases (SASs) and small alarmone hydrolases (SAHs). Their phylogenetic relationships were studied across all domains of life |CITS: |. The mechanism of action of RelA has been studied both genetically and biochemically. It is a ribosome-associated (p)ppGpp synthetase that is activated by the binding of uncharged tRNA to its cognate codon on the acceptor site (A site) of a translating ribosome in response to amino acid starvation |CITS: |. Under these conditions ppGpp is synthesized and accumulates and stable RNA synthesis (rRNA, tRNA) is inhibited. This inhibition of stable RNA synthesis during the stringent response is "relaxed" in relA mutants (reviewed in Cashel et. al. (1996) "The Stringent Response", chapter 92, in |CITS: |). Detailed in vitro studies using recombinant RelA have allowed models of RelA function to be proposed. In one study it was determined that although the presence of a deacylated tRNA on the ribosomal A site was essential for RelA-mediated ppGpp synthesis, the binding of RelA to ribosomes was dependent upon the presence of a protruding 3' extension of mRNA on the ribosome. RelA binding was independent of ribosomal protein L11, the product of gene relC (rplK). Synthesis of ppGpp by RelA reduced its binding to the ribosome. These findings led to a model in which RelA may hop between blocked ribosomal complexes during the stringent response, allowing a relatively low concentration of the enzyme to produce sufficient ppGpp |CITS: |. Another study implicated ribosomal protein L11 in the regulation of RelA activity |CITS: |. Antiobiotics that block ribosome function at different sites, such as thiostrepton and tetracycline, inhibit pppGpp synthesis |CITS: |. More recently, an in vivo, single molecule tracking methodology was developed to monitor the intracellular RelA catalytic cycle using fluorescence imaging. Results suggested that RelA is ribosome-associated under nonstarvation conditions, but dissociates for an extended time period after activation to perform its catalytic cycle. Ribosome association was not necessary to trigger each ppGpp biosynthesis cycle. Heat stress caused fast activation of RelA with a rapid return to its inactive state, suggesting an excitable response mechanism for rapid adaptation to environmental changes |CITS: |. In contrast, the results of a quantitative and more extensive fluorescent imaging study were consistant with the hypothesis that ppGpp is synthesized during starvation while RelA is bound to the ribosome |CITS: |. Two studies suggested that oligomerization, or dimerization of RelA via its C-terminal domain (amino acid residues 456-744) may have a role in regulation of (p)ppGpp synthetase activity. They supported a model in which oligomeric RelA is enzymatically inactive and is activated during the stringent response by dissociation to a monomer |CITS: |. Apart from its known function, mutant studies have also suggested that RelA may have other as yet undefined roles in ribosome function apart from its (p)ppGpp synthetase activity |CITS: |. It has also been shown that E. coli RelA carries a functionally important EXDD motif that has been implicated in a preference for GDP as pyrophosphate acceptor. This is in contrast to earlier reports that GTP is preferred. The EXDD motif may also provide this enzyme with the ability to synthesize pGpp at a low level, the significance of which has yet to be determined |CITS: |. Several relA mutant alleles were shown to confer temperature-sensitive phenotypes, suggesting that ppGpp may be required for the expression of genes involved in thermotolerance |CITS: |. Native RelA has been purified to homogeneity |CITS: |. By itself it has little activity and must be activated in vitro by a complex of 70S ribosomes, mRNA and uncharged tRNA. In a non-ribosomal based assay it can be activated by solvents such as ethanol or methanol at concentrations of about 20% |CITS: |. A relA spoT mutant was found to form biofilms with reduced catalase activity and elevated levels of hydroxyl radicals; the mutant biofilms are more sensitive to the antibiotics ofloxacin and tobramycin than wild type |CITS: |. A putative alarmone |FRAME: CPD0-1415| from Enterococcus faecalis showed inhibition of rrnB operon transcription by E. coli RNA polymerase, and activation of E. coli RelA synthetase activity in the presence of both pGpp and ppGpp |CITS: |. pGpp is an inhibitor of E. coli |FRAME: SPOT-MONOMER "SpoT"| |CITS: |.

Merged_Functions: The article identifies b3302 as the structural gene for ribosomal protein L30 (rpmD). L30 is a component of the 50S ribosomal subunit and plays a crucial role in ribosome assembly. Mutations in this gene impair growth at low temperatures (partial cold‑sensitive phenotype) and disrupt the assembly of ribosomal particles, especially at 20 °C. Thus, b3302 encodes a 50S ribosomal protein required for proper ribosomal biogenesis and normal cellular growth. {PubMed:327286}. The article lists rpmD as one of the ten ribosomal protein genes in the Escherichia coli spc operon. Specifically, rpmD corresponds to the ribosomal protein L30. Thus, rpmD encodes a ribosomal protein component that is part of the bacterial ribosome and participates in the assembly and function of the ribosome during protein synthesis. {PubMed:6222285}. The rpmD gene encodes ribosomal protein L30, a structural component of the 50S ribosomal subunit in Escherichia coli. L30 is required for proper ribosome assembly, especially at low temperatures (20 °C), where mutations in rpmD cause partial cold‑sensitive growth defects and impair the formation of mature 70S ribosomes. The gene resides in a transcriptional unit together with other ribosomal protein genes (rpsE for S5 and rpsH for S8) and has been used as a genetic marker for mapping these loci. {PubMed:327286}.
Curated_Functions: Encodes ribosomal protein L30, a structural component of the 50S ribosomal subunit. {PubMed:327286, PubMed:6222285}. Required for proper ribosome assembly and formation of mature 70S ribosomes, particularly at low temperature (20 °C). {PubMed:327286, PubMed:6222285}. Essential for normal cellular growth; mutations cause a partial cold‑sensitive growth phenotype. {PubMed:327286, PubMed:6222285}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Sbp is a periplasmic sulfate/thiosulfate binding protein; Sbp is one of two periplasmic binding proteins that separately interact with an ABC transporter permease (CysAUW) to mediate high affinity uptake of sulfate and thiosulfate. Double cysP sbp mutants (cysP::Cat sbp::Kan) are cysteine auxotrophs; growth on sulfate (and thiosulfate) as sole sulfur source can be restored in the double mutant by multicopy expression of either cysP or sbp however growth is impaired compared to the wild type strain; CysP and Sbp have overlapping specificity and both are required for wild-type levels of sulfate/thiosulfate transport |CITS: |. Sbp was identified in a set of 'sulfate starvation induced' (SSI) proteins which were induced when cells were grown with sulfur sources (eg.methionine, glutathione, ethanesulfonate) other than sulfate and cysteine |CITS: |. When grown with lanthionine or glutathione as the sulfur source, the level of Sbp is significantly reduced in a |FRAME: G7071 "cbl"| null mutant compared to wild type |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: PstS is the periplasmic, phosphate binding protein of the ATP dependent, high affinity phosphate transport sytem in E. coli K-12. PstS consists of two globular domains separated by a deep cleft which forms the phosphate binding site |CITS: |. PstS binds monobasic (H2PO4-) and dibasic (H2PO42-) phosphates but discriminates against sulphate |CITS: |. The aspartate residue at position 81 forms a short (low barrier) hydrogen bond with phosphate |CITS: |. PstS can discriminate phosphate from arsenate up to an 800 fold molar excess of arsenate |CITS: |. A pstS D81N mutant has no effect on phosphate binding but disturbs the discrimination against arsenate approximately 10-fold and the discrimination against sulfate about 100-fold |CITS: |. pstS insertion mutants were identified in a screen for genes that are important for surviving exposure to ionizing radiation (IR). A pstS deletion mutant has a substantial decrease in survival upon exposure to increasing doses of IR |CITS: |. It was determined by Genomic SELEX screening that the upstream region of the gene pstS is a target of the transcriptional factor CusR |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: FadL is an outer membrane, ligand gated channel that functions in the uptake of long chain (C12-C18) fatty acids (LCFAs) |CITS: |. FadL also serves as the receptor site for bacteriophage T2 |CITS: |. Bacteriophage T2 binding specificity resides in the amino terminal region of FadL |CITS: |. Mutations in FadL can be generated that distinguish regions required for binding from those required for transport |CITS: |. FadL binding affinity is highest for oleic acid and palmitic acid; no binding of decanoic acid is detected |CITS: |. FadL crystal structures at 2.6 and 2.8 Å indicate that the protein forms a 14-stranded antiparallel β barrel. The amino terminus forms a small "hatch" domain which plugs the barrel on the extracellular side. A prominent hydrophobic pocket is located inside the barrel towards the extracellular side of the membrane and forms a high affinity substrate binding site; a hydrophobic groove formed between two extracellular loops may constitute a low-affinity site for initial interaction with LCFAs. β-strand S3 adopts an unusual conformation which disrupts interstrand H bonding and results in a gap in the barrel wall. There is no channel connecting the extracellular space with the periplasm |CITS: |. The transport of long chain fatty acids through FadL is thought to involve diffusion of the substrate coupled with conformational change of FadL |CITS: |. A FadL mutant (A77E S100R) in which the lateral opening in the barrel wall is constricted does not transport substrate. This result supports a lateral diffusion model for transport whereby long-chain fatty acids exit into the outer membrane through an opening in the FadL barrel wall and then diffuse into the periplasm |CITS:|. High affinity binding of LCFAs results in conformational change that drives the formation of a membrane facing exit channel and release of substrate |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: HycC is a polytopic integral membrane protein that, together with HycD, forms the membrane‑anchoring domain of the Escherichia coli formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex. It anchors the soluble core components (HycB, HycE, HycF, HycG, and the formate dehydrogenase subunit FdhF) to the cytoplasmic side of the membrane, thereby linking the catalytic core to the membrane and contributing to the overall architecture of the FHL complex. {PubMed:25157147}. HycC encodes one of the two integral membrane subunits of the Escherichia coli formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex. Together with HycD, HycC anchors the soluble catalytic domain of FHL to the inner membrane. It is homologous to the antiporter‑like NuoL/M/N subunits of respiratory Complex I and contains conserved charged residues (e.g., E135 and K239) that are analogous to residues implicated in proton translocation in Complex I. However, extensive site‑directed mutagenesis of HycC (17 single‑amino‑acid substitutions) did not identify any residue essential for FHL activity, and none of the mutations impaired either the forward (formate‑dependent H₂ production) or reverse (CO₂/H₂‑dependent formate production) reactions. Genetic deletion of hycC (or hycD) abolishes both forward and reverse FHL activities, indicating that HycC is required for proper assembly or activation of the enzyme complex, but it does not appear to be directly involved in catalysis or essential proton pumping. {PubMed:27139710}. The JW2693 strain carries a plasmid‑encoded hycC L208K allele (a Leu→Lys substitution at position 208 of the HycC membrane subunit of the formate hydrogenlyase complex).  This mutation does not impair FHL activity and, in fact, yields a modestly higher CO₂/H₂‑dependent formate production (the reverse FHL reaction) compared with the wild‑type hycC complement, indicating that the L208K change slightly enhances the reverse activity of the FHL complex. {PubMed:27139710}.
Curated_Functions: Anchors the soluble catalytic subunits (HycB, HycE, HycF, HycG, and FdhF) of the formate hydrogenlyase complex to the cytoplasmic side of the inner membrane together with HycD. {PubMed:25157147, PubMed:27139710}. Is required for proper assembly or activation of the formate hydrogenlyase complex; deletion of hycC abolishes both forward (formate‑dependent H₂ production) and reverse (CO₂/H₂‑dependent formate production) activities, indicating a structural rather than catalytic role. {PubMed:27139710}. Shows homology to antiporter‑like NuoL/M/N subunits of respiratory Complex I and contains conserved charged residues analogous to proton‑translocating residues, although mutagenesis shows these residues are not essential for FHL activity. {PubMed:27139710}. The L208K substitution slightly enhances the reverse CO₂/H₂‑dependent formate production activity of the FHL complex. {PubMed:27139710}.

Merged_Functions: The hevD region encodes the hydrophilic extra‑viral domain (HEVD) of the canine distemper virus (CDV) H glycoprotein.  This domain (amino acids 59‑607 of the H protein) is highly expressed in E. coli, retains strong antigenicity, and contains major epitopes recognized by anti‑CDV antibodies.  Because of its excellent antigenic properties, the HEVD protein is used as a recombinant antigen for serological diagnostics, such as ELISA, dot‑blot, and one‑step immunochromatography rapid tests, to detect and quantify anti‑CDV antibodies in canine serum. {PubMed:25234325}. HycD is a polytopic integral membrane protein that forms part of the membrane domain of the Escherichia coli formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex. Together with HycC, it is believed to anchor the soluble core components (HycB, HycE, HycF, HycG, and the formate dehydrogenase subunit FdhF) to the cytoplasmic side of the membrane, thereby mediating membrane attachment of the FHL complex. By analogy to respiratory Complex I, HycD (along with HycC) may also participate in coupling the enzymatic reaction to the membrane proton‑motive force, although its primary described role in the article is as an anchoring membrane subunit. {PubMed:25157147}. The hycD gene encodes HycD, one of the two integral membrane subunits of the Escherichia coli formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex. HycD is homologous to the NuoH subunit of respiratory Complex I and contains a series of highly conserved glutamate residues that are thought to participate in charge transmission within the membrane domain. Experimental evidence in the article shows that HycD is essential for FHL activity in vivo: deletion of hycD abolishes both the forward (formate‑dependent H₂ production) and reverse (CO₂/H₂‑dependent formate production) reactions. Site‑directed mutagenesis identified three conserved acidic residues—E138 (located in a transmembrane helix), and E199, E201, E203 (located in a cytoplasmic loop)—as critical for FHL function; alanine substitution of these residues markedly reduced activity of both reaction directions, likely because the mutations impair proper assembly or stability of the membrane‑attached FHL complex. Thus, HycD functions as a structural component of the FHL membrane domain that is required for correct assembly and full catalytic activity of the enzyme, although it does not appear to be directly involved in proton translocation. {PubMed:27139710}. The article indicates that hycD encodes a subunit of the formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex, also referred to as Hyd3, in Klebsiella oxytoca HP1. As part of this multi‑subunit hydrogenase complex, HycD contributes to the overall hydrogen production activity, especially under oxygen‑stressed conditions, although its precise biochemical role is not detailed beyond being a component of the Hyd3/FHL assembly. {PubMed:21187144}.
Curated_Functions: Acts as a recombinant antigen with strong antigenicity, containing major epitopes recognized by anti‑CDV antibodies, and is employed in serological diagnostic assays (ELISA, dot‑blot, rapid immunochromatography) to detect and quantify anti‑CDV antibodies in canine serum. {PubMed:25234325}. Anchors the soluble core components of the formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex to the cytoplasmic membrane, serving as a structural membrane subunit whose conserved acidic residues (E138, E199, E201, E203) are critical for assembly, stability and charge transmission, though it does not directly translocate protons. {PubMed:25157147, PubMed:27139710}. Contributes to overall hydrogen production, especially under oxygen‑stressed conditions, as a component of the Hyd3/FHL assembly in Klebsiella oxytoca. {PubMed:21187144}.

Merged_Functions: HycE encodes the large subunit of Escherichia coli hydrogenase 3, the catalytic component of the [NiFe] hydrogenase enzyme that catalyzes fermentative hydrogen production. The HycE polypeptide contains the dinuclear active site—a Fe(CN)₂(CO) cluster coordinated to a nickel ion—required for hydrogen turnover. During maturation, HycE first receives an iron‑containing cofactor via the HypCDEF proteins; subsequently, the nickel insertion proteins HypA, HypB, and SlyD interact with the HycE precursor to deliver nickel, a step that depends on an intact NikABCDE nickel transporter. Fully processed HycE assembles into the membrane‑associated formate hydrogen lyase complex, localizing near the inner membrane where hydrogen production occurs. {PubMed:22016389}. hycE encodes the precursor (pre‑HycE) of the large catalytic subunit of Escherichia coli hydrogenase 3, a [NiFe]‑hydrogenase. The protein carries the metal‑binding motifs that coordinate the Ni‑Fe centre (Cys^241, Cys^244, Cys^531 and Cys^534). During maturation, pre‑HycE forms a complex with the chaperone‑type protein HypC; this interaction masks Cys^241, allows iron to bind at Cys^244, and later permits nickel insertion at Cys^531. After nickel incorporation, the C‑terminal extension of pre‑HycE is proteolytically removed, and Cys^534 provides the thiolate that closes the bridge between the iron and nickel atoms, completing the active site. Thus, hycE is essential for assembly of the functional Ni‑Fe centre and for the activity of hydrogenase 3. {PubMed:10783387}. hycE encodes the large catalytic subunit of Escherichia coli hydrogenase 3, a [NiFe] hydrogenase that is a core component of the formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex. The protein provides the active site for the reversible reaction 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂, enabling both hydrogen production (synthesis) and hydrogen consumption (uptake). Deletion of hycE abolishes hydrogen evolution and significantly reduces hydrogen uptake, while plasmid‑mediated complementation restores both activities. Thus, hycE is essential for the bidirectional hydrogenase activity of hydrogenase 3 and for coupling formate oxidation to hydrogen metabolism in E. coli. {PubMed:17668201}. Encodes the large subunit of Escherichia coli hydrogenase 3, a [NiFe] hydrogenase that is a structural component of the formate hydrogen‑lyase complex. The enzyme catalyzes the disproportionation of formate into hydrogen gas (H₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) during fermentative growth, accepting electrons from formate dehydrogenase H. HycE is initially synthesized as a Ni‑free precursor (pre‑HycE) and requires post‑translational maturation: incorporation of the Ni‑Fe metallocenter by the accessory proteins HypA, HypB, HypC, HypD, HypE, and HypF, followed by C‑terminal proteolytic cleavage by the HycI protease to generate the active large subunit. {PubMed:9485446}. The hycE gene encodes HYCE, the large catalytic subunit of Escherichia coli hydrogenase 3, a NiFe‑type hydrogenase that is part of the formate‑hydrogenlyase complex. HYCE contains the two conserved nickel‑binding motifs (RXCXXC and DPCXXCXXH) and binds approximately one nickel ion per subunit, which is essential for its activity. After nickel insertion, the precursor HYCE undergoes a specific C‑terminal proteolytic cleavage at Arg537, removing a ~3.85 kDa peptide and generating the mature, active large subunit. Thus, hycE provides the structural framework for nickel coordination and the catalytic core of hydrogenase 3, and its product requires post‑translational maturation (nickel incorporation and C‑terminal processing) to become functional. {PubMed:8125094}. HycE encodes the large catalytic subunit of the [NiFe]-hydrogenase (Hyd‑3) that forms the core of the formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex in *Escherichia coli*. The C‑terminal domain (aa 175‑537) contains the four conserved cysteine residues that coordinate the NiFe active site and directly catalyzes the reduction of protons to H₂ using electrons derived from formate oxidation by the associated formate dehydrogenase (FdhH). The N‑terminal domain (aa 9‑194) does not bind cofactors but is essential for proper assembly and stability of the FHL complex: it drives the incorporation of the small hydrogenase subunit HycG, stabilises the core Fe‑S proteins, and determines correct complex formation. Deletion of the N‑terminal domain abolishes FHL activity, whereas physical separation of the two domains retains most catalytic function, indicating a complex‑specific assembly role. HycE is evolutionarily related to the NuoCD fusion protein of respiratory complex I, sharing a similar domain architecture but performing distinct functions in the respective complexes. {PubMed:31925988}. HycE encodes the catalytic α‑subunit of the [NiFe] hydrogenase component (Hyd‑3) of the Escherichia coli formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex. It forms the core hydrogen‑evolving module of FHL, receiving electrons from the formate dehydrogenase (FdhF) via the Fe‑S proteins HycB, HycF and HycG, and catalyzes the reduction of protons to molecular hydrogen (2 H⁺ + 2 e⁻ → H₂). HycE consists of an N‑terminal domain (residues 1–166) homologous to the 30‑kDa subunit of NADH dehydrogenase and a C‑terminal domain (residues 172–539) that contains the conserved motifs for binding the NiFe cofactor. The protein is essential for formate‑dependent H₂ evolution during anaerobic fermentation, exhibits unusually weak product inhibition by H₂, and shows relatively high tolerance to CO inhibition. {PubMed:25157147}. The hycE gene encodes a subunit of the formate hydrogen‑lyase (FHL) complex, specifically the catalytic component of hydrogenase‑3 (Hyd‑3). In Escherichia coli, HycE is essential for anaerobic hydrogen (H₂) production during the fermentation of sugars such as those derived from spent coffee grounds. Deletion of hycE abolishes H₂ evolution, indicating that Hyd‑3 is the primary enzyme responsible for converting formate into H₂ and CO₂ under the studied conditions. The loss of HycE also reduces the specific growth rate and alters extracellular pH, reflecting its role in maintaining proton motive force and overall bioenergetic balance during mixed‑acid fermentation. {PubMed:32463433}. The hycE gene encodes the catalytic large subunit of the [NiFe] hydrogenase‑3 (Hyd‑3) that forms the core of the membrane‑bound formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex in Escherichia coli. HycE carries the Ni‑Fe active site that reduces protons to H₂ using electrons derived from formate oxidation by the associated formate dehydrogenase (FDH‑H). Its maturation requires delivery of the Fe(CN)₂CO cofactor by the Hyp proteins, insertion of nickel by HypAB, and C‑terminal proteolytic processing by the specific endoprotease HycI. Once processed, HycE interacts with its small subunit HycG and the electron‑transfer subunits HycF, HycB, and HycG to assemble a functional FHL complex that couples formate oxidation to hydrogen evolution. The article also notes that HycE can be affinity‑purified via a chromosomal His‑tag and that the chaperone HycH specifically binds the unprocessed precursor of HycE during early stages of assembly. {PubMed:28718449}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the reversible reduction of protons to molecular hydrogen using electrons derived from formate oxidation and also catalyzes hydrogen uptake. {PubMed:22016389, PubMed:17668201, PubMed:25157147, PubMed:9485446, PubMed:8125094, PubMed:31925988}. Binds a Ni‑Fe metallocenter composed of a Fe(CN)₂CO cluster coordinated to a nickel ion, employing conserved cysteine motifs (RXCXXC, DPCXXCXXH) for active‑site coordination. {PubMed:22016389, PubMed:10783387, PubMed:8125094, PubMed:9485446}. Undergoes post‑translational maturation involving delivery of the Fe(CN)₂CO cofactor by HypCDEF proteins, nickel insertion by HypA, HypB (and SlyD), and C‑terminal proteolytic cleavage by the specific endoprotease HycI to generate the mature large subunit. {PubMed:22016389, PubMed:10783387, PubMed:9485446, PubMed:28718449}. Interacts with the small hydrogenase subunit HycG and electron‑transfer subunits HycF, HycB, as well as the chaperone HycH, to assemble the membrane‑associated formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex; the N‑terminal domain is required for proper assembly and stability of the complex. {PubMed:31925988, PubMed:25157147, PubMed:28718449}. Couples formate oxidation by formate dehydrogenase (FdhH/FdhF) to hydrogen evolution, catalyzing the disproportionation of formate into H₂ and CO₂ during fermentative growth. {PubMed:9485446, PubMed:17668201, PubMed:32463433}. Is essential for anaerobic hydrogen production and for maintaining proton motive force and optimal growth during mixed‑acid fermentation; deletion abolishes H₂ evolution and reduces the specific growth rate. {PubMed:32463433, PubMed:22016389}. Localizes near the inner membrane as part of the membrane‑associated FHL complex. {PubMed:22016389}.

Merged_Functions: hycG encodes the small subunit of the [NiFe] hydrogenase component (Hyd‑3) of the Escherichia coli formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex. The HycG protein is predicted to bind a single 4Fe–4S cluster and to act as the direct electron‑transfer partner for the catalytic large subunit HycE. Together with HycB, HycE, and HycF, HycG forms the stable soluble core (≈131 kDa) of FHL; loss of hycG destabilises the entire complex, leaving only HycE detectable. Site‑directed mutagenesis of HycG was performed to introduce additional cysteines in an attempt to confer oxygen tolerance, indicating its role in the proximal Fe‑S cluster that influences sensitivity to O₂. Overall, HycG is essential for proper assembly, stability, and electron transfer within the FHL hydrogenase module. {PubMed:26358294}. HycG encodes a small iron‑sulfur protein that is a core component of the Escherichia coli formate hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex. It is predicted to contain a single [4Fe‑4S] cluster and functions as the β‑subunit of the Hyd‑3 [NiFe] hydrogenase, partnering with the catalytic α‑subunit HycE. Within the FHL complex, HycG participates in the electron‑transfer chain that shuttles electrons from the formate dehydrogenase (FdhF) through the Fe‑S proteins HycB and HycF to the hydrogenase active site, enabling reduction of protons to H₂ during formate disproportionation. HycG is membrane‑associated as part of the soluble core pentameric subcomplex (HycB, HycF, HycG, HycE, and FdhF). {PubMed:25157147}. hycG encodes the small subunit of the [NiFe] hydrogenase Hyd3 in Klebsiella oxytoca HP1. The protein contains three conserved cysteine‑rich motifs (CxxC, GxCx…G, and GCPP) characteristic of hydrogenase small subunits. As part of the Hyd3 (formate hydrogenlyase) complex, HycG is presumed to function as the small subunit that participates in electron transfer within the complex and contributes to the proper assembly and activity of the NiFe catalytic center. {PubMed:21187144}. HycG encodes the small, iron–sulfur‑cluster‑containing subunit of the [NiFe]‑hydrogenase Hyd‑3 (part of the formate hydrogenlyase complex). It is predicted to bind a single [Fe‑S] cluster and serves as the electron‑transfer conduit that links the large catalytic subunit HycE to the downstream components of the FHL complex. The presence of HycG is required for hydrogen‑dependent reduction of the artificial electron acceptor benzyl viologen; strains lacking hycG show no measurable hydrogenase activity, which can be restored by supplying hycG in trans. {PubMed:21717143}. According to the article, hycG encodes the small subunit of the Escherichia coli hydrogenase‑3 (Hyc) that is part of the formate‑hydrogen lyase complex. The HycG protein is an iron‑sulfur‑binding subunit (containing a single [4Fe‑4S] cluster) that interacts with the large nickel‑containing subunit (HycE) and participates in electron transfer within the hydrogenase complex. {PubMed:9546662}. Encodes a tightly membrane‑bound subunit of the formate‑hydrogenlyase (FHL) complex (hydrogenase 3). Deletion of hycG abolishes hydrogenase 3 activity and markedly reduces formate dehydrogenase H activity, demonstrating that HycG is essential for the functional assembly and activity of hydrogenase 3. Immunoblotting shows HycG is firmly attached to the membrane, and sequence analysis indicates similarity to the small subunits of hydrogenases and homology to NADH‑ubiquinone‑oxidoreductase subunits, suggesting a role in electron transfer within the FHL complex. {PubMed:1625581}.
Curated_Functions: Binds a single [4Fe‑4S] cluster. {PubMed:26358294, PubMed:25157147, PubMed:21717143, PubMed:9546662, PubMed:1625581}. Acts as the small (β) subunit of the Hyd‑3 [NiFe] hydrogenase, directly interacting with the large catalytic subunit HycE and serving as an electron‑transfer conduit to downstream components of the formate hydrogenlyase complex. {PubMed:26358294, PubMed:25157147, PubMed:21187144, PubMed:9546662, PubMed:1625581}. Contains three conserved cysteine‑rich motifs (CxxC, GxCx…G, GCPP) characteristic of hydrogenase small subunits, contributing to proper assembly of the NiFe catalytic center. {PubMed:21187144}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Farnesyl diphosphate synthase can utilize both dimethylallyl and geranyl diphosphates as substrates, generating geranyl and farnesyl diphosphate, respectively. Therefore the enzyme can catalyze two sequential reactions in the polyisoprenoid biosynthetic pathway |CITS: |. Isoprenoid product chain length specificity determinants within IspA were identified by random PCR mutagenesis |CITS: |. Substrate selectivity and stereoselectivity of the enzyme have been investigated |CITS: |. Crystal structures of ternary complexes of the enzyme with substrate(s) or an inhibitor have been solved, revealing the contribution of three Mg2+ ions to substrate binding and catalysis |CITS: |. ispA null mutants are viable, with near-wild type growth yield under anaerobic conditions and a slight reduction in growth yield under aerobic conditions. The mutant contains less than 13% and 18%, respectively, of ubiquinone-8 and menaquinone-8 and 40-70% of the wild-type levels of undecaprenyl phosphate. A low level of geranyl diphosphate synthase activity was detected, which may be due to the activity of other prenyltransferases |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: 6-hydroxymethyl-7,8-dihydropterin pyrophosphokinase (HPPK) catalyzes a reaction in the folate biosynthesis pathway, the transfer of pyrophosphate from ATP to 6-hydroxymethyl-7,8-dihydropterin |CITS: |. HPPK is essential in microorganisms, and the enzyme is not present in mammals; it is therefore a target for the development of antimicrobial drugs. Various crystal and solution structures of HPPK have been solved and have elucidated the reaction mechanism and kinetics. The protein undergoes conformational changes during the catalytic cycle. |CITS: | The enzyme binds ATP first, which then enables faster binding of 6-hydroxymethyl-7,8-dihydropterin (HMDP) |CITS: |. Mg2+ is important for binding of both ATP and HMDP |CITS: |. The roles in substrate binding and catalysis of several amino acid residues in the flexible loop 3 have been investigated by site-directed mutagenesis |CITS: |. Substrate site inhibitors have been synthesized and tested |CITS: |. Comparative genomics has suggested a functional association between |FRAME: 3-METHYL-2-OXOBUT-OHCH3XFER-CPLX PanB| and FolK. The proposed hypothesis is that a side reaction catalyzed by PanB damages 5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate (CH2-THF), and FolK subsequently recycles the resulting pterin moiety to folate. In support of this hypothesis, overexpression of panB increases the cells' sensitivity to antifolate drugs sulfathiazole and trimethoprim. However, overexpression of panB increases the intracellular folate pool. Kinetic modeling of the folate synthesis pathway suggests that a regulatory effect, whereby an initial drop in THF concentration upon PanB overexpression leads to increased expression of enzymes in the THF synthesis pathway, can explain this effect |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: Glutamyl-Q tRNAAsp synthetase (Glu-Q-RS, GluQ) catalyzes the addition of a glutamate residue to the queosine-modified wobble base of tRNAAsp. The GluQ protein shows similarity to the amino terminal part of bacterial glutamyl-tRNA synthetases, although it lacks the tRNA anticodon interaction domain |CITS: |. The protein is not capable of using tRNAGlu or tRNAGln as a substrate in vitro or in vivo, but can modify tRNAAsp with glutamate |CITS: |. There, glutamate is not esterified to the 3' terminal adenosine, but the 2-amino-5-(4,5-dihydroxy-2-cyclopenten-1-yl) moiety of queosine, which occupies the wobble position of the tRNAAsp anticodon |CITS: |. This tRNA modification is present in the normal E. coli tRNA pool |CITS: |. The glutamylated tRNAAsp does not bind elongation factor Tu and may therefore not be involved in ribosomal protein synthesis |CITS: |. Discrimination against other tRNAs that contain queosine at the wobble position is due to the C38 and C32 nucleotides of tRNAAsp |CITS: |. Homologs of GluQ have so far only been found in bacteria |CITS: |; functional similarity to the YadB protein of Neisseria meningitidis suggests a ubiquitous function |CITS: |. Crystal structures of Glu-Q-RS alone |CITS: | and in complex with glutamate |CITS: | have been solved at 1.5 and 1.75 Å resolution. A Zn2+ atom is predicted to be present and coordinated by cysteine and tyrosine ligands |CITS: |. A C101S/C103S mutant still contains 0.2 moles of zinc |CITS: |. Comparison with the structure of GluRS-Glu complex allowed insight into the structural elements that distinguish the catalytic properties of the two enzymes |CITS: |. Disruption of the gluQ gene does not cause a detectable phenotype on rich or minimal growth media |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |
