Merged_Functions: Encodes a soluble NAD(P)H‑binding quinone oxidoreductase (QorA) that is strongly up‑regulated by oxidative stress (e.g., exposure to the redox‑cycling agent 9,10‑phenanthrenequinone). QorA catalyzes NADPH‑dependent reduction of quinones, predominantly via a one‑electron pathway that generates semiquinone radicals which rapidly react with oxygen to produce superoxide anion; only a small amount of the two‑electron reduced hydroquinone is formed. The protein forms multimers under physiological conditions, is cytoplasmic, and is transcribed as part of a polycistronic operon together with the adjacent genes SA1990 and SA1988. These properties indicate that QorA functions as an oxidative‑stress‑responsive quinone reductase in Staphylococcus aureus. {PubMed:12624201}. The qor gene encodes a soluble, NAD(P)H‑dependent quinone oxidoreductase (QOR) in Escherichia coli.  QOR functions as a homodimeric enzyme that binds NADPH in a Rossmann‑fold nucleotide‑binding domain and catalyzes the reduction of a range of synthetic quinone substrates (but not menadione).  The enzyme therefore participates in quinone metabolism, likely contributing to the detoxification or processing of quinone compounds, although its precise physiological role in the cell remains to be fully elucidated. {PubMed:7602590}. The article identifies QOR (NAD(P)H‑quinone oxidoreductase) as an enzyme that possesses flavin reductase activity, using NAD(P)H to reduce free flavins (FAD, FMN, riboflavin). Recombinant QOR (rQOR) also displays free flavin‑dependent ferric reductase activity, enabling the reduction of ferric iron stored in E. coli ferritin A and bacterioferritin and thereby promoting the release of ferrous iron. Compared with other flavin‑reducing enzymes (Fre, AhpF), rQOR shows markedly lower flavin reductase and ferrous‑iron‑release activities, but it still contributes to the overall pathway whereby free flavins mediate electron transfer from NAD(P)H to ferric iron in iron‑storage proteins. {PubMed:31281172}. The qor gene encodes Escherichia coli quinone oxidoreductase, a member of the medium‑chain dehydrogenase/reductase (MDR) superfamily that functions as a NAD(P)H‑dependent reductase. QOR catalyzes the reduction of quinone substrates using NADPH (and also NADH) as the electron donor. Unlike zinc‑containing dehydrogenases in the same family, QOR lacks catalytic and structural zinc ions, and its active site contains residues adapted for quinone reduction rather than metal coordination. The enzyme adopts the typical MDR fold with a Rossmann‑type nucleotide‑binding domain and a catalytic domain, but displays unique sequence insertions that accommodate NADPH binding and a more solvent‑accessible substrate‑binding cleft. {PubMed:8638928}. The qor gene encodes a soluble Escherichia coli quinone oxidoreductase (QOR) of about 35 kDa that forms a homodimer. QOR catalyzes the NAD(P)H‑dependent two‑electron reduction of a variety of simple quinones, showing a general preference for NADPH over NADH as the electron donor. By converting quinones to their corresponding hydroquinones, QOR is implicated in the detoxification of quinone compounds, similar to the role described for the related ζ‑crystallin proteins in other species. {PubMed:8046753}. The qor gene encodes a soluble quinone oxidoreductase (QOR_Tt) that belongs to the medium‑chain dehydrogenase/reductase superfamily. The enzyme binds NADPH preferentially over NADH and catalyzes the NADPH‑dependent two‑electron reduction of quinones, showing measurable activity toward p‑benzoquinone but little or no activity toward larger substrates such as 5‑hydroxy‑1,4‑naphthoquinone and phenanthraquinone. Structural analysis indicates that the substrate‑binding pocket is restricted to small molecules, suggesting a role in detoxifying low‑molecular‑weight quinones. The protein forms a thermostable homodimer and contains a flexible lid that closes over the NADPH‑binding cleft upon cofactor binding. Overall, QOR_Tt functions as an NADPH‑dependent quinone reductase likely involved in cellular protection against quinone‑derived oxidative stress. {PubMed:12837796}. The qor1 gene encodes a soluble, NAD(P)H‑dependent quinone oxidoreductase (QOR) that catalyzes the two‑electron reduction of a range of synthetic quinone substrates. The enzyme binds NADPH in a Rossmann‑fold domain and uses the catalytic domain to transfer a hydride to quinone molecules, converting them to hydroquinones. Although inactive toward the natural quinone menadione, QOR is inhibited by the quinone‑oxidoreductase inhibitor dicumerol. The protein forms a homodimer and shares structural similarity with horse liver alcohol dehydrogenase and ζ‑crystallin. While its precise physiological role in *E. coli* remains unclear, the described activity suggests a function in quinone metabolism and possibly cellular protection against quinone‑derived toxicity. {PubMed:7602590}. The qor1 gene encodes Escherichia coli quinone oxidoreductase (QOR), a member of the medium‑chain dehydrogenase/reductase (MDR) superfamily that functions as a NAD(P)H‑dependent reductase. QOR catalyzes the reduction of quinone substrates, using NADPH (and to a lesser extent NADH) as the electron donor. Unlike the zinc‑containing dehydrogenases in the same family, QOR lacks both catalytic and structural zinc ions, and its active site residues have been altered to accommodate quinone reduction rather than alcohol oxidation. The enzyme adopts the typical MDR fold with a Rossmann‑type nucleotide‑binding domain and a catalytic domain, but displays a widened substrate‑binding cleft and specific residues (e.g., Val 172, Lys 177, Arg 317) that confer NADPH specificity and facilitate quinone reduction. {PubMed:8638928}. The qor1 gene encodes a soluble Escherichia coli quinone oxidoreductase (QOR) of ~35 kDa that forms a homodimer. QOR catalyzes the NAD(P)H‑dependent two‑electron reduction of a variety of simple quinones, showing a preference for NADPH over NADH as the electron donor. This activity places QOR in a third class of bacterial quinone reductases distinct from membrane‑bound NADH‑quinone oxidoreductases. By reducing quinones to hydroquinones, QOR is implicated in the detoxification of quinone compounds and possibly other xenobiotics, analogous to the detoxifying role of the related eukaryotic ζ‑crystallin. {PubMed:8046753}. Encodes a soluble quinone oxidoreductase that belongs to the medium‑chain dehydrogenase/reductase superfamily. The enzyme preferentially binds NADPH (rather than NADH) and catalyzes NADPH‑dependent reduction of quinones, showing weak activity toward p‑benzoquinone and no activity toward larger substrates such as 5‑hydroxy‑1,4‑naphthoquinone and phenanthraquinone. Structural features include a blocked substrate‑binding pocket that limits access to small substrates, a flexible lid that closes over the NADPH‑binding cleft, and formation of a homodimer. The protein is highly thermostable (denaturation ~80 °C) and is thought to function in quinone detoxification or metabolism, contributing to oxidative‑stress resistance. {PubMed:12837796}. qorA encodes a soluble, NADPH‑dependent quinone oxidoreductase in Staphylococcus aureus. The 333‑aa protein contains an NAD(P)H‑binding motif, forms multimers under physiological conditions, and catalyzes the one‑electron reduction of quinones such as 9,10‑phenanthrenequinone. This reaction consumes NADPH and generates semiquinone radicals that rapidly react with oxygen to produce superoxide anions, with only a minor amount of two‑electron (hydroquinone) product formed. Expression of qorA is strongly up‑regulated by oxidative stress (e.g., exposure to the redox‑cycling agent 9,10‑phenanthrenequinone), suggesting a role in the bacterial oxidative‑stress response. {PubMed:12624201}. The qorA gene encodes a soluble, NAD(P)H‑dependent quinone oxidoreductase (QOR) that forms a homodimeric enzyme capable of reducing a variety of synthetic quinone substrates. The enzyme binds NADPH in a Rossmann‑fold nucleotide‑binding domain and catalyzes electron transfer from the reduced nicotinamide cofactor to quinone molecules, generating semiquinone or hydroquinone products. Although the physiological role is not fully resolved, the article notes that QOR activity may contribute to cellular protection against quinone‑induced cytotoxicity and could be involved in quinone detoxification. {PubMed:7602590}. The qorA gene encodes NAD(P)H‑quinone oxidoreductase (QOR), an enzyme that exhibits flavin reductase activity, reducing free flavins (FAD, FMN, riboflavin) using NADH or NADPH. QOR also functions as a free flavin‑dependent ferric reductase, facilitating the reduction of ferric iron stored in ferritin A and bacterioferritin to ferrous iron, thereby promoting iron release from these iron‑storage proteins. Its activity is markedly lower than that of Fre and AhpF but still contributes to the overall flavin‑mediated iron‑release pathway in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:31281172}. The qorA gene encodes Escherichia coli quinone oxidoreductase (QOR), a member of the medium‑chain dehydrogenase/reductase (MDR) superfamily that functions as a NAD(P)H‑dependent reductase. QOR catalyzes the reduction of quinone substrates using NADPH (and to a lesser extent NADH) as electron donors. Unlike zinc‑containing dehydrogenases in the same family, QOR lacks catalytic and structural zinc ions, and its active site contains residues adapted for quinone reduction rather than metal coordination. The enzyme adopts the typical MDR fold with a Rossmann‑type nucleotide‑binding domain and a catalytic domain, and it exhibits substrate‑binding clefts that are more solvent‑accessible due to the absence of the zinc‑binding loop. {PubMed:8638928}. The qorA gene encodes a soluble Escherichia coli NAD(P)H‑dependent quinone oxidoreductase (QOR) of ~35 kDa that forms a homodimer. QOR catalyzes the two‑electron reduction of a variety of simple quinones, preferentially using NADPH rather than NADH as the electron donor. This activity is linked to the detoxification of quinones and possibly other xenobiotics, analogous to the function of ζ‑crystallin in other organisms. {PubMed:8046753}. The qorA gene encodes a soluble quinone oxidoreductase (QOR_T) belonging to the medium‑chain dehydrogenase/reductase superfamily. The enzyme is a homodimeric, highly thermostable protein that binds NADPH preferentially over NADH via a positively charged pocket that accommodates the 2′‑phosphate of NADPH. QOR_T catalyzes NADPH‑dependent reduction of quinones, showing measurable activity toward p‑benzoquinone but very weak or no activity toward larger quinone substrates such as 5‑hydroxy‑1,4‑naphthoquinone and phenanthraquinone. The substrate‑binding site is largely occluded, restricting access to small molecules. The protein lacks the zinc‑binding residues typical of dehydrogenases, confirming its classification as a reductase. Based on its quinone‑reducing activity and similarity to ζ‑crystallin, QOR_T is presumed to participate in cellular detoxification of quinones and protection against oxidative stress. {PubMed:12837796}.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Curlin is the structural subunit of the curli fimbriae. Curli are coiled surface structures that assemble preferentially at growth temperatures below 37 degrees Celsius. Curli can bind to fibronectin.
MetaCyc_Comment: csgA encodes curlin - the major subunit protein of curli which are thin, coiled surface structures involved in inert surface colonization, biofilm formation, and bacterial binding to a variety of extracellular matrix and serum proteins |CITS: |. Curli production requires CsgA and the nucleator protein |FRAME: G6547-MONOMER "CsgB"|; soluble monomeric curlin is secreted from a csgB- strain and can be polymerized into curli on the surface of a csgA- strain grown in close proximity |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Secretion of CsgA is mediated by the |FRAME: CPLX-3945 "curli secretion and assembly complex"| |CITS: | and requires the curli assembly component |FRAME: G6545-MONOMER "CsgE"| |CITS: |. The periplasmic chaperone, |FRAME: G6548-MONOMER "CsgC"| maintains CsgA in a solule monomeric state |CITS: |. Purified CsgA polymerizes into amyloid fibrils in vitro |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Mature CsgA contains an N-terminal domain followed by a repeat domain that contains five, functionally important, imperfect repeats (R1 - R5) |CITS: |. The mechanism of curli nucleation and growth is the subject of ongoing investigation |CITS: |. The curli specific genes are present in two divergently transcribed operons, csgBAC and csgDEFG |CITS: | which encode the structural, accessory and regulatory proteins of the curli biosynthetic pathway (reviewed in |CITS: |). Curli are produced at low temperatures, at low osmolarity and in stationary phase and expression is controlled by a complex regulatory network (see |CITS: |). E. coli strains vary in their capacity to produce curli |CITS: |; E. coli K-12 MG1655 is proficient in curli production (see |CITS: |). The ompR234 regulatory mutation activates curli expression in E. coli K-12 MG1655 |CITS: | (see also |CITS: |). Related reviews: |CITS: |

Merged_Functions: bglX encodes a periplasmic β‑D‑glucosidase (EC 3.2.1.21) that is exported to the periplasm via an N‑terminal signal peptide and matures into a 745‑amino‑acid (~81 kDa) enzyme. The protein belongs to the BglX family of glycosyl‑hydrolase family 3 and contains conserved catalytic residues (e.g., Asp267) typical of β‑glucosidases. Biochemically, BglX hydrolyzes β‑glucosidic bonds such as those in the chromogenic substrate o‑nitrophenyl‑β‑D‑glucopyranoside, exhibiting a Kₘ of ~18 mM and a Vₘₐₓ of ~3 µmol min⁻¹. The gene is located at 47.8 min (≈2225 kb) on the E. coli chromosome, adjacent to the dld gene, and is transcribed divergently from it. Functional assays show that BglX can cleave β‑glucosides in the periplasm, potentially releasing free glucose for uptake, although overproduction or deletion of bglX did not affect growth on common β‑glucosides, indicating that its natural substrates remain unidentified. The authors suggest possible roles in utilization of environmental β‑glucosides or in metabolism of cell‑wall polysaccharides such as peptidoglycan or LPS. {PubMed:8757730}. The bglX gene (identified as the xynB5/CCNA_03149 locus in Caulobacter crescentus) encodes a GH3 family protein that contains a conserved BglX β‑glucosidase‑β‑xylosidase domain (and a C‑terminal fibronectin type III‑like domain). The recombinant BglX‑V‑Ara protein is a multifunctional hydrolase that catalyzes three reactions: (i) β‑glucosidase activity on p‑nitrophenyl‑β‑D‑glucoside (pNPG), (ii) β‑xylosidase activity on p‑nitrophenyl‑β‑D‑xyloside (pNPX), and (iii) α‑L‑arabinosidase activity on p‑nitrophenyl‑α‑L‑arabinofuranoside (pNPA). It displays the highest affinity and catalytic efficiency for the β‑glucosidase reaction (Km ≈ 0.24 mM, Kcat/Km ≈ 0.27 mM⁻¹ s⁻¹), with lower but measurable activity toward the other two substrates. The enzyme functions optimally at pH 6 for all three activities; the optimal temperature is 50 °C for β‑glucosidase and α‑L‑arabinosidase, and 60 °C for β‑xylosidase. BglX is predicted to act in the periplasmic space of Gram‑negative bacteria and participates in the degradation of hemicellulose by hydrolyzing glucose‑, xylose‑, and arabinose‑containing oligosaccharides, thereby contributing to carbon recycling and offering potential for biotechnological applications such as simultaneous saccharification of lignocellulosic biomass. {PubMed:26264062}. The bglX gene encodes a 787‑amino‑acid β‑D‑glucosidase (approximately 95 kDa) that functions as an exo‑type enzyme hydrolyzing β‑D‑glucosidic linkages in natural O‑glycosides. In Bifidobacterium longum H‑1 it catalyzes the conversion of ginsenoside Rb1 to ginsenoside Rd (a step toward the bioactive compound K), and also hydrolyzes other plant glycosides such as loganin to loganetin, arctiin to arctigenin, and arbutin to hydroquinone. The enzyme shows optimal activity at pH 5.5 and 35–37 °C, is not affected by NaCl, but is strongly inhibited by Cu²⁺ and Ni²⁺. It does not act on C‑glycosides (e.g., mangiferin) or other glycosides lacking β‑D‑glucose residues. Thus, bglX provides the bacterium with the ability to metabolize dietary glycosylated compounds, contributing to the biotransformation of herbal constituents by intestinal microflora. {PubMed:22466563}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Transketolase catalyzes the reversible transfer of a ketol group between several donor and acceptor substrates. This key enzyme is a reversible link between glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway. The enzyme is involved in the catabolism of pentose sugars, the formation of D-ribose 5-phosphate, and the provision of D-erythrose 4-phosphate, a precursor of aromatic amino acids and PLP |CITS: |. E. coli contains two transketolase isozymes, TktA and TktB. TktB is responsible for the minor transketolase activity |CITS: |. The subunit structure of transketolase 2 (TktB) has not been explicitly determined. However, transketolase 1 (TktA) is homodimeric |CITS: |. Overproduction of TktB suppresses the tktA mutant phenotype |CITS: |. A tktA tktB double mutant requires pyridoxine (or 4-hydroxy-L-threonine or glycolaldehyde), aromatic amino acids and vitamins for growth |CITS: |. Mutations that suppress the growth defect of a tktA tktB double mutant in LB were found to constitutively express glpK or inactivate deoB, suggesting that disrupted ribose-5-P metabolism results in glycerol-3-P limitation |CITS: |. Expression of tktB is increased in a tyrR mutant in the presence of phenylalanine |CITS: |. tktB expression is increased in stationary phase and positively regulated by RpoS |CITS: | and ppGpp |CITS: |. Expression of tktA and tktB is complementary, resulting in approximately constant levels of transketolase expression throughout growth |CITS: |. A tktB mutant has lower acetate yield, but increased biomass yield under aerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. Levels of TktB protein increase during osmotic stress under aerobic, but not anaerobic growth conditions |CITS: |. TktB appears to be associated with the degradosome |CITS: | and may connect carbon metabolism to replication |CITS: |. Filament formation of a dnaE486 mutant is partially suppressed by deletion of tktB |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: NikA is the periplasmic binding protein of a high affinity Ni2+ uptake system in Escherichia coli. The identity of the nickel species bound by NikA has not been conclusively established. Purified NikA is monomeric and binds one atom of nickel per molecule of protein with a Kd of less than 0.1μM; purified NikA binds Ni2+ with at least 10-fold higher affinity than for other divalent metals |CITS: |. Purified NikA binds nickel selctively over cobalt with a Kd of 1µM for Ni2+ and 246µM for Co2+ |CITS: |. NikA mediates Tar dependent nickel-repellent chemotaxis |CITS: |. Purified, crystallized NikA consists of two lobes connected by a hinge; a hydrophobic pocket shaped to fit a penta-coordinate-hydrated nickel ion forms the ligand binding site; nickel does not form direct contacts with NikA but hydrogen bonds to a coordinating water molecule; nickel remains accessible to solvent while bound to NikA |CITS:|. The details of this binding site were later challenged by |CITS:| who reported that NikA (aerobically overexpressed and purified in the presence of EDTA) binds Fe(III)EDTA(H2O)- with high affinity and suggested that NikA would transport nickel complexed to a chemically similar metallophore (possibly butane-1,2,4-tricarboxylate |CITS: |) in vivo. Ni2+ binds a natural metallophore; His416 is the only direct metal-NikA contact |CITS: |. L-histidine is required for NikABCDE dependent nickel uptake in E. coli; purified NikA binds a Ni-(L-His)2 complex; deletion of nikA decreases the uptake of both labeled Ni and labeled L-His, 4 fold |CITS: |. Nickel, in a NikA-Ni-(L-His)2 complex, is coordinated by four nitrogen atoms and one carboxylate group from the two free histidines and one nitrogen atom from His416 of NikA |CITS: |.

Merged_Functions: The mqo gene (formerly yojH) encodes the membrane‑associated malate:quinone oxidoreductase (MQO), a flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)‑ and lipid‑dependent peripheral membrane enzyme that catalyzes the irreversible oxidation of L‑malate to oxaloacetate while transferring the electrons to the quinone pool (ubiquinone or menaquinone) of the electron‑transport chain. MQO thus provides a route for malate oxidation in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle that is distinct from the NAD‑dependent cytoplasmic malate dehydrogenase (MDH). Its activity is highest during exponential growth, is strongly influenced by the carbon source (low on glucose, high on non‑fermentable substrates), and is regulated by the ArcA‑ArcB two‑component system as well as by catabolite control. Deletion of mqo alone does not produce a measurable growth defect under the conditions tested, but in an mdh deletion background the absence of MQO further reduces growth rates, indicating that MQO can partially substitute for MDH in supplying oxaloacetate. Overexpression of mqo is deleterious, likely because it perturbs the balance between MQO and MDH activities and alters intracellular oxaloacetate levels. {PubMed:11092847}. Encodes a membrane‑associated malate:quinone oxidoreductase (MQO, EC 1.1.5.4) that catalyzes the oxidation of L‑malate to oxaloacetate by transferring electrons to a quinone cofactor (pyrroloquinoline quinone, PQQ). In Pseudomonas taetrolens the MQO exhibits a novel substrate specificity: it also oxidizes disaccharides that possess a reducing‑end glucosyl residue, most notably lactose, converting lactose into lactobionic acid (LBA). The enzyme is a ~54 kDa protein anchored to the periplasmic side of the inner membrane, shows optimal activity at pH 7.0 and 30 °C, requires PQQ as an electron acceptor, and its activity is enhanced by Fe³⁺ while being inhibited by Zn²⁺, Al³⁺ and Cu²⁺. Thus, the mqo gene provides both the canonical malate‑oxidizing activity of MQO and a unique lactose‑oxidizing activity that can be harnessed for microbial production of lactobionic acid. {PubMed:33166455}. The article identifies mqo as encoding malate dehydrogenase, an enzyme present in Escherichia coli but absent in Mannheimia succiniciproducens. It participates in the central metabolic pathway, catalyzing the interconversion of malate and oxaloacetate within the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. In the study, mqo was targeted for deletion to block a reverse flux from succinic acid, thereby aiming to redirect metabolic flow toward enhanced succinic acid production. {PubMed:16332763}. The mqo gene encodes the membrane‑associated malate dehydrogenase (acceptor), also called malate:quinone oxidoreductase (Mqo).  Mqo catalyzes the oxidation of L‑malate to oxaloacetate while transferring the electrons to a quinone (e.g., ubiquinone‑1) in the electron‑transfer chain; NAD is not used as an electron acceptor.  As a peripheral membrane protein, Mqo can be released from the membrane by chelators or mild detergents and requires a tightly bound FAD prosthetic group and activation by lipids/quinones.  The enzyme participates in the citric acid (TCA) cycle, providing a quinone‑dependent route for malate oxidation that is thermodynamically favorable (ΔG° ≈ –55 kJ·mol⁻¹ with ubiquinone) and complements the cytoplasmic NAD‑dependent malate dehydrogenase.  Loss of mqo activity impairs growth on several carbon sources, indicating its physiological importance for efficient malate oxidation and integration of reducing equivalents into the respiratory chain. {PubMed:9660197}. The mqo gene (HP0086) encodes a membrane‑associated, flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)‑dependent malate:quinone oxidoreductase (MQO). This enzyme catalyzes the oxidation of L‑malate to oxaloacetate, transferring the electrons from malate to quinone molecules of the electron‑transfer chain (predominantly menaquinone in H. pylori). By doing so, MQO links the citric acid cycle to the respiratory chain, providing a route for electron flow without involving NAD/NADH. The enzyme is loosely associated with the membrane, lacks transmembrane helices, and is activated by its tightly bound FAD cofactor. Experimental evidence shows that MQO from H. pylori can complement mqo deletion mutants in Escherichia coli and Corynebacterium glutamicum, restoring high MQO activity. Importantly, the H. pylori MQO does not catalyze the reverse reaction (oxaloacetate reduction), indicating it functions only in the oxidative direction of the citric acid cycle. {PubMed:10809701}. Encodes the membrane‑associated malate:quinone oxidoreductase (MQO). MQO catalyzes the irreversible oxidation of L‑malate to oxaloacetate, transferring the electrons to quinone carriers (ubiquinone or menaquinone) in the respiratory chain. It is an FAD‑dependent peripheral membrane protein that participates in the citric acid (TCA) cycle by providing oxaloacetate. The gene, formerly called yojH, is regulated by carbon source, growth phase, and the ArcA‑ArcB two‑component system; expression is low on glucose, high on non‑fermentable substrates, and activity peaks during exponential growth. Deletion of yojH (mqo) shows little phenotype alone but, when combined with a deletion of the NAD‑dependent malate dehydrogenase (mdh), reveals that MQO can partially replace MDH in malate oxidation. {PubMed:11092847}.
Curated_Functions: Oxidizes L‑malate to oxaloacetate while transferring electrons to quinone carriers (ubiquinone or menaquinone) in the respiratory chain. {PubMed:11092847, PubMed:9660197, PubMed:10809701}. Provides a quinone‑dependent route for malate oxidation in the tricarboxylic acid cycle that can partially substitute for the NAD‑dependent malate dehydrogenase. {PubMed:11092847, PubMed:9660197}. Is expressed preferentially during exponential growth and is up‑regulated on non‑fermentable carbon sources, being controlled by the ArcA‑ArcB two‑component system and catabolite repression. {PubMed:11092847}. Deletion alone shows little phenotype, but combined deletion with mdh reduces growth rates, whereas overexpression is deleterious, indicating a need for balanced MQO/MDH activities. {PubMed:11092847}. Oxidizes lactose and other reducing‑end glucosyl disaccharides to lactobionic acid, requiring pyrroloquinoline quinone as electron acceptor and being stimulated by Fe³⁺ and inhibited by Zn²⁺, Al³⁺ and Cu²⁺. {PubMed:33166455}. Acts as a peripheral membrane protein that binds a tightly associated FAD cofactor, requires lipid/quinone activation, and can be released from membranes by chelators or mild detergents; the enzyme is ~54 kDa, periplasmic‑side anchored, optimal at pH 7.0 and 30 °C. {PubMed:33166455, PubMed:9660197}. Functions only in the oxidative direction of the citric acid cycle, does not reduce oxaloacetate, and links the cycle to the respiratory chain without using NAD/NADH. {PubMed:10809701}. Loss of activity impairs growth on several carbon sources, highlighting its role in efficient malate oxidation and integration of reducing equivalents into the respiratory chain. {PubMed:9660197}. Deletion was employed to block reverse flux from succinic acid, thereby redirecting metabolic flow toward enhanced succinate production. {PubMed:16332763}.

Merged_Functions: The product of b0981 encodes Etk, an inner‑membrane bacterial protein‑tyrosine kinase (BY‑kinase) in Escherichia coli. Etk regulates the polymerization and trans‑envelope transport of capsular polysaccharide (CPS) by autophosphorylating a key upstream tyrosine residue (Y574). In its unphosphorylated state Y574 sterically blocks the active site; phosphorylation of Y574 induces a side‑chain rotation that allows interaction with a conserved arginine (R614), opening the active site for subsequent phosphorylation of a C‑terminal Tyr‑rich cluster. The degree of phosphorylation on this cluster controls Etk’s oligomeric state and its interaction with other components of the CPS export machinery (e.g., the outer‑membrane channel Wza), thereby influencing capsule assembly and contributing to polymyxin‑B resistance. The protein also contains Walker‑A and Walker‑B motifs for ATP binding and shares structural similarity with MinD ATPases, but possesses a distinct activation mechanism unique to Gram‑negative BY‑kinases. {PubMed:18497741}. Encodes the PLP‑dependent homotaurine:2‑oxoglutarate aminotransferase (annotated as GabT, EC 2.6.1.19). This enzyme catalyzes the first step of homotaurine catabolism in Cupriavidus necator H16 by transferring the amino group from homotaurine (or GABA) to 2‑oxoglutarate, yielding L‑glutamate and 3‑sulfopropanal. The reaction initiates the assimilatory pathway that converts homotaurine nitrogen into cellular material and ultimately produces 3‑sulfopropanoate for excretion. The protein is a ~44 kDa subunit forming a homomultimer (~120 kDa native size), is inducibly expressed during growth on homotaurine or GABA, and is cotranscribed with gabD1 as part of the gabTD operon. {PubMed:19648235}. Encodes Etk, a membrane‑spanning bacterial protein‑tyrosine kinase that is a key component of the group 4 capsule secretion system in Escherichia coli. Etk autophosphorylates on a tyrosine‑rich C‑terminal tail (requiring the conserved Lys545 for catalytic activity). Cyclic phosphorylation of Etk followed by dephosphorylation by the adjacent low‑molecular‑weight phosphatase Etp is required for the production of the O127 group 4 polysaccharide capsule. {PubMed:22675501}. The yccC gene (renamed ansZ) encodes a functional L‑asparaginase that catalyzes the conversion of L‑asparagine to L‑aspartate and ammonium. Its expression is tightly regulated: it is strongly induced during nitrogen‑limited growth by the nitrogen‑regulatory transcription factor TnrA, which binds to a specific site upstream of the ansZ promoter. Under nitrogen‑excess conditions, ansZ expression is low. Thus, yccC/ansZ provides a nitrogen‑scavenging enzymatic activity that contributes to cellular adaptation to nitrogen limitation. {PubMed:11914346}. Etk is a membrane‑bound tyrosine kinase of Escherichia coli that functions as a regulatory component of the Wzy‑dependent capsular polysaccharide (CPS) export system. It forms part of a protein complex that spans the inner and outer membranes, interacting with the outer‑membrane channel protein YccZ (analogous to the Wzc‑Wza complex). Etk undergoes autophosphorylation of a C‑terminal tyrosine cluster, which modulates its kinase activity and thereby controls CPS export and contributes to bacterial virulence. The periplasmic domain of Etk directly contacts the outer‑membrane channel, likely transmitting conformational signals from the cytoplasmic kinase domain across the membrane. {PubMed:26363120}. Etk is a bacterial protein‑tyrosine autokinase that is essential for the synthesis of the group 4 capsule in Escherichia coli. It forms a trans‑membrane hairpin with periplasmic and cytoplasmic domains; the C‑terminal cytoplasmic domain contains the catalytic PTK (protein‑tyrosine kinase) activity. Autophosphorylation of Etk’s tyrosine‑rich C‑terminal tail occurs in trans and is required for capsule assembly. Etk’s phosphorylation state is dynamically regulated by the adjacent low‑molecular‑weight protein‑tyrosine phosphatase Etp, which dephosphorylates Etk in vivo. Mutations that inactivate the kinase (e.g., Lys545→Met) abolish Etk autophosphorylation and prevent group 4 capsule production, demonstrating that the catalytic activity and the cyclic phosphorylation/dephosphorylation of Etk are critical regulatory steps in the capsule biosynthetic/export pathway. {PubMed:22675501}. Etk encodes an inner‑membrane protein tyrosine kinase (a bacterial PTK or BY‑kinase) in Escherichia coli. Its cytoplasmic kinase domain autophosphorylates a conserved tyrosine (Y574); phosphorylation of Y574 causes a side‑chain conformational change that removes steric blockage of the active site by interacting with Arg‑614, thereby enabling subsequent phosphorylation of a C‑terminal Tyr‑rich cluster. This two‑step autophosphorylation regulates the synthesis, polymerization and trans‑envelope transport of capsular polysaccharide (CPS) and extracellular polysaccharide (EPS). Through this regulation Etk influences capsule assembly, bacterial virulence, and antibiotic (polymyxin‑B) resistance, and likely participates in the CPS export complex together with periplasmic partners such as the outer‑membrane channel Wza. {PubMed:18497741}. Etk is one of the two classical bacterial tyrosine (BY) kinases identified in Escherichia coli. It contains the conserved Walker A, A', and B motifs of P‑loop NTPases and a C‑terminal cluster of autophosphorylatable tyrosine residues. Etk autophosphorylates this tyrosine cluster and phosphorylates other cellular proteins, contributing substantially to the global phosphotyrosine proteome—its activity is markedly higher in the pathogenic EHEC O157:H7 strain, as evidenced by increased phosphorylation of Etk itself and many downstream sites. Classical BY kinases, including Etk, have been linked to exopolysaccharide/capsule synthesis, antibiotic resistance, phage lysogenization, and the heat‑shock response, and they can affect virulence through capsule formation. However, deletion of etk (alone or together with the second BY kinase wzc) did not alter type III secretion system‑dependent attaching‑and‑effacing lesion formation or the ability to metabolize diverse carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur sources, indicating functional redundancy with other, as yet unidentified, tyrosine kinases. Overall, Etk functions as a bacterial tyrosine kinase that modulates protein tyrosine phosphorylation and is associated with capsule/exopolysaccharide biosynthesis and potential virulence regulation, but is not essential for the measured virulence or metabolic phenotypes in the experimental conditions described. {PubMed:23785281}. The etk gene encodes a protein‑tyrosine kinase (Etk) that is expressed in Escherichia coli K‑12 under the experimental growth conditions. Etk is essential for resistance to the cationic antimicrobial peptide polymyxin B: deletion of etk reduces survival to ~3–7 % in polymyxin assays, while complementation with a plasmid‑borne etk restores wild‑type levels of resistance. Unlike the related kinase Wzc, Etk cannot be functionally substituted by Wzc, indicating a specific role. Etk is capable of phosphorylating the UDP‑glucose dehydrogenase Ugd in vitro, suggesting it may regulate the biosynthetic pathway that produces UDP‑glucuronic acid, a precursor for the L‑Ara4N modification of lipid A that diminishes polymyxin binding. Etk is part of an operon required for group‑4 capsule formation, and its activity appears to be modulated by the cognate phosphotyrosine phosphatase Etp, implying a regulatory cycle of phosphorylation/dephosphorylation that influences polymyxin resistance. In summary, Etk functions as a specific protein‑tyrosine kinase that promotes polymyxin B resistance, likely through modulation of lipid A modification and/or capsule biosynthesis. {PubMed:16814990}. Etk is an inner‑membrane protein tyrosine kinase of *Escherichia coli* whose cytoplasmic kinase domain catalyzes ATP‑dependent autophosphorylation of a C‑terminal tyrosine cluster. This autophosphorylation regulates the export of pathogenic capsular polysaccharide (CPS) by modulating the activity of the CPS export channel (Wza/YccZ). Activation of Etk occurs in two steps: (1) intramolecular autophosphorylation of a conserved tyrosine (Y574) near the active site, which triggers a side‑chain flip of phospho‑Y574 toward Arg614, thereby unblocking the active site; (2) subsequent intermolecular autophosphorylation of the C‑terminal tyrosine cluster. The enzyme’s activity is further modulated by Arg572, which transiently interacts with phospho‑Y574 and slows the opening of the active site. Mutations that disrupt these interactions (e.g., R572A) increase kinase activity, while Y574F greatly reduces activity. Thus, Etk functions as a regulatory tyrosine kinase that controls CPS export through a unique activation mechanism involving a single‑residue side‑chain flip. {PubMed:19634880}. Etk is a bacterial BY‑kinase (tyrosine kinase) encoded near the 22‑minute mark of the E. coli chromosome. Like the related kinase Wzc, Etk autophosphorylates on multiple tyrosine residues and can phosphorylate endogenous target proteins. The article demonstrates that Etk phosphorylates the UDP‑glucose dehydrogenase Ugd on Tyr71, which activates Ugd’s enzymatic activity and promotes the synthesis of UDP‑glucuronic acid, a precursor for the L‑Ara4N modification of lipopolysaccharide that confers resistance to the cationic antimicrobial peptide polymyxin. Thus, Etk‑mediated Ugd phosphorylation is required for full polymyxin resistance. Etk is also described as a polysaccharide co‑polymerase (PCP) component of transmembrane complexes involved in extracellular polysaccharide synthesis/export, and it has been implicated in the heat‑shock response through phosphorylation of sigma and anti‑sigma factors. Etk expression is induced under stress conditions such as low pH and low Mg²⁺/Fe³⁺ concentrations, which are the same conditions that trigger polymyxin‑resistance mechanisms. {PubMed:18725960}. Etk is a protein encoded within the gfc operon that is specifically required for the polymerization of O‑antigen repeat units into the long polysaccharide chains that constitute the group 4 capsule (G4C) and for the subsequent assembly of this capsule on the bacterial surface. Loss of etk abolishes capsule formation, leading to enhanced production of LPS O‑side chains, increased attachment to epithelial cells, faster actin pedestal formation, and higher efficiency of type III secretion system (TTSS)–mediated Tir translocation. Etk expression is negatively regulated by the Ler transcriptional activator, which represses the gfc promoter when TTSS genes are induced, thereby coordinating inverse temporal expression of the capsule and the TTSS. {PubMed:18502854}.
Curated_Functions: Autophosphorylates a conserved tyrosine (Y574) and subsequently a C‑terminal tyrosine cluster in a two‑step mechanism that activates its kinase activity. {PubMed:18497741, PubMed:22675501, PubMed:19634880}. Regulates synthesis, polymerization and trans‑envelope transport of capsular polysaccharide by modulating the activity of the CPS export channel (Wza/YccZ) and interacting with other components of the export machinery. {PubMed:18497741, PubMed:26363120, PubMed:22675501, PubMed:18502854}. Functions as a polysaccharide co‑polymerase component of the group 4 capsule secretion system, forming part of a trans‑membrane complex that spans the inner and outer membranes. {PubMed:18497741, PubMed:22675501, PubMed:18502854}. Undergoes dynamic dephosphorylation by the low‑molecular‑weight phosphatase Etp, establishing a phosphorylation/dephosphorylation cycle that controls its activity. {PubMed:22675501}. Phosphorylates the UDP‑glucose dehydrogenase Ugd, activating Ugd and promoting UDP‑glucuronic acid synthesis required for L‑Ara4N modification of lipid A and conferring polymyxin B resistance. {PubMed:16814990, PubMed:18725960}. Contributes to polymyxin B resistance, likely through modulation of lipid A modification and/or capsule biosynthesis. {PubMed:16814990, PubMed:18497741}. Influences bacterial virulence by controlling capsule formation; loss of Etk abolishes capsule production, enhances cell attachment and alters type III secretion system efficiency. {PubMed:18502854, PubMed:23785281}. Participates in global protein‑tyrosine phosphorylation, phosphorylating multiple cellular proteins. {PubMed:23785281}. Is expressed under stress conditions such as low pH or low Mg²⁺/Fe³⁺ and is negatively regulated by the Ler transcriptional activator, coordinating capsule and TTSS expression. {PubMed:18502854, PubMed:18725960}. Binds ATP via conserved Walker A, A' and B motifs and shares structural similarity with MinD ATPases. {PubMed:18497741}. Catalyzes the transamination of homotaurine or GABA to 2‑oxoglutarate, producing L‑glutamate and 3‑sulfopropanal as the first step of homotaurine catabolism. {PubMed:19648235}. Provides a nitrogen‑scavenging activity by converting L‑asparagine to L‑aspartate and ammonium; expression is induced under nitrogen limitation via the TnrA regulator. {PubMed:11914346}.

MetaCyc_Comment: GntT is one of four known transporters for gluconate in E. coli, the others being the homologous GntU, GntP and IdnT transporters. Whole cell experiments have shown that the cloned gntT gene was able to complement a gluconate transport negative mutant and confers high affinity gluconate transport with a Km of approx 6 μM |CITS: |. Transcriptional analysis has shown that gntT constitutes a monocistronic operon. Analysis of gntT-lacZ fusions has indicated that gntT expression is induced at low levels of gluconate, partially repressed by glucose, and increased in early logarithmic phase |CITS: |. Expression of both gntT and gntU is controlled by the GntR repressor and by cyclic AMP-CRP |CITS: |. GntT is a member of the Gnt family of gluconate transporters |CITS: |. Gluconate uptake has been reported to occur via a proton-symport mechanism in E. coli |CITS: |. It seems likely that GntT is a high affinity gluconate uptake system that functions via D-gluconate/proton symport. Imported gluconate is metabolised primarily via the Entner-Douderoff pathway and secondarily via the pentose phosphate pathway.

MetaCyc_Comment: Early work in E. coli indicated that there are two genetically separable transport systems for inorganic phosphate (Pi) - a high affinity, low velocity Pst (phosphate specific transport) system (the |FRAME: ABC-27-CPLX|) and a low affinity, high velocity Pit (Pi transport) system |CITS: |*. This latter system is constitutive in nature and catalyses an electrogenic metal phosphate:H+ symport |CITS: |. Pi uptake via Pit is dependent on the presence of divalent cations, like Mg2+, Ca2+, Co2+, or Mn2+, which form soluble metal phosphate (MeHP04) complexes |CITS: |. The Pit system in E. coli K-12 consists of two transporters - PitA and PitB - which have 81% sequence identity at the protein level; pitA is likely constitutive while pitB is repressed or inactivated through the pho regulon; chromosomally encoded PitB catalyses Pi uptake in a phoB-phoR deleted strain; both proteins may have contributed to the kinetic values and substrate specificities determined in earlier studies |CITS: |. The Pit proteins are predicted to contain 10 transmembrane helices |CITS: |. The Pit system also transports the phosphate analogue, arsenate |CITS: |. The PitB phosphate transporter is a member of the Inorganic Phosphate Transporter (PiT) family |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: | * The Pit system is lacking in many E. coli K-10 strains |CITS: |.

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Pore-forming subunit of a potassium efflux system that confers protection against electrophiles. Catalyzes K(+)/H(+) antiport. {ECO:0000255|HAMAP-Rule:MF_01412, ECO:0000269|PubMed:3301813, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9023177}.
MetaCyc_Comment: KefB and KefC are two independent glutathione-regulated potassium efflux systems, which play a role in protecting the cell from electrophile toxicity. Mutations in kefB and kefC affect potassium efflux at neutral pH, can be complemented by the cloned genes and probably function via potassium/proton antiport |CITS: |. Potassium efflux by KefB or KefC is activated by adducts formed by reaction of glutathione with electrophilic compounds such as N-ethylmaleimide, methylglyoxal and chlorodinitrobenzene |CITS: |. Potassium efflux mediated by KefB and KefC leads to acidification of the cytoplasm, which protects the cell from electrophile toxicity |CITS: |. KefB and KefC differ in their activation by methylglyoxal, with KefC only weakly activated |CITS: |. KefB is a member of the CPA2 family of monovalent cation:proton antiporters. In addition to KefB and KefC, additional unidentified potassium efflux systems exist.

MetaCyc_Comment: FkpA is a heat shock peptidyl-prolyl isomerase (PPIase) which also has chaperone function. Deletion or overexpression of fkpA does not cause a detectable phenotype |CITS: |. Deletion mutants lacking either the N- or C-terminal domains suggest that the catalytic PPIase activity resides in the C-terminal domain, while the chaperone activity resides in the N-terminal domain |CITS: |. Mutation studies involving four PPIases present in Escherichia coli (FkpA, PpiA, PpiD, and SurA) showed that three triple mutants have growth defects, while one does not |CITS:|. The quadruple mutant had the most pronounced defect as well as increased antibiotic sensitivity compared with other surA mutants |CITS:|. No single or double mutants were shown to have growth defects in this study |CITS:|. Mutation of surA also resulted in reduced piliation in cells expressing the P and type 1 pilus operons suggesting a role for SurA and possibly the other PPIases in survival outside the laboratory or in pathogenesis |CITS:|. In vivo homodimeric FkpA interaction can be detected in cross-linking experiments. Interaction between FkpA and the 30S ribosomal protein |FRAME: EG10905-MONOMER "RpsF"| was also detected |CITS: |. FkpA is required for killing Escherichia coli by colicin M entering from outside the cell |CITS: |. The crystal structure of FkpA has been determined in three different forms |CITS: |. Targeting of FkpA to the Sec-translocase for transport across the inner membrane is SecB-dependent |CITS:|. Regulation has been described |CITS: |. The regulation of the fkpA, gapA, and hslT genes is affected by evolution under conditions of chronic heat stress |CITS: |.

Experiments in |CITS: | were done with proteins from E. coli BL21(DE3). FrlD: "fructoselysine" |CITS: |

Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Catalyzes the hydrolysis of phosphorylated glyceryl acetates in which the presence of a phosphate group is required for the enzymatic hydrolysis. No activity with various sugar phosphates, with various nitrophenylphosphate or nitrophenylphosphonate derivatives, or with phosphorylated or non-phosphorylated sugar lactones tested. Does not hydrolyze non-phosphorylated carboxyesters with long chain leaving groups (PubMed:30277746). No general esterase, aminopeptidase, sulfatase, phosphatase, carbonic anhydrase, phosphodiesterase, and phosphotriesterase activities detected when tested with the following non-specific substrates: p-nitrophenyl acetate, L-alanine nitroanilide, p-nitrophenyl sulfate, bis(p-nitrophenyl) phosphate, paraoxon, and p-nitrophenyl phosphate (PubMed:9548740). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:30277746, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9548740}.

FUNCTION: Involved in the synthesis of autoinducer 2 (AI-2) which is secreted by bacteria and is used to communicate both the cell density and the metabolic potential of the environment. The regulation of gene expression in response to changes in cell density is called quorum sensing. Catalyzes the transformation of S-ribosylhomocysteine (RHC) to homocysteine (HC) and 4,5-dihydroxy-2,3-pentadione (DPD). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:9618536, ECO:0000269|PubMed:9990077}.

MetaCyc_Comment: LuxS is involved in biosynthesis of AI-2, the hormone-like signal that mediates cell-cell communication during quorum sensing, the response to increased cell density |CITS: |. LuxS is the synthase that catalyzes formation of AI-2 by cleavage of S-ribosylhomocysteine |CITS: |. LuxS also participates in recycling of S-adenosylhomocysteine via the |FRAME: PWY-6151| |CITS: |. Stochastic modelling has predicted an alternative pathway for AI-2 formation |CITS: |. It was later found that AI-2 can form spontaneously from ribulose-5-phosphate, but this reaction may not be relevant in wild type E. coli |CITS: |. A catalytic mechanism for LuxS has been proposed |CITS: |. The DH5α strain has a luxS mutation that prevents autoinducer production, whereas the MG1655 strain produces autoinducer |CITS: |. The differences between wild type and luxS mutants have been examined by gene expression |CITS: | and phenotype |CITS: | microarrays and by profiling the metabolites of the |FRAME: PWY-6151| |CITS: |. A luxS mutant shows increased swimming motility and synthesis of flagella |CITS: |. The expression of luxS, as well as the accumulation of AI-2, is decreased in uvrY and hfq mutant strains, and it is marginally decreased in a uvrY crp double mutant. A csrB mutant strain showed marginally increased expression of luxS; on the other hand, cya, crp, and csrA mutant strains and a uvrY cya double mutant strain showed constitutive expression of luxS. In the case of the csrA mutant, there was an increase in AI-2 levels that was associated with the stability of luxR mRNA and mediated by CsrA in this strain |CITS: |. Transcription of luxS is induced by acetate |CITS: | or by acidic pH |CITS: |. Expression of luxS is posttranscriptionally regulated by the small RNA CyaR |CITS: |. The MicA small RNA appears to regulate processing of both luxS primary transcripts by RNase III |CITS: |. A luxS mutant does not produce AI-2 and has a different biofilm architecture than wild type |CITS: |. Coexpression of LuxS with recombinant proteins in E. coli was found to enhance the yield of recombinant protein. Coincident upregulation of the chaperone GroEL (GroL) was also found, demonstrating that this chaperone is positively regulated at the posttranscriptional level by AI-2 |CITS: |. Reviews: |CITS: |

FUNCTION: Involved in outer membrane lipid homeostasis (PubMed:33046656, PubMed:34781743, PubMed:35226662, PubMed:38913742, PubMed:39638236). Likely transports phospholipids between the inner membrane and the outer membrane (PubMed:33046656, PubMed:34781743, PubMed:35226662, PubMed:38913742, PubMed:39638236). It would provide a bridge-like structure that protects phospholipids as they travel across the periplasm (PubMed:34781743, PubMed:39638236). The phosphate-containing molecules are captured along the length of a hydrophobic groove that is continuous along all but the extreme N-terminus of the protein (PubMed:39638236). It also appears to control, directly or indirectly, levels of cyclic enterobacterial common antigen (cyclic ECA), a soluble cyclic ECA molecule present in the periplasm (PubMed:30087168). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:30087168, ECO:0000269|PubMed:33046656, ECO:0000269|PubMed:34781743, ECO:0000269|PubMed:35226662, ECO:0000269|PubMed:38913742, ECO:0000269|PubMed:39638236}.; FUNCTION: TamB, YdbH and YhdP are redundant, but not equivalent, in performing an essential function for growth and maintaining lipid homeostasis in the outer membrane (PubMed:34781743). The transport functions of TamB and YhdP could be differentiated according to the fatty acid saturation state of the phospholipids, with TamB transporting more unsaturated phospholipids and YhdP more saturated phospholipids (PubMed:38913742). Any of these three proteins is sufficient for growth (PubMed:34781743). {ECO:0000269|PubMed:34781743, ECO:0000269|PubMed:38913742}.

Expression of yhhW is induced by exposure to hydroquinone; this induction is abolished in a yhaJ mutant |CITS: |.

Catalytic activity: CATALYTIC ACTIVITY: Reaction=cytidine(34) in tRNA(Ile2) + L-lysine + ATP = lysidine(34) in tRNA(Ile2) + AMP + diphosphate + H(+); Xref=Rhea:RHEA:43744, Rhea:RHEA-COMP:10625, Rhea:RHEA-COMP:10670, ChEBI:CHEBI:15378, ChEBI:CHEBI:30616, ChEBI:CHEBI:32551, ChEBI:CHEBI:33019, ChEBI:CHEBI:82748, ChEBI:CHEBI:83665, ChEBI:CHEBI:456215; EC=6.3.4.19; Evidence={ECO:0000269|PubMed:14527414};
MetaCyc_Comment: TilS is a tRNAIle-lysidine synthetase, the enzyme responsible for modifying the wobble base of the CAU anticodon of tRNAIle at the keto group in position 2 of C34 such that it exhibits proper recognition of the AUA codon rather than the AUG codon |CITS: |. This modification is necessary and sufficient for correct charging of the tRNA with isoleucine (not methionine) |CITS: |. TilS recognizes and modifies the precursor form of tRNAIle, thus ensuring the fidelity and avoiding errors in translation. Unmodified C34 is only found in pre-tRNAIle; mature tRNAIle contains the modified L34 base. Thus, it is not possible to generate mischarged Met-tRNAIleCAU |CITS: |. TilS recognizes the antidodon loop, the anticodon stem, and the acceptor stem of tRNA, allowing it to discriminate between tRNAIle and tRNAMet, which are structurally similar and share the same anticodon loop |CITS: |. t6A-modified tRNAIleCAU is a better substrate for TilS than the unmodified tRNA |CITS: |. Various analogs of L-lysine have been tested as inhibitors or alternative substrates for the enzyme |CITS: |. tilS is an essential gene |CITS: |. A tilS reduction-of-function mutation causes defects in translation of AUA codons |CITS: |. TilS: tRNA(Ile)-lysidine synthetase |CITS: | Reviews: |CITS: |

This charging reaction provides the histidyl‑tRNA required for incorporation of histidine during ribosomal protein synthesis. MetaCyc_Comment: Histidine-tRNA ligase (HisRS) is a member of the family of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which interpret the genetic code by covalently linking amino acids to their specific tRNA molecules. The reaction is driven by ATP hydrolysis. HisRS belongs to the Class II aminoacyl tRNA synthetases, which share three regions of homology |CITS: |. HisRS is a dimer in solution |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain of the protein is required for dimerization, while the N-terminal domain contains most of the catalytic activity. The two domains do not complement each other in trans |CITS: |. Minimal active site fragments likely representing the ancestral "urzyme" have been studied |CITS: |. Specificity determinants within tRNAHis that are important for recognition by HisRS have been identified; the unique G-1:C73 base pair was found to play a crucial role |CITS: |. Specificity determinants and residues within HisRS that are important for catalytic activity have been investigated |CITS: |, and a model for the catalytic cycle was proposed |CITS: |. The C-terminal domain of HisRS was found to be largely responsible for recognition of the tRNAHis anticodon |CITS: |. Crystal structures of HisRS have been determined, and a reaction mechanism was proposed |CITS: |. Various types of experiments support a substrate-assisted concerted reaction mechanism |CITS: |. Catalysis may occur at sites alternating between the two monomers; conformational changes may be rate-limiting for product formation |CITS: |. The mechanisms of substrate discrimination |CITS: | and the aminoacylation reaction |CITS: | have been modeled. Reviews: |CITS: |

MetaCyc_Comment: The purified BacA protein has undecaprenyl pyrophosphate (Und-PP or C55-PP) phosphatase activity, but not undecaprenol phosphokinase activity |CITS: |. The bacA gene product is not essential for growth, but the product of the BacA catalysed reaction, undecaprenyl phosphate, is essential for the synthesis of peptidoglycan and other cell wall components. At least three additional gene products, |FRAME: G6439-MONOMER "YbjG"|, |FRAME: PGPPHOSPHAB-MONOMER "PgpB"|, and |FRAME: G7146-MONOMER "LpxT"|, are thought to have undecaprenyl pyrophosphate phosphatase activity in E. coli |CITS: |. BacA accounts for approximately three quarters of the total C55-PP phosphatase activity |CITS: |. BacA catalyses C55-PP dephosphorylation on the periplasmic side of the inner membrane |CITS: |. Purified BacA dephosphorylates farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP); the optimal pH for this assay is 6.5-7 and the enzyme requires Mg2+ or Ca2+ for activity; bacitracin inhibits the dephosphorylation of FPP by BacA |CITS: | BacA is predicted to contain 8 transmembrane helices with the N and C-termini located in the cytoplasm; two conserved motifs - region I and region II - and a conserved histidine residue (His-30) are thought to form the catalytic core of the enzyme |CITS: |. A structural model of BacA in complex with C55-PP and a magnesium ion has been predicted and a catalytic mechanism with a central role for His-30 proposed |CITS: |. Experimental analysis of BacA topology indicates that it contains 7 transmembrane segments with the C-terminus located in the cytoplasm and the two conserved BacA signature motifs located within periplasmic loops. This suggests that BacA catalyses C55-PP dephosphorylation on the periplasmic face of the inner membrane |CITS: |. His-30 is not essential for catalysis; a catalytic mechanism with a central role for Ser-27 is proposed |CITS: |. Crystal structures of BacA have been determined: the protein contains 10 α-helices, 6 of these span the membrane completely, the remaining 4 make up two antiparallel reentrant helix-loop-helix regions that likely form the active site; the protein contains a deep cleft or pocket that is open to both the periplasm and the periplasmic leaflet of the membrane and provides substrate access to the active site |CITS: |. BacA has structural similarity to a number of transport proteins raising the possibility that, in addition to its function as a C55-PP phosphatase, it is involved in transporting or flipping C55-P across the membrane |CITS: |. Simultaneous inactivation of bacA, ybjG and pgpB is lethal. Depletion of BacA in a ΔybjG ΔpgpB strain results in accumulation of the peptidoglycan precursor, UDP-MurNAc-pentapeptide, changes in cell morphology and eventual lysis. Overexpression of bacA, lpxT, ybjG or pgpB leads to increased C55-PP phosphatase activity in crude membrane extracts. Expression of C55-PP phosphatase activity from any one of the three genes bacA, ybjG or pgpB appears to be sufficient for synthesis of undecaprenyl phosphate and survival |CITS: |. bacA ybjG double and bacA ybjG lpxT triple deletion mutants are hypersensitive to the undecaprenyl phosphate biosynthesis inhibitor fosmidomycin |CITS: |. When supplied on a multicopy plasmid, bacA confers resistance to bacitracin |CITS: |. The bacA gene belongs to the σE regulon, which is responsive to extracytoplasmic stress |CITS: |. Encodes the β‑carbonic anhydrase YadF, which catalyzes the reversible hydration of CO₂ to HCO₃⁻ (CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺). Deletion of yadF blocks growth unless CO₂ is provided at high partial pressure or the alternative β‑carbonic anhydrase CynT is induced, demonstrating YadF’s critical role in maintaining HCO₃⁻ levels under normal atmospheric CO₂ conditions. {PubMed:12784642}. The yadF gene (renamed can) encodes a β‑class carbonic anhydrase that catalyzes the reversible hydration of CO₂ to bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). This enzymatic activity supplies the intracellular bicarbonate required for numerous essential metabolic processes in Escherichia coli, including biosynthesis of arginine, pyrimidines, purines, fatty‑acid synthesis, and several carboxylation reactions in central metabolism. Because spontaneous CO₂ hydration is far too slow to meet the cellular demand (10³–10⁴‑fold insufficient), the Can enzyme is essential for growth in normal atmospheric CO₂ levels. The gene is expressed continuously, with expression levels modulated by growth rate, cell density, heat shock, and stationary‑phase signals, but it is not autoregulated nor directly responsive to external CO₂ concentration. {PubMed:14563877}. It contains the characteristic carbonic anhydrase motif and requires a Zn²⁺ ion as a catalytic cofactor; a zinc ion was observed in the active site of the crystal structure.  Thus, YadF functions as a zinc‑binding carbonic anhydrase‑type protein involved in the bacterial stress response. {PubMed:26660914}. The enzyme can be functionally replaced by the paralog CynT when induced, or by heterologous CAs, indicating its primary role is to provide sufficient bicarbonate for metabolism. {PubMed:14563877}. The b0126 locus encodes the protein Can (formerly YadF), a β‑class carbonic anhydrase (CA) that catalyzes the reversible hydration of CO₂ to bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻). This enzymatic activity supplies the intracellular bicarbonate required for several essential metabolic processes in Escherichia coli, including biosynthesis of arginine, pyrimidines and purines, fatty‑acid synthesis, and central metabolic carboxylation reactions (e.g., phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, carbamoyl‑phosphate synthetase, biotin carboxylase). Under aerobic growth in air, the uncatalyzed hydration of CO₂ is insufficient to meet the cellular demand for bicarbonate, making Can essential for growth unless the external CO₂ partial pressure is high or anaerobic/acidic conditions provide abundant endogenous CO₂. Can can be functionally replaced by the paralog CynT when induced, by a γ‑CA from Methanosarcina thermophila, or by elevated environmental CO₂. Expression of can is constitutive but modulated: it does not respond to CO₂ levels or autoregulate, but increases when growth rate slows, at higher cell density, during heat shock, and modestly in stationary phase via RpoS. {PubMed:14563877}. cynT2 (also called YadF or Can2) encodes the main β‑class carbonic anhydrase of Escherichia coli. This enzyme catalyzes the rapid interconversion of CO₂ and bicarbonate, thereby maintaining intracellular bicarbonate levels that are required as substrates for essential metabolic reactions. As the primary carbonic anhydrase, YadF supports bacterial growth by supplying bicarbonate for crucial enzymatic processes. {PubMed:28139278}. The cynT2 gene encodes the β‑carbonic anhydrase EcoCAβ, an enzyme that catalyzes the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide to bicarbonate and a proton (CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺). This activity provides a rapid source of bicarbonate required for numerous carboxylation reactions and pH regulation in Escherichia coli. The enzyme displays substantial catalytic efficiency (kcat ≈ 5.3 × 10⁵ s⁻¹, KM ≈ 12.9 mM) comparable to human CA I, and its activity can be modulated by various amino acids and amines. By supplying bicarbonate for essential metabolic pathways, CynT2‑encoded CA likely supports bacterial growth, virulence, and host colonisation. {PubMed:32576029}. The cynT2 gene encodes a β‑class carbonic anhydrase (CynT2) that catalyzes the reversible hydration of CO₂ to bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) and a proton (H⁺). In Escherichia coli this enzyme is localized in the cytoplasm and is indispensable for bacterial growth under low (atmospheric) CO₂ concentrations (pCO₂). By providing bicarbonate, CynT2 contributes to the cellular balance of CO₂ and HCO₃⁻ and supports the downstream cyanate detoxification reaction catalyzed by cyanase (NCO⁻ + 3 H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ → 2 CO₂ + NH₄⁺). Thus, CynT2 is essential for the E. coli life cycle, particularly for survival and proliferation when ambient CO₂ levels are limited. {PubMed:32545297}. cynT2 encodes a second β‑carbonic anhydrase (also called Can or yadF) in Escherichia coli.  It catalyzes the reversible hydration of carbon dioxide to bicarbonate and a proton (CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺), providing a rapid source of intracellular bicarbonate.  This activity prevents depletion of cellular bicarbonate, which is subsequently used by the cyanase (CynS) in the cyanate‑to‑ammonia conversion pathway.  CynT2 is essential for bacterial growth under atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, indicating its key role in maintaining the CO₂/HCO₃⁻ balance required for central metabolism and pH homeostasis.  The enzyme functions as a dimeric/tetrameric Zn²⁺‑dependent metalloenzyme belonging to the β‑CA class. {PubMed:32486444}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes the rapid, Zn²⁺‑dependent reversible hydration of CO₂ to HCO₃⁻ and H⁺. {PubMed:28139278, PubMed:10957638, PubMed:32486444, PubMed:12784642, PubMed:16814929, PubMed:14563877, PubMed:26660914, PubMed:16557001, PubMed:32576029, PubMed:32545297}. Supplies intracellular bicarbonate required for essential metabolic reactions such as arginine, pyrimidine, purine biosynthesis, fatty‑acid synthesis and carboxylation reactions (e.g., carbamoyl‑phosphate synthetase, acetyl‑CoA carboxylase, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase). {PubMed:28139278, PubMed:12784642, PubMed:16814929, PubMed:14563877, PubMed:16557001, PubMed:32486444, PubMed:32576029}. Ensures bacterial growth at atmospheric CO₂ concentrations; loss of function causes a capnophilic phenotype that can be rescued by high CO₂, bicarbonate addition or expression of the paralog CynT or heterologous carbonic anhydrases. {PubMed:28139278, PubMed:12784642, PubMed:16814929, PubMed:14563877, PubMed:16557001, PubMed:32486444, PubMed:32545297}. Binds one Zn²⁺ ion per subunit and functions as a dimeric/tetrameric metalloenzyme of the β‑carbonic anhydrase family. {PubMed:28139278, PubMed:26660914, PubMed:14563877, PubMed:32486444}.

Under anaerobiosis, FNR represses can gene expression, but it is not known if this regulation is direct or indirect |CITS: |. Carbonic anhydrase 2 belongs to a set of native E. coli proteins that is a common contaminant during recombinant His-tagged protein purification using immobilized metal affinity chromatography |CITS: | and was also found during crystal structure determination of a presumed recombinant survivin |CITS: |. The physiological function of Fiu may be to recapture the hydrolytic products of enterobactin such as 2,3-dihydroxybenzoylserine and dihydroxybenzoate |CITS: |. Fiu serves as a receptor for microcins E492, M and H47 |CITS: |, microcin E492 and its modified form, the siderophore-peptide microcin E492m |CITS: |. Fiu is the receptor for |FRAME: Salmochelins "salmochelin"| (see |CITS: |). Fiu is implicated in uptake of the siderophore cephalosporin, Cefiderocol |CITS: |. Fiu is able to provide the cell with iron when it is present as the only outer-membrane iron transporter, likely through the transport of iron-complexed enterobactin breakdown products although this may not be its physiological (high-affinity) substrate |CITS: |. Fiu consists of a 22-stranded transmembrane β-barrel with a number of extended extracellular loops; the protein contains an internal, gated cavity large enough to accomodate an iron-complexed catecholate complex; Fiu may import its substrate via a two-step mechanism which avoids formation of a membrane-spanning channel |CITS: |. MetaCyc_Comment: LsrF is the final enzyme in the pathway for degradation of the intercellular signaling molecule AI-2. It acts as a 3-hydroxy-2,4-pentadione 5-phosphate (P-HPD) thiolase, catalyzing the transfer of the acetyl group of P-HPD to coenzyme A |CITS: |. LsrF was noted to have similarity to class I aldolases |CITS: |, and the activity described in |CITS: | is novel for this family of enzymes. Kinetic measurements showed a positive Hill coefficient for both substrates, P-HPD and coenzyme A, indicating cooperativity |CITS: |. Crystal structures of LsrF were solved in both the apo form and in complex with phospho-AI-2 analogs. The protein is a homodecamer of (αβ)8 barrels with domain-swapped N termini, and the structure is similar to that of class I aldolases that process phosphorylated sugars. The structural conservation extends to the predicted ligand binding sites and catalytic residues such as Lys203 |CITS: |. The K203A, D251A and D57A mutants show no catalytic activity; based on these results, a reaction mechanism was proposed |CITS: |. LsrF is expressed as part of the lsr operon involved in AI-2 transport and processing |CITS: |. Deletion of lsrF leads to accumulation of phospho-AI-2 |CITS: |. LsrF: "LuxS regulated"

An E. coli K-12 strain lacking all three murein endopeptidases MepH, |FRAME: G7147-MONOMER "MepS"| and |FRAME: EG10013-MONOMER "MepM"| exhibits extensive cell lysis and a terminal phenotype. Under aerobic growth conditions deletion of rcnA results in decreased resistance to nickel and cobalt and increased intracellular accumulation of Ni2+ can be directly demonstrated |CITS: , |. rcnA expressed in trans in a strain lacking chromosomal rcnA results in increased resistance to Ni2+ and Co2+ compared to wild type |CITS: |. RcnA is involved in Ni2+ homeostasis under anaerobic conditions and at low nickel concentrations (10nM Ni2+). Under these conditions deletion of rcnA results in reduced nickel accumulation and decreased |FRAME: HYDROG3-CPLX| activity. Deletion of rcnA results in increased |FRAME: EG11519-MONOMER "NikR"| activity which impacts nickel import via the high affinity |FRAME: ABC-20-CPLX| |CITS: |. RcnA contains 6 predicted transmembrane regions and a histidine rich domain in the center of the protein that may be associated with nickel binding |CITS: | Exposure of rcnA mutants to subinhibitory concentrations of nickel promotes the formation of biofilm structure |CITS: |. rcnA expression is regulated by the |FRAME: G7137-MONOMER "RcnR transcritional repressor"| |CITS:, , |.rcnA forms an operon with |FRAME: G7139-MONOMER "rcnB"| |CITS: |. RcnA is a member of the Nickel-Cobalt (NicO) family of transporters |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: ArnT is a transferase that catalyzes the addition of L-Ara4N residues from |FRAME: CPD0-1189| to lipid A. This modification confers on the organism resistance to the antibiotic polymyxin |CITS:|. It should be noted that K-12 derived strains express ArnT, but do not synthesize |FRAME: CPD0-1189| under normal conditions, and thus are sensitive to polymyxin. The enzyme from E. coli has not been studied much, but the Salmonella typhimurium enzyme has been purified and characterized |CITS:|. It has been suggested, although not proven, that the enzyme is involved not only in the attachment of L-Ara4N to lipid A but also in the transport of L-Ara4N from the cytoplasm, where it is synthesized, to the periplasmic side of the inner membrane, where the attachment takes place. Deletion of arnT results in defective attachment of L-Ara4N to the lipid A core, but does not affect the transport of undecaprenyl phosphate-α-L-Ara4N across the inner membrane |CITS:|. A lpxM mutant lacking the secondary linked myristoyl group of lipid A is unable to attach L-Ara4N to lipid A |CITS:|. Expression of the arnBCADTEF operon increased during growth with elevated FeSO4, FeCl3, or ZnSO4 and was dependent upon the BasSR two-component signal transduction system |CITS:,|. The arnT transcript levels were increased under growth conditions with low Mg2+ concentrations, but these expression levels decreased significantly in the pmrD mutant strain compared with the wild-type strain |CITS: |.

MetaCyc_Comment: YfeX belongs to the family of dye-decolorizing (DyP-type) peroxidases and is able to oxidize both protoporphyrinogen IX and coproporphyrinogen III to their corresponding porphyrins |CITS: |. A crystal structure of heme-bound YfeX from E. coli O157:H7 str. Sakai has been solved at 2.09 Å resolution. Site-directed mutagenesis of the predicted active site residues D143 And R232 indicate that their importance for catalysis is dependent on the substrate |CITS: |. The sequences of the E. coli O157:H7 str. Sakai and K-12 MG1655 proteins are 99% identical. Additional mutants in predicted active site residues were tested for heme binding ability |CITS: |. The authors of |CITS: | were unable to reproduce dechelation of iron from protoheme or mesoheme, disputing the results of |CITS: |, described below: Due to the lack of an outer membrane receptor for heme, E. coli K-12 is unable to utilize heme as a source of iron |CITS: |. However, expression of the heme receptor protein HasR from Serratia marcescens enables utilization of heme as a source of iron. This requires the presence of either the Dpp |FRAME: ABC-8-CPLX| or of the EfeUO transporter, which is not functional in E. coli K-12 due to a frameshift mutation disrupting efeU. Once transported to the cytoplasm, the YfeX protein is able to release iron from hemin without destroying the tetrapyrrol ring. The EfeB protein, although it is normally transported to the periplasm, is able to catalyze the same cytoplasmic reaction. A yfeX efeB double mutant in a HasR-expressing strain is unable to use heme as an external source of iron |CITS: |. Overproduction of YfeX disrupts heme homeostasis |CITS: |. Purified YfeX binds both hemin and protoporphyrin IX; the H215 residue is the predicted iron ligand and is required for binding of both substrates |CITS: |. YfeX expression is upregulated under glucose-limited fed-batch conditions |CITS: |. Both knockout and overexpression data suggest that YfeX is involved in tolerance to high concentrations of sodium chloride |CITS: |.

Merged_Functions: glxR encodes a 227‑amino‑acid, cAMP‑binding transcriptional regulator belonging to the CRP/FNR family. The GlxR protein forms dimers and, in the presence of cyclic AMP, binds specifically to the promoter region of the aceB gene (malate synthase) and likely to aceA (isocitrate lyase), thereby repressing transcription of these glyoxylate bypass genes. Overexpression of glxR reduces the activities of isocitrate lyase and malate synthase, especially when cells are grown on acetate, indicating its role as a negative regulator of the glyoxylate bypass pathway. GlxR can also complement an E. coli crp mutant, demonstrating functional similarity to the cAMP receptor protein. {PubMed:15150232}. GlxR is a cAMP‑responsive global transcription regulator in Corynebacterium glutamicum.  It binds specific DNA motifs in a cAMP‑dependent manner and directly activates transcription of target genes, exemplified by its positive regulation of the ramA promoter (binding at –290 relative to the ramA transcription start site).  In addition to activating ramA, GlxR has been shown to activate genes involved in glycolysis (e.g., gapA, pfk), ATP synthesis, and cytochrome c oxidase, while repressing genes of the glyoxylate shunt such as aceB (malate synthase) and aceA (isocitrate lyase).  Thus, GlxR functions as a key node in the regulatory network that integrates intracellular cAMP levels with carbon‑source‑dependent expression of central metabolic pathways. {PubMed:23396909}. GlxR encodes a cAMP‑receptor‑protein (CRP)–like transcriptional regulator in Corynebacterium glutamicum. It binds cyclic AMP and specifically interacts with CRP‑binding sites located upstream of the gluconate permease (gntP) and gluconate kinase (gntK) promoters, thereby mediating carbon catabolite repression of these genes. Overexpression of glxR modestly reduces gntP and gntK transcription, while disruption attempts failed, indicating that glxR is essential for cell viability. In addition to regulating the gnt operon, GlxR has been implicated in the control of other carbon‑responsive genes such as aceB (malate synthase). Thus, GlxR functions as a global, cAMP‑dependent regulator that modulates expression of genes involved in carbon metabolism. {PubMed:16385030}. glxR encodes a cAMP‑dependent DNA‑binding transcription regulator belonging to the CRP/FNR protein family. It functions as a global regulator (regulatory hub) that directly controls the expression of at least 96 genes organized in 53 transcription units. GlxR binds a conserved 16‑bp operator motif (consensus TGTGANNTANNTCACA) located upstream of target genes and can act as both an activator and a repressor, depending on the position of the site relative to the promoter. Through these interactions GlxR coordinates a wide range of cellular processes, including (i) sugar uptake and central carbohydrate metabolism (glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, glyoxylate bypass), (ii) utilization of acetate, lactate, gluconate and ethanol, (iii) aromatic compound degradation, (iv) aerobic and anaerobic respiration, (v) glutamate uptake and nitrogen assimilation, (vi) fatty‑acid biosynthesis, (vii) deoxyribonucleotide biosynthesis, (viii) cellular stress responses, and (ix) resuscitation processes. The regulator also participates in regulatory cascades by controlling other transcription factors and is subject to negative autoregulation. {PubMed:18573287}. GlxR is a cAMP‑dependent CRP homologue that acts as a global transcriptional regulator of carbon metabolism in Corynebacterium glutamicum. It binds the consensus sequence TGTGANGTCACA in target promoters when complexed with cAMP. GlxR represses the glyoxylate‑shunt gene aceB and the TCA‑cycle genes gltA and sdhCAB, and it participates together with RamA and RamB in regulating aceB expression. It also influences expression of acetate, gluconate and ethanol metabolism genes, aromatic‑compound degradation genes, fatty‑acid biosynthesis genes, deoxyribonucleotide biosynthesis genes, stress‑response genes, and resuscitation genes. Predicted targets include the glycolytic genes gapA and pfkA, as well as the sugar‑uptake genes ptsG and ptsI‑fruR, suggesting coordination of central carbon flux with other regulators (SugR, RamA, RamB). GlxR contributes to carbon catabolite repression: it represses a glutamate transporter in the presence of glucose, and its over‑expression reduces isocitrate lyase and malate synthase activities in acetate medium. Overall, GlxR integrates intracellular cAMP signals to modulate transcription of a broad regulon involved in central and peripheral carbon metabolism. {PubMed:21277916}. GlxR is a cAMP‑binding homodimeric transcription factor belonging to the CRP/FNR family in Corynebacterium glutamicum.  It functions as a global regulator that, upon binding cAMP, activates transcription of genes involved in aerobic respiration, glycolysis, and ATP synthesis.  The protein exhibits allosteric regulation without a detectable conformational change, whereby ligand binding modulates global low‑frequency backbone motions that influence its DNA‑binding activity. {PubMed:24058293}. GlxR is a CRP‑FNR family transcriptional regulator from Corynebacterium glutamicum that controls the glyoxylate bypass pathway. The article notes that GlxR belongs to the same subfamily as Crp^Sco, that it has been implicated in cAMP‑dependent regulation (binding of purified GlxR to its target promoter was observed only in the presence of cAMP), and that it functions as the regulator of the glyoxylate bypass in C. glutamicum. {PubMed:15541386}.
Curated_Functions: Binds cyclic AMP and forms homodimers. {PubMed:15150232, PubMed:15541386, PubMed:24058293}. Binds a conserved 16‑bp operator motif in a cAMP‑dependent manner to regulate transcription. {PubMed:18573287, PubMed:21277916, PubMed:23396909}. Activates transcription of genes involved in glycolysis, ATP synthesis, aerobic respiration and cytochrome c oxidase, including gapA, pfk and ramA. {PubMed:23396909, PubMed:24058293}. Represses transcription of glyoxylate‑shunt genes aceA and aceB and of TCA‑cycle genes gltA and sdhCAB, thereby inhibiting the glyoxylate bypass pathway. {PubMed:15150232, PubMed:21277916, PubMed:16385030}. Mediates carbon catabolite repression of gluconate utilization genes gntP and gntK and of a glutamate transporter in the presence of glucose. {PubMed:16385030, PubMed:21277916}. Regulates utilization of alternative carbon sources such as acetate, lactate, gluconate and ethanol and controls aromatic‑compound degradation pathways. {PubMed:18573287, PubMed:21277916}. Controls fatty‑acid biosynthesis, deoxyribonucleotide biosynthesis, nitrogen assimilation, cellular stress responses and resuscitation processes. {PubMed:18573287, PubMed:21277916}. Participates in regulatory cascades by controlling other transcription factors and is subject to negative autoregulation. {PubMed:18573287}. Is essential for cell viability. {PubMed:16385030}. Exhibits allosteric regulation whereby cAMP binding modulates low‑frequency backbone motions that affect DNA‑binding activity without a detectable conformational change. {PubMed:24058293}.
