MetaCyc_Comment: The DtpA protein (formerly TppB) is a member of the POT (proton-dependent oligopeptide transporter) family of peptide transporters |CITS:| also known as the PTR (peptide transport) family. DtpA is responsible for proton-dependent transport of di- and tripeptides as well as some structurally related peptidomimetics like B-lactam antibiotics |CITS:, |. DtpA transports the tetrapeptide, tetraalanine in vitro |CITS: | however tetraalanine does not function as an inhibitor in competitive transport assays |CITS: |. DtpA shows a preference for di- and tripeptides composed of L amino acids and for peptides containing a positively charged side chain in the N-terminal position |CITS: |. Transmission electron microscopy of solubilised DtpA suggests a monomeric crown-like structure with a pore of approximately 8 nm |CITS:|. DtpA is predicted to contain 14 transmembrane regions with both termini located in the cytoplasm |CITS: |. Characterisation of DtpA embedded in a lipid membrane indicates that the protein adopts two alternate conformational states defined largely by the stabilisation of transmembrane helix 2 (TMH2). Binding of an inhibitor molecule shifts the equilibrium between these two states towards the conformation containing a stabilised TMH2 |CITS: |. dtpA was identified as a member of the OmpR regulon in a DNA microarray experiment |CITS: |. dtpA expression is transcriptionally regulated by OmpR, but is not sensitive to changes in medium osmolarity |CITS:|. tpp: tripeptide permeasedtpA: dipeptide and tripeptide permease A

FUNCTION: Part of a signaling cascade that regulates curli biosynthesis. PdeR does not play a global regulatory role; csgD transcription may be its only target. PdeR acts antagonistically to DgcM |CITS: |. Genetic analysis using epistasis experiments elucidated the presence of a signaling cascade, with the DgcE/PdeH diguanylate cyclase (DGC)/phosphodiesterase (PDE) pair acting upstream of PdeR, which itself is upstream of the DGC DgcM, and all acting upstream of the MlrA transcription factor. The direct interaction between PdeR and DgcM appears to inhibit the DGC activity of DgcM |CITS: |. PdeR contains PAS, GGDEF, and EAL domains and displays c-di-GMP phosphodiesterase activity in vitro |CITS: |. PdeR interacts directly with DgcM and MlrA, primarily via its C-terminal EAL domain. The EAL domain is also required for transmitting information from the DgcE/PdeH system to DgcM/MlrA. The protein binds GTP via its GGDEF domain |CITS: |. Curli-shaped fibers are overproduced. Transcription of csgD, which controls production of curli, is elevated in a pdeR mutant at 28°C |CITS: |. In contrast, an EAL domain point mutant of pdeR reduces csgB (and thus curli) expression in a wild type background and loses sensitivity to mutations in dgcE and pdeH |CITS: |. A pdeR deletion mutant contains slightly higher levels of cytoplasmic c-di-GMP |CITS: |. Expression of pdeR is increased during the transition to stationary phase and is dependent on σS under a number of stress conditions |CITS: |. H-NS plays a role in regulating pdeR expression |CITS: |. At 28°C, pdeR expression is higher on solid medium than in liquid medium |CITS: |. A pdeR mutant exhibits 3-fold elevated RNase II abundance as a result of decreased protein turnover, compared to wild type, and thus lacks the regulation of RNase II abundance that is observed in wild type in response to changes in growth environment |CITS: |. Function [CC]: FUNCTION: Mechanosensitive channel that opens in response to membrane tension and specific ionic conditions. Requires high concentrations of external K(+), NH(4)(+), Rb(+) or Cs(+) to gate. May participate in the regulation of osmotic pressure changes within the cell, although it does not appear to have a major role in osmolarity regulation. Forms an ion channel of 1.0 nanosiemens conductance. The channel can remain active for between 30 seconds and over 3 minutes; it does not desensitize upon extended pressure. Its activity is masked in wild-type cells by the MscS channel. {ECO:0000269|PubMed:10202137, ECO:0000269|PubMed:11985727, ECO:0000269|PubMed:12374733}.
MetaCyc_Comment: MscK is a potassium-dependent, mechanosensitive channel of small conductance. mscK encodes a mechanosensitive channel with similar or slightly lower conductance to the |FRAME: EG11160-MONOMER "MscS"| channel of small conductance (0.8 - 1nS) |CITS: |; MscK does not desensitize upon extended pressure application; ΔmscK cells survive the transition to low osmolarity media as do Δ(mscK mscS) double mutants |CITS: |. E. coli strain RQ2 carrying the kefA2 allele is unable to grow in high (0.6M) K+ medium in the presence of compatible solutes; the mutant strain exhibits a complex K+ specific phenotype that likely results from aberrant gating of the MscK channel |CITS: | (see further |CITS: |). MscK is highly regulated; normal gating requires both membrane tension and high external K+ concentration; smaller ions such as Li+ and Na+ cannot substitute for K+, while larger ions such as NH4+, Rb+, and Cs+ can |CITS: |. MscK is predicted to consist of a large amino terminal domain located in the periplasm, an inner membrane domain with11 transmembrane regions and a cytoplasmic C-terminus; MscK contains a 33 residue signal sequence, that is required to organize the large hydrophilic domain in the periplasm |CITS: |. MscK fluorescent fusion proteins, expressed at basal levels, are evenly distributed and mobile throughout the membrane |CITS: |. A strain lacking MscS, MscK and MscL exhibits defects in Z-ring placement in the presence of the septation inhibitor, cephalexin |CITS: |. Early studies implicated MscK (formerly KefA) in a system of potassium efflux that responded to osmotic downshock |CITS: |. Seven mechanosensitive ion channels have been characterised in E. coli K-12: |FRAME: CPLX0-7627 "MscL"|, MscS, MscK, |FRAME: CPLX0-7985 "MscM"|, |FRAME: CPLX0-7982 "YnaI"|, |FRAME: CPLX0-7983 "YbiO"| and |FRAME: CPLX0-7981 "YbdG"|. A strain lacking all seven of these proteins fails to demonstrate channel opening in patch clamp experiments |CITS: |. Related reviews: |CITS: |.

Crystal structures of SsuE in the apo, FMN-bound, and FMNH2-bound forms have been solved |CITS: |. SsuE forms a dimer of dimers in the crystal structure; in solution, the protein is in a dimer-tetramer equilibrium that depends on the presence of FMN. A general catalytic cycle involving FMN binding before NADPH was proposed |CITS: |, thus revising the catalytic mechanism proposed earlier |CITS: |. Expression of SsuE appears to be induced by sulfate or cysteine starvation |CITS: |. Transcription of ssuE is repressed by sulfate or cysteine, and the effect requires the transcriptional regulator Cbl |CITS: |. Merged_Functions: The uxaB gene encodes altronate (also called altonate) oxidoreductase, an enzyme that participates in the Ashwell pathway for catabolism of hexuronates such as D‑galacturonate and D‑glucuronate. It acts in the early steps of galacturonate metabolism, following the products of exuT and uxaC, and preceding uxaA. Expression of uxaB is induced by substrates including galacturonate, tagaturonate, and fructuronate, and its transcription is regulated by the ExuR repressor and subject to catabolite repression. {PubMed:3525742}. The uxaB gene encodes an altronate oxidoreductase that participates in the three‑step catabolic pathway converting galacturonate (and, via a parallel route, glucuronate) into 2‑keto‑3‑deoxygluconate (KDG). It is part of the uxaC‑uxaB‑uxaA operon, whose expression is regulated by the exuR repressor. The enzyme catalyzes the oxidation of the intermediate altronate (produced after uronate isomerization by UxaC) to the next metabolite in the pathway leading toward KDG formation. {PubMed:3029026}. The uxaB gene encodes altronate oxidoreductase, an enzyme that participates in the degradative pathway of galacturonate in Escherichia coli K12. This enzyme is involved in the catabolism of galacturonate, allowing the sugar to be used as a carbon source through an inducible hexuronate degradation system. {PubMed:6343794}. The article states that uxaB encodes the structural gene for enzyme III of the hexuronate (exu) regulon. Enzyme III is an aldonic oxidoreductase (mannonate oxidoreductase, EC 1.1.1.57) that catalyzes the reduction step in the degradation of galacturonate and glucuronate: it reduces tagaturonate to altronate in the galacturonate pathway and reduces fructuronate to mannonate in the glucuronate pathway. Thus, uxaB provides the enzymatic activity required for the third step of hexuronate catabolism. {PubMed:7026975}. The article indicates that the uxaB gene encodes the enzyme responsible for altronate oxidoreductase activity in Escherichia coli. This activity is part of a catabolic pathway and is normally inducible. The expression of uxaB is controlled by a promoter‑operator region that is repressed by the ExuR protein; deletion of exuR leads to constitutive expression. The study used the uxaB promoter to drive transcription of a uidA (β‑glucuronidase) reporter, demonstrating that the uxaB promoter functions similarly to its native chromosomal context. {PubMed:2841575}. UxaB encodes the D‑altronate dehydrogenase (also called D‑AltA dehydrogenase) that catalyzes the NAD(H)-dependent interconversion of D‑tagaturonate (D‑TagA) and D‑altronate (D‑AltA). In the canonical Escherichia coli D‑galacturonate catabolic pathway, UxaB acts after the UxaC isomerase, reducing D‑TagA to D‑AltA, which is then hydrolyzed by UxaA to produce 2‑keto‑3‑deoxy‑D‑gluconate (KDG). The gene is absent from Thermotoga maritima, which instead employs the UxaE‑mediated epimerization step. {PubMed:22925190}. The article describes b1521 as the uxaB gene, which encodes altronate (altonate) oxidoreductase. This enzyme participates in the Ashwell pathway for catabolism of the aldoxuronates D‑glucuronate and D‑galacturonate, converting altronate as part of the sequence of reactions carried out by the exu regulon (exuT, uxaC, uxaB, uxaA). Its expression is induced by natural inducers of the hexuronate system (galacturonate, tagaturonate, fructuronate, mannonic amide), is subject to catabolite repression by glucose, and is negatively regulated by the ExuR repressor. {PubMed:7026975}. The article states that uxaC encodes the enzyme catalyzing the first step of glucuronate catabolism in Escherichia coli. Specifically, UxaC converts glucuronate into fructuronate, the intermediate that induces the UxuR regulon. Consequently, uxaC is essential for growth on glucuronate, as a uxaC mutant cannot grow on this substrate. {PubMed:15516583}. Encodes uronate isomerase, the first enzyme of the three‑step catabolic pathway that converts galacturonate (and, via a parallel route, glucuronate) into 2‑keto‑3‑deoxygluconate (KDG). UxaC catalyzes the isomerization of galacturonate to the intermediate tagaturonate, initiating the conversion of hexuronates toward KDG, which is further processed by UxaB and UxaA. {PubMed:3029026}. UxaC is a hexuronate isomerase that catalyzes the first step of D‑galacturonate (D‑GalA) and D‑glucuronate (D‑GlcA) catabolism. It converts D‑GalA to D‑tagaturonate (D‑TagA) and D‑GlcA to D‑fructuronate (D‑FruA). In Thermotoga maritima, the enzyme (tm_UxaC, TM0064) shows comparable affinity for both substrates but a ~7.8‑fold higher catalytic efficiency for D‑GalA, indicating dual specificity and a key role in the D‑GalA utilization pathway. {PubMed:22925190}. The uxaC gene in Escherichia coli encodes a component of the native pathway that degrades D‑glucuronic acid (GlcUA). Inactivation of uxaC prevents the catabolism of GlcUA, thereby allowing accumulation of the product during whole‑cell bioconversion. The study demonstrated that deletion of uxaC (creating strain BWΔuxaC) resulted in ~98 % of added GlcUA remaining after 12 h, compared with only ~74 % remaining in the wild‑type strain, indicating that uxaC is responsible for GlcUA degradation. {PubMed:31088620}. The b3092 gene encodes GntP, an inner‑membrane protein of the major facilitator superfamily with 12 transmembrane segments that functions as the primary fructuronate transporter in Escherichia coli. GntP is a member of the UxuR regulon: its transcription is repressed by the UxuR repressor and is strongly induced by fructuronate (the true inducer) and, indirectly, by glucuronate via its conversion to fructuronate. Expression also requires activation by the cAMP‑CRP complex and is subject to catabolite repression by glucose. A b3092 (gntP) mutant cannot grow on fructuronate as the sole carbon source, confirming its essential role in fructuronate uptake, whereas it does not affect growth on glucuronate, gluconate, glucose, or galacturonate. Merged_Functions: The ybjN gene encodes a putative sensory transduction regulator protein.  Over‑expression of ybjN can suppress the temperature‑sensitive growth defects caused by unstable mutant proteins, notably the L236F mutant pantothenate kinase (CoaA1) and other CoaA temperature‑sensitive alleles (coaA14, coaA15), as well as the ilu‑1 mutation.  This suggests that YbjN functions as a general stabilizer of certain unstable proteins, possibly acting as a stress‑response factor that helps maintain protein integrity under non‑permissive temperatures. {PubMed:16701556}. The ybjN gene (named amyR in Erwinia amylovora) encodes an enterobacteria‑specific orphan protein that acts as a broad negative regulator of exopolysaccharide (EPS) production and associated virulence traits.  Deletion of ybjN/amyR causes an ~8‑fold increase in the production of the acidic heteropolymer amylovoran, accompanied by up‑regulation of the ams biosynthetic operon (amsA‑L) and the rcsA regulatory gene, indicating that YbjN normally represses transcription of these EPS‑related genes.  Conversely, multicopy expression of ybjN/amyR strongly suppresses amylovoran synthesis, reduces levan (a fructan EPS) production, and markedly diminishes disease severity on apple shoots, leaves, and immature pear fruits, often rendering the bacterium non‑pathogenic.  Transcriptomic analyses show that YbjN influences a wide regulon, including down‑regulation of membrane‑protein genes, glycogen‑biosynthetic genes, flagellar genes, and genes involved in histidine metabolism, suggesting a role in coordinating multicellular behavior, metabolism, and stress responses.  Overall, YbjN functions as a general suppressor of EPS biosynthesis and virulence factor expression in E. amylovora. {PubMed:23028751}. YbjN is a conserved stress‑responsive regulatory protein in Enterobacteriaceae. Its expression is induced by various stress conditions (temperature shifts, growth phase, acid, radiation, etc.). Over‑expression of ybjN triggers a pleiotropic transcriptional response that up‑regulates stress‑related genes (toxin‑antitoxin modules, SOS response, cold‑shock and phage‑shock genes) and down‑regulates metabolic and biosynthetic pathways, leading to slower growth, reduced swarming motility, decreased capsule and biofilm formation, and increased acid susceptibility. In Erwinia amylovora, the ybjN ortholog AmyR controls virulence‑associated exopolysaccharide production: loss of amyR causes an 8‑fold increase in amylovoran synthesis and a mucoid phenotype, whereas over‑expression strongly represses amylovoran and levan synthesis and diminishes pathogenicity. AmyR/YbjN likely exerts its effects through protein‑protein interactions rather than enzymatic activity, possibly binding and modulating components of the Rcs phosphorelay system or other transcriptional regulators, thereby influencing the transcription of the ams operon and galactose‑metabolism genes. Although its fold resembles class I type III secretion chaperones, YbjN proteins are not involved in T3SS function; instead they act as sensory transduction regulators that mediate stress responses and virulence factor expression via specific protein interactions. {PubMed:28426806}. Over‑expression of YbjN can suppress the temperature‑sensitive growth defects caused by destabilized pantothenate kinase (CoaA[L236F]) and several other temperature‑sensitive mutations (including coaA14, coaA15, and ilu‑1). This suggests that YbjN acts as a general stabilizer of unstable proteins, possibly by enhancing their structural integrity rather than by affecting folding intermediates. YbjN expression is up‑regulated under stress conditions such as acidic pH and when the transcriptional regulator MarA is constitutively active, indicating a role in stress response. Overall, JW0837/YbjN functions as a multi‑copy suppressor that can partially rescue protein‑instability phenotypes in E. coli. {PubMed:16701556}. The b0853 gene, also known as ybjN, encodes a putative sensory transduction regulator protein.  In the study, over‑expression of ybjN was found to suppress the temperature‑sensitive growth defects caused by destabilized pantothenate kinase (CoaA) mutants (e.g., coaA1/L236F) and other temperature‑sensitive alleles such as ilu‑1.  This suppression suggests that YbjN can act as a general stabilizer of unstable proteins, helping cells tolerate mutations that compromise protein stability.  No specific biochemical activity of YbjN is described beyond its role as a multi‑copy suppressor and possible stress‑response protein. {PubMed:16701556}.

YfaE functions as an electron donor that reduces the met‑β₂ form of the class Ia ribonucleotide reductase β subunit. This activity places YfaE in the “maintenance” pathway that regenerates the Y• cofactor during normal turnover, and the authors propose that YfaE also participates in the “biosynthetic” pathway that builds the cofactor de novo. YfaE encodes a small (84‑aa) 2Fe‑2S ferredoxin that is genomically linked to the nrdAB operon encoding the α and β subunits of class Ia ribonucleotide reductase (RNR). This reduction is stoichiometric (one YfaE oxidized reduces one Fe³⁺ in β₂) and enables rapid O₂‑driven reassembly of the active diferric‑tyrosyl‑radical (Y•) cofactor.  Thus YfaE functions as the electron‑transfer partner in the “maintenance” pathway that regenerates the Y• cofactor, and the authors propose that it also participates in the “biosynthetic” pathway that assembles the cofactor de novo. In iron‑replete, unstressed cells YfaE is not required for NrdAB activity. {PubMed:21338418}. YfaE therefore participates directly in both the biosynthetic and maintenance pathways for the diferric Y• cofactor of class Ia ribonucleotide reductase, facilitating cofactor assembly and ensuring proper iron loading of β. {PubMed:18314964}.

The article reports that FIII is required, together with FI and FII, for the formation of the 70S initiation complex that contains fMet‑tRNA, poly(U,G) messenger RNA, and the ribosome. Its presence is almost absolutely necessary for maximal incorporation of both fMet‑tRNA and poly(U,G) into the 70S complex, indicating that FIII facilitates the binding of the initiator tRNA and mRNA to the ribosomal subunits during the early steps of protein synthesis. No additional activities (such as ribosome dissociation) are attributed to FIII in the article. {PubMed:5277078}. Within these complexes it participates in the vectorial translocation and phosphorylation of specific carbohydrates. Importantly, the presence of FIII is required for the chemotactic response to those substrates: mutants lacking FIII fail to exhibit chemotaxis toward D‑glucose despite having the membrane‑bound EIIB′ component. Thus, FIII functions both as an essential component of the transport/phosphorylation machinery of specific PTS enzyme II systems and as a critical element of the chemoreceptor mechanism that mediates substrate‑specific chemotaxis in *Escherichia coli* K12. {PubMed:7035817}. The article describes fla as a set of flagellar genes in Caulobacter crescentus that are essential for flagellum biosynthesis. At least 30 flagellar (fla, flb, flg) genes are required to build the flagellum, and the fla genes are transcribed in a periodic, cell‑cycle‑dependent manner that corresponds to the timing of protein assembly into the flagellum. Their expression is organized into a regulatory hierarchy in which activation of genes at one level is required for transcription of genes at the next lower level, driving a cascade that initiates flagellar assembly independently of external signals. Thus, fla genes encode products that form structural and functional components of the flagellum and are tightly controlled during the swarmer‑cell to stalked‑cell transition. {PubMed:2644197}. In this study, the fla‑encoded flagellin was used as a carrier protein into which a 15‑amino‑acid linear epitope from the CFA/I fimbria was genetically inserted. The resulting hybrid flagellin (Fla II) retained its immunogenic properties and was able to prime and boost IgG antibody responses against both homologous (CFA/I) and heterologous (CS1, CS2, PCFO166) colonization factor antigens of enterotoxigenic E. coli. Thus, fla functions to produce flagellin, a structural flagellar protein that also serves as a versatile vaccine carrier for heterologous peptide epitopes. {PubMed:11037135}. Merged_Functions: The ygiW gene encodes a small periplasmic protein of the oligonucleotide/oligosaccharide‑binding (OB‑fold) family that is co‑transcribed with the qseBC two‑component system as part of a single operon. Its transcription is driven by a promoter located 372 bp upstream of ygiW and requires the QseB response regulator and the functional periplasmic sensor domain of QseC, indicating that ygiW expression is controlled by the QseBC signaling pathway. Functional YgiW protein influences biofilm development in Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans: an in‑frame, non‑polar deletion of ygiW does not alter biofilm depth but causes a significant increase in surface coverage, and complementation restores the wild‑type phenotype. Thus, YgiW acts as a regulator of biofilm growth, likely through a mechanism distinct from that of QseBC, and may also contribute to stress‑related functions typical of OB‑fold periplasmic proteins, although its specific ligand or biochemical activity remains unidentified. {PubMed:23519160}. The ygiW gene encodes a small, predicted periplasmic protein belonging to the bacterial OB‑fold (BOF) superfamily. It is transcribed as part of the ygiW‑firRS operon and its expression is strongly up‑regulated (≈6‑fold higher than the downstream firR‑firS transcript) by the FirRS two‑component system in response to ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), zinc, and cold shock. FirR acts as an auto‑activator, and the presence of an attenuator between ygiW and firR ensures higher levels of the ygiW transcript. Although the precise biochemical activity of YgiW is not defined, the article suggests it functions as the main effector of the FirRS system, likely participating in the bacterial response to elevated Fe²⁺/Zn²⁺ or related stress conditions. Deletion of ygiW attenuates Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae in a mouse pulmonary infection model, indicating that YgiW contributes to virulence in the lung. Overall, ygiW appears to be a periplasmic BOF‑domain protein involved in ferrous‑iron‑responsive signaling and pathogenic fitness. {PubMed:22961857}. YgiW is a previously uncharacterized Escherichia coli protein that functions as a stress‑response factor. Deletion of ygiW makes cells markedly more sensitive to hydrogen peroxide (≈35‑fold lower survival) and to cadmium, indicating that YgiW contributes to oxidative‑metal stress resistance. The mutant also forms significantly more biofilm than wild‑type, and over‑expression of ygiW restores normal biofilm levels, suggesting a role in regulating biofilm formation. Transcriptomic data show that ygiW is induced by H₂O₂ exposure and by the acid‑resistance regulator AriR, and it lies between the quorum‑sensing regulators qseB and mqsR, implying integration into broader stress and signaling networks. Overall, YgiW participates in a complex stress network that protects E. coli against oxidative and metal stresses and modulates biofilm development. {PubMed:19919618}. YgiW is identified in this study as a SecB‑dependent secretory protein. Pulse‑labeling experiments showed that, in a secB null mutant, the precursor form of YgiW accumulates, indicating that its efficient translocation across the cytoplasmic membrane requires the chaperone SecB. No additional specific biochemical or physiological role for YgiW is described in the article. {PubMed:16352602}. The article reports that ygiW encodes a predicted periplasmic protein whose transcription is positively regulated by the stationary‑phase sigma factor RpoS. In strains expressing wild‑type RpoS, ygiW mRNA levels are higher, whereas a K173E mutation in RpoS reduces ygiW transcription by ~3.8‑fold. Despite this regulation, deletion of ygiW (Keio mutant JW2992) does not cause a significant change in the frequency of spontaneous plasmid transformation, indicating that while ygiW is RpoS‑responsive, it is not individually required for the plasmid DNA uptake process described in the study. {PubMed:22438941}. The YgiW homolog (PA0320) in Pseudomonas aeruginosa functions as a stress‑response protein that contributes to resistance against tributyltin (TBT). Deletion of the gene reduces growth in the presence of TBT and increases susceptibility to several other stressors, including cadmium, mercury, hydrogen peroxide, and acidic pH. These phenotypes indicate that YgiW provides cross‑protection against oxidative stress‑inducing agents and helps the bacterium tolerate multiple environmental pollutants. {PubMed:22990488}. YgiW (encoded by b3024) is a previously uncharacterized protein that functions as a stress‑response factor in Escherichia coli. Deletion of ygiW makes cells markedly more sensitive to hydrogen peroxide and cadmium, and the mutant forms increased biofilm, indicating YgiW contributes to resistance against oxidative and metal stress and modulates biofilm formation. The gene is transcriptionally induced by H₂O₂ and by the acid‑resistance regulator AriR, and it resides between the quorum‑sensing regulators qseB (b3025) and mqsR (b3022). Overall, YgiW participates in a broader network of proteins that protect the cell from multiple environmental stresses. {PubMed:19919618}. JW2992 corresponds to the gene ygiW, which is predicted to encode a periplasmic protein. Its transcription is up‑regulated by the stationary‑phase sigma factor RpoS and is significantly reduced (≈3.8‑fold) when the RpoS K173E mutation is present. Although ygiW expression is RpoS‑dependent, deletion of JW2992 (ygiW) does not cause a measurable decrease in the frequency of spontaneous plasmid transformation in E. coli, indicating that this gene alone is not essential for that process. {PubMed:22438941}.

Merged_Functions: The article reports that the Escherichia coli YhbY protein is a small (~10 kDa) cytoplasmic factor that co‑sediments with and tightly associates with pre‑50S ribosomal subunits. YhbY specifically co‑immunoprecipitates immature (pre‑processed) 23S rRNA, indicating that it binds to precursor 50S particles during ribosome assembly. Deletion of yhbY leads to accumulation of pre‑50S subunits and a reduction in mature 50S particles, supporting a role in the maturation of the large ribosomal subunit. Together with structural data showing similarity to RNA‑binding domains, the findings suggest that YhbY functions as an RNA‑binding assembly factor required for proper 50S ribosomal subunit maturation. {PubMed:17105995}. The article describes yhbY as the Escherichia coli representative of the conserved UPF0044 protein family. Structural analysis shows that YhbY adopts an IF3C-like fold, a fold known to bind rRNA, and possesses a highly basic β‑sheet surface and a conserved GkxG loop that together form a putative RNA‑binding site. Bioinformatic context (association with ribosomal protein genes in archaea) and experimental observations (cosedimentation with free 50S ribosomal subunits) suggest that YhbY functions as an RNA‑binding protein, likely participating in translation‑related processes in bacteria. {PubMed:12429100}. YhbY is a broadly conserved, putative RNA‑binding protein that is essential for normal ribosome biogenesis in Escherichia coli.  Genetic‑interaction data and follow‑up experiments demonstrated that YhbY is required for proper 30S subunit assembly, specifically facilitating the maturation of 16S rRNA (cleavage of the 5′‑end precursor) and the incorporation of the small‑subunit protein S5 while buffering the inhibitory effects of RimM and RimP on S13 incorporation.  Loss of YhbY leads to accumulation of incompletely processed 17S rRNA, altered levels of several 30S biogenesis factors (e.g., reduced RimM, Rne, RsmC; increased RbfA), and defects in translational fidelity.  YhbY also impacts 50S subunit biogenesis: it interacts genetically with early‑binding large‑subunit proteins (L1, L4, L23, L32, L35) and its deletion reduces incorporation of early‑binding proteins such as L22 and alters the abundance of later‑binding proteins (e.g., L28) in mature 50S particles.  Overall, YhbY functions as a critical factor in both 30S and 50S ribosomal subunit assembly, ensuring proper rRNA processing, ribosomal protein incorporation, and efficient protein synthesis. {PubMed:27732863}. The article reports that a CRS1/YhbY domain protein, which is co‑expressed with the Arabidopsis RNase E/G‑like gene, is implicated in group II intron splicing in plastids. This indicates that the yhbY gene product functions in plastid RNA metabolism, specifically contributing to the processing/splicing of group II introns. {PubMed:18515828}. The article describes yhbY as a member of the conserved UPF0044 (COG1534) protein family. Structural analyses of YhbY (and its homologs) reveal an α/β fold similar to the C‑terminal domain of prokaryotic translation initiation factor 3, a known RNA‑binding domain. Consequently, YhbY is inferred to be a putative RNA‑binding protein that may participate in RNA splicing or translation, although its precise biological role remains unconfirmed. {PubMed:15213438}.

The gutR gene encodes the repressor protein of the glucitol (gut) operon in Escherichia coli. The GutR protein (~257 amino acids, ~28 kDa) binds to the operator/promoter region of the gut operon and inhibits transcription of the catabolic genes (gutA, gutB, gutD, etc.). Its repressive activity is modulated by the inducer glucitol; when glucitol binds to GutR, the repressor dissociates from DNA, allowing transcription. gutR possesses its own promoter located within the gutM coding region, but most of its expression results from transcriptional read‑through of the polycistronic gut operon mRNA. GutR functions together with the positive regulator GutM and the global activator cAMP‑CRP to fine‑tune gut operon expression. {PubMed:3062173}. gutR encodes the glucitol operon‑specific transcriptional repressor, which negatively regulates expression of the genes within the E. coli glucitol (gut) operon. {PubMed:2134185}. The article notes that the GatR protein encoded in the gat operon shares similarity to GutR, indicating that GutR functions as a DNA‑binding repressor regulating sugar‑phosphate metabolism. {PubMed:8955298}. GutR is a 95‑kDa transcription activator that regulates the Bacillus subtilis glucitol (gut) operon. In the absence of ligand it exists as a monomeric protein that can bind a specific 29‑bp inverted repeat upstream of the gut promoter, but the DNA‑protein complex is short‑lived. Binding of the inducer glucitol induces a conformational change in GutR, dramatically increasing its DNA‑binding affinity (half‑life >19 h) and exposing a nucleotide‑binding site. The glucitol‑bound GutR then binds ATP (or GTP) via Walker A and B motifs; ATP binding triggers a second conformational change that makes the GutR‑DNA complex less stable, allowing controlled dissociation (t½ ≈ 274 min with ATP, ≈82 min with ADP). This ATP‑dependent step is essential for transcription activation, as demonstrated by the severe reduction in gut‑operon expression when the conserved Asp‑288 in the Walker B motif is mutated to Ala (GutR(D288A)). Thus, GutR functions as a glucitol‑responsive, ATP‑modulated transcriptional activator that tightly binds the gut promoter in the presence of glucitol and requires ATP binding (and possibly hydrolysis) to activate transcription. {PubMed:11390381}. GutR encodes a PRD‑containing transcriptional regulator that functions as the primary activator of the L. casei gut operon (gutFRMCBA). It possesses an N‑terminal helix‑turn‑helix DNA‑binding domain and two PTS‑regulated domains (an EIIB‑like domain and an EIIA‑like domain). GutR binds directly to a 35‑bp inverted‑repeat motif located upstream of the gut promoter, protecting this region from DNase I digestion. Activation of the operon requires GutR; a gutR frameshift mutant loses gut operon transcription and sorbitol uptake, which can be restored by complementation. GutR activity is modulated by phosphorylation: a conserved histidine in PRD2 (His‑310) is likely phosphorylated by P~His‑HPr (positive regulation), while a histidine in the C‑terminal EIIA domain (His‑537) is likely phosphorylated by the sorbitol‑specific EIIBC^Gut (negative regulation). Thus, GutR integrates PTS signaling to induce expression of the sorbitol utilization genes in response to sorbitol and is essential for sorbitol transport and metabolism. {PubMed:18676710}. The gutR gene encodes the repressor protein of the gut operon. It negatively regulates transcription of the operon, which includes the genes gutA, gutB, gutD, and gutM. In the wild‑type strain, GutR keeps expression of the glucitol phosphotransferase system (PTS) genes under control, allowing inducible expression. A chromosomal mutation in gutR results in loss of repression, causing constitutive (high‑level) expression of the gut operon; this leads to growth inhibition on gluconeogenic substrates and reduced activities of key gluconeogenic enzymes (phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase and phosphoenolpyruvate synthase). {PubMed:2824435}. gutR encodes a specific negative regulator (repressor) of the gut (srl) operon, which controls the synthesis of the D‑glucitol transport system in E. coli K12. Temperature‑sensitive, trans‑recessive mutations in gutR also lead to constitutive operon expression at the permissive temperature, further supporting its role as a repressor. Thus, gutR functions as a regulatory gene that negatively controls gut operon transcription. {PubMed:360044}. Merged_Functions: Encodes the bifunctional purine‑biosynthesis protein PurH, which catalyzes the last two steps of de novo purine biosynthesis. The N‑terminal domain possesses IMP cyclohydrolase activity, converting 5‑formyl‑AICAR (FAICAR) to inosine‑5′‑monophosphate (IMP). The C‑terminal domain possesses AICAR transformylase activity, transferring a formyl group from N10‑formyltetrahydrofolate to aminoimidazole‑4‑carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) to generate FAICAR, which then cyclizes to IMP. Coupling of these two domains is essential for the overall conversion of AICAR to IMP, providing the precursor for the synthesis of GMP and AMP. {PubMed:22139174}. The article reports that purH encodes a protein involved in purine biosynthesis. Its transcription is up‑regulated (approximately two‑fold) in Escherichia coli cells treated with the monoterpene citral, indicating activation of nucleotide synthesis pathways required for DNA and RNA production during the stress response. {PubMed:28644990}. purH encodes phosphoribosylaminoimidazolecarboxamide formyltransferase, an enzyme involved in the de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides. In the study, higher PurH protein levels in the acetate‑tolerant mutant DA19 (compared with DH5α) indicated an enhanced capacity for de novo purine biosynthesis under nitrogen‑limited conditions. When adenine was supplied (MNAd medium), both strains relied more on the salvage pathway for purine synthesis, reducing the relative importance of purH expression. {PubMed:20700606}. purH encodes a bifunctional enzyme (AICAR transformylase/IMP cyclohydrolase) that catalyzes the conversion of the purine intermediate AICAR (ZMP) first to FAICAR and then to inosine monophosphate (IMP). This reaction is a key step in the de novo purine biosynthetic pathway and provides a route for recycling AICAR into ATP, which is the substrate required by the first enzyme of the histidine biosynthetic pathway (HisG). In the study, overexpression of purH (together with purA) was shown to enhance the conversion of AICAR to ATP, thereby relieving AICAR‑mediated inhibition of HisG and improving L‑histidine production. {PubMed:29544475}. The purH gene encodes a single polypeptide of ~57 kDa that is bifunctional, possessing both 5‑amino‑4‑imidazolecarboxamide‑ribotide (AICAR) transformylase activity (EC 2.1.2.3) and IMP cyclohydrolase activity (EC 3.5.4.10). These two enzymatic functions catalyze the ninth and tenth reactions of the de novo purine biosynthetic pathway, respectively: AICAR transformylase transfers a formyl group from N10‑formyl‑tetrahydrofolate to AICAR to produce FAICAR, and IMP cyclohydrolase then cyclizes FAICAR to generate inosine monophosphate (IMP), the first complete purine nucleotide. The purH product therefore converts AICAR to IMP in a two‑step process and is a key component of the purHD operon, which is co‑regulated with other purine biosynthetic genes by the PurR repressor. {PubMed:2192230}. purH encodes a bifunctional enzyme that carries out the AICAR transformylase and IMP cyclohydrolase activities in the de novo synthesis of purine nucleotides. The AICAR transformylase domain catalyzes the formylation of 5′‑phosphoribosyl‑5‑amino‑imidazole‑4‑carboxamide (AICAR) to produce formyl‑AICAR, and the IMP cyclohydrolase domain subsequently converts this intermediate to inosine monophosphate (IMP). Thus, purH is essential for the final two steps of the pathway that converts 5‑phosphoribosyl‑1‑pyrophosphate to IMP. {PubMed:1954258}. The purH gene encodes a bifunctional enzyme, 5‑aminoimidazole‑4‑carboxamide‑ribotide (AICAR) transformylase‑inosine monophosphate (IMP) cyclohydrolase (ATIC). In the de novo purine nucleotide biosynthetic pathway it catalyzes the last two reactions (steps 9 and 10): (1) it transfers a formyl group from N^10‑formyl‑tetrahydrofolate to AICAR, producing 5‑formyl‑AICAR (FAICAR) and tetrahydrofolate; (2) it then promotes cyclohydrolase activity that closes the imidazole ring of FAICAR, releasing water and forming IMP. Thus, PurH is essential for the conversion of AICAR to IMP, completing purine synthesis. {PubMed:1937050}. The N‑terminal domain functions as AICAR transformylase (EC 2.1.2.3), transferring a formyl group from N¹⁰‑formyl‑THF to AICAR, while the C‑terminal domain acts as IMP cyclohydrolase (EC 3.5.4.10), converting FAICAR to IMP. MetaCyc_Comment: In bacteria and eukaryotes the last two reactions of the de novo purine biosynthetic pathway for IMP biosynthesis are sequentially catalyzed by a bifunctional enzyme containing aminoimidazole carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase and IMP cyclohydrolase activities. To date, much of the biochemical and structural characterization has been done on the enzyme from organisms other than E. coli (see for example |CITS: |). In E. coli early studies suggested an association between AICAR transformylase and IMP cyclohydrolase |CITS: |. Later studies concluded that AICAR transformylase and IMP cyclohydrolase form a bifunctional enzyme with both activities residing on a single polypeptide |CITS: |. Complementation studies suggested that the N-terminal domain contains the IMP cyclohydrolase activity and the C-terminal domain contains the AICAR transformylase activity |CITS: |. More recently recombinant, N-terminally His6-tagged enzyme from E. coli has been expressed, purified, crystallized, and subjected to preliminary X-ray diffraction analysis |CITS: |. The transformylation reaction is the second of two such reactions in the de novo biosynthesis of purine nucleotides. Like the glycinamide ribonucleotide (GAR) transformylase, AICAR transformylase also utilizes 10-formyl-tetrahydrofolate as the formyl donor. The synthesis of IMP in both E. coli and Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium is under the control of a common regulatory protein, the product of the purR gene |CITS: |. The final step in IMP biosynthesis is the ring closure of 5-formylamino-4-imidazolecarboxamide-ribonucleotide (FAICAR) to form IMP which is the first complete purine nucleotide. Review: |CITS: |

Merged_Functions: The gene encodes the amylomaltase MalQ, an enzyme essential for Escherichia coli maltose and maltodextrin metabolism. MalQ catalyzes transglycosylation/disproportionation reactions in which glycosyl or dextrinyl units are transferred among linear maltodextrins of various lengths. It converts short maltodextrins such as maltose and maltotriose into longer maltodextrins and glucose, thereby providing substrates for the phosphorolytic enzyme MalP and contributing to the production of glucose‑1‑phosphate and glucose‑6‑phosphate for glycolysis. MalQ functions together with MalP and MalZ as a major player in the catabolic degradation of maltodextrins, and its activity is modulated by intracellular glucose levels. {PubMed:26139606}. The b3416 gene (malQ) encodes the enzyme amylomaltase (also called 4‑α‑glucanotransferase). Amylomaltase catalyzes the catabolism of maltose, glycogen and maltodextrins by cleaving these α‑glucans and transferring the non‑reducing end glucose unit of maltose onto a growing dextrin chain, thereby releasing free glucose. This activity contributes to maltose and maltodextrin metabolism in Escherichia coli. In addition, the malQ product can be employed as a reporter protein in gene‑fusion studies because its activity is detectable at very low expression levels and it remains functional even when its extreme N‑ or C‑termini are altered. {PubMed:2845225}. MalA encodes a hydrophobic membrane protein with 12 predicted transmembrane segments that functions as the sole protein required for maltose transport in Bacillus stearothermophilus. When expressed in Escherichia coli, MalA restores growth of mutants defective in maltose transport (malE, malK, or complete malB deletions) by providing a high‑affinity maltose/H⁺ symport activity (Kₘ ≈ 2.5–3.5 µM). Sequence analysis shows similarity to members of the major facilitator superfamily, including LacY, CscB, and the E. coli MalG component of the binding‑protein‑dependent transport system, indicating that MalA operates as a sugar:H⁺ symporter. Although it can complement transport defects, the protein is very poorly expressed in E. coli, resulting in low transport rates. {PubMed:8190087}. The malQ gene encodes the amylomaltase MalQ, an essential enzyme for the metabolism of maltose and linear maltodextrins in Escherichia coli. MalQ catalyzes transglycosylation (disproportionation) reactions in which a non‑reducing dextrinyl fragment is cleaved from a donor maltodextrin and transferred to an acceptor molecule (another maltodextrin or glucose). This results in the interconversion of maltodextrins of varying lengths and the production of free glucose. MalQ works together with the phosphorolytic enzyme MalP to channel maltodextrins into glycolysis via glucose‑1‑phosphate, and with MalZ in the maltose system. The enzyme displays very low hydrolytic activity, favoring retention of the α‑anomeric configuration during transfer. Its activity determines the equilibrium distribution of maltodextrin products, which depends on the initial substrate chain length, and it plays a key role in balancing intracellular glucose levels and supplying substrates for downstream metabolic pathways. {PubMed:26139606}. malQ encodes the enzyme amylomaltase (also called 4‑α‑glucanotransferase), the structural gene of the second position in the malPQ operon of Escherichia coli. Amylomaltase catalyzes the catabolism of maltose, glycogen and maltodextrins by cleaving these substrates to release glucose and by transferring the non‑reducing end glucosyl unit of maltose onto a growing dextrin chain. Thus, malQ provides the enzymatic activity required for maltose‑derived carbohydrate metabolism within the maltose regulon. {PubMed:2845225}. Amylomaltase (MalQ) is a maltodextrin glucanotransferase that catalyzes the conversion of maltose and other maltodextrins into glucose and larger maltodextrins. It plays a central role in maltose metabolism by (i) removing the inducer maltotriose through repolymerization of maltotriose into higher‑order dextrins plus glucose, thereby lowering endogenous mal gene induction, and (ii) in the presence of MalZ, reforming maltotriose from maltose, helping maintain sufficient inducer levels. MalQ activity is strongly feedback‑inhibited by low concentrations of free cytoplasmic glucose; removal of glucose by glucokinase relieves this inhibition, allowing MalQ to remain active. Thus, MalQ both processes maltose/maltodextrins for carbon utilization and modulates the level of the maltose‑system inducer. {PubMed:19028900}. The article states that malQ encodes the enzyme amylomaltase, which is the key enzyme for degrading maltodextrins in Escherichia coli. Cells lacking malQ (malQ mutants) are unable to grow on maltose because they cannot process maltodextrins, and they become sensitive to maltose due to intracellular accumulation of the sugar. Thus, malQ is essential for maltose utilization by providing amylomaltase activity that converts maltodextrins into metabolites that can be further catabolized. {PubMed:9401025}. malQ encodes the enzyme amylomaltase, an obligatory glucanosyl‑transferase that remodels linear maltodextrins. The enzyme catalyzes intramolecular glucosyl transfer reactions, converting any linear maltodextrin into a mixture of shorter maltodextrins and free glucose. This activity generates maltotriose from longer dextrins, providing the inducer for the maltose/maltodextrin regulon, and contributes to the overall metabolism of maltodextrins. Mutants lacking malQ (amylomaltase) cannot grow on maltose but can grow on maltodextrins of four or more glucose units, indicating that amylomaltase is essential for maltose utilization but not strictly required for the use of longer maltodextrins. {PubMed:16321936}. MalQ encodes the enzyme maltodextrin glucanotransferase (also called amylomaltase). It is an obligatory glucanotransferase that cleaves any linear maltodextrin, releasing the reducing‑end glucose (or a short dextrin) and transferring the non‑reducing dextrinyl moiety onto glucose or another maltodextrin. Consequently, MalQ can both degrade and synthesize maltotriose, continuously reshuffling maltodextrins (including maltose) into a mixture of longer maltodextrins and glucose while keeping the total number of glycosidic linkages constant. This activity prevents accumulation of the inducer maltotriose; in malQ‑deficient strains maltotriose builds up, leading to constitutive (endogenous) activation of the maltose regulon via MalT. Thus, MalQ functions to recycle maltodextrins derived from glycogen degradation, ensuring balanced maltodextrin metabolism and low basal induction of the maltose/maltodextrin system. {PubMed:16321937}. In Escherichia coli, malQ encodes the cytosolic amylomaltase (also called disproportionating enzyme) that catalyzes the transfer of maltosyl and longer dextrinyl residues among glucose, maltose, and short maltodextrins (typically G3‑G7). This reaction converts maltose and small maltodextrins into free glucose and elongates other glucan chains, thereby enabling the bacterium to metabolize maltose and maltodextrins as carbon sources. MalQ activity is essential for growth on maltose; malQ‑deficient strains cannot grow on maltose and accumulate excess maltose. The enzyme works in concert with maltodextrin phosphorylase (MalP) in the cytoplasmic maltose/maltodextrin metabolic pathway. {PubMed:16980562}. The malQ gene encodes the enzyme amylomaltase (also called 4‑α‑glucanotransferase). In both Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, amylomaltase is a component of the maltose regulon and is required for growth on maltose. It catalyzes the intramolecular transfer of α‑1,4‑linked glucose residues, remodeling maltodextrins and contributing to their utilization. The article demonstrates that malQ is part of the malPQ operon, that its expression is necessary for the Mal⁺ phenotype (growth on maltose), and that the amylomaltase protein produced from malQ has a molecular weight of ~75 kDa. The gene’s promoter and coding region are conserved enough to allow functional interchangeability between the two species. {PubMed:2946664}. The article identifies malQ as a metabolic gene encoding an amylomaltase (also called maltodextrin glucosyltransferase) that participates in intracellular maltose metabolism, i.e., the enzymatic processing of maltose after it has been transported into the cell. The cloned Bacillus DNA fragment did not complement a malQ deficiency, indicating that malQ’s role is distinct from the maltose transport function provided by the malA gene. {PubMed:8190087}. The article indicates that malQ encodes the enzyme amylomaltase, a protein required for maltose metabolism. Expression of malQ (amylomaltase synthesis) is controlled by the malPQ promoter; deletions affecting this promoter drastically reduce amylomaltase levels, demonstrating its role as the functional product of the malQ gene. {PubMed:6339728}.

MetaCyc_Comment: Amylomaltase (MalQ) was first described as a maltose-inducible enzyme that catalyzes a reversible transglycosidase reaction |CITS: |. The enzyme belongs to the glycoside hydrolase family GH77 of 4-α-glucanotransferases |CITS: | that catalyzes transglycosylation of maltose and maltodextrins. MalQ does not have maltase activity, i.e. it does not hydrolyze maltose to form two molecules of glucose |CITS: |. The specificity of MalQ for donor and acceptor molecules of the transglycosylation reaction has been difficult to ascertain. It was initially reported that maltose serves as an acceptor substrate of the enzyme |CITS: |. Further experiments using more highly purified maltose suggested that maltose is a poor acceptor |CITS: |. Later, it was demonstrated that the enzyme can utilize purified 14C-maltose to produce labeled maltodextrins and glucose |CITS: |. Maltotetraose appears to be the most efficient substrate |CITS: |. Kinetic data of the utilization of maltose and higher oligomers alone or with the addition of glucose have been measured |CITS: |. MalQ transfers glycosyl chains of 1-9 glucosyl units from the nonreducing end of donor molecules onto the nonreducing end of maltodextrin acceptors, including maltose and glucose |CITS: |. Glucose feedback-inhibits the reaction at concentrations above 0.1 mM |CITS: |. Studies using malP, malQ and glgA deletion mutants demonstrated that MalQ can catalyze glycogen formation from maltodextrins. In vitro, MalQ is able to produce glycogen from maltose when the liberated glucose was removed enzymatically and the glycogen branching enzyme GlgB was added |CITS: |. Conversely, a Delta;malQ mutant grown on glucose shows increased accumulation of glycogen; in vitro, MalQ enhances glycogen breakdown when added to a reaction mixture with GlgX and GlgP |CITS: |. Crystal structures of apo-MalQ, MalQ in complex with maltose, and MalQ in complex with the inhibitory transition state analog acarviosine-glucose-acarbose have been solved at 2.80, 2.10 and 2.10 Å resolution, respectively. Each structure revealed a distinct state of the enzyme, suggesting that major conformational changes occur during catalysis. Assay data showed that the equilibrium concentration of glucose and maltodextrins produced by MalQ is dependent on the initial average number of glycosidic bonds per molecule of substrate, with less glucose formed from longer substrates |CITS: |. malQ mutants are unable to utilize maltose as the sole source of carbon |CITS: |. A malQ mutant in a malB+ background secretes acetylmaltose and acetylated maltodextrins |CITS: |. Review: |CITS: |

The speC gene encodes ornithine decarboxylase (ODCase), the enzyme that catalyzes the decarboxylation of L‑ornithine to produce putrescine, a key step in the biosynthetic pathway leading to polyamines such as spermidine. In Escherichia coli the speC locus maps at 63.4 minutes on the chromosome. Cloning of speC into plasmid pODC1 resulted in a 13‑fold increase in ODCase activity and restored ODCase activity in a ΔspeC strain, confirming that speC provides the structural gene for the 80 kDa ODCase protein. {PubMed:6392022}. The speC gene encodes the biosynthetic ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) enzyme in Escherichia coli. This enzyme catalyzes the decarboxylation of L‑ornithine to produce putrescine, a key polyamine required for normal replication, transcription and translation. speC‑derived ODC is constitutively expressed under neutral pH conditions, is negatively regulated at the transcriptional level by cAMP‑CRP, and its activity is feedback‑inhibited by putrescine. The encoded protein is a ~79.5 kDa, 711‑amino‑acid pyridoxal‑phosphate‑dependent decarboxylase that forms dimers of approximately 80 kDa. {PubMed:7828866}. The speC gene encodes the structural protein of streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxin C (SPE C), a 23.8 kDa secreted toxin produced by Streptococcus pyogenes. SPE C functions as a superantigen: it is pyrogenic (induces fever), mitogenic for lymphocytes (stimulates rabbit splenocyte proliferation), and enhances host susceptibility to lethal endotoxin shock. The gene product is biologically active when expressed in Escherichia coli, retaining the same molecular weight, immunological reactivity, and biological activities as the native streptococcal toxin. {PubMed:2836707}. The speC gene encodes the biosynthetic ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) isoenzyme in Escherichia coli. This enzyme catalyzes the decarboxylation of L‑ornithine to produce putrescine, a polyamine that can be further converted to spermidine. In the context of the study, speC (together with speF) was deleted to block the conversion of ornithine to putrescine, thereby preventing the loss of the agmatine precursor and facilitating agmatine accumulation. {PubMed:32624951}. SpeC encodes an ornithine decarboxylase that catalyzes the conversion of ornithine to putrescine, providing one of the two biosynthetic routes for putrescine production in Escherichia coli. Deletion of speC (together with speAB) creates a polyamine‑deficient strain, indicating its essential role in intracellular putrescine synthesis. {PubMed:19493013}.

Merged_Functions: The ycaC gene (b0897) encodes a ~23 kDa protein (ycaCgp) that assembles into an octameric enzyme with a hydrolase‑like fold. Structural comparisons place it in a diverse family of bacterial hydrolases related to N‑carbamoylsarcosine amidohydrolase, EntB and PncA enzymes, and it contains a conserved catalytic cysteine (Cys118) and a non‑proline cis peptide bond in the active‑site cleft. Although its exact biochemical role and natural substrate have not been identified, the protein is described as a hydrolase of unknown specificity. {PubMed:9782055}. Encodes a ~23 kDa protein (ycaC gene product) that forms an octameric bacterial hydrolase. Structural analysis shows it belongs to a diverse family of hydrolases related to N‑carbamoylsarcosine amidohydrolase (CSHase), EntB, and nicotinamidase (PncA) enzymes. The protein contains a conserved catalytic cysteine (Cys118) and a non‑proline cis peptide bond in the active‑site cleft, suggesting it catalyzes a hydrolytic reaction, although its natural substrate and precise biochemical role remain unknown. {PubMed:9782055}. The ycaC gene encodes a ~23 kDa protein that assembles into an octameric hydrolase. Structural studies reveal it belongs to a diverse family of bacterial hydrolases related to N‑carbamoylsarcosine amidohydrolase (CSHase), EntB and PncA enzymes. The protein contains a conserved catalytic cysteine (Cys118) and a non‑proline cis peptide bond within a solvent‑accessible cleft at the interface of two subunits, indicating it catalyzes a hydrolytic reaction. However, the natural substrate and precise biochemical role of the enzyme remain unknown. {PubMed:9782055}. The article identifies ycaC as encoding an isochorismatase hydrolase (YcaC). Proteomic analysis showed that YcaC levels were markedly reduced (to ~35% of wild‑type) in the membrane fraction of an apidaecin 1b‑resistant E. coli strain, while its cytosolic level remained unchanged. Structural similarity suggests that YcaC possesses hydrolase activity, although it has not been studied extensively. Functional assays demonstrated that a ΔycaC knockout mutant of E. coli BW25113 exhibited an eight‑fold increase in resistance to apidaecin 1b (and to the related peptide Api88), indicating that YcaC contributes to the susceptibility of E. coli to these proline‑rich antimicrobial peptides. The authors speculate that YcaC may interact with membrane components or form a pore, potentially influencing peptide uptake, but the exact mechanism remains unresolved. {PubMed:27405093}. The article states that YcaC (Escherichia coli) is a protein of unknown physiological function, described as a hydrolase of unknown specificity. Structural analysis shows that YcaC shares a fold with the pyrazinamidase PH999 and N‑carbamoylsarcosine amidohydrolase (CSHase), possessing a conserved catalytic triad (C118, R84, D19) and a characteristic cis‑peptide bond, which are typical of active sites in related hydrolases. Thus, while its exact biological role is not defined, YcaC is inferred to be a catalytic hydrolase with a putative active site similar to that of pyrazinamidases. {PubMed:11714269}.
Curated_Functions: Catalyzes a hydrolytic reaction of unknown substrate specificity, consistent with a conserved catalytic cysteine and cis‑peptide bond characteristic of bacterial hydrolases. {PubMed:9782055, PubMed:11714269}. Contributes to susceptibility of Escherichia coli to the proline‑rich antimicrobial peptides apidaecin 1b and Api88, as loss of YcaC markedly increases resistance. {PubMed:27405093}.

Merged_Functions: The article identifies the phmA locus as the nmpC gene, which encodes NmpC, an outer‑membrane protein that functions as a porin. NmpC shares about 58 % identity with other E. coli porins (OmpF, OmpC, PhoE) and can form a channel in the outer membrane, especially when the major porins OmpF and OmpC are absent. The protein is produced from a gene located within the defective lambdoid prophage qsr′ and its expression is modulated by external pH, catabolite repression, and the CRP‑cAMP complex, but its primary biochemical role is that of a non‑specific outer‑membrane porin. {PubMed:8057841}. phmA is one of six pH‑modulated (phm) loci identified in Escherichia coli. It encodes a non‑essential protein located in the cell envelope whose transcription is strongly up‑regulated (up to ~20‑fold) when cells are grown at neutral to alkaline external pH (7.0–8.5) and repressed at acidic pH (≈5.0). Its expression is also influenced by internal pH changes, osmolarity (showing a two‑fold increase in high‑osmolarity medium), and anaerobic growth (induced under anaerobiosis). Regulation is largely independent of the EnvZ/OmpR two‑component system, although a minor effect of EnvZ on phmA expression was observed. The gene appears to participate in the adaptive response of E. coli to external pH, possibly as part of a transport‑related cell‑envelope system, although its precise biochemical role is not defined in the article. {PubMed:1833617}. NmpC encodes an outer‑membrane protein that functions as a porin.  The protein forms a channel in the outer membrane and can substitute for the major porins OmpF and OmpC when they are absent.  Its expression is controlled by a promoter that responds to external pH (repressed at acidic pH), catabolite repression via the CRP‑cAMP complex, osmolarity, and benzoate, and the gene resides within the defective lambdoid prophage qsr'. {PubMed:8057841}. The nmpC gene encodes the outer membrane porin NmpC, a protein that forms pores in the outer membrane of Escherichia coli and permits selective passage of hydrophilic solutes. In the heat‑resistant strain E. coli AW1.7, NmpC is expressed (absent in the heat‑sensitive strain GGG10 due to an IS5 insertion) and its presence in the outer membrane was confirmed by SDS‑PAGE and LC‑MS/MS. Overexpression of nmpC in the sensitive strain markedly increased survival during lethal heat treatment (60 °C), indicating that NmpC contributes to heat resistance, likely by enhancing solute transport and supporting intracellular osmolyte balance under stress conditions. {PubMed:21398480}. The article describes nmpC as a silent outer‑membrane porin gene located in the defective qsr' prophage of *Escherichia coli* K‑12. It is transcribed at a level comparable to the phage lc gene, but the resulting mRNA is rapidly degraded (due to an IS5 insertion in its 3′ end), preventing accumulation of a stable mRNA pool and consequently limiting production of the NmpC porin protein. Thus, nmpC encodes a porin that is normally not expressed as a functional protein under the conditions examined. {PubMed:3032909}. Encodes an outer‑membrane porin (NmpC) that contributes to heat resistance in Escherichia coli. The presence of NmpC increases survival of cells exposed to elevated temperatures (e.g., 60 °C), enhancing viability by 50‑ to 1,000‑fold. By forming a channel in the outer membrane, NmpC influences membrane permeability and helps the bacterium cope with heat‑induced stress, thereby playing a protective role during thermal treatments. {PubMed:27857712}.

Enhances survival during lethal heat treatment (e.g., 60 °C) and protects cells from thermal stress, likely by facilitating solute transport and osmolyte balance. {PubMed:21398480, PubMed:27857712}. Is encoded within the defective lambdoid prophage qsr′ and normally remains silent because its mRNA is rapidly degraded due to an IS5 insertion. {PubMed:3032909}.

Merged_Functions: FliO encodes a membrane‑bound component of the Helicobacter pylori flagellar protein export apparatus. It is required for normal flagellar biogenesis and wild‑type levels of bacterial motility. Deletion of fliO markedly reduces transcription of RpoN‑dependent (e.g., flaB, flgE) and FliA‑dependent (flaA) flagellar genes, although expression of upstream regulators (flgS, flgR, fliA, RpoN) remains unchanged. FliO also supports the accumulation of the export apparatus protein FlhA in the membrane, suggesting a role in the assembly or stability of other export components. The transmembrane region of FliO is the critical determinant for these functions, while its large N‑terminal periplasmic domain and C‑terminal cytoplasmic domain are individually dispensable for flagellar gene regulation and assembly. {PubMed:24837287}. FliO is a conserved component of the flagellar type‑III secretion system. It is one of the eight proteins (FliH, FliI, FliO, FliP, FliQ, FliR, FlhA and FlhB) that together form the export apparatus required for flagellar assembly. {PubMed:15817382}. Encodes a component of the flagellum‑specific protein export apparatus (together with fliP, fliQ, fliR, and flhA). It is a class II flagellar gene that is transcribed from a divergent promoter overlapping the flgB promoter and its expression is regulated by the cell‑cycle response regulator CtrA. The protein contributes to the export of flagellar structural components required for assembly of the polar flagellum in Caulobacter crescentus. {PubMed:11133968}. flbD (renamed fliO) is a flagellar gene located in the flaA operon of Escherichia coli. Complementation experiments showed that loss of flbD results in defective motility and chemotaxis, and that plasmids carrying flbD restore wild‑type swimming behavior. Thus, flbD encodes a protein required for normal flagellar function, likely contributing to the membrane‑associated switch complex that controls flagellar rotation. {PubMed:2651416}. FlbD is a transcription factor that functions at the class II level of the Caulobacter crescentus flagellar regulatory hierarchy. It is required for the activation of class III and class IV flagellar genes, thereby enabling expression of later-stage flagellar components such as the outer basal body, hook, and filament. FlbD binds to specific promoter elements (including ftr sequences) upstream of class III operons and can also act as a repressor of class II promoters, exemplified by its inhibition of the fliF class‑II promoter that controls its own transcription. Thus, FlbD serves both as an activator of downstream flagellar genes and as a regulator that modulates earlier‑stage transcription within the flagellar gene cascade. {PubMed:11133968}. FlbD is a transcriptional activator that globally regulates the expression of σ⁵⁴‑dependent class III and class IV flagellar (fla) genes in Caulobacter crescentus. It binds specifically to conserved upstream DNA elements called ftr sequences (located ~100 bp upstream of the transcription start sites) and, through these interactions, stimulates open‑complex formation by the Eσ⁵⁴ RNA polymerase holoenzyme, thereby initiating transcription of downstream flagellar genes such as flbG, flgF, flgI, and fljK. FlbD functions without apparent phosphorylation in vitro, although it can be phosphorylated in vivo and phosphoramidate enhances its activity, suggesting a possible regulatory role for modification. Mutations that disrupt the ftr sites markedly reduce FlbD‑dependent transcription both in vitro and in vivo, indicating that intact ftr elements are essential for full activation. Overall, FlbD acts as a global activator linking cell‑cycle cues to the coordinated synthesis of the polar flagellum. {PubMed:7768824}. flbD is described as the fleQ homolog in Caulobacter crescentus. It functions as a transcriptional regulator involved in flagellar biogenesis and is positively regulated by the master cell‑cycle regulator CtrA. {PubMed:12218009}. Encodes a protein of unknown function; it is a unique flagellar gene in Borrelia burgdorferi that shows homology to an ORF from the same operon of Treponema pallidum, but no specific role or known homologs in other bacteria are described in the article. {PubMed:9168127}. FlbD is a transcription activator protein that works together with the σ⁵⁴ (RpoN) sigma factor to initiate transcription from σ⁵⁴‑dependent promoters. In Caulobacter crescentus it is required for activation of the σ⁵⁴‑dependent fljK promoter (a flagellin gene) and, more broadly, for transcription of the Class III and IV flagellar genes that are expressed later in the cell cycle. The gene flbD is part of the Class II flagellar gene cluster and its product is essential for σ⁵⁴‑dependent transcriptional activation during flagellar biosynthesis. {PubMed:9261176}. The gene b1947 encodes the Escherichia coli deoxyinosine 3'-endonuclease (also known as endonuclease V, nfi, or orf225). This enzyme specifically recognizes DNA containing deoxyinosine, various base mismatches, and insertion/deletion mismatch (IDM) structures such as hairpins, loops, flap, and pseudo‑Y DNA. It cleaves these substrates on the strand that carries the lesion, typically one nucleotide 3' to the mismatch or structural anomaly, and can also perform a weak 5'→3' exonucleolytic activity. By processing IDM and other secondary DNA structures generated during replication—especially on the lagging strand where 5' nicks are present—the enzyme is proposed to initiate a MutS‑independent repair pathway that helps maintain microsatellite stability and overall genome integrity. Its activities are functionally analogous to eukaryotic flap endonucleases (FEN1) and yeast RTH1 nucleases. {PubMed:8940043}. Encodes Escherichia coli Exonuclease IX (ExoIX), a member of the flap endonuclease (FEN) family. ExoIX functions as a DNA‑processing enzyme required for replication and repair; it removes RNA or DNA flaps generated during lagging‑strand synthesis and can perform 5′‑3′ exonucleolytic cleavage of duplex DNA. Unlike most FENs, ExoIX lacks the second catalytic metal‑binding (Cat2) site but retains a functional Cat1 site that binds a pair of Mg²⁺ ions to carry out phosphodiester hydrolysis via a two‑metal‑ion mechanism. A distinctive K⁺‑binding site in the C‑terminal H3TH motif, coordinated mainly by main‑chain carbonyls, is essential for high‑affinity DNA binding, interacting directly with a DNA phosphate backbone. The enzyme’s activity is potassium‑dependent, and loss of either ExoIX or the Pol I FEN domain is lethal, indicating its essential role in maintaining genomic integrity. {PubMed:23821668}. The article identifies JW5316 as the gene encoding FleQ, the principal transcriptional activator governing flagellar biogenesis in Pseudomonas aeruginosa. FleQ functions as the highest‑level regulator in the hierarchical flagellar cascade, activating expression of multiple downstream flagellar genes and operons. Its transcription is driven by a σ⁷⁰‑dependent promoter; the -10 region of this promoter overlaps a Vfr (CRP‑homolog) binding site. Binding of Vfr to this site represses fleQ transcription by sterically hindering σ⁷⁰ binding, thereby down‑regulating flagellar synthesis. Post‑translationally, FleQ activity is also modulated by the antiactivator FleN. Overall, JW5316/FleQ is essential for flagellum assembly, motility, and chemotaxis, and its expression is subject to both transcriptional repression by Vfr and protein‑protein inhibition by FleN. {PubMed:12218009}.

Merged_Functions: The b1708 gene (formerly yvcE, renamed cwlO) encodes a 473‑amino‑acid peptidoglycan hydrolase belonging to the NLPC/P60 (DL‑endopeptidase family II) superfamily. It possesses an N‑terminal signal peptide for secretion and a C‑terminal catalytic domain that functions as a D,L‑endopeptidase, specifically cleaving the bond between D‑glutamic acid and meso‑diaminopimelic acid in the peptide stem of Bacillus subtilis peptidoglycan. The enzyme is expressed as a monocistronic mRNA during the vegetative growth phase, is released into the extracellular medium (appearing as degradation products of the full‑length protein), and exhibits cell wall‑hydrolyzing activity in vitro. Disruption of b1708 does not affect vegetative growth rate, cell morphology, motility, sporulation, or germination, indicating that while it has peptidoglycan‑hydrolytic activity, it is not essential for these processes under the conditions tested. {PubMed:16233686}. The nlpC gene encodes the NlpC/P60 domain of the membrane‑anchored lipoprotein Spr in Escherichia coli.  This domain functions as a cysteine peptidase (γ‑D‑glutamyl‑L‑diaminopropionic acid‑endopeptidase) that hydrolyzes specific peptide bonds in the bacterial peptidoglycan cell wall.  It therefore acts as a cell‑wall hydrolase involved in cell‑wall remodeling during growth, division, or lysis/invasion, and represents a potential target for antibiotic development. {PubMed:18715016}. The nlpC gene encodes the C‑terminal NlpC/P60 domain of the bifunctional cell‑wall hydrolase CwlT. This domain is a papain‑like cysteine peptidase (γ‑D‑Glu‑L‑diaminopimelic acid/L‑lysine endopeptidase) that hydrolyzes the γ‑D‑glutamyl‑DAP (or γ‑D‑Glu‑L‑Lys) linkage in peptidoglycan cross‑links. It contains a conserved catalytic triad (Cys‑His‑His) and a Tyr residue that together form the active site required for cleavage of the peptide bond in the murein tetrapeptide, thereby contributing to cell‑wall degradation during conjugative transposon transfer. {PubMed:24051416}. The article reports that the nlpC gene encodes a hypothetical protein belonging to the NlpC/P60 family. Members of this family possess protease, amidase, or acyl‑transferase activities and are involved in the hydrolysis of cell‑wall peptides and in bacterial cell division. The protein is highly conserved among Corynebacterium pseudotuberculosis and Corynebacterium ulcerans strains, suggesting a fundamental role in cell‑wall metabolism. Additionally, NlpC/P60 proteins have been shown in related bacteria (e.g., Mycobacterium avium paratuberculosis and Mycobacterium tuberculosis) to be antigenic and to participate in growth and cell‑wall formation, indicating that the C. pseudotuberculosis NlpC/P60 protein may also serve as an immunogenic antigen useful for diagnostics or vaccine development. {PubMed:28934943}.

The surface‑localized α‑amylase hydrolyzes starch into smaller sugars, enabling the engineered E. coli strains to directly utilize starch as a carbon source for the production of 1,2‑propanediol and 1,3‑propanediol. {PubMed:32909101}. MetaCyc_Comment: AmyA is a cytoplasmic α-amylase. Amylose, a linear α-glucan, is the most effective substrate in vitro; starch and amylopectin, a lightly branched α-glucan, can serve as good substrates, while the highly branched α-glucan glycogen is a poor substrate. Linear oligomeric α-glucans of six or more glucose moieties are good substrates of AmyA |CITS: |. The physiological role of AmyA is uncertain. Although under experimental conditions glycogen is a poor substrate for the enzyme, it is the most likely natural substrate since it is the only polysaccharide present in appreciable amounts in the cytoplasm. It has been hypothesized that in the absence of exogenous oligosaccharides that could act as primers for glycogen synthesis, the cytoplasmic amylase might provide oligosaccharides through catabolism of existing cellular glycogen, which would then act as the source of primers for the synthesis of more molecules of glycogen |CITS: |. AmyA is one of two α-amylases present in E. coli. The second enzyme, |FRAME: ALPHA-AMYL-PERI-MONOMER "MalS"|, is periplasmic.

Merged_Functions: hsrA encodes a predicted 475‑amino‑acid efflux protein (member of a family of multidrug extrusion proteins). When overexpressed, HsrA does not confer resistance to tested antibiotics but interferes with the conversion of homocysteine (HC) to methionine, likely by exporting a cofactor required for the MetE enzyme. This causes intracellular accumulation of HC, which is subsequently cyclized to homocysteine thiolactone (HCTL). Elevated HCTL acts as a positive effector of the stationary‑phase sigma factor σ⁽ˢ⁾, restoring σ⁽ˢ⁾ levels that are otherwise reduced by overexpression of RspA. Thus, hsrA functions as a high‑copy suppressor of RspA‑mediated σ⁽ˢ⁾ inhibition by modulating HC/HCTL metabolism. {PubMed:10754234}. The yieO gene encodes a protein (renamed HsrA) that belongs to a family of putative efflux pumps.  HsrA is required for the high‑copy suppressor activity that reverses RspA‑mediated inhibition of σ⁽ˢ⁾ accumulation.  Although predicted to have multidrug extrusion activity, overproduction of HsrA does not confer resistance to tested antibiotics.  Instead, excess HsrA interferes with the conversion of homocysteine (HC) to methionine, creating a growth requirement for exogenous methionine or cobalamin.  This effect is thought to arise from extrusion of a cofactor needed by the MetE enzyme, leading to accumulation of HC and its cyclic derivative homocysteine thiolactone (HCTL).  Elevated HCTL acts as a positive effector of σ⁽ˢ⁾ levels, linking HsrA activity to the regulation of the stationary‑phase response. {PubMed:10754234}.

Merged_Functions: PqqL encodes a periplasmic, zinc‑dependent metalloprotease that is up‑regulated under iron‑limiting conditions (Fur‑regulated) and is co‑expressed with the outer‑membrane transporter YddB. It belongs to the M16 family and is structurally analogous to the FusC protease of the ferredoxin uptake system. PqqL functions as the processing protease that cleaves a specific imported protein substrate after it has been translocated into the periplasm by the YddB/TonB‑dependent transporter, thereby facilitating iron acquisition from host‑derived iron‑containing proteins. The enzyme displays narrow peptide‑sequence specificity (preferring F/Y‑F/Y‑V/A motifs) and adopts flexible open and closed conformations characteristic of substrate capture and proteolysis. {PubMed:31613892}. The article identifies pqqL as a gene encoding an inner‑membrane‑associated zinc metallopeptidase that is part of the yddABpqqL operon. Transposon insertions in pqqL caused a significant fitness defect for uropathogenic E. coli during mouse systemic infection, indicating that pqqL contributes to bacterial survival in the spleen. The yddABpqqL locus is highly up‑regulated (>30‑fold) when the bacteria grow in human urine, suggesting a role in adapting to the urinary tract environment. Although the precise biochemical activity is not defined, the authors note that pqqL can complement PQQ‑biosynthetic genes (pqqE and pqqF) in another bacterium, hinting that it may be involved in uptake or processing of pyrrolo‑quinoline quinone (PQQ), a cofactor for certain quinoproteins. Thus, pqqL functions as a putative zinc metallopeptidase that enhances UPEC fitness during systemic infection, possibly through a role in PQQ handling. {PubMed:24339777}.
