Merged_Functions: The fepE gene encodes the Escherichia coli O157:H7 FepE protein, a member of the polysaccharide co‑polymerase class 1a (PCP1a) family. FepE regulates the length of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) O‑antigen (Oag) polysaccharide chain, conferring a very long (VL) modal chain length of greater than 80 O‑antigen repeat units. Specific residues located inside the oligomeric cavity of FepE (notably Leu168 and Asp268) are essential for this length‑determination activity. While FepE forms oligomers (up to a hexamer in vivo), the oligomeric state does not consistently correlate with its functional activity. Overall, FepE’s primary role is to control the modal chain length of the LPS O‑antigen, thereby influencing the bacterial surface polysaccharide structure. {PubMed:23393150}. The article describes fepE (also referred to as wzz_fepE) as a gene that modulates the length of the O‑antigen polysaccharide chain in the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) capsule of Enterobacteria. It was originally named fepE and was thought to be part of the enterobactin (iron‑siderophore) uptake system, but its role in iron transport has not been confirmed. The primary function highlighted in the study is its involvement in O‑antigen chain‑length control, which can affect polysaccharide capsule properties and may influence swarming motility. {PubMed:15941987}. fepE encodes a ~43 kDa membrane-associated protein that is required for ferric enterobactin uptake in Escherichia coli. Mutations disrupting fepE abolish iron transport via enterobactin, indicating that the gene product functions as a component of the inner‑membrane permease complex that works together with FepC (and likely FepD and FepF) to translocate ferric enterobactin across the cytoplasmic membrane after it has been bound by the periplasmic protein FepB. {PubMed:2956250}. In Salmonella typhimurium, the fepE gene encodes a Wzz family protein (designated Wzz_fepE) that regulates the polymerization of O‑antigen (Oag) polysaccharide chains, specifically conferring a very long (VL) modal length of >100 repeat units. This very long Oag chain contributes to the bimodal distribution of LPS O‑antigen lengths together with the other Wzz protein (Wzz_ST), and is essential for maintaining complement resistance and full virulence when combined with the long‑chain Wzz_ST pathway. Mutational inactivation of fepE abolishes the VL Oag population without affecting iron‑enterochelin transport under iron‑limiting conditions. {PubMed:12603743}. According to the article, fepE encodes a protein that is highly homologous to other O‑antigen chain‑length determinant (Cld) proteins. It is thought to be part of the enterobactin iron‑uptake system in Escherichia coli, possibly acting as a component of an enterobactin permease, since transposon insertions in fepE disrupt iron uptake. The authors suggest that, because of its similarity to known Cld proteins, fepE may also function as a chain‑length determinant influencing O‑antigen polymerisation, although how it would affect ferric enterobactin uptake remains unclear. {PubMed:7532605}. FepE encodes a cytoplasmic membrane protein that participates in the enterobactin iron‑transport system. Together with other Fep proteins (FepC, FepB, FepA), it is required for the movement of the ferrienterobactin complex across the bacterial envelope, facilitating uptake of iron bound to the siderophore enterobactin. {PubMed:1846151}. The fepE gene encodes the WzzFepE protein, a polysaccharide co‑polymerase (PCP) that resides in the inner membrane of Gram‑negative bacteria and functions as an O‑antigen chain‑length regulator.  WzzFepE forms oligomeric assemblies (nonameric in the periplasmic domain) that interact with the O‑antigen polymerization machinery (Wzy polymerase) to impose a specific modal length distribution on the lipopolysaccharide O‑antigen polysaccharide.  Mutations or deletions in the loop L4 region of WzzFepE dramatically alter its ability to produce very long O‑antigen polymers, demonstrating that the protein’s surface‑exposed residues are critical for determining the final length of the O‑antigen chains. {PubMed:22437828}. Encodes a member of the polysaccharide co‑polymerase (Wzz) family that forms periplasmic oligomers and contributes to the regulation of lipopolysaccharide O‑antigen chain length in Gram‑negative bacteria. The crystal structure of FepE shows it adopts an α‑helical barrel (α‑helix 8) that participates in inter‑monomer interactions, supporting its role as a scaffold that influences the preferred length of the O‑antigen side chain. {PubMed:22069314}. Encodes the enzyme L‑aspartate oxidase (NadB), which catalyzes the first step of the de novo NAD biosynthetic pathway in Escherichia coli by oxidizing L‑aspartate to iminoaspartate (which is further converted to quinolinate). This activity provides the cell with the ability to synthesize NAD and NADP from aspartate; loss of NadB function (e.g., the Ala28Val mutation described) results in nicotinamide/quinolinate auxotrophy. {PubMed:22174382}.
Curated_Functions: Controls the modal length of the lipopolysaccharide O‑antigen polysaccharide, generating very long chains (>80–100 repeat units). {PubMed:23393150, PubMed:15941987, PubMed:12603743, PubMed:22437828, PubMed:22069314}. Forms periplasmic oligomeric assemblies (up to nonameric) and interacts with the O‑antigen polymerase Wzy to impose the specific chain‑length distribution. {PubMed:23393150, PubMed:22437828, PubMed:22069314}. Requires specific periplasmic residues (e.g., Leu168, Asp268, loop L4) for length‑determination activity. {PubMed:23393150, PubMed:22437828}. Contributes to complement resistance and full virulence by providing the very‑long O‑antigen population together with other Wzz proteins. {PubMed:12603743}. Acts as a component of the inner‑membrane ferric enterobactin permease complex (with FepC/D/F) required for uptake of iron bound to enterobactin. {PubMed:2956250, PubMed:1846151, PubMed:7532605, PubMed:15941987}. Modulates polysaccharide capsule properties and swarming motility through O‑antigen chain‑length control. {PubMed:15941987}. Catalyzes oxidation of L‑aspartate to iminoaspartate, the first step of de novo NAD biosynthesis; loss leads to nicotinamide/quinolinate auxotrophy. {PubMed:22174382}.

Merged_Functions: OmpC is an outer‑membrane porin protein of Escherichia coli that forms channels for passive diffusion of small molecules across the outer membrane. In the context of this study, OmpC functions as a primary receptor for bacteriophage Bp7: it binds reversibly to the phage’s receptor‑binding protein (gp38) during the initial adsorption step. Deletion of ompC reduces Bp7 adsorption by ~50 % and, together with lamB deletion, abolishes infection, demonstrating that OmpC is essential for efficient phage attachment and entry. {PubMed:32238583}. The ompC gene encodes a major outer membrane protein (a porin) in Escherichia coli. Its expression is controlled by the osmolarity‑responsive regulatory system consisting of the ompR and envZ genes. The OmpR protein activates transcription of ompC by binding to an upstream regulatory region located ~60 bp upstream of the -35 promoter element, thereby enhancing production of the OmpC porin under appropriate environmental conditions. {PubMed:3531187}. OmpC encodes a 36 kDa outer membrane porin that forms channels for the transport of small hydrophilic molecules, notably the amino acids arginine and lysine and their decarboxylated products. The study shows that deletion of ompC (alone or together with ompF) diminishes Escherichia coli’s acidic resistance, particularly the arginine‑dependent (AR3) and lysine‑dependent (AR4) acid‑resistance systems, by reducing the expression and activity of the corresponding decarboxylases (adiA and cadB). Complementation with an ompC‑containing plasmid restores acid survival, indicating that OmpC is essential for importing these amino acids (and possibly exporting their decarboxylated amines) across the outer membrane, thereby supporting cytoplasmic pH homeostasis under extreme acidic conditions. {PubMed:21372380}. Encodes the major outer membrane matrix porin OmpC, a passive diffusion pore that permits uptake of nutrients such as sugars and amino acids. Expression of ompC is induced under high‑osmolarity conditions and is regulated by the ompB operon. The OmpC protein also functions as the receptor for bacteriophage TuIb. {PubMed:6297988}.
Curated_Functions: Forms passive diffusion channels for small hydrophilic molecules, allowing uptake of nutrients such as sugars, amino acids, arginine and lysine across the outer membrane. {PubMed:32238583, PubMed:6297988}. Acts as a primary receptor for bacteriophages Bp7 and TuIb, binding their receptor‑binding proteins during adsorption and facilitating efficient phage attachment and entry. {PubMed:32238583, PubMed:6297988}. Is transcriptionally activated by the EnvZ/OmpR two‑component system, which binds an upstream regulatory region, and its expression is induced under high‑osmolarity conditions and controlled by the ompB operon. {PubMed:3531187, PubMed:6297988}. Contributes to acid resistance by importing arginine and lysine (and possibly exporting their decarboxylated amines), thereby supporting cytoplasmic pH homeostasis under extreme acidic conditions. {PubMed:21372380}.

Merged_Functions: The b4566 gene (yhjX) encodes a putative major facilitator superfamily transporter that is strongly up‑regulated during the first exposure of Escherichia coli to sub‑inhibitory concentrations of gentamicin. Its expression is controlled by the YpdA/YpdB two‑component system and is induced by extracellular pyruvate, although the protein does not act as a pyruvate efflux pump. Deletion of b4566 improves bacterial growth in medium containing sub‑MIC gentamicin and abolishes the adaptive resistance normally observed after a second gentamicin exposure, indicating that b4566 mediates the adaptive resistance response. The protein appears to be involved in regulating growth and metabolism under stress conditions, possibly by influencing the decrease of extracellular pyruvate after a sharp increase, rather than directly transporting pyruvate. {PubMed:31191496}. yjhX encodes an 85‑amino‑acid toxin (renamed TopAI) that is the toxic component of a newly identified yjhX‑yjhQ toxin‑antitoxin operon in Escherichia coli. Upon expression, YjhX causes rapid growth arrest and cell death by specifically inhibiting DNA topoisomerase I (TopA). YjhX binds to the N‑terminal domain of TopA (TopA67) and, in the presence of DNA, forms a stable TopA‑DNA‑YjhX complex that blocks the nicking/relaxation activity of TopA without directly binding DNA or RNA. This inhibition leads to accumulation of hyper‑negatively supercoiled plasmid DNA, cessation of DNA replication and RNA synthesis, while protein synthesis is only modestly affected. The cognate antitoxin YjhQ (181 aa) neutralizes YjhX toxicity by forming a stable TA complex. Thus, yjhX functions as an endogenous, specific inhibitor of topoisomerase I, acting as the toxin component of a type II TA system. {PubMed:26553797}. YhjX encodes a putative Major Facilitator Superfamily transporter that is highly up‑regulated during the first exposure of Escherichia coli to a sub‑inhibitory concentration of gentamicin. It is the sole target of the YpdA/YpdB two‑component system (normally induced by pyruvate), although its induction by gentamicin occurs without a change in ypdB expression. Deletion of yhjX improves bacterial growth in medium containing ½ MIC gentamicin and eliminates the adaptive‑resistance phenotype observed after a second gentamicin exposure, while complementation restores this phenotype. Extracellular pyruvate measurements show that YhjX does not function as a pyruvate efflux pump; rather, it is associated with the rapid decrease of extracellular pyruvate following a sharp increase. Consequently, YhjX acts as a stress‑responsive transporter that regulates growth and metabolism of E. coli under nutrient‑limited or energy‑scarce conditions and mediates adaptive resistance to gentamicin. {PubMed:31191496}. YhjX (locus tag JW5968) encodes a putative major‑facilitator‑superfamily transporter that is the sole transcriptional target of the YpdA/YpdB two‑component system. In Escherichia coli it is dramatically up‑regulated during the first exposure to a sub‑inhibitory concentration of gentamicin and down‑regulated on re‑exposure. Deletion of JW5968 improves bacterial growth in medium containing ½ MIC gentamicin but abolishes the adaptive‑resistance phenotype seen after a pretreatment, indicating that the protein mediates adaptive resistance to gentamicin. The gene does not alter the minimum inhibitory concentrations of gentamicin or other tested antibiotics. Although annotated as a pyruvate transporter, experimental data show that JW5968 does not act as a pyruvate efflux pump; rather, it is associated with the rapid decrease of extracellular pyruvate after a transient increase, suggesting a role in regulating metabolism under nutrient‑limited or stress conditions. Overall, JW5968 functions as a stress‑responsive transporter that modulates growth and adaptive resistance to gentamicin in E. coli. {PubMed:31191496}.

Forms a type II toxin‑antitoxin system with antitoxin YjhQ, which neutralizes YjhX toxicity via a stable TA complex. {PubMed:26553797}.

Merged_Functions: The article reports that yibT encodes a membrane‑associated protein whose reduced expression or deletion enhances n‑butanol tolerance in Escherichia coli. Merged_Functions: RodZ (yfgA) encodes an inner‑membrane protein that regulates the rod‑shaped morphology of E. coli.  In this study it was identified as an essential gene for cell‑to‑cell plasmid transfer, being required for the acceptance of extracellular plasmid DNA by recipient cells.  The rodZ mutant could still be transformed by standard artificial methods (CaCl₂, PEG, electroporation), indicating that RodZ is not needed for general plasmid uptake or maintenance, but is specifically required for the natural‑like, cell‑to‑cell transfer process.  RodZ possesses a cytoplasmic helix‑turn‑helix DNA‑binding motif and may participate in Ca²⁺‑mediated DNA uptake across the cell envelope, suggesting a dual role in DNA passage and possibly extracellular DNA secretion. {PubMed:22497891}. RodZ (encoded by yfgA) is a conserved, moderately abundant bitopic membrane protein that is an essential component of the MreB actin cytoskeleton in Escherichia coli. It is required for the proper spiral‑like assembly of MreB filaments underneath the cytoplasmic membrane, thereby maintaining the characteristic rod shape of the cell. RodZ directly interacts with MreB (and more weakly with MreC) as shown by bacterial two‑hybrid assays, and colocalizes with MreB in a helical pattern. The basic juxta‑membrane (JM) domain of RodZ is strictly required for rod‑shape maintenance, while the transmembrane segment anchors the protein and the N‑terminal helix‑turn‑helix (HTH) domain and the C‑terminal periplasmic domain contribute to its association with the cytoskeleton and proper localization. Loss of RodZ causes misassembly of MreB into large, non‑spiral clusters, leading to spherical or irregular cell shapes, division defects, and a severe growth defect in minimal medium; these phenotypes can be partially suppressed by overproduction of FtsZ or by balancing the cellular MreB‑to‑RodZ ratio. {PubMed:19078962}. The article reports that yfgA encodes a protein of previously unknown function that is important for the integrity of the outer membrane in Escherichia coli. Deletion of yfgA reduces the levels of major outer‑membrane proteins (OmpA, OmpC, OmpF, LamB), indicating a role in maintaining membrane protein composition. Genetically, yfgA interacts with the periplasmic chaperone gene surA: a ΔyfgA ΔsurA double mutant is synthetically lethal, and ΔyfgA shows synthetic lethality with other uncharacterized genes (yciB, yciM, yhcB). Mutants lacking yfgA are also more sensitive to membrane‑perturbing agents such as SDS and the antibiotic novobiocin. Together, these data suggest that YfgA is required for proper outer‑membrane biogenesis and stability. {PubMed:18180259}. The article describes yfgA (also called rodZ) as an inner‑membrane protein that plays a key role in maintaining cell‑wall integrity and rod‑shaped morphology in Escherichia coli. Deletion of yfgA causes a severe reduction (~80%) in peptidoglycan synthesis, leading to spherical, osmotically fragile cells that lyse under hypo‑osmotic conditions. The protein contains a helix‑turn‑helix (HTH) domain that is essential for its activity; loss of the HTH motif abolishes complementation of the mutant phenotypes. RodZ interacts with the actin‑like protein MreB and is thought to help coordinate lateral peptidoglycan synthesis with cell growth. Although the ΔrodZ mutant shows markedly reduced expression of most flagellar class‑2 and class‑3 genes (while the master regulator flhDC is unaffected), the cells still assemble flagella, indicating that RodZ influences motility indirectly, likely through cell‑wall stress signalling. yfgA is co‑transcribed with the downstream essential gene ispG, and its absence alters ispG expression, suggesting a functional link to isoprenoid metabolism that supports peptidoglycan biosynthesis. Importantly, RodZ is not absolutely required for rod shape, as spontaneous pseudorevertants can regain near‑rod morphology and higher peptidoglycan levels, implying that other mechanisms can partially compensate for its loss. {PubMed:20528937}. The gene encodes RodZ, an inner‑membrane protein that plays a key role in the synthesis and coordination of peptidoglycan during cell‑wall growth. It interacts with the bacterial actin homolog MreB, helping to position the cell‑wall synthetic machinery and thereby influencing rod‑shaped morphology.  Deletion of the gene leads to a severe reduction (~80 %) in peptidoglycan content, hypersensitivity to hypo‑osmotic stress, spherical cell shape, and loss of motility despite the presence of flagella, indicating that RodZ is also important for proper expression of many flagellar genes (except the master regulator flhDC).  RodZ and the downstream essential gene ispG are co‑transcribed as an operon, and loss of RodZ alters ispG expression, suggesting a functional link between RodZ and isoprenoid‑dependent steps of peptidoglycan biosynthesis.  Although not absolutely required for rod shape—pseudorevertants can regain a rod‑like morphology—RodZ is essential for optimal cell‑wall synthesis, normal cell shape, and full motility in *E. coli*. {PubMed:20528937}.

Merged_Functions: YebA is one of four Escherichia coli LytM‑domain proteins (EnvC, NlpD, YgeR, YebA).  It is predicted to be a bitopic inner‑membrane protein (N‑in/C‑out) that contains a C‑terminal LytM domain, suggesting it functions as a metallo‑endopeptidase that can act on peptidoglycan.  In the experiments reported, loss of YebA alone caused no obvious division defect, but when combined with deletions of the major LytM factors (especially EnvC and NlpD) it modestly worsened the severe cell‑chain phenotype, indicating that YebA contributes a minor, supportive role to septal peptidoglycan splitting and daughter‑cell separation.  Fluorescent YebA‑mCherry fusions showed a largely uniform peripheral localization with some enrichment at the cell poles and did not display strong recruitment to the division site, consistent with its secondary role in cell division.  Overall, YebA is a putative peptidoglycan‑hydrolyzing LytM protein that plays a minor, auxiliary role in promoting proper cell separation during cytokinesis. {PubMed:19525345}. YebA encodes a DD‑endopeptidase (a member of the MEROPS M23/LytM metallopeptidase family) that hydrolyzes the peptide cross‑links of the peptidoglycan sacculus in Escherichia coli. Together with the other two newly identified endopeptidases Spr and YdhO, YebA is collectively essential for cell‑wall growth: it cleaves existing DD‑cross‑links, creating space that allows the incorporation of newly synthesized peptidoglycan material during elongation. Depletion or catalytic inactivation of YebA (along with Spr and YdhO) blocks new PG incorporation, leading to growth arrest and cell lysis. In vitro, purified YebA shows DD‑endopeptidase activity against soluble cross‑linked muropeptides and can also hydrolyse DD‑cross‑links in intact sacculi, although with weaker activity compared with soluble substrates. {PubMed:23066944}. YebA encodes a LytM family metalloprotease that possesses peptidoglycan‑cleaving activity. In NTHI it localizes primarily to the outer‑membrane fraction (periplasmic/extracytoplasmic) and contributes to proper cell division by facilitating peptidoglycan remodeling required for cell separation. Loss of yebA results in elongated, bent cells with defective septum formation, increased bacterial clumping, and excessive release of outer‑membrane vesicles, indicating a role in maintaining membrane stability. Thus, YebA functions as a peptidoglycan‑hydrolyzing enzyme essential for normal cell morphology, division, and outer‑membrane integrity. {PubMed:25714719}. Predicted to encode a membrane protein that is homologous to eukaryotic cyclic nucleotide‑gated (CNG) and cGMP‑gated channel proteins. The product is expected to contain transmembrane‑spanning helices, suggesting a role in ion or small‑molecule transport across the membrane. {PubMed:8969499}. YebA is a lysostaphin (M23) family metallo‑endopeptidase that cleaves the D‑alanine–meso‑diaminopimelic acid (D‑Ala‑mDAP) peptide cross‑links in Escherichia coli peptidoglycan. It functions as a DD‑endopeptidase (space‑maker) required for breaking existing cross‑links to permit insertion of new glycan strands during peptidoglycan synthesis. YebA, together with Spr and YdhO, is redundantly essential for normal growth and viability; loss of all three enzymes prevents new murein incorporation and causes rapid cell lysis. Its activity depends on a divalent metal ion, with Zn²⁺ providing optimal catalysis. {PubMed:23062283}.

Merged_Functions: The yeaA gene encodes the protein MsrB, a methionine sulfoxide reductase that catalyzes the reduction of methionine sulfoxide (MetSO) back to methionine. MsrB acts on free MetSO as well as on MetSO residues within oxidized proteins, such as calmodulin, thereby repairing oxidative damage to proteins. In Escherichia coli, MsrB contributes to cellular resistance against cadmium-induced oxidative stress. Thus, yeaA/MSrB functions as a repair enzyme that restores the activity of oxidatively damaged proteins and enhances metal stress resistance. {PubMed:11677230}. Merged_Functions: Encodes a small nitroreductase that forms a homodimeric protein binding flavin mononucleotide (FMN) at the dimer interface. As a member of the nitroreductase family, YdjA catalyzes the reduction of hazardous nitroaromatic compounds (e.g., nitrotoluenes, nitrofurans, nitroimidazoles) by transferring electrons from NAD(P)H to the substrate via the FMN cofactor. The absence of two internal helices creates a wider, more flexible active site, giving YdjA specificity for larger substrates and suggesting potential applications in bioremediation and pro‑drug activation. {PubMed:18241886}. The ydjA gene encodes a small (fewer than 190 amino acids) putative nitroreductase that belongs to the nitroreductase family. It is expected to catalyze the reduction of nitroaromatic compounds, transferring reducing equivalents from NADH, NADPH or other nicotinamides to the substrate via a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) cofactor. {PubMed:18084095}. YdjA is an Escherichia coli homodimeric, FMN‑binding oxidoreductase that shares sequence similarity with members of the nitroreductase superfamily and has been described in the literature as a “minimal nitroreductase.” In the context of this study, YdjA showed no detectable nitroreductase activity toward a range of nitroaromatic substrates, including the prodrug CB1954, and was therefore used as a negative control for prodrug activation. Separate reports (cited in the article) have implicated YdjA as a key enzyme in biohydrogen production, but its precise biochemical role remains undefined in the present work. {PubMed:24996412}.

Merged_Functions: The article reports that ybjA encodes a protein that is homologous to members of the ATP‑binding cassette (ABC) transporter family.  The predicted YbjA protein contains a conserved ATP‑binding domain and, like SurB, is expected to be an integral membrane protein with multiple transmembrane‑spanning regions.  ybjA lies immediately upstream of surB and may be co‑transcribed with it, suggesting that YbjA and SurB could function together as subunits of a common transport system.  Physical mapping links ybjA (or surB) to the previously described cydC/cydD locus, whose products are required for the assembly of functional cytochrome d oxidase complexes.  Thus, YbjA is predicted to act as an ABC‑type transporter component that participates in a transport pathway important for cytochrome d oxidase biogenesis and for the ability of starved E. coli cells to resume growth under certain conditions. {PubMed:8276245}. The product of ECOK12F023 (identified in the article as SurB, also known as YbjA or CydC) is an integral membrane protein that belongs to the ATP‑binding cassette (ABC) family of transporters. SurB contains multiple transmembrane‑spanning regions and a cytoplasmic ATP‑binding domain, indicating it functions as a membrane‑associated transporter. Genetic and physiological analyses showed that SurB is not required for cell viability during stationary phase, but is essential for starved E. coli cells to re‑initiate aerobic growth under restrictive conditions (high temperature). Mutants lacking SurB can sense nutrients and initiate early RNA and protein synthesis but arrest before the first cell division, indicating a role in the regulatory pathway that controls exit from stationary phase. In addition, loss of SurB results in the absence of functional cytochrome d oxidase, suggesting that SurB (or its operon partner YbjA) is also required for the assembly or activity of this terminal oxidase complex. Thus, ECOK12F023 encodes an ABC‑type membrane transporter that is required for proper outgrowth from stationary phase and for the formation of functional cytochrome d oxidase, with likely additional regulatory functions in growth resumption. {PubMed:8276245}.

Merged_Functions: YbiB is the defining member of the novel TrpD2 family of prokaryotic proteins. It forms a homodimer that presents two positively charged DNA‑binding grooves, but due to negative cooperativity only one groove is occupied in vitro. YbiB binds single‑stranded and double‑stranded DNA (and also RNA) with high affinity (KD ≈ 10–100 nM) without detectable sequence specificity, and multiple YbiB dimers can bind cooperatively to longer DNA molecules. The protein lacks detectable anthranilate phosphoribosyltransferase or nucleoside phosphorylase activity, indicating it functions as a DNA‑binding protein rather than an enzyme. The ybiB gene is organized in an operon with the DNA helicase gene dinG and is under LexA repression; its expression is induced by DNA‑damaging agents, suggesting a role in the LexA‑controlled SOS response in bacteria. {PubMed:26063803}. The ECOK12F022 gene encodes YbiB, the defining member of the novel TrpD2 family of prokaryotic proteins. YbiB adopts a phosphoribosyltransferase‑class III fold but, unlike its enzymatic homologues (TrpD and NP‑II), it does not catalyze phosphoribosyl transfer or nucleoside phosphorylase reactions. Instead, YbiB functions as a high‑affinity, sequence‑non‑specific nucleic‑acid binding protein. It forms a homodimer that presents two positively charged grooves; however, negative cooperativity within the dimer restricts DNA binding to a single groove under in‑vitro conditions. Each groove can accommodate 6–10 nucleotides, and multiple YbiB dimers bind cooperatively to longer DNA molecules. YbiB binds both single‑stranded and double‑stranded DNA, as well as RNA, with dissociation constants in the low nanomolar range (K_D ≈ 10–100 nM). The ybiB gene is organized in an operon with the DNA helicase gene dinG and is under LexA repression; its expression is induced by DNA‑damaging agents, suggesting a role in the bacterial SOS response. In summary, ECOK12F022 encodes a dimeric DNA‑binding protein of the TrpD2 family that likely participates in LexA‑controlled DNA repair or stress‑response pathways. {PubMed:26063803}.

Merged_Functions: The ybhA gene encodes a pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) phosphatase that dephosphorylates PLP to pyridoxal, thereby maintaining PLP homeostasis in Escherichia coli. Overproduction of YbhA lowers intracellular PLP levels and slows growth, while its absence makes cells sensitive to PLP accumulation caused by overexpression of the PL kinases PdxK or PdxY. YbhA thus protects cells from both excess and shortage of PLP, influencing amino‑acid metabolism and growth initiation. {PubMed:29187681}. YbhA is a bifunctional enzyme that exhibits both sugar phosphatase and phosphotransferase activities.  In vitro assays showed that YbhA can dephosphorylate a range of sugar phosphates (e.g., ribose‑5‑phosphate, glucose‑6‑phosphate, glycerol‑3‑phosphate) with relatively similar specific activities, indicating loose substrate specificity for its phosphatase function.  Additionally, YbhA catalyzes a phosphotransfer reaction, converting glycerol and inorganic phosphate into glycerol‑phosphate (a glycerol kinase‑like activity), although this activity is weaker than its phosphatase activity.  The enzyme can use mono‑phosphate compounds as phosphate donors but does not utilize nucleoside di‑ or tri‑phosphates.  Overall, YbhA functions as a broad‑specificity sugar phosphatase/phosphotransferase in Escherichia coli. {PubMed:16889420}.

Merged_Functions: In Escherichia coli, YbdB is a hot‑dog‑fold thioesterase that participates in the biosynthesis of the siderophore enterobactin. It acts as a proofreading enzyme, hydrolyzing aberrant aroyl‑holoEntB thioesters that accumulate as dead‑end intermediates and would otherwise block enterobactin formation. Structurally, YbdB forms a dimer‑of‑dimers and contains a conserved CoA‑binding pocket that recognizes CoA‑based thioesters; catalysis relies on a conserved Glu63* (and supporting residues such as His89*, Gln48, His54) to cleave the thioester bond, thereby clearing the pathway for proper enterobactin production. {PubMed:25010423}. YbdB is a hot‑dog‑fold thioesterase that functions as a proofreading/housekeeping enzyme in the enterobactin siderophore biosynthetic pathway of *Escherichia coli*. It hydrolyzes aberrant aroyl‑holoEntB thioesters (e.g., 2,3‑dihydroxybenzoyl‑holoEntB, 2,4‑dihydroxybenzoyl‑holoEntB, and benzoyl‑holoEntB) that can arise as dead‑end intermediates during enterobactin assembly, thereby preventing accumulation of stalled intermediates. YbdB also shows activity toward benzoyl‑CoA and related aromatic CoA thioesters, but has little activity on aliphatic acyl‑CoA substrates. Its expression is controlled by the iron‑responsive regulator Fur and is induced under iron‑starvation conditions, linking its role to iron acquisition via enterobactin production. {PubMed:24992697}. The ybdB gene encodes the hot‑dog fold protein EntH, a thioesterase that is specifically expressed under iron‑limiting conditions as part of the entCEBA‑ybdB operon. EntH interacts in vivo with the aryl carrier protein (ArCP) domain of EntB, an interaction that requires the phosphopantetheinyl (Ppant) modification of EntB. Through this interaction EntH performs a proofreading role during enterobactin biosynthesis: it hydrolyzes thioester bonds linking incorrectly loaded precursor molecules (e.g., salicylate) to the Ppant arm of EntB, thereby preventing blockage of the non‑ribosomal synthesis pathway. Deletion of ybdB reduces enterobactin production and impairs growth when the pathway is challenged with salicylate, while moderate expression restores normal production. Conversely, overproduction of EntH decreases siderophore output, indicating that precise cellular levels of EntH are required for optimal enterobactin synthesis. {PubMed:17675380}.

Merged_Functions: Encodes a 43‑kDa integral cytoplasmic membrane protein that shows homology to proton‑motive‑force‑dependent membrane transporters, but its specific physiological role has not been determined. {PubMed:11222606}. The ybdA gene encodes the 43 kDa inner‑membrane protein P43, a member of the Major Facilitator Superfamily (MFS) with twelve predicted transmembrane helices. P43 functions as the primary active exporter of the siderophore enterobactin in Escherichia coli. It transports newly synthesized, iron‑free enterobactin from the cytoplasm across the inner membrane into the periplasm and ultimately to the extracellular environment. Loss of ybdA (P43) results in a severe reduction of enterobactin secretion, accumulation of enterobactin breakdown products (DHBS monomer, dimer, trimer) in the medium, and no intracellular buildup of enterobactin, indicating that the protein is essential for normal enterobactin export. Based on this role, the authors propose renaming ybdA to entS (enterobactin secretor). {PubMed:12068807}.

Exports newly synthesized iron‑free enterobactin from the cytoplasm across the inner membrane into the periplasm and extracellular environment. {PubMed:12068807}. Merged_Functions: The ybbA gene encodes a putative esterase that is required for Bacillus subtilis to respond to the siderophore enterobactin. Located downstream of the feuABC operon and regulated by Fur, YbbA shares sequence similarity with E. coli esterases that hydrolyze trilactone siderophores. In B. subtilis, YbbA is necessary for enterobactin‑mediated acceleration of sporulation gene expression (P_sspB‑yfp reporter activation) and for the utilization of iron bound to enterobactin under iron‑starved conditions. Deletion of ybbA abolishes the sporulation‑promoting effect of enterobactin, while complementation restores it, indicating that YbbA likely hydrolyzes enterobactin to release iron, enabling the iron‑dependent sporulation cue. {PubMed:28283524}.

Promotes enterobactin‑mediated acceleration of sporulation gene expression. {PubMed:28283524}. Expression is regulated by the ferric uptake regulator Fur. {PubMed:28283524}.

Merged_Functions: YacA (also known as MesJ) is a universally conserved protein that is essential for growth in Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae and Bacillus subtilis. Bioinformatic and structural analyses suggest that YacA contains an N‑terminal pyrophosphate‑binding domain of the adenine nucleotide α‑hydrolase fold, indicating ATP‑dependent pyrophosphate hydrolysis activity. The authors propose that YacA functions as a novel phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) synthase, catalyzing the synthesis of PRPP from ATP and ribose‑phosphate. PRPP is a key precursor for purine phosphoribosyltransferases (e.g., HprT, Xpt) in the purine salvage pathway, linking YacA to purine nucleotide biosynthesis. {PubMed:15044829}.
Curated_Functions: Is essential for growth of Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae and Bacillus subtilis. {PubMed:15044829}. Catalyzes ATP‑dependent hydrolysis of pyrophosphate and synthesis of phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) from ATP and ribose‑phosphate. {PubMed:15044829}. Contributes to purine nucleotide biosynthesis by supplying PRPP for purine phosphoribosyltransferases in the salvage pathway. {PubMed:15044829}.

Merged_Functions: The yffB gene encodes a ~13 kDa protein that adopts a thioredoxin‑like fold closely resembling the arsenate reductase (ArsC) from E. coli.  Structural analysis shows a catalytic cysteine (Cys11) in the active‑site loop, three conserved arginine residues (Arg60, Arg94, Arg107 in ArsC; Lys91, Arg60, Arg94 in YffB) that are positioned to bind substrate, and a positively charged surface that would favor anion binding.  Mass‑spectrometry experiments demonstrated that YffB can bind one molecule of glutathione (GSH), indicating that its catalytic cycle is coupled to GSH.  Consequently, the authors conclude that YffB most likely functions as a glutathione‑dependent thiol reductase, analogous to ArsC, although the natural substrate has not yet been identified. {PubMed:15102337}.
Curated_Functions: Binds one molecule of glutathione (GSH). {PubMed:15102337}. Functions as a glutathione‑dependent thiol reductase, analogous to the arsenate reductase (ArsC). {PubMed:15102337}.

Merged_Functions: The yfcB gene encodes the N5‑glutamine methyltransferase (also called PrmB) that specifically methylates ribosomal protein L3 at the nitrogen of the side‑chain amide of Gln150. This modification is required for proper ribosome assembly; loss of yfcB results in a cryosensitive growth phenotype that can be rescued by expressing a wild‑type yfcB allele. YfcB does not methylate peptide release factors (RF1 or RF2); its activity is limited to ribosomal protein L3. {PubMed:11847124}.

Loss causes a cryosensitive growth phenotype, which can be rescued by expression of a wild‑type yfcB allele. {PubMed:11847124}. Activity is limited to ribosomal protein L3 and does not target peptide release factors RF1 or RF2. {PubMed:11847124}.

Merged_Functions: The ypaA gene encodes a putative riboflavin transport protein. Its expression is controlled by an FMN‑responsive riboswitch located in the 5' untranslated region. Binding of FMN to the conserved RFN element induces a structural rearrangement that sequesters the Shine–Dalgarno (SD) ribosome‑binding site, thereby preventing ribosome access and down‑regulating translation of the ypaA mRNA. Thus, ypaA functions as a riboflavin transporter whose synthesis is repressed when intracellular FMN levels are high. {PubMed:12456892}.
